body.text:
śrīrastu
satyasiddhiśāstram
body.translated_text:
May there be prosperity.
<s>Satyasiddhiśāstra</s> (Treatise on the Establishment of Truth)

body.text: śrīmadācāryaharivarmaṇaḥ kṛtiḥ
body.translated_text: A composition of the illustrious master <s>Harivarman</s>.

body.text: 1 prasthānaskandhe buddharatnādhikāre ādyasampadvarga
body.translated_text: 1. In the <s>Prasthānaskandha</s> (Section on Approach), in the chapter on the <s>Buddharatna</s> (Buddha-jewel): the first section on attainments (<s>Ādyasampadvarga</s>).

children.translated_text: 1. Having first reverently saluted the most worthy of salutation, the perfectly self-awakened one,
the omniscient, worthy teacher, the great one, benefactor of the world—
2. and the well-purified true <s>Dharma</s>, and the community of noble disciples (<s>Āryaśrāvakamaṇḍala</s>)—
I wish to expound, for the benefit of the world, the utterance of the <s>Jina</s> (Conqueror).
3. A treatise that accords with the <s>sūtras</s>, that does not deviate from the true nature of things (<s>dharmatā</s>),
that leads to tranquility (<s>śama</s>)—such is indeed rightly called a treatise of true knowledge (<s>jñānaśāstra</s>).
4. Just as the moon and sun, by nature exceedingly luminous, are not seen
when obscured in the sky by smoke, clouds, dust, fog, and the like—
5. so too the true meaning of the <s>sūtras</s>, when surrounded by false treatises, does not shine forth;
because the true meaning has become unclear, the door to false knowledge has been thrown open.
6. Offenses, ill repute, mental remorse, torpor, and the like,
distraction of mind and weariness—these are thrown open by false knowledge.
7. One who wishes to remove the sufferings headed by offenses

children.text: samyak śāstrecchayā gacchet gabhīrajñāninaṃ sa ca ||
children.translated_text: should, with desire for the true treatise, approach a teacher of profound knowledge.
8. Devotion to that very true treatise is the root;
for from the cause of the true treatise arise excellent merit and so forth.
9. Even one who has studied a hundred thousand false treatises, though sharp of intellect,
does not attain eloquence, fame, or gain in the assembly.
10. Knowing the excellent <s>Dharma</s> of the <s>Buddha</s>, and that his teaching brings happiness,

children.text: cirakālañca dharmasya sthitaye na tu kīrtaye ||
children.translated_text: this is for the long endurance of the <s>Dharma</s>, not merely for fame.
11. Having examined with wisdom the views of the various schools and the intentions of the wise,
I wish to compose this treatise of truth (<s>Tattvaśāstra</s>), which is solely the knowledge of the omniscient one.
12. The <s>Buddha</s> heard completely the monks of the various schools;
therefore I undertake to harmonize the meaning of the <s>Tripiṭaka</s> (Three Baskets).

body.text: atra vicāryate | (pṛ) nanu bhavatā satyasiddhiśāstraṃ vakṣyata iti jñātmasmābhiḥ | ādau bhavatoktaṃ abhivadyābhivandyaṃ prāgiti | sa ca budo [bhagavān] | kasmāt tasya buddha ityākhyā | kena guṇenābhivandyaḥ | (u) bhagavān prakṛtyā manuṣyabhūtaḥ sarvākārajñānena sarvadharmāṇāṃ svalakṣaṇavibhāgān prajānāti | sarvākuśalavinirmuktaḥ sañcitasarvakuśalaḥ sarvasattvānāṃ
body.translated_text: Here it is examined. (Question) "Surely we understand that you intend to expound the <s>Satyasiddhiśāstra</s>. At the outset you have said 'Having first reverently saluted the most worthy of salutation'—and that is the <s>Buddha</s>, the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Why is he called '<s>Buddha</s>'? By what quality is he worthy of salutation?" (Answer) The <s>Bhagavān</s>, though by nature a human being, through omniscient knowledge (<s>sarvākārajñāna</s>) comprehends the distinguishing characteristics of all <s>dharmas</s>. Completely freed from all unwholesome states, having accumulated all wholesome states, and being a well-wisher of all beings—

body.text: hitaiṣī cetyato buddha ityucyate | [sattvān] śikṣayitumupadiṣṭaṃ dharma ityucyate | taṃ dharmaṃ ye pratipadyante te saṅgha ityucyante | ityeteṣāṃ triratnānāmabhivandananidānaṃ vakṣye | bhagavān pañca[dharma]skandhasaṃpannaḥ ityato devamanuṣyāṇāṃ pūjyaḥ |
body.translated_text: therefore he is called '<s>Buddha</s>.' The <s>Dharma</s> is what he taught in order to instruct beings. Those who practice that <s>Dharma</s> are called the <s>Saṅgha</s>. Thus I shall speak of the reason for paying homage to these Three Jewels (<s>Triratna</s>). The <s>Bhagavān</s> is endowed with five aggregates of qualities (<s>pañcadharmaskandha</s>), and therefore is worthy of worship by gods and humans.

body.text:
(pṛ) anye 'pi āryapugdalāḥ pañcadharmaskandhasamanvitāḥ | tathāgatasya ko viśeṣaḥ | (u) tathāgatasya pañcaguṇaskandhasaṃpadaḥ pariśuddhāḥ | tatkasya hetoḥ | kāyikādiṣu karmasu apramattatvāt śīlaskandhasaṃpat [pariśuddhā] | bhagavān śīlasaṃvara evāvipannaḥ | kimuta vaktavyaṃ mūlāpattau | kiñca cirasañcitamaitrīkasya nākuśalacittamudeti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- bhagavānavocadānandam | ājanma yo maitrīmabhyasyati tasyākuśalacittamudeti na vā | no bhagavan iti | tathāgataścirasañcitakuśalasvabhāvaḥ, nātmatrāṇārthaṃ kintu apakīrtibhīrutayā saṃvaraśīlaṃ dhatte | apramāṇabuddheṣu dīrghābhyastaśīlacaryaḥ unmūlitatriviṣamūlātyantaniśśeṣavāsanaḥ | ityādibhiḥ pratyayaiḥ śīlaskandhasampannaḥ |
samādhiskandhasampannaḥ | tathāgata imaṃ samādhiṃ niśritya sarvajñajñānaṃ labdhavān | ataḥ samādhiskandhasampanna iti jñāyate | yathā ghṛtatailabahulaḥ pradīpaḥ vartikāmahimnā mahān prakāśate | tathāgataḥ sunirūḍhastambhavat dṛḍhasamādhikaḥ | anye tu jalarūḍhastambhavat apratilabdhacirasamādhikāḥ | tathāgatasya dhyānasamādhirapramāṇakalpeṣu kramaśaḥ saṃsiddhaḥ | ata staṃ paripūrayati | tathāgatasya samādhiḥ puruṣaṃ sthānaṃ dharmopadeśaṃ vā ityādipratyayagaṇān nopakṣate | na tathānyeṣām | tathāgataḥ sadā gabhīrabhāvitasamādhirbhavati | yathā kaścit ātmānaṃ saṃrakṣan sadā smarati na vismarati | tathāgataḥ dhyānasamādhimupasampadya na cittabalamadhitiṣṭhati | tadyathā kaścit svāvasaṃthaṃ prāpya vadati kṣemaprāptaḥ akhinna iti | na samādhisthastathāgataḥ punarevam | ata ucyate tathāgataḥ nityasamādhisthita iti | dhyānasamādhiprakampino
body.translated_text:
(Question) Other noble individuals (<s>āryapudgala</s>) also possess the five aggregates of qualities. What is the distinction of the <s>Tathāgata</s>? (Answer) The <s>Tathāgata</s>'s attainment of the five aggregates of qualities is completely purified. For what reason? Because of non-negligence in bodily and other actions, his attainment of the aggregate of moral conduct (<s>śīlaskandha</s>) is purified. The <s>Bhagavān</s> is unfailing in the discipline of moral conduct (<s>śīlasaṃvara</s>) itself—how much more so with respect to root offenses! Furthermore, for one who has long cultivated loving-kindness (<s>maitrī</s>), no unwholesome thought arises. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: "The <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed <s>Ānanda</s>: 'For one who has practiced <s>maitrī</s> from birth, does an unwholesome thought arise or not?' 'No, <s>Bhagavān</s>.'" The <s>Tathāgata</s>, whose nature is of long-accumulated wholesome states, maintains the discipline of moral restraint not for self-protection, but out of fear of disrepute. Having practiced moral conduct for a long time under innumerable <s>Buddhas</s>, he has uprooted the three roots of poison and completely eradicated their residual impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>). Through these and other reasons, he is endowed with the aggregate of moral conduct.
He is endowed with the aggregate of concentration (<s>samādhiskandha</s>). The <s>Tathāgata</s>, relying on this <s>samādhi</s>, has obtained omniscient knowledge. Therefore it is known that he is endowed with the aggregate of concentration. Just as a lamp rich in ghee and oil shines greatly by the power of its wick, so the <s>Tathāgata</s> is firm in concentration like a pillar rooted on solid ground; others, however, are like pillars rooted in water, not having attained lasting concentration. The <s>Tathāgata</s>'s <s>dhyāna</s>-concentration has been gradually perfected over immeasurable <s>kalpas</s>; therefore he fulfills it completely. The <s>Tathāgata</s>'s concentration does not diminish due to the person, the place, the teaching of <s>Dharma</s>, or any other group of conditions—but it is not so for others. The <s>Tathāgata</s> always abides in profoundly cultivated concentration. Just as someone protecting himself always remembers and does not forget, so the <s>Tathāgata</s>, having entered <s>dhyāna</s>-concentration, does not exert mental force to maintain it. It is as if someone, having reached his own dwelling, says 'I have reached safety, I am unwearied'—so too the <s>Tathāgata</s> in concentration does not experience it as effort. Therefore it is said that the <s>Tathāgata</s> always abides in concentration. The states that cause disturbance to <s>dhyāna</s>-concentration—

body.text: mahāprāmodyādayo dharmāḥ tathāgatasya sarve prahīṇāḥ | cirasamādhivipākapratilabdhaiśvaryadivyābhijñānāṃ paramo 'graṇīḥ | ṛddhividhinā ekasminneva kṣaṇe daśadikṣu apramāṇadhātuṣu parikrāmati | sarvāṇi kṛtyāni yatheṣṭaṃ karoti | sarvanirmiteṣu apratihataṃ prabhavati | anye sattvā māgacchantviti sarvadharmānugacitto bhavati |
body.translated_text: such as great elation (<s>mahāprāmodya</s>) and others—are all abandoned by the <s>Tathāgata</s>. He is the supreme foremost among those who have attained sovereign divine super-knowledges (<s>divyābhijñā</s>) as the fruit of long-practiced concentration. By the method of supernatural power (<s>ṛddhividhi</s>), in a single instant he traverses immeasurable realms in the ten directions. He accomplishes all tasks as he wishes. He exercises unobstructed mastery over all magical creations. His mind accords with all <s>dharmas</s>, thinking 'may other beings come.'

body.text: tathāgatasya āryavaśitāsamanvitasya sukhe asukhasaṃjñotpadyate | asukhe ca sukhasaṃjñotpadyate sukhāsukhe ca upekṣāsaṃjñotpadyate | (pṛ)asukhe upekṣā jāyeta | kathaṃ sukhasaṃjñā jāyeta | (u) subhāvitacittatvāt vākpāruṣyādyasukhadharmeṣu na pratibandhaṃ manyate | anyāsu divyābhijñāsu divyacakṣurdivyaśrotraparacittajñānapūrvanivāsānusmṛtiṣu apratihato bhavati | samādhibalena apratihatadivyābhijño bhavati | dhyānasamādhiṣu suvyaktābhisamayaḥ | tānanye sattvā na śṛṇvanti | tathāgata evāpratihataṃ praviśati vyuttiṣṭhate ca | tathāgatasya dhyānasamādhi rbalamityākhyāyate | yathā daśabalavarge vakṣyate | anyeṣāṃ pugdalānāṃ nāsti [tādṛśaṃ] kiñcit | ataḥ tathāgata samādhiskandhasampannaḥ |
body.translated_text: For the <s>Tathāgata</s>, who possesses noble mastery (<s>āryavaśitā</s>), in pleasure the perception of non-pleasure arises, in non-pleasure the perception of pleasure arises, and in both pleasure and non-pleasure the perception of equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>) arises. (Question) In non-pleasure, equanimity may arise—but how can the perception of pleasure arise? (Answer) Because his mind is well-cultivated, he does not regard unpleasant states such as harsh speech and the like as obstructions. Regarding the other super-knowledges—the divine eye (<s>divyacakṣus</s>), the divine ear (<s>divyaśrotra</s>), knowledge of others' minds (<s>paracittajñāna</s>), and recollection of former lives (<s>pūrvanivāsānusmṛti</s>)—he is unobstructed. By the power of concentration, his divine super-knowledges are unobstructed. In <s>dhyāna</s>-concentrations, his insight is perfectly clear. Others cannot hear those; only the <s>Tathāgata</s> enters and emerges from them without obstruction. The <s>Tathāgata</s>'s <s>dhyāna</s>-concentration is called 'power' (<s>bala</s>), as will be explained in the chapter on the ten powers (<s>Daśabalavarga</s>). Other individuals do not possess anything like it. Therefore the <s>Tathāgata</s> is endowed with the aggregate of concentration.

body.text: prajñāskandhasampanna iti | dhyānāvaraṇaṃ kleśotpāda iti dvividhāvidyā tathāgatasya sarvathā prahīṇā | viruddhasya prahāṇāt prajñāskandhasampannaḥ | svato dharmalābhī [tathāgataḥ] na parataḥ śrutvā | niruktikuśalaḥ arthagatijñānasujñānakuśalaḥ anavasannapratibhānaḥ akṣīṇaprajñaśca | anye sattvā steṣu kauśalaṃ na saṃpādayāṃbabhūvuḥ | bhagavānena anapakṛṣṭakṣayajñānaḥ | atastathāgataḥ prajñāskandhasampannaḥ |
body.translated_text: He is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom (<s>prajñāskandha</s>). The twofold ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)—namely, the obstruction of <s>dhyāna</s> and the arising of defilements (<s>kleśa</s>)—is completely abandoned by the <s>Tathāgata</s>. Through the abandonment of what is opposed to wisdom, he is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom. The <s>Tathāgata</s> attains the <s>Dharma</s> by himself, not by hearing from others. He is skilled in etymology (<s>nirukti</s>), skilled in the knowledge of meaning and in right understanding, unfailing in eloquence (<s>pratibhāna</s>), and inexhaustible in wisdom. Other beings have not been able to accomplish such skill. The <s>Bhagavān</s> possesses undiminished knowledge of destruction (<s>kṣayajñāna</s>). Therefore the <s>Tathāgata</s> is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom.

body.text: bhagavadbhāṣito dharmaḥ arthagatau kuśalaḥ | nānyairalpajñai rbhāṣitaḥ samarthaḥ niravadyaḥ | tathāgata bhāṣita evānavadyaḥ | atastathāgata prajñāskandhasampannaḥ | apramāṇaguṇasādhanīyā prajñeti [tāṃ] sampādayati | dharmaṃ praṇītamaviparītañca bhāṣitavān | yathā aśubhabhāvanā
body.translated_text: The <s>Dharma</s> spoken by the <s>Bhagavān</s> is skilled in conveying meaning. That spoken by others of little knowledge is not capable and not faultless; only that spoken by the <s>Tathāgata</s> is faultless. Therefore the <s>Tathāgata</s> is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom. His wisdom accomplishes immeasurable virtues, and he has spoken the <s>Dharma</s> as excellent and unerring. Just as the contemplation of impurity (<s>aśubhabhāvanā</s>)

body.text: kāmarāgabhedinītyādayaḥ | prajñāprakarṣāt prakṛṣṭeryāpathaśca bhavati ityādibhiḥ pratyayaiḥ prajñāskandhasampannaḥ |
body.translated_text: destroys sensual desire (<s>kāmarāga</s>), and so forth—through the excellence of wisdom, excellent deportment (<s>īryāpatha</s>) also arises. Through these and other reasons, he is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom.

body.text: vimuktiskandhasampanna iti | avidyādvayāccittaṃ vimuktam | nānyāsti vāsanā, sarvathānivṛtā ityādinā vimuktisampannaḥ |
body.translated_text: He is endowed with the aggregate of liberation (<s>vimuktiskandha</s>). The mind is liberated from the twofold ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). There are no remaining residual impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>); they are completely and in every way eradicated—through these and other reasons, he is endowed with liberation.

body.text: vimuktijñānadarśanasampanna iti | sarvasmin saṃyojanaprahāṇamārge pratikṣaṇaṃ smṛtijñānakuśalaḥ | yathā kaścit vṛkṣaṃ chettuṃ haste dhṛtakuṭhāraḥ pāryantikaṃ jānānaḥ prajānāti śākhāḥ praśākhāḥ | tathā bhagavānapi saṃyojanaprahāṇajñānasya pratikṣaṇaṃ kṣīyamāṇaṃ sarvamavayavaśaḥ prajānāti | sattvānāmāśayaṃ jñātvā yathāyogaṃ dharmamupadiśati | yena [te] vimucyante | ataḥ sattvānāṃ sarvavimuktimārge jñānadarśanasampannaḥ |
body.translated_text: He is endowed with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (<s>vimuktijñānadarśana</s>). On the path of abandoning all fetters (<s>saṃyojana</s>), at every moment he is skilled in mindfulness and knowledge. Just as someone holding an axe in hand to cut a tree, knowing it thoroughly, understands its branches and sub-branches, so too the <s>Bhagavān</s>, at every moment, comprehends in all its parts the gradual diminishing of the knowledge of abandoning fetters. Knowing the dispositions (<s>āśaya</s>) of beings, he teaches the <s>Dharma</s> as appropriate, by which they are liberated. Therefore he is endowed with the knowledge and vision of the path of complete liberation for all beings.

body.text: kiñca bhagavān kālaṃ jñātvā dharmamupadiśati yathā timburukabrāhmaṇādinām | tathāgataḥ dharmāṇāṃ vibhāgajñānakuśalaḥ | ayaṃ pudgalaḥ asya dharmasyārha iti | yathā bhagavānānandamāmantrya chandakasya yogyaṃ bhāvābhāvavyāvartakaṃ sūtramupadiśati | atastathāgato vimuktijñānakuśalaḥ | kiñcopāyakuśalaḥ sattvamalaṃ hāpayati yathā nandasya kāmaprajihīrṣāyai [dharma]mupadiśati | sattvānāñca śraddhendriyādiparipākaṃ jñātvā paścāt dharmamupadiśati yathā rāhulasya | kecit sattvāḥ karmavipākāvṛtāḥ na vimuktiṃ labhante | bhagavān [taṃ]nāśayitvā dharmamupadiśati | kecit sattvāḥ kālapakṣye kṣīṇāsravā bhavanti yathā jāyāpatisūtra upadiṣṭam | kecit sattvāḥ puruṣaviśeṣamapekṣya kṣīṇāsravāḥ bhavanti yathā śāriputra aśvajitamapekṣya | kecit sattvā deśamapekṣya kṣīṇāsravāḥ yathā rājā pukkasātiḥ | kecit sattvā satīrthyamapekṣya
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the <s>Bhagavān</s> teaches the <s>Dharma</s> knowing the right time, as in the case of the Brahmin <s>Timburuka</s> and others. The <s>Tathāgata</s> is skilled in the knowledge of distinguishing <s>dharmas</s>: 'This individual is worthy of this <s>dharma</s>.' For example, the <s>Bhagavān</s>, addressing <s>Ānanda</s>, teaches <s>Chandaka</s> the appropriate <s>sūtra</s> that turns him away from existence and non-existence. Therefore the <s>Tathāgata</s> is skilled in the knowledge of liberation. Furthermore, being skilled in means (<s>upāyakuśala</s>), he removes the defilements of beings—as when he teaches the <s>Dharma</s> to <s>Nanda</s> in order to make him relinquish desire. And knowing the ripening of the faculties such as faith (<s>śraddhendriya</s>) of beings, he teaches the <s>Dharma</s> afterward, as in the case of <s>Rāhula</s>. Some beings, obscured by the ripening of <s>karma</s>, do not attain liberation; the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having removed that obstruction, teaches the <s>Dharma</s>. Some beings become ones whose outflows are exhausted (<s>kṣīṇāsrava</s>) at the decline of a particular time period, as taught in the <s>Jāyāpatisūtra</s> (Husband and Wife Sūtra). Some beings become <s>kṣīṇāsrava</s> depending on a particular person, as <s>Śāriputra</s> depending on <s>Aśvajit</s>. Some beings become <s>kṣīṇāsrava</s> depending on a particular place, as King <s>Pukkasāti</s>. Some beings, depending on a fellow practitioner—

body.text: kṣīṇāsravāḥ yathā gopāla nandaḥ ajitagrāmīṇādīnapekṣya | kecit sattvā bhagavataḥ tāttvikakāyamapekṣya nirmitakāya ñcāpekṣya kṣīṇāsravā bhavanti | bhagavān pratipatiṃ jñātvā dharmamupadiśati [atha]vimocayati | kiñca bhagavān vividhān saddharmānupadiya sarvān vimuktyāvaraṇadharmān paribhedayati ato vimuktijñānadarśanasampanna ityucyate |
body.translated_text: become <s>kṣīṇāsrava</s>, as <s>Gopāla</s>, <s>Nanda</s>, and others depending on <s>Ajita</s>, the villagers, and others. Some beings become <s>kṣīṇāsrava</s> depending on the <s>Bhagavān</s>'s real body (<s>tāttvikakāya</s>) or depending on his emanation body (<s>nirmitakāya</s>). The <s>Bhagavān</s>, knowing the right practice, teaches the <s>Dharma</s> and thereby liberates them. Furthermore, the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having taught the various true <s>Dharmas</s>, breaks through all the states that obstruct liberation; therefore he is said to be endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation (<s>vimuktijñānadarśana</s>).

body.text: bhagavān dharmārthagatikuśalo dharmamupadiśati nānarthamavipākam | bhagavān saṃkhyāgaṇanavat kramaśo vimuktimārgamupadiśati | ataḥ suvimoko bhavati | bhagavān satvānāṃ pūrvanivāsaṃ kuśalamūla ñca jñātvā kramaśo dharmamupadiśati | bhagavān vimuktiṃ pratyakṣīkṛtya parasyopaśati na parataḥśratvā | jinaśāsanaṃ vahvībhiḥ kalābhiḥ sampannam | yathā bhaiṣajyakalāsampanno vyādhīn śamayati | tathā jinaśāsanamapi pratipakṣakalāpamukhena sarvān kleśān vyāvartayati | yathā navasaṃjñādīn mahatyo 'lpā vā saṃyojanā na punaḥ kṣapayanti | ataḥ kauśalasampanna eva kleśān paribhedayati | anuttamopāyaiḥ sattvān santārayati, kadācit sukumāravacanaiḥ kadācit kaṭuvacanaiḥ kadācit punaḥ sukumārakaṭuvacanaiśca | tadarthameva tathāgato vimuktijñānadarśanasampannaḥ iti |
body.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s>, being skilled in understanding the purpose of the <s>Dharma</s>, teaches the <s>Dharma</s>—not what is meaningless or without fruit. The <s>Bhagavān</s> teaches the path of liberation step by step, like counting and calculation; therefore liberation is well-accomplished. The <s>Bhagavān</s>, knowing the former abodes and wholesome roots (<s>kuśalamūla</s>) of beings, teaches the <s>Dharma</s> progressively. The <s>Bhagavān</s> teaches others having directly realized liberation himself, not by hearing from others. The teaching of the <s>Jina</s> is endowed with many skillful methods. Just as one skilled in the art of medicine cures diseases, so too the teaching of the <s>Jina</s>, through the application of antidotes (<s>pratipakṣa</s>), turns away all defilements (<s>kleśa</s>). As with the nine perceptions and so forth, whether the fetters are great or small, they do not diminish again without skill; therefore only one endowed with skill breaks through the defilements. By unsurpassed means he delivers beings across—sometimes with gentle words, sometimes with harsh words, and sometimes with both gentle and harsh words. For that very purpose the <s>Tathāgata</s> is endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation (<s>vimuktijñānadarśana</s>).

body.text: prasthānaskandhe buddharatnādhikāre ādyasampadvargaḥ prathamaḥ |
body.translated_text: In the <s>Prasthānaskandha</s> (Section on Approach), in the chapter on the <s>Buddharatna</s> (Buddha-jewel): the first section on attainments (<s>Ādyasampadvarga</s>), chapter one.

body.text: 2 daśabalavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 2. Chapter on the Ten Powers (<s>Daśabalavarga</s>)

body.text: atha bhagavān daśa balasamanvāgamāt prajñāsampannaḥ | hetupratyayapratilomakatayoktāni daśabalāni | talādyaṃ sthānāsthānajñānabalam | idaṃ kāryakāraṇanaiyatyajñānam | asmāt īdṛśaṃ phalaṃ bhavati na tādṛśam | ayamācāraḥ akuśalo 'vayaṃ duḥkhavipākaḥ na sukhavipāka iti jñānam | sthānaṃ nāma bhāvavastu | asthānamabhāvavastu | ādyaṃ balamidaṃ sarvabalānāṃ mūlam |
body.translated_text: Now, the Blessed One is endowed with wisdom by virtue of possessing the ten powers (<s>daśabala</s>). The ten powers are stated in reverse order of causes and conditions. The first of these is the power of knowledge of what is possible and impossible (<s>sthānāsthānajñānabala</s>). This is the knowledge of the fixed relation between cause and effect — from this, such a result arises and not another. This conduct is unwholesome; this has a result of suffering, not a result of happiness — such is the knowledge. 'Possible' (<s>sthāna</s>) means a thing that exists; 'impossible' (<s>asthāna</s>) means a thing that does not exist. This first power is the root of all the powers.

body.text: (pṛ) [nanu]laukikā api jānanti hetuphalayoḥ sthānāsthānam | yathā yavādyava eva jāyate na brīhyādaya iti | (u) sthānāsthānabalena karmādīnāṃ jñānāt idaṃ balamatigahanaṃ paramaṃ devamanuṣyāṇāṃ na prāptuṃ śakyam | jātadharmasya hetusamanantarādhipatipratyayān pratyāyayatītyata idaṃ balaṃ praṇītam |
body.translated_text: (Objection) [But] even worldly people know what is possible and impossible regarding cause and effect — for example, that from barley only barley is born and not rice, etc. (Reply) Through the power of knowing the possible and impossible, because of the knowledge of <s>karma</s> and other [factors], this power is extremely profound and supreme — it cannot be attained by gods and humans. Because it makes known the causal (<s>hetu</s>), immediately preceding (<s>samanantara</s>), and dominant (<s>adhipati</s>) conditions of arisen <s>dharmas</s>, this power is declared to be excellent.

body.text: (2) yat atitānāgatapratyutpannāni karmāṇi sarvadharmasamādānāni ca prajānāti | teṣāṃ sthānaṃ prajānāti vastu prajānāti hetuṃ prajānāti vipākañca prajānāti | ata idaṃ jñānaṃ balamākhyāyate | triṣu adhvasu sthānavastuhetuvipākaprajñāpakatvāt gahanam | kasmāt | kecidvadanti atītānāgatā abhāvadharmā iti | ato bhagavataḥ teṣāṃ kathanaṃ balaṃ bhavati | atītānāgatādhvagatān dharmān adṛṣṭākārānapi bhagavān sākṣātprajānāti |
body.translated_text: (2) That which fully knows the actions (<s>karma</s>) of the past, future, and present, and all undertakings of <s>dharmas</s> — he fully knows their basis, their substance, their cause, and their ripening (<s>vipāka</s>). Therefore this knowledge is called a power. Because it makes known the basis, substance, cause, and ripening across the three time periods (<s>adhvan</s>), it is profound. Why? Because some say that past and future <s>dharmas</s> are non-existent. Therefore the Blessed One's declaration of them constitutes a power. The Blessed One directly knows the <s>dharmas</s> belonging to the past and future time periods, even those of unseen aspects.

body.text: atha karma dvividhaṃ kuśalamakuśalamiti | kecit kuśalakarmavanto dṛṣṭe duḥkhavedanāḥ yathā śīlaṃ dhṛtvā kleśānanubhavanti | kecitpāpakarmāṇaḥ dṛṣṭe sukhavedanāḥ yathā śīlaṃ bhitvā svairaṃ caranti | ataḥ kecit saṃśerate anāgatādhvāpi pratyutpannasama iti | atastathāgataḥ karmakrameṇa vedanāmupadiśati |
body.translated_text: Now, <s>karma</s> is twofold: wholesome (<s>kuśala</s>) and unwholesome (<s>akuśala</s>). Some who have performed wholesome <s>karma</s> experience suffering in this life — for example, those who maintain moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>) yet experience afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>). Some who have performed unwholesome <s>karma</s> experience happiness in this life — for example, those who break moral conduct and act as they please. Therefore some doubt whether the future is the same as the present. Therefore the <s>Tathāgata</s> teaches about feelings (<s>vedanā</s>) according to the sequence of <s>karma</s>.

body.text: catvāri dharmasamādānāni pratyutpannaṃ duḥkhaṃ āyatyāṃ sukhavipākam, pratyutpannaṃ sukhamāyatyāṃ duḥkhavipākam, pratyutpannaṃ sukham āyatyāṃ sukhavipākam, pratyutpannaṃ duḥkhamāyatyāṃ duḥkhavipākam iti | bhagavān saṃprati āyatyāñca [teṣāṃ] sthānaṃ, vastu, hetuṃ vipākañca prajānāti | sthānaṃ nāma vedakaḥ | vastu deyapadārthaḥ | heturdānacittam | yathoktaṃ sūtre pūrvañca pramuditacittaḥ dānakāle ca viśuddhacitto dattvā ca yanna vipratisarati | tat phalaprāpakaṃ karma vipāka mākhyāyate | bhagavāneva prajānāti taratamaṃ karma yadi niyatamaniyataṃ vā dṛṣṭavipākam upapadyavipākaṃ tadūrdhvavipākaṃ vā ityādi | nānyaḥ | ato balamityucyate |
body.translated_text: There are four undertakings of <s>dharma</s> (<s>dharmasamādāna</s>): present suffering with future ripening of happiness, present happiness with future ripening of suffering, present happiness with future ripening of happiness, and present suffering with future ripening of suffering. The Blessed One fully knows the basis, substance, cause, and ripening of those [undertakings] both in the present and in the future. 'Basis' means the one who experiences; 'substance' means the object to be given; 'cause' means the mental intention of giving. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Previously with a joyful mind, at the time of giving with a purified mind, and having given, one does not regret.' That <s>karma</s> which brings about the result is called ripening (<s>vipāka</s>). Only the Blessed One fully knows whether <s>karma</s> is of greater or lesser [degree], whether it is determined or undetermined, whether its ripening is in the present life, in the next rebirth, or in lives beyond that, and so forth. No other [can know this]. Therefore it is called a power.

body.text: (3) bhagavān sarvadhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpattīnāṃ saṃkleśaṃ prajānāti sthitiṃ prajānāti upacayaṃ prajānāti vyavadānañca prajānāti | tatra dhyānaṃ nāma catvāri dhyānāni catvāra ārūpyasamādhayaśca | tadeva rūpārūpyadhātukaṃ karma | vimokṣo nāma yadutāṣṭau vimokṣāḥ taktarmakṣepakāḥ | dhyānāni ārūpyasamādhayo 'ṣṭavimokṣāśca samādhayo bhavanti | eṣāṃ samādhīnāṃ vṛtterābhimukhyalābhaḥ samāpattiḥ | samāpattayaścaturdhā vibhaktāḥ saṃkleśataḥ sthitita upacayato vyavadānataśceti | saṃkleśajñāninaḥ saṃkleśataḥ samādhiḥ | sthitijñāninaḥ sthityā samādhiḥ | upacayajñānina upacayataḥ samādhiḥ | vyavadānajñāninaḥ prativedhataḥ samādhiḥ | prativedhataḥ samādhikasya ūṣmamūrdhakṣāntyādayaścaturdharmā bhavanti | tathāgatasyaiva teṣu sarveṣu jñānaṃ bhavati | nānyeṣām iti balaṃ bhavati |
body.translated_text: (3) The Blessed One fully knows the defilement (<s>saṃkleśa</s>), stability (<s>sthiti</s>), increase (<s>upacaya</s>), and purification (<s>vyavadāna</s>) of all <s>dhyānas</s> (meditations), <s>vimokṣas</s> (liberations), <s>samādhis</s> (concentrations), and <s>samāpattis</s> (attainments). Therein, 'meditation' (<s>dhyāna</s>) means the four <s>dhyānas</s> and the four formless concentrations (<s>ārūpyasamādhi</s>) — these constitute the <s>karma</s> of the form and formless realms. 'Liberation' (<s>vimokṣa</s>) means the eight liberations, which are action-directing. The <s>dhyānas</s>, formless concentrations, and eight liberations are [all types of] <s>samādhi</s>. The attainment (<s>samāpatti</s>) of these concentrations is the gaining of access to their functioning. The attainments are divided fourfold: by defilement, by stability, by increase, and by purification. For one who knows defilement, the <s>samādhi</s> is [characterized] by defilement. For one who knows stability, the <s>samādhi</s> is [characterized] by stability. For one who knows increase, the <s>samādhi</s> is [characterized] by increase. For one who knows purification, the <s>samādhi</s> is [characterized] by penetration. For one whose <s>samādhi</s> is [characterized] by penetration, the four <s>dharmas</s> beginning with warmth (<s>uṣman</s>), summit (<s>mūrdhan</s>), and patience (<s>kṣānti</s>) arise. Only the <s>Tathāgata</s> has knowledge regarding all of these. Because others do not, it is a power.

body.text: (4) tathāgataḥ sattvānāmindriyāṇi tīkṣṇāni mandāni [yathābhūtaṃ] prajānāni | średdhendriyādīnāṃ prādhānyāt tīkṣṇatā yathā tathāgatādīnām | mandatā tadaprāptiḥ yathā nāgadāsakādīnām | madhyendriyasya tu nāsti aniyatatvāt | tīkṣṇendriyasyāsti kāṣṭhā
body.translated_text: (4) The <s>Tathāgata</s> fully knows the faculties (<s>indriya</s>) of beings as sharp or dull [as they truly are]. Due to the predominance of the five faculties beginning with the faith-faculty (<s>śraddhendriya</s>), there is sharpness, as in the case of the <s>Tathāgata</s> and others. Dullness is the non-attainment of that, as in the case of <s>Nāgadāsaka</s> and others. But for one of middling faculties, there is no [fixed characterization] because of its indeterminate nature. For one of sharp faculties there is an ultimate limit

body.text: yathā tathāgatāḥ | mṛdvindriyasyāsti kāṣṭha yathā nāgadāsakaḥ | madhyamasya nāsti kāṣṭheti madhyendriyasya nocyate | atha śraddhāpratipat dharmapratipat iti dvividho mārgaḥ | punarapi dvividhaḥ durmārgaḥ sumārga iti | asmāt mārgadvayādanyo madhyamaḥ | tīkṣṇamandapudgalau pratīkṣya madhyamo bhavati | adhimuktitaścendriyāṇi bhidyante | śraddhendriyādhimuktikāḥ śraddhābahulāḥ | prājñajanā viśiṣṭendriyā adhimuktita upakṛtā średdhendriyapradhānāśca bhavanti | imānīndriyāṇi sarvāṇi [tathāgataḥ] prajānāti | nānye | ityatastadvalam |
body.translated_text: as in the case of the <s>Tathāgatas</s>. For one of dull faculties there is an ultimate limit, as in the case of <s>Nāgadāsaka</s>. Because there is no ultimate limit for the middling, the middling faculty is not mentioned. Now, there are two kinds of path: the path of faith-practice (<s>śraddhāpratipat</s>) and the path of <s>Dharma</s>-practice (<s>dharmapratipat</s>). Again there are two kinds: the wrong path (<s>durmārga</s>) and the good path (<s>sumārga</s>). Apart from these two paths, there is the middle one. The middling [person] is determined in relation to the sharp and dull individuals. Faculties are differentiated by inclination (<s>adhimukti</s>). Those of faith-faculty inclination are predominant in faith (<s>śraddhā</s>). Wise persons have superior faculties and, aided by inclination, become predominant in the faith-faculty. The <s>Tathāgata</s> fully knows all these faculties. Others do not. Therefore that is a power.

body.text: (5) tathāgato nānādhimuktikaṃ lokaṃ [yathābhūtaṃ] prajānāti | adhimuktirnāma icchā | tadyathā surāyāmadhimuktaḥ surāmicchati | tathāgato yathādhimukti pratipattiṃ prajānāti yadutāyaṃ sattvaḥ pañcakāmanāsvadhimuktaḥ bhāvanāmārge bādhimukta ityevaṃ viditvā yathārhaṃ dharmamupadiśati | ataḥ sarvasattvāśca santārayati |
body.translated_text: (5) The <s>Tathāgata</s> fully knows the world of diverse inclinations (<s>nānādhimukti</s>) [as it truly is]. Inclination (<s>adhimukti</s>) means desire. For example, one inclined toward liquor desires liquor. The <s>Tathāgata</s> fully knows the practice according to each inclination — namely, this being is inclined toward the five sense-pleasures (<s>pañcakāma</s>), that one is inclined toward the path of cultivation (<s>bhāvanāmārga</s>) — and having thus known, teaches the <s>Dharma</s> appropriately. Therefore he ferries across all beings.

body.text: (6) tathāgato nānādhātukānapramāṇalokāṃśca [yathābhūtaṃ] prajānāti | sattvānāṃ yat dīrghakālamabhyasya abhirocate sa dhātuḥ sidhyati | yathā devadattādayastathāgatamadhvanyadhvani duṣayanto 'kuśalacittapravṛttagahanānuśayadhātukā bhavanti | tathā kuśalasvabhāvā api | kecit sattvāḥ svabhāvataḥ pravṛttarāgāḥ kecit dṛṣṭaṃ pratītya pravṛttarāgāḥ | tathāgato 'dhimuktiṃ dhātuñca sarvaṃ [teṣāṃ] prajānātītyata[stat]balamucyate |
body.translated_text: (6) The <s>Tathāgata</s> fully knows the diverse elements (<s>nānādhātu</s>) and the immeasurable worlds [as they truly are]. That which beings have long practiced and have come to delight in — that element (<s>dhātu</s>) is established. For example, <s>Devadatta</s> and others, harming the <s>Tathāgata</s> in one life after another, have elements characterized by deep-seated unwholesome mental tendencies (<s>anuśaya</s>). Likewise, those of wholesome nature also [have their respective elements]. Some beings have passion arisen from their nature; some have passion arisen from what they have seen. The <s>Tathāgata</s> fully knows all of their inclinations and elements — therefore that is called a power.

body.text: (7) tathāgataḥ sarvatragāminīṃ pratipadaṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti | imāṃ pratipadaṃ pratipanno naraka utpadyate yāvatsvarge iti ca prajānāti | imāṃ pratipadaṃ pratipanno yāvannirvāṇamanuprāpnoti | idaṃ karma indriyarāgasvabhāvapravṛttam, sāsravakarmakaḥ pañcagatiṣūtpadyate | anāsravakarmako nirvāṇamanuprāpnoti iti prajānāti |
body.translated_text: (7) The <s>Tathāgata</s> fully knows the path leading everywhere (<s>sarvatragāminī pratipad</s>) as it truly is. He fully knows that one established on this path is reborn in hell, and so on up to heaven. He fully knows that one established on this path attains <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. This <s>karma</s>, proceeding from the nature of the faculties and passion, is with outflows (<s>sāsrava</s>) — one of such <s>karma</s> is reborn in the five destinies (<s>pañcagati</s>). One of <s>karma</s> without outflows (<s>anāsrava</s>) attains <s>Nirvāṇa</s> — thus he fully knows.

body.text: pūrvamuktaṃ mārgaḥ | idānīmuktantu mārgaphalam | pūrvaṃ sāmānyata uktam | idānīṃ vivicyocyate īdṛśakarmaṇā narakaṃ yāti, īdṛśakarmaṇā nirvāṇaṃ prāpnoti iti | narakapratitasyāpi pravibhāgo 'sti anena karmaṇā sañjīvanarake patiṣyati, anena karmaṇā kālasūtranarake patiṣyati iti | atastathāgataḥ saptamabale sthitaḥ sukṣmaṃ karma prajānāti | anye sattvā jānanto 'pi na vivecayanti | atastat balamucyate |
body.translated_text: What was stated earlier is the path; what is stated now is the fruit of the path. Earlier it was stated in general terms; now it is explained in detail — by such <s>karma</s> one goes to hell, by such <s>karma</s> one attains <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Even for one destined for hell there is a subdivision: by this <s>karma</s> one will fall into the <s>Saṃjīva</s> hell, by this <s>karma</s> one will fall into the <s>Kālasūtra</s> hell. Therefore the <s>Tathāgata</s>, established in the seventh power, fully knows even subtle <s>karma</s>. Other beings, even if they know [in general], do not discriminate [the details]. Therefore that is called a power.

body.text: (8) evaṃ tathāgatasya atītakarmaṇāṃ phalajñānaṃ pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabalamityucyate | tathāgataḥ sattvānāṃ pūrvamācaritāṃ pratipadaṃ jñātvā dharmamupadiśati | ataḥ pūrvanivāsavyākaraṇe 'sti jñānabalama | tathāgato 'tītaṃ sarvamupapattisthānaṃ rūpadhātau vā ārupyadhātau vā ityanusmarati | ātmano 'pi prajānāti | anyeṣāmapi satvānāṃ prajānāti | ata[stat] balamucyate |
body.translated_text: (8) Thus, the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s knowledge of the fruits of past actions is called the power of the knowledge of recollecting previous abodes (<s>pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala</s>). The <s>Tathāgata</s>, having known the path previously practiced by beings, teaches the <s>Dharma</s>. Therefore in the declaration of previous abodes there is a power of knowledge. The <s>Tathāgata</s> recollects all past places of rebirth — whether in the form realm (<s>rūpadhātu</s>) or the formless realm (<s>ārūpyadhātu</s>). He fully knows his own [past lives] and also fully knows those of other beings. Therefore that is called a power.

body.text: (9) tathāgato divyena cakṣuṣā paśyati anāgatādhvani tribhavasantānān trividhāni karmāṇi caturdharmasamādānāni ca jñātvā vyākaroti | tatrāpratighapratyāyanaṃ balamucyate |
body.translated_text: (9) The <s>Tathāgata</s>, with the divine eye (<s>divyacakṣus</s>), sees in the future time-period the continuities of the three realms of existence (<s>tribhava</s>), and having known the three kinds of <s>karma</s> and the four undertakings of <s>dharma</s>, makes declarations. Therein, the unobstructed convincing [of others] is called a power.

body.text: (10) āsravakṣaya[jñāna]balena santānanivṛttiṃ prajānāti | sattvā āyuṣonte kecit sasantānā bhavanti, kecit nivṛttasantānā bhavanti | idaṃ balaṃ sarvasattvagāmisthānamārgabalaṃ bhavati | sāmānyato nirvāṇamārga ityucyate | asya balasya savistaravibhāgo vakṣyate | tathāgataḥ saṃkleśavyavadānahetordaśabalasamanvāgataḥ | navabalalābhitvāt jñānasamanvitaḥ | daśamabalalābhitvāt prahāṇasamanvitaḥ | jñānaprahāṇasampannatvāt bhagavān devamanuṣyairabhivandyaḥ |
body.translated_text: (10) Through the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (<s>āsravakṣayajñānabala</s>), he fully knows the cessation of the continuity [of existence]. When beings' lifespans end, some have [further] continuity and some have cessation of continuity. This power is the power of the path to the abodes of all beings. In general terms, it is called the path to <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. A detailed analysis of this power will be stated [later]. The <s>Tathāgata</s> is endowed with the ten powers because of the causes of defilement and purification. Through attaining the [first] nine powers, he is endowed with knowledge. Through attaining the tenth power, he is endowed with abandonment (<s>prahāṇa</s>). Because of being accomplished in both knowledge and abandonment, the Blessed One is worthy of veneration by gods and humans.

body.text: daśabalavargo dvitīyaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the second chapter, the Chapter on the Ten Powers (<s>daśabalavarga</s>).

body.text: 3 caturvaiśāradyavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 3. Chapter on the Four Fearlessnesses (<s>caturvaiśāradyavarga</s>)

body.text: tathāgataścaturvaiśāradyasamanvitatvāccābhivandyaḥ | tathāgatapratilabdhāni catvāri vaiśāradyāni- sarva[dharmā]bhisambodhi[vaiśāradyam], sarvāsravakṣaya [jñānavaiśāradyaṃ], mārgāntarāyikavyākaraṇa [vaiśāradyaṃ], duḥkhanairyāṇikapratipa[dvaiśāradyam] | eṣu caturṣu yadi kaścidāgatya yathā dharmaṃ codayet | tatrāhaṃ vaiśādya[prāpta] iti |
body.translated_text: The <s>Tathāgata</s> is also worthy of veneration because of being endowed with the four fearlessnesses (<s>caturvaiśāradya</s>). The four fearlessnesses attained by the <s>Tathāgata</s> are: the fearlessness of complete awakening to all <s>dharmas</s> (<s>sarvadharmābhisambodhivaiśāradya</s>), the fearlessness of the knowledge of the destruction of all outflows (<s>sarvāsravakṣayajñānavaiśāradya</s>), the fearlessness of declaring the path-obstructing [dharmas] (<s>mārgāntarāyikavyākaraṇavaiśāradya</s>), and the fearlessness of the path leading to the cessation of suffering (<s>duḥkhanairyāṇikapratipadyaiśāradya</s>). If anyone were to come and challenge [the <s>Tathāgata</s>] according to the <s>Dharma</s> regarding these four — therein, 'I have attained fearlessness,' [he declares].

body.text: ādyaṃ vaiśāradyaṃ sarva[dharmā]bhisambodhiḥ navabalātmakam | dvitīyamāsravakṣayo daśamabalameva | kṣayajñānasampannatvāt tathāgata ātmaguṇasampannaḥ | antye dve vaiśāradye parasampadaṃ kurutaḥ | tathāgato vyākaroti āntarāyikamāntarāyikamārgadharmān yadutākuśalaṃ sāsravaṃ kuśalañca | vimuktyantarāyatvāt āntarāyikadharma ityucyate | antarāyavisaṃyogitayā nairyāṇikapratipadityucyate |
body.translated_text: The first fearlessness, complete awakening to all <s>dharmas</s> (<s>sarvadharmābhisambodhi</s>), has the nature of the [first] nine powers. The second, the destruction of outflows (<s>āsravakṣaya</s>), is the tenth power itself. Through being accomplished in the knowledge of destruction, the <s>Tathāgata</s> is accomplished in his own qualities. The last two fearlessnesses accomplish the perfection of others. The <s>Tathāgata</s> declares as obstructive the obstructive path-<s>dharmas</s> — namely, the unwholesome and the wholesome with outflows (<s>sāsrava</s>). Because they obstruct liberation, they are called obstructive <s>dharmas</s>. Through disjoining from obstructions, it is called the path leading to liberation (<s>nairyāṇikapratipad</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) nanu bhavaduktarītyā balānyeva vaiśādyāni | ataḥ ko bhedo balavaiśāradyayoḥ | (u) abhisambodhirbalaṃ bhavati | tena balenopādeyaṃ vaiśāradyamityākhyāyate | kecinmūḍhā nirapatrapā bahūpādadate | tathāgatasyopādānantu prajñāsambhūtam | abhisambudhya parebhyo 'bhayaprāpta iti vaiśāradyam | kasmāt | satyapyabhisambodhe [parebhyaḥ] paritrāsasambhavāt | abhisambodho balātmakaḥ | tadabhisambodhavyākaraṇaṃ vaiśāradyamityākhyāyate | kasmāt | keṣāñcitpuruṣāṇāṃ jñāne satyapi vyākaraṇakauśalābhāvāt parapuruṣāṇāṃ vijayo vaiśāradyam | kasmāt | satyapi jñāne keṣāñcit paravijayāsambhavāt | akṣīṇo 'bhisambodho balam | akṣīṇaṃ pratibhānaṃ vaiśāradyam | atha punarbhavagativyākaraṇaṃ balam | vyākaraṇe vaśitā vaiśāradyam | heturbalam | phalaṃ vaiśāradyam | abhisambodhādvaiśāradyasambhavāt | ya ājanma paritrastaḥ sa paścāt kiñcit jñānaṃ labdhvā viśārado bhavati | kiṃ punarbhagavān sudūrakālāt mahodāracittaḥ sarvākārābhisambodhiñca labdhvā bibheṣyati | kaścit paravijayāśaktatvāt sabhītiko bhavati | tatra na kaścidasti yaṃ tathāgato na vijitavān | ato viśāradaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Objection) According to what you have said, the powers themselves are the fearlessnesses. Then what is the difference between powers and fearlessnesses? (Reply) Complete awakening (<s>abhisambodhi</s>) is a power. Through that power, the appropriation is called fearlessness. Certain deluded and shameless persons appropriate much. But the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s appropriation is born of wisdom. Having fully awakened, one who has attained fearlessness toward others — that is fearlessness (<s>vaiśāradya</s>). Why? Because even though there is complete awakening, fear may arise [toward others]. Complete awakening is of the nature of power. The declaration of that awakening is called fearlessness. Why? Because even though some persons have knowledge, they lack skill in declaration, and other persons prevail over them. Victory [over others] is fearlessness. Why? Because even though there is knowledge, some cannot prevail over others. Inexhaustible awakening is a power. Inexhaustible eloquence is fearlessness. Furthermore, the declaration of existence and destiny is a power. Mastery in declaration is fearlessness. The cause is power; the fruit is fearlessness — because fearlessness arises from complete awakening. One who has been fearful from birth, who later obtains some knowledge and becomes confident — how much less will the Blessed One, who has had a supremely great mind since long ago and has obtained complete awakening of all aspects, be afraid? Some are afraid because they are unable to prevail over others. But there is no one whom the <s>Tathāgata</s> has not vanquished. Therefore he is fearless (<s>viśārada</s>).

body.text: yo vādī vacanakuśalaḥ arthakuśalaśca sa viśāradaḥ | tathāgata evāyam | sarvajñatālābhāt arthakuśalaḥ | apratighapratibhānalābhāt vacanakuśalaḥ | kecitpunarvastuṣu [jñāna]balavihīnāḥ santaḥ sañjātabhītikā bhavanti | tathāgatastu sarvajñānalābhitvāt sarvavastuṣu na balavihīnaḥ, sarvasūtrāṇi sarvaśāstrāṇi ca pratividhya praśnavisarjanaṃ paridīpayatīti viśāradaḥ | kecitpunaḥ kule gotre rūpe śīlabāhuśrutyajñānādiṣu vā vikalā ityataḥ sāvadyaṃ śāstramadhigacchanti | tathāgatastu tatra sarvatrāvikalaḥ | ato viśāradaḥ |
body.translated_text: One who is skilled in speech and skilled in meaning — he is '<s>Vaiśāradya</s>' (assured). The <s>Tathāgata</s> alone is such. Because of attaining omniscience, he is skilled in meaning. Because of attaining unobstructed eloquence (<s>apratighapratibhāna</s>), he is skilled in speech. Some, being devoid of the power of knowledge regarding things, become fearful. But the <s>Tathāgata</s>, because of having attained all knowledge, is not powerless in any matter; having mastered all <s>sūtras</s> and all <s>śāstras</s>, he illuminates the answering of questions — thus he is 'assured.' Some, being deficient in family, lineage, beauty, moral conduct, learning, knowledge, and so forth, therefore engage in faulty teachings. But the <s>Tathāgata</s> is not deficient in any of those. Therefore he is 'assured.'

body.text: yo yathābhūtadharmavādī sa na kampyaḥ | sa ca tathāgata eva | yathāvocat asurabrāhmaṇo bhagavantam- yathābhūtadharmavādī durjayo duṣprakampaḥ | tathaivānulomamārgavādī tarkavādī sahetuvādī ca | iti | yaḥ punaścaturbhirvāda dharmaiḥ samanvitaḥ so 'pi durjayaḥ duṣprakampaḥ | [catvāro vādadharmā yaduta] samyak pratijñāpratiṣṭhāpanam, hetvahetūpādānam, dṛṣṭāntopādānam vādadharmapratiṣṭhāpanamiti | tathāgata ebhiścaturbhiḥ sampannaḥ | devamanuṣyā api taṃ na jetuṃ śaknuvanti ityato viśāradaḥ | yaśca kalyāṇamitramanupasevya vādaṃ karoti sa sukampaḥ | tathāgatastu dīpaṅkarādiṣu apramāṇabuddheṣu pūrvamevābhyastavādadharmā ityato na prakampyaḥ | bhagavānupadiśati satyadvayaṃ yaduta lokasatyaṃ paramārthasatyamiti | ataḥ prājño na kampayituṃ śakyaḥ | prākṛtairajñaiśca saha na vivadate | tathāgataśca lokena saha na vivadate | loke 'sti tathāgataḥ [paraṃ maraṇāt] iti vadati | bhagavānapi vadati astīti | nāstīti vadati loke nāstīti vadati | ato nāsti vivādaḥ | tena saha vivādābhāvāt aprakampyaḥ |
body.translated_text: One who speaks the <s>Dharma</s> as it truly is — he is unshakeable. And that is the <s>Tathāgata</s> alone. As the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> <s>Asura</s> said to the Blessed One: 'One who speaks the <s>Dharma</s> as it truly is, is hard to defeat and hard to shake.' Likewise, one who speaks in accordance with the path, who speaks with reasoning, who speaks with causes — [is hard to shake]. Furthermore, one who is endowed with the four qualities of debate is also hard to defeat and hard to shake. The four qualities of debate are: the correct establishment of the thesis, the employment of valid and invalid reasons, the employment of examples, and the establishment of the rules of debate. The <s>Tathāgata</s> is endowed with these four. Even gods and humans cannot defeat him — therefore he is 'assured.' One who debates without having attended upon a good spiritual friend is easily shaken. But the <s>Tathāgata</s> has already practiced the qualities of debate under innumerable <s>Buddhas</s> beginning with <s>Dīpaṅkara</s> — therefore he is not to be shaken. The Blessed One teaches the two truths, namely conventional truth (<s>lokasatya</s>) and ultimate truth (<s>paramārthasatya</s>). Therefore the wise one cannot be shaken. Ordinary, ignorant people do not dispute with him. And the <s>Tathāgata</s> does not dispute with the world. When the world says 'the <s>Tathāgata</s> exists [after death],' the Blessed One also says 'it exists.' When it says 'it does not exist,' he says 'it does not exist.' Therefore there is no dispute. Because of the absence of dispute with him, he is unshakeable.

body.text: śāstraṃ puna dvividhaṃ tattvaśāstraṃ śaṭhaśāstram iti | tīrthikānāṃ bhūyasā śaṭhaśāstram | tathāgatasya tu tattvaśāstram | ato 'pi na prakampyaḥ | jinaśāsane sucaritapariśuddhatvāt upadeśo 'pi pariśuddhaḥ | sucaritapariśuddhirnāma duḥkhahetukṣayaḥ | tīrthikānāṃ śāstrāṇi sahetvābhāsāni na sahetukāni iti na vijayasamarthāni bhavanti | bhagavataḥ sūtrāṇi pariśuddhapravacanārthagatikāni tattvalakṣaṇāvilomakāni na tīrthikīyasamānāni | bhagavadupadiṣṭo
body.translated_text: Furthermore, treatises are of two kinds: truthful treatises (<s>tattvaśāstra</s>) and deceitful treatises (<s>śaṭhaśāstra</s>). The treatises of the <s>tīrthikas</s> (non-Buddhist teachers) are mostly deceitful. But the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s treatise is truthful. Therefore too he is unshakeable. Because of the purity of good conduct in the <s>Jina</s>'s teaching, the instruction too is pure. Purity of good conduct means the destruction of the causes of suffering. The treatises of the <s>tīrthikas</s> have only the appearance of reasons, not genuine reasons — therefore they are not capable of [producing] victory. The <s>sūtras</s> of the Blessed One convey the pure meaning of the teaching and are in conformity with the characteristics of reality, not like those of the <s>tīrthikas</s>. The path taught by the Blessed One

body.text: mārgo na yathārutagrahaṇarthaḥ | api tu ādhyātmikajñānacittakaḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- bhagavān bhikṣūnāmantyāha mā bhikṣavo mama vacanādhimuktikā bhavata | kintu bhavadbhirādhyātmikajñānasya kāyena sākṣātkāribhirbhavitavyam | iti | kiñcāha- aśaṭhā yūyamāgacchata | prātarvo dharmaṃ bhāṣamāṇe mayi sāyaṃ mārga labhedhvam | sāyaṃ dharmaṃ bhāṣamāṇe prātarmārgaṃ labhedhvam | iti | yaḥ kaśmiṃściddharme 'prabuddhaḥ sa [tūṣṇī]tiṣṭhet | na pravacanaṃ kuryāt | yatkiñcitpravadannapi avaśyaṃ prakampyaḥ | tathāgatastu nāprabuddha iti vaiśāradyasamarthaḥ | kiñca tathāgataḥ pratilabdhāpratighābhisambodhaḥ | na sarvadharmeṣvapratibuddha iti viśāradaḥ | alpajñā na jānanti mahāpuruṣāṇāṃ yadadhigatam | mahāpuruṣāstu jānanti alpajñānāmadhigatam | bhagavān sattvānāmuttamo mahān iti alpajñānāṃ śāstraṃ jānāti | ato viśāradaḥ | tīrthikānāṃ śāstraṃ yāṃ kāñcit dṛṣṭimupādāya pravṛttam | bhagavāṃstu prajānāti dṛṣṭiriyaṃ pratītya samutpanneti | tatsamudayaṃ prajānāti, nirodhaṃ prajānāti, āsvādaṃ prajānāti, ādīnavaṃ prajānāti, nairyāṇikañca prajānāti | tīrthikādayo na kṣayajñānasamarthā iti [mitho] vivadante | tathāgatastu sarvākārajñaḥ sarvadharmajñaḥ sarvaparaśāstrāṇāṃ dārako na paraśāstrairdāryo bhavati | ato viśāradaḥ | ityādayaḥ pratyayā balavaiśāradyapravibhāgārthā bhavanti |
body.translated_text: is not to be grasped merely according to the letter. Rather, it is directed toward inner knowledge (<s>ādhyātmikajñāna</s>) of the mind. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The Blessed One addressed the monks: "O monks, do not be those who merely accept my words on faith. Rather, you should become ones who directly realize inner knowledge with your own bodies."' And he further said: 'Come to me without deceit. If in the morning I teach you the <s>Dharma</s>, you may attain the path by evening. If in the evening I teach you the <s>Dharma</s>, you may attain the path by morning.' One who has not awakened to some <s>dharma</s> should remain silent. He should not expound the teaching. Whatever he says, he will certainly be shaken. But the <s>Tathāgata</s> is not unawakened — therefore he is capable of the assurance (<s>vaiśāradya</s>). Moreover, the <s>Tathāgata</s> has attained unobstructed awakening (<s>apratighābhisaṃbodha</s>). Because he is not unawakened regarding any <s>dharma</s>, he is 'assured.' Those of little knowledge do not know what great beings have realized. But great beings know what those of little knowledge have realized. Since the Blessed One is the foremost and greatest among beings, he knows the teachings of those with little knowledge. Therefore he is 'assured.' The teachings of the <s>tīrthikas</s> proceed by taking up some view or other. But the Blessed One knows: 'This view has arisen dependently (<s>pratītyasamutpanna</s>).' He knows its origin, he knows its cessation, he knows its gratification, he knows its danger, and he knows the way of escape from it. The <s>tīrthikas</s> and others, not being capable of the knowledge of destruction, dispute among themselves. But the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the knower of all aspects, the knower of all <s>dharmas</s>, breaks through all rival teachings and is not broken through by rival teachings. Therefore he is 'assured.' These and similar considerations serve to distinguish the powers (<s>bala</s>) from the assurances (<s>vaiśāradya</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) tathāgataḥ sarvadharmeṣu viśāradaḥ | kasmāducyante | catvāryeva vaiśāradyāni | (u)yānyuktāni tāni sarvavaiśāradyānāṃ sāmānyavacanāni | kasmāt | ādyaṃ vaiśāradyadvayamātmanaḥ kṣayajñānābhidhāyakam | antimadvayaṃ parasya mārgāntarāyikadharmābhidhāyakam | duḥkhakṣayamārgābhidhāyakaṃ [sat]kṣayajñānamityucyate | sa śrāvakaḥ śāstā kṣayajñānasampanna ityataḥ sarvāṇi vaiśāradyāni sāmānyata uktāni |
body.translated_text: (Objection:) The <s>Tathāgata</s> is assured in all <s>dharmas</s>. Why then are only four assurances stated? (Reply:) Those that have been stated are general expressions for all assurances. Why? The first pair of assurances proclaims one's own knowledge of destruction. The latter pair proclaims the <s>dharmas</s> that obstruct the path for others. [The assurance that] proclaims the path to the destruction of suffering is called the knowledge of destruction. He, the <s>Śrāvaka</s> [turned] teacher, being endowed with the knowledge of destruction — therefore all assurances are stated in general terms.

body.text: (pṛ) sattvāḥ kasmāt saṃśerate tathāgato 'sarvajñaḥ puruṣa iti | (u) bhagavatoktaṃ vacanaṃ kadācidasarvajña[vacana]kalpamasti | tadyathā bhagavān pratyāha- kuto yūyamāgacchatha ityādi | yathoktaṃ sūtre- yaḥ kaścit nagaraṃ praviśya tannāma nāgarikān pṛcchati | nāhaṃ vadāmi taṃ sarvajñam iti | śrotāsya sūtrasya saṃśete tathāgato 'sarvajñaḥ puruṣa iti | bhagavadvacanaṃ sarāgavacanakalpamasti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- bhagavānāha svāgataṃ vo bhikṣavaḥ anena
body.translated_text: (Objection:) Why do beings doubt whether the <s>Tathāgata</s> is an omniscient person? (Reply:) There are some words spoken by the Blessed One that resemble the speech of a non-omniscient person. For example, the Blessed One asked: 'Where have you come from?' and so forth. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Whoever enters a city and asks the citizens its name — I do not call him omniscient.' One who hears this <s>sūtra</s> doubts whether the <s>Tathāgata</s> is omniscient. There are words of the Blessed One that resemble the speech of one with attachment. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The Blessed One said: "Welcome, O monks! By this

body.text: kāyena mahārthalābhāya mama śāsanamanuvartadhvam | tadā pramuditaḥ syām iti | dveṣikalpamapyasti vacanam | yathoktam- tvaṃ khalu devadatta śavabhūtaḥ kheṭāśano 'si | iti | ābhimānikakalpo 'pyasti vyavahāraḥ | yathātmānamadhikṛtyāha ahaṃ pariṣadi siṃhakalpo daśabalaiścaturbhirvaiśāradyaiśca samanvitaḥ mahāpariṣadi siṃhanādaṃ nadāmi iti | mithyādṛṣṭikakalpo 'pyasti vyavahāraḥ | sandhārayāmyātmadharma yathā tailapātnam | āha ca devadattam- nāhaṃ dadāmi saṅghaṃ śāriputramaugdalyāyanādibhyo 'pi kiṃ punardāsyāmi tubhyam | iti | alpajñā imāni vacanāni śrutvā vadanti tathāgatasyasravā akṣīṇā iti |
body.translated_text: body, for the sake of great benefit, follow my teaching. Then I would be gladdened."' There are also words resembling those of one with aversion. As stated: 'You indeed, <s>Devadatta</s>, are like a corpse, eating phlegm!' There is also behavior resembling that of one with pride. As when he said of himself: 'I, like a lion in the assembly, endowed with the ten powers and the four assurances, roar the lion's roar in the great assembly.' There is also behavior resembling that of one with wrong view. 'I hold to the <s>Dharma</s> of the self, like an oil-lamp.' And he said to <s>Devadatta</s>: 'I do not give the <s>Saṅgha</s> even to <s>Śāriputra</s> and <s>Maudgalyāyana</s> — how much less would I give it to you!' Those of little knowledge, hearing these words, say that the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s defilements (<s>āsrava</s>) have not been destroyed.

body.text: kiñcāha bhagavān- kāmā mārgāntarāyikā dharmaḥ | kecittu [kāmān] vedayanto 'pi mārgaṃ labhante | iti | vinaye 'pyuktam- viramaṇadharmābhdraṣṭo 'pi mārgaṃ spṛśati | iti | ato 'lpajñāḥ saṃśerate tathāgata āvaraṇadharmānabhijña iti | kecinmārgaṃ bhāvayanto 'pi saṃyojanairanuśayavantaḥ | ato 'lpajñāḥ saṃśerate āryamārgaḥ saṃyojanānāṃ na kṣayakṛta iti | saṃyojanāni aprahāya ko duḥkhaṃ viyojayet | atastathāgatasteṣu caturṣu dharmeṣu viśāradaḥ |
body.translated_text: Moreover, the Blessed One said: 'Sensual pleasures are <s>dharmas</s> that obstruct the path. Yet some, even while experiencing sensual pleasures, attain the path.' In the <s>Vinaya</s> too it is said: 'Even one who has not seen the <s>dharmas</s> of abstinence may touch the path.' Therefore those of little knowledge doubt whether the <s>Tathāgata</s> does not know the obstructing <s>dharmas</s>. Some, even while cultivating the path, are still bound by fetters (<s>saṃyojana</s>) and latent tendencies (<s>anuśaya</s>). Therefore those of little knowledge doubt whether the noble path does not destroy the fetters. Without abandoning the fetters, who could separate [beings] from suffering? Therefore the <s>Tathāgata</s> is assured regarding these four <s>dharmas</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) kathaṃ yathoddiṣṭāḥ saṃśayā parihīṣyante | (u) bhagavān saṃvṛtimanuvartate | yathā laukikā jānanto 'pi praṣṭāro na duṣyanti | tathā bhagavānapi lokavartitvāt saṃvṛtimanuvartya pṛcchati | laukikā anāsaṅgacittā api āsaṅgikalpaṃ vadanti īdṛśamiti | tathā bhagavānapi sattvānāṃ hitāyadṛṣṭe vyavaharati | kāmā nāntarāyikadharmā iti sati vacane tatra tathāgata upadiśati kāmā vastuta āntarāyikadharmā iti | yasya kāmāścittagatāḥ sa na mārgaṃ bhāvayati | ato 'vaśyaṃ kāmān pūrvaṃ parityajya paścānmārgaṃ spṛśati | āpattidharme satyapi
body.translated_text: (Objection:) How will the doubts that have been enumerated be removed? (Reply:) The Blessed One follows convention (<s>saṃvṛti</s>). Just as in the world, those who already know [the answer] are not at fault for asking — so too the Blessed One, being one who follows worldly convention, asks in accordance with convention. Worldly people, even those without attachment of mind, speak in ways that resemble attachment, such as saying 'it is like this.' So too the Blessed One, for the benefit of beings, engages in visible behavior. When [someone says] 'sensual pleasures are not obstructing <s>dharmas</s>,' the <s>Tathāgata</s> teaches there: 'Sensual pleasures are in reality obstructing <s>dharmas</s>.' One for whom sensual desires have entered the mind does not cultivate the path. Therefore one must first abandon sensual desires and then afterward touch the path. Even when there is the <s>dharma</s> of transgression

body.text: mārgaḥprāpyata iti brūvato 'vaśyaṃ paribhinne 'pyāpattidharme mārgo na prāpyate | yasya vastuto nāstyāpattiḥ | tasya gurupratyayatvāt bhagavān punaḥkhayamāśrāvayet nāstyāpattidharmo vināśayitum iti | yanmārgaṃ bhāvayatāmapi saṃyojanamastīti | ayaṃ mārgaḥ sarvasaṃyojanānuśayānāṃ vināśakaḥ, asampannatvāttu na vināśayituṃ prabhavati | tadyathā prakṛtito dadhi tāpaśamanam | kintu [puruṣasya] alpavasanatve na tatparipācanaṃ bhavati | tathā mārgabhāvanāpīti anavadyam | tathāgata ścaturvaiśāradyasamanvita ityato 'bhivandyaḥ |
body.translated_text: the path is attained — so says [the objector]. But [the reply is:] even when the <s>dharma</s> of transgression is present, the path is certainly not attained. For one who truly has no transgression, because the Blessed One would have him hear again about destruction [of defilements] — it is not for the purpose of destroying the <s>dharma</s> of transgression. As for the statement that even those cultivating the path still have fetters — this path is the destroyer of all fetters and latent tendencies, but because it is not yet perfected, it is unable to destroy them. Just as, by nature, yogurt is a cooler of heat, but if a person wears too little clothing, that cooling effect does not fully ripen. So too with the cultivation of the path — there is nothing blameworthy. Since the <s>Tathāgata</s> is endowed with the four assurances, he is worthy of veneration.

body.text: caturvaiśāradyavargastṛtīyaḥ
body.translated_text: End of the Third Chapter on the Four Assurances (<s>Caturvaiśāradyavarga</s>).

body.text: 4 daśanāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: Chapter 4: The Chapter on the Ten Names (<s>Daśanāvarga</s>).

body.text: atha sūtra uktaṃ- tathāgatādīnāṃ daśa guṇāḥ yaduta tathāgataḥ arhan samyak sambuddho vidyācaraṇasampannaḥ sugato lokavit anuttarapuruṣadaumyasārathiḥ śāstā devamanuṣyāṇāṃ buddho bhagavān iti |
body.translated_text: Now, in the <s>sūtra</s> it is stated: 'The <s>Tathāgata</s> and others have ten qualities, namely: <s>Tathāgata</s>, <s>Arhat</s>, <s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s> (Perfectly Awakened One), <s>Vidyācaraṇasampanna</s> (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct), <s>Sugata</s> (Well-Gone), <s>Lokavit</s> (Knower of the World), <s>Anuttarapuruṣadamyasārathi</s> (Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men to be Tamed), <s>Śāstā Devamanuṣyāṇām</s> (Teacher of Gods and Men), <s>Buddha</s>, <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One).'

body.text: tathāgata iti yathābhūtamārgayānena saṃsādhitasamyaksambodhitvāt tathāgata ityucyate | yadyadupadiśati sarvaṃ tattvameva bhavati na mṛṣā | yathā bhagavānānandamāmantryāha- tathāgataproktamubhayakoṭikaṃ na vā | no bhagavana iti | atastathāvādītyucyate |
body.translated_text: He is called '<s>Tathāgata</s>' because he has accomplished perfect awakening (<s>samyaksaṃbodhi</s>) by means of the path as it truly is (<s>yathābhūtamārgayāna</s>). Whatever he teaches, all of it is truly real and not false. As the Blessed One addressed <s>Ānanda</s>: 'Is what the <s>Tathāgata</s> has said of both extremes, or not?' 'No, Blessed One.' Therefore he is called 'one who speaks what is true' (<s>tathāvādin</s>).

body.text: atha punastathāgato yāṃ rātrimabhisambuddhaḥ | yāñca rātriṃ parinirvṛtaḥ | atrāntarāle yat bhāṣate tat satyameva bhavati nānyathā | tasmādyathārthavādītyucyate | sarvākārasarvajñajñānena pūrvāparaṃ parīkṣya paścādupadiśatītyata upadiṣṭaṃ satyameva bhavati | kiñca buddhānāṃ bhagavatāṃ smṛtirdṛḍhā bhavati na muṣitā | kecidanumāya yadupadiśaṃti tat kadācit sūtrānuyāyi bhavati | kecittu pratyakṣato dṛṣṭvaivopadiśanti | tairupadiṣṭhaṃ lābhāya vā bhavati hānāya vā | yathoktaṃ sūtre- anumāturvacanaṃ lābhāya kadācit bhavati hānāya vā kadācit | tathāgatastu
body.translated_text: Furthermore, from the night the <s>Tathāgata</s> was fully awakened to the night he attained <s>Parinirvāṇa</s>, whatever he spoke in the interval — all of it is true and not otherwise. Therefore he is called 'one who speaks what is truly so.' Having examined the past and future with the knowledge of omniscience in all its aspects, he then teaches — therefore what he teaches is truly real. Moreover, the memory of the <s>Buddhas</s>, the Blessed Ones, is firm and not confused. Some teach on the basis of inference, and what they teach sometimes accords with the <s>sūtras</s> and sometimes does not. But some teach having directly seen with direct perception. What they teach may be either beneficial or harmful. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The words of one who infers may sometimes be beneficial and sometimes harmful.' But the <s>Tathāgata</s>

body.text: dharmānabhisambudhyopadiśati | iti | tasmādakampyavacanastattvopadeṣṭetyucyate | bhagavatopadiṣṭaṃ tattvavacanaṃ bhavati nānyeṣāmiva satattvamatattvañcetyato 'kampyam |
body.translated_text: teaches <s>dharmas</s> having fully awakened to them. Therefore he is called 'one whose speech is unshakeable, a teacher of reality.' The words taught by the Blessed One are words of reality, not like those of others — sometimes true and sometimes untrue — and therefore they are unshakeable.

body.text: kālānurūpañcopadiṣṭam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- bhagavān sattvānāṃ cittaprāmodyamadhimukti ñca prajñāya mārgamupadiśati iti | yathārthavaktā bhavati | yadupadeśārhaṃ tadevopadiśyate | yathoktaṃ kiṃśukaśirṣaka sūtre yo dharma upadeśārhaḥ tamupadiśati saṃkṣepato vistarato vā skandhāyatanādimukhena iti | ata upadiṣṭaṃ naiva mṛṣā bhavati |
body.translated_text: And [his teaching is] appropriate to the occasion. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The Blessed One, knowing the mental joy and inclination of beings through wisdom, teaches the path.' He speaks what is true to the purpose. Only that which is worthy of teaching is taught. As stated in the <s>Kiṃśukaśīrṣaka Sūtra</s>: 'He teaches that <s>dharma</s> which is worthy of teaching — whether in brief or in detail, by way of the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>), sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>), and so forth.' Therefore what is taught is never false.

body.text: atha punardharmāvavādo dvividhaḥ saṃvṛtitaḥ paramārthata iti | tathāgata idaṃ satyadvayaṃ niśrityopadiśatītyata upadiṣṭaṃ sarvaṃ tattvaṃ bhavati | bhagavān nopadiśati yat saṃvṛtisatyaṃ tat paramārthasatyamiti | na ca yat paramārthasatyaṃ tat saṃvṛtisatyamiti | ato vacanadvayaṃ na virudhyate | atha tathāgatena yadi vā saṃvriyate yadi vā vivriyate tadubhayamapyaviruddham | yat saṃvaraṇāya bhavati na tat vibriyate | yat vivaraṇāya bhavati na tat saṃvriyate | ato yatkimapi vacanamaviruddham |
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the teaching of <s>Dharma</s> is twofold: in terms of <s>saṃvṛti</s> (conventional truth) and in terms of <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate truth). The <s>Tathāgata</s> teaches depending on these two truths, and therefore everything he has taught is true. The Blessed One does not teach that what is <s>saṃvṛti-satya</s> (conventional truth) is <s>paramārtha-satya</s> (ultimate truth), nor that what is <s>paramārtha-satya</s> (ultimate truth) is <s>saṃvṛti-satya</s> (conventional truth). Therefore the two [kinds of] statements do not contradict each other. Moreover, whether the <s>Tathāgata</s> conceals or reveals, both are non-contradictory. What is for the purpose of concealing is not revealed; what is for the purpose of revealing is not concealed. Therefore, whatever statement [he makes] is non-contradictory.

body.text: kiñca trividhā avavādadharmā dṛṣṭijo 'bhimānajaḥ prajñaptijaśceti | bhagavato nāsti ādyāvavādadvayam | tṛtīyo 'vavādastu pariśuddho 'malaḥ | santi ca caturvidhā avavādāḥ darśanaśravaṇamananidhyaptidharmā iti | bhagavāneṣu caturṣu dharmeṣu yadyadupadiśati tat sarvaṃ cittavyavadānāya bhavati nāsaṅgāya | pañcavidhā api avavādadharmāḥ atītānāgatapratyutpannāsaṃskṛtāvaktavyā iti | eṣu pañcasu bhagavān sambuddhaḥ san vyaktaramabhijñāyopadiśati | ato yathārthavādītyucyate | yathābhūtavacane naipuṇyāt tathāgata ityucyate |
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the teachings of <s>Dharma</s> are of three kinds: those born of [wrong] views, those born of conceit, and those born of designation. The Blessed One does not have the first two kinds of teaching. But the third kind of teaching is pure and stainless. There are also four kinds of teachings: those pertaining to seeing, hearing, thinking, and meditative realization. In these four aspects of <s>Dharma</s>, whatever the Blessed One teaches, all of it is for the purification of the mind, not for attachment. The teachings of <s>Dharma</s> are also of five kinds: past, future, present, unconditioned, and inexpressible. Among these five, the Blessed One, being fully awakened, teaches with clear direct knowledge. Therefore he is called 'one who speaks in accordance with reality.' Because of his skill in speaking in accordance with how things truly are, he is called <s>Tathāgata</s> (Thus-Come One).

body.text: kṣīṇakleśatvāt imaṃ dharma labdhavān | rāgadveṣamohādayo mṛṣāvādasya mūlam | tāni saṃyojanāni niruddhavān iti arhan | atha tathāgatasyopadeśo 'rhan | saṃyojananirodhaḥ samyaksambodhāt bhavati | anityatādinā dharmān samyak bhāvayataḥ kleśāḥ kṣīyante | ataḥ samyaksambodhimupādāya arhaddharmaḥ pravartate | samyaksambodhiriyaṃ vidyācaraṇajanitā | pūrvāntāparāntayośca nāsti santatiriti samyak pratisambudhyata iti samyak sambuddha iti nāma |
body.translated_text: Because his defilements are destroyed, he has attained this <s>Dharma</s>. Passion, hatred, delusion, and the like are the root of false speech. He has put an end to those fetters — therefore he is an <s>Arhat</s> (Worthy One). Now, the teaching of the <s>Tathāgata</s> is worthy (<s>arhat</s>). The cessation of fetters comes from <s>samyaksaṃbodhi</s> (perfect awakening). When one rightly cultivates <s>dharmas</s> through [contemplating] impermanence and so forth, the defilements are destroyed. Therefore, based on <s>samyaksaṃbodhi</s>, the quality of <s>Arhatship</s> operates. This <s>samyaksaṃbodhi</s> is born of <s>vidyācaraṇa</s> (knowledge and conduct). And because there is no continuity of the prior and posterior limits [of existence], he perfectly realizes — therefore he is named <s>Samyak-saṃbuddha</s> (Perfectly Awakened One).

body.text: dānādipāramitāḥ samācaratīti vidyācaraṇasampannaḥ | anye 'pi puruṣā anādisaṃsāre dānādīn dharmānācaranti na samyagācarantīti na sugata ityucyante | bhagavān punardānādicaryāḥ samyaṅmārgeṇa caritavāniti sugata ityucyate | dānādipañcadharmāṇāṃ lābhī tathāgataḥ svārthaguṇasampannaḥ | samyaksambodhimanuprāpya lokānāṃ manasi cintitaṃ prajānāti | [ato lokavit] | cintitañca prajñāya dharmamupadiśatīti anuttaraḥ puruṣadaumyasārathiḥ | vinetavyā nāvinītā bhavanti | vinītāśca na bhraśyanti | vinetavyāśca devamanuṣyāḥ | ato devamanuṣyāṇāṃ śāstā | kecit vicikitsante kathaṃ manuṣyeṇa devā avavadituṃ śakyanta iti | ata āha- ahaṃ devamanuṣyāṇāṃ śāstā iti | buddha iti atītānāgatapratyutpannānāṃ saṃskṛtāsaṃskṛtasakṣayākṣayāṇāṃ sthūlasūkṣmādīnāṃ vā sarveṣāṃ dharmāṇām | bodhimūle niṣadya avidyāmiddhamavidhya sarvajñānojvalitāṃ mahābodhiṃ labdhavāniti buddhaḥ | evaṃ navabhirguṇaiḥ sampanna triṣu adhvasu daśasu dikṣu sarvalokadhātuṣu ca pūjya iti bhagavān | bhagavān daśanāmasampannaḥ svātmasampadā parasampadā ca ātmānamupakaroti parāṃścopakarotītyato 'bhivandyaḥ ||
body.translated_text: Because he practices the <s>pāramitās</s> (perfections) such as <s>dāna</s> (generosity) and the rest, he is called <s>Vidyācaraṇa-sampanna</s> (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct). Other persons too, in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, practice <s>dharmas</s> such as giving and the rest, but they do not practice them rightly — therefore they are not called <s>Sugata</s> (Well-Gone One). But the Blessed One has practiced the conduct of giving and the rest through the right path — therefore he is called <s>Sugata</s>. The <s>Tathāgata</s>, who has obtained the five <s>dharmas</s> beginning with <s>dāna</s> (generosity), is endowed with the qualities that benefit himself. Having attained <s>samyaksaṃbodhi</s>, he knows what is thought in the minds of beings — therefore [he is called] <s>Lokavid</s> (Knower of the World). And having known their thoughts, he teaches the <s>Dharma</s> — therefore he is the <s>Anuttara-puruṣa-damya-sārathi</s> (Unsurpassed Charioteer of Persons to be Tamed). Those to be tamed do not remain untamed, and those who are tamed do not fall away. Those to be tamed are gods and humans — therefore he is the <s>Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām</s> (Teacher of Gods and Humans). Some doubt: 'How can a human being instruct gods?' Therefore he says: 'I am the teacher of gods and humans.' As for <s>Buddha</s>: of all <s>dharmas</s> — past, future, present, conditioned and unconditioned, perishable and imperishable, gross and subtle, and so forth — having sat at the foot of the <s>Bodhi</s> tree, having pierced the darkness of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), he attained the great <s>Bodhi</s> (awakening) blazing with omniscient knowledge — therefore he is <s>Buddha</s> (Awakened One). Thus, endowed with these nine qualities, he is worshipped in all three time-periods, in the ten directions, and in all world-realms — therefore he is <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One). The Blessed One, endowed with the ten names, benefits himself through his own accomplishment and benefits others through the accomplishment of others — therefore he is worthy of veneration.

body.text: daśanāmavargaścaturthaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Ten Names.

body.text: 5 trividhārakṣāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 5. Chapter on the Threefold Non-Guardedness

body.text: tathāgatasya kāyikavācikamānasikakarmāṇi arakṣyāṇi | kutaḥ | na hi santi tathāgatasya kāyikavācikamānasikaduścaritāni yāni[tathāgato rakṣitu]micchet mā paro drakṣyāt mā ca jñāsīt iti | anyeṣāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ santi kadācidavyākṛtābhāsāni kāyikavācikamānasikaduścaritāni vidvadgarhaṇīyāni | tathāgatasya tu na santi | kasmāt | tathāgatasya sarvāṇi karmāṇi prajñāsamyaksmṛtibhyāmutpadyante | ye muṣitasmṛtikā duṣprajñāḥ | na ta īdṛśakarmāṇo bhavanti | laukikāḥ kadācit vyativṛttabhrāntavādino bhavanti |
body.translated_text: The bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the <s>Tathāgata</s> need not be guarded. Why? Because the <s>Tathāgata</s> does not have any bodily, verbal, or mental misconduct that he would wish to guard, thinking 'Let others not see it or know it.' Other persons sometimes have bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct that appears neutral but is blameworthy by the wise. But the <s>Tathāgata</s> does not have such [misconduct]. Why? Because all the actions of the <s>Tathāgata</s> arise from <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom) and right <s>smṛti</s> (mindfulness). Those who are of confused mindfulness and poor wisdom do not have such actions. Worldly persons sometimes speak with error and confusion.

body.text: tathāgatastu na tatsamaḥ | tathāgataḥ kāyena subhāvitavān śīlasamādhiprajñā stattulyān dharmāśca | ataḥ sarvāṇyakuśalāni akuśalābhāsāni ca karmāṇi sarvathā parikṣīṇāni | bhagavān dirghakālādārabhya saddharmacaryāṃ bhāvitavān nedānīmeva | atastatkarmāṇi viśuddhasvabhāvāni nārakṣyāṇi | tathāgataḥ sadā śīlamācarati adhimuktito na durgatipatanabhayādinā | tathāgatasya ca sarvāṇi kāyikavācikamānasikakarmāṇi paropakārāya bhavanti iti nākuśalāni | akuśalābhāvānnārakṣyāṇi | viśuddhatvādarakṣyaṃ karma ityato 'bhivandyaḥ | tathāgatastrividhasmṛtyupasthānasamanvitaḥ yenābhivandanīye bhavati |
body.translated_text: But the <s>Tathāgata</s> is not equal to them. The <s>Tathāgata</s> has well-cultivated his body, <s>śīla</s> (moral conduct), <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom), and <s>dharmas</s> equal to those. Therefore all unwholesome actions and actions that have the appearance of unwholesomeness are completely exhausted. The Blessed One has cultivated the practice of the true <s>Dharma</s> since a long time ago, not only now. Therefore those actions are of a purified nature and need not be guarded. The <s>Tathāgata</s> always practices <s>śīla</s> (moral conduct) out of conviction, not out of fear of falling into lower realms and the like. And all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the <s>Tathāgata</s> are for the benefit of others — therefore they are not unwholesome. Because of the absence of the unwholesome, they need not be guarded. Because of their purity, his actions need not be guarded — therefore he is worthy of veneration. The <s>Tathāgata</s> is endowed with the three <s>smṛtyupasthānas</s> (foundations of mindfulness), by which he is worthy of veneration.

body.text: dharma upadiśyamāne yadi śrotā ekāgracitto bhavati | nānena [tathāgatasya] saumanasyaṃ bhavati | yadi naikāgracitto bhavati | nānena daurmanasyaṃ bhavati | sarvadā tu upekṣācittamācarati | kasmāt | tathāgate rāgadveṣavāsanāyā avaśeṣitatvāt | sarvadharmāṇāmatyantaśūnyatāṃ jñātavāniti na daurmanasyaṃ na vā saumanasyam | susañcitamahākaruṇācittatvāt tathāgataḥ kuśale akuśale ca vinā saumanasyadaurmanasyādi mahākaruṇāmevotpādayati | tathāgataḥ sattvānāṃ pṛthak pṛthak svabhāvamatigahanaṃ parijñātavānityato yadi kaścit kuśalacittaḥ śṛṇoti nānena sumanasko bhavati | yadi akuśacittaḥ śṛṇoti nānena durmanasko bhavati | prakṛtitaḥ sarvadā upekṣācittamācarati | kiñca tathāgato mahāpṛthivīvat dhruvacitto bhavati | guruvastunyapagate nonnato bhavati | tasmin prakṣipte 'pi na punaravanato bhavati | anye prākṛtā janāstu yathoditacittā bhavanti | kiñcidārope 'vanatā bhavanti | kiñcidavarope unnatā bhavanti | buddho bhagavān mahākāruṇika ityato devamanuṣyāṇāmabhivandanīyaḥ |
body.translated_text: When the <s>Dharma</s> is being taught, if the listener is single-pointed in mind, the <s>Tathāgata</s> does not experience elation thereby. If [the listener] is not single-pointed in mind, the <s>Tathāgata</s> does not experience dejection thereby. He always maintains an attitude of equanimity. Why? Because in the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the residual impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) of passion and aversion have been exhausted. Having known the ultimate emptiness of all <s>dharmas</s>, he has neither dejection nor elation. Because his mind is well-accumulated with great compassion (<s>mahākaruṇā</s>), the <s>Tathāgata</s>, whether in the wholesome or the unwholesome, without elation or dejection, generates only great compassion. The <s>Tathāgata</s> has thoroughly known the individual natures of beings, which are extremely profound — therefore, if someone listens with a wholesome mind, he does not become pleased thereby; if someone listens with an unwholesome mind, he does not become displeased thereby. By nature he always maintains an attitude of equanimity. Furthermore, the <s>Tathāgata</s> is steady-minded like the great earth. When a heavy object is removed, it does not rise up; even when [something heavy] is placed upon it, it does not sink down. But other ordinary persons have minds that fluctuate as described — when something is added, they sink; when something is removed, they rise. The <s>Buddha</s>, the Blessed One, is the great compassionate one — therefore he is worthy of veneration by gods and humans.

body.text: paramaṃ dhyānasamādhisukhamupekṣya janānāṃ dharmamupadiśati | anyeṣāṃ karuṇācittaṃ na kṛtyakṛt | bhagavatastu mahākaruṇā sattvānāmupakāriṇīti phalavatī bhavati | mahākaruṇayā saṃsādhito 'nuttaro mārgo na punaranyaiḥ kāraṇaiḥ | atha punastathāgatasya nāsti kāpīcchā- mama paramā santuṣṭiriti | mahākāruṇikatvāt svātmānaṃ kleśayati | tathāgataḥ prakṛtyā sūrataḥ | mahākāruṇikatvāt bhavaduḥkhahṛdvacanena mahopāye na sattvānāmuddharaṇāya vyavasāyaduḥkhānyupādatte | tathāgato mahākaruṇayā sattvānāmuddharaṇāya loke 'smin taptāyaḥpiṇḍavat kṣaṇamapyasahyaṃ pañcaskandhātmakaṃ kāyamupādāya viharati | bhagavān buddhaḥ subhāvitopākṣācittaḥ tadupekṣācittamupekṣya sadā mahākaruṇācittamācarati | ataḥ pūjanīyaḥ |
body.translated_text: Relinquishing the supreme bliss of <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) and <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), he teaches the <s>Dharma</s> to beings. The compassionate mind of others does not accomplish its purpose. But the great compassion of the Blessed One is beneficial to beings — therefore it is fruitful. The unsurpassed path has been accomplished through great compassion, not through other causes. Moreover, the <s>Tathāgata</s> does not have any desire, thinking 'I have supreme contentment.' Because of his great compassion, he exerts himself [even to the point of hardship]. The <s>Tathāgata</s> is by nature gentle. Because of his great compassion, with words about the suffering of existence as a great expedient, he undertakes the suffering of effort for the deliverance of beings.
