body.translated_text: — and the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya). Karma is the causal condition (hetupratyaya). Consciousness (vijñāna) is the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), because consciousness arises immediately after [the preceding] consciousness. Form (rūpa) is the object condition (ālambanapratyaya). The eye [and other sense faculties] constitute the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya). Therein, consciousness arises from two causes — namely, the eye and form, up to the mind and dharmas. These constitute the twelve sense-bases (dvādaśāyatana). With the addition of consciousness, the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśa dhātu) come into being — the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu), the form-element (rūpadhātu), the eye-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu), and so forth.

body.text: skandhādayo dharmāḥ kathamutpadyeran | dvādaśasu parvasu vartitvāt dvādaśa nidānāni bhavanti | tatrāvidyā kleśāḥ | saṃskāraḥ karma | imau dvāvupādāya kramaśa utpadyante- vijñānaṃ nāmarūpaṃ ṣaḍāyatanaṃ sparśo vedanā ca | tṛṣṇopādānākhyau dvau dharmau kleśau | bhavaḥ karma | anāgate 'dhvani kāyopādānasyādyaṃ vijñānaṃ jātirityucyate | anyat jarāmaraṇam | imāni dvādaśa nidānāni atītānāgatavartamānasandarśanāni kevalamupādanapratyayarūpāṇi anātmakāni |
body.translated_text: How do dharmas such as the aggregates (skandha) and others arise? Because they operate through twelve junctures, the twelve links (nidāna) come into being. Therein, ignorance (avidyā) constitutes the defilements (kleśa). Formations (saṃskāra) constitute karma. Based on these two, there arise in succession: consciousness (vijñāna), name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana), contact (sparśa), and feeling (vedanā). The two dharmas called craving (tṛṣṇā) and clinging (upādāna) are defilements. Becoming (bhava) is karma. In the future course of time, the first consciousness of the appropriation of a body is called birth (jāti). The rest is aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa). These twelve links are indicators of past, future, and present — they are merely of the nature of appropriation and conditions, and are without self (anātmaka).

body.text: upapattimaraṇapunaḥ sandhinivṛtyarthakāni dvāviṃśatirindriyāṇyucyante | sarvasattvānāmādyaśarīrānubhavo vijñānamūlakaḥ | tadvijñānaṃ cakṣurādibhyaḥ ṣoḍhā samutpadyate iti ṣaḍindriyāṇyucyante yat cakṣurindriyaṃ yāvanmanaindriyamiti | ṣaḍvivajñānajanakatvādindriyāṇi ṣaḍeva | yena strīpuruṣalakṣaṇaṃ vikalpyate tat strīpuruṣendriyam | kecidvadanti- ayaṃ kāyendriyaikadeśa iti | tāni ṣaḍindriyāṇi kadācit ṣaḍāyatanānītyucyante | ebhyaḥ ṣaḍbhya utpadyamānaṃ ṣoḍhā vijñānaṃ jīvitamityucyate | kasmāt | imāni ṣaḍāyatanānīti ṣaḍvijñānānīti santānapravṛttiṃ labhanto ityato jīvitamityucyate | ata eṣāṃ jīvitamityākhyā | tatra kimindrim | yaducyate karma | karmahetutayā ṣaḍāyatanaṣaḍvijñānāni santānena pravartante | jīvite cāsmin karma jīvitendriyāmityākhyāyate | karmedaṃ vedanābhya utpadyate | vedanā eva sukhādīni pañcendriyāṇi | tebhyaḥ pañcendriyebhyaḥ kāmatṛṣṇādayaḥ sarve kleśāḥ kāyikavācikakarmāṇi ca prādurbhavanti | tatkarmapratyayaṃ punarjātimaraṇamupādīyate | ayaṃ saṃkleśadharmo jātimaraṇapratyayaṃ santānaṃ karoti |
body.translated_text: For the purpose of explaining birth, death, and the cessation of the continuity of rebirth, twenty-two faculties (indriya) are taught. The primordial experience of the body of all beings is rooted in consciousness. That consciousness arises in six ways from the eye and other [faculties] — therefore six faculties are taught, namely the eye-faculty (cakṣurindriya) up to the mind-faculty (manaindriya). Because they generate six kinds of cognition, the faculties are six alone. That by which the characteristics of female and male are distinguished is the female faculty (strīndriya) and male faculty (puruṣendriya). Some say: 'These are a portion of the body-faculty (kāyendriya).' Those six faculties are sometimes called the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana). The sixfold consciousness arising from these six is called the life-force (jīvita). Why? Because through these six sense-bases and the six kinds of consciousness, continuity proceeds — therefore it is called the life-force. Hence their designation as 'life.' Therein, what is the faculty? That which is called karma. Through karma as cause, the six sense-bases and six kinds of consciousness proceed in continuity. And in this life, karma is designated as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya). This karma arises from feelings (vedanā). The feelings themselves are the five faculties of pleasure and the rest. From these five faculties arise all defilements such as craving for sense-pleasures (kāmatṛṣṇā) and others, as well as bodily and verbal karmas. Conditioned by that karma, one again takes up birth and death. This is the dharma of affliction (saṃkleśadharma), which creates the continuity conditioned by birth and death.

body.text: kiṃpratyayaṃ vyavadānaṃ bhavati | niyamena śraddhādīnupādāya | śraddhādicaturdharmapratyayā prajñā bhavati | prajñā ca traikālikī yat anājñātamājñāsyāmi, ājñā, ājñātāvī ti | bhāvanāyāṃ kriyamāṇāyāṃ tānīndriyāṇi jñāna[rūpa]prajñāviśeṣabhūtāni | tathāgataḥ saṃsārasthitipravṛttinivṛttitryavadānārthakatvena dvāviṃśatīndriyāṇyavocat | evamādayo dharmā duḥkhasatyasaṅgṛhītāḥ | tatparijñātā duḥkhasatyajñānakuśala ityucyate |
body.translated_text: By what condition does purification (vyavadāna) arise? Necessarily by taking up faith (śraddhā) and the rest. Wisdom (prajñā) arises conditioned by the four dharmas beginning with faith. And wisdom is threefold in terms of the three times: 'I shall come to know what has not yet been known' (anājñātamājñāsyāmi), final knowledge (ājñā), and the possessor of final knowledge (ājñātāvin). When cultivation (bhāvanā) is practiced, those faculties become special forms of knowledge and wisdom. The <s>Tathāgata</s> taught the twenty-two faculties for the purpose of [explaining] the continuity of <s>saṃsāra</s>, its cessation, and the three aspects of purification. Such and similar <s>dharmas</s> are comprised within the truth of suffering (<s>duḥkhasatya</s>). One who has fully comprehended that is called skilled in the knowledge of the truth of suffering.

body.text: samudayasatyamiti | karma kleśāḥ | karma karmaskandhe vakṣyate | kleśāḥ kleśaskandhe | karmakleśāḥ pūnarbhavanidānatvātsamudayasatyamityākhyāyate |
body.translated_text: Regarding the truth of the origin (<s>samudayasatya</s>): [it comprises] <s>karma</s> and defilements (<s>kleśa</s>). <s>Karma</s> will be explained in the section on the aggregate of <s>karma</s> (<s>karmaskandha</s>). The defilements [will be explained] in the section on the aggregate of defilements (<s>kleśaskandha</s>). <s>Karma</s> and defilements are called the truth of the origin because they are the cause of further becoming (<s>punarbhava</s>).

body.text: nirodhasatyamiti | paścādvistareṇa nirodhaskandhe vakṣyate | yat prajñapticittaṃ dharmacittaṃ śūnyatācittamityeṣāṃ trayāṇāṃ cittānāṃ nirodho nirodhasatyamityucyate |
body.translated_text: Regarding the truth of cessation (<s>nirodhasatya</s>): this will be explained later in detail in the section on the aggregate of cessation (<s>nirodhaskandha</s>). The cessation of three kinds of mind — the designating mind (<s>prajñapticittam</s>), the <s>Dharma</s>-mind (<s>dharmacittam</s>), and the emptiness-mind (<s>śūnyatācittam</s>) — is called the truth of cessation.

body.text: mārgasatyamiti | yatsaptatriṃśadvodhipakṣikā dharmāḥ catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni catvāri pradhānāni catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ pañcendriyāṇi pañca balāni saptabodhyaṅgāni aṣṭāvāryamārgāṅgāni iti | catvāri samyak smṛtyupasthānāni iti | kāyavedanācittadharmeṣu samyak smṛtisthāpanam | smṛtiśca prajñā bhavati | kāyo 'nitya ityādi bhāvanayā tadālambane viharaṇaṃ kāyasmṛtyupasthānam | iyaṃ smṛtiḥ prajñayā saha kramaśo bhūyo vivṛddhā vedanāṃ vikalpayatīti vedanāsmṛtyupasthānam | bhūyaśca pariśuddhā cittaṃ vikalpayatīti cittasmṛtyupasthānam | samyak caryayā dharmān vikalpayatīti dharmasmṛtyupasthānam |
body.translated_text: Regarding the truth of the path (<s>mārgasatya</s>): the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (<s>saptatriṃśad bodhipakṣikā dharmāḥ</s>) are: the four foundations of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>), the four right efforts (<s>pradhāna</s>), the four bases of supernatural power (<s>ṛddhipāda</s>), the five faculties (<s>indriya</s>), the five powers (<s>bala</s>), the seven factors of awakening (<s>bodhyaṅga</s>), and the eight noble path-factors (<s>āryamārgāṅga</s>). The four right foundations of mindfulness: the proper establishment of mindfulness (<s>smṛti</s>) regarding body, feelings, mind, and <s>dharmas</s>. And mindfulness here is wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>). Contemplating 'the body is impermanent' and so forth, dwelling with that as one's object — this is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (<s>kāyasmṛtyupasthāna</s>). This mindfulness, gradually increasing together with wisdom, discriminates feelings — this is the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (<s>vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna</s>). Further purified, it discriminates the mind — this is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (<s>cittasmṛtyupasthāna</s>). Through right practice, it discriminates <s>dharmas</s> — this is the foundation of mindfulness of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>dharmasmṛtyupasthāna</s>).

body.text: catvāri samyak pradhānānīti | utpannānāṃ pāpakānāmakuśalānāṃ dharmāṇāmādīnavaṃ paśyan tatprahāṇāya chandaṃ janayati vīryamārabhate | tatprahāṇopāyo yat tatpratyayajñānadarśanapratyayaḥ | anutpannānāṃ pāpakānāmakuśalānāṃ dharmāṇāmanutpādāya chandaṃ janayati vīryamārabhate | anutpādopāyo yat jñānadarśanapratyayaḥ | anutpannānāṃ kuśalānāṃ dharmāṇāmutpādāya chandaṃ janayati
body.translated_text: The four right efforts (<s>samyak pradhāna</s>): seeing the danger in arisen evil and unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>, one generates the desire for their abandonment and arouses vigor. The means of their abandonment is the condition of the knowledge and vision of their causes. For the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>, one generates desire and arouses vigor. The means of non-arising is the condition of knowledge and vision. For the arising of unarisen wholesome <s>dharmas</s>, one generates desire —

body.text: vīryamārabhate | utpādopāyo yat jñānadarśanapratyayaḥ | utpannānāṃ kuśalānāṃ dharmaṇāṃ vaipulyāya chandaṃ janayati vīryamārabhate | uttamamadhyamādhamakrameṇopāyaḥ | avinivartanīyatvāt [tasya] |
body.translated_text: — and arouses vigor. The means of arising is the condition of knowledge and vision. For the increase of arisen wholesome <s>dharmas</s>, one generates desire and arouses vigor. The method proceeds in the order of superior, middling, and inferior. Because of its irreversibility.

body.text: catvāra ṛddhipādā iti | chandasamādhi saṃskārasamanvāgatarddhipādabhāvanā | chandamupādāyotpannaḥ samādhiścandasamādhiḥ | chandavīryaśraddhāpraśrabdhismṛtisamprajanyacetanopekṣādidharmasahagataḥ saṃskārasamanvāgato nāma | guṇānāṃ vivṛddhayarthatvena ṛddhipādaḥ | chandravivṛddhaye vīryakaraṇam | ayaṃ dvitīya [ṛddhipādaḥ] | yogī sacchandaḥ savīryaśca cittasamādhiṃ prajñāñca bhāvayati | cittasamādhipratilambha eva samādhirityucyate | mīmāṃsāsamādhireva prajñā |
body.translated_text: The four bases of supernatural power (<s>ṛddhipāda</s>): the cultivation of the base of supernatural power endowed with the <s>samādhi</s> of desire (<s>chanda</s>) and with volitional formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>). The <s>samādhi</s> arisen based on desire is called the <s>samādhi</s> of desire (<s>chandasamādhi</s>). 'Endowed with volitional formations' means accompanied by <s>dharmas</s> such as desire, vigor, faith, tranquility (<s>praśrabdhi</s>), mindfulness, clear comprehension (<s>samprajanya</s>), volition (<s>cetanā</s>), equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>), and so forth. Because it serves the purpose of the increase of virtuous qualities, it is a base of supernatural power. Making effort for the increase of desire — this is the second [base of supernatural power]. The <s>yogī</s>, possessed of desire and vigor, cultivates the <s>samādhi</s> of mind (<s>cittasamādhi</s>) and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>). The very attainment of the <s>samādhi</s> of mind is called <s>samādhi</s>. The <s>samādhi</s> of investigation (<s>mīmāṃsāsamādhi</s>) is wisdom itself.

body.text: pañcendriyāṇīti | dharmaśravaṇajā śraddhā śradvendriyam | saśraddhaḥ san saṃkleśadharmāṇāṃ prahāṇāya vyavadānadharmāṇāmadhigamāya ca vīryamārabhate | idaṃ vīryendriyam | caturṇāṃ smṛtyupasthānānāmabhyāsaḥ smṛtīndriyam | smṛtimupādāya samādhinirvartanaṃ samādhīndriyam | samādhimupādāya samutpannā prajñā prajñendriyam | imāni pañcendriyāṇi vivṛddhāni balavantīti pañcabalānītyucyante |
body.translated_text: The five faculties (<s>pañcendriya</s>): faith born from hearing the <s>Dharma</s> is the faith-faculty (<s>śraddhendriya</s>). Having faith, one arouses vigor for the abandonment of defiled <s>dharmas</s> and the attainment of purified <s>dharmas</s> — this is the vigor-faculty (<s>vīryendriya</s>). The practice of the four foundations of mindfulness is the mindfulness-faculty (<s>smṛtīndriya</s>). Based on mindfulness, the production of <s>samādhi</s> is the <s>samādhi</s>-faculty (<s>samādhīndriya</s>). Based on <s>samādhi</s>, the wisdom that arises is the wisdom-faculty (<s>prajñendriya</s>). These five faculties, when they have increased and become powerful, are called the five powers (<s>pañcabala</s>).

body.text: aṣṭāvāryamārgāṅgānīti | śrutamayaprajñaḥ śraddadhate pañcaskandhā anityā duḥkhā ityādi | iyaṃ samyak dṛṣṭiḥ | prajñeyaṃ yadi cintāmayī bhavati | tadā samyak saṅkalpaḥ | samyak saṅkalpenākuśalānāṃ prahāṇāya kuśalānāṃ karmaṇā bhāvanāyai ca yat vīryamācarati sa samyak vyāyāmaḥ | tataḥ krameṇa pravrajitaḥ śīlamupādāya samyagvācaṃ samyak karmāntaṃ samyagājīvañca trīṇi mārgāṅgānyanuprāpnoti | asmāt samyak saṃvarātkramaśaḥ smṛtyupasthānāni dhyānasamādhayaśca saṃsidhyanti | tāṃśca smṛtisamādhīnupādāya yathābhūtajñānamanuprāpnoti | ityevamāryāṣṭamārgāṅgānāṃ
body.translated_text: The eight noble path-factors (<s>āryamārgāṅga</s>): one with wisdom born of learning (<s>śrutamayaprajñā</s>) has faith that the five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) are impermanent, suffering, and so forth — this is right view (<s>samyak dṛṣṭi</s>). When this wisdom becomes born of reflection (<s>cintāmayī</s>), it is right intention (<s>samyak saṅkalpa</s>). The vigor one exerts through right intention for the abandonment of the unwholesome and for the cultivation of wholesome <s>karma</s> is right effort (<s>samyak vyāyāma</s>). Then, in due course, having gone forth as a renunciant and taken up moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), one attains the three path-factors of right speech (<s>samyagvāc</s>), right action (<s>samyak karmānta</s>), and right livelihood (<s>samyagājīva</s>). From this right restraint (<s>samyak saṃvara</s>), the foundations of mindfulness and <s>dhyāna</s>-<s>samādhis</s> are gradually accomplished. Based on those mindfulness and <s>samādhi</s> [practices], one attains knowledge of things as they truly are (<s>yathābhūtajñāna</s>). Thus is the sequence of the eight noble path-factors —

body.text: kramaḥ | atha mārgāṅgeṣu śīlaṃ prāthamikaṃ syāt | kasmāt | śīlasamādhiprajñāskandhānāmārthikakramatvāt | samyaksmṛtiḥ samyaksamādhiśca samādhiskandhaḥ | vyāyāmaḥ sarvatra samudācarati | prajñāskandho mārgapratyāsanna ityata ādāvuktaḥ | sā ca prajñā dvividhā audārikī sūkṣmā ceti | audārikīti yā śrutamayī cintāmayī ca prajñā | ayaṃ samyak saṅkalpa ityucyate | sūkṣmeti bhāvanāmayī prajñā yā ūṣmādidharmagatā prajñaptisatpañcaskandhān vidārayati | iyaṃ samyak dṛṣṭiḥ | anayā samyagdṛṣṭayā yaḥ pañcaskandhānāṃ nirodhaṃ paśyati | ayaṃ prathamābhisambuddha ityucyate | tadupādāya saptabodhyaṅgānyanuprāpnoti |
body.translated_text: — the sequence. Now, among the path-factors, moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>) should be primary. Why? Because the aggregates of moral conduct, concentration (<s>samādhi</s>), and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) follow a purposive sequence. Right mindfulness (<s>samyaksmṛti</s>) and right concentration (<s>samyaksamādhi</s>) constitute the aggregate of concentration. Effort (<s>vyāyāma</s>) operates everywhere. The aggregate of wisdom, being proximate to the path, is stated first. And that wisdom is twofold: coarse and subtle. 'Coarse' refers to wisdom born of learning (<s>śrutamayī</s>) and reflection (<s>cintāmayī</s>) — this is called right intention (<s>samyak saṅkalpa</s>). 'Subtle' refers to wisdom born of meditation (<s>bhāvanāmayī</s>), which, having entered into the <s>dharmas</s> of warmth (<s>ūṣma</s>) and the rest, pierces through the five aggregates as mere designations. This is right view (<s>samyak dṛṣṭi</s>). Through this right view, one who sees the cessation of the five aggregates is called 'one who has first awakened' (<s>prathamābhisambuddha</s>). Based on that, one attains the seven factors of awakening (<s>bodhyaṅga</s>).

body.text: smṛtisambodhyaṅgam- śaikṣaḥ puruṣaḥ smṛtipramoṣe kleśā uttiṣṭhantītyataḥ samyak smṛtyupasthānaṃ badhnāti | baddhasmṛtiḥ san pūrvāgamalabdhāṃ samyak dṛṣṭiṃ labhate | ayaṃ dharmapravicayaḥ | dharmapravicayāparityāgo vīryam | vīryamācarataḥ kleśānāṃ tanutve citte prītirjāyate | iayaṃ prītiḥ | prītyā kāyaḥ praśramyate | iyaṃ praśrabdhiḥ | praśrabdhyā sukhī bhavati | sukhitve cittaṃ samādhīyate | ayaṃ samādhiḥ durlabho vajropama ityākhyāyate | phale 'nāsajya prītidaurmanasyādīnāṃ prahāṇamupekṣā | iyamuttamā caryā | upekṣā ca nonmajjanaṃ nanimajjanaṃ, kintu tayościttasamatā | sambodhirnāmāśaikṣajñānam | imāni sapta bhāvayan sambodhiṃ labhata iti sambodhyaṅgamityucyate |
body.translated_text: The mindfulness factor of awakening (<s>smṛtisambodhyaṅga</s>): a learner (<s>śaikṣa</s>), [knowing that] defilements arise when mindfulness lapses, binds himself to the right foundation of mindfulness. Being bound in mindfulness, he obtains the right view previously gained through learning — this is the investigation of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>dharmapravicaya</s>). Not abandoning the investigation of <s>dharmas</s> is vigor (<s>vīrya</s>). For one who practices vigor, when defilements become weakened, joy (<s>prīti</s>) arises in the mind — this is joy. Through joy, the body becomes calm — this is tranquility (<s>praśrabdhi</s>). Through tranquility, one becomes happy. When happy, the mind becomes concentrated — this <s>samādhi</s> is said to be difficult to obtain, called 'vajra-like' (<s>vajropama</s>). Without clinging to the fruit, the abandonment of elation, dejection, and the like is equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>). This is the supreme practice. And equanimity is neither rising up nor sinking down, but rather the evenness of mind between the two. Awakening (<s>sambodhi</s>) is the knowledge of a non-learner (<s>aśaikṣajñāna</s>). One who cultivates these seven attains awakening — therefore they are called factors of awakening.

body.text: ebhiḥ saptatriṃśabdodhipakṣikaiścatvāri śrāmaṇyaphalāni labhate | srotaāpattiphalamiti yaḥ śūnyatābhi samayaḥ | anena śūnyatājñānena trīṇi saṃyojanāni prajahāti | sakṛdāgāmiphalamiti yat imameva mārgaṃ bhāvayan kleśān tanūkṛtya kāmadhātau sakṛdutpadyate | anāgāmiphalamiti kāmadhātukasarvakleśānāṃ prahāṇam | arhatphalamiti sarvakleśānāṃ prahāṇam | ya idaṃ tathāgatadharmaśāstramadhyeti sa catvāri satyāni abhisametya catvāri śrāmaṇyaphalāni pratilabhate | ata idaṃ tathāgataśāsanaśāstramabhyasitavyam ||
body.translated_text: Through these thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, one obtains the four fruits of the ascetic life (<s>śrāmaṇyaphala</s>). The fruit of stream-entry (<s>srotāpattiphala</s>) is the realization of emptiness (<s>śūnyatābhisamaya</s>). Through this knowledge of emptiness, one abandons the three fetters (<s>saṃyojana</s>). The fruit of once-returning (<s>sakṛdāgāmiphala</s>): cultivating this very path, one thins out the defilements and is reborn once in the desire-realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>). The fruit of non-returning (<s>anāgāmiphala</s>): the complete abandonment of all defilements pertaining to the desire-realm. The fruit of <s>Arhat</s>-ship (<s>arhatphala</s>): the complete abandonment of all defilements. One who takes up this treatise on the <s>Dharma</s> of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, having fully comprehended the Four Truths, obtains the four fruits of the ascetic life. Therefore this treatise on the teaching of the <s>Tathāgata</s> should be studied.

body.text: catussatyavargaḥ saptadaśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the seventeenth chapter, the Chapter on the Four Truths (<s>catussatyavarga</s>).

body.text: 18 dharmaskandhavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 18. Chapter on the Aggregates of <s>Dharmas</s> (<s>dharmaskandhavarga</s>)

body.text: athaitacchāsrābhyāsī jñeyādidharmaskandhānabhisameti | abhisamayāt tīrthikamithyāśāstrānabhibhūtaḥ kṣipraṃ kleśānupaśamayati | ātmano duḥkhaparihārakuśalaḥ parānapi trāyati |
body.translated_text: Now, one who studies this treatise comprehends the aggregates of <s>dharmas</s> beginning with the knowable (<s>jñeya</s>) and so forth. Through this comprehension, being unconquered by the false treatises of the <s>tīrthikas</s>, one quickly pacifies the defilements. Being skilled in the removal of one's own suffering, one also rescues others.

body.text: jñeyādidharmaskandha iti yaduta jñeyadharmā vijñeyadharmā rūpadharmā ārūpyadharmāḥ sanidarśanadharmā anidarśanadharmāḥ sapratighadharmā apratighadharmāḥ sāsravadharmā anāsravadharmāḥ saṃskṛta dharmā asaṃskṛtadharmāścittadharmā acittadharmāścaitasikadharmā acaitasikadharmāścittasaṃprayukta dharmāścittaviprayuktadharmāścittasahabhūdharmāścittāsahabhūdharmāścittānucaradharmāścittānanucaradharmā ādhyātmikadharmā bāhyadharmā audārikadharmāḥ sūkṣmadharmā uttamadharmā avaradharmāḥ sannikṛṣṭadharmā viprakṛṣṭadharmā upādānadharmā anupādānadharmā nairyāṇikadharmā anairyāṇikadharmāḥ prākṛtadharmā aprākṛtadharmāḥ samanantaradharmā asamanantaradharmāḥ kramikadharmā akramikadharmā ityevamādayo dvidhā dharmāḥ |
body.translated_text: The aggregates of <s>dharmas</s> beginning with the knowable are: knowable <s>dharmas</s> (<s>jñeya</s>) and to-be-known <s>dharmas</s> (<s>vijñeya</s>); form <s>dharmas</s> (<s>rūpa</s>) and formless <s>dharmas</s> (<s>ārūpya</s>); <s>dharmas</s> with indication (<s>sanidarśana</s>) and without indication (<s>anidarśana</s>); <s>dharmas</s> with resistance (<s>sapratigha</s>) and without resistance (<s>apratigha</s>); <s>dharmas</s> with outflows (<s>sāsrava</s>) and without outflows (<s>anāsrava</s>); conditioned <s>dharmas</s> (<s>saṃskṛta</s>) and unconditioned <s>dharmas</s> (<s>asaṃskṛta</s>); <s>dharmas</s> with mind (<s>citta</s>) and without mind (<s>acitta</s>); mental-factor <s>dharmas</s> (<s>caitasika</s>) and non-mental-factor <s>dharmas</s> (<s>acaitasika</s>); <s>dharmas</s> associated with mind (<s>cittasaṃprayukta</s>) and dissociated from mind (<s>cittaviprayukta</s>); <s>dharmas</s> co-existent with mind (<s>cittasahabhū</s>) and not co-existent with mind (<s>cittāsahabhū</s>); <s>dharmas</s> that follow mind (<s>cittānucara</s>) and that do not follow mind (<s>cittānānucara</s>); internal <s>dharmas</s> (<s>ādhyātmika</s>) and external <s>dharmas</s> (<s>bāhya</s>); coarse <s>dharmas</s> (<s>audārika</s>) and subtle <s>dharmas</s> (<s>sūkṣma</s>); superior <s>dharmas</s> (<s>uttama</s>) and inferior <s>dharmas</s> (<s>avara</s>); near <s>dharmas</s> (<s>sannikṛṣṭa</s>) and distant <s>dharmas</s> (<s>viprakṛṣṭa</s>); <s>dharmas</s> of clinging (<s>upādāna</s>) and without clinging (<s>anupādāna</s>); <s>dharmas</s> leading to emancipation (<s>nairyāṇika</s>) and not leading to emancipation (<s>anairyāṇika</s>); natural <s>dharmas</s> (<s>prākṛta</s>) and non-natural <s>dharmas</s> (<s>aprākṛta</s>); immediately successive <s>dharmas</s> (<s>samanantara</s>) and non-immediately successive <s>dharmas</s> (<s>asamanantara</s>); sequential <s>dharmas</s> (<s>kramika</s>) and non-sequential <s>dharmas</s> (<s>akramika</s>) — thus the <s>dharmas</s> are classified in twofold [pairs].

body.text: tridhā ca santi dharmāḥ- rūpadharmāścittadharmāścittaviprayuktadharmā iti | atītadharmā anāgatadharmāḥ pratyutpannadharmāḥ | kuśaladharmā akuśaladharmā avyākṛtadharmāḥ | śaikṣadharmā aśaikṣadharmā naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣadharmāḥ | satyadarśanaheyadharmā bhāvanāheyadharmā aheyadharmā ityevamādayastridhā dharmāḥ |
body.translated_text: Dharmas are of three kinds: form-dharmas, mind-dharmas, and dharmas disjoined from mind. Past dharmas, future dharmas, and present dharmas. Wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, and indeterminate dharmas. Dharmas of learners, dharmas of non-learners, and dharmas that are neither of learners nor of non-learners. Dharmas to be abandoned by truth-seeing, dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation, and dharmas not to be abandoned — thus and so forth are the threefold dharmas.

body.text: catuvirdhāśca santi dharmāḥ kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktadharmā rūpadhātupratisaṃyuktadharmā ārūpyadhātupratisaṃyuktadharmā apratisaṃyuktadharmā iti | catasraḥ pratipadaḥ duścarā duḥkhapratipat sucarā duḥkhapratipat duścarā sukhapratipat sucarā sukhapratipat iti | catvāra āsvādāḥ- pravrajyāsvādo visaṃyogāsvāda upaśamāsvādaḥ samyaksambodhāsvād iti | catvāraḥ sākṣātkṛtadharmāḥ- kāyasākṣātkṛtadharmāḥ smṛtisākṣātkṛtadharmā indriyasākṣātkṛtadharmāḥ prajñāsākṣātkṛtadharmā iti | catvāra upādānakāyāḥ catasro garbhāvakrāntayaḥ, catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ, catasraḥ śraddhāḥ, catvāri āryagotrāṇi, catvāri duścaritāni ityevamādayaścatvāro dharmāḥ |
body.translated_text: And dharmas are of four kinds: dharmas associated with the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>), dharmas associated with the form realm (<s>rūpadhātu</s>), dharmas associated with the formless realm (<s>ārūpyadhātu</s>), and unassociated dharmas. There are four practices (<s>pratipat</s>): difficult practice with painful progress, easy practice with painful progress, difficult practice with pleasant progress, and easy practice with pleasant progress. There are four relishes (<s>āsvāda</s>): the relish of going forth (<s>pravrajyāsvāda</s>), the relish of disengagement (<s>visaṃyogāsvāda</s>), the relish of tranquility (<s>upaśamāsvāda</s>), and the relish of perfect awakening (<s>samyaksambodhāsvāda</s>). There are four directly realized dharmas: dharmas directly realized through the body, dharmas directly realized through mindfulness, dharmas directly realized through the faculties, and dharmas directly realized through wisdom. There are four bodies of clinging (<s>upādānakāya</s>), four entries into the womb (<s>garbhāvakrānti</s>), four conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>), four kinds of faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), four noble lineages (<s>āryagotra</s>), and four kinds of misconduct (<s>duścarita</s>) — thus and so forth are the fourfold dharmas.

body.text: pañca skandhāḥ | ṣaḍ dhātavaḥ ṣaḍādhyātmikāyatanāni, ṣaḍ bāhyāyatanāni, ṣaḍ jātisvabhāvāḥ, ṣaḍ saumanasyopavicārā ṣaḍ daurmanasyopavicārā ṣaḍupekṣopavicārāḥ ṣaḍ sucaritāni | sapta viśuddhayaḥ | aṣṭa puṇyajanmāni | navānupūrvasamāpattayaḥ | daśāryāvāsāḥ | dvādaśa nidānāni | ityevamādayo dharmaskandhā apramāṇā anantā iti nāvasānaṃ vaktuṃ śakyate |
body.translated_text: Five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>). Six elements (<s>dhātu</s>), six internal sense-bases (<s>ādhyātmikāyatana</s>), six external sense-bases (<s>bāhyāyatana</s>), six natures of birth (<s>jātisvabhāva</s>), six investigations associated with mental pleasure (<s>saumanasyopavicāra</s>), six investigations associated with mental displeasure (<s>daurmanasyopavicāra</s>), six investigations associated with equanimity (<s>upekṣopavicāra</s>), and six kinds of good conduct (<s>sucarita</s>). Seven purifications (<s>viśuddhi</s>). Eight births of merit (<s>puṇyajanman</s>). Nine successive attainments (<s>anupūrvasamāpatti</s>). Ten noble abodes (<s>āryāvāsa</s>). Twelve links of dependent origination (<s>nidāna</s>). Thus and so forth, the heaps of dharmas (<s>dharmaskandha</s>) are immeasurable and infinite — it is impossible to state their end.

body.text: teṣu prādhānyataḥ saṃkṣipāmi | jñeyadharma iti pāramārthikaṃ satyam | vijñeyadharma iti yat laukikaṃ satyam | rūpadharmā iti rūparasagandhasparśāḥ | arūpadharmā iti cittāsaṃskṛtadharmāḥ | sanidarśanadharmā iti yāni rūpāyatanāni sapratidhadharmā iti rūpadharmāḥ | sāsravadharmā iti ya āsravāṇāmutpādakā yathā anarhatāṃ prajñaptidharmeṣu cittam | tadviparītā anāsravadharmāḥ | saṃskṛtadharmā iti pratītyasamutpannāḥ pañca skandhāḥ | asaṃskṛtadharmā iti pañcaskandhānāṃ nirodho 'yam | cittadharmā iti ālambakaṃ cittam | caitasikadharmā iti yadvijñānamālambate tatsamanantarajātāḥ saṃjñādayaḥ | cittasaṃprayuktadharmā iti yadvijñānamālambate tatsamanantarajātam | yathā saṃjñādayaḥ | cittasahabhūdharmā iti ye dharmāścittena sahabhuvaḥ | yathā rūpaṃ cittaviprayuktaṃ gocarībhavati | cittānucaradharmā iti ye dharmāścitte sati utpadyante nāsati yathā kāyavāgbhyāmakṛtaṃ karma | ādhyātmikadharmā iti svakāyasyāntaḥsthitāni ṣaḍāyatanāni | audārikasūkṣmadharmā iti parasparamapekṣyabhāvinaḥ | yathā pañca kāmānapekṣya rūpadhyānaṃ sūkṣmam | ārūpyadhyānamapekṣya rūpadhyānamaudārikam | uttamāvaradharmā apyevam | sannikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭadharmā iti keciddeśabhedādviprakṛṣṭāḥ | kecidasārūpyādviprakṛṣṭāḥ | upādānadharmā iti kāyikādharmāḥ | nairyāṇikadharmā iti ye kuśaladharmā | prākṛtadharmā iti sāsravadharmāḥ | samanantara dharmā iti anyasmāt samanantarajātāḥ | kramikadharmā iti [ye] kramajanakāḥ |
body.translated_text: Among them I shall summarize according to primacy. 'Knowable dharma' (<s>jñeyadharma</s>) refers to ultimate truth (<s>pāramārthikasatya</s>). 'To be cognized' (<s>vijñeyadharma</s>) refers to conventional truth (<s>laukikasatya</s>). 'Form-dharmas' are form, taste, smell, and touch. 'Formless dharmas' are mind and unconditioned dharmas. 'Visible dharmas' (<s>sanidarśanadharma</s>) are the objects of the form sense-base (<s>rūpāyatana</s>). 'Resistant dharmas' (<s>sapratidhadharma</s>) are form-dharmas. 'Dharmas with outflows' (<s>sāsravadharma</s>) are those that produce outflows — such as the consciousness directed toward designated dharmas in those who are not <s>Arhats</s>. The opposite of these are 'dharmas without outflows' (<s>anāsravadharma</s>). 'Conditioned dharmas' (<s>saṃskṛtadharma</s>) are the five aggregates arisen through dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>). 'Unconditioned dharmas' (<s>asaṃskṛtadharma</s>) are the cessation of the five aggregates. 'Mind-dharmas' (<s>cittadharma</s>) are the mind that apprehends an object. 'Mental-factor dharmas' (<s>caitasikadharma</s>) are perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>) and so forth that arise immediately together with what consciousness apprehends. 'Dharmas associated with mind' (<s>cittasaṃprayuktadharma</s>) are those that arise immediately together with what consciousness apprehends — such as perception and the rest. 'Dharmas co-existent with mind' (<s>cittasahabhūdharma</s>) are dharmas that arise together with mind — for instance, form disjoined from mind becomes an object of mind. 'Dharmas that follow mind' (<s>cittānucaradharma</s>) are dharmas that arise when mind is present and do not arise when it is absent — such as karma not enacted through body and speech. 'Internal dharmas' (<s>ādhyātmikadharma</s>) are the six sense-bases situated within one's own body. 'Gross and subtle dharmas' are relative to each other — for instance, the form-realm <s>dhyāna</s> is subtle in comparison with the five sense pleasures, while the form-realm <s>dhyāna</s> is gross in comparison with the formless-realm <s>dhyāna</s>. 'Superior and inferior dharmas' are likewise. 'Proximate and remote dharmas' — some are remote due to spatial distinction, others are remote due to dissimilarity. 'Dharmas of clinging' (<s>upādānadharma</s>) are bodily dharmas. 'Dharmas leading to deliverance' (<s>nairyāṇikadharma</s>) are wholesome dharmas. 'Ordinary dharmas' (<s>prākṛtadharma</s>) are dharmas with outflows. 'Immediately succeeding dharmas' are those arising immediately after another. 'Sequential dharmas' (<s>kramikadharma</s>) are those that produce effects in sequence.

body.text: rūpadharmā iti rūpādayaḥ pañcadharmāḥ | cittadharmā iti yathopariṣṭāduktāḥ | cittaviprayuktadharmā iti avijñaptikarma | atītadharmā iti niruddhā dharmāḥ | anāgatadharmā iti utpatsyamānā dharmāḥ | pratyutpannadharmā iti uptadyamānā aniruddhāśca dharmāḥ | kuśaladharmā iti parasattvānāṃ hitakṛddharmāḥ padārthābhisambodhaśca | tadvaparītā akuśaladharmāḥ | ubhābhyāṃ viruddhā avyākṛtadharmāḥ | śaikṣadharmā iti śaikṣāṇāmanāsravacittadharmāḥ | aśaikṣadharmā iti aśaikṣāṇāṃ paramārthagataṃ cittam | anye naivaśaikṣānāśaikṣā dharmāḥ | satyadarśanaheyadharmā iti yat
body.translated_text: 'Form-dharmas' are the five dharmas of form and so forth. 'Mind-dharmas' are as stated above. 'Dharmas disjoined from mind' are non-informative karma (<s>avijñaptikarma</s>). 'Past dharmas' are dharmas that have ceased. 'Future dharmas' are dharmas that will arise. 'Present dharmas' are dharmas that are arising and have not yet ceased. 'Wholesome dharmas' are dharmas that bring benefit to other beings and the comprehension of the true meaning of things. The opposite of these are 'unwholesome dharmas.' Those opposed to both are 'indeterminate dharmas' (<s>avyākṛta</s>). 'Dharmas of the learner' (<s>śaikṣadharma</s>) are the undefiled mind-dharmas of learners. 'Dharmas of the non-learner' (<s>aśaikṣadharma</s>) are the mind that has reached the ultimate in those who are non-learners. Others are 'dharmas neither of learners nor non-learners.' 'Dharmas to be abandoned by truth-seeing' are those

body.text: srotaāpannānāṃ heyā nimittasandarśanāsmimānatajjā dharmāḥ | bhāvanāheyadharmā iti yat srotaāpannasakṛdāgāmyanāgāmināṃ heyā animittasandarśanāsmimānatajjā dharmāḥ | aheyadharmā iti ye 'nāsravāḥ |
body.translated_text: dharmas to be abandoned by stream-enterers (<s>srotāpanna</s>) — namely, the dharmas born from the views of signs (<s>nimitta</s>), the false perception of 'I am' (<s>asmimāna</s>), and related defilements. 'Dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation' (<s>bhāvanāheyadharma</s>) are those dharmas to be abandoned by stream-enterers, once-returners (<s>sakṛdāgāmin</s>), and non-returners (<s>anāgāmin</s>) — namely, the dharmas born from the signless perception, the false perception of 'I am,' and related defilements. 'Dharmas not to be abandoned' are those that are undefiled (<s>anāsrava</s>).

body.text: kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktadharmā iti ye dharmā vipākalabdhā avīcinarakāt yāvatparanirmitavaśavartino devān | rūpadhātupratisaṃyuktadharmā iti ābrahmalokāt ācākaniṣṭhadevebhyaḥ | ārūpyadhātupratisaṃyuktadharmā iti catvāryārūpyāṇi | apratisaṃyuktadharmā iti anāsravadharmāḥ | duścarā duḥkhapratipat iti mṛdvindriyasya samādhiṃ labdhvā mārgacāriṇaḥ | sucarā duḥkhapratipat iti tīkṣṇendriyasya samādhiṃ labdhvā mārgacāriṇaḥ | duścarā sukhapratipat iti mṛdvindriyasya prajñāṃ labdhvā mārgacāriṇaḥ | sucarā sukhapratipat iti tīkṣṇendriyasya prajñāṃ labdhvā mārgacāriṇaḥ || pravrajyāsvāda iti gṛhātpravrajya mārgaparyeṣaṇam | visaṃyogāsvāda iti kāyacittapravivekaḥ | upaśamāsvāda iti dhyānasamādhipratilambhaḥ | samyaksambodhāsvāda iti catussatyābhisamayaḥ || smṛtisākṣātkṛtadharmā iti catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni | tānyupādāya catvāri dhyānānyutpadyante | caturṇāṃ satyānāmabhisamayaḥ prajñāsākṣātkṛta ityucyate | catvāra upādānakāyā iti kaścidātmānaṃ hinasti na parān || kaścitparān hinasti nātmānam | kaścidātmanaṃ hinasti parāṃśca hinasti | kaścinnātmānaṃ hinasti na parān | catasro garbhāvakrāntaya iti kaścidasamprajānanneva mātuḥ kukṣāvavatarati | asamprajānaṃśca [mātuḥkukṣau]tiṣṭhati | asamprajānaṃśca mātuḥkukṣerniṣkramati | kaścitsamprajānan mātuḥ kukṣāvavatarati | asaṃprajānan mātuḥ kukṣau tiṣṭhati | asamprajānan mātuḥ kukṣerniṣkramati | kaścitsamprajānan mātuḥ kukṣāvavatarati | samprajānān mātuḥ kukṣau tiṣṭhati | samprajānan mātuḥ kukṣerniṣkramati viparyastamativikṣepānnātmānaṃ samprajānāti | cittārjavenāvikṣepādātmānaṃ samprajānāti || catvāraḥ pratyayā iti hetupratyayo yo janakahetuḥ vāsanāheturāśrayahetuḥ | janakahetu yo dharmo jāyamānasya hetukṛtyaṃ karoti | yathā vipākātmakaṃ karma | vāsanāhetuḥ kāmarāgavāsanāyāṃ kāmarāgo 'bhivardhate | āśrayahetuḥ yathā cittacaittānāṃ rūpagandhādaya āśrayāḥ | ime hetupratyayā ityucyante | samanantarapratyaya iti yathā pūrvacittanirodhātsamanantaracittamutpadyate | ālambanapratyaya iti yadālambya dharma utpadyate | yathā
body.translated_text: 'Dharmas associated with the desire realm' are dharmas obtained through the ripening of karma, from <s>Avīci</s> hell up to the <s>Paranirmitavaśavartin</s> gods. 'Dharmas associated with the form realm' are those from <s>Brahmaloka</s> up to the <s>Akaniṣṭha</s> gods. 'Dharmas associated with the formless realm' are the four formless attainments. 'Unassociated dharmas' are the undefiled dharmas. 'Difficult practice with painful progress' means one of dull faculties who, having attained <s>samādhi</s>, practices the path. 'Easy practice with painful progress' means one of sharp faculties who, having attained <s>samādhi</s>, practices the path. 'Difficult practice with pleasant progress' means one of dull faculties who, having attained wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), practices the path. 'Easy practice with pleasant progress' means one of sharp faculties who, having attained wisdom, practices the path. 'The relish of going forth' means leaving the household life and seeking the path. 'The relish of disengagement' means the seclusion of body and mind. 'The relish of tranquility' means the attainment of <s>dhyānas</s> and <s>samādhis</s>. 'The relish of perfect awakening' means the realization of the four truths (<s>catussatyābhisamaya</s>). 'Dharmas directly realized through mindfulness' are the four foundations of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>). On the basis of these, the four <s>dhyānas</s> arise. The realization of the four truths is called 'directly realized through wisdom.' The four bodies of clinging: a certain one harms himself but not others; a certain one harms others but not himself; a certain one harms both himself and others; a certain one harms neither himself nor others. The four entries into the womb: a certain one enters the mother's womb without awareness, abides in the mother's womb without awareness, and emerges from the mother's womb without awareness. A certain one enters the mother's womb with awareness, abides in the mother's womb without awareness, and emerges from the mother's womb without awareness. A certain one enters the mother's womb with awareness, abides in the mother's womb with awareness, and emerges from the mother's womb with awareness. Due to distracted mind with perverted understanding, one does not comprehend oneself; through straightforwardness of mind without distraction, one comprehends oneself. The four conditions: the causal condition (<s>hetupratyaya</s>) is the generative cause (<s>janakahetu</s>), the habitual cause (<s>vāsanāhetu</s>), and the support cause (<s>āśrayahetu</s>). The generative cause is the dharma that performs the function of cause for that which is being born — as for instance, karma that has the nature of ripening (<s>vipāka</s>). The habitual cause: through the habituation of desire-passion, desire-passion increases. The support cause: for instance, form, smell, and so forth are supports for mind and mental factors. These are called causal conditions. The immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>): as when, from the cessation of the preceding mind, the immediately succeeding mind arises. The object condition (<s>ālambanapratyaya</s>): the dharma that arises depending on an object — as

body.text: cakṣurvijñānasya janakaṃ rūpam | adhipatipratyaya iti yajjāyamānasya dharmasyānye pratyayāḥ || catasraḥ śraddhā iti | (1) tathāgataśraddhā yat tattvajñānaṃ labdhā tathāgate prasannacitto niścinoti tathāgataḥ sattveṣu śreṣṭha iti | (2) asmin tattvajñāne śraddhaiva dharmaśraddhā | (3) etattattvajñānalābhī sarvasaṅgheṣu paramottama itīyaṃ saṅghaśraddhā | (4) āryāṇāṃ priyaṃ saṃvaraṃ labdhvā adhyāśayenāpi nāhamakuśalāni karomi ahamimaṃ saṃvaramupādāya triṣu ratneṣu ca śraddhāvāniti ca prajānāti iti yadiyaṃ śraddhā saṃvarabalāditi saṃvaraśraddhetyucyate || caturāryagotratvāt na cīvarārthatṛṣṇayā kliśyate | nānnapānaśayanāsanārthaṃ kāyikatṛṣṇayā kliśyate | iti catvāryāryagotrāṇi || catvāri duścaritānīti | rāgadveṣamohasantrāsairdurgatau patati |
body.translated_text: form is the generator of visual consciousness. The dominant condition (<s>adhipatipratyaya</s>) is the other conditions for the dharma that is arising. The four kinds of faith: (1) Faith in the <s>Tathāgata</s> — having obtained the knowledge of reality, with a mind well-disposed toward the <s>Tathāgata</s>, one ascertains: 'The <s>Tathāgata</s> is the highest among beings.' (2) Having faith in this knowledge of reality itself is faith in the <s>Dharma</s>. (3) 'One who obtains this knowledge of reality is the supreme among all <s>Saṅghas</s>' — this is faith in the <s>Saṅgha</s>. (4) Having obtained the restraint (<s>saṃvara</s>) dear to the noble ones, with sincere intention one resolves: 'I shall not do unwholesome deeds; relying on this restraint, I have faith in the Three Jewels' — knowing this, this faith, arising from the power of restraint, is called faith in restraint (<s>saṃvaraśraddhā</s>). Because of possessing the four noble lineages, one is not afflicted by craving for robes, nor afflicted by bodily craving for food, drink, bedding, and seats — thus there are four noble lineages. The four kinds of misconduct: through passion (<s>rāga</s>), hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>), delusion (<s>moha</s>), and fear (<s>santrāsa</s>), one falls into a lower realm.

body.text: rūpaskandha iti rūpādayaḥ pañca | vedanāskandha iti ālambakadharmāḥ | saṃjñāskandha iti prajñaptivikalpā dharmāḥ | saṃskāraskandha iti punarbhavajanakā dharmāḥ | vijñānaskandha iti viṣayamātravijñānadharmāḥ || pṛthivīdhāturiti rūpasagandhasparśasamavāyaḥ khaṭkalakṣaṇabahulaḥ pṛthivīdhāturiti vyapadiśyate | snehabahulo 'bdhātuḥ | uṣṇalakṣaṇabahulastejodhātuḥ | laghimalakṣaṇabahulo vāyudhātuḥ | rūpalakṣaṇavirahita ākāśadhātuḥ | ālambamāno dharmo vijñānadhātuḥ | cakṣurāyatanamiti cāturmautikaṃ cakṣurvijñānāśrayaścakṣurdhāturityucyate | śrotraghrāṇajihvākāyāyatanānyapyevam | mana āyatanamiti yaduta cittam || rūpāyatanamiti cakṣurvijñānasyālambyadharmaḥ | tathā śabdagandharasaspṛṣṭavyā api || ṣaḍ jātisvabhāvā iti yat kṛṣṇasvabhāvaḥ puruṣaḥ kṛṣṇaṃ dharmaṃ niṣevate | śuklaṃ dharmaṃ kṛṣṇaśuklaṃ dharmañca niṣevate | tathā śuklasvabhāvaḥ puruṣo 'pi || ṣaṭ saumanasyopavicārā iti rāgacittāśritāḥ || ṣaḍ daurmanasyopavicārā iti dveṣacittāśritāḥ | ṣaḍupekṣopavicārā iti mohacittāśritāḥ | ṣaṭ sucaritānīti tattvajñānāśritāni |
body.translated_text: The form aggregate (<s>rūpaskandha</s>) consists of the five dharmas beginning with form. The feeling aggregate (<s>vedanāskandha</s>) consists of dharmas that apprehend objects. The perception aggregate (<s>saṃjñāskandha</s>) consists of dharmas that conceptually designate. The formations aggregate (<s>saṃskāraskandha</s>) consists of dharmas that generate renewed existence. The consciousness aggregate (<s>vijñānaskandha</s>) consists of dharmas that cognize mere objects. The earth element (<s>pṛthivīdhātu</s>): the combination of form, smell, and touch, predominantly characterized by hardness, is designated as the earth element. That which is predominantly moist is the water element (<s>abdhātu</s>). That which is predominantly characterized by heat is the fire element (<s>tejodhātu</s>). That which is predominantly characterized by lightness is the wind element (<s>vāyudhātu</s>). That which is devoid of the characteristic of form is the space element (<s>ākāśadhātu</s>). The dharma that apprehends an object is the consciousness element (<s>vijñānadhātu</s>). The eye sense-base (<s>cakṣurāyatana</s>): consisting of the four great elements, the support of visual consciousness, is called the eye element. The ear, nose, tongue, and body sense-bases are likewise. The mind sense-base (<s>mana āyatana</s>) is mind (<s>citta</s>). The form sense-base (<s>rūpāyatana</s>) is the dharma that is the object of visual consciousness. Likewise sound, smell, taste, and tangibles. The six natures of birth: a person of dark nature pursues dark dharmas, or pursues bright dharmas, or pursues mixed dark-and-bright dharmas. Likewise a person of bright nature. The six investigations associated with mental pleasure are those dependent on a mind of passion. The six investigations associated with displeasure are those dependent on a mind of hatred. The six investigations associated with equanimity are those dependent on a mind of delusion. The six kinds of good conduct are those dependent on the knowledge of reality.

body.text: sapta viśuddha yaḥ | śīlaviśuddhiriti śīlasaṃvaraṇam | cittaviśuddhiriti dhyānasamādhīnāmupasampat | dṛṣṭiviśuddhiriti satkāyadṛṣṭisamucchedaḥ | kāṅkṣāvitaraṇaviśuddhiriti |
body.translated_text: The seven purifications (<s>viśuddhi</s>): purification of moral conduct (<s>śīlaviśuddhi</s>) is the restraint of moral conduct. Purification of mind (<s>cittaviśuddhi</s>) is the attainment of <s>dhyānas</s> and <s>samādhis</s>. Purification of views (<s>dṛṣṭiviśuddhi</s>) is the eradication of the view of the personal self (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>). Purification by overcoming doubt (<s>kāṅkṣāvitaraṇaviśuddhi</s>) is

body.text: kāṅkṣāsaṃyojanasamucchedaḥ | mārgāmārgajñānadarśanaviśuddhiriti | śīlavrataparāmarśasamucchedaḥ | pratipadājñānadarśanaviśuddhiriti bhāvanāmārgaḥ | jñānadarśanaviśuddhiriti aśaikṣamārgaḥ |
body.translated_text: the eradication of the fetter of doubt (<s>kāṅkṣāsaṃyojana</s>). Purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (<s>mārgāmārgajñānadarśanaviśuddhi</s>) is the eradication of clinging to rites and vows (<s>śīlavrataparāmarśa</s>). Purification by knowledge and vision of the way of practice (<s>pratipadājñānadarśanaviśuddhi</s>) is the path of cultivation (<s>bhāvanāmārga</s>). Purification by knowledge and vision (<s>jñānadarśanaviśuddhi</s>) is the path of the non-learner (<s>aśaikṣamārga</s>).

body.text: aṣṭau puṇya sargā iti manuṣyeṣvāḍhya ābrahmalokāt | puṇyavipākasukhanāmeṣu atibahulatvāt ime 'ṣṭāvucyante ||
body.translated_text: The eight births of merit (<s>puṇyasarga</s>): among humans, the wealthy, and up to <s>Brahmaloka</s>. Because the happiness resulting from the ripening of merit is exceedingly abundant in these, they are called the eight births of merit.

body.text: navānupūrvasamāpattaya iti prathamadhyānamupasampadyamāno vācaṃ niyacchati | dvitīyadhyānamupasampadyamāno vitarkavicārān | tṛtīyadhyānamupasaṃpadyamānaḥ prītim | caturthadhyāne ānāpānam | ākāśānantyāyatane rūpalakṣaṇam | vijñānānantyāyatana ākāśalakṣaṇam | ākiñcanyāyatane vijñānalakṣaṇam | naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana ākiñcanyāyatanalakṣaṇam | nirodhasamāpattimupasampadyamānaḥ saṃjñāveditaṃ niyacchatiḥ ||
body.translated_text: The nine successive attainments (<s>navānupūrvasamāpatti</s>) are: when entering the first <s>dhyāna</s>, one restrains speech; when entering the second <s>dhyāna</s>, one restrains discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>) and investigation (<s>vicāra</s>); when entering the third <s>dhyāna</s>, one restrains joy (<s>prīti</s>); in the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>, one restrains breathing (<s>ānāpāna</s>); in the base of infinite space (<s>ākāśānantyāyatana</s>), one restrains the mark of form; in the base of infinite consciousness (<s>vijñānānantyāyatana</s>), one restrains the mark of space; in the base of nothingness (<s>ākiñcanyāyatana</s>), one restrains the mark of consciousness; in the base of neither perception nor non-perception (<s>naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana</s>), one restrains the mark of the base of nothingness; when entering the cessation attainment (<s>nirodhasamāpatti</s>), one restrains perception and feeling (<s>saṃjñāvedita</s>).

body.text: daśāryāvāsā iti | āryaḥ pudgalaḥ (1) pañcāṅgaviprahīno bhavati | (2) ṣaḍaṅgasamanvāgataḥ | (3) ekārakṣaḥ | (4) caturapāśrayaḥ | (5) praṇunnapratyekasatyaḥ | (6) samavasṛṣṭeṣaṇaḥ | (7) anāvilasaṅkalpaḥ | (8) praśrabdhakāyasaṃskāraḥ | (9) suviviktacittaḥ | (10) suvimuktaprajñaḥ kṛtakṛtyaḥ san kevalo 'sahāyī bhavati | (1) pañcāṅgaviprahīno bhavatīti | ūrdhvabhāgīyāni pañcasaṃyojanāni prahāya sarvasaṃyojanakṣayarūpārhatvalābhī bhavati | (2) ṣaḍaṅgasamanvāgata iti | yataścakṣurādibhiḥ rūpādi dṛṣṭvā naivā sumanā bhavati na durmanā upekṣako viharati smṛtaḥ saṃprajānan | (3) ekārakṣa iti | smṛtyārakṣeṇa cetasā samanvāgato bhavati | (4) caturapāśraya iti | bhikṣādīṃścaturo dharmānāśrayate | kecitpunarāhuḥ- caturapāśraya iti ārya [ekaṃ] dharmaṃ parivarjayati | [ekaṃ]
body.translated_text: The ten abodes of the Noble Ones (<s>daśāryāvāsa</s>) are: A Noble person (<s>ārya pudgala</s>) (1) is free from five limbs (<s>pañcāṅgaviprahīna</s>); (2) is endowed with six limbs (<s>ṣaḍaṅgasamanvāgata</s>); (3) has one guard (<s>ekārakṣa</s>); (4) relies on four supports (<s>caturapāśraya</s>); (5) has dispelled individual truths (<s>praṇunnapratyekasatya</s>); (6) has completely abandoned the three quests (<s>samavasṛṣṭeṣaṇa</s>); (7) has unturbid intentions (<s>anāvilasaṅkalpa</s>); (8) has tranquilized bodily formations (<s>praśrabdhakāyasaṃskāra</s>); (9) has a well-secluded mind (<s>suviviktacitta</s>); (10) has well-liberated wisdom (<s>suvimuktaprajña</s>), having accomplished what was to be done (<s>kṛtakṛtya</s>), he dwells alone without a companion. (1) 'Free from five limbs' means: having abandoned the five higher fetters (<s>ūrdhvabhāgīyasaṃyojana</s>), through the destruction of all fetters, he attains <s>Arhat</s>-ship. (2) 'Endowed with six limbs' means: having seen form and other objects through the eye and other senses, he is neither pleased nor displeased, but dwells in equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>), mindful and fully aware. (3) 'One guard' means: he is endowed with mindfulness as his guard of mind. (4) 'Four supports' means: he relies on the four <s>dharmas</s> beginning with alms-food. Some further say: 'Four supports' means the Noble One avoids one <s>dharma</s>, [follows] one

body.text: dharma pratisevate | ekaṃ dharmaṃ vinodayati | ekaṃ dharmamadhivāsayati || (5) viśuddhaśīladhāraṇāt tattvalakṣaṇaṃ pratibudhyan praṇunnapratyekasatya ityucyate | samucchinnasarvadṛṣṭika ādyaphalasya lābhī bhavati | (6) samavasṛṣṭeṣaṇa iti kāmeṣaṇā [prahīṇā] bhavati | bhaveṣaṇā prahīṇā bhavati | brahmacaryeṣaṇā pratipraśrabdhā | ādyaphalalābhitvāt prajānāti saṃskṛtadharmā mṛṣeti | īṣaṇātrayaprahāṇaṃ vajropamasamādhiṃ lapsya itīcchayā śaikṣamārgaṃ prajahāti | tadā kṣayakuśalaḥ samasṛṣṭeṣaṇā ityucyate | (7) anāvilasaṅkalpa iti | prahīṇaṣaḍvitarkaḥ viśuddhacittastrīṇi viṣāṇi tanūkṛtya dvitīyaphalaṃ labhate | praśamitakāmaśokaḥ san tṛtīyaphalamanuprāpnuvan anāvilasaṅkalpa ityucyate | (8) praśrabdhakāyasaṃskāra iti | kāmadhātukasaṃyojanāni vihāya catvāri dhyānānyupasampadya viharatītyataḥ praśrabdhakāyasaṃskāro bhavati | kṣayajñānalābhā (9) tsuviviktacitto bhavati ityucyate | anutpādajñānalābhāt (10) suvimuktaprajñobhavati | āryāṇāṃ cittameṣu daśasu sthāneṣu āvasatīti āryāvāsaḥ | kṛtatathāgatadharmo 'vaśyaṃ duḥkhasyāntaṃ kuryādityataḥ kṛtakṛtya iti kathyate | pṛthagjanaiḥ śaikṣajanaiśca vivikta ityato 'sahāyīti | taccitaṃ sarvadharmān vidhūya atyantaśūnyatāpratiṣṭhitamityataḥ kevala ityākhyāyate ||
body.translated_text: <s>dharma</s>, pursues one <s>dharma</s>, dispels one <s>dharma</s>, and endures one <s>dharma</s>. (5) Through the maintenance of purified moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), awakening to the mark of reality, he is called 'one who has dispelled individual truths' — having cut off all views, he obtains the first fruit. (6) 'One who has completely abandoned the quests' (<s>samavasṛṣṭeṣaṇa</s>) means: the quest for sensual pleasures (<s>kāmeṣaṇā</s>) is abandoned; the quest for existence (<s>bhaveṣaṇā</s>) is abandoned; the quest for the holy life (<s>brahmacaryeṣaṇā</s>) is allayed. Because of having obtained the first fruit, he understands that conditioned <s>dharmas</s> are false. Wishing to attain the <s>vajropamasamādhi</s> (diamond-like concentration) through the abandonment of the three quests, he relinquishes the path of the learner (<s>śaikṣamārga</s>). Then, being skilled in destruction, he is called 'one who has completely abandoned the quests.' (7) 'Unturbid intentions' means: having abandoned the six kinds of discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>), with purified mind, having thinned the three poisons, he obtains the second fruit. Having pacified sensual desire and grief, upon attaining the third fruit, he is called 'one of unturbid intentions.' (8) 'Tranquilized bodily formations' means: having abandoned the fetters belonging to the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>), he enters and abides in the four <s>dhyānas</s> — therefore his bodily formations are tranquilized. (9) Through the attainment of the knowledge of destruction (<s>kṣayajñāna</s>), he is said to have a well-secluded mind. (10) Through the attainment of the knowledge of non-arising (<s>anutpādajñāna</s>), he has well-liberated wisdom. The mind of the Noble Ones dwells in these ten stations, therefore they are called 'abodes of the Noble Ones' (<s>āryāvāsa</s>). One who has accomplished the <s>Dharma</s> of the <s>Tathāgata</s> will certainly make an end of suffering — therefore he is called 'one who has accomplished what was to be done' (<s>kṛtakṛtya</s>). Being separate from ordinary beings and learners, he is called 'without a companion.' His mind, having dispelled all <s>dharmas</s>, is established in ultimate emptiness (<s>atyantaśūnyatā</s>) — therefore he is called 'alone' (<s>kevala</s>).

body.text: dvādaśanidānāni | tatrāvidyeti yat prajñaptyanuyāyicittam | tadviparyayacittamupādāya karmāṇi sañcinotīti avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārā ityucyante | vijñānaṃ karmānuyāyi iti satkāyamupādatte | ataḥ saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam iti | satkāyamupādāya nāmarūpaṣaḍāyatanasparśavedanā bhavanti | imāni aṅgāni kālakrameṇa vardhante | sarvā api vedanā anubhavan prajñaptimāśrayate ityatastatra tṛṣṇāṃ janayati | tṛṣṇāmupādāyānye kleśā bhavantīti ta upādānamityucyante | tṛṣṇopādānapratyayo bhavaḥ | sa ca trikāṇḍaḥ | ebhyaḥ karmakleśapratyayebhya aurdhvakālikī jātiḥ | jātipratyayājjarāmaraṇādayo bhavanti |
body.translated_text: The twelve links of dependent origination (<s>dvādaśanidāna</s>): Therein, 'ignorance' (<s>avidyā</s>) is the mind that follows conventional designations. Based on that deluded mind, one accumulates <s>karmas</s> — therefore it is said: 'Conditioned by ignorance, formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) arise.' Consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), following <s>karma</s>, takes up a body — therefore 'conditioned by formations, consciousness arises.' Having taken up a body, name-and-form (<s>nāmarūpa</s>), the six sense-bases (<s>ṣaḍāyatana</s>), contact (<s>sparśa</s>), and feeling (<s>vedanā</s>) come into being. These limbs grow in temporal sequence. Experiencing all feelings, one relies on designations, and thereby generates craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>). Based on craving, other defilements arise — these are called clinging (<s>upādāna</s>). Conditioned by craving and clinging, there is becoming (<s>bhava</s>). And that is threefold. From these conditions of <s>karma</s> and defilements, future birth (<s>jāti</s>) arises. Conditioned by birth, aging, death, and the rest come into being.

body.text: tatra yaducyate avidyā pratyayāḥ saṃskārā iti tadatītādhvaprakāśanaṃ śāśvatadṛṣṭisamucchedakam | jñāyate hi anādisaṃsāre ājavañjavibhāve karmakleśapratyayebhyaḥ kāyo vedyata iti | yaducyate jātimaraṇamiti | tadanāgatādhvaprakāśanamucchedadṛṣṭi samucchekadam | yasya tattvajñānaṃ na bhavati | tasya jātimaraṇayornāstyanto duḥkhaphalamātramasti | yaducyante madhye 'ṣṭāvaṅgāni | tatpratyutpannadharmaprakāśanam, pratyayakalāpamātrāt santatyā pravartate, nāsti tattvajñānamiti | tatrāvidyā saṃskārāśca pūrvādhvapratyayāḥ | tatpratyayaṃ phalaṃ yaduta vijñānaṃ nāmarūpaṃ ṣaḍāyatanaṃ sparśo vedanā ca | ebhyaḥ pañcabhya utpadyate tṛṣṇopādānaṃ bhavaśca | ime 'nāgatādhvahetavaḥ | tatpratyayaṃ phalaṃ yat jātijarāmaraṇam | vedanā vedayataḥ punastṛṣṇopādānañca bhavati | ata idaṃ dvādaśāṅgaṃ[bhava]cakramanavasthaṃ pravartate | tattvajñānaṃ labhamānaḥ karmāṇi na sañcinoti | karmaṇāmasañcaye na bhavati jātiḥ | jātirhi pravṛttisādhanī ||
body.translated_text: Therein, the statement 'conditioned by ignorance, formations arise' illuminates the past period (<s>atītādhva</s>) and cuts off the eternalist view (<s>śāśvatadṛṣṭi</s>). For it is known that in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, through the twisting and turning [of rebirth], the body is experienced through the conditions of <s>karma</s> and defilements. The statement about birth and death illuminates the future period (<s>anāgatādhva</s>) and cuts off the annihilationist view (<s>ucchedadṛṣṭi</s>). For one who does not have the knowledge of reality, there is no end to birth and death — there is only the fruit of suffering. The eight limbs stated in the middle illuminate the present (<s>pratyutpanna</s>) <s>dharmas</s>, showing that [existence] proceeds merely through the aggregation of conditions in a continuum, without any knowledge of reality. Therein, ignorance and formations are the conditions of the past period. Their resultant fruit is consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-bases, contact, and feeling. From these five arise craving, clinging, and becoming. These are the causes of the future period. Their resultant fruit is birth, aging, and death. While experiencing feeling, craving and clinging again arise. Thus this twelve-limbed wheel of becoming (<s>bhavacakra</s>) revolves without cessation. One who attains the knowledge of reality does not accumulate <s>karmas</s>. When <s>karmas</s> are not accumulated, there is no birth. For birth is what brings about continued activity.

body.text: ya idaṃ samyacchāstraṃ niṣevate sa dharmāḥ svalakṣaṇaśūnyā iti prajñāya na karmāṇi sañcinoti | karmaṇāmasañcaye na bhavati jātiḥ | jātyabhāvājjarāmaraṇaśokaparidevaduḥkhopāyāsāḥ sarve nirudhyante | ata ātmahitaṃ satvahitañca kāmayamānaḥ kramaśastathāgatamārgaṃ prasādhya svadharmamādīpayan paradharmaṃ yo nirākaroti tenedaṃ śāstraṃ niṣevitavyam ||
body.translated_text: One who takes up this true treatise, understanding that <s>dharmas</s> are empty of own-characteristics (<s>svalakṣaṇaśūnya</s>), does not accumulate <s>karmas</s>. When <s>karmas</s> are not accumulated, there is no birth. Through the absence of birth, aging, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress — all cease. Therefore, one who desires benefit for oneself and benefit for beings, gradually accomplishing the path of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, illuminating one's own <s>Dharma</s> and refuting the <s>dharma</s> of others — he should take up this treatise.

body.text: dharmaskandhavargo 'ṣṭādaśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the eighteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Aggregates of <s>Dharmas</s> (<s>dharmaskandhavarga</s>).

body.text: 19 daśasu vādeṣu ādyaṃ sattālakṣaṇam
body.translated_text: 19. Among the ten disputations, the first: the mark of existence (<s>sattālakṣaṇa</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) śāstrārambha uktaṃ bhavatā- niṣevya bhinnavādāṃśceti tathāgatadharmavicārayiṣayā | ke te vibhinnā vādāḥ | (u) tripiṭake santi bahavo vibhinnā vādāḥ | puruṣāṇāṃ bhūyasā pramodāya paraṃ vivādaśāstrapravartakairabhihitam- yaduta (1) astyadhvadvayaṃ nāstyadhvadvayam, (2) sarvamasti sarvaṃ nāsti, (3) astyantarā bhavo nāstyantarā bhavaḥ, (4) catussatyānāmānupūrveṇa lābhaḥ ekakṣaṇena lābhaḥ (5) asti parihāṇiḥ nāsti parihāṇiḥ (6) anuśayāścittasamprayuktāḥ cittaviprayuktāḥ, (7) cittaṃ prakṛtipariśuddham, na prakṛtipariśuddham, (8) upāttavipākaṃ karma kiñcidasti kiñcinnāsti, (9) tathāgataḥ saṅghagaṇitaḥ, na saṅghagaṇitaḥ, (10) asti pudgalo nāsti pudgala iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) At the beginning of the treatise, you stated: 'Having investigated the various views (<s>bhinnavāda</s>)' — with the intention of examining the <s>Dharma</s> of the <s>Tathāgata</s>. What are these divergent views? (Answer) In the <s>Tripiṭaka</s> there are many divergent views. For the great delight of people, those who promulgate disputational treatises have stated [ten issues]: (1) the two periods of time exist / the two periods of time do not exist; (2) everything exists / everything does not exist; (3) the intermediate state of becoming (<s>antarābhava</s>) exists / does not exist; (4) the Four Noble Truths are obtained sequentially / obtained in a single moment; (5) decline exists / decline does not exist; (6) latent tendencies (<s>anuśaya</s>) are associated with mind / dissociated from mind; (7) the mind is naturally pure / not naturally pure; (8) <s>karma</s> with appropriated result partly exists, partly does not; (9) the <s>Tathāgata</s> is counted among the <s>Saṅgha</s> / not counted among the <s>Saṅgha</s>; (10) a person (<s>pudgala</s>) exists / a person does not exist.

body.text: kecidāhuḥ- asti adhvayadharma iti | kecidāhuḥ nāstīti | kena pratyayena astīti vadanti kena pratyayena nāstīti | (u) astīti yaḥ san dharmaḥ tatra cittamutpadyate | tryadhvadharme cittamutpadyata ityato jñātavyaṃ tadastīti ||
body.translated_text: Some say: 'The <s>dharma</s> of the two periods of time exists.' Others say: 'It does not exist.' For what reason do they say it exists? For what reason do they say it does not? (Answer) Those who say 'it exists' [argue that] the mind arises with respect to an existing <s>dharma</s>. Since the mind arises with respect to <s>dharmas</s> of the three periods of time, it should be known that they exist.

body.text: (pṛ) prathamamucyatāṃ sattālakṣaṇam | (u) jñānaṃ yatra pracarati[tat]sattālakṣaṇam |
body.translated_text: (Question) First, let the mark of existence (<s>sattālakṣaṇa</s>) be stated. (Answer) That toward which knowledge operates — that is the mark of existence.

body.text: dūṣaṇam- jñānamavidyamāne 'pi pracarati | kasmāt | yathādhimukti avinīlakaṃ dṛṣṭvā vinīlakaṃ paśyati | kṛtakaṃ māyāvastu asadapi sat paśyati | akiñcanasya jñānādākiñcanyāyatanasamādhimupasampanno bhavati | aṅgulyā ca nirdiśya [vadati] candradvayamahaṃ paśyāmīti | sūtre coktam- ahaṃ prajānāmi nādhyātmamasti chandarāga iti | uktañca sūtre- yathā yo rūpe chandarāgaḥ taṃ prajahīt | evaṃvastadrūpaṃ prahīṇaṃ bhavati iti | yathā ca svapne asadapi mithyā [sat] paśyati | ityādibhiḥ kāraṇairjñānamavidyamāne 'pi pracarati | jñānapracarāspadatvādastīti na sambhavati |
body.translated_text: Refutation: Knowledge operates even with respect to what does not exist. Why? Just as one with a fixed belief (<s>adhimukti</s>), seeing something that is not blue, perceives it as blue. Concerning an artificial magical object (<s>māyāvastu</s>), even though it is unreal, one perceives it as real. From the knowledge of nothingness, one enters the attainment of the base of nothingness (<s>ākiñcanyāyatana</s>). And pointing with a finger, one says: 'I see two moons.' It is also stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'I know that internally there is no desire-and-passion (<s>chandarāga</s>).' And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Just as that desire-and-passion toward form — when one abandons it, that form is abandoned.' And just as in a dream, even what is unreal is falsely perceived as real. By these and other reasons, knowledge operates even with respect to what does not exist. Therefore, the claim that something exists because it is the domain of knowledge's operation is untenable.

body.text: ucyate | avidyamāne 'pi jñānaṃ pracaratīti na bhavati | kasmāt | āśrayālambanātmaka dharmadvayaṃ pratītya hi vijñānamutpadyate | yadyanālambanaṃ vijñānamudeśyati | anāśrayamapi vijñānamutpannaṃ syāt | tathā ca dharmadvayaṃ niṣprayojanaṃ syāt | evaṃ vināpi vimuktiṃ tadvijñānaṃ sadotpadyate | ato jñāyate vijñānaṃ nāvidyamāne pracaratīti | atha yat kiñcana vijānātīti vijñānam | yat na kiñcana vijānāti na tat vijñānam | vijñānaṃ viṣayaṃ vijānāti vacanaṃ cakṣurvijñānaṃ rūpaṃ vijānāti yāvanmanovijñānaṃ dharmān vijānāti ityetasyābhidhānam | yadi matam anālambanaṃ vijñānamastīti | tadvijñānaṃ kasya vijñānaṃ bhavet | kiñca anālambanaṃ vijñānamastīti vādinastat bhrāntaṃ syāt | yathā kecidvadanti bhrāntavikṣiptacitto 'haṃ loke 'vidyamānamapyātmānaṃ paśyāmīti | yadi kiñcidavidyamānaṃ jānīyāt | saṃśayo na syāt | kiñcittu jñātuḥ saṃśaya utpadyate | uktañca sūtre- yo 'yaṃ lokato 'vidyamāna ātmā, tasya jñānaṃ darśanaṃ veti nedaṃ sthānaṃ vidyate iti |
body.translated_text: It is replied: It is not the case that knowledge operates with respect to what does not exist. Why? Because consciousness arises dependent upon two <s>dharmas</s> — a basis (<s>āśraya</s>) and an object (<s>ālambana</s>). If consciousness could arise without an object, then it could also arise without a basis. In that case, the two <s>dharmas</s> would be purposeless. Moreover, without liberation too, that consciousness would always arise. Therefore it is known that consciousness does not operate with respect to what does not exist. Now, 'cognizing something' is consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>); what does not cognize anything is not consciousness. 'Consciousness cognizes objects' means: eye-consciousness cognizes form, up to mind-consciousness cognizes <s>dharmas</s> — such is the designation. If you hold that consciousness without an object exists, then whose consciousness would it be? Furthermore, the claim that consciousness without an object exists would itself be erroneous — just as some say: 'I, with a confused and distracted mind, perceive in the world a self that does not exist.' If one could know something non-existent, there would be no doubt. But doubt does arise for the knower. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'That there would be knowledge or vision of a self that does not exist in the world — this situation is not found.'

body.text: bhavadvavacanaṃ svato virūddham | yadyasat, kasya jñānaṃ syāt | uktañca sūtre- cittacaittā ālambamānadharmāḥ iti | kiñcāha- sarve dharmā ālambyā iti | natu tatroktam avidyamāno dharma ālambvyaṃ bhavatīti | atha sarve viṣayadharmā vijñānotpādahetavaḥ | yadyavidyamānaḥ ko heturbhavati | uktañca sūtre- trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | avidyamānānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ kaḥ sannipātaḥ | athāsadālambanaṃ jñānaṃ kathamupalabhyeta | yasya jñānaṃ na tadasat | yannāsti na tasya jñānam | ato nāstyasadālambanaṃ jñānam |
body.translated_text: Your statement is self-contradictory. If [the object] is non-existent, whose knowledge would it be? And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Mind and mental factors are <s>dharmas</s> that take objects (<s>ālambanadharma</s>).' Furthermore, it is said: 'All <s>dharmas</s> are objects.' But it is not stated there that a non-existent <s>dharma</s> becomes an object. Moreover, all object-<s>dharmas</s> are causes for the arising of consciousness. If something does not exist, how can it be a cause? And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The conjunction of three is contact (<s>sparśa</s>).' How could there be a conjunction of non-existent <s>dharmas</s>? Furthermore, if knowledge took a non-existent object, how could it be apprehended? What has knowledge is not non-existent; what does not exist has no knowledge. Therefore there is no knowledge with a non-existent object.

body.text: yaduktaṃ bhavatā jñānamavidyamāne 'pi pracarati | yathādhimukti avinīlakaṃ dṛṣṭvā vinīlakamiti paśyatīti nedaṃ sthānaṃ vidyate | kasmāt | avinīlake 'pi tattvato 'sti vinīlakasvabhāvaḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- astyasmin vṛkṣe viśuddhatā iti |
body.translated_text: As for your statement that 'knowledge operates even with respect to what does not exist — just as one with fixed belief, seeing something not blue, perceives it as blue' — this situation is not found. Why? Because even in what is not blue, there truly exists the nature of blue. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'In this tree there exists purity.'

body.text: nīlalakṣaṇagrāhīcittabalāt sarvaṃ nīlaṃ pariṇamate natvanīlalakṣaṇamiti | māyājālasūtrañcāha- asti māyā māyāvastu | asati sattve sattvābhāsaṃ paśyantīti māyā iti | bhavatoktam akiñcanasya jñānādākiñcanyāyatanamupasampanna iti | samādhibalāt tadasallakṣaṇaṃ
body.translated_text: By the power of the mind that grasps the mark of blue, everything is transformed into blue — it is not that the mark of non-blue [is perceived]. The <s>Māyājālasūtra</s> also states: 'There exists illusion (<s>māyā</s>) and the illusory object (<s>māyāvastu</s>). When a being does not exist, they perceive an appearance of a being — that is called illusion.' Your statement that 'from the knowledge of nothingness, one enters the base of nothingness' — [this is explained as follows:] by the power of <s>samādhi</s>, that mark of the non-existent

body.text: bhavati na tu asattadbhavati | yathā vastutaḥ sadapirūpamapohyate śūnyarūpamiti | samādhimupasampannenālpaṃ dṛśyata ityato 'sadicyate | yathālpalavaṇamalavaṇamityucyate | alpajño 'jña iti | yathā ca naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanamucyate | tatra vastutaḥ saṃjñāyāṃ satyāmapi naivāsti na nāstīti vyapadiśyate | uktañca bhavatā- aṅgulyā nidiśyātmānaṃ candradvayaṃ paśyāmīti | anibhṛtatvāt ekaṃ dvidhā paśyati | ya ekāgracakṣuṣkaḥ sa na paśyati | ahaṃ prajānāmi nādhyātmamasti chandarāga iti yadbhavatoktam | sa pañcanīvaraṇaviruddhāni saptabodhyaṅgāni dṛṣṭvā manaskāraṃ janayati- ahaṃ prajānāmi antaśchandābhāvamiti | na tu [ekāntato] nāstīti prajānāti | kiñcoktaṃ bhavatā- yat rūpe chandarāgaṃ prahīṇaṃ prajānāti | tadrūpaprahāṇamiti | paramārthaprajñādarśanasya mithyādhimuktiṃ prati virodhitvāt chandarāgaprahāṇamityucyate | svapne 'sadapi paśyatīti yat bhavānāha | tatra pūrvaṃ dṛṣṭaśrutasmṛtavikalpita bhāvitānyupādāya hi svapnadarśanam | vātapittaśleṣmaṇāṃ vaśācca svapnadarśanamanuyāti | kadācit karmapratyayācca svapno bhavati | yathā purā bodhisattvasya mahāsvapnā abhūvan | kadācit devā āgamya svapnamupadarśayanti | ataḥ svapnadarśane nāsato jñānaṃ bhavati |
body.translated_text: it exists, but what is non-existent does not come into being from that. Just as in reality, even existent form is negated as 'empty form.' One who has entered <s>samādhi</s> sees only a little — therefore it is called 'non-existent.' Just as a small amount of salt is called 'unsalted,' and one of little knowledge is called 'ignorant.' And just as the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (<s>naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana</s>) is so called — therein, though perception truly exists in reality, it is designated as 'neither exists nor does not exist.' And as you have said: 'Pointing at oneself with a finger, one sees two moons.' Because of unsteadiness, one sees one as two. One whose eye is focused sees [only one]. As for what you have said: 'I know there is no desire-and-passion (<s>chandarāga</s>) internally' — he, having seen the seven factors of awakening (<s>saptabodhyaṅga</s>) which are opposed to the five hindrances (<s>pañcanīvaraṇa</s>), generates the attention: 'I know there is no desire internally.' But he does not know that it [absolutely] does not exist. Furthermore, as you have said: 'He knows that desire-and-passion toward form has been abandoned — that is the abandonment of form.' Because the seeing of ultimate wisdom (<s>paramārthaprajñādarśana</s>) is opposed to wrong inclination (<s>mithyādhimukti</s>), it is called the abandonment of desire-and-passion. As for what you have said — 'Even in dreams one sees what is non-existent' — therein, dream-perception occurs by taking up what was previously seen, heard, remembered, conceptualized, and cultivated. And dream-perception follows from the influence of wind, bile, and phlegm (<s>vāta</s>, <s>pitta</s>, <s>śleṣman</s>). Sometimes dreams arise from the condition of <s>karma</s> — just as in the past, the <s>Bodhisattva</s> had great dreams. Sometimes deities come and display dreams. Therefore, in dream-perception, there is no knowledge of the non-existent.

body.text: dūṣaṇam- yat bhavānavocat- dvābhyāṃ pratyayābhyāṃ vijñānamutpadyata iti | idamayuktam | tathāgataḥ pudgaladūṣaṇayāha- dvābhyāṃ pratyayābhyāṃ vijñānamutpadyata iti | na tu tanniṣṭhayā | bhavatoktam- vijñeyasattvādvijñānamastīti | vijñeyadharme sati astīti jñānam | asati nāstīti jñānam | yadīdaṃ vastu nāsti | tadvastu nāstīti śūnyaṃ paśyati | kiñca trividhanirodho nirodhasatyamityucyate | yadi nāsti śūnyacittam kiṃ nirūdhyate | [yat]bhavānavocat cakṣurvijñānaṃ rūpaṃ vijānāti yāvanmanovijñānaṃ dharmān vijānāti iti | tat vijñānaṃ viṣayamātraṃ vijānāti na vicinoti san vā asan vā iti | yadapi bhavānāha- yadyanālambanaṃ vijñānamasti | tadbhrāntamiti | tadā asti asajjñānasya
body.translated_text: Refutation: What you have said — 'Consciousness arises from two conditions' — this is incorrect. The <s>Tathāgata</s> said 'consciousness arises from two conditions' for the purpose of refuting the person (<s>pudgala</s>), not as a definitive statement. You have said: 'Because the knowable (<s>vijñeya</s>) exists, consciousness exists.' When the knowable <s>dharma</s> exists, there is the knowledge 'it exists.' When it does not exist, there is the knowledge 'it does not exist.' If this thing does not exist, one sees it as empty, [knowing] that this thing does not exist. Furthermore, the threefold cessation is called the truth of cessation (<s>nirodhasatya</s>). If the empty mind does not exist, what is it that ceases? As you have said: 'Eye-consciousness cognizes form, and so on up to mind-consciousness cognizes <s>dharmas</s>' — that consciousness cognizes only the object, it does not discern whether it is existent or non-existent. And as you have said: 'If objectless consciousness exists, then it is deluded' — then there exists knowledge of the non-existent

body.text: jñānam | yathā madamattaḥ puruṣaḥ paśyati avidyamānamapi | bhavānavocat- yadi asajjānīyāt, saṃśayo na bhavediti | kimasti kiṃ vā nāstīti yadi saṃśayaḥ, tadā anālambanaṃ jñānamasti | āha ca bhavān- yathoktaṃ sūtre yallokato 'vidyamāna ātmā tasya jñānaṃ darśanaṃ veti nedaṃ sthānaṃ vidyata iti | idaṃ sūtraṃ na dharmalakṣaṇānugatam abuddhavacanaṃ tadābhāsaṃ vā | samādhirvā evam | tatsamādhimupasampannena yatkiñcit dṛśyate sarvaṃ sadeva | tatsamādhitvādevamucyate | [mama vacanaṃ prati]svato viruddhamiti bhavānavocat | asti asadālambanaṃ jñānamiti mama vacanaṃ na svato viruddham | avocacca bhavān- cittacaittā ālambamānāḥ | sarve dharmā ālambyā iti | santi ca cittacaittā anālambamānāḥ | cittacaittā na paramāyārthālambanāḥ | ato 'nālambamānā bhavanti | dharmāṇāṃ yatparamārthalakṣaṇaṃ tallakṣaṇairviyuktatvāt cittacaittā nālambamānā bhavanti | yat bhavān bravīti viṣayā vijñānajanakahetavaḥ | teṣāmasattve ko hetuḥ syāditi | tadvijñānaṃ saddhetukameva | trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | yatra trīṇyupalabhyante tatra teṣāṃ sannipātaḥ | na tu sarvatra trīṇi santi | abravīcca bhavān- yasya jñānaṃ, na tadasadbhavati | yannāsti, na tasya jñānamiti | yadi sadālambanaṃ jñānamiti | tatrāpi samo doṣaḥ | yat bhavānāha- yathā vṛkṣe 'sti viśuddhateti | nedaṃ yujyate | satkāryadoṣāt | yadbhavatoktaṃ [nīla]lakṣaṇagrāhicittaṃ vipulaṃ pariṇamata iti | tadapi na yuktam | nīlalakṣaṇālpamūlaṃ sarvāṃ mahāpṛthivīṃ yat nīlaṃ paśyati | tadabhūtadarśanam | tathā alpanīlabhāvanayā tu sarvaṃ jambūdvīpaṃ yat nīlaṃ paśyati na tadabhūtadarśanam | bhavān bravīti- māyājālasūtramāha- asti māyā māyāvastu iti | asati sattve sattvābhāsaṃ sattva iti paśyati | tadvastu paramārthato 'satpaśyati | tadā anālambanaṃ jñānaṃ bhavati | āha ca bhavān- samādhibalāttallakṣaṇaṃ bhavati yathā vastutaḥ sadapi rūpaṃ śūnyatayāpohyata iti | yadi rūpaṃ vastusadapohyate śūnyarūpamiti | tadā viparyayaḥ | alpasya sato 'sattāvacanamapi viparyaya eva | anibhṛtatvādekaṃ dvidhā paśyatīti yadvacanam | tadapi na yujyate | yathā timiropahatacakṣuṣka ākāśe keśān paśyati | te 'vastusantaḥ | āha ca bhavān pañcanīvaraṇaviruddhāni saptabodhyaṅgāni dṛṣṭvā manaskāraṃ janayati ahamasat prajānāmīti | saptabodhyāṅgāni bhinnāni |
body.translated_text: — knowledge. Just as a person intoxicated with drink sees even what does not exist. You have said: 'If one could know the non-existent, there would be no doubt.' If there is doubt about whether something exists or does not exist, then objectless knowledge exists. And you have said: 'As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: That which is non-existent in the world as a self — that there is knowledge and vision of it, this is not possible.' This <s>sūtra</s> does not accord with the marks of <s>Dharma</s> — it is either not the word of the <s>Buddha</s> or it is a mere semblance. Or else, it refers to a particular <s>samādhi</s> — whatever is seen by one who has entered that <s>samādhi</s> is all existent; because it is that particular <s>samādhi</s>, it is spoken of thus. You have said 'my statement is self-contradictory.' [But] my statement that there exists knowledge with a non-existent object is not self-contradictory. And you have said: 'Mind and mental factors are apprehending; all <s>dharmas</s> are objects of apprehension.' But there are mind and mental factors that do not apprehend. Mind and mental factors do not apprehend ultimate reality (<s>paramārtha</s>). Therefore they are non-apprehending. Because the ultimate characteristic of <s>dharmas</s> is dissociated from those characteristics, mind and mental factors do not apprehend [it]. As for what you say — 'Objects are causes that generate consciousness; in their non-existence, what would be the cause?' — that consciousness indeed has an existent cause. 'The conjunction of three is contact (<s>sparśa</s>)' — where three are found, there is their conjunction; but not everywhere are all three present. And you have said: 'That of which there is knowledge — that is not non-existent; what does not exist — of that there is no knowledge.' If [you hold that] knowledge has an existent object, the same fault applies there too. As for what you have said — 'Purity exists in the tree' — this is not correct, because of the fault of the doctrine of pre-existent effects (<s>satkāryavāda</s>). What you have said — 'The mind that grasps the characteristic of blue expands' — that too is not correct. The small basis of the blue characteristic — [when one] sees the entire great earth as blue, that is a seeing of what is unreal. But when, through the cultivation of a small [amount of] blue, one sees all of <s>Jambudvīpa</s> as blue, that is not a seeing of what is unreal. You say: 'The <s>Māyājālasūtra</s> states: There is illusion and there is the basis of illusion.' When beings do not [truly] exist, one sees the semblance of beings as beings. One sees that thing as ultimately non-existent. Then there is objectless knowledge. And you have said: 'By the power of <s>samādhi</s>, that characteristic arises — just as in reality, even existent form is negated as emptiness.' If form, though existent in reality, is negated as 'empty form,' then that is a perversion. Calling a small existent 'non-existent' is also indeed a perversion. As for your statement — 'Because of unsteadiness, one sees one as two' — that too is not correct. Just as one whose eye is impaired by cataracts (<s>timira</s>) sees hairs in the sky — those have no real substance. And you have said: 'Having seen the seven factors of awakening opposed to the five hindrances, one generates the attention: I know the non-existent.' But the seven factors of awakening are distinct,

body.text: chandarāgābhāvaśca bhinnaḥ | kathamekaḥ syāt | bhavān bravīti- paramārthaprajñādarśanasya mithyādhimuktiṃ prati virodhitaiva chandarāgaprahāṇamiti | mithyādhimuktirhi abhūtabhāvanā | ata ucyate chandarāgaprahāṇaṃ prajñāya rūpaprahāṇaṃ bhavatīti | paramārthaprajñā tu anityabhāvanā | yat bhavān kathayati- svapne vastusan dṛśyata iti | tadayuktam | yathā svapne [paśyati] kuṭyāṃ patatīva | na vastutaḥ patati | ato 'sti asajjñānasya jñānam | na tu yatna jñānaṃ pracaratīti sattālakṣaṇam ||
body.translated_text: and the absence of desire-and-passion is distinct. How could they be one?
