(Reply) The Blessed One said 'I will be worshipped' with the intention of [promoting] worship of the <s>Saṅgha</s>. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'One who looks upon the sick sees me.' (Objection) Some, such as <s>Śāriputra</s> and others who are endowed with noble qualities, are included within the <s>Saṅgha</s> — by similarity of characteristics, the Blessed One too should be likewise. (Reply) If [it is argued] by similarity of characteristics, then all ordinary persons (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) and even those called non-beings would be admitted into the <s>Saṅgha</s>. This is not tenable in reality. Therefore it is known that the Blessed One is not included within the <s>Saṅgha</s>. Furthermore, the Blessed One has not entered the formal acts of the <s>Saṅgha</s> (<s>saṅghakarma</s>), nor is he equal to other matters of the <s>Saṅgha</s>. Because of the distinction of the Three Jewels (<s>Ratnatraya</s>), the Blessed One is not included within the <s>Saṅgha</s>.

body.text: ratnadvayavivādavargastrayastriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the thirty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Dispute Concerning the Two Jewels (<s>ratnadvayavivādavarga</s>).

body.text: 34 nāstipudgalavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 34. Chapter on the Non-Existence of the Person (<s>nāstipudgalavarga</s>)

body.text: śāstramāha- vātsīputrīyā vadanti asti pudgala iti | anye vadanti nāstīti | (pṛ) kiṃ tattvam | (u) nāsti pudgaladharma iti tattvam | kasmāt | yathā bahuṣu sūtreṣu tathāgato bhikṣūnāha- nāmamātrataḥ prajñaptimātrata upayogamātrataḥ pudgala ityucyate | iti | nāmamātrata ityādinā jñāyate na paramārtha iti | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre-
body.translated_text: The treatise says: The <s>Vātsīputrīyas</s> say: 'The person (<s>pudgala</s>) exists.' Others say: 'It does not exist.' (Question) What is the truth? (Answer) The truth is that the <s>dharma</s> of the person does not exist. Why? Because, as the <s>Tathāgata</s> said to the monks in many <s>sūtras</s>: 'It is only by name, only by designation, only by convention that it is called a person (<s>pudgala</s>).' From the expression 'only by name' and so forth, it is known that [the person] is not [an entity in] the ultimate sense (<s>paramārtha</s>). Furthermore, it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>:

body.text:
yo na paśyati duḥkhañca sa ātmānantu paśyati |
duḥkhadarśī yathābhūtaṃ sa ātmānaṃ na paśyati || iti |
body.translated_text:
One who does not see suffering sees the self;
one who sees suffering as it truly is does not see the self — thus it is said.

body.text: yadi vastu san ātmā, duḥkhadarśyapi ātmānaṃ paśyet | āryāḥ punaḥ saṃvṛtimātrato vadanti astyātmeti | api ca sūtre bhagavānavocat- yatrāsmīti tatreñjitam iti | yadvastu sat na tatreñjitaṃ bhavati yathā cakṣuḥ, tasya vastusattvāt na [tatra] iñjitamasti | tatra tatra sūtre ca ātmavādaḥ pratiṣiddhaḥ | yathā āryā bhikṣuṇī māramavocat-
body.translated_text: If the self (<s>ātman</s>) were a real entity, one who sees suffering would also see the self. But the Noble Ones speak only conventionally (<s>saṃvṛtimātrataḥ</s>), saying 'the self exists.' Furthermore, in the <s>sūtra</s> the Blessed One said: 'Where there is the [notion] "I am," there is agitation (<s>iñjita</s>).' That which is a real entity — there is no agitation regarding it, just as with the eye; because of its real existence, there is no agitation there. And in various <s>sūtras</s>, the doctrine of self (<s>ātmavāda</s>) is prohibited. As the Noble <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> said to <s>Māra</s>:

body.text:
kiṃ nu satveti pratyeṣi māradṛṣṭigataṃ nu te |
śuddhasaṃskārapuñjo 'yaṃ neha sattva upalabhyate || iti |
body.translated_text:
Why do you believe in a 'being'? Is this a view of <s>Māra</s> in you?
This is merely a heap of pure formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) — no being is found here — thus it is said.

body.text: kiñcāha-
body.translated_text: Furthermore it says:

body.text:
saṃskārāṇāṃ kalāpo hi santānena pravartate |
māyānirmitamevedaṃ prakṛtānāñca vañcanam |
hṛdgatena sadṛśaṃ śalyenedaṃ sapatnakam |
naivāsti sāravadvastu................ | iti
kiñcāha-
body.translated_text: Furthermore it says:

children.text: nāstyātmā na cātmīyaṃ na sattvo nāpi mānavaḥ |
children.translated_text: There is no self, nor anything belonging to self, no being, nor a human person.
The five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) are merely empty, characterized by arising and ceasing.
There is <s>karma</s> and its ripening (<s>vipāka</s>), but no doer (<s>kāraka</s>) is apprehended.

body.text: ityevamādinā bhagavān nānāsūtreṣu ātmavādaṃ pratiṣiddhavān | ato nāstyātmā | sūtre ca vijñānārthā vibhaktāḥ | kasmāt vijñānamiti | yaduta rūpaṃ vijānāti yāvaddharmān vijānātīti | na coktaṃ ātmānaṃ vijānātīti | ato nāstyātmā |
body.translated_text: By these and other [statements], the Blessed One has prohibited the doctrine of self (<s>ātmavāda</s>) in various <s>sūtras</s>. Therefore the self does not exist. And in the <s>sūtra</s>, the meanings of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) are analyzed: 'Why is it called consciousness? Because it cognizes form, up to because it cognizes <s>dharmas</s>.' But it is not said: 'It cognizes the self.' Therefore the self does not exist.

body.text: cundabhikṣurbhagavantamapṛcchat- ko nu khalu vijñānāhāramāhārayati | bhagavān pratyavadat | na kalyaḥ praśnaḥ | vijñānāhāramāhārayatīti nāhaṃ vadāmi | iti | yadyasti ātmā | ātmā vijñānāhāramāhārayatīti vadet | ato jñātavyaṃ nāstyātmeti | bimbisārapratyudgamanasūtre bhagavān bhikṣūnāmantryāha- vibhāvayata yūyaṃ bhikṣavaḥ prākṛtānāṃ prajñaptimanurudhya vadāmi astyātmeti | paramārthastu nāsti pañcaskandheṣu ātmātmīyaṃ vā | iti | kiñcāha- pañcaskandhānupādāyāsti nānāvidhaṃ nāma yaduta ātmā sattvo mānavo deva iti | evaṃpramāṇāni nāmāni pañcaskandhānupādāya santi | yadyātmāsti | ātmānamupādāyeti vadet | sthavirapūrṇakaḥ kaścit tīrthikaḥ āha- yadi puruṣo mithyādṛṣṭayā asantamastīti vadati | bhagavān prahīṇaitanmithyābhimānaḥ aprahīṇasattva
body.translated_text: The monk <s>Cunda</s> asked the Blessed One: 'Who indeed feeds on consciousness-as-nutriment (<s>vijñānāhāra</s>)?' The Blessed One replied: 'This is not a proper question. I do not say that someone feeds on consciousness-as-nutriment.' If the self existed, he would have said: 'The self feeds on consciousness-as-nutriment.' Therefore it should be known that the self does not exist. In the <s>Bimbisārapratyudgamanasūtra</s>, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'O monks, make it clear! Following the designation of ordinary people (<s>prākṛta</s>), I say: The self exists. But in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārtha</s>), there is no self nor anything belonging to self in the five aggregates.' Furthermore he said: 'Depending on the five aggregates, there are various names, such as self, being, human person, god, and so forth. Such names exist depending on the five aggregates.' If the self existed, he would have said: 'Depending on the self.' The Elder <s>Pūrṇaka</s>, a certain <s>tīrthika</s>, said: 'If a person, through wrong view, speaks of what does not exist as existing — the Blessed One, whose such false conceit has been abandoned, [is one whose] being has not been abandoned

body.text: ityato nāstyātmā | yamakasūtre śāriputro yamakamavocat- kiṃ yamaka samanupaśyasi rūpaskandho 'rhan iti | uttaramāha- no hīdamāyuṣman iti | kiṃ samanupaśyasi vedanā saṃjñā saṃskārā vijñānamarhan iti | nohīda[māyuṣman] | kiṃ samanupaśyasi pañcaskandhakalāpo 'rhan iti | nohīdamāyuṣman | kiṃ samanupaśyasi pañcaskandhādanyatra arhan iti | nohīdamāyuṣman śāriputro 'vocat | yadevaṃ parimṛgya [dṛṣṭa eva dharme satyataḥ sthirataḥ] nopalabhyate | tatkalyaṃ nu te vyākaraṇaṃ arhan [kāyasya bhedāducchidyate vinaśyati] na bhavati paraṃ maraṇāditi | abhūtkhalu me [āyuṣman] śāriputra pūrvaṃ pāpakaṃ dṛṣṭigatam, idaṃ punarāyuṣmataḥ śāriputrasya dharmadeśanāṃ śrutvā tacca pāpakaṃ dṛṣṭigataṃ prahīṇam | iti | yadyasti ātmā, pāpakaṃ dṛṣṭigataṃ iti na vadet |
body.translated_text: ' — therefore the self does not exist. In the <s>Yamakasūtra</s>, <s>Śāriputra</s> said to <s>Yamaka</s>: 'What do you think, <s>Yamaka</s>? Is the form aggregate an <s>Arhat</s>?' He answered: 'No indeed, Venerable One.' 'Is feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness an <s>Arhat</s>?' 'No indeed, Venerable One.' 'Is the aggregate of the five <s>skandhas</s> an <s>Arhat</s>?' 'No indeed, Venerable One.' 'Is the <s>Arhat</s> found apart from the five <s>skandhas</s>?' 'No indeed, Venerable One.' <s>Śāriputra</s> said: 'If thus, when sought in this very life, [the <s>Arhat</s>] truly and firmly is not apprehended — is it proper for you to declare that the <s>Arhat</s>, at the breaking up of the body, is cut off, perishes, and does not exist after death?' [<s>Yamaka</s> replied:] 'Indeed, Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>, previously there arose in me an evil view. But now, having heard the Venerable <s>Śāriputra</s>'s teaching of the <s>Dharma</s>, that evil view has been abandoned.' If the self existed, he would not have called it 'an evil view.'

body.text: caturṣūpādāneṣu uktamātmavādopādānamiti | yadyastyātmā ātmopādānamiti brūyāt yathā kāmopādānamityādi | na brūyādātmavādopādānamiti | uktañcaśreṇikasūtre- trayāṇāṃ śāstṝṇāṃ yo nopalabhate pratyutpannamātmānamūrdhvabhāvinaṃ vātmānaṃ tamahaṃ śāstāraṃ buddhaṃ vadāmi iti | bhagavatānupalabdhatvāt nāstyātmeti jñāyate | anātmani ātmeti saṃjñā viparyayaḥ | yadi mataṃ satyātmani ātmeti saṃjñā na viparyāsa iti | na yuktamidam | kasmāt | bhagavānāha- yatsattvā ātmeti samanupaśyantaḥ samanupaśyanti | imāneva pañcaskandhān [ātmata ātmītayataśca] samanupaśyanti | iti | ato nāstyātmā | kiñcāha- sattvāḥ vividhān pūrvanivāsānanusmarantaḥ pañcaskandhānanusmaranti | iti | yadyastyātmā, tamapyanusmareyuḥ | ananusmaraṇānnāstīti jñātavyam | yadi manyase- kiñcitsūtramāha sattvānusmaraṇamapi | yathā amukaḥ sattvaḥ tatrāhamamukanāmaka iti |
body.translated_text: Among the four kinds of clinging (<s>upādāna</s>), the clinging to the doctrine of self (<s>ātmavādopādāna</s>) is mentioned. If the self existed, one would say 'clinging to the self' (<s>ātmopādāna</s>), just as one says 'clinging to sense-pleasures' (<s>kāmopādāna</s>) and so forth — one would not say 'clinging to the doctrine of self.' And it is stated in the <s>Śreṇikasūtra</s>: 'Among three teachers, the one who does not apprehend either a present self or a future self — him I call a teacher, a <s>Buddha</s>.' Because the Blessed One does not apprehend [a self], it is known that the self does not exist. The perception of self in what is without self is a perversion (<s>viparyaya</s>). If you think: 'When the self truly exists, the perception of self is not a perversion' — this is not correct. Why? Because the Blessed One said: 'When beings perceive a self, they perceive precisely these five aggregates as self and as belonging to self.' Therefore the self does not exist. Furthermore he says: 'Beings, when recollecting their various previous abodes (<s>pūrvanivāsa</s>), recollect the five aggregates.' If the self existed, they would recollect that too. Since it is not recollected, it should be known to be non-existent. If you think: 'Some <s>sūtra</s> also speaks of the recollection of a being — as in: Such-and-such a being, there I was, bearing such-and-such a name'

body.text: tadayuktam | taddhi lokasatyavikalpāduktam | paramārthatastu pañcaskandhānevānusmarati na sattvam | kutaḥ | manovijñānena hi smarati | manovijñānañca dharmamātrālambanam | tasmānnāsti kiñcitsmaraṇaṃ sattvānusmaraṇaṃ nāma | astyekāntata ātmeti yo vadati sa ṣaṇṇāṃ mithyādṛṣṭīnīmanyatamasyāmanupatati | yadi manyase nāstyātmeti vacanamapi mithyādṛṣṭiriti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | satyadvayasya sattvāt | lokasatyato nāstyātmā | paramārthatastu astyātmeti brūvato hi doṣo bhavati | ahantu vadāmi paramārthato nāstyātmā | lokasatyatastu astīti | ato 'navadyam |
body.translated_text: — that is not correct. That is spoken from the perspective of the conceptualization of worldly truth (<s>lokasatya</s>). But in the ultimate sense, one recollects only the five aggregates, not a being. Why? Because one recollects through mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>), and mental consciousness takes only <s>dharmas</s> as its object. Therefore there is nothing called the recollection of a being. One who says absolutely 'the self exists' falls into one of the six wrong views (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>). If you think: 'The statement "the self does not exist" is also a wrong view' — that is not correct. Why? Because of the reality of the two truths (<s>satyadvaya</s>). From the standpoint of worldly truth (<s>lokasatya</s>), the self does not exist. But one who says 'the self exists' in the ultimate sense — that is faulty. I, however, say: 'In the ultimate sense, the self does not exist. But from the standpoint of worldly truth, it exists.' Therefore there is no fault.

body.text: api cātmadṛṣṭimūloddharaṇāyāha bhagavān yathā mogharāja [māṇava]pṛcchāyāṃ bhagavān mogharājaṃ pratyāha-
body.translated_text: Furthermore, for the purpose of uprooting the root of the view of self (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>), the Blessed One spoke, as in the question of <s>Mogharāja</s> the young man (<s>māṇava</s>), when the Blessed One replied to <s>Mogharāja</s>:

children.translated_text: Regard the world as empty, O <s>Mogharāja</s>, being ever mindful;
having uprooted the view that follows the self (<s>ātmānudṛṣṭi</s>) — [thus you may cross beyond death;

children.text: evaṃ lokamavekṣantaṃ] mṛtyurājo na paśyati || iti
children.translated_text: one who regards the world thus] — the king of death (<s>Mṛtyu</s>) does not see — thus it is said.

body.text: ātmāstivādānāṃ kāraṇāni prītidaurmanasyādīni sarvāṇi pañcaskandhavartīni | tīrthikānāmātmadṛṣṭikāraṇakhaṇḍanānnāstyātmā ||
body.translated_text: The reasons for the doctrines asserting the existence of the self — such as pleasure, displeasure, and the like — all abide in the five aggregates. By refuting the causes of the self-view (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>) of the <s>tīrthikas</s>, it is established that the self does not exist.

body.text: nāsti pudgalavargaścatustriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the thirty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Existence of the Person (<s>nāstipudgalavarga</s>).

body.text: 35 pudgalāstināstitāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 35. Chapter on the Existence and Non-Existence of the Person (<s>pudgalāstināstitāvarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) nāstyātmeti bhavato vacanamayuktam | kasmāt caturṣu vyākaraṇeṣu caturtha sthapanīyaṃ vyākaraṇaṃ yaduta bhavati puruṣaḥ paraṃ maraṇāt na bhavati [puruṣaḥ paraṃ maraṇāt] bhavati ca na bhavati ca [puruṣaḥ paraṃ maraṇāt], naiva bhavati na na bhavati [puruṣaḥ paraṃ maraṇāt] | yadi paramārthato nāstyātmā, na syādidaṃ sthapanīyaṃ vyākaraṇam | ūrdhvakāyavedakaḥ
body.translated_text: (Objection) Your statement 'the self does not exist' is incorrect. Why? Among the four types of answers (<s>vyākaraṇa</s>), the fourth is the question to be set aside (<s>sthāpanīya</s>), namely: 'Does a person exist after death? Does a person not exist after death? Does a person both exist and not exist after death? Does a person neither exist nor not exist after death?' If the self does not exist in the ultimate sense, this question to be set aside would not apply. One who experiences the body in the higher [rebirths]

body.text: sattvo nāstīti yat keṣāñcit vacanam | mithyādṛṣṭiriyam | dvādaśāṅgapravacane cāsti jātakam | tatra bhagavānevamāha- tasmin samaye ahameva mahāsudarśano rājā evaṃkāya ityādi | pūrvakebhya utpannā idānīntanāḥ pañcaskandhāḥ na tu purāṇā eva | tasmādastyātmā [yaḥ] pūrvakebhyo 'dya yāvat bhavati | kiñcāha bhagavān-
body.translated_text: — 'Such a being does not exist' — the statement of certain people is a wrong view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>). In the twelve divisions of the teaching (<s>dvādaśāṅgapravacana</s>), there are the <s>Jātaka</s> stories. Therein the Blessed One himself said: 'At that time, I myself was King <s>Mahāsudarśana</s>, of such-and-such a body' and so forth. The present five aggregates arose from the previous ones, but they are not the very same ancient ones. Therefore the self exists, [as that] which continues from the previous [existence] up to now. Furthermore, the Blessed One said:

body.text: iha nandati pretya nandati kṛtapuṇyo ubhayanna nandati | iti |
body.translated_text: He rejoices here and rejoices hereafter — one who has done merit rejoices in both — thus it is said.

body.text: yadi pañcaskandhamātramasti, ubhayatra nandirna syāt | uktañcasūtre- cittasaṃkleśāt sattvāḥ saṃkliśyante | cittavyavadānāt sattvā viśudhyanti | iti | ekatyaḥ pudgala utpadyate loke bahūnāṃ vipattyanutāpāya | ekatyaḥ pudgala utpadyate loke bahūnāṃ lābhāya | yat kuśalākuśalakarmaṇāṃ samudācaraṇaṃ sarvaṃ tat sattvopagam | tatra tatra ca sūtre bhagavān svayamāha- ahaṃ vadāmi sattvā ūrdhvakāyaṃ vedayante iti | ātmahite kuśalaḥ na parahita ityādi | evamādikāraṇairjñāyate astyātmeti |
body.translated_text: If only the five aggregates exist, there would be no rejoicing in both [lives]. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.' 'A certain person is born in the world for the grief and remorse of many. A certain person is born in the world for the benefit of many.' 'Whatever accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome <s>karma</s> — all of that accrues to the being.' And in various <s>sūtras</s>, the Blessed One himself says: 'I say that beings experience the body in the higher [rebirths].' 'One who is skilled in self-benefit is not [necessarily skilled] in the benefit of others' — and so forth. By these and other reasons, it is known that the self exists.

body.text: bhavatā yadyapi pūrvamuktaṃ nāmamātrata ityādi | na yuktamidam | kasmāt | pañcaskandhavyatirikto nityo 'vināśilakṣaṇo 'styātmeti tīrthikāḥ parikalpayanti | teṣāṃ mithyādṛṣṭivyavacchedāya bhagavānāha nāstyātmeti | vayantu vadāmaḥ pañcaskandhasamavāya ātmeti | ato 'navadyam | yadyapyāha ātmā nāmamātramiti | tadvacanaṃ pragāḍhaṃ cintanīyam | yadi sattvo nāmamātramiti | yathā mṛṇmayagohanane nāsti pāpam | tathā vāstavikagohanane 'pi pāpaṃ na bhavet | yathā bālakānāṃ nāmamātreṇa vastudānaṃ savipākaṃ syāt | tathā mahatāṃ dānavratamapi vipākaṃ prāpnuyāt | vastutastu na yujyate | nāmamātrato 'sadapi astīti vādina āryā mṛṣāvādinaḥ syuḥ | satyavādinaḥ khalvāryāḥ | ato jñāyate astyātmeti |
body.translated_text: Although you have previously stated 'only by name' and so forth — this is not correct. Why? The <s>tīrthikas</s> conceive of a self that is separate from the five aggregates, permanent, and of indestructible nature. For the purpose of eliminating their wrong views, the Blessed One said: 'The self does not exist.' But we say: 'The self is the combination of the five aggregates (<s>pañcaskandhasamavāya</s>).' Therefore there is no fault. Although he says: 'The self is merely a name' — that statement must be deeply contemplated. If a being is merely a name, then just as there is no sin in killing a clay cow, there would be no sin in killing an actual cow either. And just as for children, merely nominal giving of an object would ripen as the actual giving of an object — so too the vows and giving of great persons would obtain their ripening. But in reality, this is not tenable. If merely by name what does not exist were said to exist, then the Noble Ones would be speakers of falsehood (<s>mṛṣāvādin</s>). But the Noble Ones are indeed speakers of truth. Therefore it is known that the self exists.

body.text: yadyāryāḥ paramārthato nairātmyadarśinaḥ vyavahārato 'styatmeti vadanti | tadā viparyayadarśinaḥ syuḥ | [anyathā dṛṣṭasya] anyathā vacanāt | yadi vyavahārato 'sadapi astīti vadatāṃ punaḥ sūtragatāni pāramārthikāni dvādaśanidānāni trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni anātmānaḥ sarvadharmā ityādi vacanaṃ na syāt | asti paraloka iti vādinamanusṛtya vadanti astīti | nāstīti vādinamanusṛtya vadanti nāstīti | vadanti ca loke ayutāni vastūni īśvarādutpannani | iti | tatādṛśā vividhamithyādṛṣṭisūtramanyāstadvavatānusāriṇaḥ syuḥ | tatu na sambhavati | ato bhavatodāhṛtaṃ sūtraṃ sarvaṃ sāmānyato dūṣitameva | ato nāsti nairātmyam |
body.translated_text: — if the Noble Ones, who see selflessness from the standpoint of ultimate truth, say from the standpoint of convention that 'there is a self,' then they would be seers of what is false — because of stating otherwise what was seen otherwise. If, speaking from the standpoint of convention, they say 'what does not exist, exists,' then the statements found in the <s>sūtras</s> that are ultimate — the twelve links of dependent origination (<s>dvādaśanidāna</s>), the three doors of liberation (<s>vimokṣamukha</s>), 'all <s>dharmas</s> are without self (<s>anātman</s>),' and so forth — those statements would not exist. Following the one who says 'the other world exists,' they say 'it exists.' Following the one who says 'it does not exist,' they say 'it does not exist.' And they say that in the world, ten thousand things are produced from <s>Īśvara</s> and so forth. If so, they would be followers of such various false-view <s>sūtras</s>. But that is not possible. Therefore the <s>sūtra</s> cited by you is entirely refuted on general grounds. Hence, selflessness does not exist [— so the objection claims].

body.text: atrocyate | yadbhavatā pūrvamuktaṃ sthapanīyavyākaraṇāt astyātmeti jñāyata iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | so 'vaktavyadharma iti paścāt nirodhasatyaskandhe vivekṣyate | ato nāsti paramārthata ātmā avaktavya iti | prajñaptimātramityucyate na paramārthasan iti | bhavatāṃ śāsane ātmā ṣadbhirvijñānairvijñāyate | yathāha bhavatāmāgamaḥ cakṣuṣā dṛśyamānaṃ rūpamupādāyetyato vināśyātmā | tadā tvayaṃ cakṣurvijñānavijñeyaḥ | tadā na vaktavyaṃ na rūpaṃ nārūpamiti | evaṃ śabdādayo 'pīti |
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: What you said earlier — 'From the fact that [the question about the self] is to be set aside (<s>sthāpanīya</s>) rather than answered, it is known that the self exists' — that is not correct. Why? That it is an inexpressible <s>dharma</s> will be examined later in the section on the aggregate of the truth of cessation (<s>nirodhasatyaskandha</s>). Therefore, the self does not ultimately exist — it is 'inexpressible,' meaning it is said to be a mere designation (<s>prajñaptimātra</s>) and not something ultimately real. In your teaching, the self is known through the six kinds of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). As your scripture states: 'Form that is seen by the eye is to be appropriated' — and therefore the self perishes. Then this [self] would be knowable by eye-consciousness. In that case, it should not be said that it is 'neither form nor non-form.' The same applies to sound and the other [sense-objects].

body.text: atha yadyātmā ṣaḍvijñānavijñeyaḥ | tadā sūtrairvirucyate | sūtre hyuktam- pañcendriyāṇi nānyopyasya viṣayān pratyanubhavanti | iti | pratyadhvavasāyasya vaiṣamyāt | yadyātmā ṣaḍvijñānavijñeyaḥ syāt | tadā ṣaḍindriyāṇi anyonyavṛttīnī syuḥ | kiñca bhavaduktaṃ pūrvāparaviruddham | yat cakṣurvijñānavijñeyaṃ na tat rūpamiti bravīṣi | bhavānāha- nāstyātmā itīyaṃ mithyādṛṣṭiriti | sūtre bhagavān svayaṃ bhikṣūnāmantryāha- asatyapyātmani saṃskārāṇāṃ
body.translated_text: Now, if the self were knowable by the six kinds of consciousness, then it would be contradicted by the <s>sūtras</s>. For it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The five faculties do not experience each other's objects.' Because of the inequality of the respective determinations [of each faculty]. If the self were knowable by the six kinds of consciousness, then the six faculties would have mutually interchangeable functions. Moreover, your statements are self-contradictory. You say: 'What is knowable by eye-consciousness is not form.' And you say: 'The [view that] there is no self is a wrong view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>).' But in the <s>sūtra</s>, the Blessed One himself addressed the monks saying: 'Even though the self does not exist, I say that through the continuity of the formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) —

body.text: santānamupādāya jananamaraṇamastīti vadāmi | paśyāmi ca divyena cakṣuṣā sattvānutpadyamānān mriyamāṇāṃśca | athāpi na vadāmi astyātmeti |
body.translated_text: — there exists birth and death based on the appropriation of continuity. And with the divine eye, I see beings being born and dying. And yet I do not say: There exists a self.'

body.text: kiñca bhavatāṃ śāsane 'sti doṣaḥ | bhavatāṃ śāsane hyucyate ātmā na jāyata iti | yo 'jātaḥ sa mātāpitṛbhyāṃ vihīnaḥ | mātāpitṛbhyāṃ vihīnasya nāstyānantaryam | anyānyapi pāpakarmāṇi na santi ityato bhavatāṃ śāsanameva mithyādarśanam |
body.translated_text: Moreover, in your teaching there is a fault. In your teaching it is said: 'The self is not born.' One who is unborn is devoid of mother and father. For one who is devoid of mother and father, there is no heinous crime (<s>ānantarya</s>). Other evil <s>karmas</s> too would not exist. Therefore your teaching itself is a wrong view.

body.text: bhavānāha bhavasya pūrvasmādutpāda iti | pañcaskandhānupādāya sudarśano nāma rājā | ta eva pañcaskandhāḥ santatyā buddho bhavati | tasmādāha- ahameva sa rājā iti | bhavatāṃ śāsane ātmana ekatvāt viśeṣo na syāt |
body.translated_text: You say: 'From a previous existence there is arising.' Based on the five aggregates (<s>pañcaskandha</s>), [one was] the king named <s>Sudarśana</s>. Those very five aggregates, through their continuity, become a <s>Buddha</s>. Therefore he said: 'I myself was that king.' In your teaching, because of the oneness of the self, there would be no distinction.

body.text: bhavānāha- kṛtapuṇya ubhayatra nandatīti | sūtre bhagavān idaṃ vastu pratiṣidhyāha- nāhaṃ vadāmi kaścidimān pañcaskandhān parityajya tān skandhānupādatta iti | kintu tatpañcaskandhānāṃ santatyā bhedābhāvādāha- ubhayatna nandatīti | yadbhavānāha- cittasaṃkleśāt sattvāḥ saṃkliśyanta iti | tato nāstyātmā paramārthata iti | yadyastyātmā, cittābhinnaḥ syāt | nocyate sattvasaṃkleśāt sattvāḥ saṃkliśyanta iti | kasmāt | na hi sambhavati tasya saṃkleśasamayaṃ [sattva] upādatta iti | kintu prajñaptyā hetupratyayānāṃ saṃkliṣṭatvāt āha- sattvāḥ saṃkliśyanta iti | ataḥ prajñaptyāstyātmā | na paramārthataḥ | bhavatāṃ śāsane cocyate na pañcaskandhā evātmeti | tadā so 'jāto 'niruddho 'puṇyapāpa ityevamādayo doṣā bhavanti | vayantu vadāmaḥ pañcaskandhānāṃ kalāpaḥ prajñaptyā ātmeti | imamātmānamupādāya asti janma asti nirodhaḥ puṇyapāpamityādi | na ca prajñaptisannāstīti | vastumātraṃ na bhavati | bhavatā pūrvamuktaṃ- tīrthikānāmāśayakhaṇḍanāya bhagavānāha- nāstyātmeti | abhūtasaṃjñayā bhavānevaṃ kalpayati na tathā bhagavadāśayaḥ | vividhā ātmavādāḥ sarve duṣṭāḥ yathā bhavān bravīti- pañcaskandhān vihāya anyo 'styātmeti tīrthikā manyanta iti | tathā bhavānapi [manyate] |
body.translated_text: You say: 'One who has made merit rejoices in both [worlds].' The Blessed One, refuting this very matter, stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'I do not say that someone relinquishes these five aggregates and then takes up those [other] aggregates.' Rather, because there is no break in the continuity of those five aggregates, he said: 'One rejoices in both.' As for what you say — 'Through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled (<s>saṃkliśyante</s>)' — from this it follows that the self does not ultimately exist. If the self exists, it would be distinct from the mind. It is not said: 'Through the defilement of beings, beings are defiled.' Why? Because it is not possible to say that a being appropriates [something] at the time of defilement. Rather, because the causes and conditions are defiled by way of designation (<s>prajñapti</s>), it is said: 'Beings are defiled.' Therefore, the self exists by designation alone, not ultimately. And in your teaching it is said: 'The five aggregates are not the self.' In that case, [the self would be] unborn, unceased, without merit or demerit — and such faults would follow. But we say: the collective assemblage (<s>kalāpa</s>) of the five aggregates is designated as 'self' by convention. Based on this self, there is birth, there is cessation, there is merit and demerit, and so forth. And what exists by designation is not non-existent — but it does not exist as a mere substance. What you said earlier — 'The Blessed One said: There is no self, in order to break the inclination of the <s>tīrthikas</s>' — you conceive this through a false notion, but the intent of the Blessed One is not like that. The various doctrines of self are all erroneous, as you yourself say: 'The <s>tīrthikas</s> think there is a self other than the five aggregates.' And you too think the same way —

body.text: kasmāt | anityā hi pañcaskandhāḥ | ātmātvavaktavyo yadi nityo 'nityo veti | [so] 'yaṃ skandhavinirmukta eva |
body.translated_text: — Why? Because the five aggregates are impermanent. The self, however, is inexpressible as to whether it is permanent or impermanent. This [self of yours] is entirely separate from the aggregates.

body.text: atha skandhasya santi trayo bhedāḥ- śīlasamādhiprajñāḥ, kuśalākuśalāvyākṛtāḥ, kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktarūpadhātupratisaṃyuktārūpyadhātupratisaṃyuktāḥ ityevaṃ vibhāgāḥ | ātmānastu tathā vibhaktā na bhavanti | ataḥ pañcaskandhebhyo 'nyaḥ | ātmā ca pudgalaḥ | pañcaskandhā na pudgalaḥ | tadā tvayamanyo bhavati | skandhāḥ pañca | ātmātvekaḥ | ityato nātmā skandhāḥ | asti cedātmā | sa ebhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ pañcaskandhebhyo 'nyaḥ syāt | loke ca nāsti ko 'pi dharma eka ityavaktavyaḥ | ato nāsti kaścidavaktavyo dharmaḥ |
body.translated_text: Now, the aggregates have three classifications: moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), concentration (<s>samādhi</s>), and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>); wholesome (<s>kuśala</s>), unwholesome (<s>akuśala</s>), and indeterminate (<s>avyākṛta</s>); associated with the desire-realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>), associated with the form-realm (<s>rūpadhātu</s>), and associated with the formless realm (<s>ārūpyadhātu</s>) — such are the divisions. But the self cannot be divided in that way. Therefore it is other than the five aggregates. And the self is a person (<s>pudgala</s>). The five aggregates are not a person. In that case, this [self] would be something else. The aggregates are five; but the self is one. Therefore the self is not the aggregates. If the self exists, it would, for these reasons, be other than the five aggregates. And in the world, there is no <s>dharma</s> whatsoever that is 'one' and yet 'inexpressible.' Therefore there is no inexpressible <s>dharma</s> whatsoever.

body.text: (pṛ) yathā agnirindhanañca na vaktuṃ śakyata evaṃ vā nānā veti | tathātmāpi syāt | (u) idaṃ sandigdhasamam | kimagniḥ kimindhanamiti | yadi tejodhāturagniḥ anye dhātava indhanam | tadā agnirindhanātpṛthak syāt | yadi tejodhāturevendhanam | kathamucyate naikamiti | yadindhanaṃ sa eva tejodhātuḥ | tejodhātuṃ vināpi [dahet] ityubhayamayuktam | ataḥ sandigdhasamam | yasyāgnirindhanavān yathā ātmā rūpavān iti | tasya satkāyadṛṣṭipātaḥ | ātmabahutvañca syāt | yathā kāṣṭhāgniranyaḥ gomayāgniścānyaḥ | evātmāpi | manuṣyaskandheṣvanya ātmā | devaskandheṣvanya ātmā itīdamātmabahutvam | yathāgnirindhanañca triṣu adhvasu vartate | evamātmāpi pañcaskandhaiḥ saha triṣu adhvasu vartamānaṃ syāt | yathā cāgnirindhanaṃñca saṃskṛtam, ātmāpi pañcaskandhaiḥ saha saṃskṛtaṃ syāt | yadyapi bhavānāha- agnirindhanena naiko na nānā iti | tathāpi cakṣuṣā paśyāmaḥ khalu nānālakṣaṇe | ātmāpi pañcaskandhāścānye syuḥ | kiñca pañcaskandhā naśyanti | ātmā tu na naśyati | asmāt lokāt cyutaḥ paraloka utpadyate | ubhayatra nandiyuktatvāt | yaḥ pañcaskandhānanusṛtya savināśaḥ sotpādaśca | sa pañcaskandhasamo nobhayatra nandiko bhavati | bhavāṃstu abhūtasaṃjñayā imamātmānaṃ vikalpya keṣāṃ hitaṃ prāpayati |
body.translated_text: (Objection) Just as fire and fuel cannot be stated to be the same or different, so too with the self. (Reply) This is an argument based on a doubtful analogy. What is fire? What is fuel? If the fire-element (<s>tejodhātu</s>) is fire and the other elements are fuel, then fire would be separate from fuel. If the fire-element itself is the fuel, how can it be said that they are not one? If the fuel is the fire-element itself, then [fire] would burn even without fuel — both [options] are untenable. Therefore this is a doubtful analogy. For one who [holds that] fire possesses fuel just as the self possesses form — for him there is the fall into the view of the personal aggregate (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>). And there would be a multiplicity of selves — just as the fire of wood is one and the fire of cow-dung is another, so too the self [would differ]: there would be one self in the human aggregates and another self in the divine aggregates — this is the multiplicity of selves. Just as fire and fuel exist in the three time-periods, so too the self, together with the five aggregates, would exist in the three time-periods. And just as fire and fuel are conditioned (<s>saṃskṛta</s>), so too the self, together with the five aggregates, would be conditioned. Although you say: 'Fire and fuel are neither one nor different,' nevertheless we see with the eye that they have different characteristics. The self too would be different from the five aggregates. Moreover, the five aggregates perish, but the self does not perish — having departed from this world, it arises in the next world, because of being endowed with joy in both. One who follows the five aggregates and is subject to their destruction and arising — if equal to the five aggregates, he would not be one who rejoices in both. But you, through a false notion, conceiving this self — whom do you benefit?

body.text: viṣayeṣu na ko 'pyasti ṣaḍvijñānavijñeyaḥ | ṣaḍvijñānavijñeya iti bhavatokta ātmā na ṣaḍviṣayarūpo bhavati | yo dvādaśāyataneṣvasaṅgṛhītaḥ | na sa āyataneṣu bhavati | caturṣu satyeṣu asaṅgraprahītaśca na satyeṣu bhavati | tasmādastyātmeti yadvacanaṃ sa mṛṣāvādaḥ |
body.translated_text: There is nothing among the sense-objects that is knowable by the six kinds of consciousness [and is also the self]. The self that you described as 'knowable by the six kinds of consciousness' does not have the nature of the six sense-objects. That which is not comprised in the twelve sense-bases (<s>dvādaśāyatana</s>) does not exist among the sense-bases. And that which is not comprised in the four truths (<s>catursatya</s>) does not exist among the truths. Therefore, the statement 'there is a self' is a false utterance.

body.text: bhavatāṃ śāsana ucyate jñeyadharmā yaduta pañcadharmakośāḥ- atītā anāgatāḥ pratyutpannā asaṃskṛtā avaktavyā iti | ātmā pañcamadharmāntargataḥ | tadā caturbhyo dharmebhyo 'nyaḥ | sa caturbhyo dharmebhyo 'nya itīcchanti khalu bhavantaḥ | ayaṃ pañcamastu na sambhavati | ātmāstitvavādasyedṛśā doṣā bhavanti | kimātmeti mithyāsaṃjñāvikalpena | ato bhavatā pūrvamuktam- tīrthikāḥ pañcaskandhān vihāya pṛthagātmāstīti manyante | vayantu na tathā iti | tadayuktam | yadbhavānāha- ātmā prajñaptimātramitīdaṃ gāḍhataraṃ cintanīyam iti | tadapyayuktam | kasmāt | jinaśāsane hyucyate lokasatyavastu na pragāḍhaṃ cintanīyam iti | yat bhavatoktaṃ mṛṣāvādino viparyayadarśinaḥ syuriti | idamapi tathaiva | yadavādīḥ "sūtragatāni pāramārthikāni" [ityādi] vacanaṃ na syāditi | tattathā prativaktavyaṃ yathā paramārtho jñāyeta | yadavocadbhavān lokoktāni sarvāṇi anusartavyāni yadvadanti īśvarādutpannāni na yutāni vastūni ityādi | na tadupādeyam | yaddhitakaraṃ paramārthāvilomakaṃ tadupādeyamityato 'navadyam | yallokasatyato guṇotpādakaṃ hitakarañca | īdṛśaṃ sarvamupādeyam iti paścādvakṣyate | yadavādīḥ- mṛṇmayagavādihanane nāsti pāpamiti | tadidānīṃ prativaktavyam | savijñānānāṃ skandhānāṃ santatyā samudācāre sati asti karma asti vipākaḥ | mṛṇmayagavādiṣu tu nedamasti | tasmāt pañcaskandhānāṃ kalāpaḥ prajñaptyā ātmā ityākhyāyate | na vastusattayā iti jñātavyam ||
body.translated_text: In your teaching it is said that knowable <s>dharmas</s> consist of five categories (<s>dharmakośa</s>): past, future, present, unconditioned, and inexpressible. The self is included in the fifth category. In that case, it is other than the four [remaining] categories. And you hold that it is other than those four categories. But this fifth [category] is not tenable. Such are the faults of the doctrine that the self exists. What then is 'the self' other than a conceptual construction arising from a false notion? Therefore, what you said earlier — 'The <s>tīrthikas</s> think there is a self separate from the five aggregates; but we do not think so' — that is untenable. And your statement that 'the self is a mere designation — this is to be thought about more deeply' — that too is untenable. Why? Because in the teaching of the <s>Jina</s> it is said that matters pertaining to conventional truth (<s>lokasatyavastu</s>) should not be thought about deeply. As for your claim that 'they would be speakers of falsehood and seers of perversion' — this too is the same [refutation]. As for your statement that the words found in the <s>sūtras</s> that are 'ultimate' would not exist — that should be replied to in such a way that the ultimate is understood. As for your statement that all worldly conventions should be followed, [including the assertion that] things are produced from <s>Īśvara</s> and the like — that should not be accepted. What is beneficial and does not contradict ultimate truth should be accepted — therefore it is blameless. Whatever, from the standpoint of conventional truth, produces virtue and is beneficial — all such things should be accepted, as will be explained later. As for your statement: 'In killing a clay cow and the like, there is no sin' — this should now be addressed. When the continuity and activity of conscious aggregates exists, there is <s>karma</s> and there is its fruit. But in clay cows and the like, this does not exist. Therefore, the assemblage of the five aggregates is designated as 'self' by convention — it should be understood that it does not exist as a real substance.

body.text: ātmāstitvanāstitvavargaḥ pañcatriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the thirty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Existence and Non-Existence of the Self (<s>ātmāstitvanāstitvavarga</s>).

body.text: satyasiddhiśāstre prathamaḥ prasthānaskandhaḥ samāptaḥ |
body.translated_text: In the <s>Satyasiddhi-śāstra</s>, the first section — the Section on the Approach (<s>prasthānaskandha</s>) — is completed.

body.text: atha duḥkhasatyaskandhaḥ |
body.translated_text: Now, the Section on the Aggregate of the Truth of Suffering (<s>duḥkhasatyaskandha</s>).

body.text: 36 duḥkhasatyaskandhe rūpādhikāre rūpalakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 36. In the Section on the Truth of Suffering, in the subsection on Form: the Chapter on the Characteristic of Form (<s>rūpalakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) pūrvamavādīḥ satyasiddhiśāstraṃ pravakṣyāmīti | idānīṃ vaktavyaṃ kiṃ tat satyamiti | (u) satyaṃ nāma catvāri [ārya]satyāni yaduta duḥkhaṃ duḥkhasamudayo duḥkhanirodho duḥkhanirodhagāminī patipat | pañcopādānaskandhā duḥkham | karmakleśāśca duḥkhasamudayaḥ | duḥkhakṣayo duḥkhanirodhaḥ | aṣṭāṅgikamārgo duḥkhanirodhagāminī pratipat | itīmaṃ dharmaṃ sādhayitumidaṃ śāstraṃ nibadhyate | tathāgataḥ svayamimaṃ dharmaṃ sādhayannapi sattvānāṃ tāraṇāya tatra tatra viprakīrṇaṃ deśitavān | caturaśītisahasrātmakaṃ dharmapiṭakaṃ sa saṃkṣipyovāca | tatra catvāri pratiśaraṇāni aṣṭau hetava [ityādi] | teṣāmarthaṃ kecidupekṣya nāvocan | kecit saṃkṣipyāvocan | athedānīṃ teṣāmarthaviniścayāya anusaṃkalayya vivakṣāmi |
body.translated_text: (Question) Previously you said: 'I shall expound the <s>Satyasiddhi-śāstra</s>.' Now it is to be stated: what is that truth? (Answer) Truth means the Four Noble Truths (<s>āryasatya</s>), namely: suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), the origin of suffering (<s>duḥkhasamudaya</s>), the cessation of suffering (<s>duḥkhanirodha</s>), and the path leading to the cessation of suffering (<s>duḥkhanirodhagāminī pratipad</s>). The five aggregates of clinging (<s>pañcopādānaskandha</s>) are suffering. <s>Karma</s> and defilements (<s>kleśa</s>) are the origin of suffering. The destruction of suffering is the cessation of suffering. The Eightfold Path (<s>aṣṭāṅgikamārga</s>) is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. In order to establish this <s>Dharma</s>, this treatise is composed. The <s>Tathāgata</s>, himself establishing this <s>Dharma</s> and for the purpose of ferrying beings across, taught it scattered here and there. He summarized the <s>Dharma</s>-treasury (<s>dharmapiṭaka</s>) consisting of eighty-four thousand [teachings]. Therein are the four refuges (<s>pratiśaraṇa</s>), the eight causes, and so forth. Some neglected their meaning and did not expound it. Some expounded it in summary form. Therefore now, for the determination of their meaning, I shall compile and expound it.

body.text: (pṛ) yadbhavānāha- pañcopādānaskandhā duḥkhasatyamiti | ke te pañca | (u) rūpaskandhaḥ, vijñānaskandhaḥ, saṃjñāvedanāsaṃskāraskandhāḥ | rūpaskandho yaduta catvāri mahābhūtāni catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya dharmāśca | catvāri mahābhūtāni tānyupādāya dharmāścābhisaṃkṣipya rūpamityucyate | catvāri mahābhūtāni pṛthivyaptejovāyavaḥ | rūparasagandhasparśānupādāya sidhyanti catvāri mahābhūtāni | tānyupādāya sidhyanti cakṣurādīni pañcendriyāṇi | teṣāṃ mithaḥ saṃsparśācchabdaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) As you have said: 'The five aggregates of clinging (<s>pañcopādānaskandha</s>) are the truth of suffering' — what are those five? (Answer) The form aggregate (<s>rūpaskandha</s>), the consciousness aggregate (<s>vijñānaskandha</s>), the perception aggregate (<s>saṃjñāskandha</s>), the feeling aggregate (<s>vedanāskandha</s>), and the formations aggregate (<s>saṃskāraskandha</s>). The form aggregate is the four great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>) and the <s>dharmas</s> derived from the four great elements. The four great elements, together with the <s>dharmas</s> derived from them, when summarized, are called 'form' (<s>rūpa</s>). The four great elements are earth (<s>pṛthivī</s>), water (<s>ap</s>), fire (<s>tejas</s>), and wind (<s>vāyu</s>). Dependent on form, taste, smell, and touch, the four great elements are established. Dependent on them, the five sense faculties (<s>indriya</s>) beginning with the eye are established. From their mutual contact, sound arises.

body.text: pṛthivīti | rūpādisamavāyaḥ kāṭhinyabahulaḥ pṛthivītyucyate | tathā snehabahulaḥ abdhātuḥ | ūṣmabahulastejodhātuḥ | ladhvīraṇabahulo vāyudhātuḥ | cakṣurindriyamiti rūpāṇi pratītya [utpannasya] cakṣurvijñānasyāśraya eva | [yastu] tatsabhāgaḥ anāśrayaḥ [tadapi] cakṣurindriyaṃ [tatsājātyāt] | tathānyānīndriyāṇyapi | rūpamiti | cakṣurvijñānasyālambanameva | tatsabhāgo 'nālambanaṃ tu [tatsājātyāt] rūpam | rasagandhasparśā apyevam | eṣāṃ mithaḥ saṃsparśācchabdo bhavati ||
body.translated_text: 'Earth' (<s>pṛthivī</s>): the combination of form and the rest, predominantly characterized by hardness, is called 'earth.' Likewise, that which is predominantly moist is the water element (<s>abdhātu</s>). That which is predominantly warm is the fire element (<s>tejodhātu</s>). That which is predominantly characterized by lightness and movement is the wind element (<s>vāyudhātu</s>). 'Eye faculty' (<s>cakṣurindriya</s>): it is precisely the support of the visual consciousness that arises dependent on forms. That which is of the same class but is not a support — that too is the eye faculty, because it is of the same kind. Likewise for the other faculties. 'Form' (<s>rūpa</s>): it is precisely the object of visual consciousness. That which is of the same class but is not an object — that too is form, because it is of the same kind. Taste, smell, and touch are likewise. From their mutual contact, sound arises.

body.text: rūpalakṣaṇavargaḥ ṣaṭtriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the thirty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of Form (<s>rūpalakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 37 rūpanāmavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 37. Chapter on the Name of Form (<s>rūpanāmavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) uktaṃ khalu sūtre- yatkiñcana rūpaṃ sarvaṃ tat catvāri mahābhūtāni catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya [rūpam] iti | kasmāduktaṃ yatkiñcana rūpaṃ tatsarvamiti | (u) yatkiñcit tatsarvamiti vadan rūpalakṣaṇaṃ nirdhārayati nānyadastīti | tīrthikā hi vadanti pañca mahābhūtānīti | tatpratyākhyānāyāha catvāri [eva] mahābhūtāni catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya [rūpam] iti | catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptitaḥ santi | vyāpitvāt mahadityucyate | arūpadharmo 'mūrtaḥ | amūrtatvāt apradeśaḥ | apradeśatvāt na mahān | audārikatvācca mahadityucyate | cittacaittānāñcādṛṣṭatvāt na mahattvam |
body.translated_text: (Question) It is indeed stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Whatever form there is, all of it is the four great elements and form derived from the four great elements.' Why was it said 'whatever form there is, all of it'? (Answer) By saying 'whatever, all of it,' one determines the characteristic of form, meaning 'there is nothing else.' For the <s>tīrthikas</s> (non-Buddhist teachers) say there are five great elements. In order to refute that, he said: 'Only four great elements and form derived from the four great elements.' The four great elements exist as designations (<s>prajñapti</s>). Because they pervade, they are called 'great' (<s>mahat</s>). A formless <s>dharma</s> is immaterial (<s>amūrta</s>). Being immaterial, it has no spatial location. Having no spatial location, it is not 'great.' And because of grossness, [form] is called 'great.' Because mind and mental factors are invisible, they do not have the quality of greatness.

body.text: (pṛ) kasmāt pṛthivyādaya eva rūpaṃ na śabdaḥ | (u) sapratighā dharmā rūpamityucyante | śabdādayo 'pi sapratighatvāt rūpam | na cittadharmādivat sākāratvāt rūpam | śabdādayo 'pi sākāratvāt rūpamityucyeran | yatkiñcan pradeśāvaraṇaṃ hi ākāraḥ | (pṛ) rūpādaya aparikṣīyamāṇākārāḥ | śabdādināntu nāsti [tādṛśa] ākāraḥ | (u) śabdādayaḥ sarve sākārāḥ | sākāratvena sapratighāḥ sāvaraṇāḥ | ato bhittyāvaraṇe na śrūyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) Why is only earth and the rest called 'form' and not sound? (Answer) <s>Dharmas</s> that offer resistance (<s>sapratigha</s>) are called 'form.' Sound and the rest, being also resistant, are form. It is not the case that form is defined by having shape (<s>sākāra</s>) like mind-<s>dharmas</s> and so forth. Sound and the rest, also having shape, would also be called form. For whatever has spatial obstruction is 'shape.' (Question) Form and the rest have shapes that are not exhausted. But sound and the rest do not have such shape. (Answer) Sound and the rest all have shape. Having shape, they are resistant and obstructive. Therefore, when obstructed by a wall, [sound] is not heard.

body.text: (pṛ) śabdādayo yadi sapratighāḥ | tadā nānyavastūnyādadyuḥ | yathā bhittyāvaraṇe na kasyacidavakāśo labhyate | (u) śabdasyātisūkṣmatvāt upādeyāstitā śakyate | yathā gandharasādayaḥ saukṣmyāt ekamākāraṃ yugapadāśrayante na mithaḥ pratighnanti | ataḥ śabdādayaḥ sāvaraṇāḥ sapratighā ityato rūpamityucyante | rūpyata iti rūpalakṣaṇam | yat chidyate bhidyate vihiṃsyata ityādi tat sarvaṃ rūpāśritam | etadviparītamarūpamiti nirdhāritam |
body.translated_text: (Question) If sound and the rest are resistant, then they would not take hold of other objects. Just as when a wall is obstructing, no space is available for anything. (Answer) Because sound is extremely subtle, its taking hold is possible. Just as smell, taste, and the rest, due to their subtlety, simultaneously occupy a single location and do not obstruct each other. Therefore, sound and the rest are obstructive and resistant — hence they are called 'form.' 'That which is formed (<s>rūpyate</s>)' — this is the characteristic of form. Whatever is cut, broken, destroyed, and so forth — all of that is based on form. The opposite of this is determined to be 'non-form.'

body.text: pūrvanivāsasthakuśalākuśalakarmāṇi nirūpayatīti rūpam | cittacaittān nirūpayatīti ca rūpam | varṇātmakañca rūpam |
body.translated_text: Form reveals (<s>nirūpayati</s>) the wholesome and unwholesome <s>karmas</s> of previous existences. And form reveals mind and mental factors. And form is that which has the nature of color (<s>varṇa</s>).

body.text: rūpanāmavargaḥ saptatriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the thirty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Name of Form (<s>rūpanāmavarga</s>).

body.text: 38 caturmahābhūtaprajñaptivargaḥ
body.translated_text: 38. Chapter on the Designation-Existence of the Four Great Elements (<s>caturmahābhūtaprajñaptivarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptisantītyayamartho 'siddhaḥ | keciddhi vadanti tāni dravyasantīti | (u) catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptitaḥ santi | kasmāt | bhagavān tīrthikebhyo 'vocat- catvāri mahābhūtāni iti | tīrthikāḥ kecidvadanti rūpādireva mahābhūtaṃ bhavatīti yathā sāṃkhyādīnām | kecidvadanti rūpādi vihāyāsti mahābhūtam iti yathā vaiśeṣikādīnām | ata idaṃ sūtramavadhārayati rūpādyupādāya pṛthivyādi mahābhūtaṃ sidhyatīti | ato jñāyate mahābhūtāni prajñaptisantīti |
body.translated_text: (Question) The meaning of 'the four great elements exist as designations (<s>prajñapti</s>)' is not established. For some say they exist as real substances (<s>dravya</s>). (Answer) The four great elements exist as designations. Why? The Blessed One said to the <s>tīrthikas</s>: 'There are four great elements.' The <s>tīrthikas</s> — some say the great element is identical with form and the rest, as the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> and others hold. Others say the great element exists apart from form and the rest, as the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> and others hold. Therefore this <s>sūtra</s> determines: 'Dependent on form and the rest, earth and the other great elements are established.' From this it is known that the great elements exist as designations.

body.text: kiñcāha sūtram- khakkhaṭaḥ kharagataḥ pṛthivīdhātuḥ iti | ato na kharamātraṃ pṛthivī | laukikāśca sarve śraddadhante mahābhūtāni prajñaptisantīti | kasmāt | te hi vadanti pṛthivīṃ paśyāmi pṛthivīṃ jighremi (dharmi) pṛthivīṃ rasayāmi pṛthivīṃ spṛśāmi iti | sūtre coktaṃ yathā sparśavatī pṛthivī draṣṭavyā | pṛthivyādisarvāyata nagato 'yaṃ puruṣaḥ paśyati rūpaṃ na kaṭhinyādi | kiñca puruṣo nirūpayati [idaṃ] pṛthivīrūpam, pṛthivīgandhaḥ, pṛthivīrasaḥ pṛthivīsparśa iti | na dravyasataḥ pṛthaṅ nirūpaṇamupalabhyate | vyāpitvāt mahadityarthaḥ | idaṃ
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the <s>sūtra</s> says: 'Hard and solid is the earth element.' Therefore, earth is not mere hardness. And all worldly people have faith that the great elements exist as designations. Why? For they say: 'I see earth, I smell earth, I taste earth, I touch earth.' And the <s>sūtra</s> also says: 'Earth should be seen as having the quality of touch.' A person, standing on the ground of earth and the rest, sees form — not hardness and so forth. Furthermore, a person distinguishes: 'This is the form of earth, this is the smell of earth, this is the taste of earth, this is the touch of earth.' Such separate distinguishing is not found in what exists as a real substance. 'Because it pervades, it is called great' — this is the meaning. This

body.text: lakṣaṇaṃ prajñaptisata ucyate | na kaṭhinyamātralakṣaṇasya | kiñcāha- pṛthivī abmaṇḍale pratiṣṭhitā iti | prajñaptisatī pṛthivī pratitiṣṭhati | na kāṭhinyamātrama | kiñcāha- ahamimāṃ mahāpṛthivīṃ dagdhvā vidhūmaṃ bhasmasātkariṣyāmīti | atra prajñaptisatīṃ pṛthivīṃ dahati na kāṭhinyamātraṃ dahati | rūpādibhyaḥ śraddadhante asti pṛthivī ityādi | na kāṭhinyamātrāt |
body.translated_text: characteristic is spoken of with respect to what exists as a designation — not of what is characterized by mere hardness. Furthermore, it says: 'Earth is established upon the circle of water.' It is the earth existing as a designation that is so established — not mere hardness. Furthermore, it says: 'I shall burn this great earth, reducing it to smokeless ashes.' Here, it is the earth existing as a designation that is burned — it is not mere hardness that is burned. From form and the rest, people have faith that 'earth exists' and so forth — not from mere hardness.

body.text: kūpopame coktam- āpo dṛśyante ca spṛśyante ceti | yadi sneha evāpaḥ | tadā na dvidhā varteran | kasmāt | bhagavānāha- pañcemānīndriyāṇi [nānāviṣayāṇi] nānyonyasya viṣayaṃ pratyanubhavanti | iti | kiñcāha bhagavān- aṣṭaguṇā āpaḥsusaṃsthitaṃ śītalaṃ mṛdu madhuraṃ śuci adurgandhaṃ pātuḥ prahlādanaṃ paridāhanivāraṇamiti | tatra yat susaṃsthitaṃ śītalaṃ sukumāraṃ tat sarvaṃ sparśāntargatam | madhuraṃ rasāntargatam | śuci rūpāntargatam | adurgandhaṃ gandhāntargatam | prahlādanaṃ paridāhanivāraṇañca tatprabhāvaḥ | eṣāmaṣṭānāṃ kalāpaḥ sāmānyamāpa ityucyate | ato jñāyate mahābhūtāni prajñaptisantīti | upādāya dharmāḥ sarve prajñaptisantaḥ na dravyasantaḥ | yathoktaṃ gāthāyām-
body.translated_text: In the Sūtra of the Well (<s>kūpopama</s>) it is said: 'Waters are seen and also touched.' If water were merely moisture, it would not function in two ways. Why? The Blessed One said: 'These five faculties have different domains and do not experience each other's domain.' Furthermore, the Blessed One said: 'Water has eight qualities: well-formed, cool, soft, sweet, pure, free from bad odor, refreshing to drink, and removing burning.' Among these, that which is well-formed, cool, and delicate — all that falls under touch. Sweet falls under taste. Pure falls under form. Free from bad odor falls under smell. Refreshing and removing burning are its efficacy. The collection of these eight constitutes what is generally called 'water.' From this it is known that the great elements exist as designations. All derived <s>dharmas</s> exist as designations, not as real substances. As stated in the verse:

body.text:
yathā hyaṅgasambhārādbhavati śabdo ratheti ca |
evaṃ skandheṣu satsveva bhavati sattveti saṃvṛtiḥ || iti |
body.translated_text:
Just as from the assemblage of parts the word 'chariot' arises,
so too, when the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) exist, there arises the convention 'being' (<s>sattva</s>).

body.text: āha cānandaḥ- pratyayamayā dharmāḥ | ātmā cāviniścayasthānaṃ bhavati iti | ye vadanti karkaśādīni mahābhūtānīti | te karkaśādīni rūpādīnāmāśrayā iti manyante |
body.translated_text: And <s>Ānanda</s> said: '<s>Dharmas</s> are constituted by conditions. And the self (<s>ātman</s>) is a matter of indeterminacy.' Those who say that hardness and the like are the great elements — they think that hardness and the like are the supports of form and the rest.

body.text:
tattu sāśrayayaṃ sādhiṣṭhānakamiti na tathāgataśāsanaṃ bhavet | ato jñāyate catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptisantīti |
dharmāṇāṃ saukṣmyasokumāryaślakṣṇatvādīni sarvāṇi sparśāyatanasaṃgṛhītāni | khakkhaṭādayaścatvāro dharmāḥ kimarthā bhavantiiti kevalaṃ mahābhūtārthā bhavati iti prāpyate | ekādicaturgrahāḥ sāvadyāḥ | ato jñāyate catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptimātrāṇi iti | vastudharmaḥ salakṣaṇaḥ prajñaptidharmaśca salakṣaṇaḥ | prajñapteśca ko 'tiśaya iti paścādvakṣyate | ataścatvāri mahābhūtāni na dravyasanti ||
body.translated_text: But [to say that form and the rest] have a support and have a basis — that would not be the teaching of the <s>Tathāgata</s>. From this it is known that the four great elements exist as designations. The subtlety, delicacy, smoothness, and the like of all <s>dharmas</s> are all included in the touch sense-base (<s>sparśāyatana</s>). What purpose then do the four <s>dharmas</s> of hardness and the rest serve? They serve solely the purpose of [defining] the great elements — so it is concluded. Grasping them individually from one to four is faulty. From this it is known that the four great elements are mere designations. A real <s>dharma</s> has its own characteristic, and a designated <s>dharma</s> also has its own characteristic. What is the distinction of designation — this will be explained later. Therefore the four great elements do not exist as real substances.

body.text: caturmahābhūtaprajñaptivargo 'ṣṭatriṃśaḥ
body.translated_text: This is the thirty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Designation-Existence of the Four Great Elements (<s>caturmahābhūtaprajñaptivarga</s>).

body.text: 39 caturmahābhūtadravyasattāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 39. Chapter on the Substance-Existence of the Four Great Elements (<s>caturmahābhūtadravyasattāvarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) catvāri mahābhūtāni dravyasanti | kasmāt | abhidharma uktam | khakkhaṭalakṣaṇaḥ pṛthivīdhātuḥ snehalakṣaṇo 'bdhātuḥ ūṣmalakṣaṇastejodhātuḥ īraṇalakṣaṇo vāyudhāturiti | ataścatvāri mahābhūtāni dravyasanti | rūpādi bhautikaṃ rūpaṃ caturbhyo mahābhūtebhyaḥ samutpadyate | na prajñaptisan dharmaṃ janayati | khakkhaṭādinā ca catvāri mahābhūtāni nirucyante yat khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ sā pṛthivīti | tasmāt khakkhaṭādīni dravyamahābhūtāni | kiñca sūtre dvābhyāmākārābhyāmucyate khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ, snehaḥ snehagatam ityādi | ato jñāyate khakkhaṭaṃ vastudharmaḥ kharagataṃ prajñaptidharma iti | evamanyānyapi mahābhūtāni | tasmāt khakkhaṭādīni dravyamahābhūtāni | kharagatadharmastu vyavahārato mahābhūtam | ato 'sti dvidhā
body.translated_text: (Question) The four great elements exist as real substances (<s>dravya</s>). Why? In the <s>Abhidharma</s> it is said: 'The earth element has the characteristic of hardness; the water element has the characteristic of moisture; the fire element has the characteristic of heat; the wind element has the characteristic of movement.' Therefore the four great elements exist as real substances. The derived material form arises from the four great elements. What exists merely as a designation does not generate a <s>dharma</s>. And by hardness and the rest, the four great elements are etymologically defined — 'what is hard and solid, that is earth.' Therefore hardness and the rest are the substantial great elements. Furthermore, in the <s>sūtra</s>, they are described in two ways: 'hard and solid, moist and fluid,' and so forth. From this it is known that hardness is a real <s>dharma</s> and solidity is a designated <s>dharma</s>. Likewise for the other great elements. Therefore hardness and the rest are the substantial great elements. Solidity and the rest are conventional great elements. Thus there are two kinds of

body.text: mahābhūtaṃ dravyarūpaṃ prajñaptirūpamiti | kiñcoktamabhidharme- saṃsthānāyatanaṃ pṛthivī, khakkhaṭalakṣaṇaḥ pṛthivīdhāturiti | tathānyānyapi mahābhūtāni |
body.translated_text: great elements: substantial form (<s>dravyarūpa</s>) and designated form (<s>prajñaptirūpa</s>). Furthermore, it is said in the <s>Abhidharma</s>: 'The sense-base of configuration is earth; the characteristic of hardness is the earth element.' Likewise for the other great elements.

body.text: sūtre cāha bhagavān- yaccakṣuṣi [māṃsa]piṇḍe khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ iyaṃ pṛthivī | yat snehaḥ snehagataṃ imā āpaḥ | yat ūṣma ūṣmagataṃ idaṃ tejaḥ | māṃsapiṇḍaṃ pṛthivī iti | asmin māṃsapiṇḍe bhagavānāha santi catvāri mahābhūtāni iti | khakkhaṭādīni dravyamahābhūtāni | tatsaṃsthānāni prajñaptimahābhūtānīti jñātavyam | kiñca bhagavānnāvocat vāyorāśrayo 'stīti | ato jñāyate vāyurdravyamahābhūtamiti |
body.translated_text: And the Blessed One said in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'In the lump of flesh of the eye, what is hard and solid — that is earth. What is moist and fluid — that is water. What is warm and heat-producing — that is fire.' The lump of flesh is earth. In this lump of flesh, the Blessed One said there are four great elements. Hardness and the rest are the substantial great elements. Their configurations are to be known as the designated great elements. Furthermore, the Blessed One did not say that wind has a support. From this it is known that wind is a substantial great element.

body.text: yadi kaścit brūyāt catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptisantīti | tadā mahābhūtalakṣaṇāni vinirbhaktāni syuḥ | yadi kharagataṃ pṛthivīti āpaḥ kharagatā iti tā api pṛthivī syuḥ | mṛtpiṇḍaḥ snehagata iti so 'pi āpaḥ syāt | yathā jvarapīḍitasya kāya utkampyate | taptaḥ kāya eva tejaḥ syāt | tanna yujyate | ato na vaktuṃ śakyate kharagataṃ pṛthivī, khakkhaṭamātraṃ pṛthivīdhāturiti | tathānyāni mahābhūtānyapi |
body.translated_text: If someone were to say that the four great elements exist as designations, then the characteristics of the great elements would be separable. If solidity is earth, then if water is also solid, it too would be earth. If a lump of clay is fluid, it too would be water. Just as when a person afflicted by fever — his body trembles; [yet] the heated body itself would be fire. That is not tenable. Therefore, it cannot be said that solidity is earth and mere hardness is the earth element. Likewise for the other great elements.

body.text: sahajātatvāt catvāri mahābhūtāni avinirbhaktāni | yathoktaṃ sūtre yatkiñcidrūpaṃ sarvaṃ tat caturmahābhūtakṛtamiti | catvāri mahābhūtāni dravyasantīti vaktustānyavinirbhaktāni bhavanti | catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptisantīti vaktustāni vinirbhaktāni syuḥ | kasmāt | khararūpādyāśrayāḥ snehādyāśrayebhyo vinirbhaktāḥ | tathā ca sati cakṣurmāsapiṇḍe catvāri mahābhūtāni na syuḥ | tathā ca sūtravirodhaḥ | sūtrasyāvirodhaṃ kāmayānasya bhavataḥ catvāri mahābhūtāni dravyāṇi bhavanti |
body.translated_text: Because they are co-born, the four great elements are inseparable. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Whatever form there is, all of it is produced by the four great elements.' For one who says the four great elements exist as real substances, they are inseparable. For one who says the four great elements exist as designations, they would be separable. Why? Because the supports of hard form and the rest are distinct from the supports of moisture and the rest. If so, there would not be four great elements in the lump of flesh of the eye. And that would contradict the <s>sūtra</s>. For one who desires non-contradiction with the <s>sūtra</s>, the four great elements are real substances.

body.text: yadbhavatā pūrvamuktam- tīrthikebhyaścatvāri mahābhūtānyavocaditi | tadayuktam | kasmāt | sarve hi tīrthikā vadanti catvāri mahābhūtāni rūpādibhirekāni yadi vānakānīti |
body.translated_text: What you said earlier — 'he taught the four great elements to the <s>tīrthikas</s>' — that is not valid. Why? For all the <s>tīrthikas</s> say that the four great elements are either identical with or different from form and the rest.

body.text: vayantu vadāmaḥ spraṣṭavyāyatanaikadeśa ścatvāri mahābhūtānīti | ato 'navadyam | kiñca vayaṃ vadāmaḥ pratyakṣadṛṣṭāni khakkhaṭādīni caturmahābhūtāni na tu vaiśeṣikāṇāmiva tānyapratyakṣadṛṣṭānyapi |
body.translated_text: But we say: the four great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>) are a portion of the tangible sense-base (<s>spraṣṭavyāyatana</s>). Therefore there is no fault. Furthermore, we say that the four great elements such as hardness and the rest are directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣadṛṣṭa</s>), and not — as for the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> — imperceptible.

body.text: yaduktaṃ bhavatā khakkhaṭaṃ kharagatamiti | tatra asti dvidhāśrayārthaḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- rūpaṃ rūpādhikaraṇam iti | āha ca cittaṃ mahatāṃ dharmāṇāmāśraya iti | asminnartha uktam khakkhaṭameva svaragataṃ na punardhamāntaramiti | tathā ca ko doṣaḥ |
body.translated_text: As for your statement that 'hardness (<s>khakkhaṭa</s>) is the same as roughness (<s>kharagata</s>)' — therein, the meaning of 'basis' (<s>āśraya</s>) is twofold. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Form is the support of form.' And it says: 'The mind is the basis of great <s>dharmas</s>.' In this sense, it has been said that hardness itself is what is characterized by roughness, not a different <s>dharma</s>. If so, what is the fault?

body.text: laukikāḥ sarve śraddadhante yāvadaṣṭaguṇā āpa iti yadbhavato vacanaṃ tat vyavahārānuvartanamātrato vadanti na dravyamahābhūtā [nuvartana]taḥ | kiñcoktaṃ bhavatā- upādāyadharmāḥ sarve prajñaptyātmakā iti | nedaṃ yujyate | kasmāt | uktaṃ hi sūtre- yadi vā ṣaṭ sparśāyatanāni yadi vā ṣaṭ sparśāyatanānyupādāya dharmā iti | kaścidbhikṣurbhagavantaṃ pṛcchati- ka tat cakṣuriti | bhagavān pratyāha- cakṣu[rbhikṣo] catvāri mahāmūtānyupādāya rūpaprasāda iti | evaṃ daśāyatanānyapi | yattu sāśrayaṃ sādhiṣṭhānakaṃ iti | na tathā vadāmaḥ | dharme dharmo vartata iti mātraṃ vadāmaḥ |
body.translated_text: Your statement that 'all worldly people believe that water has up to eight qualities' — they speak merely in conformity with conventional usage, not in conformity with the great elements as substances (<s>dravya</s>). Furthermore, you have said: 'All derivative <s>dharmas</s> (<s>upādāyadharma</s>) are merely designations (<s>prajñaptyātmaka</s>).' This is not valid. Why? For it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There are either the six bases of contact (<s>sparśāyatana</s>) or <s>dharmas</s> derived from the six bases of contact.' A certain monk asked the Blessed One: 'What is the eye?' The Blessed One replied: 'The eye, O monk, is the material transparency (<s>rūpaprasāda</s>) derived from the four great elements.' The ten sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>) are likewise. As for the statement 'with a basis, with a support' — we do not say it in that way. We say merely that 'one <s>dharma</s> operates in [relation to] another <s>dharma</s>.'

body.text: yadbhavānāha- khakkhaṭādayaḥ kimarthā bhavantīti kevalaṃ mahābhūtārthā iti bhavanti iti prāpyate iti | khakkhaṭādayaḥ sārthakā yaduta khakkhaṭa lakṣaṇaṃ sandhatta iti | ablakṣaṇaṃ snehayatīti | tejolakṣaṇaṃ paripācayatīti | vāyulakṣaṇam abhinirvartayatīti | ataścatvāri mahābhūtāni dravyāṇi santi ||
body.translated_text: Your statement: 'For what purpose do hardness and the rest exist? They exist merely for the purpose of the great elements' — it follows that hardness and the rest have meaning, namely: the characteristic of hardness (<s>khakkhaṭa</s>) binds together; the characteristic of water (<s>ap</s>) moistens; the characteristic of fire (<s>tejas</s>) ripens; the characteristic of wind (<s>vāyu</s>) brings forth. Therefore the four great elements are substances (<s>dravya</s>).

body.text: caturmahābhūtadravyasattāvarga ekonacatvāriṃśaḥ
body.translated_text: This is the thirty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Substantial Existence of the Four Great Elements (<s>caturmahābhūtadravyasattāvarga</s>).

body.text: 40 tadaprāmāṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 40. Chapter on the Invalidity of That [View] (<s>tadaprāmāṇavarga</s>)

body.text: atra pratibrūmaḥ | tadayuktam | catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptimātrāṇi | yadyapyuktaṃ bhavatā abhidharma uktaṃ- khakkhaṭalakṣaṇaḥ pṛthivīdhātuḥ | ityādi | na tadyujyate | kasmāt |
body.translated_text: Here we reply: That is not valid. The four great elements are mere designations (<s>prajñaptimātra</s>). Although you have stated that 'it is said in the <s>Abhidharma</s>: The earth element (<s>pṛthivīdhātu</s>) has the characteristic of hardness' — and so forth — that is not valid. Why?

body.text: bhagavān hi svayamāha- khakkhaṭaḥ kharagataśca pṛthivī iti | na khakkhaṭamātra[māha] | ato nāyaṃ samyag hetuḥ |
body.translated_text: For the Blessed One himself said: 'Hardness and roughness constitute earth (<s>pṛthivī</s>).' He did not say 'hardness alone.' Therefore this is not a correct reason.

body.text: rūpādikaṃ caturbhyo mahābhūtebhyaḥ samutpadyata iti bhavaduktaṃ na yujyate | kasmāt | rūpādiḥ karmakleśānnapānamaithunarāgādibhyaḥ samutpadyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- cakṣuḥ kimupādāya bhavati | karmopādāya bhavati | iti | kiñcāha- sukhāsaṅgasamudayādrūpasamudaya iti | yathā cānando bhikṣuṇīśikṣaṇāya bhaginīmāha- ayaṃ kāyaḥ āhārasambhūtaḥ tṛṣṇāsambhūto mānasambhūto maithunasambhūta iti | ato jñāyate rūpādi rna caturmahābhūtasambhūt iti | (pṛ) yadyapi rūpādi karmasambhūtam | tathāpi catvāri mahābhūtāni ca aṃśena hetavaḥ syuḥ | yathā karmavaśāt vrīhirbhavati | sa brīhirbījādyapekṣya ca prādurbhavati | tathā cakṣurādīnāṃ karmasambhūtatve 'pi catvāri mahābhūtāni aṃśato hetavo bhavanti | (u) kadācit kiñcidvastu vināpi hetupratyayān utpadyate | yathā kalpāvasāne kalpādau ca mahatī vṛṣṭiḥ | tā āpaḥ kasmātsambhavanti | devānāmabhīpsitamanusmaraṇamātrāllabhyeta | yathā dhyānaniṣaṇṇasya bhadantasya cābhīpsitaṃ chandamanuvartate | asya ke pratyayāḥ | na[nu] karmamātram | yathā ca rūpasantānaḥ vyucchidya punaḥ pratisandhīyate | yo 'rūpadhātāvupapadya punā rūpadhātāvupapadyate | rūpasyāsya kiṃ mūlam |
body.translated_text: Your statement that 'form and the rest arise from the four great elements' is not valid. Why? Form and the rest arise from <s>karma</s>, defilements (<s>kleśa</s>), food, sexual desire, and the like. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'What does the eye depend upon for its existence? It depends upon <s>karma</s>.' And it says: 'From the arising of attachment to pleasure, the arising of form [occurs].' And just as <s>Ānanda</s> said to a nun for her instruction: 'This body is born of food, born of craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), born of conceit (<s>māna</s>), born of sexual intercourse (<s>maithuna</s>).' From this it is known that form and the rest are not born from the four great elements. (Question) Even if form and the rest are born of <s>karma</s>, the four great elements may still be partial causes. Just as rice comes into being through the power of <s>karma</s>, but that rice also depends on seeds and other [conditions] to appear. Likewise, even though the eye and the rest are born of <s>karma</s>, the four great elements are partial causes. (Answer) Sometimes a certain thing arises even without causal conditions. Just as at the end and beginning of a cosmic age (<s>kalpa</s>), there is great rainfall — from what do those waters arise? They are obtained merely through the recollection of the gods' wishes. Just as the wishes of the venerable one seated in <s>dhyāna</s> are fulfilled — what are the conditions for that? It is merely <s>karma</s>. And just as the continuum of form, having been interrupted, is reconnected — one who is reborn in the formless realm (<s>arūpadhātu</s>) and again reborn in the form realm (<s>rūpadhātu</s>) — what is the root of that form?

body.text: (pṛ) kasmāt kiñcit karmamātrādutpadyate kiñcittu bāhyapratyayamapekṣyotpadyate | (u) yaḥ sattvo 'varakarmabalo bhavati | sa bījasāmagrīsāhāyyataḥ sādhayati | utkaṭakarmabalastu na bāhyapratyayamapekṣate tathā dharmā api syuḥ | kecit sakarmakāḥ | kecit sadharmakāḥ | keṣāñcidupapattyāyatanaṃ karmabalamātrāllabhyate | na bāhyapratyayamapekṣya | hetupratyayāpekṣī vadet bījamaṅkurādīnāṃ heturiti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Why does some [form] arise from <s>karma</s> alone while other [form] arises depending on external conditions? (Answer) A being whose <s>karma</s>-power is weak accomplishes [its result] with the assistance of the aggregate of seeds and conditions. But one whose <s>karma</s>-power is intense does not depend on external conditions. Likewise, <s>dharmas</s> too may be so — some depend on <s>karma</s>, some depend on [other] <s>dharmas</s>. For some, the place of rebirth (<s>upapattyāyatana</s>) is obtained merely through the power of <s>karma</s>, not depending on external conditions. One who holds that [things] depend on causal conditions would say: 'A seed is the cause of sprouts and the rest.'

body.text: kasmāducyate khakkhaṭādimupādāya [rūpādi]rutpadyate | kenārthena khakkhaṭādito rūpādirutpadyate na rūpāditaḥ khakkhaṭādiḥ | tayośca sahajātatvāt kathamucyate khakkhaṭādimupādāya
body.translated_text: Why is it said that 'form and the rest arise depending on hardness and the like'? For what reason do form and the rest arise from hardness and the like, rather than hardness and the like from form and the rest? And since the two are co-arisen (<s>sahajāta</s>), how can it be said that

body.text: rūpādirbhavati | na rūpādimupādāya khakkhaṭādiriti | nahyekakālīnaryordharmayoranyonyahetutvaṃ bhavati | yathā śṛṅgadvayaṃ yugapajjāyamānam | na vaktuṃ śakyaṃ vāmadakṣiṇe hetū iti |
body.translated_text: form and the rest depend on hardness and the like, rather than hardness and the like depending on form and the rest? For between two <s>dharmas</s> that arise simultaneously, there is no mutual causal relationship — just as two horns arising simultaneously: one cannot say that the left and the right are causes [of each other].

body.text: (pṛ) yathā pradīpaprakāśayorekakālikayorapi pradīpamupādāya prakāśa ityucyate | na prakāśamupādāya pradīpa iti | tathedamapi | (u) pradīpo na prakāśādanyaḥ | pradīpo hi rūpaṃ prakāśa iti dharmadvayasamavāyātmakaḥ | rūpameva prakāśa iti na pradīpaḥ pṛthagbhavati | evamasya dṛṣṭāntasya tathyaṃ na cintitavānasi | (pṛ) prakāśaḥ pradipādanyatra gacchatīti anyaḥ syāt | (u) nānyatra gacchati | idaṃ prakāśarūpaṃ pradīpa eva pratyakṣamupalabhyate | yadyanyatra gacchati | pradīpaṃ vihāyāpyupalabhyeta | na tūpalabhyate vastutaḥ | tadrūpaṃ na pradīpādanyaditi jñātavyam |
body.translated_text: (Question) Just as between a lamp and its light, which are simultaneous, it is said that 'the light depends on the lamp,' not that 'the lamp depends on the light' — so too here. (Answer) The lamp is not different from the light. For the lamp is comprised of both form and light — the two <s>dharmas</s> are inseparably conjoined. Light itself is form — the lamp does not exist separately. You have not correctly considered the truth of this example. (Question) The light goes elsewhere from the lamp, so it would be different. (Answer) It does not go elsewhere. This luminous form is directly perceived in the lamp itself. If it went elsewhere, it would be apprehended even apart from the lamp. But in reality it is not apprehended [apart from the lamp]. Therefore it should be known that that form is not different from the lamp.

body.text: (pṛ) yugapajjāyamānayorapi dharmayorhetuphalabhāvo 'sti | yathā sapratidhe vijñānasya cakṣūrūpaṃ hetupratyayo bhavati | na tu cakṣūrūpasya vijñānam | (u) na yujyate | cakṣurvijñānasya pūrvacittaṃ hetuḥ cakṣūrūpaṃ pratyayaḥ | pūrvaniruddhaṃ cittaṃ hetuḥ iti kathaṃ yugapajjāyamānaṃ bhavati | yo dharmo yaṃ hetumanuvartyotpadyate sa tasya hetuḥ | yaccittaṃ yadindriyāṇyupādāya bhavati sa tadupādāya dharmaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) Even between <s>dharmas</s> arising simultaneously, there is a cause-and-effect relationship. Just as in the case of obstructive consciousness, the eye and form serve as the causal condition (<s>hetupratyaya</s>) of consciousness, but consciousness is not [the cause] of eye and form. (Answer) This is not valid. The cause of eye-consciousness is the preceding mind-moment, while eye and form are its conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>). Since the preceding mind that has ceased is the cause, how can [two things] arising simultaneously be [in a causal relationship]? That <s>dharma</s> which arises following a [certain] cause — that is its cause. Whatever consciousness arises depending on certain sense-faculties — that is a <s>dharma</s> derived from those [faculties].

body.text: atha catvāri mahābhūtānyeva [na] rūpakarāṇi | [sarūpa]hetusambhūtatvāt | pratyakṣamupalabhāmaḥ khalu loke vastūni sarūpahetorjāyamānāni | yathā sāleśśālirbhavati, yavādyavaḥ | evaṃ pṛthivītaḥ pṛthivī bhavati nābādayaḥ | evaṃ rūpādrūpaṃ bhavati ityevamādi |
body.translated_text: Moreover, the four great elements alone do not produce form. Because [things arise] from causes of a similar nature (<s>sarūpahetu</s>). We directly perceive in the world that things are born from causes of a similar nature. Just as from rice comes rice, from barley comes barley. Likewise, from earth comes earth, not from water and the rest. Similarly, from form comes form — and so forth.

body.text: (pṛ) dṛśyate sa kiñcidvastu asarūpahetorjāyata iti | yathā vyākīrṇagopurīṣakūṭe kṛmirjāyate | śṛṅgakūṭe tṛṇaṃ prarohati | (u) na vayaṃ vadāmaḥ asarūpahetorna jāyata iti | kintu sarūpahetau ca sati jāyata iti vadāmaḥ | tasmāducyate rūpādibhyo
body.translated_text: (Question) It is seen that certain things arise from causes of a dissimilar nature. Just as worms arise in scattered heaps of cow-dung, and grass sprouts from piles of horns. (Answer) We do not say that nothing arises from causes of a dissimilar nature. Rather, we say that when a cause of a similar nature is also present, [things] arise. Therefore it is said that from form and the rest

body.text: rūpādayo jāyante na caturmahābhūtebhya eva jāyanta iti | ato nābadhāraṇaṃ bhavati rūpādayaścaturmahābhūtebhya eva jāyanta iti |
body.translated_text: form and the rest arise — they do not arise solely from the four great elements. Therefore, the definitive determination that 'form and the rest arise only from the four great elements' does not hold.

body.text: khakkhaṭādinā catvāri mahābhūtāni nirūpyanta iti yadavocadbhavān | tadayuktam | kasmāt | niyataiḥ khakkhāṭādilakṣaṇaiḥ catvāraḥ saṅghātā vibhaktavyāḥ | saukumāryādestu aniyataḥ kadācit khakkhaṭabahule saṅghāte vartate | kadācitsnehabahule saṅghāte vartate | ato nānena [saukumāryādinā] saṅghātā vibhaktavyāḥ | tathānyairapi | khakkhaṭādīnāṃ sparśaviśeṣāḥ saukumāryādaya ucyante | kimiti | yadi snehena utpattisvabhāvenāpi sukumārasūkṣmaślakṣṇāni bhavanti | khakkhaṭalakṣaṇabahulatvāt khakkhaṭaṃ kharamaudārikaṃ karkaśamityevamādi bhavati | ataḥ khakkhaṭādimātreṇa catvāraḥ saṅghātā vibhajyante | yathoktaṃ sūtre- khakkhaṭā[di]gatānīti caturṇāṃ mahābhūtānāṃ vibhāgā nirdiśyanta iti | ato jñāyate khakkhaṭagatadharmaḥ pṛthivīdhātuḥ na tu khakkhaṭamātralakṣaṇa iti | tasmāt khakkhaṭalakṣaṇaṃ pṛthivīprasādhanaheturityucyate | pṛthivīprasādhane ca khakkhaṭatvaṃ pradhānahetuḥ | ataḥ pṛthakkṛtyocyate | tathānyāni lakṣaṇānyapi [vaktavyāni] | saṃjñākriyāyai yat kiñcan khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ sarvaṃ tat pṛthividhātuḥ | kecidvadanti kevalaṃ khakkhaṭalakṣaṇaṃ pṛthivīdhāturiti | tatpratyākhyānāya bhagavānāha- khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ pṛthivīdhāturiti | anyadapyevam | khakkhaṭalakṣaṇasaṅghāte khakkhaṭasya bāhulyāt dvidhāsti vyavahāraḥ | sarveṣu saṅghāteṣu khakkhaṭādisparśāḥ santi | yat khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ sa pṛthivīdhātuḥ | yat snigdhaṃ snigdhagataṃ sa āpodhātuḥ | yat uṣṇaṃ uṣṇagataṃ sa tejodhātuḥ |
body.translated_text: Your statement that 'the four great elements are determined by hardness and the rest' is not valid. Why? The four aggregates (<s>saṅghāta</s>) should be distinguished by the fixed characteristics of hardness and the like. But [qualities like] softness (<s>saukumārya</s>) and the rest are not fixed — sometimes softness occurs in an aggregate predominated by hardness, sometimes in an aggregate predominated by moisture. Therefore the aggregates should not be distinguished by softness and the rest, nor by other [such qualities]. The touch-particularities such as softness and the like are said to be varieties of the touches beginning with hardness. Why? If [things are] soft, subtle, and smooth by the nature of moisture, they are so because of the predominance of the characteristic of hardness [in contrast]. When predominated by the characteristic of hardness, [things are] hard, rough, coarse, and harsh, and so forth. Therefore the four aggregates are distinguished by hardness and the rest alone. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The characteristics such as hardness and roughness indicate the divisions of the four great elements.' From this it is known that the <s>dharma</s> characterized by hardness and roughness is the earth element (<s>pṛthivīdhātu</s>), not merely the characteristic of hardness. Therefore, the characteristic of hardness is said to be the principal reason for establishing the earth [element]. And in establishing the earth [element], hardness is the principal cause. Therefore it is stated separately. The other characteristics too should be stated likewise. For the purpose of designation and action, whatever is hard and rough — all of that is the earth element. Some say: 'The earth element is characterized merely by hardness.' In order to refute that, the Blessed One said: 'Hardness and roughness constitute the earth element.' The same applies to the others. In an aggregate characterized by hardness, because hardness predominates, there is a twofold usage. In all aggregates, the touches of hardness and the rest exist. That which is hard and rough is the earth element. That which is moist and viscous is the water element (<s>āpodhātu</s>).
