That which is hot and heat-producing is the fire element (<s>tejodhātu</s>).

body.text: khakkhaṭaṃ pṛthivīprasādhanasya pradhānaheturityatastatra pṛthivīti nāma | prajñaptitaḥ prasiddhe hetau prajñaptitaḥ saṃjñā bhavati yathā vadanti- paśyāmyahaṃ vṛkṣasya chettāraṃ puruṣamiti |
body.translated_text: Hardness is the principal reason for establishing earth — therefore it is named 'earth' there. A designation (<s>prajñapti</s>) based on a well-known cause [gives rise to] a designation-name — just as people say: 'I see the man who is the feller of the tree.'

body.text: dvābhyāmākārābhyāmiti yadavocaḥ | tadayuktam | yadi vyavahārabhaṅgīmanusṛtya tattvaṃ bhavati | tadā dvādaśāyatanādīni tattvāni na syuḥ | ataścakṣuḥ pratītya rūpañcotpadyate cakṣurvijñānamitīdamatattvaṃ syāt | vyavahārabhaṅgayā abhāvāt | idañca mithyāśāstraṃ syāt | kiñca tathāgate tejovatī samādhimupasampanne tatkāyā dvividhāni jvālārūpāṇi niścaranti | tatra kimitti tejo dhāturna bhavati | rūpādīnā tejaḥ sidhyati natūṣmamātralakṣaṇataḥ | kiñcāha bhagavān- kāyo 'yaṃ karaṇḍaka iti | tatra nakhalomakeśādayaḥ samṛddhāḥ santi | yathoktaṃ sūtre- santi kāye 'smin nakhalomakeśādaya iti | ato nakhalomakeśādayaḥ pṛthivīdhātuḥ | na hi dhatuvādo 'stīti dravyadharmo bhavati | uktañcabīja sūtre yataḥ pṛthivīdhātuḥ syāt nābdhātuḥ na bījāni vṛddhiṃ [virūḍhiṃ vipulatā] māpadyanta iti | tatra kiṃ pṛthivīdhātuḥ yaduta prajñaptitaḥ kṣetram, na tu khakkhaṭamātralakṣaṇam | āpo 'pi prajñaptitaḥ na snehamātralakṣaṇam | ekasya dharmasya dravyatvaṃ prajñaptitvamiti dviprakāro 'pi nopalabhyate | kasmāt, rūpādīni dravyāṇi | cakṣurādīni prajñaptitaḥ santi | mahābhūtāni tu dravyataśca prajñaptitaśca santīdaṃ mithyāśāstram | ṣaḍdhātu sūtre ca bhagavānāha- keśalomanakhādīni pṛthivīdhāturiti | hastipadopamasūtre coktam- keśā lomā nakhā ityādīni ayamucyate pṛthivīdhāturiti | kenārthena dhāturdravyaṃ na prajñaptirityucyate | na ca so 'rthaḥ sūtrārūḍhaḥ |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'by two aspects' is untenable. If reality (<s>tattva</s>) were established by following conventional usage, then the twelve sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>) and the rest would not be realities. Therefore the statement 'Depending on the eye and form, eye-consciousness arises' would be non-real, because it does not conform to conventional usage. And this treatise would be a false treatise. Furthermore, when the <s>Tathāgata</s> enters the fire-radiance <s>samādhi</s> (<s>tejovatī samādhi</s>), from his body two kinds of flame-forms emerge. How, then, could [one say] that the fire element (<s>tejodhātu</s>) does not exist? Fire is established through form and the rest, not merely through the characteristic of heat (<s>uṣmamātra</s>). Furthermore, the Blessed One said: 'This body is a basket.' Therein, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs, and the rest abundantly exist. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'In this body there are nails, body-hairs, head-hairs, and the rest.' Therefore nails, body-hairs, head-hairs, and the rest are the earth element (<s>pṛthivīdhātu</s>). The statement 'element exists' does not constitute a substantial <s>dharma</s> (<s>dravyadharma</s>). And it is stated in the Seed <s>Sūtra</s> (<s>Bījasūtra</s>): 'Where the earth element exists but the water element does not, seeds do not grow, [sprout, or become abundant].' Therein, what is the earth element? It is the field (<s>kṣetra</s>) as designated (<s>prajñaptitaḥ</s>), not merely the characteristic of hardness (<s>khakkhaṭa</s>). Water too exists as designated, not merely as the characteristic of moisture (<s>sneha</s>). That a single <s>dharma</s> is both a substance (<s>dravya</s>) and a designation (<s>prajñapti</s>) — neither of these two modes is apprehended. Why? Form and the rest are substances. The eye and the rest exist as designations. But that the great elements exist both as substances and as designations — this is a false teaching. In the <s>Ṣaḍdhātusūtra</s>, the Blessed One said: 'Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, and the rest are the earth element.' In the <s>Hastipadopamasūtra</s> (Simile of the Elephant's Footprint <s>Sūtra</s>) it is also said: 'Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, and so forth — these are called the earth element.' By what argument is the element (<s>dhātu</s>) said to be a substance and not a designation? That meaning is not found in the <s>sūtras</s>.

body.text: yadavādīḥ bhagavānāha- yaccakṣurmāsapiṇḍe khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ iyaṃ pṛthivī ityādi | vacanenānena bhagavān pradarśayati pañcendriyāṇi catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya bhavanti iti | kecidvadanti ahaṅkārasambhūtamindriyamiti | kecidvadanti mahābhūtavyatiriktamindriyamastīti | kecidvadanti indriyāṇi nānāsvabhāvajāni yaduta pṛthivīmahābhūtāt sambhūtaṃ ghrāṇamityādi | tatpratyākhyānāya bhagavānāha- cakṣurādīndriyāṇi caturmahābhūtasamavāyātmakāni śūnyānyavastūni iti | vikalpaḥ prajñapterhetuṃ pratyayaṃ sādhayati | [sā] prajñaptirapi nāsti | asmin māṃsapiṇḍe santi catvāro bhāgāḥ khakkhaṭaṃ kharagatamityādi vacanena bhagavān pradarśayati sarvapadārthāḥ caturmahābhūtasambhūtā iti |
body.translated_text: You have said that the Blessed One stated: 'Whatever in this lump of flesh is hard and rough — that is earth' and so forth. By this statement, the Blessed One shows that the five sense-faculties (<s>indriya</s>) arise depending on the four great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>). Some say: 'The sense-faculty arises from the ego-principle (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>).' Some say: 'The sense-faculty is something distinct from the great elements.' Some say: 'The sense-faculties arise from individual natures — that is, the organ of smell is born from the earth great element,' and so forth. To refute these [views], the Blessed One said: 'The sense-faculties beginning with the eye are constituted by the combination of the four great elements — they are empty, without real substance (<s>avastu</s>).' Conceptualization (<s>vikalpa</s>) establishes causes and conditions for the designation (<s>prajñapti</s>). [But] that designation too does not exist [ultimately]. By the statement 'In this lump of flesh there are four aspects — what is hard and rough' and so forth, the Blessed One shows that all entities arise from the four great elements.

body.text: bhagavānnāvocat- dvayorāśrayo 'stītyato dravyamahābhūtaṃ [vāyu]riti yadavocaḥ | tadayuktam | kasmāt | vāyorlaghutvaṃ viśiṣṭaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ na laghugatadharmaḥ | pṛthivyādīnāṃ khakkhaṭagatadharmādayo viśiṣṭāḥ vāyostu na tathā | laghugatadharmaścālpa iti nāvocat | yadavādīḥ catvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptisantīti vaktuḥ tanmahābhūtalakṣaṇāni vinirbhaktāni syuriti | tadayuktam | yat khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ caturmahābhūtasambhūtaṃ [sa]pṛthivīdhātuḥ | na tūcyate 'nyadvastu lakṣaṇasyāśraya iti | yo dharmo lakṣaṇādanya na sa āśrayaḥ | ayameva lakṣaṇasya [a]vinirbhāgaḥ | (pṛ) yadutpadyamānaṃ na sa āśrayo bhavati | āśrayo hi [yat]anyadvastu [tat] āśrayatāmupayāti | (u) āśraya iti saṃjñāyate nānyadvastu lakṣaṇasyāśraya iti | utpadyamānasya pravibhāgāt | yathā vadanti ākāśaṃ sarvagāmīti | vastutastu nāsti tat yadgacchati |
body.translated_text: The Blessed One did not say 'there is a support for both [substance and designation].' Therefore your statement 'wind (<s>vāyu</s>) is a substantial great element' is untenable. Why? Lightness (<s>laghutva</s>) is the distinguishing characteristic of wind, not the quality of being light-in-movement (<s>laghugatadharma</s>). For earth and the rest, the qualities of hardness and so forth are distinctive, but for wind it is not so. And the quality of being light-in-movement is minimal — therefore it is not stated [to be distinctive]. Your statement 'the four great elements exist as designations, and therefore the characteristics of the great elements would be separable from [their bearer]' — that is untenable. What is hard and rough, born from the combination of the four great elements — that is the earth element. But it is not said that there is another entity which serves as the support of the characteristic. A <s>dharma</s> that is other than its characteristic is not a support. This itself is the inseparability of the characteristic. (Objection) That which is arising is not the support. For a support is another entity that enters into the state of being a support. (Reply) It is designated as a 'support' — [but] another entity is not the support of the characteristic, because of the separability of what is arising. Just as they say: 'Space is all-pervasive.' But in reality, there is nothing that moves.

body.text: yaduktaṃ bhavatā catvāri mahābhūtāni sahajātānīti | tadayuktam | yathā ātape kevalaṃ rūpayuktaḥ sparśa upalabhyate nānye dharmaḥ | candrikāyāṃ kevalaṃ rūpayuktaḥ śītasparśa upalabhyate nānye dharmāḥ | tasmānna sarveṣu padārtheṣu caturmahābhūtāni santi | tadyathā kiñcidvastu nīrasaṃ yathā suvarṇavajrādi | kiñcidvastu nirgandhaṃ yathā suvarṇarajatādi | kiñcidvastu nīrūpaṃ yathā gṛha[prāsāda]dharma | kiñcidvastu
body.translated_text: Your statement 'the four great elements are co-arising (<s>sahajāta</s>)' is untenable. For example, in sunlight, only a touch (<s>sparśa</s>) accompanied by form (<s>rūpa</s>) is perceived — no other <s>dharmas</s>. In moonlight, only a cold touch accompanied by form is perceived — no other <s>dharmas</s>. Therefore the four great elements do not exist in all entities. For example, some things are without flavor (<s>nīrasa</s>), such as gold, diamond, and the like. Some things are without smell (<s>nirgandha</s>), such as gold, silver, and the like. Some things are without form (<s>nīrūpa</s>), as in the case of [the <s>dharma</s> of] a house or palace. Some things

body.text: nirūṣma yathā candra[kānta]ādi | kiñcidvastu niśśītam yathā teja ādi | kiñcidvastu īraṇalakṣaṇaṃ yathā vāyvādi | kiñcidvastu nirīraṇaṃ yathā pāṣāṇaghaṇḍaḥ | evaṃ kiñcidvastu niṣkarkaśam | kiñcinnisneham | kiñcinnirūṣma | kiñcinnirīraṇam | ataścatvāri mahābhūtāni nāvinirbhāgavartīni |
body.translated_text: are without heat (<s>nirūṣma</s>), such as moonstone and the like. Some things are without cold, such as fire and the like. Some things have the characteristic of impulsion (<s>īraṇa</s>), such as wind and the like. Some things are without impulsion, such as a solid rock. Thus, some things are without hardness, some without moisture, some without heat, and some without impulsion. Therefore the four great elements do not exist inseparably together.

body.text: (pṛ) bāhyaiḥ kāraṇairmahābhūtānāṃ svabhāva āvirbhavati | yathā suvarṇapāṣāṇādau dravalakṣaṇaṃ teja apekṣyāvirbhavati | apsu kāṭhinyalakṣaṇa atiśaityamupādāyodbhavati | vāyau śītoṣmalakṣaṇa aptejasī upādāyodbhavati | tṛṇavṛkṣeṣu īraṇalakṣaṇaṃ vāyuṃ prāpyodbhavati | tasmāt pūrvavartinaḥ svabhāvāḥ pratyayamapekṣodbhavanti | ataścatvāri mahābhūtāni na vinirbhāgalābhina iti jñāyate | yadi purvamasan [sa]svabhāvaḥ | kathamudbhavet | (u) tathā cet vāyau kadācidgandho 'stīti gandho vāyugataḥ syāt | yathā vāsitatailagandhastailagataḥ | natvidaṃ yujyate | na hi mahābhūtebhyo bhautikaṃ rūpamutpadyate | yathā snehāt sneho bhavati | tathā rūpādrūpaṃ bhavati | yadi [tāni] avinirbhāgavartīni | tadā satkāryaṃ syāt | yathā kanyāyāṃ putraḥ anne 'medhyādiḥ | na vayaṃ brūmaḥ satkāryam | yadyapi nāsti payasi dadhi | tathāpi dadhi payasa utpadyate | evaṃ kiṃ saṃjñānusmaraṇavikalpena yaduta catvāri mahābhūtāni sahajātāni apṛthagbhāgavartīnīti ||
body.translated_text: (Objection) Through external causes, the intrinsic nature of the great elements becomes manifest. For example, in gold and stone, the characteristic of liquidity becomes manifest in dependence on fire. In water, the characteristic of hardness arises in dependence on extreme cold. In wind, the characteristics of cold and heat arise in dependence on water and fire. In grass and trees, the characteristic of impulsion arises on encountering wind. Therefore, the previously existing intrinsic natures become manifest in dependence on conditions. From this it is known that the four great elements are not obtained separately. If previously non-existent, how would [a characteristic] arise? (Reply) If that were so, then the smell that sometimes exists in wind would be inherent in wind — just as the fragrance of perfumed oil is inherent in oil. But this is not tenable. For material form (<s>bhautika rūpa</s>) does not arise from the great elements. Just as from moisture comes moisture, so from form comes form. If [the elements] exist inseparably, then it would be the theory of pre-existent effects (<s>satkārya</s>) — as a son in a maiden, or impurity in food. We do not assert the pre-existence of effects. Even though curd does not exist in milk, still curd arises from milk. Why then should one, through the conceptualization and memory of designations, [assert] that the four great elements are co-arisen and inseparably present?

body.text: tadapramāṇavargaścatvāriṃśaḥ
body.translated_text: This is the fortieth chapter, the Chapter on the Invalidity of That [View] (<s>tadapramāṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 41 pūrvatanasiddhāntaprakāśanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 41. Chapter on the Clarification of the Previous Doctrine (<s>pūrvatanasiddhāntaprakāśanavarga</s>)

body.text: pūrvaṃ yadavādīḥ- na vayaṃ brūmaḥ catvāri mahābhūtāni rūpādibhirekāni yadi vānekāni ityato 'navadyam iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | tīrthikāḥ sarve siṣādhayiṣantītyata ścaturṇāṃ mahābhūtānāmekatvanānātve udāharanti | ato bhagavān prajñaptau catarṇāṃ mahābhūtānāmudāhṛtatvāt teṣāmarthamupadiśati | tathā no cet na brūyāt | laukikāḥ svabhāvataḥ pṛthivyādimahābhūtāni jānanto 'pi na vidanti [teṣāṃ] vastubhāvam | ata upadeśaṃ karoti | nopadiśati hastādi | yadi khakkhaṭādibhiścatvāri mahābhūtāni bhavanti iti | ka upakāro bhavet |
body.translated_text: You previously said: 'We do not say whether the four great elements are identical with or different from form and the rest — therefore there is no fault.' This is untenable. Why? Because all <s>tīrthikas</s> wish to establish [their views], they present the unity or plurality of the four great elements as examples. Therefore, since the Blessed One has spoken of the four great elements in the context of designation (<s>prajñapti</s>), he teaches their meaning. If it were not so, he would not have spoken [of them]. Worldly people, while knowing the great elements of earth and the rest by their own nature, do not know their real status as entities. Therefore he gives instruction. He does not instruct about hands and the like. If the four great elements consist of hardness and the like — what benefit would there be?

body.text: asti dvidhā āśrayārtha ityuktvā mahābhūtāni dravyāṇīti yadavocaḥ | tatra na pratīmo- ayamāśrayārthaḥ, [ta]danyo yaḥ sa prajñaptisan iti | [aṣṭaguṇā āpa iti] vyavahārānuvartanato vadanti na tu dravyamahābhūtā[nuvartana]ta iti yadvacanaṃ tadayuktam | kasmāt | yadi vā pravacane yadi vā loke na hetupratyayairvinā rūpādiṣu caturmahābhūta saṃjñāṃ kurvanti | yathā loke vadanti paśyāmyahaṃ puruṣamiti | rūpādiṣu hi puruṣa iti saṃjñā na hetupratyayairvinā bhavati | yo vināpi sudṛḍhahetupratyayaiḥ saṃjñāṃ karoti so 'śvaṃ dṛṣṭvā puruṣa ityāhvayet | vastutastu na tathā | kasmācchabde pṛthivīti na vadanti | laukikāḥ sadā [pṛthag] vadanti pṛthivīti śabda iti | na kadācidapi vadanti śabdaḥ pṛthivīti | yo vinā sudṛḍhahetupratyayaiḥ saṃjñāṃ karoti | sa śabdaṃ pṛthivīti āhvayet | vastutastu na tathā | tasmādrūpādayaścatvāro dharmā [eva] pṛthivī | pṛthivībhāge ['pi] pṛthivīti saṃjñā bhavati | yathārūpamidaṃ prajñapterhetuṃ sādhayati tatra puruṣa iti saṃjñā | vṛkṣeṣu vanamiti saṃjñā | bhikṣuṣu saṅgha iti saṃjñā | evaṃ rūpādiṣu dharmeṣu catvāri mahābhūtānīti saṃjñāṃ vadanti |
body.translated_text: You have said: 'There are two kinds of basis-meaning,' and thereby asserted that the great elements are substances. But we do not accept this — that this is the basis-meaning, and that which is other is an existent designation. Your statement 'eight qualities of water, and so forth, are spoken following conventional usage, not following substantial great elements' — that is untenable. Why? Because neither in the [Buddha's] teaching nor in the world does one apply the designation of the four great elements to form and the rest without causes and conditions. Just as in the world they say: 'I see a person.' The designation 'person' applied to form and the rest does not arise without causes and conditions. One who makes a designation without firm causes and conditions would, upon seeing a horse, call it a 'person.' But in reality it is not so. Why do they not call sound 'earth'? Worldly people always say separately 'earth' and 'sound.' They never say: 'Sound is earth.' One who makes a designation without firm causes and conditions would call sound 'earth.' But in reality it is not so. Therefore, the four <s>dharmas</s> of form and the rest are [themselves] earth. Even in a portion of earth, the designation 'earth' applies. Just as form establishes the cause for designation, therein the designation 'person' [arises]. In trees, the designation 'forest' [arises]. In monks, the designation '<s>Saṅgha</s>' [arises]. Thus, in <s>dharmas</s> of form and the rest, they apply the designation 'four great elements.'

body.text: yadavocaḥ- yadi vā ṣaṭ sparśāyatanāni yadi vā ṣaṭ sparśāyatanānyupādāya siddhā [dharmā] iti | nedaṃ sūtraṃ yuktam | yathā bhavatāṃ śāsane bhautikaṃ rūpaṃ na kasyacijjanakam | tathā mama śāsane 'pi prajñaptau na [tat]kasyacit janyam | ata idaṃ sūtraṃ na bhavet | asti cettasyārtho 'nyathayitavyaḥ | yadavādīḥ- catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya bhautiko rūpaprasādaḥ cakṣuriti | tadayuktam | caturṇāṃ mahābhūtānāṃ samavāyaḥ prajñaptau cakṣurityucyate | prajñaptisanti catvāri mahābhūtāni rūpam | tadrūpaprasādaścakṣuḥ | yadyupyuktaṃ bhavatā dharme dharmo vartate nirāśrayo niradhiṣṭhātā ceti | [tatra yo dharmaḥ] sa evāśrayaḥ adhiṣṭhātā ca | yena vartate sa āśrayaḥ | yasmin dharme tiṣṭhati so 'dhiṣṭhātā | yadavocaḥ- khakkhaṭalakṣaṇaṃ "saṃghatta" ityādi | nedaṃ yujyate | na khakkhaṭalakṣaṇaṃ kevalaṃ dhatte | api tu hetupratyayasāmagrīñcāpekṣate | tathānyānyapi | tasmāccatvāri mahābhūtāni prajñaptisanti ||
body.translated_text: Your statement 'whether the six bases of contact, or <s>dharmas</s> established depending on the six bases of contact' — this <s>sūtra</s> is not applicable [here]. Just as in your teaching, material form (<s>bhautika rūpa</s>) is not the producer of anything — so too in my teaching, in the context of designation, [that] is not the producer of anything. Therefore this <s>sūtra</s> would not apply. If there is [an applicable meaning], its meaning must be explained otherwise. Your statement 'Depending on the four great elements, the material form-clarity (<s>rūpaprasāda</s>) is the eye' — that is untenable. The combination (<s>samavāya</s>) of the four great elements, in the context of designation, is called 'the eye.' The four great elements existing as designations are form. The form-clarity of that [form] is the eye. Although you have said: 'A <s>dharma</s> abides in a <s>dharma</s>, without a support and without a controller' — [in our view,] that very <s>dharma</s> is itself the support and the controller. That by which it operates is the support. That <s>dharma</s> in which it abides is the controller. Your statement 'The hardness characteristic [is called] "friction"' and so forth — this is not tenable. The hardness characteristic does not function by itself alone; rather, it depends on the assemblage of causes and conditions. So too with the others. Therefore the four great elements exist as designations.

body.text: pūrvatanasiddhāntaprakāśanavargaṃ ekacatvāriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-first chapter, the Chapter on the Clarification of the Previous Doctrine (<s>pūrvatanasiddhāntaprakāśanavarga</s>).

body.text: 42 khakkhaṭalakṣaṇāsattāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 42. Chapter on the Non-Existence of the Hardness Characteristic (<s>khakkhaṭalakṣaṇāsattāvarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) yadāha bhavān- khakkhaṭabahulo rūpādi [samavāyaḥ] pṛthivīmahābhūtamityataḥ pṛthivyādayaḥ prajñaptisanta iti | nedaṃ yujyate | kasmāt | khakkhaṭadharma eva nāsti | kiṃ punaḥ prajñaptisatī pṛthivī | (1) yo mṛtpiṇḍaḥ khakkhaṭaḥ sa eva [kadācit] mṛduḥ | ato jñāyate khakkhaṭalakṣaṇamaniyatamiti | (2) alpatarakāraṇena ca khakkhaṭabuddhirbhavati | aṇūnāṃ viśliṣṭasamavāye mṛduriti buddhirbhavati | saṃśliṣṭasamavāye khakkhaṭamiti | ato 'niyatam | (3) nahyekasmin dharme sparśadvayaṃ bhavati | yena khakkhaṭaḥ kāyaḥ mṛduḥ kāya iti buddhirbhavet | ato 'niyataṃ khakkhaṭalakṣaṇam | (4) aniyatā khakkhaṭatā mṛdutā cānyonyamapekṣyāsti | yathā kambalamapekṣya paṭaṃ mṛdu bhavati | paṭamapekṣya kambalaṃ karkaśaṃ bhavati | na hi [tāttvikaḥ] sparśadharmaḥ anyonyamapekṣyāsti | (5) suvarṇapāṣāṇe cakṣuṣā draṣṭurjñāyate
body.translated_text: (Objection) Your statement 'A combination of form and the rest, predominantly hard, is the earth great element — therefore earth and the rest exist as designations' — this is not tenable. Why? Because the <s>dharma</s> of hardness itself does not exist. How much less could earth exist as a designation? (1) A lump of clay that is hard itself [sometimes] becomes soft. Therefore it is known that the hardness characteristic is indeterminate. (2) The cognition of hardness arises from a minor cause. When atoms (<s>aṇu</s>) are loosely combined, the cognition 'it is soft' arises. When tightly combined, [the cognition] 'it is hard' [arises]. Therefore it is indeterminate. (3) Two kinds of touch (<s>sparśa</s>) do not occur in a single <s>dharma</s> — by which there would be the cognition 'the body is hard' or 'the body is soft.' Therefore the hardness characteristic is indeterminate. (4) Hardness and softness exist only in mutual dependence — they are indeterminate. Just as, in comparison with a blanket, cloth is soft; in comparison with cloth, a blanket is rough. For the true touch-<s>dharma</s> does not exist in mutual dependence. (5) In gold and stone, through the eye, one who sees knows

body.text: idaṃ khakkhaṭamiti | na hi sparśaścakṣuṣopalabhyate | ato nāsti khakkhaṭatā | anenaiva kāraṇena mṛdvādayaḥ sparśā api na santi ||
body.translated_text: 'This is hard.' But touch (<s>sparśa</s>) is not apprehended by the eye. Therefore hardness does not exist. By this very reasoning, soft and other tangible qualities (<s>sparśa</s>) also do not exist.

body.text: khakkhaṭalakṣaṇāsattāvargo dvipaṃñcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Existence of the Characteristic of Hardness (<s>khakkhaṭalakṣaṇāsattāvarga</s>).

body.text: 43 khakkhaṭalakṣaṇasattāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 43. Chapter on the Existence of the Characteristic of Hardness (<s>khakkhaṭalakṣaṇasattāvarga</s>)

body.text: atrocyate | dravyasat khakkhaṭalakṣaṇam | yadyapyāha bhavān- yo mṛtpiṇḍaḥ khakkhaṭaḥ sa eva [kadācit] mṛduriti (1) | tadayuktam | kasmāt | nahyastyasmākaṃ dravyato mṛtpiṇḍaḥ | bahūnāṃ dharmāṇāṃ kalāpaḥ prajñaptyā mṛtpiṇḍa ityucyate | alpatarakāraṇena ca khakkhaṭabuddhirbhavatīti yadavocaḥ (2) | na tadyujyate | mama saṃśliṣṭasaṃṅghātāṇuṣu idaṃ khakkhaṭalakṣaṇaṃ labhyata iti asti khakkhaṭatā | asaṃśliṣṭeṣu tanmṛdulakṣaṇaṃ labhyate, ityato nāsti doṣaḥ | yo dharma upalabhyate | sa evāstītyucyate | yadapyuktaṃ- nahyekasmin dharme sparśadvayamastīti (3) | tadayuktam | upalabhyante kilāsmābhiḥ ekasminneva dharme bahavaḥ sparśāḥ khakkhaṭo 'pi mṛdurapīti | yadapyuktam- khakkhaṭatā mṛdutā cānyonyamapekṣata iti nāsti niyateti (4) tannayujyate | yathā hrasvadīrghatvādi anyonyamapekṣyāpyasti | yathā sitopalārasamāsvādayiturasitopalārasaḥ kaṭurbhavati | harītakīrasamāsvādayiturasitopalāraso madhuro bhavati | yadyanyonyāpekṣaṇānnāsti | tadā rasa eva na syāt | (pṛ) asitopalāyāṃ dvividho 'sti rasaḥ madhuraḥ kaṭuriti | (u) [tarhi]paṭe 'pi dvau sparśau staḥ khakkhaṭo mṛduśceti |
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: The characteristic of hardness exists as a real substance (<s>dravyasat</s>). Although you have said (1): 'The same lump of clay that is hard is [sometimes] also soft' — that is not correct. Why? Because for us, a lump of clay does not exist as a substance. An assemblage (<s>kalāpa</s>) of many <s>dharmas</s> is called 'a lump of clay' by designation (<s>prajñapti</s>). And as for what you said (2) — 'The cognition of hardness arises from a lesser cause' — that is not correct. In my view, this characteristic of hardness is obtained in atoms (<s>aṇu</s>) that are tightly conjoined in an aggregate — therefore hardness exists. In those that are not tightly conjoined, the characteristic of softness is obtained — therefore there is no fault. Whatever <s>dharma</s> is apprehended — that alone is said to exist. As for what you have said (3) — 'In one <s>dharma</s> there cannot be two tangible qualities' — that is not correct. Indeed, we apprehend in a single <s>dharma</s> many tangible qualities, both hard and soft. As for what you have said (4) — 'Hardness and softness are mutually dependent and therefore not fixed' — that is not correct. Just as shortness and length and so forth, though mutually dependent, still exist. For example, for one who has tasted the juice of raw sugar, the juice of raw sugar tastes bitter. For one who has tasted the juice of <s>harītakī</s>, the juice of raw sugar tastes sweet. If [you say that] because of mutual dependence it does not exist, then taste itself would not exist. (Objection) In raw sugar there are two kinds of taste — sweet and bitter. (Reply) Then in cloth too there are two tangible qualities — hard and soft.

body.text: pāṣāṇadarśane khakkhaṭatā jñāyata iti yaduktam | tadayuktam | na hi cakṣuṣā jñeyā khakkhaṭatā | sparśapūrvakamanumīyate | yathāgniṃ dṛṣṭvā ūṣma jñāyate iti noṣma dṛśyaṃ bhavati | yathā puruṣaḥ kambalaṃ dṛṣṭvā saṃśete kimidaṃ kaṭhinaṃ kiṃ vā mṛdu iti | ataḥ sparśo na cakṣuṣā dṛśyaḥ | ataḥ santi khakkhaṭādayaḥ sparśāḥ |
body.translated_text: As for what you have said — 'Upon seeing a stone, hardness is known' — that is not correct. For hardness is not to be known by the eye. It is inferred on the basis of [previous] touch. Just as upon seeing fire, heat is known — but heat is not visible. Just as a person, upon seeing a blanket, doubts: 'Is this hard or soft?' Therefore touch is not visible through the eye. Therefore tangible qualities such as hardness and the rest do exist.

body.text: atha khakkhaṭādayo dravyasantaḥ | kasmāt | vikalpacittasyotpādakatvāt | yadi nāsti khakkhaṭatā | tadā kiṃ vikalpyeta | khakkhaṭaḥ [sva]cittasya pratyayaṃ karoti | yatra takṣṇādi karmāntaraṃ kriyate | mṛdusnidghalakṣaṇaviruddhaṃ yat tat khakkhaṭamityucyate | sandhāraṇasya pratyayatvāt khakkhaṭam | karādīn pratihantīti khakkhaṭam | pratyakṣataḥ khalu jānīma idaṃ khakkhaṭamiti | pratyakṣaparijñāte ca vastuni na hetupratyayāpekṣāsti | loke tadvastu khakkhaṭamityākhyāyate | tathānyānyapi | ato jñāyate 'sti khakkhaṭamiti ||
body.translated_text: Now, hardness and the rest exist as real substances. Why? Because they give rise to conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpacitta</s>). If hardness does not exist, then what would be conceptualized? Hardness serves as a condition for [the arising of] one's own cognition. Where actions such as carving and the like are performed — that which is opposed to the characteristics of softness and smoothness is called 'hard.' Because it is a condition for resistance (<s>sandhāraṇa</s>), it is 'hard.' Because it strikes back against the hand and the like, it is 'hard.' We directly perceive (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) that 'this is hard.' And when a thing is known through direct perception, there is no need to rely on reasoning from cause and condition. In the world, that thing is called 'hard.' Likewise with other [tangible qualities] as well. Therefore it is known that hardness exists.

body.text: khakkhaṭalakṣaṇasattāvargastricatvāriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Existence of the Characteristic of Hardness (<s>khakkhaṭalakṣaṇasattāvarga</s>).

body.text: 44 caturmahābhūtalakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 44. Chapter on the Characteristics of the Four Great Elements (<s>caturmahābhūtalakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) asti khakkhaṭadharma iti jñātamevāsmābhiḥ | parantu paśyāmastapte suvarṇe dravatvam | āpo ghanībhūtāḥ karakāḥ | kimidaṃ suvarṇaṃ khakkhaṭatvāt pārthivam | kiṃ vā dravatvādāpyam | (u) asti pratyekaṃ svalakṣaṇam | yo dharmaḥ khakkhaṭaḥ kharagataḥ sa pṛthivīdhātuḥ | yaḥ snigdhaḥ snigdhagataḥ so 'bdhātuḥ | (pṛ) suvarṇaṃ khakkhaṭaṃ sat [tejaso yogāt] dravībhavati | āpaḥ snigdhā atiśaityāt karakā bhāvanti iti kathaṃ mahābhūtāni na svalakṣaṇaṃ jahati | yathāha sūtram- caturṇāṃ mahābhūtānāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ kadācit vikāryaṃ catvāraḥ śrāddhā nānyathopalabhyante | iti | (u) nāsmākaṃ khakkhaṭato dravo bhavati | snigdhaṃ vā khakkhaṭaṃ bhavati | kintu khakkhaṭo dravasya hetuṃ karoti | snigdhañca khakkhaṭasya hetuṃ karoti | ato na jahāti svalakṣaṇam |
body.translated_text: (Objection) We have indeed understood that the quality of hardness exists. But we observe that when gold is heated, it becomes liquid. And water, when solidified, becomes hailstones (<s>karaka</s>). Is this gold, being hard, earthy (<s>pārthiva</s>)? Or is it watery (<s>āpya</s>) because of its liquidity? (Reply) Each has its own characteristic. The <s>dharma</s> that is hard and of the nature of hardness is the earth element (<s>pṛthivīdhātu</s>). That which is moist and of the nature of moisture is the water element (<s>abdhātu</s>). (Objection) Gold, being hard, becomes liquid through the conjunction with fire (<s>tejas</s>). Water, being moist, becomes hailstones due to extreme cold. How then do the great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>) not abandon their own characteristics? As the <s>sūtra</s> states: 'The characteristics of the four great elements may sometimes be modified, but the four bases (<s>śrāddhā</s>) are not apprehended otherwise.' (Reply) For us, hardness does not become liquid, nor does moisture become hard. Rather, hardness serves as a cause for liquidity, and moisture serves as a cause for hardness. Therefore they do not abandon their own characteristics.

body.text: (pṛ) abhidharma uktam- apāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ sneha iti | kecidvadanti drava apāṃ lakṣaṇamiti | uktaṃ sūtre- syandanamapāṃ lakṣaṇamiti | kiṃ pāramārthikaṃ tattvam | (u) dravasnehasyandanāni
body.translated_text: (Objection) In the <s>Abhidharma</s> it is stated: 'The characteristic of water is moisture (<s>sneha</s>).' Some say: 'Liquidity (<s>drava</s>) is the characteristic of water.' It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Flowing (<s>syandana</s>) is the characteristic of water.' What is the ultimate truth (<s>pāramārthika tattva</s>) [here]? (Reply) Liquidity, moisture, and flowing

body.text: apāṃ nāmāntarāṇi | (pṛ) apāṃ karma dravaścakṣuṣā dṛśyamāno dharmaḥ | ato drava eva [lakṣaṇam] na tu snehaḥ syandanaṃ vā | (u) snehasyandanābhyāṃ dravo bhavati | snigdhaṃ hi adhomukhaṃ yāti | ato dravaḥ syandaḥ | snehasyandau cāpāṃ lakṣaṇam | dravastu apāṃ karma |
body.translated_text: are different names for water. (Objection) The function of water is liquidity, and liquidity is a <s>dharma</s> visible to the eye. Therefore liquidity alone is [the characteristic], not moisture or flowing. (Reply) Liquidity arises from moisture and flowing. For what is moist flows downward. Therefore liquidity is flowing. Moisture and flowing are the characteristics of water. But liquidity is the function of water.

body.text: (pṛ) laghusamudīraṇatvaṃ vāyorlakṣaṇamuktam | [tatra] laghutvamanyat samudīraṇatvamanyat | laghutvaṃ sparśāyatanasaṅgṛhītam | samudīraṇatvaṃ rūpāyatanasaṅgṛhītam | kimidānīṃ vāyurdharmadvayātmakaḥ sambhavati | (u) laghutvaṃ vāyorlakṣaṇam | samudīraṇatvaṃ vāyoḥ karma | karmaṇā saṃyujya [lakṣaṇa]muktam | (pṛ) nāsti samudīraṇalakṣaṇam | sarvadharmāṇāṃ kṣaṇikatvāt | nānyatra prāptirasti | anyatra prāptirhi samudīraṇamucyate | prāptigamanasamudīraṇānāmekārthatvāt | (u) karmeti kevalaṃ lokasatyato vadāmaḥ na tu paramārthataḥ laghudharmamupādāya deśāntare jananadharmaḥ karmeti saṃjñāṃ labhate | tasminneva samaye gacchatītyucyate | (pṛ) laghutvamaniyatalakṣaṇam | kasmāt | anyonyamapekṣya satvāt | yathā daśapalaṃ vastu viṃśatipalavastvapekṣya laghu pañcapalavastvapekṣa tu guru | (u) gurutvaparimāṇadharmaścittādi dharmamupādāya anyonyamapekṣya cāsti | yathā kaściddharmaḥ anyamapekṣya dīrghaḥ | kaścittu dharmo 'nyamapekṣya hrasvaḥ | sāmānyalakṣaṇantu [yat] cittamupādāyāsti tadeva lakṣaṇam | yadi laghutvadharmo 'nyonyāpekṣitatvānnāsti | etadādyapi na syāt | na tu tadyujyate | ato 'nyonyāpekṣikatvaṃ na samyagdhetuḥ |
body.translated_text: (Objection) It is stated that lightness (<s>laghu</s>) and stirring (<s>samudīraṇa</s>) are the characteristics of wind (<s>vāyu</s>). Lightness is one thing and stirring is another. Lightness belongs to the tangible sense-base (<s>sparśāyatana</s>). Stirring belongs to the visible sense-base (<s>rūpāyatana</s>). How then can wind be composed of two <s>dharmas</s>? (Reply) Lightness is the characteristic of wind. Stirring is the function of wind. [The characteristic] is stated together with the function. (Objection) The characteristic of stirring does not exist, because all <s>dharmas</s> are momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>). There is no arrival at another place. For arrival at another place is what is called 'stirring.' Because arrival, going, and stirring have the same meaning. (Reply) We speak of 'function' only from the standpoint of conventional truth (<s>lokasatya</s>), not from the standpoint of ultimate truth (<s>paramārtha</s>). The light <s>dharma</s>, by taking up [its nature], is a <s>dharma</s> that produces [an effect] in another place — this obtains the designation of 'function.' At that very moment it is said to 'go.' (Objection) Lightness is an indeterminate characteristic. Why? Because it exists in mutual dependence. For example, an object weighing ten <s>palas</s> is light relative to an object weighing twenty <s>palas</s>, but heavy relative to an object weighing five <s>palas</s>. (Reply) The qualities of heaviness and measure, and <s>dharmas</s> such as mind and the rest, exist in mutual dependence. Just as a certain <s>dharma</s> is long relative to another, and a certain <s>dharma</s> is short relative to another. The general characteristic that exists depending on mind — that alone is the characteristic. If the quality of lightness does not exist because of mutual dependence, then these other [qualities] too would not exist. But that is not correct. Therefore mutual dependence is not a valid objection.

body.text: kiñca laghutvaṃ nānyonyāpekṣaṇādasti | kintu atulyamasti | atulyaṃ vastu yathā dṛtimadhyagato vāyuḥ | ato nāpekṣyāsti | kevalaṃ gurutvadharma āpekṣikaḥ | vigatagurukaṃ vastu atulyam | (pṛ) yadyatulyaṃ vastu laghu ityucyate | gurutvavarjitā anye rūpādayo dharmā atulyatvāt laghavaḥ syuḥ | tattu na yujyate | ato bhavaduktaṃ na laghulakṣaṇama | (u) na vayamaṅgīkurmo rūpādīn vihāya dharmāntaraṃ guru bhavatīti | rūpādaya eva dharmāḥ
body.translated_text: Furthermore, lightness does not exist by mutual dependence — rather, it exists as unequal (<s>atulya</s>). An unequal thing — for example, wind contained within a bellows (<s>dṛti</s>) — therefore it does not exist by dependence. Only the quality of heaviness is relative. A thing devoid of heaviness is unequal. (Objection) If an unequal thing is called 'light,' then other <s>dharmas</s> such as form and the rest, being devoid of heaviness, would be light because of being unequal. But that is not correct. Therefore what you have said is not the characteristic of lightness. (Reply) We do not accept that, apart from form and the rest, some other <s>dharma</s> is heavy. The <s>dharmas</s> of form and the rest themselves

body.text: kecit tulyasvabhāvā utpadyante | yathā khakkhaṭamakhakkhaṭaṃ balamabalaṃ navaṃ purāṇamupacitamanucitaṃ kṣīṇamakṣīṇaṃ sthūlaṃ sūkṣmam ityādayaḥ | te 'pi na rūpādīn vihāya santi | evaṃ gurulakṣaṇamapi | ayaṃ rūpādisaṅghāto yadi pārthiva āpyo vā | tadā tulyo bhavet | yadi vāyavīyastaijaso vā | tadā na tulyaḥ syāt |
body.translated_text: — some arise with an equal nature. For example, hard and non-hard, strong and weak, new and old, developed and undeveloped, diminished and undiminished, gross and subtle, and so forth. These too do not exist apart from form and the rest. Likewise with the characteristic of heaviness. If this aggregate of form and the rest is earthy or watery, then it would be equal [in heaviness]. If it is of the nature of wind or fire, then it would not be equal.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi gurutvadharmo na rūpādīn vihāyāsti | laghatvamapi rūpādīn vihāyana syāt | (u) satyamevam | rūpādīn vihāya nāsti pṛthag laghutvam | kintu rūpādigaṇakalāpo laghurbhavati | (pṛ) maivam | gurulaghutvavikalpo 'vaśyaṃ kāyendriyeṇeṣyata ityato na gururlaghuḥ rūpādisaṅghātaḥ | (u) te ca khakkhaṭādayaḥ kadācit cakṣuṣā kadācit śrotrādīnā vikalpyante | te ca khakkhaṭādayaḥ padārthā na rūpādīn vihāya santi | tathā gururlaghurapi | [tatra] yadyapi kāyendriyaṃ vyāpriyate | na [tāvatā] punastat lakṣaṇāntaraṃ bhavati | na ca kāyendriyamaspṛśya kāyavijñaptimutpādayati | idaṃ gurutvalakṣaṇaṃ kāyenāspṛṣṭamapi [tasya] vijñaptimutpādayati | yathā gurudravye dravyāntargatāpekṣayāpi tadgurutvaṃ jñāyate | (pṛ) na tasmin samaye jñāyata idaṃ gurulakṣaṇamiti | (u) yathā parihitavastraḥ puruṣo 'spṛṣṭo 'pi jñāyate [ayaṃ] balavān abalavān iti | tathā gururlaghurapi | kasmāt | vividhebhyaḥ sparśebhyo vividhāḥ kāyavijñaptayo bhavanti | yathā kadācidāvedhapīḍanābhyāṃ kaṭhinasukumāra [sparśa]vijñaptirjāyate | kadācidutkṣepaṇakampanābhyāṃ gurulaghuvijñaptirjāyate | kadācidādānasaṃsparśābhyāṃ dṛḍhabalbajavijñaptirbhavati | kadācit saṃsparśapratighātābhyāṃ śītoṣṇavijñaptirbhavati | kadācinmārjanaparāmarśābhyāṃ karkaśaślakṣṇavijñaptirbhavati | kadācidabhiṣavasaṃmardābhyāṃ balīyastundilavijñaptirbhavati | chedanavedhanābhyāṃ daṇḍāghātena vā dhātvantaravijñaptirbhavati | kecitsparśāḥ sadākāyagatāḥ na śītoṣṇādivat bāhyamapekṣyāgāminaḥ yaduta praśrabdhisukhaṃ styānaprakarṣaḥ astyānaprakarṣaḥ rogo viśeṣovā kāyataikṣṇyaṃ kāyamāndyam ālasyagurutā mūrchā unmādaḥ pakṣavāyujṛmbhaṇabubhukṣāparitarṣaṇaparitarpaṇasukhāsukhalolupatājaḍatādayaḥ sparśāḥ | [te] pratyekaṃ pṛthak pṛthagvijñaptijanakāḥ |
body.translated_text: (Objection) If the quality of heaviness does not exist apart from form and the rest, then lightness too would not exist apart from form and the rest. (Reply) That is indeed so. Apart from form and the rest, there is no separate lightness. Rather, the aggregate of form and the rest [as a whole] is light. (Objection) This should not be so. The conceptualization of heaviness and lightness is necessarily held to [be cognized] through the body-faculty (<s>kāyendriya</s>) — therefore the aggregate of form and the rest is neither heavy nor light [in itself]. (Reply) Hardness and other such [qualities] are sometimes conceptualized through the eye, sometimes through the ear and other [senses]. And those qualities such as hardness do not exist apart from form and the rest. Likewise with heaviness and lightness. Although the body-faculty is active [in cognizing them], that does not make them a separate characteristic. And the body-faculty does not produce bodily cognition (<s>kāyavijñapti</s>) without touching. But this characteristic of heaviness produces cognition even without being touched by the body. Just as in a heavy object, the heaviness is known even by considering other objects contained within it. (Objection) At that moment, one does not know 'this is a characteristic of heaviness.' (Reply) Just as a person wearing clothes, even without being touched, is known to be 'strong or weak.' Likewise with heaviness and lightness. Why? Because from various tangible qualities, various bodily cognitions arise. For example, sometimes through piercing and pressing, the cognition of hard and delicate touch arises. Sometimes through lifting and shaking, the cognition of heavy and light arises. Sometimes through grasping and touching, the cognition of firm and loose arises. Sometimes through contact and impact, the cognition of cold and hot arises. Sometimes through rubbing and stroking, the cognition of rough and smooth arises. Sometimes through squeezing and pressing together, the cognition of strong and supple arises. Through cutting and piercing, or through the blow of a stick, the cognition of other elements arises. Certain tangible qualities are always present in the body and do not come from external [sources] like cold and heat — namely, the bliss of tranquility (<s>praśrabdhisukha</s>), the intensity of torpor (<s>styāna</s>), the absence of torpor, illness, distinguishing sensations, bodily sharpness, bodily dullness, the heaviness of laziness, fainting (<s>mūrcchā</s>), madness (<s>unmāda</s>), paralysis, yawning, hunger, thirst, satisfaction, pleasant and unpleasant [sensations], fickleness, torpidity, and so forth. Each of these produces distinct cognition.

body.text: (pṛ) yat gurulaghulakṣaṇaṃ sa rūpādisaṅghāta eva | kathaṃ tadrūpādīnāṃ kāyavijñaptiṃ prati pratyayatvam | (u) na rūpādisaṅghātasya kāyavijñaptiṃ prati pratyayanavyāpāraḥ | kevalaṃ tadavayavasparśaḥ kāyavijñaptiṃ prati pratyayaḥ | yathā khakkhaṭākhakkhaṭatvādayo rūpādisaṅghātavartino 'pi
body.translated_text: (Objection) The characteristic of heaviness and lightness is just this aggregate of form and the rest. How then can that be a condition for the bodily cognition of form and the rest? (Reply) It is not that the aggregate of form and the rest has no active role as a condition for bodily cognition. Rather, the tangible quality that is a component [of the aggregate] is the condition for bodily cognition. Just as hardness, non-hardness, and other such [qualities], though existing within the aggregate of form and the rest,

body.text: cakṣuṣā dṛṣṭvā jñātuṃ śakyante | yathā ca praśrabdhisukhādayo rūpādisaṅghātātmakakāyenāpi vijñāya vikalpyante | tathedamapi |
body.translated_text: can be known by seeing with the eye. And just as the bliss of tranquility (<s>praśrabdhisukha</s>) and the rest, though of the nature of the body which is the aggregate of form and the rest, are cognized and conceptualized [by it]. Likewise with this [heaviness and lightness] as well.

body.text: yadi gururlaghuḥ sparśamātram [ityabhyupagamyate] ko doṣaḥ kimanayā rūpādisaṅghātavikalpakriyayā | (u) yathā laukikā vadanti pratnadhānyaṃ pūtidhānyamiti | idaṃ pratnapūtila kṣaṇaṃ rūpādibhyo 'nyat syāt | vastutastu na tathā | rūpādīnāṃ prāthamika utpādaḥ pratnamityucyate | yadīdaṃ pratnalakṣaṇaṃ rūpādisaṅghāta eva | kathaṃ gurulakṣaṇaṃ na tathā | (pṛ) yadi laghugurvādayo rūpādisaṅghātā eva | laghulakṣaṇañca vāyau tejasi ca vartate | tadā laghutvabahulo rūpādisaṅghāto vāyuḥ syāt | tathā cetteja eva vāyuḥ syāt | (u) yatna [ya]llakṣaṇabāhulyaṃ [tasya] tanmahābhūtamiti nāma | tejasi laghūṣmalakṣaṇañcāsti | ūṣmabahulamityatasteja ityucyate | na tu laghutvabāhulyādvāyurbhavati | vāyau laghutvamātramasti | na tūṣma | ato laghumātreṇākhyā bhavati | nāsmākaṃ laghumātreṇa vāyurbhavati | kiṃntu yo laghuḥ san samudīraṇasya hetuṃ karoti | sa vāyurityucyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- laghusamudīraṇalakṣaṇo vāyuriti | tatra laghutvaṃ vāyorlakṣaṇaṃ samudīraṇatvaṃ vāyoḥ karma |
body.translated_text: If heavy and light were accepted as mere touch, what would be the fault? What need is there for this activity of distinguishing aggregates of form and the rest? (Answer) Just as worldly people say 'old grain' and 'rotten grain' — this 'old' and 'rotten' moment would be something other than form and the rest. But in reality it is not so. The initial arising of form and the rest is called 'old.' If this characteristic of 'oldness' is itself an aggregate of form and the rest, why would the characteristic of heaviness not be likewise? (Question) If lightness, heaviness, and the rest are merely aggregates of form and the rest, and the characteristic of lightness occurs in both wind and fire, then the aggregate of form and the rest that is predominated by lightness would be wind. And if so, fire itself would be wind. (Answer) That in which a certain characteristic predominates — that is named after that great element. In fire, there are both the characteristics of lightness and heat. Because heat predominates, it is called fire. It is not that wind exists merely because lightness predominates. In wind, there is only lightness — not heat. Therefore it is named solely by lightness. [But] according to our view, wind does not exist merely because of lightness. Rather, that which, being light, serves as the cause of agitation — that is called wind. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Wind is characterized by lightness and agitation.' Therein, lightness is the characteristic of wind, and agitation is the function of wind.

body.text: (pṛ) vāyuḥ parvatamapi avamūrdhayati | yadi | laghudravyam | kathaṃ tathā kuryāt | (u) vāyuḥ sthūlaḥ san baliṣṭho bhavati | tathā prabhāvakṣamo bhavati | yathā kadācidvāyuralpakaṃ tṛṇaṃ kampayati | kadācitparvatamunmūlayati | īdṛśaṃ vāyoḥ karmeti jñātavyam |
body.translated_text: (Question) Wind topples even a mountain. If it is a light substance, how could it do so? (Answer) When wind is massive, it becomes powerful. And thus it is capable of great effects. Just as sometimes wind shakes a small blade of grass, and sometimes it uproots a mountain. Such should be known as the function of wind.

body.text: (pṛ) pṛthivyādimahābhūtāni kimaviśeṣeṇa rūparasagandhasparśasaṅghātāḥ | (u) nāsti niyamaḥ | yathā pṛthivyāṃ santi rūparasagandhasparśāḥ | kadācit kevalaṃ rūpasparśau staḥ yathā suvarṇajatādiṣu | apsu kadācit rūparasagandhasparśāḥ santi | kadācit trayo rūparasasparśāḥ santi tejasi kadācit rūparasagandhasparśāḥ santi | kadācit trayo rūpagandhasparśāḥ santi | kadācitkevalaṃ rūpasparśau staḥ | ato nāsti niyamaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) Are the great elements such as earth and the rest invariably aggregates of form, taste, smell, and touch? (Answer) There is no fixed rule. In earth there are form, taste, smell, and touch. But sometimes there are only form and touch — as in gold, lac, and the like. In water, sometimes there are form, taste, smell, and touch. Sometimes there are three — form, taste, and touch. In fire, sometimes there are form, taste, smell, and touch. Sometimes there are three — form, smell, and touch. Sometimes there are only form and touch. Therefore there is no fixed rule.

body.text: (pṛ) vāyoḥ sparśaḥ kīdṛśaḥ | (u) śītoṣṇakaṭhinasukumārādayaḥ sparśāḥ yanmahābhūtasantatāvavinirbhāgavartinaḥ tasya mahābhūtasya sparśā iti jñātavyam | (pṛ) bhiṣajo vadanti vāyurūpaṃ kṛṣṇamiti | kiṃ pāramārthikam | (u) vāyuḥ kṛṣṇarūpasya hetuḥ | yathā vātarogiṇo mukhe tiktaraso 'stīti na sa bhiṣagvavati vāyau raso 'stīti | tadā vāyū rasasya heturiti bhavati | (pṛ) kecidvadanti vāyuḥ śīto na tu laghuriti | kiṃ paramārthikam |
body.translated_text: (Question) What kind of touch does wind have? (Answer) Cold, hot, hard, soft, and the rest — whatever touches exist inseparably in the continuum of a great element, those should be known as the touches of that great element. (Question) Physicians say: 'The color of wind is dark.' Is that ultimately true? (Answer) Wind is the cause of dark color. Just as a person afflicted by wind-disease has a bitter taste in his mouth — but the physician does not say 'wind has taste.' Rather, wind is the cause of that taste. (Question) Some say: 'Wind is cold but not light.' What is ultimately true?

body.text: (u) nāsti yaḥ śītaḥ sa vāyuriti | yathā himaṃ śītaṃ sat na vāyurbhavati | vāyuśaityañcānyat | kasmāt | yathoṣṇavāyuranuṣṇāśītavāyuśca vāyurityākhyāyate | ato laghutvāśrayaḥ saṅghāto vāyurbhavati | kiñca rūparahitasparśādidharmajanano vāyuḥ | na tu [yat] śītaṃ [sa] vāyuḥ |
body.translated_text: (Answer) It is not the case that whatever is cold is wind. For instance, snow is cold but is not wind. And the coldness of wind is something else. Why? Because hot wind, and neither-hot-nor-cold wind are also designated as 'wind.' Therefore, the aggregate based on lightness is wind. Furthermore, wind is that which generates <s>dharmas</s> of touch and the like that are devoid of form. But it is not the case that whatever is cold is wind.

body.text: (pṛ) vāyu rūparasavattve ko doṣaḥ | (u) vāyau rūparasau nopalabhyete | sattve 'pi saukṣmyānnopalabhyata iti vaktuścitta eva saṃjñānusmaraṇavikalpaḥ syāt yaduta vāyau rūparasau sta iti | natvidaṃ yujyate | na hi vayaṃ vadāmaḥ satkāryam | tasmāt yatphala upalabhyate nāvaśyaṃ taddhetau pūrvamasti | ayaṃ caturṇāṃ mahābhūtānāṃ paramārthaḥ siddhaḥ ||
body.translated_text: (Question) What is the fault in wind possessing form and taste? (Answer) Form and taste are not apprehended in wind. Even if they existed, [one might say] they are not apprehended due to their subtlety — but that would be a mere conceptual construction of the mind of the speaker, namely: 'Wind has form and taste.' This is not tenable. For we do not hold the doctrine of pre-existent effects (<s>satkāryavāda</s>). Therefore, what is apprehended in the fruit does not necessarily pre-exist in the cause. This establishes the ultimate nature of the four great elements.

body.text: caturmahābhūtalakṣaṇavargaścatuścatvāriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of the Four Great Elements (<s>caturmahābhūtalakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 45 indriyaprajñaptivargaḥ
body.translated_text: 45. Chapter on the Designation of the Sense Faculties (<s>indriyaprajñaptivarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) cakṣurādīnīndriyāṇi kiṃ caturmahābhūtaiḥ sahaikāni utānyāni | (u) karmataścatvāri mahābhūtāni pratītya cakṣurādīnīndriyāṇi bhavanti | ataścaturmahābhūtebhyo nānyāni | cakṣurvikalpayan bhagavānevaṃ vacanamāha yaccakṣuṣi māṃsapiṇḍe khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ sa pṛthivīdhāturiti | kasmāt | khakkhaṭādivikalpamātraṃ, na punaranyadasti cakṣuḥ | bhagavān cakṣuḥ śūnyamiti janānāṃ jijñāpayiṣayaivedṛśaṃ vacanamāha | tathā no cet cakṣuṣi khakkhaṭādikamanyadasti khakkhaṭādau vā anyadāsti cakṣuḥ [iti]khakkhaṭādīnāṃ vikalpe 'pi nāsti kaścanopakāraḥ | ataḥ sarvāṇīndriyāṇi na caturmahābhūtebhyo 'nyāni | ṣaḍdhātusūtre coktaṃ- ṣaḍdhāturayaṃ puruṣa iti | yadīndriyāṇi [na] caturmahābhūtebhyo 'nyāni | tadā cakṣurādīni na puruṣapratyayā iti sidhyati | rūpādīnupādāya catvāri mahābhūtāni bhavanti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Are the sense faculties such as the eye and the rest identical with the four great elements, or are they different? (Answer) Dependent on the four great elements through the force of <s>karma</s>, the sense faculties such as the eye and the rest come into being. Therefore they are not different from the four great elements. The Blessed One, analyzing the eye, spoke thus: 'In the lump of flesh of the eye, what is hard and solid — that is the earth element.' Why? Because there is merely the distinction of hardness and the rest — there is no other thing called 'the eye.' The Blessed One spoke in this way in order to make people understand that the eye is empty (<s>śūnya</s>). If it were otherwise — that in the eye there is something other than hardness and the rest, or that in hardness and the rest there is another thing called 'the eye' — then even the analysis of hardness and the rest would serve no purpose. Therefore all the sense faculties are not different from the four great elements. And it is stated in the <s>Ṣaḍdhātusūtra</s> (Sūtra on the Six Elements): 'This person consists of six elements.' If the sense faculties are not different from the four great elements, then it is established that the eye and the rest are not additional constituents of the person. Dependent on form and the rest, the four great elements come into being.

body.text: tathā śabdo 'pi puruṣapratyaya iti sidhyet | ṣaḍdhātumātre puruṣa iti prajñapyate | ato jñāyata indriyāṇi na caturmahābhūtebhyo 'nyānīti |
body.translated_text: Likewise, it would be established that sound too is a constituent of the person. The person is designated as consisting merely of six elements. From this it is known that the sense faculties are not different from the four great elements.

body.text: kaścidbhikṣurbhagavantaṃ pṛcchati katamaccakṣuriti | bhagavān pratyāha- catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya rūpi anidarśanaṃ sapratighaṃ cakṣuḥ iti | ato na caturmahābhūtebhyo 'nyaditi jñāyate | ayaṃ bhikṣustīkṣṇendriyaḥ prājñaḥ | tasya cakṣurādiṣu kāṃkṣā samapadyata | laukikāḥ sarve prajānanti rūpadarśanaṃ cakṣuryāvat sparśanaṃ kāya iti | tasya bhikṣoścakṣurādīndriyeṣu nāstīti śaṅkodapādi | kasmāt kecidācāryā vadanti pañcasvabhāvāḥ pañcendriyāṇīti | anye kecidvadanti ekasvabhāvā iti | [ato] 'yaṃ bhikṣurbhagavataḥ śāsanamimāṃsayā bhagavantaṃ papraccha | pañcendriyāṇi caturmahābhūtamayānīti parididṛkṣayā bhagavān pratyāha- cakṣurbhikṣo [ādhyātmikamāyatana] catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya rūpamanidarśanaṃ sapratighamiti | yo dharmo dravyasan na sa upādāyāsti | prajñaptimupādāya dharmaḥ prajñaptireva | yathā vṛkṣānupādāya vanam |
body.translated_text: A certain monk asked the Blessed One: 'What is the eye?' The Blessed One replied: 'The material form (<s>rūpa</s>) derived from the four great elements, invisible (<s>anidarśana</s>) and resistant (<s>sapratigha</s>) — that is the eye.' From this it is known that [the eye] is not different from the four great elements. This monk was one of sharp faculties and great wisdom. A doubt arose in him regarding the eye and the rest. All worldly people know that seeing form is the eye, and so on down to touching is the body. In this monk, regarding the sense faculties of the eye and the rest, the suspicion arose that they do not exist. Why? Because some teachers say: 'The five sense faculties have five natures.' Others say: 'They have a single nature.' Therefore this monk, investigating the teaching of the Blessed One through critical inquiry, asked the Blessed One. Wishing to show that the five sense faculties are composed of the four great elements, the Blessed One replied: 'The eye, O monk, is the internal sense-base (<s>ādhyātmikāyatana</s>), the material form derived from the four great elements, invisible and resistant.' A <s>dharma</s> that exists as a real substance would not be described as 'derived from.' A <s>dharma</s> that is dependent on a designation is itself a designation — just as a forest is [a designation] dependent on trees.

body.text: (pṛ) kecidvadanti rūpaprasādhanaṃ cakṣuriti | katamatpāramārthikam | (u) yatprasādhanaṃ tadaprasādhameva | karmahetujāni catvāri mahābhūtāni cakṣurādīndriyāṇītyākhyāyante | tathā nocet asya bhikṣoścakṣurādiṣu indriyeṣu śaṅkā naivocchidyeta | kasmāt | bhagavān prāha- cakṣurādīnindriyāṇi catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya bhavantītyato 'yaṃ bhikṣurjānāti adravyasan cakṣurdharma iti | ato jñāyate cakṣurādīni na caturmahābhūtebhyo 'nyānīti | bhagavān cakṣuṣaḥ śūnyatvapradarśanāya tatra catvāri mahābhūtāni vikalpayati | yathā prajñayā aprapañcayitā vadati- ayaṃ kāyaḥ ṣaṭsu dhātuṣu vibhaktaḥ yat khakkhaṭaṃ kharagataṃ sa pṛthivīdhāturityādi pratyavekṣeteti | evaṃ pañcadhātubhyo viraktasya ekaṃ vijñānamātramasti | tadyathāpi
body.translated_text: (Question) Some say: 'Transparency of form (<s>rūpaprasādhana</s>) is the eye.' What is ultimately true? (Answer) What is called 'transparency' is itself a non-transparent [substance]. The four great elements born of <s>karma</s> are designated as the sense faculties of the eye and the rest. If it were otherwise, the doubt of this monk regarding the sense faculties of the eye and the rest would not have been resolved. Why? The Blessed One said: 'The sense faculties of the eye and the rest come into being derived from the four great elements' — therefore this monk knew that the eye is a <s>dharma</s> that does not exist as a real substance. From this it is known that the eye and the rest are not different from the four great elements. The Blessed One analyzed the four great elements within the eye in order to demonstrate the emptiness of the eye. Just as one who, examining without conceptual proliferation (<s>prapañca</s>), says: 'This body, divided into the six elements — what is hard and solid is the earth element' and so forth, should be examined. Thus, for one who is dispassionate toward the five elements, there remains only consciousness alone. Just as

body.text: godhātakasya | hastipadopamasūtre catvāri mahābhūtāni vikalpitāni na punaścakṣuḥ | yadyasti pṛthak cakṣuḥ, vikalpyeta | vātsaputrīyādaya abhidharmikā api īdṛśaṃ vacanaṃ kurvanti | aduṣṭatvāt śraddhātavyaṃ syāt |
body.translated_text: in the case of [the Elder] <s>Godhātaka</s>. In the <s>Hastipadopama-sūtra</s> (Sūtra of the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint), the four great elements are analyzed, but the eye is not [separately analyzed]. If the eye existed separately, it would be analyzed. The <s>Vātsīputrīya</s> and other <s>Abhidharmikas</s> also make such statements. Because they are not corrupt, this should be believed.

body.text: (pṛ) pañcendriyāṇi caturmahābhūtebhyo 'nyāni | kasmāt | cakṣurādīni cakṣurādyāyatanasaṃgṛhītāni | catvāri mahābhūtāni spraṣṭavyāyatanasaṃgṛhītāni | cakṣurādīnyādhyātmikāyatanāni | catvāri mahābhūtāni bāhyāyatanāni | cakṣurādīnīndriyāṇi, catvāri mahābhūtāni anindriyāṇi | cakṣurādīni bhautikarūpaprasādhanāni | na tathā catvāri mahābhūtāni | ato jñāyata indriyāṇi na caturmahābhūtāni |
body.translated_text: (Question) The five sense faculties are different from the four great elements. Why? The eye and the rest are included in the eye sense-base and so forth. The four great elements are included in the tangible sense-base (<s>spraṣṭavyāyatana</s>). The eye and the rest are internal sense-bases (<s>ādhyātmikāyatana</s>). The four great elements are external sense-bases (<s>bāhyāyatana</s>). The eye and the rest are faculties (<s>indriya</s>); the four great elements are non-faculties. The eye and the rest are transparencies of derived material form (<s>bhautikarūpaprasādhana</s>); not so the four great elements. From this it is known that the sense faculties are not the four great elements.

body.text: (u) ekameva vastu pratyayavaśānnānocyate | yathā śraddhādīni pañcendriyāṇyapi saṃskāraskandha ityākhyāyante | yāni catvāri mahābhūtāni karmajāni cakṣurādisaṅgṛhītāni [tāni] ādhyātmikamāyātanam indriyam iti ca kathyante | tānyeva [indriya]prasādhanāni | yathā cakrādayaśśakaṭasādhanāni | cakrameva hi śakaṭam | tathedamapi |
body.translated_text: (Answer) One and the same thing is called by different names due to conditions. Just as faith and the other five faculties are also designated as the formations aggregate (<s>saṃskāraskandha</s>). Those four great elements that are born of <s>karma</s> and are included in the eye and the rest are spoken of as 'internal sense-bases' and as 'faculties.' Those very same [elements] are the transparencies [of the faculties]. Just as wheels and the rest are the means of accomplishing a chariot. The wheel itself is the chariot. So too is this.

body.text: (pṛ) maivam | yathā śraddhā nāma cittaprasādaḥ | anyā ca śraddhā anyat cittam | tathedamapi | (u) na yujyata [idam] yathā prasādamupādāya āpaḥ sphaṭikam | āpa eva prasannā āpa iti prasāda āpa eva | evaṃ pratilabdhaśraddhāsphaṭikaṃ cittasrotaḥ prasādaḥ | ayaṃ cittaprasādaśca cittameva | na vayamasmin śāstre vadāmaścittādanyadasti śraddheti | ato nāyaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ sambhavati | indriyāṇi ca prajñaptayaḥ | na ca prajñaptiḥ tatsādhanahetoranyeti vaktuṃ śakyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) This is not correct. Just as faith is called the purification of mind (<s>cittaprasāda</s>) — faith is one thing and mind is another. So too here. (Answer) That is not tenable. Just as, with reference to transparency, water [that is] crystal-clear — the water itself, when clear, is called transparent water. The transparency is just the water. Likewise, the stream of mind that has obtained the crystal-clarity of faith is the transparency. And this mental transparency is mind itself. We do not say in this <s>śāstra</s> that there exists faith separate from mind. Therefore your analogy does not hold. The sense faculties are designations. And it cannot be said that a designation is different from the cause that establishes it.

body.text: (pṛ) ekamityapi na vaktuṃ śakyate | (u) caturmahābhūtaprasādhita indriyamiti
body.translated_text: (Question) It cannot be said that [they are] identical either. (Answer) It is designated that the sense faculty is that which is accomplished by the four great elements

body.text: prajñapyate | na caturmahābhūtamātramidriyam | ato jñāyate indriyāṇi na caturmahābhūtebhyo 'nyānīti ||
body.translated_text: . It is not the case that the four great elements alone constitute a sense faculty. From this it is known that the sense faculties are not different from the four great elements.

body.text: indriyaprajñaptivargaḥ pañcacatvāriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Designation of the Sense Faculties (<s>indriyaprajñaptivarga</s>).

body.text: 46 indriyavikalpavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 46. Chapter on the Analysis of the Sense Faculties (<s>indriyavikalpavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) indriyeṣu kiṃ mahābhūtaṃ nyūnaṃ kimadhikam | (u) na kiñcit nyūnamadhikaṃ vā | (pṛ) yadi sarvāṇi bhūta[mayā]ni | kasmātkiñcidrūpaṃ paśyati | kiñcinna paśyati | (u) sarvaṃ karmajam | karmajacākṣuṣacaturmahābhūtabalaṃ rūpaṃ paśyati tathānyānyapīndriyāṇi | (pṛ) yadi karmajam | kasmānnaikendriyeṇa sarvān viṣayān jānāti | (u) idaṃ karma pañcadhā vibhaktam | kiñcitkarma darśanasya hetuṃ karoti | yathā pradīpadānaṃ cakṣurindriyavipākam | tathā śabdādīnāmapi | karmaviśeṣāt indriyabalaṃ bhidyate | (pṛ) yadīdaṃ karmabalam | indriyāṇāṃ kāpekṣā | karmajaṃ vijñānamātraṃ sarvaviṣayān gṛhṇīyāt | (u) maivam | pratyakṣaṃ paśyāmaḥ khalu anindriyāṇāṃ vijñānaṃ notpadyata iti | tathā hi yathāndho na paśyati | na badhiraḥ śṛṇoti | pratyakṣadṛṣṭe vastuni nirarthikā pratyayatā syāt | naitaddūṣaṇaṃ bhavati | dharmatā ca tathā- ya indriyavirahitāḥ teṣāṃ vijñānaṃ notpadyata iti | na bāhyāni catvāri mahābhūtāni anindriyāṇi janayanti iti dharmatā tadapekṣeta | indriyālaṅkṛtāḥ sattvānāṃ kāyā ityataḥ karmajam | yathā dhānyakāraṇakarmapratilambhāt dhānyaṃ bījāṅkurakāṇḍanālapatrāṇyapekṣyāpi kramaśo jāyate | evamidamapi |
body.translated_text: (Question) Among the sense faculties, is any great element deficient or in excess? (Answer) None is deficient or in excess. (Question) If all [faculties] are composed of the [same] elements, why does one [faculty] see form while another does not? (Answer) Everything is born of <s>karma</s>. The power of the four great elements of the eye born of <s>karma</s> sees form. Likewise for the other sense faculties. (Question) If it is born of <s>karma</s>, why does one not know all objects through a single faculty? (Answer) This <s>karma</s> is divided fivefold. A certain <s>karma</s> serves as the cause of seeing — just as the giving of a lamp results in the ripened fruit of the eye faculty. Likewise for sound and the rest. Through the distinction of <s>karma</s>, the power of the faculties differs. (Question) If this is the power of <s>karma</s>, what need is there for the sense faculties? <s>Karma</s>-born consciousness alone would apprehend all objects. (Answer) That is not correct. We directly perceive that for those lacking sense faculties, consciousness does not arise. For instance, a blind person does not see; a deaf person does not hear. If a contrary reasoning were to be offered against a directly perceived fact, it would be pointless. This objection does not hold. It is the nature of things (<s>dharmatā</s>) that for those devoid of sense faculties, consciousness does not arise. It is not the external four great elements — those that are non-faculties — that generate [consciousness]. The nature of things requires this. The bodies of beings are adorned with faculties — and therefore [consciousness] is born of <s>karma</s>. Just as grain comes into being through the acquisition of the <s>karma</s> of its cause, and that grain also depends on seeds, sprouts, stalks, stems, and leaves, arising progressively — so too is this.

body.text: (pṛ) kasmānna tathā cittam | yathā cakṣurvijñānaṃ cakṣurindriyakaṃ samanantaraniruddhacittamupādāya ca bhavati | cittantu samanantaraniruddhacittamātrendriyakam | na punarasti cakṣurādīnāmiva indriyāyatanam | vaktavyaśca pratyayaḥ | (u) niyatānāṃ pañcaviṣayāṇāṃ niyatāni pañcavijñānāni santi | naivaṃ cittasya | cittadharmaśca tathā syāt- yat samanantaraniruddhacittendriyakaṃ bhavati nānyatkiñcidapekṣata iti | yathātītānāgatadharmā asanto 'pi manasa ālambanāni bhavanti | cittacaittā apyevamitīdamapi yujyate | idañca bhavatāṃ
body.translated_text: (Question) Why is mind (<s>citta</s>) not the same [as the five sense-consciousnesses]? Just as eye-consciousness arises depending on the eye-faculty (<s>cakṣurindriya</s>) and the immediately preceding ceased mind — mind, however, has only the immediately preceding ceased mind as its faculty. It does not have a separate faculty-base (<s>indriyāyatana</s>) like the eye and the rest. The condition must be stated. (Answer) For the five fixed objects, there are five fixed consciousnesses. This is not the case for mind. The nature of mind-<s>dharma</s> is such that it arises depending only on the immediately preceding ceased mind as its faculty, without depending on anything else. Just as past and future <s>dharmas</s>, even though non-existent, serve as objects (<s>ālambana</s>) of the mind — mind and mental factors likewise function in this way. And this accords with your own

body.text: siddhāntena samam | bhavatāṃ siddhāntaśca- rūpādiviṣayeṣu vijñānamindriyamapekṣyotpadyate | samanantaraniruddhacittamapekṣya manovijñānamutpadyata iti |
body.translated_text: established doctrine. Your established doctrine is: 'In the case of objects such as form and the rest, consciousness arises depending on the sense-faculty. Mind-consciousness arises depending on the immediately preceding ceased mind.'

body.text: (pṛ) yadi manovijñānasya na punarindriyamasti | kutrāśritya bhavati | (u) caturmahābhūtakāyamāśritya bhavati | (pṛ) ārūpyadhātau ka āśrayaḥ | (u) ārūpyadhātuvijñānasya na kaścanāśrayo 'sti | dharmateyaṃ yannirāśrayaṃ tiṣṭhatīti | kasmāt | lakṣaṇaviśeṣāt | manovijñānameva jānāti asti nāstīti | rūpiṇa āśrayo bhavati | arūpamapi tiṣṭhatīti ārūpyadhātāvapi nirāśrayaṃ tiṣṭhati | pratyayasāmagryā vijñānamutpadyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- manaḥ pratītya dharmāṃśca manovijñānamutpadyata iti | asya ka āśrayaḥ | nāsti tu puruṣāṇāmiva bhittyādiḥ | sarve dharmāḥ prakṛtipratiṣṭhāḥ ||
body.translated_text: (Question) If mind-consciousness has no further sense-faculty, on what basis does it exist? (Answer) It exists based on the body constituted of the four great elements (<s>caturmahābhūtakāya</s>). (Question) In the formless realm (<s>ārūpyadhātu</s>), what is its basis? (Answer) The consciousness of the formless realm has no basis whatsoever. It is its nature (<s>dharmatā</s>) that it subsists without a basis. Why? Because of a distinctive characteristic. Mind-consciousness alone knows 'it exists' and 'it does not exist.' For one with form, there is a basis. But the formless also subsists — therefore, even in the formless realm, it subsists without a basis. Consciousness arises through the aggregate of conditions (<s>pratyayasāmagrī</s>). As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Dependent on mind (<s>manas</s>) and <s>dharmas</s>, mind-consciousness arises.' What is its basis? It does not have [a basis] like a wall and such for persons. All <s>dharmas</s> are established in their own nature (<s>prakṛtipratiṣṭha</s>).

body.text: indriyavikalpavargaḥ ṣaṭcatvāriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Analysis of the Faculties (<s>indriyavikalpavarga</s>).

body.text: 47 indriyāṇāṃ samabhūtatāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 47. Chapter on the Equal Elemental Composition of the Faculties (<s>indriyāṇāṃ samabhūtatāvarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) tīrthikā vadanti- pañcendriyāṇi pañcabhūtebhyo jātānīti | kiṃ paramārthikam | (u) na [tebhyo jātāni] | kasmāt | ākāśasyābhāvāt | idañca dīpitameva | tasmānna pañcabhūtebhyo jātāni |
body.translated_text: (Question) The <s>tīrthikas</s> (non-Buddhist teachers) say: 'The five sense faculties are born from the five elements (<s>bhūta</s>).' Is this ultimately true? (Answer) [They are] not [born from the five elements]. Why? Because space (<s>ākāśa</s>) does not [truly] exist. This has already been demonstrated. Therefore they are not born from the five elements.

body.text: (pṛ) tīrthikā vadanti- cakṣuṣi tejomahābhūtaṃ bahulam | kasmāt | karmasārūpyahetoḥ | pradīpadānamupādāya cakṣurlabhate | yathokta sūtre- paṭaṃ datvā rūpaṃ labhate | annaṃ datvā rūpaṃ labhate | annaṃ datvā balaṃ labhate | yānaṃ datvā sukhaṃ labhate | pradīpaṃ datvā cakṣurlabhate | iti | ataścakṣuṣi tejomahābhūtaṃ bahulam | cakṣuścālokamapekṣya paśyati |
body.translated_text: (Question) The <s>tīrthikas</s> say: 'In the eye, the fire great element (<s>tejas</s>) predominates.' Why? Because of the correspondence between <s>karma</s> and its fruit. By giving a lamp, one obtains the eye. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'By giving cloth, one obtains [beautiful] form. By giving food, one obtains strength. By giving a vehicle, one obtains comfort. By giving a lamp, one obtains the eye.' Therefore, in the eye, the fire great element predominates. And the eye sees depending on light.

body.text: ālokavigataṃ na paśyati | ato jñāyate tejomahābhūtaṃ bahulamiti | tejaśca sudūraṃ prakāśayati | saprabhatvāt cakṣuḥ sudūraṃ rūpaṃ pratihanti | vadanti ca mriyamāṇasya cakṣuḥ sūryaṃ pratigacchatīti | ato jñāyate sūryo mūlaprakṛtiriti | cakṣurniyamena rūpameva paśyati | rūpañca taijasamityataḥ punarātmabhāvameva paśyati | evamākāśapṛthivyabvāyava indriyato nyūnādhikāḥ | mriyamāṇasya śrotramākāśaṃ pratigacchati | śrotraṃ niyamena śabdaṃ śṛṇoti | śabdaścākāśa[gataḥ] | evanyānyānyapi | ata indriyeṣu mahābhūtāni nyūnādhikāni bhavanti | [na samāni] | iti |
body.translated_text: Without light, it does not see. From this it is known that the fire great element predominates. And fire illuminates over a great distance. Because the eye has luminosity (<s>saprabhatva</s>), it apprehends form over a great distance. They also say: 'The eye of a dying person returns to the sun.' From this it is known that the sun is the root-nature (<s>mūlaprakṛti</s>). The eye invariably sees only form. And form is fiery in nature — therefore [the eye] sees only its own nature. Likewise, space, earth, water, and wind are distributed in lesser and greater proportions in the sense faculties. The ear of a dying person returns to space. The ear invariably hears only sound. And sound resides in space. Similarly with the others. Therefore, in the sense faculties, the great elements are present in unequal proportions.

body.text: atrocyate | yadbhavānavocat- karmasārūpyahetoriti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | kiñciddarśanaṃ saphalaṃ vinā karmasārūpyahetoḥ | yathā vadanti- annaṃ datvā pañcavastu- vipākān labhata iti | yadi cakṣuṣi tejo bahulam | pradīpādibāhyālokamanapekṣya [paśyet] | yadi bāhyālokāpekṣiṇo 'pi cakṣuṣastejo bahulam | tadā śrotrādīndriyeṣvapi ākāśādayo bahulāḥ syuḥ | na bāhyākāśādīnapekṣeran | vastutastu bāhyānapekṣante | ato 'hetuḥ | āpaścakṣuṣa upakurvanti | yathā kṣālitacakṣuṣkasya puruṣasya cakṣuḥ sphuṭameva pratyeti | tadā abbahulaṃ syāt | tejaśca cakṣurvināśayati yathā sūryaprabhādayaḥ | yadīme svaprakṛtayaḥ, nātmānaṃ vighaṭayeyuḥ | ato jñāyate na tejo[bahulam] iti | divyaṃ cakṣurālokamantarāpi rūpaṃ paśyati | ato na taijasaṃ cakṣuḥ | candrikāyāñca rūpaṃ draṣṭuṃ śaknoti | candraśca na tejaḥprakṛtikaḥ | tathā cakṣuṣo dharmaśaktirapi | kiñciccakṣurālokamapekṣya paśyati | kiñcidanapekṣyāpi paśyati | yathā cakṣurākāśādipratyayaṃ labdhvā rūpamaprāpyāpi sudūraṃ paśyati | īdṛśī cakṣuṣo dharmatā | ato na kāryaḥ saṃjñānusmaraṇavikalpoi yaduta tejobahulaṃ [cakṣu]riti |
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: Your statement 'because of the correspondence between <s>karma</s> and its fruit' is not valid. Why? Certain results of seeing are fruitful without correspondence to <s>karma</s>. As they say: 'By giving food, one obtains five kinds of ripened results.' If in the eye the fire [element] predominates, it would see without depending on external light such as a lamp. If, even though the eye depends on external light, fire predominates in it — then in the ear and other faculties too, space and the rest would predominate, and they would not depend on external space and the rest. But in reality they do depend on them. Therefore that is not a valid reason. Water also benefits the eye — just as the eye of a person whose eyes have been washed perceives clearly. In that case, water would predominate. And fire destroys the eye, as in the case of sunlight and the like. If these were of the same nature [as the eye], they would not damage it. From this it is known that [fire] does not predominate. And the divine eye (<s>divyacakṣus</s>) sees form even without light. Therefore the eye is not fiery in nature. And one can see form in moonlight — and the moon is not of a fiery nature. Such too is the natural power (<s>dharmaśakti</s>) of the eye. Sometimes the eye sees depending on light, sometimes it sees even without depending [on light]. Just as the eye, having obtained conditions such as space, sees form even without reaching [it physically], over a great distance. Such is the nature of the eye. Therefore, one should not engage in the conceptual elaboration of remembering labels, [thinking:] 'fire predominates in the eye.'

body.text: yadbhavānavocat- ālokamantarā na paśyatīti | yadyākāśaṃ manaskāraṃ rūpañcāntarā na paśyati | tadā ākāśādayo 'pi bahulāḥ syuḥ | na hi sarvaṃ cakṣurbāhyālokamapekṣate | yathā ulūkādayaḥ pakṣiṇo viḍālasṛgālādayastīryañca bāhyāmālokamanapekṣyāpi draṣṭuṃ śaknuvanti | ato na tejobahulam | tejaḥ prajvalat sadoṣmalakṣaṇam | cakṣustu na tathā |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'without light, it does not see' — if it does not see without space, mental attention (<s>manaskāra</s>), and form, then space and the rest would also predominate. For not every eye depends on external light. Just as owls and other birds, cats, jackals, and other animals can see even without depending on external light. Therefore fire does not predominate. Fire, when blazing, always has the characteristic of heat. But the eye is not like that.

body.text: yadbhavānavādīḥ- cakṣuḥ saprabhatvāt sudūraṃ rūpaṃ patihantīti | tad dūṣitameva | niṣprabhatvāccakṣuṣaḥ | yaduktaṃ sūryaṃ pratigacchatīti | cakṣustadā nityaṃ syāt | sūryādayaśca
body.translated_text: Your statement 'because the eye has luminosity, it apprehends form over a great distance' — that has already been refuted, because the eye has no luminosity. Your statement 'it returns to the sun' — then the eye would be permanent. And the sun and the rest

body.text: nendriyāṇi | cakṣuḥ kasmāt pratigacchati | yadi sūryo mriyate | sūryendriyaṃ sūryaśca kutra punaḥ pratigacchati | ato 'yuktam | upari devānāṃ mriyamāṇānāṃ cakṣuḥ kutra pratigacchati | tata upari sūryābhāvāt | ākāśamakriyaṃ sat apratiśaraṇaṃ bhavati | indriyāṇi na pratigacchanti | saṃskṛtadharmāṇāṃ kṣaṇikatvāt |
body.translated_text: are not sense faculties. Why would the eye return [to the sun]? If the sun dies, where would the sun's faculty and the sun itself return to? Therefore that is untenable. Where would the eye of dying gods in the higher realms return to? Because there is no sun above them. Space (<s>ākāśa</s>), being inactive, cannot serve as a refuge. The sense faculties do not return [anywhere], because conditioned <s>dharmas</s> (<s>saṃskṛtadharma</s>) are momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>).

body.text: yadbhavatoktaṃ- cakṣurniyamena rūpameva paśyati | rūpañca taijasamityataḥ punarātmabhāvameva paśyatīti | nedaṃ yuktam | nirupayogahetutvāt | śabda ākāśagata ityādirapi evaṃ [vācyaḥ] | tasmādindriyeṣu mahābhūtāni nyūnādhikāni bhavantīti bhavadvacanaṃ dūṣitameva |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'the eye invariably sees only form, and form is fiery in nature, therefore it sees only its own nature' — this is not valid, because it is a useless reason. The statement that 'sound resides in space' and the rest should be criticized in the same way. Therefore your statement that 'the great elements are present in unequal proportions in the sense faculties' has been refuted.

body.text: (pṛ) kecidācāryā āhuḥ- ekamindriyamekasvabhāvam | iti | pṛthivyāṃ [kevalaṃ] guṇabahutvāt gandho 'sti gandhajñānotpādakaḥ | abtejovāyuṣu rūparasasparśāḥ santi iti rūparasasparśajñānotpādakā bhavanti | kiṃ pāramārthikam | (u) uktapūrvaṃ mayā nāsti niyama iti | pṛthivyāṃ gandho 'nye 'pi santi | ato 'hetuḥ | mahābhūtāni ca sambhūya sambhavanti | na hi dṛśyate kācitpṛthivī abādiviyuktā | yadi gandhavattvāt pṛthivī gandhajñānotpādinī | rūpādijñānopādinyapi syāt | guṇacatuṣṭayopetatvātpṛthivyāḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) Certain teachers say: 'Each sense faculty has a single elemental nature.' In earth alone, because of the predominance of qualities, there is smell — which produces the cognition of smell. In water, fire, and wind, there are form, taste, and touch — which produce the cognition of form, taste, and touch respectively. Is this ultimately true? (Answer) As I have stated before, there is no such fixed rule. In earth there is smell, but other [qualities] also exist. Therefore that is not a valid reason. And the great elements arise in combination. For no earth is ever seen that is devoid of water and the rest. If, because it possesses smell, earth produces the cognition of smell — then it should also produce the cognition of form and the rest, since earth possesses all four qualities.

body.text: (pṛ) gandhamātraṃ pṛthivyāmasti | ghrāṇaṃ pārthivamityato gandhamātraṃ jñāpayati | (u) pṛthivīguṇaḥ pṛthivīmātre 'sti | ghrāṇaṃ kṣīṇa[gandha]jñānaṃ syāt | apāṃ śītasparśamātraṃ tejasa uṣṇasparśamātraṃ jivhācakṣurbhyāṃ jñātuṃ śaknuyāt | na tu yujyate vastutaḥ | dravyaṃ nāstīti indriyaṃ nāsti | indriyāṇāṃ balavṛttirviṣayasaṃyogāt jñānaṃ janayatīti | saṃyoge ca bhagne nendriyavṛttiḥ | tasmānaikasvabhāvamindriyam ||
body.translated_text: (Question) Only smell belongs to earth alone. The nose, being earthen, cognizes only smell. (Answer) The quality of earth exists in earth alone. The nose would then cognize only diminished smell. Water's cold touch alone, fire's hot touch alone — the tongue and eye could cognize only those. But in reality this is not valid. Since substance (<s>dravya</s>) does not [ultimately] exist, the sense faculty does not [exist in that way]. The forceful activity of the sense faculties, through conjunction with the object, generates knowledge. When the conjunction is broken, the faculty does not function. Therefore, a sense faculty does not have a single elemental nature.

body.text: indriyāṇāṃ samabhūtatāvargaḥ saptacatvāriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Equal Elemental Composition of the Faculties (<s>indriyāṇāṃ samabhūtatāvarga</s>).

body.text: 48 na vijānātīndriyavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 48. Chapter on Whether the Sense Faculty Cognizes (<s>na vijānātīndriyavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) indriyāṇi viṣayān kiṃ prāpya vijānanti utāprāpya vijānanti | (u) nendriyaṃ vijānāti | kasmāt | yadīndriyaṃ viṣayaṃ vijānāti | tadā sarvān viṣayānekakālaṃ vijānīyāt | vastutastu na vijānāti | ato vijñānaṃ vijānāti | bhavato hṛdayam- yatkecidvadanti indriyaṃ vijñānamapekṣya saha vijānāti na tu vijñānaviyuktaṃ vijānātīti | tadayuktam | na kaściddharmo 'nyaṃ dharmamapekṣya kiñcitkartuṃ samarthaḥ | yadīndriyaṃ vijānāti | kā vijñānasyāpekṣā | yadīndriyaṃ vijānāti idamindriyakarma idaṃ vijñānakarma iti vivektavyam |
body.translated_text: (Question) Do the sense faculties cognize objects by reaching them, or do they cognize without reaching them? (Answer) The sense faculty does not cognize. Why?
