If the sense faculty cognized the object, it would cognize all objects simultaneously. But in reality it does not cognize [all at once]. Therefore, it is consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) that cognizes. Your [unstated] thought: 'Some say that the sense faculty cognizes together with consciousness — it does not cognize when dissociated from consciousness.' That is not valid. No <s>dharma</s> can accomplish anything while depending on another <s>dharma</s>. If the sense faculty cognizes, what need is there for consciousness? If the sense faculty cognizes, then one should distinguish: 'This is the function of the sense faculty; this is the function of consciousness.'

body.text: (pṛ) prakāśanamindriyakarma | vijñāpanaṃ vijñaptikarma | (u) nāyaṃ viveko [yuktaḥ] | katamat prakāśanam | bhavatāṃ śāsane śrotrādīnīndriyāṇi na tejaḥprakṛtikāni iti na prakāśayeyuḥ | yadīndriyāṇi vijñānasya pradīpakalpāni | tadendriyāṇi punaḥ prakāśakāni syuḥ | yathā pradīpaḥ | tadā prakāśakasya punaḥ prakāśaka ityevamanavasthā syāt | yadi punaḥ prakāśakaṃ vināpi indriyamātraṃ prakāśayati | [tadā] vinendriyāmapi vijñānamātraṃ vijānīyāt | ataḥ prakāśanaṃ nendriyakarma | kiñcendriyaṃ na vijānāti | yathā pradīpaḥ prakāśayannapi na vijānāti | ato 'vaśyaṃ vijñānasyāśrayakṛtyaṃ karotīdamindriyakarma | ato vijñānamātraṃ vijānāti | nendriyāṇi | sati vijñāne jñānaṃ nāsati | yathā sati tejasi ūṣma nāsati iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Illumination (<s>prakāśana</s>) is the function of the sense faculty. Making known (<s>vijñāpana</s>) is the function of consciousness. (Answer) This distinction is not valid. What is illumination? In your teaching, the ear and other sense faculties are not fiery in nature — therefore they would not illuminate. If the sense faculties are like lamps for consciousness, then the sense faculties would themselves need further illuminators — just as a lamp [requires fuel]. Then there would be an infinite regress of illuminators needing further illuminators. If, on the other hand, the sense faculty alone illuminates without a further illuminator, then consciousness alone too could cognize without a sense faculty. Therefore, illumination is not the function of the sense faculty. Furthermore, the sense faculty does not cognize — just as a lamp, even while illuminating, does not cognize. Therefore, the sense faculty necessarily performs the function of being a support (<s>āśraya</s>) for consciousness — this is the function of the sense faculty. Therefore, consciousness alone cognizes — not the sense faculties. When consciousness is present, there is knowledge; when it is absent, there is not — just as when fire is present, there is heat; when it is absent, there is not.

body.text: (pṛ) sūtra uktaṃ- cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā na nimittagrāhī syāditi | tathā śrotrādīnyapi | ato jñāyate cakṣūrūpaṃ gṛhṇātīti | cakṣurādīnīndriyāṇi yadi na vijānanti | kenendriyatvam | uktañca sūtre- vayaṃ māṇavakāḥ susūkṣmamaṣi vastu jānīmaḥ | tadyathā cakṣurbhyāṃ dṛśyata iti | yadi cakṣurna paśyati | tadā jinaurasā na kiñcana paśyeyuḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Having seen forms with the eye, one should not grasp at signs (<s>nimitta</s>).' Likewise for the ear and the rest. From this it is known that the eye grasps form. If the eye and other sense faculties do not cognize, what makes them 'faculties'? And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'We young men know even the most subtle things — namely, what is seen by the eyes.' If the eye does not see, then the sons of the <s>Jina</s> (Victor) would not see anything.

body.text: nedaṃ saṃbhavati | ata indriyāṇi niyamena viṣayān gṛhṇanti | indriyeṇa viṣayo gṛhyate vijñānena vikalpyate ityayamevendriyavijñānayorbhedaḥ |
body.translated_text: That is not possible. Therefore, the sense faculties necessarily grasp their objects. The object is grasped by the sense faculty; it is discriminated by consciousness — this alone is the distinction between the sense faculty and consciousness.

body.text: (u) sūtre bhagavān svayamāha- cakṣu[brāhmaṇa]dvāraṃ[yāvadeva] rūpāṇāṃ darśanāya iti | ataścakṣurna paśyati | cakṣuṣā dvārībhūtena tatrasthaṃ vijñānaṃ paśyati | ata ucyate cakṣuḥ paśyatīti | (pṛ) āha ca- mano dvāraṃ [yāvadeva] dharmāṇāṃ vijñānāye ti | kiṃ sambhavati manasā dvārībhūtena vijānātīti | (u) mano [vijñānasyā]pi samanantaraniruddhaṃ cittaṃ dvāram | ato na mano vijānāti | manovijñānantu vijānāti | sūtre bhagavānāha- cakṣuḥ priyarūpāṇi kāmyati | iti | cakṣurhi rūpaprakṛtikamaviveki | ato na vastutaḥ kāmyati | tadvijñānameva kāmyati | kiñcāha bhagavān- cakṣurvijñeyāni rupāṇi iti | vijñānaṃ rūpaṃ vijānāti | na cakṣuḥ | kiñca laukikā vyavaharanti- cakṣuḥ paśyati śrotraṃ śṛṇoti iti | tadbhagavānapyanuvadati | kimiti rūpamātraṃ draṣṭavyaṃ nānyat | āha ca bhagavān- paśyāmi rāgādīn doṣān iti | candraḥ kṣīṇa iti laukikānāṃ vacanaṃ bhagavānapyanuvadati | yathā daridraḥ puruṣaḥ prabhuriti nigadyate | tathā bhagavānapyanuvadati | nahi tathāgato lokaiḥ saha vivaditumabhilaṣati | yathā mṛgāramātā ityādi | ato jñātavyaṃ vyavahārānuvartanādbhagavānāha cakṣuḥ paśyatīti |
body.translated_text: (Reply) In the <s>sūtra</s>, the Blessed One himself stated: 'The eye, O <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, is the door for the seeing of forms.' Therefore the eye does not see. Through the eye serving as a door, the consciousness stationed there sees. Therefore it is said: 'The eye sees.' (Question) He also said: 'The mind is the door for the cognizing of <s>dharmas</s>.' Is it possible that the mind, serving as a door, cognizes? (Reply) For mind-consciousness too, the immediately preceding ceased mind-moment is the door. Therefore the mind does not cognize — rather, mind-consciousness cognizes. In the <s>sūtra</s>, the Blessed One said: 'The eye desires pleasing forms.' But the eye, being of the nature of form and non-discriminating, does not actually desire. It is the consciousness [associated with the eye] that desires. Moreover, the Blessed One said: 'Forms are to be cognized by the eye.' [But] it is consciousness that cognizes form, not the eye. Furthermore, worldly people conventionally say: 'The eye sees, the ear hears.' The Blessed One too follows this convention. For what reason is only form to be seen and nothing else? The Blessed One also said: 'I see the faults of passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the rest.' The worldly saying 'the moon has waned' — the Blessed One too follows this. Just as a poor man is called 'a lord' [in polite convention], so too the Blessed One follows along. For the <s>Tathāgata</s> does not wish to dispute with the world. Just as [the conventional usage] '<s>Mṛgāramātā</s>' and so forth. Therefore it should be known that following conventional usage, the Blessed One said: 'The eye sees.'

body.text: (pṛ) loke kasmādevaṃ vyavaharati | (u) cakṣuṣo vijñānāśrayahetutāmanusṛtya tasmin hetau paśyatīti vadanti | yathā vadanti sa puruṣaḥ paśyati ayaṃ puruṣaḥ paśyatīti | yathā ca vadanti janāḥ puṇyapāpādīni kurvanti | tathāgatā devā ṛṣayaśca paśyantīti | yathā ca vadanti vāmacakṣuṣā paśyati dakṣiṇacakṣuṣā paśyatīti | vadanti ca sūryācandramasābhyāṃ paśyati sūryācandramasau paśyataḥ | kadācidakāśaṃ paśyati | kadācinmadhyaṃ paśyati
body.translated_text: (Question) Why does the world speak in this way? (Reply) Following the fact that the eye is the basis and cause of consciousness, they say of that cause: 'It sees.' Just as they say: 'That person sees, this person sees.' And just as they say: 'People perform merit and sin and the like. <s>Tathāgatas</s>, gods, and sages see.' And just as they say: 'One sees with the left eye, one sees with the right eye.' They also say: 'One sees by means of the sun and moon; the sun and moon see.' Sometimes one says: 'One sees the sky.' Sometimes one says: 'One sees the middle —'

body.text: yat dvāramadhyaṃ [tat] paśyati iti | dagdhe padārthe vadanti ayaṃ dahati | sa dahati iti | kadācidvadanti tṛṇendhanaṃ dahati | gopurīṣaṃ dahati | tailaṃ dahati | dhṛtaṃ dahati | tejo dahati | sūryo dahati iti | vastutastu agnireva hahati | anyāni dahatīti prajñaptyā vyavahriyante | sa vyavahāro na pāryantikaḥ | vaktavyañca cakṣuṣā dvāreṇa rūpaṃ paśyatīti | cakṣuḥ puruṣāṇāmupabhogopakaraṇam | puruṣāḥ prajñaptikāriṇa iti upabhogopakaraṇena bhavitavyam | cakṣurupādāya vijñāne paśyati cakṣuḥ paśyatīti vyavahāraḥ | yathā mañcastheṣu puruṣeṣu krośatsu mañcāḥ krośantīti vyavahāraḥ | cakṣuḥpratisaṃyuktaṃ vijñānakarma ityatastatra cakṣuṣi vijñānakarma vyavaharanti | yathā hastapādapratisaṃyukte puruṣe vartamānaṃ puruṣakarma hastakarmeti vyavaharanti | cakṣurvijñānasya hetuścakṣuḥ | kāraṇe kāryopacāraḥ | yathā vadanti amukaḥ puruṣo 'mukaṃ grāmaṃ dahatīti | yathā ca vadanti suvarṇa mattīti | suvarṇa māyuḥ | tṛṇāni gopaśava iti | idaṃ sarvaṃ kāraṇe kāryopacāraḥ | evaṃ cakṣurbhyomutpannaṃ vijñānaṃ rūpaṃ paśyatītyataścakṣuḥ paśyatīti vyavaharanti | cakṣuḥsannikṛṣṭe vijñāne rūpaṃ paśyati cakṣuḥ paśyatīti vyavahāraḥ | yathā gaṅgāsannikṛṣṭe ghoṣe gaṅgāyāṃ [ghoṣa] iti [vadanti] | cakṣuṣā cākṣuṣaṃ vijñānaṃ vivicyata ityataścakṣuṣi cākṣuṣavijñānakarmāropyate | yathā daṇḍī brāhmaṇa iti | cakṣuścākṣuṣavijñānaṃ sādhayatītyatastatra cakṣurvijñānakarmocyate | yathā dhane prahīṇe puruṣaḥ prahīṇa iti vadanti | pravivṛddhe ca dhane pravivṛddhaḥ puruṣa iti | cakṣurvijñāne cakṣuṣā saṃyujya paśyati sati cakṣuḥ paśyatīti vadanti | yathā vṛkṣe puruṣeṇa saṃyujya chidyamāne sati puruṣo vṛkṣaṃ chinnattīti vyavahāraḥ | yathā vā kṛṣṇavarṇasaṃyukte paṭe kṛṣṇaḥ paṭa iti vyavahāraḥ | sarve ca dharmā mithaḥ saṃkīrya vyavahriyante | yathā prajñākarma vedanādiṣūcyate | cakṣūṣā rūpaṃ paśyatīti vaktavye saṃkṣipya vyavaharantaḥ kevalamāhuḥ cakṣuḥ paśyatīti | yathā ca pāṣāṇamauṣadhamiti ekavedanāvaśā vyavahāraḥ |
body.translated_text: — 'one sees through the middle of the door.' When a substance is burned, they say: 'This burns, that burns.' Sometimes they say: 'Grass-fuel burns, cow-dung burns, oil burns, ghee burns, radiance burns, the sun burns.' But in reality, it is only fire that burns. The others are said to burn by way of designation (<s>prajñapti</s>). That convention is not ultimate. And it should be said that 'through the eye as a door, one sees form.' The eye is an instrument of experience for persons. Persons are the agents of designation, and so there must be an instrument of experience. When consciousness sees by depending on the eye, the convention is: 'The eye sees.' Just as when persons standing on a platform cry out, the convention is: 'The platforms cry out.' The action of consciousness is connected with the eye — therefore the action of consciousness is conventionally attributed to the eye. Just as when an action of a person is connected with hands and feet, the person's action is conventionally called 'the action of the hand.' The eye is the cause of eye-consciousness — the effect is figuratively attributed to the cause. Just as they say: 'Such-and-such a person burns such-and-such a village.' And just as they say: 'Gold is drunk' [meaning intoxicated by gold], 'gold is life,' 'grass is cattle.' All of this is the figurative attribution of the effect to the cause. Thus, because consciousness arises from the eye and sees form, they conventionally say: 'The eye sees.' When consciousness that is proximate to the eye sees form, the convention is: 'The eye sees.' Just as when a sound is proximate to the <s>Gaṅgā</s>, they say: 'A sound in the <s>Gaṅgā</s>.' Because eye-consciousness is distinguished by the eye, the action of eye-consciousness is attributed to the eye. Just as [one says]: 'The <s>brāhmaṇa</s> with a staff.' The eye accomplishes eye-consciousness — therefore the action of consciousness is attributed to the eye. Just as when wealth is lost, they say: 'The person is lost.' And when wealth increases, they say: 'The person has increased.' When eye-consciousness sees by being conjoined with the eye, they say: 'The eye sees.' Just as when a tree is cut by a person being conjoined [with an axe], the convention is: 'The person cuts the tree.' Or just as when a cloth is conjoined with black color, the convention is: 'The cloth is black.' And all <s>dharmas</s> are mixed together in conventional usage. Just as the action of wisdom is attributed to feeling and the rest. Instead of saying 'one sees form through the eye,' they speak in abbreviation and say merely: 'The eye sees.' And just as [saying] 'the stone is medicine' — it is a convention governed by a single perception.

body.text: yadbhavanāha apaśyataḥ kathamindriyatvamiti | bhavānidaṃ prativaktavyaḥ cakṣurādayaḥ pañcadharmā stadanyarūpādīnatiśerata ityata indriyamiti vyavahriyante | (pṛ) cakṣurādayaḥ pañcadharmāstadanyarūpādibhirmilitāḥ | daśeme dharmā na yugapadviṣayān vijānanti | yathā cakṣurādīnāṃ viyoge vijñānaṃ notpadyate, tathā yadi rūpādīnāṃ viyoge 'pi vijñānaṃ notpadyate | tadā kena [teṣā]matiśayaḥ | (u) indriyairvijñānaṃ viśeṣyate cakṣurvijñānaṃ śrotravijñānamiti | yathā bheridaṇḍasaṃyoge śabdo bhavati | [tatra] bheryāḥ prādhānyāt bherīśabda iti vadanti | pṛthivīyavādisaṃyoge aṅkuro jāyate | [tatra] yavasya prādhānyāt yavāṅkura iti vadanti | tathā vijñānānyapi | āśrayato vyavahāro viśeṣyate na pratyayataḥ | rūpavijñānamityukte saṃśayaḥ prasajyate kimidaṃ cakṣurvijñānaṃ kiṃ vā rūpaṃ pratītya manovijñānamiti | indriye 'sti vijñānaṃ na viṣaye | cakṣurādiṣu ātmasaṃmohanaṃ cittaṃ bhavati | vijñānasyāśraya āyatanamindriyaṃ na viṣayaḥ | svakāyasaṃkhyāte sthitamindriyaṃ na viṣaye | puruṣasyopabhogopakaraṇamindriyaṃ na viṣayaḥ | indriyaṃ sattvasaṃkhyātaṃ na viṣayaḥ | indriye 'pratīkṣṇe vijñānaṃ na sphuṭaṃ bhavati | prasanne tu indriye vijñānaṃ viśadaṃ bhavati | indriyāṇāmuttamamadhyamādhamatvāt vijñānamanuvibhajyate | ebhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ prādhānyaṃ kathyate | indriyamasādhāraṇam | eko viṣayo bahūnāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ sādhāraṇa upalabhyate | indriyaṃ vijñānena sahaikakarmavipākaḥ | viṣayastu naivam | indriyaṃ hetuḥ viṣayaḥ pratyayaḥ | kasmāt | indriyabhedāt vijñānaṃ viśeṣyate na viṣayaḥ | yathā bījaṃ hetuḥ pṛthivyādayaḥ pratyayāḥ | bījabhedātparasparaṃ bhedaḥ | pratyayātiśayihetutvādindriyamityākhyāyate |
body.translated_text: As for your statement: 'If it does not see, how can it be a sense-faculty (<s>indriya</s>)?' — you should be answered as follows: the five <s>dharmas</s> beginning with the eye surpass the other [<s>dharmas</s>] such as form and the rest — therefore they are conventionally called 'sense-faculties.' (Question) The five <s>dharmas</s> beginning with the eye, combined with the other [<s>dharmas</s>] such as form and the rest — these ten <s>dharmas</s> do not simultaneously cognize objects. Just as when the eye and the rest are separated [from their objects], consciousness does not arise — likewise, if even when form and the rest are separated, consciousness does not arise, then in what way do [the sense-faculties] surpass? (Reply) Consciousness is distinguished by the sense-faculties — as 'eye-consciousness,' 'ear-consciousness,' and so forth. Just as when a drum and a stick are conjoined, a sound occurs — [therein] because of the predominance of the drum, they say: 'The sound of the drum.' When earth and barley-seeds and the like are conjoined, a sprout arises — [therein] because of the predominance of the barley, they say: 'A barley-sprout.' Likewise with the kinds of consciousness. The convention is distinguished by the basis, not by the object-condition. If one says 'form-consciousness,' ambiguity arises — is this eye-consciousness, or is it mind-consciousness that has arisen dependent on form? In the sense-faculty there is consciousness, not in the sense-object. In the eye and the rest, the mind of self-delusion arises. The basis (<s>āśraya</s>) and sense-base (<s>āyatana</s>) of consciousness is the sense-faculty, not the sense-object. The sense-faculty abides within one's own body, not in the sense-object. The sense-faculty is an instrument of experience for the person, not the sense-object. The sense-faculty is reckoned as [belonging to] a sentient being (<s>sattva</s>), not the sense-object. When the sense-faculty is dull, consciousness is not clear. But when the sense-faculty is clear, consciousness is vivid. Due to the superior, middling, and inferior grades of the sense-faculties, consciousness is correspondingly differentiated. For these reasons, the predominance [of the sense-faculties] is stated. The sense-faculty is uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>). A single sense-object is found to be common to many persons. The sense-faculty together with consciousness shares a single <s>karma</s>-result. But the sense-object is not like that. The sense-faculty is the cause (<s>hetu</s>); the sense-object is the condition (<s>pratyaya</s>). Why? Because consciousness is distinguished by the difference of sense-faculties, not by the sense-object. Just as the seed is the cause, while earth and the rest are conditions. From the difference of seeds comes mutual difference [in the sprouts]. Because the sense-faculty is a cause that surpasses the conditions, it is designated as 'sense-faculty' (<s>indriya</s>).

body.text: yadbhavānavādīḥ- vayaṃ māṇavakāḥ susūkṣmamapi vastu jānīmaḥ tadyathā cakṣurmyāṃ dṛśyate iti | idaṃ saṃvṛtitaḥ | laukikāścakṣuḥ paśyatīti vadantītyata āhuḥ tadyathā cakṣurbhyāṃ dṛśyata iti | yathā ha bhagavān-
body.translated_text: As for your statement: 'We students know even the most subtle object — namely, that which is seen by the eyes' — that is [spoken] from the standpoint of conventional truth (<s>saṃvṛti</s>). Worldly people say 'the eye sees' — therefore they say 'that which is seen by the eyes.' As the Blessed One said:

body.text:
muhūrtamapi cedvijñaḥ paṇḍitaṃ paryupāsate |
[kṣipraṃ dharmaṃ vijānāti] jihvā [sūpa]rasaṃ yathā |
acetanāpi jihvā tu na darvībhājanopamā || iti |
body.translated_text:
Even if a wise person attends upon a learned one for but a moment,
he quickly knows the <s>Dharma</s>, just as the tongue [knows] the taste of broth.
Even the tongue, though non-sentient, is not comparable to a ladle or a vessel.

body.text: jihvāśritaṃ mano jihvāvijñānaṃ janayatītyata āha jihvā [sūpa]rasaṃ vettīti | tathā cakṣurāśritya samutpanne vijñāne cakṣuḥ paśyatīti vadanti | ata āha- jinaurasāḥ paśyanti tadyathā cakṣurbhyāṃ dṛśyata iti |
body.translated_text: Because the mind, situated in the tongue, generates tongue-consciousness, it is said: 'The tongue knows the taste of broth.' Likewise, when consciousness arises situated in the eye, they say: 'The eye sees.' Therefore it is said: 'The true sons of the <s>Jina</s> see — namely, that which is seen by the eyes.'

body.text: yadbhavānavādīḥ- indriyeṇa viṣayo gṛhyate vijñānena vikalpyate iti | idaṃ pratyuktam | indriyasyāvijñātṛtvāt | na ca yūyaṃ bravītha indriyasyaivaṃ bhavati ahaṃ viśiṣṭalakṣaṇa iti | ata indriyāṇi na viṣayān gṛhṇanti | bhavatāṃ jñānāni nendriyamapekṣya jāyante | kasmāt | mahadahaṅkārādīni hi indriyebhyaḥ pūrvamutpadyante | bhavatāṃ mahadādīni tattvāni na santi | mūlaprakṛtyabhāvāt | bhavatāṃ śāsanaṃ- mūlaprakṛtivikārā mahadādīnīti | mūlaprakṛtiśca nāstītyuktameva | na tu nendriyamiti ||
body.translated_text: As for your statement: 'The sense-faculty grasps the object, while consciousness discriminates' — that has been refuted. Because the sense-faculty is not a cognizer. And you do not say that the sense-faculty has [the thought]: 'I am one of distinguished characteristics.' Therefore the sense-faculties do not grasp objects. In your [<s>Sāṃkhya</s>] teaching, cognitions do not arise depending on the sense-faculties. Why? Because <s>Mahat</s> (the Great), <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-principle), and the rest arise prior to the sense-faculties. [But] in your teaching, the principles (<s>tattva</s>) such as <s>Mahat</s> and the rest do not exist — because of the non-existence of the root-nature (<s>Mūlaprakṛti</s>). Your teaching holds that <s>Mahat</s> and the rest are transformations (<s>vikāra</s>) of the root-nature. But that the root-nature does not exist has already been stated. It is not [the case], however, that they do not [arise] depending on the sense-faculties.

body.text: na vijānātīndriyavargo 'ṣṭacatvāriṃśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-eighth chapter, the Chapter [showing that the Sense-Faculty] Does Not Cognize (<s>na vijānātīndriyavarga</s>).

body.text: 49 viṣayendriyasaṃyogaviyogavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 49. Chapter on the Contact and Separation of Sense-Object and Sense-Faculty (<s>viṣayendriyasaṃyogaviyogavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) yadbhavānavocat- vijñānaṃ vijānāti nendriyamiti | tatprasādhitam | idānīṃ kiṃ viṣayendriyasaṃyogādvijñānamutpadyate kiṃ vā tadviyogāt | (u) cakṣurvijñānaṃ na prāptimapekṣya viṣayān vijānāti | kasmāt | candrādayo viprakṛṣṭapadārthā api dṛśyante | candrarūpaṃ na gandhavinirmuktamāgacchet | ākāśālokāvapekṣya rūpaṃ paśyati | yadi cakṣūrūpaṃ prāpnoti | tadā nāntarākāśālokau syātām | yathā cakṣuṣi pracchādite cakṣurna paśyati | ato jñātavyaṃ cakṣurvijñānaṃ na prāpya vijānāti | iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) As you stated: 'Consciousness cognizes, not the sense-faculty' — that has been established. Now, does consciousness arise from the contact of sense-object and sense-faculty, or from their separation? (Reply) Eye-consciousness cognizes objects without requiring contact (<s>prāpti</s>). Why? Because even distant objects such as the moon and the rest are seen. The form of the moon could not come [to the eye] separated from its smell. One sees form depending on space and light. If the eye reached [the object of] form, then there would be no intervening space or light. Just as when the eye is covered, the eye does not see. Therefore it should be known that eye-consciousness cognizes without contact.

body.text: śrotrādivijñānaṃ dvividham- kiñcitprāpya vijānāti kiñcidaprāpya vijānāti | śrotraṃ ruditaṃ prāpya vijānāti | ghanagarjitamaprāpya vijānāti | anyāni trīṇi vijñānāni indriyaprāptaṃ vijānanti | kasmāt | dṛṣṭaṃ khalu trayāṇāmeṣāmindriyāṇāṃ viṣayaiḥ saṃyogāt vijñānaṃ labhyata iti | manaindriyamarūpi | ato 'prāptaviṣayam | [viṣayaṃ] na prāpnoti |
body.translated_text: The consciousness [associated with] the ear and the rest is twofold: some cognizes through contact, some cognizes without contact. The ear cognizes a whisper through contact [with proximate sound], but cognizes the rumbling of dense clouds without contact. The other three kinds of consciousness [nose, tongue, body] cognize what has reached the sense-faculty. Why? Because it is observed that for these three sense-faculties, consciousness is obtained from the contact with their objects. The mind-faculty (<s>manaindriya</s>) is formless (<s>arūpi</s>). Therefore its object is not contacted — it does not reach [the object].

body.text: (pṛ) cakṣūrūpamaprāpya vijānāti iti bhavadvacanamayuktam | kasmāt | asti cakṣuṣi raśmiḥ | ayaṃ raśmī rūpadarśanāya gacchati | raśmiścāyaṃ taijasaṃ dravyam | cakṣuśca tejaḥsamutpannam | tejasaḥ saraśmitvāt yadyaprāpya paśyati | kasmātsarvāṇi rūpāṇi na paśyati | cakṣūraśmirhi sapratighe 'pi gacchati | avibhutvāt na sarvāṇi paśyati | yathoktaṃ sūtre- trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | yadyaprāpnoti | kathaṃ sannipātaḥ | pañcendriyāṇi sapratighāni | viṣayeṣu pratihanyanta iti sapratighāni | ghrāṇaṃ gandhe jihvā rase kāyaḥ spraṣṭavye cakṣūrūpe śrotraṃ śabde yadyaprāptam | tadā apratigham | pratyutpanneṣu pañcaviṣayeṣu jñānamutpadyate | ataḥ pañca vijñānāni prāpya vijānanti | yadyaprāpya vijānanti atītamanāgataṃ rūpamapi vijānīyuḥ | na vijānanti vastutaḥ | bahupratyayasāmagryā ca jñānamutpadyate iti cakṣūraśmirviṣayasaṃyogāya gacchati | rūpe raśmiprāptirhi sannipātaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Objection) Your statement that 'the eye cognizes form without contact' is untenable. Why? There exist rays (<s>raśmi</s>) in the eye. These rays go forth for the seeing of form. And these rays are a luminous substance (<s>taijasa dravya</s>). The eye too arises from the fire-element (<s>tejas</s>). Because the fire-element has rays, if it sees without contact, why does it not see all forms? The eye-rays indeed travel even to resistant [objects]. Because they are not all-pervading, they do not see everything. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The conjunction of three is contact (<s>sparśa</s>).' If [the eye] does not reach [the object], how can there be conjunction? The five sense-faculties are resistant (<s>sapratigha</s>). They collide with their objects — therefore they are called 'resistant.' The nose [collides] with smell, the tongue with taste, the body with tangibles, the eye with form, the ear with sound — if [the eye] does not reach [the object], then it would be non-resistant (<s>apratigha</s>). With respect to present objects of the five senses, knowledge arises. Therefore the five kinds of consciousness cognize through contact. If they cognized without contact, they would also cognize past and future forms. But in reality they do not. And knowledge arises from the aggregate of many conditions — therefore the eye-rays go forth for conjunction with the object. The reaching of the rays to form is indeed the conjunction.

body.text: śabdo 'pi śrotraṃ prāpya śrūyate | kasmāt | viprakṛṣṭadeśavartini puruṣe mandaṃ bhāṣamāṇe na śrūyate | yadi śabdaṃ rūpavadaprāpyāpi vijānāti | mandamapi śabdaṃ śṛṇuyāt | na tu śṛṇoti | ato jñāyate prāpya śṛṇotīti | śabdo dūrato 'pi śrūyate | yadyaprāpya śrūyate | āvaraṇe satyapi śrūyeta | dūrataḥ śrūyamāṇaḥ śabdo na pratyāyayati | sannikṛṣṭaṃ śrūyamāṇassu pratyāyayati | aprāpya śravaṇe tu sa vibhāgo na syāt | ato jñāyate śabdaḥ prāpya śrūyata iti | kiñcānukūlavāyau śabdaḥ pratyāyayati | na pratikūlavāyau | ato 'pi prāpya śrūyate | śabdaḥ sākalyena śrūyate | aprāpya śravaṇe tu na sākalyena śrūyeta | yathā rūpasyāprāptyā darśānāt na sākalyena darśanam | ato jñāyate na rūpasamaḥ śabda iti | aprāpya śravaṇe tu rūpasamaḥ syāt | yathā rūpasyekadeśaṃ dṛṣṭvā avaśiṣṭamapi ālokamapekṣya paśyati | tathā śabdo 'pi syāt | na vastutastathā bhavati | ato 'prāpya na śrūyate |
body.translated_text: Sound too is heard only upon reaching the ear. Why? Because when a person speaking softly is situated in a distant place, [the sound] is not heard. If one could know sound without it reaching [the ear], just as with form, one would hear even a faint sound. But one does not hear it. Therefore it is known that one hears [only] upon [the sound] reaching [the ear]. Sound is heard even from a distance. If it were heard without reaching [the ear], it would be heard even when there is an obstruction. Sound heard from a distance does not convey [meaning clearly]. Sound heard from nearby does convey [meaning clearly]. But if hearing occurred without reaching [the ear], this distinction would not exist. Therefore it is known that sound is heard upon reaching [the ear]. Furthermore, sound conveys [meaning clearly] when the wind is favorable, but not when the wind is unfavorable. From this too, it is heard upon reaching [the ear]. Sound is heard in its entirety. But if hearing occurred without reaching [the ear], it would not be heard in its entirety — just as form, being seen without reaching [the eye], is not seen in its entirety. Therefore it is known that sound is not like form. But if hearing occurred without reaching [the ear], it would be like form — just as one who sees one part of a form, depending on illumination, then sees the remainder as well. Sound too would be like that. But in reality, it is not so. Therefore, it is not heard without reaching [the ear].

body.text: yadbhavānāha- śrotrādīnīndriyāṇi viṣayamaprāpya vijānantīti | tadayuktam | śabdagandharūparasasparśā indriyamāgaccheyuḥ | yadidānīmindriyaṃ gacchatīti | tadyuktam | śrotrādīnāmindriyāṇāṃ nīraśmikatvāt | tejo mahābhūtamekameva saraśmikam | ato na gacchati | śabdaṃ yadi ghananibiḍaṃ jalādyāvṛtamapi śrotraṃ śrotuṃ śaknoti | yadi saraśmi, tadindriyam | naivaṃ śaknuyāt | ato jñāyate śrotrendriyaṃ nīraśmikamiti | śrotramandhakāre 'pi viṣayaṃ vijānāti | yadi saraśmikam, nāndhakāre vijānīyāt | saraśmikamindriyañca diśamapekṣya vijānāti | ekāṃ diśaṃ draṣṭuṃ śaknoti naikasmin samaye sarvā diśo draṣṭuṃ śaknoti | yathā pūrvābhimukhaḥ puruṣaḥ pūrvāṃ diśaṃ rūpañca paśyati nānyā diśaḥ |
body.translated_text: As for what you have said — 'The sense-faculties beginning with the ear cognize objects without reaching [them]' — that is not correct. Sound, smell, form, taste, and touch should come to the sense-faculty. Now, [the view] that 'the sense-faculty goes [to the object]' — that is correct. Because the sense-faculties beginning with the ear are without rays (<s>nīraśmika</s>). Only the fire great element (<s>tejas</s>) has rays. Therefore [the other senses] do not go [to their objects]. If the ear could hear sound even when it is densely covered by water and the like — if it had rays, that sense-faculty could not do so. Therefore it is known that the ear-faculty is without rays. The ear cognizes its object even in darkness. If it had rays, it would not cognize in darkness. A sense-faculty that has rays cognizes [only] in dependence on direction. It can see in one direction but cannot see all directions simultaneously. Just as a person facing east sees the eastern direction and forms but not other directions.

body.text: vadanti ca mano gacchatīti | ataḥ prāpya viṣayaṃ vijānāti | yathoktaṃ sūtre-
body.translated_text: They also say that the mind goes [to the object]. Therefore [the senses] cognize the six objects upon reaching [them]. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s> —

body.text:
dūraṅgamamekacaramaśarīraṃ guhāśayam
sūryasya raśmiriva cittaṃ carati viprakīrṇataḥ |
matsyo yathā sthale kṣipta [okamokata uddhṛtaḥ |]
parispandatīdaṃ cittaṃ svābhīṣṭañca yathā caratyadaḥ || iti |
body.translated_text:
Far-going, solitary-wandering, bodiless, dwelling in a cave —
like the rays of the sun, the mind ranges about dispersedly.
Just as a fish thrown on dry land [drawn out from water]
thrashes about — so this mind wanders as it pleases.

body.text: ataḥ ṣaḍviṣayān prāpya vijānanti |
body.translated_text: Therefore [the senses] cognize upon reaching the six objects.

body.text: atrocyate | raśmirgacchatīti bhavadvacanamayuktam | kasmāt | yathā puruṣo dūrataḥ sthāṇuṃ dṛṣṭvā saṃśete kimayaṃ puruṣa iti | yadi raśmirgarcchati | kasmāt saṃśayo bhavet | atisannikṛṣṭañca cakṣurna paśyati | yathā cakṣussaṃsaktaṃ tṛṇaroma na paśyati | ato raśmirgacchannapi atisannikarṣānna paśyati | yadi raśmistatra gacchati | kasmāt sthūlaṃ paśyati na sūkṣmaṃ
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: Your statement that 'rays go [to objects]' is not correct. Why? Just as a person seeing a post from a distance doubts: 'Is this a person?' If rays went [there], why would there be doubt? And the eye does not see what is extremely close — just as the eye does not see a blade of grass or hair touching it. Therefore, even though the ray goes [there], due to extreme proximity, it does not see. If the ray goes there, why does it see the gross but not discriminate

body.text: vivecayati | rūpadarśane 'sti dvibhāgaḥ yaduta pūrvasyāṃ paścimāyāṃ vā diśi rūpamiti | sannikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭavibhāgo 'pyasti | yadi cakṣuḥ prāpya vijānāti | tādṛśavibhāgo na syāt | kasmāt | gandharasasparśeṣu nāyaṃ vibhāgo 'sti | ato nayanaraśmiraprāpya vijānāti | nayanaraśmiryadi pūrvameva dṛṣṭavān | kimarthaṃ punargacchati | yadi pūrvamadṛṣṭvā gacchati | kutra gacchati | yadi sannikṛṣṭarūpaṃ viprakṛṣṭarūpañca ekadā yugapatpaśyati | na tathā gamanadharmaḥ | ato nayanaraśmirna gacchati | yadi sa gacchati | madhye mārgaṃ rūpāṇi paśyet | vastutastu na paśyati | ato jñāyate na gacchatīti | raśmirgacchatīti raśmiḥ kāyabdahirgato nendriyaṃ bhavet | yathāṅgulau kāyātsamucchidya viyujyamānāyāṃ nāsti kāyabuddhiḥ | na cakṣuḥ svāśrayaṃ tyajat paśyāmaḥ | sapakṣābhāve nāsti hetuḥ | tasya nayanaraśme rasati draṣṭari sa na syāt |
body.translated_text: the subtle? In the seeing of form, there is a twofold division — namely, whether the form is in the eastern or western direction. There is also a division of near and far. If the eye cognizes upon reaching [the object], such a division would not exist. Why? Because in smell, taste, and touch, this division does not exist. Therefore the visual ray (<s>nayanaraśmi</s>) cognizes without reaching [the object]. If the visual ray had already seen [the object] previously, for what purpose would it go again? If it goes without having previously seen, where does it go? If it sees both near and far forms simultaneously, that is not the nature of going. Therefore the visual ray does not go. If it goes, it would see the forms along the way in between. But in reality it does not see them. Therefore it is known that it does not go. If the ray goes, the ray having gone outside the body would not be a sense-faculty — just as when a finger is severed and separated from the body, there is no bodily cognition. And we do not see the eye leaving its own support. In the absence of a supporting instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>), there is no proof. If that visual ray moved [and] the one seeing [with it were separate], he would not [perceive].

body.text: (pṛ) astīyaṃ nāyanaraśmiḥ sūryaraśmitiraskṛtā na dṛśyate | yathā sūryaraśmau nakṣatrāṇi na pratyakṣāṇi | (u) tathā cedrātnau dṛśyeta | (pṛ) rūpa dharmā avaśyaṃ bāhyaṃ prakāśamapekṣya dṛśyante | rātrau ca bāhyaprakāśo nāsti | yena na dṛśyante | (u) yadīyaṃ raśmirdivāniśamubhayatna nopalabhyate | tadāsyā atyantānupalabdhiḥ | (pṛ) biḍālasṛgālamūṣikādīnāṃ sarveṣāṃ rātriñcarāṇāṃ nāyano raśmirupalabhyate | (u) idaṃ dṛśyarūpaṃ viḍālādīnāṃ cakṣuṣi vartate | yathā khadyotasya prakāśātmakaṃ rūpaṃ tatkāyavarti | nāyaṃ raśmiḥ | yathā ca rātriñcarā jantavo 'ndhakāre paśyanti | manuṣyāśca na paśyanti | tathā ca teṣāmeva raśmiḥ syāt | nānyeṣām | tathaiva dharmatā syāt |
body.translated_text: (Objection) This visual ray exists but is concealed by the rays of the sun and is therefore not visible. Just as the stars are not visible in the presence of sunlight. (Reply) If that were so, it would be visible at night. (Objection) Form-<s>dharmas</s> are necessarily seen in dependence on external light. At night there is no external light, and therefore they are not seen. (Reply) If this ray is not apprehended either by day or by night, then it is altogether unapprehended. (Objection) In cats, jackals, mice, and all nocturnal creatures, the visual ray is apprehended. (Reply) This visible luminous form exists in the eyes of cats and the like. Just as in a firefly, the luminous form exists in its body. This is not a ray. And just as nocturnal creatures see in darkness while humans do not see — if that is so, then only they would have rays, not others. The nature of things would be just so.

body.text: yadavādīḥ- yadyaprāpya paśyati | sarvāṇi rūpāṇi paśyediti | yat rūpaṃ jñānasya
body.translated_text: As for what you have said — 'If one sees without reaching [the object], one would see all forms' — whatever form falls within the range

body.text: gocaraṃ tat dṛśyam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- cakṣuranupahataṃ bhavati | viṣaya ābhāsagato bhavati | tadā sa dṛśyo bhavati | iti | (pṛ) ko nāmābhāsagataḥ | (u) yadā rūpacakṣuṣoḥ sannipātaḥ | sa ābhāsagataḥ | (pṛ) yadi cakṣurna prāpnoti kaḥ sannipātaḥ | (u) samānamidam, yathā bhavataścakṣū rūpaṃ prāpyāpi kadācitpaśyati kadācinna paśyati | tadyathā cakṣuḥ sūryaṃ prāpya sūryamaṇḍalaṃ paśyati na tu sūryakarma | evaṃ mamāpi cakṣuragatvāpi yadrūpamābhāsagataṃ bhavati | tat paśyati | yadābhāsagataṃ na bhavati na tatpaśyati | (pṛ) nayanaraśmiḥ sudūraṃ gacchati | vegaprakarṣāttu sūryakarma na paśyati | (u) yadi vegaprakarṣātsūkṣmaṃ karma na paśyati, sthūlaṃ sūryamaṇḍalaparimāṇaṃ kasmānna paśyati | na hīdaṃ yujyate | yadi raśmimastatra gatvā paśyatīti | kasmād dūrasthaṃ sūryamaṇḍalaṃ dṛṣṭvāpi karma na paśyati tat pāṭaliputrādi āsannaṃ janapadanagaram | yadi bhavān manyate pāṭaliputrādi na ābhāsagatamityato na paśyatīti | mama cakṣuraprāpyāpi rūpaṃ nābhāsāgatamityato na paśyati |
body.translated_text: of knowledge, that is visible. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The eye is unimpaired; the object has come into the field of appearance (<s>ābhāsa</s>)' — then it becomes visible. (Objection) What does 'come into the field of appearance' mean? (Reply) When there is a conjunction of form and the eye — that is 'come into the field of appearance.' (Objection) If the eye does not reach [the object], what conjunction is there? (Reply) This is the same [difficulty] — for your eye too, even upon reaching form, sometimes sees and sometimes does not see. For example, the eye, reaching the sun, sees the solar disc but not the [details of] the sun's activity. Likewise for me too, the eye, even without going [to the object], when a form has come into the field of appearance, sees it; when it has not come into the field of appearance, it does not see it. (Objection) The visual ray goes very far. But because of the intensity of its speed, it does not see the subtle activity [of the sun]. (Reply) If because of the intensity of speed it does not see subtle activity, why does it not see the gross solar disc in its full extent? This is not tenable. If your ray goes there and sees [the sun] — why, upon seeing the solar disc at a distance, does it not also see the activity of a nearby city such as <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> and the like? If you think 'because <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> and the like have not come into the field of appearance, they are not seen' — [then I say,] for my eye too, even without reaching [the object], when a form has not come into the field of appearance, it does not see it.

body.text: (pṛ) sarvāṇi rūpāṇi ābhāsagatāni dṛśyānīti jñātameva | idānīṃ kiṃ dṛśyaṃ kimadṛśyam | (u) adhvāvaraṇānna dṛśyate yathātītamanāgatam | rūpasyābhibhāvakaviśeṣānna dṛśyate yathā rātrau tejo dṛśyamanyadadṛśyam | bhūmiviśeṣānna dṛśyate yathā prathamadhyānagatacakṣuṣā dvitīyadhyānagataṃ rūpaṃ na dṛśyate | tama āvāvaraṇānna dṛśyate yathā tamasi ghaṭaḥ | ṛddhibalānna dṛśyate yathā bhūtādīnāṃ dehaḥ | atighanamālāvṛtatvānna dṛśyate | yathā parvatasya bāhyaṃ rūpam | atidūrānna dṛśyate yathānye lokadhātavaḥ | atisāmīpyānna dṛśyate yathā cakṣupyañjanam | aprāptyā na dṛśyate yathā prabhāgatā aṇavoḥ dṛśyāḥ prabhābāhyāstu adṛśyāḥ | saukṣmyānna dṛśyate yathā puruṣākāraḥ sthāṇurna vivektuṃ śakyaḥ | samānābhihārānna dṛśyate yathā mahārāśigatamekaṃ śālidhānyam | yathā ca kākavṛndagata ekaḥ kākaḥ | pūvoktaviparītamābhāsagatamityucyate |
body.translated_text: (Objection) It is already understood that all forms that have come into the field of appearance are visible. Now, what is visible and what is invisible? (Reply) Due to the obstruction of the time-period (<s>adhvan</s>), [forms] are not seen — for example, the past and the future. Due to specific overpowering of form, [they] are not seen — for example, at night fire-light is visible but other [things] are not. Due to the distinction of [meditative] level, [they] are not seen — for example, the eye of one in the first <s>dhyāna</s> does not see form belonging to the second <s>dhyāna</s>. Due to the obstruction of darkness, [they] are not seen — for example, a pot in the dark. Due to the power of supernatural ability (<s>ṛddhi</s>), [they] are not seen — for example, the bodies of spirits (<s>bhūta</s>) and the like. Due to being covered by an extremely dense mass, [they] are not seen — for example, the external form of a mountain. Due to extreme distance, [they] are not seen — for example, other world-systems. Due to extreme proximity, [they] are not seen — for example, ointment applied to the eye. Due to non-arrival [into the field of appearance], [they] are not seen — for example, atoms within the range of light are visible, but those outside the range of light are invisible. Due to subtlety, [they] are not seen — for example, a post in the form of a person cannot be distinguished. Due to uniformity of presentation, [they] are not seen — for example, a single grain of rice within a large pile, or a single crow within a flock of crows. The opposite of what was previously stated is called 'having come into the field of appearance.'

body.text: (pṛ) kaścakṣuṣa upaghātaḥ | (u) vātoṣmaśītādibhirvyādhibhiḥ pratighātaḥ | yat vātopahataṃ cakṣuḥ tat viparyastaṃ nīlakṛṣṇādirūpaṃ paśyet | yadūṣmopahataṃ tat pītaraktāgnijvālādi paśyati | yacchītopahataṃ tat bhūyasāvadātahradajalādirūpaṃ paśyati | yat jāgaraṇopahataṃ
body.translated_text: (Objection) What is the impairment of the eye? (Reply) Impairment by ailments such as wind, heat, cold, and the like. An eye impaired by wind sees perverted forms such as blue, black, and the like. An eye impaired by heat sees yellow, red, [or] fire-flame [forms] and the like. An eye impaired by cold sees predominantly white [forms], such as the surface of a lake, and the like. An eye impaired by sleeplessness

body.text: cakṣuḥ tat kampitavṛkṣādirūpaṃ prāyaḥ paśyati | yat parikhedopahataṃ cakṣuḥ tat rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā na budhyate | bhāgaśaḥ praṇuditamekaṃ cakṣuścandradvayaṃ paśyati | bhūtādyāviṣṭaṃ vikṛtaṃ paśyati | pāpakarmavaśātkurūpaṃ paśyati | puṇyakarmavaśātsurūpaṃ paśyati | pittopahataṃ cakṣurjvālādirūpaṃ paśyati | sattvā apariniṣpannacakṣustvādvikalaṃ paśyanti | ghanatimirāvṛtacakṣuṣkā na paśyanti | yadupahataṃ cakṣurindriyaṃ na paśyati | sa cakṣuṣa upaghātaḥ | tallakṣaṇaviparito 'nupāghātaḥ | śrotrādīnīndriyāṇyapi [tathā]rthavaśādvivektavyāni |
body.translated_text: mostly sees trembling forms such as swaying trees and the like. An eye impaired by fatigue, upon seeing a form, does not comprehend it. An eye partially impaired sees two moons. [An eye] possessed by spirits (<s>bhūta</s>) and the like sees distorted [forms]. Due to the influence of unwholesome <s>karma</s>, one sees ugly forms. Due to the influence of meritorious <s>karma</s>, one sees beautiful forms. An eye impaired by bile sees flame-like forms and the like. Beings with incompletely developed eyes see incompletely. Those whose eyes are covered by dense cataracts (<s>timira</s>) do not see at all. When the eye-faculty is impaired, it does not see — that is the impairment of the eye. The opposite of that characteristic is non-impairment. The sense-faculties of the ear and the rest should likewise be analyzed according to their respective [objects].

body.text: (pṛ) pañca viṣayāḥ jñānābhāsagatatvāt jñeyā bhavantīti jñātameva | katame dharmā jñānasyābhāsagatā na bhavanti | (u) ūrdhvabhūmikatvānna jñāyate yathā prathamadhyānacittaṃ dvitīyadhyānatadūrdhvadharmān na vijānāti | indriyaviśeṣānna jñāyate yathā mandendriyasya cittaṃ tīkṣṇendriyasya cittagatadharmān na vijānāti | puruṣaviśeṣānna jñāyate yathā śrotraāpannaḥ sakṛdāgāminaścittagatadharmān na vijānāti | balaprabhedānna jñāyate yathā yanmanovijñānaṃ yasmin dharme balavihīnaṃ na tena manovijñānena sa dharmo jñāyate | tadyathā samāhitacitta(sya) manovijñānavijñeyadharmo na vikṣiptacittakamanovijñānena vijñātuṃ śakyo bhavati | yathā pratyekabuddhamanovijñānabalavijñeyadharmo na śrāvakamano[vijñāna]balena vijñātuṃ śakyo bhavati | yathordhvapakṣikadharmo nāvarapakṣikamanovijñānena vijñātuṃ śakyaḥ | atisūkṣmā dharmā na jñātuṃ śakyāḥ | yathoktamabhidharme kena cittena smaryate | yaduta pratītipratyāyakaṃ pūrvānubhavitṛ, tena smaryate nānanubhavitrā | yathā janāḥ saṃsāre pūrvānubhūtaṃ dharmaṃ smaranti | ananubhūtaṃ na smaranti | āryāstu yadi vānubhūtaṃ yadivānanubhūtaṃ sarvaṃ tadāryajñānabalādvijānanti | viśiṣṭaviṣayatvāt jñāyate yathā rūpadhātukacittamanubhūya kāmadhātukadharmān vijānānti | viparyayāvṛtatvānna jñāyate yathā satkāyadṛṣṭikacittaṃ pañcaskandhālambanaṃ nairātmyaṃ paśyati | tathā anityaṃ duḥkhamapi | balāvṛtatvānna jñāyate yathā mṛdvindriyaḥ puruṣastīkṣṇendriyasya cittamāvṛtatayā na vijānāti | [yat] pūrvoktalakṣaṇaviparītaṃ tadābhāsagatamityucyate |
body.translated_text: (Objection) It is already understood that the five objects become knowable when they come into the field of appearance of knowledge. Now, what <s>dharmas</s> do not come into the field of appearance of knowledge? (Reply) Due to belonging to a higher [meditative] level, [they] are not known — for example, the mind of the first <s>dhyāna</s> does not cognize <s>dharmas</s> belonging to the second <s>dhyāna</s> and above. Due to the distinction of faculties, [they] are not known — for example, the mind of one with dull faculties does not cognize <s>dharmas</s> in the mind of one with sharp faculties. Due to the distinction of persons, [they] are not known — for example, a stream-enterer (<s>srotāpanna</s>) does not cognize <s>dharmas</s> in the mind of a once-returner (<s>sakṛdāgāmin</s>). Due to the division of powers, [they] are not known — for example, whatever <s>dharma</s> the mind-consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) is powerless regarding, that <s>dharma</s> is not known by that mind-consciousness. For instance, the <s>dharma</s> knowable by the mind-consciousness of one in a concentrated state (<s>samāhitacitta</s>) cannot be known by the mind-consciousness of one with a distracted mind (<s>vikṣiptacitta</s>). And the <s>dharma</s> knowable by the power of the mind-consciousness of a <s>Pratyekabuddha</s> cannot be known by the power of a disciple's (<s>śrāvaka</s>) mind-consciousness. And <s>dharmas</s> belonging to the upper portion [of practice] cannot be known by the mind-consciousness of one in the lower portion. Extremely subtle <s>dharmas</s> cannot be known. As stated in the <s>Abhidharma</s>: 'By what mind does one remember? By that which has come into contact and been experienced previously — by that one remembers, not by one that has not experienced [it].' Just as beings in <s>saṃsāra</s> remember <s>dharmas</s> previously experienced but do not remember those not experienced. But the Noble Ones, whether [a <s>dharma</s>] has been experienced or not, know everything through the power of noble knowledge (<s>āryajñānabala</s>). Due to the specificity of the object, [some things] are known — for example, the mind of the form realm (<s>rūpadhātu</s>), upon experiencing [it], cognizes <s>dharmas</s> of the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>). Due to being covered by perversion (<s>viparyaya</s>), [they] are not known — for example, the mind characterized by the view of the personal self (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>), taking the five aggregates as its object, [does not] see selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>). Likewise with impermanence and suffering. Due to being covered by [lesser] power, [they] are not known — for example, a person of dull faculties does not know the mind of one with sharp faculties because it is covered [to him]. The opposite of the characteristics previously stated is called 'having come into the field of appearance.'

body.text: (pṛ) ko nāma manasa upaghātaḥ | (u) vikṣepaviparyayabhūtāveśā mānamadacittapramoṣā madyena vā auṣadhavyāmohena vā cittavibhramaḥ, kadācit rāgrikruddhatādikleśaparipuṣṭa
body.translated_text: (Question) What is meant by damage to the mind (<s>manas</s>)? (Answer) Distraction (<s>vikṣepa</s>), perversion (<s>viparyaya</s>), spirit-possession (<s>bhūtāveśa</s>), pride (<s>māna</s>), intoxication (<s>mada</s>), loss of awareness (<s>cittapramoṣa</s>), mental derangement due to liquor or drug-induced delusion (<s>auṣadhavyāmoha</s>), sometimes nourished by defilements (<s>kleśa</s>) such as passion and anger

body.text: pramādapranaṣṭacittatā yathā śvapākakaivartādīnām | sannipātena vā cittaptyopaghāto bhavati | jarāvyādhimaraṇānyapi cittasyopaghātāḥ | yaccittaṃ kuśaladharmagataṃ yadavyākṛtadharmanimagnam | tadanupahataṃ nāma | evamādibhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ sattvo viṣayān vijānāti | tasmādyadyaprāpya paśyati kasmānna sarvāṇi rūpāṇi paśyatīti bhavadvacanamayuktam |
body.translated_text: — the state of awareness lost through negligence (<s>pramāda</s>), as in the case of <s>Śvapākas</s> (outcaste hunters), <s>Kaivartas</s> (fishermen), and the like. Or through the conjunction [of humors], there is damage to the arising of consciousness. Old age, illness, and death are also damages to the mind. Whatever mind is established in wholesome <s>dharmas</s>, or is immersed in indeterminate <s>dharmas</s> — that is called undamaged. By these and other reasons, a being cognizes objects. Therefore your statement 'If he sees without reaching [the object], why does he not see all forms?' is untenable.

body.text: yadavocaḥ- trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | indriyaviṣayavijñānānugamanakālaḥ sparśaḥ nāvaśyaṃ prāptilakṣaṇaḥ | kasmāt | manaindriyasyāpyuktaṃ trayāṇāṃ sannipāta iti | na tatra prāptilakṣaṇo 'sti sparśaḥ | [sparśasya] prāptilakṣaṇatvāt [indriyāṇi] sapratighānīti bhavadvacanamayuktam | na hyasti pratihantilakṣaṇam ityuktatvāt | pratyutpanneṣu jñānamutpadyata iti yadavādīḥ tatra ṣaṣṭhaṃ vijñānamapi pratyutpannamātraṃ jñāpayet paracittajñānavat | bahupratyayasāmagryā jñānamutpadyata iti yadavādīḥ | tat ṣaṣṭhamanaindriyeṇa pratyuktameva yaduta indriyaviṣayavijñānānugamakālaḥ sannipāta iti | pratītya mano dharmāṃśca manovijñānamutpadyata itīdaṃ vacanañca tadā vyarthaṃ syāt prāptyabhāvāt | pratiniyataniyamo hi sannipāto nāma | cakṣurvijñānaṃ cakṣurmātraṃ nānyadāśritya nānāśritya bhavati | [tathā] rūpamātraṃ pratītya nānyatpratītya nāpratītya bhavati | evaṃ yāvanmanovijñānamapi |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'The conjunction of three is contact (<s>sparśa</s>)' — contact (<s>sparśa</s>) is the time of the concurrence of sense-faculty, object, and consciousness; it does not necessarily have the characteristic of physical reaching (<s>prāpti</s>). Why? Because even for the mind-faculty (<s>manaindriya</s>), it is said: 'The conjunction of three is [contact].' But there is no contact with the characteristic of physical reaching there. Your statement 'Because contact has the characteristic of reaching, the sense-faculties have resistance (<s>sapratigha</s>)' is untenable — because, as has been stated, there is no characteristic of striking back (<s>pratihanti</s>). Your statement 'Knowledge arises with respect to present [objects]' — therein, the sixth consciousness (mind-consciousness) too would cognize only what is present, like the knowledge of others' minds (<s>paracittajñāna</s>). Your statement 'Knowledge arises from the assemblage of many conditions' — that is already answered by the sixth mind-faculty, namely that the time of the concurrence of sense-faculty, object, and consciousness is [what is called] conjunction. And the statement 'Depending on the mind and <s>dharmas</s>, mind-consciousness arises' would then be purposeless, due to the absence of [physical] reaching. For what is called 'conjunction' is a fixed and determinate [concurrence]. Eye-consciousness arises depending on the eye alone — not depending on anything else, nor without depending [on something]. [Likewise,] depending on form alone — not depending on anything else, nor without depending [on it]. So too up to mind-consciousness.

body.text: viṣayendriyasaṃyogaviyogavarga ekonapañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the forty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Conjunction and Disjunction of Object and Sense-Faculty (<s>viṣayendriyasaṃyogaviyogavarga</s>).

body.text: 50 śabdaśravaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 50. Chapter on the Hearing of Sound (<s>śabdaśravaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: yadavādīḥ viprakṛṣṭadeśavartini puruṣe mandaṃ bhāṣamāṇe na śabdaḥ śrūyate | ato jñāyate śabdaḥ śrotraṃ prāpnotīti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | yathā bhavānāha viprakṛṣṭadeśavartini puruṣe bhāṣamāṇe śabdāt śabdasantatyā tanurbhūtvā na punarudbhavatītyato na śrūyata iti | evaṃ mamāpi syāt | śabdo 'prāpyāpi so 'lpīyāniti na śrūyate | yathā bhavato nayanaraśmirgatvāpi sūryamaṇḍalamātraṃ paśyati na sūryasya karma | evaṃ mamāpi | śrotramaprāpyāpi
body.translated_text: Your statement 'When a person at a distant place speaks softly, the sound is not heard — therefore it is known that sound reaches the ear' — that is untenable. Why? Just as you have said: 'When a person at a distant place speaks, the sound, through the continuity of sounds, becomes attenuated and does not arise again — therefore it is not heard.' So too for my [position]: sound, even without reaching [the ear], being too faint, is not heard. Just as in your view the visual ray (<s>nayanaraśmi</s>), even having traveled, sees only the disc of the sun but not the activity of the sun — so too for me: even without reaching the ear

body.text: śabda audārikaḥ san śrūyate sūkṣmastu na śrūyate | yathā bhavato nayanaraśmiḥ sudūraṃ gacchannapi na śatasahasrāyutayojanāni prāpnoti | prasannasalilādyāvṛtaṃ suṣṭhu paśyannapi bhittyādyāvṛtaṃ tu na paśyati | sūryamaṇḍalaṃ dṛṣṭvāpi na paśyati sūryakarma | tathā mamāpi śrotramaprāpyāpi śabdamaudārikaṃ śṛṇoti | na tu śaknoti sūkṣmaṃ vivecayitum |
body.translated_text: , a gross sound is heard, but a subtle one is not heard. Just as in your view the visual ray, even traveling very far, does not reach a hundred thousand <s>ayutayojanas</s> (<s>koṭis</s> of <s>yojanas</s>); clearly seeing through clear water and the like, it does not see through a wall and the like; even seeing the disc of the sun, it does not see the activity of the sun — so too for me: even without reaching the ear, one hears gross sound but cannot discern the subtle.

body.text: yadavādīḥ- anukūlavāyau pratyāyayati iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | tadā tu na kaścitpratikūle vāyau śṛṇotīti syāt | yathā gandhaḥ pratikūlavāyau na jighrayate | tadā śabdo 'pi pratikūlavāyau na kiñcidapi na śrotavyaḥ syāt | vastutastu śrūyate | ato jñāyate śabdo 'prāpya śrūyata iti | yadalpaṃ śabdaḥ śrūyate tat vāyvāvaraṇāt | kiñca śabdo gandhavat pravāhyaḥ | kimanukūlapratikūla vāyuvikalpanayā |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'A favorable wind conveys [the sound]' is untenable. Why? Then it would follow that no one at all hears in an unfavorable wind. Just as smell is not smelled in an unfavorable wind, so too sound in an unfavorable wind should not be heard at all. But in reality, it is heard. Therefore it is known that sound is heard without reaching [the ear]. That a small amount of sound is heard [less clearly] is due to the obstruction of wind. Furthermore, sound, like smell, is carried along. What need is there for the conceptualization of favorable and unfavorable wind?

body.text: yadavocaḥ śabdaḥ sākalyena śrūyata ityataḥ prāptipakṣe na rūpasama iti | na yuktamidam | śabdadharmo yat sākalyena śrūyata iti | na tathā rūpadharmaḥ | padārthāḥ salakṣaṇavilakṣaṇā bhavanti | jñeyaviṣayatvena samāḥ | sākalyāsākalyajñānatvena viṣamāḥ | ghaṇṭāśabdo ghaṇṭāyāṃ śrūyate | kenedaṃ jñāyate | tadyathā puruṣaḥ ghaṇṭānādaśuśrūṣayā karṇena ghaṇṭāmupeti | śabdaśca guṇatvānna gacchati | guṇānāmakarmakāritvāt |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'Sound is heard in its entirety, and therefore in the reaching-thesis it is not similar to form' — this is not correct. It is a property of sound (<s>śabdadharma</s>) that it is heard in its entirety. It is not so with the property of form. Objects are both similar and dissimilar in their characteristics — they are equal in being objects of knowledge, but unequal in being known in entirety or not. [As for] the sound of a bell being heard in the bell — how is this known? For example: a person, desiring to hear the bell-sound, approaches the bell with his ear. And sound, being a quality (<s>guṇa</s>), does not travel — because qualities do not perform action.

body.text: (pṛ) śabdaparamparayotpadyamāne śabdaguṇe vīcītaraṅgavacchabdo gacchatītyucyate | (u) śabdataraṅgasya kena saha dṛṣṭāntaḥ | ablakṣaṇe bherīcarmaṇi sati taraṅga utpadyeta | idānīṃ śabde kaḥ punaḥ śabdaḥ yaḥ śabdāntaraṃ janayati | yadi manyase śabdaḥ śabdāntaraṃ janayatīti | kasmānna mūlapradeśe janayati nānyatra | apāmablakṣaṇaviruddhatvāt taraṅgo jāyate | yo vadati- puruṣaḥ śabdaṃ karotīti | [tasya] karṇameva vaktṛ syāt | vastutastu na sambhavati | ato jñāyate śabdo noccarito gacchatīti | yadi ghaṇṭātaḥ śabdasantatirutpadyate, tarhi ghaṇṭā śabdavihīnā na syāt | yadi śabdastaraṅgavatsantatyā pravartate iti | niyatamāpo nistaraṅgāḥ syuḥ | evaṃ ghaṇṭātaḥ śabda [udgate] sati ghaṇṭā niśśabdā syāt | na vastuta idaṃ yujyate | ato jñāyate śabdo ghaṇṭāyāṃ vartata iti | ghaṇṭāyāṃ gṛhītāyāṃ śabda uparamati | ato jñāyate śabdaḥsadā ghaṇṭāmāśrayata iti | yadi śabdo ghaṇṭāmāśrito ghaṇṭātaścāpi viyujyata iti | ghaṇṭāyāṃ gṛhītāyāṃ ghaṇṭāmāśritaḥ
body.translated_text: (Objection) Sound, arising in successive generations as a quality of sound — like waves and ripples — is said to 'travel.' (Reply) With what is the wave of sound to be compared? If the bell-skin had the characteristic of water, a wave would arise. But now, in sound, what further sound is there that generates another sound? If you think 'sound generates another sound' — why does it not generate [it] at the original location and not elsewhere? Because of the opposition to the water-characteristic, a wave arises [in water, but not in sound]. As for one who says 'a person produces sound' — [in that case] only the ear would be the speaker. But in reality this is not possible. Therefore it is known that uttered sound does not travel. If from a bell a continuity of sound arises, then the bell would never be devoid of sound. If sound proceeds in continuity like waves — then necessarily the waters would be without waves [at some point]. Likewise, from the bell, once the sound has gone forth, the bell would be soundless. But in reality this is not tenable. Therefore it is known that sound abides in the bell. When the bell is grasped [to stop it], the sound ceases. Therefore it is known that sound always depends on the bell. If sound depends on the bell and also separates from the bell — then when the bell is grasped, the sound depending on the bell

body.text: śabdo 'niruddhaḥ syāt | ghaṇṭāviyuktaḥ śabdo 'nuvarteta | dṛṣṭe vyavahāre ca nāsti kiñcit yathā ghaṇṭāsantatirutpadyata iti | śabdasya cāsti digbhāgabhedo yaduta prācīśabdaḥ karṇadeśaṃ prāpnoti tadā na syāt ayaṃ vibhāgaḥ | yadi śabda āgacchati | tadā divyaśrotraṃ niṣprayojanaṃ syāt | kasmāt | śatasahasralokadhātūn śabdaḥ kathamāgacchati | yathā viddhaśabdaḥ śabdadeśaṃ lakṣayati | tathā yadi śabdaḥ śrotramāgacchati | svayameva śrotraṃ vidhyāt | tathā no cet viddhaśabda iti nocyeta | yaḥ śabdo viprakṛṣṭaḥ sannikṛṣṭaśca tau yugapat śrūyetām |
body.translated_text: would not cease. And the sound separated from the bell would continue. In observed practice, there is nothing like 'a continuity of sound arises from the bell.' And sound has a distinction of direction — namely, when a sound from the east reaches the region of the ear, there would be no such distinction if sound traveled. If sound came [to the ear], then the divine ear (<s>divyaśrotra</s>) would be purposeless. Why? How could sound come from a hundred thousand world-systems (<s>lokadhātu</s>)? Just as a struck sound indicates the location of the sound — so too, if sound came to the ear, it would itself strike the ear. If it did not, it would not be called 'a struck sound.' [Furthermore,] a sound that is distant and one that is near would both be heard simultaneously.

body.text: śabdaśca kṣaṇikatvānna śabdāntaramutpādayati | na hi paśyāmaḥ kṣaṇikadharmaḥ kasyacijjanaka iti | ato na śabdaḥ śabdāntaraṃ janayati | yathā kṣaṇikaṃ karma na karmāntaramutpādayati | yadi śabdaḥ śabdāntaramutpādayati | karmāpi karmāntaramutpādayet | ekañca na karma karmotpādakamiti vacanaṃ praṇaṣṭaṃ syāt | bhavatāṃ śāsane śabdaḥ śabdāntareṇa viruddhaḥ pṛthak, naikasthānikaḥ | yadi śabdaḥ śabdantareṇaikasthānikaḥ, na sa viruddho nāma | yadi naikasthānikaḥ | tadā pūrvaśabde niruddhe 'nantaraśabdaḥ svayamutpadyate | ato na śabdaḥ śabdāntaramutpādayati | śabdaścaiko dharmaḥ, kathaṃ śabdāntaramutpādayati | nahyekaṃ vastūtpādakaṃ paśyāmaḥ | (pṛ) yathā saṃyoga ekaḥ san vastunāmutpādakaḥ | evaṃ śabdo 'pi ekadharmaḥ sannapi śabdāntarasyotpādakaḥ | (u) paśyasi khalu saṃyoga ekaḥ san yaṃ śabdamutpādayati [so] 'pi tathā syāt | rūpamapi ekaṃ sat rūpāntaramutpādayet | tathā gandharasasparśā api | evañca dravyaṃ pañcasvabhāvaṃ trisvabhāvaṃ dvisvabhāvaṃ na syāt |
body.translated_text: And because sound is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), it does not produce another sound. For we do not see that a momentary <s>dharma</s> produces anything. Therefore sound does not generate another sound. Just as momentary <s>karma</s> does not produce another <s>karma</s>. If sound produced another sound, then <s>karma</s> too would produce another <s>karma</s>. And the statement 'a single <s>karma</s> does not produce <s>karma</s>' would be destroyed. In your teaching, sound is opposed to another sound — they are separate, not co-locational. If sound were co-locational with another sound, then they would not be called 'opposed.' If not co-locational, then when the preceding sound has ceased, the subsequent sound arises by itself. Therefore sound does not produce another sound. And sound is a single <s>dharma</s> — how could it produce another sound? For we do not see that a single thing produces [another]. (Objection) Just as a single conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) produces things — so too, even though sound is a single <s>dharma</s>, it produces another sound. (Reply) You see indeed that a single conjunction produces such a sound — so it should be likewise [for all]. Then form too, being a single [thing], would produce another form. Likewise smell, taste, and touch. In that case, a substance (<s>dravya</s>) of five natures, of three natures, or of two natures would not exist.

body.text: karmasāmyācca | śabdaḥ karmaṇā tulyalakṣaṇaḥ | yathā vadanti śabdo guṇo 'pi
body.translated_text: And because of similarity to action (<s>karma</s>): sound has the same characteristic as action. Just as they say: 'Sound is a quality, yet

body.text: karmaṇā tulyo nirudhyate | yathāṅgulisphoṭasvaṅgaspandakarmāṇi śabdavanti | na hi spandaḥ khaḍgagādviyujyate | evaṃ śabdo 'pi karagṛhīte khaḍge śabdaḥ spandena sahoparamati | ato jñāyate karma na karmāntarasyotpādakam | śabdo 'pi na punaḥ śabdānantarasyotpādaka iti | yathā kalpayasi ādyakarmaṇaḥ saṃskāra uttarottarakarmotpādaka iti | tathā ādyaśabdātsaṃskāra utpadyate | saṃskārāduttarottarakarmāṇi samutpadyanta iti | tatra nāsti saṃskārādutpadyamānaṃ saṃskārāntaram | kāraṇakarma saṃskāramutpādayati | na śabdaḥ | karmanirodhācca na kāraṇadravyaṃ bhavati | kasmāt | pūrvaṃ karmaṇi niruddhe hi tadanantaraṃ dravyamutpadyate | evaṃ śabdo 'pi | pūrvaśabde niruddhe 'nantaraṃ śabdaḥ svayamutpadyate | ityanantaraśabdo na kāraṇavān syāt | athāpi yadi vadasi pūrvaśabdaḥ śabdānantaramutpādayatīti | tadā śabdo 'kṣaṇikaḥ syāt | kasmāt | śabdotpattikāla prathamaḥ kṣaṇaḥ | śabdāntarotpattikālo dvitīyaḥ kṣaṇaḥ | utpannaśabdāntara [kālaḥ] tṛtīyaḥ kṣaṇaḥ | pūrvaśabdanirodhakālaścaturtha ityakṣaṇikaḥ syāt |
body.translated_text: it ceases together with action in the same manner.' Just as finger-snapping and the trembling-actions of one's own body produce sound — for vibration (<s>spanda</s>) is not separated from a sword and the like. Likewise, sound too — when a sword is grasped, the sound ceases together with the vibration. Therefore it is known that action does not produce another action; sound too does not produce a subsequent sound. Just as you assume 'from the initial action, a formative impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) arises that produces successive subsequent actions' — so too, from the initial sound, a formative impression arises, and from the formative impression, successive subsequent actions arise. Therein, there is no other formative impression arising from a formative impression. The causal action produces the formative impression — not the sound. And upon the cessation of action, there is no causal substance (<s>kāraṇadravya</s>). Why? Because when the prior action has ceased, the subsequent substance arises. Likewise with sound too — when the prior sound has ceased, the subsequent sound arises by itself. Therefore the subsequent sound would be without a cause. Moreover, if you say: 'The prior sound produces a subsequent sound' — then sound would not be momentary. Why? The first moment is the time of the arising of sound. The second moment is the time of the arising of another sound. The third moment is the time of the arisen other sound. The fourth [moment] would be the time of the cessation of the prior sound — thus it would be non-momentary.

body.text: śabdaḥ kathaṃ śabdāntareṇa viruddhaḥ | kiṃ yathā khalu viṣaṃ viṣauṣadhena viruddham | auṣadhaṃ vā vyādhyā viruddham | tathā no cet ghaṇṭā na śabdadvayavatīti [na] syāt | yadyekasmin kṣaṇe ghaṇṭā śabdadvayavatī, tadā kṣaṇasahasre 'pi śabdadvayavatī syāt | yathā guṇe 'sati drvyasyāgnisaṃyogād guṇa utpadyate | pūrvakṛṣṇarūpe niruddhe raktarūpamutpadyate | evaṃ śabdo 'pi- pūrvaśabde niruddhe śabdāntaramutpadyate | tathā no cet ekasminneva kṣaṇe ghaṇṭā śabdadvayavatī syāt | vastutastu na dvayavatī | ato 'yuktam | yadi śabdāt śabdāntaramutpadyate tadā na hetumanuvarteta | vastutastu ghaṇṭātaḥ śabda utpadyate | sa tu hetumanuvartate | idañca śabdāntaramakhaṇṭāśabdaḥ syāt | tacca śabdāntaraṃ naivaṃ samucchidyeta | hetusamucchedābhāvāt |
body.translated_text: How is sound opposed to another sound? Is it opposed as poison is opposed to an antidote, or as medicine is opposed to disease? If not, then it should not be the case that a bell does not have two sounds. If at one moment a bell has two sounds, then even in a thousand moments it would have two sounds. Just as when a quality does not exist, from the conjunction of a substance with fire, a quality arises — when the prior black form has ceased, a red form arises — so too with sound: when the prior sound has ceased, another sound arises. If it were not so, at one and the same moment the bell would have two sounds. But in reality, it does not have two. Therefore [your view] is untenable. If from sound another sound arises, then [the sound] would not follow its cause. But in reality, sound arises from the bell and follows its cause. Moreover, this other sound would be a non-bell sound. And that other sound would never be cut off, because there is no cessation of its cause.

body.text: (pṛ) ādyaśabdāt sūkṣmaśabdaḥ pariṇamata ityato 'sti samucchedaḥ | (u) kasmātsūkṣmaśabdaḥ pariṇamate | yathābhighātaṃ saṃskārābhivyaktiḥ | yathābhivyakti ādyaśabdaḥ | dvitīyaśabdatadavayavādayo 'pi yathābhivyaktiviśeṣaṃ bhavanti | tāḍanahetvabhāvāt saṃskārābhivyaktistu
body.translated_text: (Objection) From the initial sound, a subtle sound gradually diminishes — therefore there is cessation. (Reply) Why does the subtle sound diminish? According to the degree of striking, the manifestation of the formative impression (<s>saṃskārābhivyakti</s>) [varies]. According to the degree of manifestation, so is the initial sound. The second sound and its components also correspond to the degree of manifestation. Due to the absence of the cause of striking, the manifestation of the formative impression

body.text: bhajyate | saṃskārābhivyaktibhaṅgāttu śabdaḥ sūkṣmaḥ pariṇamate | yasya śabdahetukaṃ śabdāntaramutpadyata iti | tasya rūpamupādāya jala ādarśe rūpamutpannaṃ syāt | evaṃ jale candra ādarśe pratibimbameva rūpaṃ bhavet | tathā ca vaiśeṣikasūtraṃ sarvaṃ naṣṭaṃ syāt |
body.translated_text: breaks down. Due to the breakdown of the manifestation of the formative impression, the sound gradually diminishes to subtlety. For one who holds that another sound arises caused by [a prior] sound — [it would follow that] from form in water, a form in a mirror would arise. Likewise, the moon in water and a reflection in a mirror would be actual form. And in that case, the entire <s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> would be destroyed.

body.text: yadvadasi vibhāgācchabdo niṣpadyata iti | tadapi na yuktam | kasmāt | na hi hastavibhāgācchabda utpadyate | saṃyogāttu śabdo bhavati | khaḍgavaṃśādīnāmavayaveṣu mithaḥ saṃśliṣṭeṣu vibhajyamāneṣu ca mitho nodanācchabdo bhavati | na ca vayaṃ vadāmaḥ saṃyogācchabdo bhavatīti | kasmāt | nahyaṅgulyākāśasaṃyoge śabda utpadyate | aṅgulīṣu mitho 'nunnāsu na śabda utpadyate | ataḥ saṃyogānnotpadyate | kevalaṃ caturṣu mahābhūteṣu saṃyukteṣu viyukteṣu vā śabda utpadyate | yathā mahābhūtānāṃ karma nityasthāyi, na tāni vihāya gacchati |
body.translated_text: Your statement that 'sound is produced from separation (<s>vibhāga</s>)' is also not valid. Why? Sound does not arise from the separation of hands. Rather, sound arises from conjunction. When the parts of swords, bamboo, and the like, which are mutually joined, are separated from each other, sound arises from their mutual impact — not from separation. But we do not say that 'sound arises from conjunction' either. Why? For sound does not arise from the conjunction of a finger with space. Nor does sound arise when fingers are mutually pressed [without impact]. Therefore it does not arise from conjunction. Sound arises solely when the four great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>) are conjoined or disjoined. Just as the action of the great elements is permanently abiding — it does not depart from them.

body.text: śabdaśravaṇavargaḥ pañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fiftieth chapter, the Chapter on Hearing Sound (<s>śabdaśravaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 51 gandhāghrāṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 51. Chapter on Smelling Odor (<s>gandhāghrāṇavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) yadyāha bhavān- gandho nāsikāṃ prāpto jighryata iti | tadapyayuktam | kasmāt | yathā śabdo dūrācchrūyate | tathā gandho viprakṛṣṭadeśastho 'pi ghrātuṃ śakyate | yadi manyase yat asmādgandhāt santatyā gandhakāraṇamutpadyata iti | tat śabdasantāna ukta eva taddoṣaḥ | (u) gandhaḥ kathaṃ [tarhi] ghrātavyaḥ | (pṛ) kusumāvayavān sūkṣmān gacchato gandho 'pyāśritya gacchati | (u) maivam | yadi kusumāvayavā gacchanti kusumāvayavasya rūpamapi draṣṭavyaṃ syāt | na tu dṛśyate | ato jñāyate na gacchantīti | (pṛ) kusumāvayavarūpamatisūkṣmatvāt na dṛśyate | (u) gandho 'pyatisūkṣmo na jighrayet | (pṛ) prabhāvamahatvādgandho jighnyate | yathā coṣyasya hiṅgāvadṛṣṭarūpe 'pi tadgandhamātraṃ jighrāmaḥ | (u) yatra sūkṣmāvayavarūpaṃ [tatra] tadgandho jighrayata iti pratyakṣadṛṣṭam | sūkṣmāvayavasya rūpaṃ kasmānna dṛśyate | yadi kusumaṃ dahyate | tadgandho vardhate | rūpaṃ paraṃ nirudhyate | ato na kusumāvayavo gandhaḥ | yadi gandha kusumāvayavaḥ, alpaṃ ghrātavyaḥ syāt | na tathā vastutaḥ | yadi kusumāvayavā gacchanti, kusumamapacīyamānaṃ syāt | natvapacīyate vastutaḥ | kenedaṃ jñāyate | yathā ekapalaṃ kuṅkuma[kusumaṃ] sadā sagandhaṃ gatvāpi sadaikapalam |
body.translated_text: (Question) If you say that 'an odor is smelled when it reaches the nose' — that too is not valid. Why? Just as sound is heard from a distance, so too an odor located in a distant place can be smelled. If you think that from this odor, a cause of odor arises in a continuum — then the same fault stated for the continuum of sound [applies here]. (Answer) How then is odor to be smelled? (Question) The odor travels depending on subtle particles of the flower that move [through the air]. (Answer) That is not so. If the particles of the flower travel, then the form of the flower-particle should also be seen. But it is not seen. Therefore it is known that they do not travel. (Question) Because the form of the flower-particle is extremely subtle, it is not seen. (Answer) Then the odor too, being extremely subtle, would not be smelled. (Question) Because of the greatness of its potency, the odor is smelled. Just as with dry <s>hiṅgu</s> (asafoetida) — even when its form is not seen, we smell only its odor. (Answer) Where the subtle particle's form is [present], there its odor is smelled — this is directly perceived. Why is the form of the subtle particle not seen? If the flower is burned, its odor increases while its form progressively ceases. Therefore, odor is not a flower-particle. If odor were a flower-particle, it should be smelled only in a small quantity. But in reality that is not the case. If flower-particles travel, the flower would be diminishing. But in reality it does not diminish. How is this known? Just as one <s>pala</s> (measure) of saffron (<s>kuṅkuma</s>) flower, even while emitting fragrance constantly, always remains one <s>pala</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) apacīyamānamatisūkṣmatvānna jñātuṃ śakyate | yathā jalaghaṭa ekabindvapagame tatkṣayo na budhyate | (u) yadi sadāpacīyate | kusumavevāsatsyāt | kiṃ punarapacīyamānaṃ na budhyata iti | yadi kusumaṃ sadāpacīyate | tadā [tadgandhasya] āghrāṇaṃ nopalabhyeta | sadāpacīyamānatvātpratikṣaṇamutpannavināśi syāt | pratikṣaṇavināśitvād dravyāntaramutpannaṃ syāt | kiṃ punarna guṇāntaramutpannamiti | vastutastu kusumasyāghrāṇamupalabhyate | ato jñāyate kusumāvayavā na gacchantīti |
body.translated_text: (Question) It diminishes, but because it is extremely subtle, it cannot be known — just as when a single drop is removed from a water-pot, its depletion is not noticed. (Answer) If it is always diminishing, the flower would eventually become non-existent. How then can it be said that what is diminishing is not noticed? If the flower is always diminishing, then its fragrance would not be obtained — because, being always diminishing, it would be destroyed moment by moment. Being destroyed moment by moment, a different substance would arise. Why then would a different quality not arise? But in reality, the fragrance of the flower is obtained. Therefore it is known that flower-particles do not travel.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi gandhamātraṃ gacchati gandho 'pi [tarhi] kṣīyeta | sadāpacīramānatvāt | gandhasya niravayatvāccaikāntikaparikṣaya eva syāt | (u) na vayaṃ [svī]kurmaḥ kusumāvayavā vāyumanuvartanta iti | nāpi vāyuḥ kusumasya gandhaṃ boḍhvā gamayatīti | kusumagandhamātramupādāya gandhāntaramugpadyate | tadupādāya gandhavāyuḥ tataḥ samutpanno gandhavāyurnāsikāṃ prāpya jighryate | ato nāsti taddoṣaḥ | kenedaṃ jñāyate | yathā jighranti tile gandhaṃ, na tu kusumāvayavagandham | kusumena vāsitatvāt | yadyayaṃ kusumāvayavīyaḥ | kiṃ vāsayati | tilam | ato jñāyate 'yaṃ gandho na kusumāvayavartīti | sa kusumagandhaḥ kusume niṣpīḍite vā niṣpiṣṭe vā saṃparitāpite vā kṣīyate | yaḥ tilavartī, na sa kṣīyate | sa kusumagandhaśca tailamātre vartate | na tu kalke | ato na kusumāvayavīyaḥ | sa ca gandho dīrghakālaṃ tile vartate | na tu kusume | ato na kusumāvayavīyaḥ | (pṛ) yadi na kusumāvayavīyaḥ | ayaṃ kasya gandhaḥ | (u) ayaṃ tilagandhaḥ kusumamupādāya samutpanno na tilādviyujyate | evaṃ kusumagandhamupādāya vāyurgandhāntaramutpādayati | idañca pradarśitameva |
body.translated_text: (Question) If only the odor travels, then the odor too would be depleted — because it is always diminishing. Because odor has no parts, there would be total depletion. (Answer) We do not accept that flower-particles follow the wind. Nor does the wind carry away the odor of the flower. Rather, depending on the flower's odor, a different odor arises in the wind. Depending on that, an odor-carrying wind arises. That odor-wind, having arisen therefrom, reaches the nose and is smelled. Therefore there is no such fault. How is this known? Just as one smells the fragrance in sesame [oil] — but it is not the fragrance of the flower-particle. [The sesame is] fragrant because it was infused by the flower. If this [fragrance] were of the flower-particle, what would it be infusing? The sesame. Therefore it is known that this odor is not one residing in flower-particles. That flower-odor, when the flower is pressed, crushed, or heated, is depleted. But the one residing in the sesame is not depleted. That flower-odor exists only in the oil, not in the cake. Therefore it is not of the flower-particle. And that odor remains in the sesame for a long time, but not in the flower. Therefore it is not of the flower-particle. (Question) If it is not of the flower-particle, whose odor is it? (Answer) It is the odor of the sesame, arisen depending on the flower, and it does not separate from the sesame. Likewise, depending on the flower-odor, the wind produces a different odor. This has already been demonstrated.

body.text: atha kadāciduṣṇavāyuśśītavāyuścānubhūyate | na tatrāpāmagnervā rūpamupalabhyate | ato jñātavyaṃ vāyau punaḥ sparśāntaramutpadyate | na tvāhṛtasya jalasyāgnervāyavā gacchantīti | yadi vāyāvuṣṇasparśastaijasaḥ, śītasparśaśca jalīyaḥ tadānuṣṇāśītasparśena pārthivena bhavitavyam | yathā jalasya tejasaśca rūpaṃ nopalabhyate, pārthivarūpamapi saukṣmānnopalabhyeta | tathā cet vāyurasparśaḥ syāt | idaṃ doṣāyaiva bhavet |
body.translated_text: Now, sometimes hot wind and sometimes cold wind is experienced. But the form of water or fire is not perceived therein. Therefore it should be known that a different touch (<s>sparśa</s>) arises in the wind. The particles of the water or fire that have been carried do not travel [in the wind]. If the hot touch in wind is fiery and the cold touch is watery, then the touch that is neither hot nor cold would have to be of earth. Just as the form of water and fire is not perceived [in wind], the form of earth too, being subtle, would not be perceived. If so, the wind would be without touch — and that would be a fault indeed.

body.text: anyasyāpi kasyacidvacanamupalabhyate- yathā vāyorudakatejaḥsaṃyogācchītoṣṇasparśaḥ, tathā vayoḥ pṛthivīsaṃyogādanuṣṇāśītasparśo 'sti iti | tatra nāsti vinigamakaṃ yadudakāvayavā stejovayavā eva vā vāyumanugacchanti, na tu pṛthivyavayavā iti | yathā bhavatāṃ sūtram- trayaḥ sparśā sparśakāyā vā na pṛthivyudakatejasāmityadṛṣṭaliṅgo vāyuriti jñāyate | anena vacanena trividhāḥ sparśā vāyau kadācidāgantukā vānāgantukā vā syuḥ | kasmāt | trividhāḥ sparśā yadyadṛṣṭaliṅgāḥ, tadā vāyavīyāḥ | bhavato mataṃ yat dṛṣṭa udake tejasi śītoṣṇaspaśau staḥ | na tau vāyavīyau | iti | evaṃ dṛṣṭapṛthivyāmanuṣṇāśītasparśo 'stīti so 'pi vāyvayavīyo na syāt | yadi pūrvamevāsti pṛthagvāyusparśo na pṛthivīsaṃyogāt | tarhi vaktavyamayaṃ sparśo vāyavīyaḥ | ādau tu na dṛśyata iti | kathaṃ jñātavyaṃ vāyusparśamātra manuṣṇāśītaṃ na tu pṛthivyavayava iti | vayamapi vadāmo rūparasagandhasparśāḥ pṛthivyāmeva santi nābādiṣu iti |
body.translated_text: Another person's statement is also found: 'Just as from the conjunction of wind with water and fire, cold and hot touches arise — so too from the conjunction of wind with earth, neither-hot-nor-cold touch exists.' Therein, there is no determining evidence that water-particles and fire-particles follow the wind but earth-particles do not. As in your <s>sūtra</s>: 'Three touches — or rather, touch-bodies — are not of earth, water, or fire; [what remains] is wind, known by an unseen mark.' By this statement, the three kinds of touch in the wind may sometimes be adventitious and sometimes non-adventitious. Why? The three kinds of touch that are known by unseen marks are of the wind. Your view is that in water and fire, cold and hot touches are directly seen, and therefore they are not of the wind. Likewise, in earth, neither-hot-nor-cold touch is directly seen — so it too would not be of the wind. If from the beginning there is a separate wind-touch, not arising from conjunction with earth, then one should be able to say 'this touch is of the wind.' But initially it is not seen. How then is it to be known that only the wind's touch is neither-hot-nor-cold and not an earth-particle? We too say that form, taste, smell, and touch exist only in earth, not in water and the rest.

body.text: yat bhavatāṃ matam- yat dṛṣṭeṣu abādiṣu rūpādikamastīti | tat pṛthivīyogād dṛśyate na tu tat tatrāsti | apsu uṣṇaliṅgavat | tatra nāsti vinigamakaṃ yadapāmuṣṇalakṣaṇaṃ tattejoyogādevāsti | na tu rūpādilakṣaṇaṃ pṛthivīyogāditi | ādau [yat] pṛthagastitvenādṛṣṭamabādīnāṃ na tat pṛthiviyogādbhavati | yadyādau dṛṣṭam | tadā sambhavati vaktum idaṃ rūpamabīyaṃ na pārthivamiti | evamabādīnāṃ vivecanaṃ syāt |
body.translated_text: Your view is that form and the rest are seen in water and the rest. [But] that is seen because of conjunction with earth — it does not exist in them [intrinsically]. Just as the hot characteristic in water [is not intrinsic but] appears due to conjunction with fire. Therein, there is no determining evidence that the hot characteristic of water exists only due to conjunction with fire and the form-characteristic does not exist due to conjunction with earth. What was initially not seen as existing separately in water and the rest does not arise from conjunction with earth.
