If initially it is seen, then one could say: 'This form is of water, not of earth.' In that way, water and the rest could be distinguished.

body.text: (pṛ) vāyau gandhāntaramutpadyata iti yadvacanam | tadayuktam, kasmāt | nirvāte keṣṭhe durādgandho jighryate | gandhastu vātaṃ prati ghrātavyaḥ | yathā pārijātataroḥ | ato jñāyate na vāyau gandhāntaramutpadyate | api tu gandhamupādāya gandhāntaramutpadyate | iti | (u) dvividhaḥ pratyayo gandhasya | yatra vāyurasti | tatra gandhavāyurutpadyate | yatra nāsti tatra gandhamupādāya gandha utpadyate ityasya ko doṣaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) Your statement that 'a different odor arises in the wind' is not valid. Why? Even in the absence of wind, the fragrance of a flower placed in a basket is smelled from a distance. Yet odor is to be smelled [only] against the wind — as with the <s>Pārijāta</s> tree. Therefore it is known that a different odor does not arise in the wind. Rather, depending on the odor, another odor arises. (Answer) There are two kinds of conditions for odor. Where wind is present, an odor-wind arises. Where wind is absent, depending on the odor, a [further] odor arises — what fault is there in this?

body.text: yadavādīḥ pūrvaṃ gandho dūrāt jighryata ityaprāptyā syāditi | tadayuktam | kasmāt | rūpasāmyābhāvāt | yadyaprāpya jighryate | tadā rūpeṇa samaṃ sadaprāpya jighryeta |
body.translated_text: Your earlier statement 'odor is smelled from a distance, and therefore without reaching [the nose]' — that is not valid. Why? Because there is no similarity with form. If [odor] is smelled without reaching [the nose], then it should be smelled at all times without reaching, just like form.

body.text: dūrāddṛṣṭadhūmagandho na jighryate | prāptau tu jighryate | ato jñāyate aprāpya na jighryata iti | divyanāsikābhāvācca prāpya jighryate | yadyaprāpya jighryate | divyanāsikā syāt | divyacakṣuḥśrotavat ||
body.translated_text: The odor of smoke seen from a distance is not smelled. But when reached, it is smelled. Therefore it is known that [odor] is not smelled without reaching [the nose]. And because there is no divine nose — [odor must be] smelled by reaching [it]. If [odor] were smelled without reaching [the nose], there would be a divine nose — like the divine eye and divine ear.

body.text: gandhāghrāṇavarga ekapañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-first chapter, the Chapter on Smelling Odor (<s>gandhāghrāṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 52 sparśabuddhivargaḥ
body.translated_text: 52. Chapter on the Cognition of Touch (<s>sparśabuddhivarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) sparśo 'pi aprāpya jñeyaḥ | kasmāt | sūryasparśasya dūre vartamānatvāt | (u) sūryasparśaḥ kathaṃ jñeyaḥ | (pṛ) tejobhāgaḥ sūryasakāśādāgatya kāyaṃ prāpto jñāyate | (u) yadi sūryāttejobhāgā āgacchanti | sūrye 'stamite tejobhāgo varteta | na tu vartate vastutaḥ | ato jñāyate nāgacchatīti | (pṛ) sūryo yadyapi astamitaḥ | tathāpi tattejo vartate iti sparśātt jñāyate | (u) tathā cettejo 'rūpaṃ syāt | bhavatāṃ sūtre nāstyarūpaṃ teja ityayameva doṣaḥ | (pṛ) tatrāsti sūkṣmaṃ rūpam | (u) tejo rūpabahulamalpasparśakam | yathā pradīrūpam tatsparśamapratibudhyāpi paśyāmaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) Touch too should be known without reaching [the body]. Why? Because the touch of the sun is experienced from a distance. (Answer) How is the touch of the sun to be known? (Question) A portion of fire (<s>tejas</s>) comes from the sun and, having reached the body, is known. (Answer) If fire-portions come from the sun, then when the sun has set, the fire-portion should still remain. But in reality it does not remain. Therefore it is known that [fire] does not come [from the sun]. (Question) Even though the sun has set, that fire still exists — this is known from the touch [of residual warmth]. (Answer) If so, that fire would be formless. In your <s>sūtra</s> it is said: 'There is no formless fire' — this itself is the fault. (Question) Therein there exists a subtle form. (Answer) Fire has predominantly form and little touch. Just as we see the form of a lamp-flame without being aware of its touch.

body.text: (pṛ) sparśaḥ kiṃ niyamena prāpya jñāyate | (u) niyamena prāpya jñāyate | kasmāt | yathā gandhamupādāya vāyau gandhāntaramutpadyate | tathā sūryamupādāya teja utpadyate | (pṛ) sūrye 'stamite tejorūpaṃ kasmānna dṛśyate | (u) kasyacit tejasaḥ sparśamātramasti na rūpam | yathā sūrye 'stamite dharma | yathā vā jvarārtasya puruṣasya tejaḥ kāyaniśritamasti | dharmagṛhe 'gnyapagame 'pi dharmāvaśiṣyate | yathā vā yavā gvāmauṣṇyādi | tat sarvaṃ sparśavadarūpam | tasmāttejaḥ kiñcitsarūpaṃ kiñcidarūpamiti śraddhātavyaṃ bhavati ||
body.translated_text: (Question) Is touch invariably known only by reaching [the body]? (Answer) It is invariably known by reaching. Why? Just as, depending on a [flower's] odor, a different odor arises in the wind — so too, depending on the sun, fire arises [in proximity]. (Question) When the sun has set, why is the form of fire not seen? (Answer) Certain fires have only touch without form — such is the nature [of things] when the sun has set. Just as the heat in the body of a person afflicted with fever — the fire is located in the body [without visible form]. And in a heated room, even after the fire has been removed, the heat remains. Just as the warmth of barley, cow's milk, and such. All of that has touch without form. Therefore, it should be accepted that some fire has form and some fire is formless.

body.text: sparśabuddhivargo dvipañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Cognition of Touch (<s>sparśabuddhivarga</s>).

body.text: 53 manovargaḥ
body.translated_text: 53. Chapter on Mind (<s>manovarga</s>)

body.text: yadavādīḥ- manaḥsañcaratīti | ṣadayuktam | kasmāt | manaḥpratikṣaṇamutpannavināśi vāyuvat karmavadvā | pratikṣaṇotpannavināśidharmasya nāsti gatilakṣaṇam | kiñca mano gacchatīti kiṃ jñātvā gacchet | utājñātvā gacchet | tadubhayamayuktan | yadi pūrvameva jñātavat kiṃ gamanena | yadyajñātavat, kimarthaṃ gamanam | yadi cittaṃ cakṣuṣi vartate | kathaṃ karṇaṃ prāpnoti | yat cittaṃ manyate śrotraṃ gamiṣyāmīti tacchrotasmaraṇam | yā śabdaśuśrūṣā saiva śabdasmṛtiḥ | yadi cakṣuṣi vartamānaṃ cittam, na tadā [śrotra]smaraṇaṃ bhavati | evamindriyāntare 'pi | ato na mano gacchati | yaḥ pumān pūrvaṃ nagarādīn dṛṣṭavān sa idānīṃ pūrvamanurudhya smarati na jānāti pratyutpannān | ato na mano gacchati | yadi [mano]dharmo gacchati, pūrvasaṃnnikṛṣṭaṃ paścādviprakṛṣṭaṃ [gacchet] | idānīntu sannikṛṣṭaṃ viprakṛṣṭa ñca yugapatsmarati | ato jñāyate na gacchatīti | yo dharmo gacchati sontarāle sarvān viṣayān jānīyāt | yathā kaścitsañcaran madhyemārgaṃ rūpādīn padārthān jānāti | na tathā manaḥ | yathā cittamasadapi jānāti yadutātītamanāgataṃ śagaśṛṅgaṃ kūrmaromāhipādaṃ vāyurūpaṃ lohitalavaṇagandhamityādīni [sarvāṇya]pijānāti | sarveṣāmaprāptatvāt | ato jñāyate na [mano] gacchatīti |
body.translated_text: Your statement that 'the mind travels' is untenable. Why? The mind arises and perishes every moment, either like wind or like <s>karma</s>. A <s>dharma</s> that arises and perishes every moment does not have the characteristic of motion. Moreover, [when you say] 'the mind goes' — does it go having cognized, or does it go without having cognized? Both are untenable. If it has already cognized previously, what need is there for going? If it has not cognized, for what purpose would it go? If the mind is operating in the eye, how does it reach the ear? The mind that thinks 'I shall go to the ear' — that is the recollection of the ear. The desire to hear a sound is itself the recollection of sound. If the mind is currently operating in the eye, there is no recollection of the ear at that time. The same applies to the other sense faculties. Therefore the mind does not travel. A person who has previously seen cities and the like now remembers by recalling the past — he does not cognize present [objects in distant places]. Therefore the mind does not travel. If the mind-<s>dharma</s> were to travel, it would go first to what is near and then to what is distant. But in fact one remembers both the near and the distant simultaneously. Therefore it is known that it does not travel. A <s>dharma</s> that travels would cognize all objects in the intervening space. Just as someone walking along the middle of a road knows objects such as form and the rest [along the way]. The mind is not like that. Just as the mind knows even what does not exist — namely, the past, the future, a hare's horn, a tortoise's hair, a snake's foot, the form of wind, the smell of red salt, and so forth — it knows all of these. Because none of them are reached [by the mind]. Therefore it is known that the mind does not travel.

body.text: yadi cittamālambanaṃ prāpnoti | tadā ajñānasaṃśayajñānamithyājñānāni na syuḥ | vastatastu santi tāni | ato jñāyate na gacchatīti | cittasyālambanaṃ nirvāṇaṃ cittaṃ yadi prāpnoti | saṃskṛtenāsaṃskṛtaṃ prāpyate | tattu na yuktam | punarāvṛttinissaraṇa[lakṣaṇa]masaskṛtaṃ saṃskṛte praviśatīdamapyayuktam | yadi paraloko 'stīti smarati | tadā cittaṃ paralokaṃ prāpnoti | tatkāyo mṛto bhavet | na punarujjīvet | ato na gacchati | cittamanāgataṃ smaradanāgataṃ prāpnoti | na hi pratyutpanno dharmo 'nāgato bhavet | atītaṃ smaraccita matīte vartate | nahyatītagato dharmaḥ pratyutpannaḥ syāt | ato jñāyate na gacchatīti, rāgacittānmukhe rūpāntaramutpadyate | tathā dveṣādibhyo 'pi | yadi cittaṃ deśāntaraṃ prāpnoti | tadā rūpabhedo na syāt | ato jñāyate na gacchatīti |
body.translated_text: If the mind were to reach its object, then ignorance, doubt-knowledge, and wrong knowledge would not exist. But in reality they do exist. Therefore it is known that [the mind] does not travel. The object of the mind is <s>Nirvāṇa</s> — if the mind reaches it, then the conditioned would reach the unconditioned. But that is not tenable. Moreover, the unconditioned, having the characteristic of irreversible liberation, entering into the conditioned — this too is untenable. If one remembers 'the other world exists,' then the mind reaches the other world. In that case, the body would be dead and would not revive. Therefore it does not travel. The mind, remembering the future, reaches the future. But a present <s>dharma</s> would not become future. Remembering the past, the mind exists in the past. But a <s>dharma</s> that has gone to the past would not be present. Therefore it is known that it does not travel. From a mind of passion (<s>rāga</s>), a different appearance arises in the face. Likewise from hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>) and the other [defilements]. If the mind were to reach another place, then there would be no change in appearance. Therefore it is known that it does not travel.

body.text: kiñcālambanasthaṃ cittaṃ vedanetyucyate | tā vedanā stistraḥ- duḥkhāḥ vā sukhā vā aduḥkhāsukhā veti | yadi cittaṃ pradeśāntaraṃ prāpnoti | tadā tā vedanā na syuḥ | ato na gacchati | cittañca kāyaniśritam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- nāmarūpāśritaṃ vijñānamiti | ataḥ kāyaṃ vihāya nānyatra gacchati | kāyaśca vijñānasaṃyuktaḥ san kāya ityucyate | yadi cittaṃ deśāntare vartate | kāyo nirvijñānaḥ syāt | ālambanaṃ vijñānasaṃyuktaṃ punaḥ sa vijñānamityucyate ato na gacchati |
body.translated_text: Moreover, the mind stationed on its object is called 'feeling' (<s>vedanā</s>). Those feelings are threefold: painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. If the mind were to reach another place, then those feelings would not exist. Therefore it does not travel. And the mind is dependent on the body. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Consciousness depends on name-and-form (<s>nāmarūpa</s>).' Therefore, abandoning the body, it does not go elsewhere. And the body, when conjoined with consciousness, is called 'body' (<s>kāya</s>). If the mind were to exist in another place, the body would be without consciousness. And the object conjoined with consciousness is further called 'that consciousness' — therefore it does not travel.

body.text: (pṛ) svapne cittamanyā diśo gacchati | (u) maivam | svapne śukraskhalanādi ceṣṭitāni sarvāṇi kāyagatāni | cittaviparyayādanyatra diśi vartate iti vadanti | na tu vastuto gacchati | svapne ca kriyāḥ sarvāstā mithyā | yathā kaścitsvapne pibati naiba tat tṛṣṇāmapanayati | svapne ca [pāpa]karmacaryādi na pātakaṃ bhavati | ataḥ mano 'pi na gacchati | cittaṃ dṛṣṭe śrute mate jñāte dharmamātre vartate | na dharmāntaraṃ carati | yadi gamanena prāpnoti tadā dharmāntaramapi jānīyāt | (pṛ) ṛddhiprabhāvitaṃ mano gacchati | anyā diśaśca prāpnoti | idañca paścādṛddhikhaṇḍanavarge vakṣyate | ato na mano gacchati ||
body.translated_text: (Question) In dreams, the mind goes to other places. (Reply) Not so. In dreams, activities such as the emission of semen and the like — all of these occur within the body. Due to the perversion of the mind, they say it exists in another place. But in reality it does not travel. And all actions in dreams are false. Just as someone who drinks in a dream — that does not actually quench his thirst. And sinful conduct and the like performed in a dream do not constitute a transgression. Therefore the mind too does not travel. The mind operates only in the seen, the heard, the thought, and the known <s>dharma</s> alone. It does not travel to another <s>dharma</s>. If it cognized by traveling, it would also know other <s>dharmas</s> [along the way]. (Question) The mind empowered by supernatural power (<s>ṛddhi</s>) does travel and reaches other places. (Reply) This too will be discussed later in the chapter on the refutation of supernatural powers. Therefore the mind does not travel.

body.text: manovargastripañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Mind (<s>manovarga</s>).

body.text: 54 indriyāniyamavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 54. Chapter on the Non-Fixedness of the Sense Faculties (<s>indriyāniyamavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) indriyāṇi kiṃ pratiniyatāni utāpratiniyatāni | (u) kiṃ nāma pratiniyataṃ kiṃ nāmāpratiniyatam | (pṛ) [yaḥ] cakṣurādīnāmindriyāṇāṃ jñeyo hetuśca | idaṃ pratiniyataṃ nāma | (u) tathā cedindriyamaniyatam | kasmāt | nendriyāṇi cakṣurādīnāṃ jñeyāni hetavaśca | (pṛ) akṣitārakājihvākāya ñca jakṣuṣā dṛśyam | śrotranāsika ñcāntarvartata ityato nopalabhyate | (u) mṛtapuruṣasyāpi tāni santi | natvindriyāṇi tāni | (pṛ) akṣitārakā dvividhā sendriyā nirindriyeti | mṛtapuruṣasyendriyatārakā kṣīṇā | anindriyatārakā tu vartate | (u) nendriyatārakā draṣṭrī | ato na cakṣurādibhirupalabhyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) Are the sense faculties fixed (<s>pratiniyata</s>) or non-fixed (<s>apratiniyata</s>)? (Reply) What do you mean by 'fixed'? What do you mean by 'non-fixed'? (Question) That [which serves as] the object (<s>jñeya</s>) and the cause (<s>hetu</s>) of the faculties such as the eye and the rest — this is called 'fixed.' (Reply) If so, the sense faculty is non-fixed. Why? Because the sense faculties are not the objects and causes of the eye and the rest. (Question) The pupil of the eye, the tongue, and the body are visible to the eye. The ear and the nose, being internal, are therefore not apprehended. (Reply) Even a dead person has those [parts]. But they are not sense faculties. (Question) The pupil of the eye is twofold: with a faculty (<s>sendriya</s>) and without a faculty (<s>nirindriya</s>). In a dead person, the faculty-pupil has perished. The non-faculty pupil remains. (Reply) The faculty-pupil is not the seer. Therefore it is not apprehended by the eye and the rest —

body.text: uktañca sūtre- pañcendriyāṇi rūpīṇyanidarśanāni sapratighānīti | yadi tat sanidarśanam | tadā vibhajyeta iyamakṣitārakā sendriyā iyamanindriyeti |
body.translated_text: — As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The five sense faculties are material (<s>rūpin</s>), invisible (<s>anidarśana</s>), and resistant (<s>sapratigha</s>).' If [the faculty] were visible (<s>sanidarśana</s>), one could distinguish: 'This pupil has a faculty; this pupil does not have a faculty.'

body.text: (pṛ) yadyuktaṃ sūtre- catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya rūpaprasādāḥ pañcendriyāṇīti | kasmātpunarucyate- pañcendriyāṇi rūpīṇyanidarśanāni | sapratighānīti | (u) ata eva śaṅkyate tadacintyakarmavalamiti | karmabalāddhi catvāri mahābhūtānīndriyāṇi pariṇamanti | bhagavān kāṃkṣāvataḥ svaśiṣyān pratyāha- karmajāni pañcendriyāṇīti | ata ucyate rūpīti | tīrthikā vadanti- pañcendriyāṇi ahaṅkārajātāni ahaṅkāraścārūpīti | kiñcāhuḥ- pañcendriyāṇi bṛhadvijānanti alpañca vijānanti | ato 'pratiniyatānīti | te 'pi manyante indriyamarūpīti | ato bhagavānāha- indriyāṇi rūpīṇi rūpādīnupādāya siddhānīti | kadācidyāni rūpādīnupādāya bhavanti tāni sanidarśanānīti brūyāt | ata āha- anidarśanānīti | nāpi śrotrādīnāṃ tadupalabhyate | tathā cedapratighānīti kaścidbūyāt | ata āha- sapratighānīti | viṣayān pratihantīti
body.translated_text: (Question) If it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The five sense faculties are the transparency (<s>rūpaprasāda</s>) of the [form] derived from the four great elements' — why is it further said: 'The five sense faculties are material, invisible, and resistant'? (Reply) Precisely because this is suspected to be an inconceivable power of <s>karma</s>. Through the power of <s>karma</s>, the four great elements are transformed into sense faculties. The Blessed One, addressing his doubting disciples, said: 'The five sense faculties are born of <s>karma</s>.' Therefore it is said 'material' (<s>rūpin</s>). The <s>tīrthikas</s> say: 'The five sense faculties are born of the ego-principle (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>), and the ego-principle is formless (<s>arūpin</s>).' Moreover, they say: 'The five sense faculties cognize extensively and also cognize minutely — therefore they are non-fixed.' They too think the sense faculty is formless. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'The sense faculties are material and are established dependent on form and the rest.' Someone might say: 'Whatever is established dependent on form and the rest is visible (<s>sanidarśana</s>).' Therefore he said: 'Invisible (<s>anidarśana</s>).' Nor are the ear and the rest apprehended [as visible]. If so, someone might say: 'Then they are non-resistant (<s>apratigha</s>).' Therefore he said: 'Resistant (<s>sapratigha</s>).' They resist their objects —

body.text: kṛtvā | yadrūpaṃ sākāraṃ sapratigham, tadaudārikaṃ cakṣurmātreṇa dṛśyaṃ bhavati | tīrthikā vadanti- saṃkhyāḥ parimāṇāni pṛthaktvaṃ saṃyogavibhāgau paratvāparatve karma sāmānyaṃ viśeṣāśca [rūpi]dravyasamavāyādarūpiṇo 'pi cākṣuṣāṇīti | ato bhagavānāha- eṣāṃ rūpamātraṃ sanidarśanam nānye dharmā iti |
body.translated_text: — this being done. Whatever form has shape (<s>sākāra</s>) and resistance (<s>sapratigha</s>) — that is gross and visible to the eye alone. The <s>tīrthikas</s> say: 'Numbers, measures, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, nearness and remoteness, <s>karma</s>, universality, and particularities — though formless, they inhere in material substance and are therefore perceptible to the eye.' Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Only form alone is visible — not other <s>dharmas</s>.'

body.text: hastādau pratihanyata iti sapratigham | (pṛ) tathā cet [ta]tsparśamanubhavet | (u) yadyapi sarvaṃ pratihanti | tathāpi na sarvatrotpadyate [tatsparśaḥ] | kāyavijñānaṃ [ta]dvijñānamanujāyata iti indriyāṇi vibhaktāni | athendriyāṇi vastuto 'pratiniyatāni | kasmāt | dharmo yadi pratiniyataḥ | hastena vastugrahaṇavadekameva vastu gṛhṇīyāt | cakṣustu mahadalpañca paśyatītyato 'niyatam | yasya pratiniyato vastusparśaḥ tasya kāritramasti | yathā tejaḥsparśe dāhaḥ khaḍgasparśe chedaḥ | cakṣustu sudūramapi paśyatītyato 'pratiniyatam | yo dharmaḥ pratiniyataḥ sa pratiniyataṃ dharmaṃ pratihanti | yathā hasto hastaṃ pratihanti | cakṣustu udakakācābhrapaṭalādibhirna pratihanyate | ato 'pratiniyatam | kiñcendriyaṃ yadi pratiniyatam | kāyasyāntareva varteta | kāyasyāntarvartitvānmanoyuktamapi na bāhyaviṣayān paśyet | vastutastu paśyati | ato 'pratiniyatam | dharmo yadi pratiniyataḥ tadā [na] saṃkhyeyāni pañcendriyāṇi | kintu cakṣurādīni dvaikāyajihvābhyaḥ sahāṣṭau syuḥ | ato 'pratiniyatam | adhiṣṭhānamātraṃ pratiniyatam | nendriyam | vāmacakṣuḥ paśyati dakṣiṇacakṣurapi vijānāti | nahyanyatpaśyati anyadvijānātīti syāt | indriyāṇāṃ vāmadakṣiṇalakṣaṇābhāvānna pratiniyatānīmāni |
body.translated_text: [A <s>dharma</s>] is resistant because it collides with the hand and the rest. (Question) If so, it would experience touch. (Reply) Although it resists everything, the experience of touch does not arise everywhere. Body-consciousness — that consciousness arises [from touch], and therefore the sense faculties are differentiated. Now, the sense faculties are in reality non-fixed. Why? If a <s>dharma</s> were fixed, it would grasp only a single object, like grasping a thing with the hand. But the eye sees both large and small — therefore it is non-fixed. That which has a fixed contact with an object has causal efficacy [upon it]. Just as contact with fire produces burning, and contact with a sword produces cutting. But the eye sees even from a great distance — therefore it is non-fixed. A <s>dharma</s> that is fixed resists a fixed <s>dharma</s>. Just as the hand resists the hand. But the eye is not resisted by water, glass, cloud-coverings, and the like — therefore it is non-fixed. Moreover, if the sense faculty were fixed, it would exist only within the body. Being situated within the body, it would not see external objects, even in conjunction with the mind. But in reality it does see. Therefore it is non-fixed. If a <s>dharma</s> were fixed, the five sense faculties would not be countable [as five]. Rather, the eye and the rest, together with the two [faculties of] body and tongue, would be eight. Therefore it is non-fixed. Only the location (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>) is fixed — not the sense faculty. The left eye sees, and the right eye also cognizes. It should not be the case that one sees [one thing] and the other cognizes [another]. Because the sense faculties lack the characteristics of left and right, they are non-fixed.

body.text: (pṛ) cakṣuṣo raśmirmahadalpaṃ paśyati sudūraṃ gatvāpi rūpamapratihataṃ paśyati | yathā sūryaraśmiḥ kāyavinirmuktaḥ paśyati | raśmirayaṃ dve cakṣuṣyupādāyaikatra militvā ekībhūto rūpaṃ paśyati | cakṣurekaṃ śrotraṃ nāsikā ca kāyasyāntarvartamānā na vibhaktuṃ śakyate | ato bhavadvacanam anyatpaśyati anyadvijānāti idaṃ nirastam | ātmano jñānaṃ nendriyasya indriyantu prayojyan | dharmasannikarṣo nopalabhyata iti yadbhavadvacanam tatprayuktam | yadādityaprakaśenābhibhūta ityādi | śrotrādīnāmindriyāṇāṃ sannikarṣo gūḍha ityato 'pi nopalabhyate | yathā vṛkṣasaṃyogasya nigūḍhā koṭirna jñāyate | ātmānamupādāya caitanyam | nendriyāṇyupādāya | indriyaṃ mautikam | mahābhūtamacetanamityata indriyamapyacetanam | ghaṭaḥ paramāṇuhetukaḥ | yathā paramāṇuracetanaḥ | ghaṭo 'pyacetanaḥ | sa viṣayāntaraṃ na jānātītyato 'cetanamiti jñāyate |
body.translated_text: (Objection) The rays of the eye see both large and small, and traveling even to a great distance, see form unobstructed. Just as the rays of the sun [travel far]. These rays, departing from the body, see. These rays, depending on the two eyes, merge at one point and become unified, and see form. The eye is one; the ear and the nose, being situated within the body, cannot be distinguished [spatially from each other]. Therefore your statement 'one sees one thing and the other cognizes another' is refuted. Knowledge belongs to the self (<s>ātman</s>), not to the sense faculty — the sense faculty is merely the instrument employed [by the self]. [As for your claim that] the contact of <s>dharmas</s> is not apprehended — that has been answered. [Regarding] what is overpowered by sunlight and so forth — the contact of the ear and other sense faculties is hidden, and therefore is also not apprehended. Just as the hidden tip of a branch conjoined with a tree is not known. Sentience belongs to the self, not to the sense faculties. The sense faculty is a pearl [i.e., a jewel]. The great elements are non-sentient — therefore the sense faculty too is non-sentient. A pot has atoms as its cause. Just as atoms are non-sentient, a pot too is non-sentient. It does not know another object — therefore it is known to be non-sentient.

body.text: atrocyate | bhavānāha- raśmirgacchati indriyamekatra sthitamiti | bhavato raśmirindriyaṃ bhavati | raśmeravyavasthitatvādindriyamapyavyavasthitam | sa ca raśmirnāstīti pūrvameva nirastam | yadavādīrekamindriyamiti | nedaṃ yujyate | ekaṃ cakṣuḥ kiñcitpaśyati dvitīyaṃ cakṣuranyatpaśyati | yadyekaṃ cakṣurvinaśyati tadā nāsti raśmiḥ | indriyāṇāṃ savyadakṣiṇatvañca pūrvameva pratyuktam | (pṛ) yadyekaṃ cakṣurvijñānajanakam | tadā dve cakṣuṣī ekamindriyaṃ syāt | kiṃ dvitīyaṃ cakṣuḥ karoti | (u) nāsikā [vivarasya] bhedānnaikaṃ bhavati | asaṃvṛtāpi pṛthagbhavatīti naikaṃ bhavati | karāṅgulyādivat | yadavocadbhavān- ātmaprayogya[mindriya]miti | tannirastapūrvam | ātmā na prayojayati |
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: You say: 'The rays travel; the sense faculty remains in one place.' [But] according to you, the rays are the sense faculty. Because of the instability of the rays, the sense faculty too would be unstable. And that the rays do not exist has already been refuted previously. Your statement that 'it is one sense faculty' — that is not tenable. One eye sees something, and the second eye sees something else. If one eye is destroyed, then there are no rays. The [objection about] left and right of the sense faculties has already been answered previously. (Question) If a single eye generates consciousness, then the two eyes would be one sense faculty. What would the second eye do? (Reply) The nostril, because of the division of its opening, is not one. Even when uncovered, [each nostril] functions separately — therefore it is not one. Like the fingers of the hand and so forth. Your statement that 'the sense faculty is an instrument employed by the self' — that has been refuted previously. The self does not employ [instruments] —

body.text: ādityaprakāśenābhibhūta ityapi dūṣitapūrvam | yadavādīḥ sannikarṣo nigūḍha ityato na dṛśyata iti | idamayuktam | kasmāt | [indriya]dharmo yadi vyavasthitaḥ | tadā sannikarṣo na bhavet | svarūpato bailakṣaṇyāt | yathā vṛkṣasaṃyogo nigūḍho 'pi tadavasāne dṛśyate | naivaṃ viṣayendriyasannikarṣo dṛśyate | yaduktam- ātmavaśāccaitanyamiti | atrātmā nāstīti vakṣyate | yabdravīṣi- bhautikānīndriyāṇīti | tadayuktam | karmabalena pariṇamitāni mahābhūtānīndriyāṇi bhūtvā vibhaktāni santi |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'it is overpowered by the radiance of the sun' has also been refuted previously. Your statement 'the contact is concealed, and therefore it is not seen' — this is untenable. Why? If the nature of the sense faculty is determined, then contact would not occur, because of the difference in intrinsic nature. Just as the conjunction of a tree, even when concealed, is seen at its end — but the contact of object and sense-faculty is not seen in that way. Your statement 'consciousness arises from the power of the self (<s>ātman</s>)' — it will be stated [later] that the self does not exist. Your statement 'the sense faculties are material (<s>bhautika</s>)' — that is untenable. The great elements, transformed by the power of <s>karma</s>, become sense faculties and are differentiated.

body.text: (pṛ) indriyāṇi niyatāni | kasmāt | tāni ca bhautikāni | catvāri mahābhūtāni niyatānīti indriyamapi niyatam | yasmāccakṣurādīnīndriyāṇi niyatāni tasmānmahābhūtādīnyupakurvanti | mahābhūtañcendriyaṃ pariṇamyate | mahābhūtasya niyatatvāt tadvikṛtadharmo 'pi niyataḥ syāt | indriyeṇa svaviṣayavatā bhāvyam | viṣayeṇa ca svendriyavatā bhāvyam | yadyaniyatam | mitho bhāvyatā na syāt | manovat syāt | ato jñāyate niyatamiti | lauki kāstārakādiṣu niyatān dharmān vijānanti | na mana ādivat [aniyatān] | ato niyatāni | indriyañca purovartinaṃ viṣayaṃ vijānāti | anyatrānumānena | ato niyatam | vidyamānamālambanaṃ vijanātīndriyam | manastvavidyamānamālambanam | tadyathātītādi | indriyārthasannikarṣādindriyajñānamutpadyate | yasmānniyatenendriyeṇa niyato viṣayaḥ pratihanyate | tasmāt jñāyate niyatamiti |
body.translated_text: (Question) The sense faculties are determined. Why? They are material. Since the four great elements are determined, the sense faculties too are determined. Because the sense faculties of the eye and the rest are determined, the great elements and the rest serve them. And the great element is transformed into the sense faculty. Because the great element is determined, the <s>dharma</s> that is its modification should also be determined. A sense faculty must possess its own object. And an object must possess its own sense faculty. If they were indeterminate, there would be no mutual correspondence — it would be like the mind. Therefore it is known that [the faculties] are determined. Worldly people know that <s>dharmas</s> such as stars and the rest are determined — unlike the mind and the like, which are indeterminate. Therefore they are determined. And the sense faculty cognizes the object present before it — otherwise, by inference. Therefore it is determined. The sense faculty cognizes an existing object. But the mind cognizes even a non-existing object — such as past [objects] and the like. From the contact of sense-faculty and object, sense-faculty knowledge arises. Because a determined sense faculty encounters a determined object, it is known that [the faculty] is determined.

body.text: atrocyate | yaduktaṃ bhavatā- indriyāṇi bhautikāni niyatānīti | sarvaṃ bhautikamapi kiñcidindriyaṃ bhavati kiñcinnendriyam | evaṃ kiñcinniyataṃ kiñcidaniyatam | yadavocaḥ- upakurvantīti | jñānasyopakurvanti na indriyasya | mahābhūtavikṛtamindriyamiti coktam | vikāro 'pi jñānārtho nendriyopakārakaḥ | caturṇāṃ mahābhūtānāṃ prasāda ityato 'niyatam | yabdravīṣi- indriyārthayormitho bhāvyateti | ayamapi manasa eva niyamaḥ | indriyasyājñatvāt | tadanye sarve manobalaviśeṣāḥ | ṣaḍ vijñānāni ityuktirapi manovijñānamapekṣyeti niścīyate | yathā catussatyābhisamaye dharmān sākṣātkṛtya [ta]ddharmatāṃ samyak bhāvayatīti sarvamidaṃ manovijñānenaiva | yathā cālātacakramāyamarīcinirmitagandharvanagarāṇi sarvāṇyasatyabhūtāni paśyati | tathā rūpāṇyapi paśyati | ataścakṣurādīni sarvāṇi mithyālambanāni bhavanti | yadavādīḥ- indriyārthasannikarṣāt jñānamutpadyata iti | kiṃ prāpya vijānāti kimaprāpyeti sarvaṃ pratyuktam |
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: Your statement 'the sense faculties are material and therefore determined' — everything material may sometimes be a sense faculty and sometimes not. Likewise, something may sometimes be determined and sometimes indeterminate. Your statement 'they serve [the faculties]' — they serve knowledge, not the sense faculty. And you said 'the sense faculty is a modification of the great elements.' The modification too is for the purpose of knowledge, not for the benefit of the sense faculty. Because of the transparency (<s>prasāda</s>) of the four great elements, [the faculty] is indeterminate. Your statement 'object and sense faculty must mutually correspond' — this too is merely a determination of the mind, not of the sense faculty, because the sense faculty is non-cognitive. All those other [arguments] are special powers of the mind. The statement 'there are six kinds of consciousness' too is determined with reference to mind-consciousness. Just as in the realization of the Four Noble Truths (<s>catussatyābhisamaya</s>), having directly realized <s>dharmas</s>, one properly cultivates their nature — all of this is by mind-consciousness alone. Just as one sees whirling firebrands, mirages, magical creations, and cities of the <s>Gandharvas</s> — all of which are unreal — so too one sees forms. Therefore the eye and the rest are all apprehending false objects. Your statement 'from the contact of sense-faculty and object, knowledge arises' — whether one cognizes by contact or without contact, all of that has been answered.

body.text: indriyāniyamavargaścatuḥpañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Indeterminacy of the Sense Faculties (<s>indriyāniyamavarga</s>).

body.text: 55 rūpāyatanalakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 55. Chapter on the Characteristics of the Form Sense-Base (<s>rūpāyatanalakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: nīlapītādirūpaṃ rūpāyatanamityucyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- [yat] cakṣurāyatanamatītarūpaviprayuktam | idamāyatanaṃ jñātavyamiti | (pṛ) kecidāhuḥ karma parimāṇañca
body.translated_text: Blue, yellow, and other colors — these are called the form sense-base (<s>rūpāyatana</s>). As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'What pertains to the eye sense-base (<s>cakṣurāyatana</s>) and is disjoined from past forms — this sense-base should be known.' (Question) Some say <s>karma</s> and spatial dimension (<s>parimāṇa</s>)

body.text: rūpāyatanamiti | kasmāt | yathoktaṃ sūtre- kṛṣṇāvadātahrasvadīrghaudārikasūkṣmāṇi rūpāṇīti | (u) saṃsthānādayo rūpasya prabhedā eva | kenedaṃ jñāyate | rūpaviyuktaṃ parimāṇādicittaṃ nopalabhyate | yadi saṃsthānādi rūpādanyat | rūpaviyukta [saṃsthāna]cittamapyutpadyeta na vastuta utpadyate | ato jñāyate nānyaditi | (pṛ) pūrvaṃ rūpabuddhirbhavati paścātsaṃsthānabuddhiḥ | kasmāt | kṛṣṇāvadātavartulaparimaṇḍalabuddhayo na yugapadbhavanti (u) hrasvadīrghādilakṣaṇaṃ sarvaṃ rūpaṃ pratītya manovijñāne samutpadyate | yathā rūpadarśanapūrvakaṃ manovijñānamutpadyate | saṃskṛtadharmāṇāṃ kṣaṇikatvāt strīpuṃnimittakarmāpi nāsti, vijñānadharmo na gatiḥ | atītaṃ hi karmetyucyate |
body.translated_text: are [included in] the form sense-base. Why? As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Forms are dark, bright, short, long, gross, and subtle.' (Answer) Configuration (<s>saṃsthāna</s>) and the rest are merely subdivisions of form. How is this known? A cognition of spatial dimension and the rest that is separated from form is not found. If configuration and the rest were different from form, a cognition of configuration separated from form would also arise — but in reality it does not arise. Therefore it is known that they are not different. (Question) First the cognition of form arises, then the cognition of configuration. Why? Because the cognitions of dark, bright, round, and circular do not arise simultaneously. (Answer) The characteristic of shortness, longness, and the rest — all of it arises in mind-consciousness dependent on form. Just as mind-consciousness arises preceded by the seeing of form. Because conditioned <s>dharmas</s> are momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), there is no <s>karma</s> of male and female signs either — the <s>dharma</s> of consciousness is not a movement (<s>gati</s>). For what is past is called <s>karma</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) atītaṃ kāyikaṃ karma | yadi nāstyatītaṃ | na tadāsti kāyikaṃ karma | (u) saṃvṛtisaṃjñāyāsti kāyikaṃ karma | na paramārthataḥ | (pṛ) yadi paramārthato nāsti kāyikaṃ karma | na syātpuṇyapāpamapi paramārthataḥ | puṇyapāpābhāvādvipāko 'pi nāsti | (u) [kasmiṃścit] dharme sthānāntara uddhite yadi parasyopakāro hiṃsā vā bhavati | tadā sidhyati puṇyapāpam ||
body.translated_text: (Question) Bodily <s>karma</s> is past. If the past does not exist, then there would be no bodily <s>karma</s>. (Answer) In conventional designation (<s>saṃvṛtisaṃjñā</s>), there is bodily <s>karma</s> — but not in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārthataḥ</s>). (Question) If bodily <s>karma</s> does not exist in the ultimate sense, then merit and sin would also not exist in the ultimate sense. And if merit and sin do not exist, their ripening (<s>vipāka</s>) also does not exist. (Answer) When a certain <s>dharma</s>, having been moved to another position, either benefits or harms another — then merit and sin are established.

body.text: rūpāyatanalakṣaṇavargaḥ pañcapañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of the Form Sense-Base (<s>rūpāyatanalakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 56 śabdalakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 56. Chapter on the Characteristics of Sound (<s>śabdalakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) kasmānnocyate śabdamupādāya mahābhūtāni bhavantīti | (u) śabdo rūpādivinirmuktaḥ | rūpādayaśca [śabdā] saṃprayuktāḥ | ato nocyate | śabdaśca na rūpādivannityasantānaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) Why is it not said 'dependent on sound, the great elements come into being'? (Answer) Sound is separate from form and the rest. Form and the rest, however, are conjoined [with each other]. Therefore it is not said [that way]. And sound does not have a continuous series (<s>santāna</s>) like form and the rest.

body.text: nāpi ca rūpādibhi sahajātaḥ | rūpādibhyaścānyathā jātaḥ | kasmāt | rūpādīni sahajātāni kramaśo mūlāṅkurakrameṇa bhavanti | śabdastu na tathā bhavati | śabdaśca padārthāllabdhanāmakaḥ | yathā vadanti ghaṭaśabda iti | na tu vadanti ghaṭe śabda iti | kadācidvadanti ghaṭaṃ paśyāmīti | kadācidvadanti ghaṭarūpaṃ paśyāmīti | na tu vadanti ghaṭaṃ śṛṇomīti | kevalaṃ vadanti ghaṭaśabdaṃ śṛṇomīti | sattvānāṃ pūrvākṣiptakarmavāsanatvādyadi padārthā nityaṃ saśabdāḥ syuḥ tadā na tātkālikaḥ [śabdaḥ] | tasmācchabdo na mahābhūtānāṃ sādhanahetuḥ |
body.translated_text: Nor is it co-born with form and the rest. And it arises differently from form and the rest. Why? Form and the rest are co-born and arise progressively in the sequence of root, sprout, and so forth. But sound does not arise in that way. And sound is named after the object (<s>padārtha</s>). As they say: 'The sound of a pot' — but they do not say: 'In the pot there is a sound.' Sometimes they say: 'I see the pot.' Sometimes they say: 'I see the form of the pot.' But they do not say: 'I hear the pot.' They merely say: 'I hear the sound of the pot.' Because beings are endowed with the habitual tendencies (<s>vāsanā</s>) of previously initiated <s>karma</s>, if objects always had sound, then there would be no occasional sounds. Therefore sound is not a cause for establishing the great elements.

body.text: (pṛ) padārthāḥ saśabdā iti kenedaṃ jñāyate | sammarde śabda udeti | mahābhūtānāṃ sadā mithaḥ sammardāt sarvaṃ saśabdaṃ syāt | (u) na padārthānāṃ mithaḥ sammardaḥ sarvaḥ śabdahetuḥ | kasmāt | cakṣuṣā paśyāmaḥ khalu nāṅgulidvayasammardaśśabdajanaka iti | (pṛ) tatra śabda utpadyate | saukṣmyānna jñāyate | (u) notpadyate [tatra śabdaḥ] yāvatsūkṣmaśabdasyāpyaśravaṇāt | yo vadati asti śabda iti | tasya pratyakṣe śraddhā na syāt | paro 'pi vadet- astyudake gandhaḥ | saukṣmyānna jighryate | asti tejasi rasaḥ | santi vāyāvākāśe ca rūpādaya iti | na santi vastutaḥ | ato na sarvaḥ sammardaḥ śabdajanakaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) How is it known that objects have sound? Sound arises from friction. Since the great elements are always in mutual friction, everything would be accompanied by sound. (Answer) Not every mutual friction of objects is a cause of sound. Why? We directly perceive that the friction of two fingers does not produce sound. (Question) Sound is produced there, but is not known due to its subtlety. (Answer) It is not produced — because even a subtle sound is not heard. One who says 'sound exists' would have no faith in direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). Another too could say: 'In water there is smell, but it is not smelled due to its subtlety. In fire there is taste. In wind and space there are form and the rest.' But in reality they do not exist. Therefore not every friction produces sound.

body.text: (pṛ) saṃvṛtitaḥ sadā vadanti śabda ākāśaguṇa iti | kenedānīṃ jñāyate caturmahābhūtaja iti | (u) pratyakṣaṃ paśyāmaḥ khalu śabdaṃ caturmahābhūtajam | asmaddarśanasya pratyakṣapūrvakatvāt | vadanti ca ghaṇṭāśabdo bherīśabda iti | ato jñāyate ghaṇṭābheryorayaṃ śabda iti | caturmahābhūtebhyo 'nyatvāt śabdo viśiṣyate yathā ghaṇṭābherīśabdāvanyau | tāmrabhājanavedhe kampitaśabdaḥ saha bhavati | gṛhīte ca saha śāmyati | kampitabhājanaśabdo 'pyevamiti jñeyam | śabdaṃ kariṣyan avaśyaṃ cāturbhautikaṃ bimbamākāṃkṣate | ato jñāyate caturmahābhūtajaḥ śabda iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Conventionally it is always said: 'Sound is a quality of space.' How is it now known that it is born of the four great elements? (Answer) We directly perceive that sound is born of the four great elements. Our view is based on direct perception. And they say: 'The sound of a bell, the sound of a drum.' From this it is known that this sound belongs to the bell and the drum. Sound is distinguished from the four great elements in the same way that the sounds of a bell and a drum are different from each other. When a copper vessel is struck, the vibrating sound arises together [with the strike]. And when [the vessel] is grasped [to stop it], [the sound] subsides together. The sound of a vibrating vessel should be understood in the same way. One who intends to produce a sound necessarily requires a material object (<s>bimba</s>) composed of the four great elements. From this it is known that sound is born of the four great elements.

body.text: karmakāraṇaśca śabdo viśiṣyate | yathā sattvānāṃ dhvaniḥ kadācitkarkaśaḥ kadācinmadhuraḥ | na karmakāraṇenākāśe guṇa utpadyeta | ato na [sa ākāśaguṇaḥ] | hetulakṣaṇatvācca | hetulakṣaṇañca- yo dharmo yasmādbhavati | sa [tabhya] hetuḥ | evaṃ kāraṇamahābhūteṣu satsu śabdo bhavati | asatsu na śabdaḥ | yathā tejasi satyauṣṇyaṃ nāsati | iti jñātavyaṃ tejasa auṣṇyaṃ bhavatīti | mahābhūtajaḥ śabdo 'pyevam | yathākāśauṣṇyayoḥ sattā |
body.translated_text: And sound is distinguished by the cause of <s>karma</s>. Just as the voice of beings is sometimes harsh and sometimes sweet. A quality would not arise in space from the cause of <s>karma</s>. Therefore it is not a quality of space. And because of the mark of causation — the mark of causation is: a <s>dharma</s> that arises from something, that something is its cause. Thus, when the causal great elements are present, sound arises; when they are absent, there is no sound. Just as when fire is present, there is heat; when it is absent, there is not. Thus it should be known that heat comes from fire. Sound born of the great elements is likewise. Just as the existence of heat and space —

body.text: ākāśe vartamāne 'pi auṣṇyamasti kadācit kadācinnetyākāśo nauṣṇyakāraṇamiti jñeyam | tadā śabdo 'pi | yathākāśabhāve śabdabhāvaḥ | ākāśe vartamāne 'pi śabdaḥ kadācidasti kadācinnāsti | ato jñāyate 'kāraṇamiti | śabda ākāśaguṇa itīdaṃ na śraddheyam | dṛṣṭe tāvanna paśyāmaḥ śabdaḥ ākāśamupādatta iti | nāpyanumānam | tatra kenānumānaṃ bhavet | sūtragranthe ca bahūni viruddhāni | evaṃ nāstyekamapi śreaddheyam | ato 'yuktamiti jñāyate |
body.translated_text: when space is present, heat sometimes exists and sometimes does not — therefore space should be known as not the cause of heat. So too with sound. Just as sound exists when space exists — when space is present, sound sometimes exists and sometimes does not. Therefore it is known that [space] is not its cause. The statement 'sound is a quality of space' should not be believed. In what is directly seen, we do not perceive that sound takes hold of space. Nor is there inference [for that]. What inference could there be in that case? And in the <s>sūtra</s>-text, there are many contradictions. Thus there is not a single thing that should be believed. Therefore it is known that [the view that sound is a quality of space] is untenable.

body.text: śabdalakṣaṇavargaḥ ṣaṭpañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of Sound (<s>śabdalakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 57 gandhalakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 57. Chapter on the Characteristics of Smell (<s>gandhalakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) tamālapatrādinānāgandhasamavāyāt tadgandho maula- [gandhā]danyaḥ | kiṃ teṣāmeva gandho gandhāntaramutpādayati ? | (u) gandhakalāpahetukaṃ gandhāntaramutpadyate | yathā nīlapītarūpasaṅkare haritarūpamutpadyate | vibhinnakarmapratyayācca vibhinnagandha utpadyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) Since there is a combination of various smells such as <s>tamālapatra</s> (bay leaf) and the rest, that smell is different from the original smell. Does their smell produce another smell? (Answer) Another smell arises caused by the aggregate of smell-factors. Just as from a mixture of blue and yellow forms, a green form arises. And from different <s>karma</s>-conditions, a different smell arises.

body.text: aulūkyā vadanti pṛthivīmātraguṇo gandha iti | kathamidam | (u) nāsti dravyamitīdaṃ pradarśitameva | ato 'yuktamiti jñāyate |
body.translated_text: The <s>Aulūkyas</s> (<s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>) say: 'Smell is a quality of earth alone.' How is this? (Answer) It has already been demonstrated that substance (<s>dravya</s>) does not exist. Therefore it is known that this is untenable.

body.text: vaiśeṣikāḥ punarāhuḥ- kāṃsyatrapusīsa[loha]suvarṇarajatatāmrādayastaijasā iti | tatrāpi gandho 'stītyato jñāyate na pṛthivīmātre 'stīti | (pṛ)kāṃsyādau pṛthivīyogādgandhaḥ | (u) nāyamāgantuko gandhaḥ | kasmāt | pūrvamanyasmin dravye 'nāghrāto 'yaṃ gandhaḥ | yo ghrātapūrvaḥ sa āgantuko vaktavyaḥ | yathā pūrvaṃ kusume gandhamāghrāya paścādvastre jighrataḥ ayamāgantukaḥ saṃbhavati | naivaṃ bhavati kāṃsyādīnāṃ gandhaḥ | ato 'hetuḥ | kāṃsyādīnāmasati nirgandhasamaye na vaktavyamāgantuka iti | mamāpi sambhavati nodakādādau rūpādīni santi | pṛthivīyogāttu kevalamupalabhyanta iti | yadi bravīṣi jalādāvasti rūpaṃ svata iti |
body.translated_text: The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> further say: 'Bronze, tin, lead, iron, gold, silver, copper, and the like are fiery substances (<s>taijasa</s>).' In those too there is smell — therefore it is known that [smell] does not belong to earth alone. (Question) In bronze and the like, the smell is due to the conjunction with earth. (Answer) This smell is not adventitious (<s>āgantuka</s>). Why? Because this smell was never previously perceived in another substance. What has been previously smelled [elsewhere and transferred] should be called adventitious. Just as when one first smells a fragrance in a flower and later smells it in a garment, this [latter] may be called adventitious. But the smell of bronze and the like is not like that. Therefore that is not a valid reason. Since there is no time when bronze and the like are without smell, it cannot be said to be adventitious. On my view too, it is possible that form and the rest do not originally exist in water and so forth. They are apprehended only due to conjunction with earth. If you say that 'in water and the like, form exists inherently' —

body.text: vayamapi vadema kāṃsyādau svata eva gandho 'stīti | yo dharmo yasya vastuno 'vinirbhāgavartī sa tasyāsti | ato yo gandho yatrāvinirbhāgavartī sa tasyaiva dravyasya gandhaḥ | jalādau ca yadyasti gandhaḥ saukṣmyānnopalabhyate | tadā ko doṣaḥ | yathā vadanti- asti candramasi tejaḥ tejasaḥ pratiniyatoṣṇatā iti | vadanti ca gharmagṛhe 'gnyapagame 'pi śiṣyamāṇasya dharmaṇo 'sti sūkṣmaṃ rūpamiti | yavāgāvasti sūkṣmaṃ śītalakṣaṇamiti ca | tathā jale 'pi gandho 'sti | na tatrāsti niyamaheturyajjalegandho nāstīti vaktam |
body.translated_text: then we too would say: 'In bronze and the like, smell exists inherently.' A <s>dharma</s> that exists inseparably in a certain substance — that belongs to that substance. Therefore, a smell that exists inseparably in something is the smell of that very substance. And if there is smell in water and the like but it is not apprehended due to its subtlety, then what is the fault? Just as they say: 'There is fire in the moon; and fire invariably has heat.' And they say: 'In a heated room, even after the fire has been removed, the remaining <s>dharma</s> has a subtle form.' And: 'In porridge there is a subtle characteristic of cold.' Likewise, in water too there is smell. There is no determining reason for saying that smell does not exist in water.

body.text: kiñca bhavato dravyāṇyaniyatalakṣaṇāni bhavatni | kasmāt | bhavatā pratijñātam "vyavasthitaḥ pṛthivyāṃ gandha" iti | vajrasphaṭikādīnāntūjvalavikṛtatvāt pārthivatve 'pi nāsti gandhaḥ | bravīṣi ca "apsu śītatā" iti | kṣīrādīnāṃ niyataśītatve 'pi ghṛtādīnāṃ gandhavattvāt pārthivatvamucyate | āha ca "tejasa uṣṇatā" iti | kāṃsyādīnāṃ taijasatve 'pi noṣṇatā | candrādayaḥ śītā api taijasā iti bravīṣi | ityevamādibhirdravyāṇi na niyatalakṣaṇāni bhavanti || tasmādgandhaḥ pṛthivīmātre vidyata itīdamayuktam | kāṃsyādayastaijasā iti yadbhavato matam | tadapyayuktam | kasmāt | uṣṇatāniyamābhāvāt | aulukyā vadanti- tejasa uṣṇatā vyavasthiteti | kāṃsyādayastvanuṣṇāḥ | (pṛ) kāṃsyādīnāmuṣṇatā kārye vartate | na tu sparśe | (u) ghṛtaṃ kāryataḥ śītamiti āpyaṃ syāt | bhavatastu matam gandhavattvātpārthivamiti | ataḥ kāryata iti vacanaṃ na hetuḥ kalpate | harītakīphalamātre uṣṇatā niyateti taijasadravyaṃ syāt | vastutastu gandhavatī pañcarasavatīti na taijasadravyamityucyate | kāryata iti vacanasyāhetutvāt | kāṃsyādīni na taijasadravyāṇi | tejaso lakṣaṇaṃ laghutvaṃ kāṃsyādīnāṃ gurutvaṃ, tejaso rūpaṃ bhāskaraṃ śuklam kāṃsyādīnāntu abhāsvaram | kāṃsyāṃdīnāṃ tejasā vailakṣaṇye 'pi tāni taijasadravyāṇīti jñāpyante | tāni ca tejaso viruddhāni | kasmāt |
body.translated_text: Furthermore, your substances do not have fixed characteristics. Why? You have asserted: 'Smell is fixed in earth.' But in diamond, crystal, and the like, although they are earthy due to their bright and lustrous transformation, smell does not exist. And you say: 'Coldness belongs to water.' But although milk and the like have a fixed characteristic of coldness, ghee and the like are said to be earthy because they possess smell. And you say: 'Heat belongs to fire.' But in bronze and the like, although they are fiery, there is no heat. And you say that the moon and the like, though cold, are fiery. By these and other [reasons], substances do not have fixed characteristics. Therefore the statement 'smell exists only in earth' is untenable. Your view that 'bronze and the like are fiery' is also untenable. Why? Because of the absence of a fixed [connection with] heat. The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> (<s>Aulūkya</s>) say: 'Heat is fixed in fire.' But bronze and the like are without heat. (Objection) The heat of bronze and the like exists in its effect, not in its touch. (Reply) Then ghee, being cold in its effect, would be watery. But your view is that it is earthy because it possesses smell. Therefore the statement 'in its effect' does not serve as a valid reason. The fruit of <s>harītakī</s> alone has heat as a fixed [quality] — so it would be a fiery substance. But in reality, because it possesses smell and the five tastes, it is not called a fiery substance. Because the statement 'in its effect' has no probative force, bronze and the like are not fiery substances. The characteristic of fire is lightness, while bronze and the like are heavy. The form of fire is luminous and white, while bronze and the like are non-luminous. Although bronze and the like differ in characteristics from fire, they are made known as fiery substances. But they are opposed to fire. Why?

body.text: agnisaṃyoge 'pacayāt | yadi taijasāni, agnisaṃyoge vivardheta | na tu vivardhate | ato na taijasadravyāṇi | asamyakcintanāt bravītha yūyaṃ- gandhaḥ pṛthivīmātre vidyata iti | parantu sa gandhaścaturṣu saṅghāteṣu vartate |
body.translated_text: Because they diminish upon conjunction with fire. If they were fiery, they would increase upon conjunction with fire. But they do not increase. Therefore they are not fiery substances. Through incorrect reasoning you say: 'Smell exists only in earth.' But that smell exists in the four aggregates.

body.text: gandhalakṣaṇavargaḥ saptapañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristic of Smell (<s>gandhalakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 58 rasalakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 58. Chapter on the Characteristic of Taste (<s>rasalakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: raso nāma mathurāmlalavaṇakaṭutiktakaṣāyādayāḥ | ime ṣaḍrasāḥ padārthavaśādviśiṣṭā bhavanti | na tu caturṣu mahābhūteṣu tāratamyena bhavanti | yathā vadanti pṛthivyā apāṃ bāhulyena madhura iti | tadayuktam | madhurasyāpramāṇā viśeṣā bhavanti | ato jñātavyam - padārthāt pṛthak [pṛthak] svabhāvo raso jāyata iti |
body.translated_text: Taste (<s>rasa</s>) means sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent, and the rest. These six tastes are differentiated according to the nature of the substance. They do not arise in the four great elements in varying degrees. As they say: 'From the predominance of earth and water, [the taste is] sweet' — that is not correct. Sweet [taste] has immeasurable varieties. Therefore it should be known that taste arises with its own nature separately from each substance.

body.text: cikitsakāvadanti- ṣaḍeva rasā iti | kathamidam | ṣaḍiti nātisīmā | kasmāt | kadācidvayo rasayoḥ samavāyaḥ, kadācit trayāṇām, kadāciccaturṇāmityevamapramāṇāḥ | na tu madhurāmlasamavāyānmadhurāmlau bhavataḥ | madhurāmlasamavāye punārasāntaramutpadyata ityevamapramāṇāḥ | saṃvṛtyā rasā vibhaktāḥ yathā janā manyante madhuraṃ madhurameva bhavatīti | rasānāṃ pākakālaḥ pṛthak pṛthaglakṣaṇasya hetuḥ | madhurarasaḥ pākakāle 'mṛtameva bhavati vikriyate vā | tathānye 'pi rasāḥ | ato dharmāṇāmastīdṛśaḥ prabhāvaḥ | na tu ṣaṇmātrā [rasā] iti ||
body.translated_text: Physicians say: 'There are exactly six tastes.' How is this [to be understood]? 'Six' is not an absolute limit. Why? Sometimes two tastes combine, sometimes three, sometimes four — thus they are immeasurable. But from the combination of sweet and sour, [the result] does not become sweet and sour [separately]. From the combination of sweet and sour, yet another taste arises — thus they are immeasurable. Conventionally, tastes are classified as people think: 'Sweet is simply sweet.' The time of cooking (<s>pākakāla</s>) is the cause of each separate characteristic. Sweet taste, at the time of cooking, becomes merely nectar-like or undergoes transformation. Likewise the other tastes too. Therefore <s>dharmas</s> have such inherent power. But [tastes] are not merely six.

body.text: rasalakṣaṇavargo 'ṣṭapañcāśaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristic of Taste (<s>rasalakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 59 sparśalakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 59. Chapter on the Characteristic of Touch (<s>sparśalakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: sparśo nāma kaṭhinaṃ mṛdu guru laghu prabalaṃ durbalaṃ śītamuṣṇaṃ karkaśaṃ ślakṣṇaṃ kṛśaṃ śthūlaṃ praśrabdhiḥ klamathamaklamathaṃ rogo viśeṣo vā kāyataikṣṇyaṃ kāyamāndyamālasyaṃ gauravaṃ sammūrchanaṃ
body.translated_text: Touch (<s>sparśa</s>) means hard, soft, heavy, light, strong, weak, cold, hot, rough, smooth, thin, thick, tranquility (<s>praśrabdhi</s>), sluggishness, non-sluggishness, illness, distinguishing sensation, bodily sharpness, bodily dullness, laziness, heaviness, fainting

body.text: sammohaḥ stambharna vyathā śūlaṃ vijṛmbhikā jighatsā pipāsā santṛptiḥ sātaṃ visātaṃ maurarvyam ityādayaḥ |
body.translated_text: , bewilderment, stiffness, pain, colic, yawning, hunger, thirst, satisfaction, comfort, discomfort, agitation, and the rest.

body.text: (pṛ) kecidāhuḥ- trayaḥ sparśāḥ śīta uṣṇo 'nuṣṇāśīta iti | kathamidam | (u) kāṭhanyādiṣu jñānamutpadyate | kāṭhinyādīn vihāya nāsti śītoṣṇajñānam | (pṛ) aulūkyā vadanti- pṛthivyā anuṣṇāśītasparśastathā vāyorapi sparśaḥ | apāṃ śītasparśaḥ tejasa uṣṇasparśa iti | kathamidam | [tādṛśa]niyamo nāstīti pūrvamevoktam- yaduta sarpirādīnāṃ niyatā śītatā kāṃsyādīnāmanuṣṇateti | kiñcoktaṃ pūrvaṃ triṣu sparśeṣu yadi vāyavīya āgantukaḥ tadā sparśāntarābhāvādvāyuraniyatalakṣaṇaḥ syāt | iti | yavāgau śīlakṣaṇānupalambhādapāmaniyataṃ śītalakṣaṇaṃ syātt |
body.translated_text: (Objection) Some say: 'There are [only] three kinds of touch — cold, hot, and neither-cold-nor-hot.' How is this [to be understood]? (Reply) Cognition arises with respect to hardness and the rest. Apart from hardness and the rest, there is no cognition of cold and hot. (Objection) The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> (<s>Aulūkya</s>) say: 'In earth, the touch is neither-cold-nor-hot; likewise the touch of wind. In water, the touch is cold. In fire, the touch is hot.' How is this [to be understood]? [Reply:] There is no such fixed determination — as was stated previously, namely that ghee and the like have a fixed characteristic of coldness, and bronze and the like are without heat. Furthermore, as was previously stated: 'Among the three touches, if the airy [touch] is adventitious, then in the absence of another touch, wind would have an indeterminate characteristic.' Because the cold characteristic is not observed in gruel, the cold characteristic of water would be indeterminate.

body.text: (pṛ) yavāgāvasti sūkṣmaṃ śītalakṣaṇam | tejasābhibhūtatvānna jñāyate | kenedaṃ jñāyate | tejaḥśaktau kṣīṇāyāṃ punaḥśītasyodayāt | (u) kāṃsyādīni sarpirādīni ca kaṭhinadravyāṇi agnisaṃyogādravī bhavanti | yadi kāṭhinye 'vinaṣṭa eva dravatvamasti | tadā kāṭhinyameva dravatvaṃ syāt | yadi kāṭhinye vinaṣṭe dravatvaṃ bhavati | tadā śītasparśe niruddhe punaśśītasparśa utpadyeta | yathānuṣṇāśītaḥ pṛthivīsparśaḥ | agnisaṃyoge sa sparśo yadi na vinaṣṭaḥ | tadā na pāko bhavet | yadi vinaṣṭaḥ | tadā sa eva sparśaḥ sparśāntaramutpādayet |
body.translated_text: (Objection) In gruel there exists a subtle cold characteristic. Because it is overpowered by fire, it is not known. How is this known? Because when the power of fire diminishes, coldness arises again. (Reply) Hard substances such as bronze, ghee, and the like become liquid upon conjunction with fire. If hardness is not destroyed while liquidity exists, then hardness itself would be liquidity. If liquidity arises when hardness is destroyed, then when the cold touch ceases, a cold touch would arise again. Just as the touch of earth is neither-cold-nor-hot — upon conjunction with fire, if that touch is not destroyed, then there would be no cooking. If it is destroyed, then that very touch would produce another touch.

body.text: evañca śītasparśe vinaṣṭe punaśśītasparśa utpadyeta | tathā cedapāṃ guṇā api pacyeran | bhavāṃstu viparyayaṃ duṣṭaṃ bravīti | virodhidharmasannipāte sarvāṇyanityāni | yathāgnisaṃyogāttṛṇādīni naśyanti | yadyāha- uṣṇasparśaḥ śītasparśa [tayā] parāvartata iti | [tadā] paro 'pi brūyāt payolakṣaṇamanirudhya kevalaṃ dadhilakṣaṇaṃ parāvartata iti | tattu nopalabhyate | yadi bravīṣi na paśyāmaḥ payaḥ punaḥ payorūpeṇeti | evañca na pākavat syāt | kasmāt | anādau saṃsāre kiṃ dravyaṃ nāgninā dagdhaṃ bhavati | dṛṣṭā ca bhūmau sadhrūmamṛt upalabhyamānā | jñātavyāñca pākāt vyāvṛtteti | ato jñāyate pāko na nityo 'parāvṛtta iti | evañca śītasparśe vinaṣṭe punaḥ śītasparśa utpadyate | kadācidagnisaṃyogātkṛṣṇarūpe vinaṣṭe punaḥ kṛṣṇarūpamutpadyate | raktarūpe vinaṣṭe punāraktarūpamutpadyate | evaṃ śītasparśo vinaṣṭaḥ sannagniviyoge punarutpadyate | tatra ko doṣaḥ |
body.translated_text: And thus, when the cold touch is destroyed, a cold touch would arise again. If that is so, then the qualities of water too could be cooked. But you, on the contrary, assert a perversion. When opposing <s>dharmas</s> come together, all [things] are impermanent. Just as upon conjunction with fire, grass and the like are destroyed. If you say: 'The hot touch merely reverses the cold touch' — then the opponent too could say: 'Without the characteristic of milk being destroyed, only the characteristic of curd reverses it.' But that is not observed. If you say: 'We do not see milk [revert to] the form of milk [after becoming curd]' — then it would not be like cooking. Why? In beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, what substance has not been burned by fire? And one sees on the ground clay with smoke, which is obtained [as evidence of past burning]. And it should be known that [the effect of] cooking has reversed. Therefore it is known that cooking is not permanent and unreversed. And thus, when the cold touch is destroyed, a cold touch arises again. Sometimes, upon conjunction with fire, when the black form is destroyed, a black form arises again. When the red form is destroyed, a red form arises again. Likewise, the cold touch, having been destroyed, upon separation from fire, arises again. What fault is there in this?

body.text: vaiśeṣikā vadanti- pṛthivīmātre pāko bhavati nāpsu iti | bhiṣajastu vadanti- yastaptāṃ yavāgūṃ pāti sa vijātīyaṃ phalaṃ labhata iti | yadi yavāgau rūpādīnāṃ nāsti [pākaḥ] | vijātīyaphalavattāniṣṭhābhaṅgaḥ | ato jñāyate 'bādayo 'pi pākavanta iti | yathāgnipakvadravyasya pūrvaguṇavināśātpurnarguṇāntaravattvāt jñāyate dravyaṃ vijātīyaguṇavaditi | evamāpo 'pi | lakṣaṇānāṃ virodhāccānityatā | yathāpogniṃ nirvāpayanti | agnirāpaḥ paripācayati | nādravyaṃ paripācayati tejobalam | api cāgnisaṃyogena śītasparśo 'pagacchati | tasmādvaiśeṣikasūtram- śītasparśavatya āpa itidamayuktam ||
body.translated_text: The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> say: 'Cooking occurs only in earth, not in water.' But physicians say: 'One who drinks hot gruel obtains a heterogeneous result.' If in gruel there is no cooking of form and the rest, the thesis of heterogeneous results would be broken. Therefore it is known that water and the rest also undergo cooking. Just as in a substance cooked by fire, because of the destruction of the prior qualities and the arising of other qualities, it is known that the substance has heterogeneous qualities — so too with water. Because of the opposition of characteristics, [there is] impermanence. Just as water extinguishes fire, and fire cooks water. What does not have a substance is not cooked by the power of fire. Furthermore, upon conjunction with fire, the cold touch disappears. Therefore the <s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> — 'Water has the cold touch' — is untenable.

body.text: sparśalakṣaṇavarga ekonaṣaṣṭitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the fifty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristic of Touch (<s>sparśalakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 60 atha duḥkhasatyaskandhe vijñānādhikāre acaitasikasthāpanam
body.translated_text: 60. Now, within the section on the truth of suffering, in the topic of consciousness: the establishment of [the view that there are] no separate mental factors (<s>acaitasikasthāpana</s>)

body.text: cittaṃ manovijñānamityekasyaiva vibhinnāni nāmāni | yat dharmālambanaṃ taccittamityucyate | (pṛ) tathā cedvedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskārādayaścaitasikā api cittāni syuḥ | sarveṣāmālambakatvāt | (u) vedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskārādayaścittaviśeṣasyākhyā bhavanti | yathā mārgavarge smṛterekasyā eva pañca nāmānyu[cyante] smṛtyupasthānaṃ smṛtīndriyaṃ smṛtibalaṃ smṛtisambodhyaṅgaṃ samyaksmṛtiriti | tathā vīryādayo 'pi | yathā caikasyā anāsravaprajñāyā duḥkhabhāvanā, sambodhirityādīni nānā pṛthak pṛthaṅ nāmāni bhavanti | eka eva samādhiḥ dhyānaṃ vimuktiḥ nissṛtiḥ samāpattirityucyate | evamekameva cittaṃ yathākālaṃ viśeṣākhyāṃ labhate | ato jñāyata ekameva cittamiti | kasmāt | yathoktaṃ sūtre- tasya kāmāsravāccittaṃ vimucyate avidyāsravaccittaṃ vimucyata iti | yadyasti pṛthak caitasikam | caitasikāccittaṃ vimucyata iti brūyāt | api coktaṃ sūtre- yadā bhagavān sattvānāṃ kallacittaṃ mṛducittaṃ dāntacittaṃ vimuktilābhapravaṇatāñca prajānāti | tataścatussatyānyupadiśati iti | tatra na caitasikamuktamasti | api coktaṃ sūtre- cittasaṃkleśātsattvāḥ saṃkliśyanti cittavyavadānātsattvā viśudhyanti | iti | kiñcāha- yo bhikṣuścatvāri dhyānānyupasampadya viśuddhākopyacitto
body.translated_text: Mind (<s>citta</s>), thought (<s>manas</s>), consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) — these are different names of one and the same [thing]. That which takes <s>dharmas</s> as its object is called 'mind' (<s>citta</s>). (Objection) If that is so, then feeling (<s>vedanā</s>), perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>), formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and other mental factors (<s>caitasika</s>) would also be minds, since all of them take objects. (Reply) Feeling, perception, formations, and the rest are designations for specific [functions] of mind. Just as in the section on the path, memory (<s>smṛti</s>) alone has five names — foundation of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>), faculty of mindfulness (<s>smṛtīndriya</s>), power of mindfulness (<s>smṛtibala</s>), mindfulness as a factor of awakening (<s>smṛtisambodhyaṅga</s>), and right mindfulness (<s>samyaksmṛti</s>). Likewise with effort (<s>vīrya</s>) and the rest. And just as a single undefiled wisdom (<s>anāsravaprajñā</s>) has various separate names such as contemplation of suffering (<s>duḥkhabhāvanā</s>), awakening (<s>sambodhi</s>), and the rest. A single <s>samādhi</s> is called <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), <s>vimukti</s> (liberation), <s>nissṛti</s> (deliverance), and <s>samāpatti</s> (attainment). Thus, one and the same mind receives specific designations according to the occasion. Therefore it is known that mind alone [exists]. Why? As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'His mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (<s>kāmāsrava</s>); his mind is liberated from the outflow of ignorance (<s>avidyāsrava</s>).' If there were separate mental factors, he would have said: 'The mind is liberated from mental factors.' Furthermore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'When the Blessed One knows that beings' minds are ready, softened, tamed, and inclined toward the attainment of liberation, then he teaches the Four Noble Truths.' Therein, no separate mental factor is mentioned. Furthermore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Through the defilement of mind, beings are defiled; through the purification of mind, beings are purified.' Furthermore it says: 'A monk, having attained the four <s>dhyānas</s>, [whose mind is] purified and unshakeable

body.text: bhavati | sa duḥkhaṃ samudayaṃ nirodhaṃ mārgamāryasatyañca yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti iti | dvādaśanidāneṣu ca saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānamityucyate | āha ca ṣaḍdhāturayaṃ puruṣa iti | kiñcāha- capalatā na cittādatyeti | iti | api coktaṃ sūtre rāṣṭrapālamāhūyāvadat idaṃ vastu punaḥ punarājavajjavaṃ mahārāja cittaṃ vadāmi iti | āha ca ādhyātmiko vijñānakāyo bāhyaṃ nāparūpamiti dvidhā bhavati | iti | vijñānakāyo 'stīti mātramāha na caitasikamastīti | kiñcāha- trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | yadi caitasikamasti na brūyāt "trayāṇām" iti | ucyate tu vastuta strayāṇāmiti | ato jñāyate cittamātramasti na caitasikamasti pṛthagiti ||
body.translated_text: knows as it truly is the truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the noble path.' And in the twelve links of dependent origination (<s>dvādaśanidāna</s>), it is said: 'Consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is conditioned by formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>).' And it says: 'This person consists of six elements (<s>ṣaḍdhātu</s>).' Furthermore it says: 'Fickleness does not come from mind [alone].' Furthermore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s> where the Blessed One, having summoned <s>Rāṣṭrapāla</s>, said: 'This thing again and again runs swiftly — O great king, I say it is the mind.' And it says: 'The internal body of consciousness (<s>vijñānakāya</s>) and the external non-similar form are twofold.' It merely says 'there is a body of consciousness' — it does not say 'there are separate mental factors.' Furthermore it says: 'The conjunction of three is contact (<s>sparśa</s>).' If mental factors existed [separately], he would not have said 'of three.' But in reality, 'of three' is stated. Therefore it is known that mind alone exists — separate mental factors do not exist.

body.text: duḥkhasatyaskandhe vijñānādhikāre 'caitasikasthāpanavargaḥ ṣaṣṭitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Within the section on the truth of suffering, in the topic of consciousness, this is the sixtieth chapter, the Chapter on the Establishment of No [Separate] Mental Factors (<s>acaitasikasthāpanavarga</s>).

body.text: 61 caitasikasthāpanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 61. Chapter on the Establishment of [Separate] Mental Factors (<s>caitasikasthāpanavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) cittamanyat caitasikadharmā anye | kasmāt | cittacaitasikānāṃ samprayogāt | yadi na santi caitasikadharmāḥ | tadā samprayogo na syāt | asti tu samprayogaḥ | ato jñāyate santi caitasikadharmā iti | yadbhavatāṃ mataṃ- cittamanyena cittena samprayujyata iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | uktaṃ hi sūtre- dūraṅgamamekacaramaśarīraṃ guhāśayam iti | tatra sadharmatāmātraṃ pratiṣidhyate | caitasikasahacaratve 'pi ekacaramityucyate | yathā bhikṣurekākī san satsvapi maśakā[di]prāṇiṣu sajātīyo nāstīti ekākītyucyate | ato
body.translated_text: (Objection) Mind is one thing and mental factors (<s>caitasikadharma</s>) are another. Why? Because of the association (<s>samprayoga</s>) of mind and mental factors. If mental factors do not exist, then there would be no association. But there is association. Therefore it is known that mental factors exist. Your view that 'mind is associated with another mind' is untenable. Why? Because it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Far-going, solitary-wandering, bodiless, dwelling in a cave.' Therein, [the objection of] mere similarity of nature is refuted. Even though [mind] accompanies mental factors, it is called 'solitary-wandering.' Just as a monk, though alone, when mosquitoes and other creatures are present, is called 'alone' because no one of the same kind is present. Therefore

body.text: jñāyate nānyacittena cittaṃ samprayujyata iti | asti tu samprayoga ityato 'sti caitasika [dharmaḥ] | cittañca saptadhātubhirekāyatanena ekaskandhena ca saṅgṛhītam | caitasikāstu ekena dhātunā ekenāyatanena tribhiḥ skandhaiśca saṅgṛhītāḥ | cittamāśrayaḥ caitasikā āśritāḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- caitasikāścittaṃ niśritya samudarācaranti | iti | yadi na santi caitasikāḥ | tadā na syuḥ pañcaskandhāḥ | na tu tatsambhavati | tayośca dvayorutpattirbhidyate | dvābhyāṃ cittamutpadyate | tribhiścaitasikāḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpañca cakṣurvijñānamutpadyate | trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśaḥ | sparśapratyayā vedanā iti | āha ca- nāmarūpasamudayādvijñānasamudayaḥ | sparśapratyayādvedanāsamudaya iti | caitasikā āśrayasaṃprayuktāḥ | samamekālambanā ekādhvavartinaśca | naivaṃ cittaṃ bhavati | tādṛśavibhāgāt jñāyate cittamanyat caitasikā anya iti | caturṣu pratiśaraṇeṣu jñānapratiśaraṇaṃ [viśiṣṭa]mucyate | na vijñānapratiśaraṇam | yadi jñānameva vijñānam | kathamidaṃ pratiśaraṇavacanaṃ syāt | ato jñāyate jñānaṃ na vijñānamiti |
body.translated_text: it is known that the mind is not associated with another mind. But association exists — therefore mental factors (<s>caitasikadharma</s>) exist. And mind (<s>citta</s>) is comprised in seven elements (<s>dhātu</s>), one sense-base (<s>āyatana</s>), and one aggregate (<s>skandha</s>). But the mental factors are comprised in one element, one sense-base, and three aggregates. Mind is the basis (<s>āśraya</s>); the mental factors are dependent upon it. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The mental factors, depending on the mind, operate together.' If mental factors did not exist, then the five aggregates would not exist. But that is not possible. And the arising of the two [mind and mental factors] differs. Mind arises from two [conditions]; mental factors arise from three. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Depending on the eye and form, eye-consciousness arises. The conjunction of three is contact (<s>sparśa</s>). Conditioned by contact is feeling (<s>vedanā</s>).' And it says: 'From the arising of name-and-form (<s>nāmarūpa</s>), the arising of consciousness. From the condition of contact, the arising of feeling.' The mental factors are associated with the basis and share the same object and abide in the same time-period. Mind does not have this nature. From such distinctions, it is known that mind is one thing and mental factors are another. Among the four refuges (<s>pratiśaraṇa</s>), taking knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>) as refuge is stated to be [the most] distinguished, not taking consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) as refuge. If knowledge were identical with consciousness, how could this statement about refuge exist? Therefore it is known that knowledge is not consciousness.

body.text: bhagavān svayamāha- ye cittajāścittaniśritāste caitasikā iti | na cāha bhagavān cittamātramasti | na caitasikā itīmamartham | paro 'pi vadet- caitasikāḥ santi na cittamiti | saṃjñāmātramiti caitāsikān dūṣayasi | cittamapi saṃjñāmātramiti dūṣayiṣyāmi | kāritrabhedāddharmāṇāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ bhidyate | yathāpaḥ snehayanti | tejaḥ paridahati | evaṃ vedanādīnāṃ kāritrabhedāt jñāyate vibhinnalakṣaṇamiti | uktañca sūtreṣu- citte vitarka udabhūditi | ataścittādanye caitasikā iti jñāyate | na hi citte svacittamutpadyeta | yathoktaṃ- cittasaṃkleśāt sattvāḥ kliśyanti | cittavyavadānātsattvā viśudhyanti | iti | yadi cittamātramasti | tadā saṃkleśo vyavadānañca nirhetukaṃ syāt | puruṣasyāvidyayā
body.translated_text: The Blessed One himself said: 'Those that are born of mind and depend on mind — those are mental factors.' And the Blessed One did not say this to mean 'only mind exists, not mental factors.' An opponent too could say: 'Mental factors exist, not mind.' You reject mental factors [by saying] they are merely designations (<s>saṃjñāmātra</s>) — [but] I would reject mind too as merely a designation. Through the difference of function (<s>kāritra</s>), the characteristics of <s>dharmas</s> are differentiated. Just as water moistens and fire burns — so too, from the difference of function of feeling (<s>vedanā</s>) and the rest, it is known that their characteristics are distinct. And it is stated in the <s>sūtras</s>: 'In the mind, discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>) arose.' From this it is known that mental factors are other than mind — for in the mind, its own mind would not arise. As it is stated: 'Through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.' If only mind existed, then defilement and purification would be without cause. Through ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), a person's

body.text: saṃkleśaḥ prajñayā vyavadānamiti na bhavet | ātmaiva saṃkleśa ātmaiva vyavadānamiti syāt | tattu na sambhavati | ataḥ santi caitasikāḥ ||
body.translated_text: defilement [occurs]; through wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), purification — this would not be possible. The self itself would be the defilement and the self itself would be the purification. But that is not possible. Therefore mental factors exist.

body.text: caitāsikasthāpanavarga ekaṣaṣṭitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-first chapter, the Chapter on Establishing Mental Factors (<s>caitasikasthāpanavarga</s>).

body.text: 62 nācaitasikavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 62. Chapter on the Non-Existence of Mental Factors (<s>nācaitasikavarga</s>)

body.text: bhavatā yadyapyuktaṃ dharmālambanaṃ cittaṃ cittaviśeṣāścaitasikā mārgavargoktavat iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | sūtre cittalakṣaṇaṃ pṛthak caitasikalakṣaṇañca pṛthagucyate | vijānātīti vijñānakṣaṇam | sukhaduḥkhānubhavo vedanālakṣaṇama | [nīlapītādi]saṃjñānaṃ saṃjñālakṣaṇam | abhisaṃskaraṇaṃ saṃskāralakṣaṇama | ataścittamanyat caitasikā anya iti | yaduktaṃ- cittaṃ vimucyata iti | tadayuktam | uktamanyasmin sūtre- avidyāvisaṃyogātprajñā vimucyata iti | na cittamātraṃ vimucyata iti | cittasya prādhānyāccittamātramuktam | laukikāḥ sarve bhūyasā cittameva vijānanti | na caitasikān | ato bhagavānekadeśamāha | sūtre bhagavān na pariniṣṭhitaṃ vakti idamasyādhivacanamiti | yathāha sūtram- ekaṃ dharmaṃ prajahītha ahamājānāmi anāgāmimārgaṃ pratilabhadhve yadidaṃ kāmacchandam | iti | vastutastu naikadeśaprahāṇena tadbhavati | tathedamapi | anena kallacittādyapi pratyuktam | yaduktaṃ bāhyamādhyātmikamiti dharmo dvidhā bhavatīti | tadapyayuktam | yaduktaṃ bāhyaṃ nāmarūpamiti sa eva caitasika[dharma] ityucyate | bāhyāyatanasaṅgṛhītatvādvāhyamityākhyā |
body.translated_text: Although you have said 'Mind that takes <s>dharmas</s> as its object, and particular modifications of mind are mental factors — as stated in the chapter on the path' — that is untenable. Why? Because in the <s>sūtra</s>, the characteristic of mind and the characteristic of mental factors are stated separately. 'It cognizes' — that is the characteristic of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). 'The experience of pleasure and pain' — that is the characteristic of feeling (<s>vedanā</s>). 'Cognizing [things as] blue, yellow, and so forth' — that is the characteristic of perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>). 'Fashioning together' — that is the characteristic of formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>). Therefore mind is one thing and mental factors are another. Your statement 'mind is liberated' — that is untenable. It is stated in another <s>sūtra</s>: 'Through the disjoining from ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) is liberated.' It is not that mind alone is liberated. Because of the predominance of mind, only mind is mentioned. All worldly people, for the most part, know only mind, not mental factors. Therefore the Blessed One spoke only partially. In the <s>sūtra</s>, the Blessed One does not speak definitively, saying 'this is the designation of that.' As the <s>sūtra</s> says: 'Abandon one <s>dharma</s> — I assure you, you will obtain the path of non-returning, namely desire-and-passion (<s>kāmacchanda</s>).' But in reality, it is not by the abandonment of a single portion that that [result] is obtained. The same applies here. By this, [the objection regarding] 'beautiful mind' (<s>kallacittā</s>) and so forth is also answered. Your statement 'external and internal — <s>dharma</s> is twofold' — that too is untenable. What is called 'external name-and-form' is itself the mental factor — it is called 'external' because it is comprised in the external sense-base (<s>bāhyāyatana</s>).

body.text: tatra bhagavān trīṇī vastūnyāha | ya ādhyātmiko 'sti vijñānakāyaḥ | tadevendriyeṇa saha vijñānamityucyate | yat bāhyaṃ sa eva viṣaya ityucyate | yaduktaṃ vijñānakāyamātramastīti | tadapyayuktam | tasmin sūtra uktaṃ bāhyalakṣaṇaṃ caitasikameva | yaduktaṃ trayāṇāṃ
body.translated_text: Therein, the Blessed One spoke of three things: that which is internal consciousness-body (<s>vijñānakāya</s>) — that, together with the sense-faculty, is called consciousness. That which is external — that itself is called the object. Your statement 'only the consciousness-body exists' — that too is untenable. In that <s>sūtra</s>, the external characteristic stated is itself the mental factor. Your statement 'the conjunction of three

body.text: sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | ayuktamidamapi | sparśo hi vedanādīnāṃ caitasikānāṃ hetūkriyate | ataḥ sparśa ucyate ||
body.translated_text: is contact (<s>sparśa</s>)' — this too is untenable. For contact serves as the cause of mental factors such as feeling (<s>vedanā</s>) and the rest. Therefore it is called contact.

body.text: na caitasikanāstitāvargo dviṣaṣṭitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Existence of Mental Factors (<s>caitasikanāstitāvarga</s>).

body.text: 63 na caitasikasattāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 63. Chapter on the Non-Existence of Mental Factors [continued] (<s>na caitasikasattāvarga</s>)

body.text: atra brūmaḥ | yadavādīḥ samprayogātsanti caitasikā iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | sarveṣāṃ dharmāṇāmekacaratvaṃ paścātsavistaraṃ vakṣyate | ataḥ samprayogo nāsti | anena cittamidamekacaramityādyapi pratyuktam | na tatra sadharmatā pratiṣidhyate | caitasikā eva pratiṣidhyante | yadavocaḥ saṅgṛhītabhedātsanti caitasikā iti | tat sūtrakartā svīyāṃ saṃjñā vyavasthāpayāmāsa | na bhagavataḥ sūtre lakṣaṇasaṅgraha ucyate | ato na santi | yadabravīḥ āśrayāśrāyibhāva iti | yathā bhavato manovijñānaṃ cittamāśrayate | āśrayatvānna caitasikamityucyate | evaṃ cittaṃ cittamāśrayata iti na nāmāntaraṃ labhate | yaduktam- pañcaskandhā na syuriti | tadayuktam | mama [mate] cittaviśeṣā eva vedanāsaṃjñādaya ityucyante | [yathā] bhavataścaitasikāḥ pṛthak trayaḥ skandhā bhavanti | yadavādīḥ utpattirbhidyata iti | tadayuktam | yadi cittaṃ caitasikāśca sahotpadyante | kasmāducyate dvābhyāṃ cittamutpadyate tribhiścaittā iti | yaścittamātraṃ bravīti | tasyāyameva nyāyaḥ | kasmāt | sa hi bravīti- pūrvaṃ vijñānasya kālaḥ paścātsaṃjñādīnām iti | yaduktaṃ samprayogālambanādhvabhijñānaṃ bhidyata iti | tat pūrvameva dūṣitam | samprayogasyābhāvāt | yadabravīḥ- jñānapratiśaraṇaṃ na
body.translated_text: Here we say: Your statement 'mental factors exist because of association (<s>samprayoga</s>)' is untenable. Why?
