That all <s>dharmas</s> operate singly (<s>ekacara</s>) will be explained later in detail. Therefore association does not exist. By this, [the statement] 'this mind operates singly' and so forth is also answered. Therein, it is not the similarity of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>sadharmatā</s>) that is denied — it is only the mental factors that are denied. Your statement 'mental factors exist because of the distinction in classification (<s>saṅgṛhītabheda</s>)' — the author of the <s>sūtra</s> established his own designations. In the <s>sūtra</s> of the Blessed One, the classification by characteristics is not stated. Therefore they do not exist. Your statement regarding the basis-and-dependent relationship (<s>āśrayāśrāyibhāva</s>) — just as in your view mind-consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) depends on mind, yet because of being the basis, it is not called a mental factor — so too mind depends on mind, and it does not acquire a different name. Your statement 'the five aggregates would not exist' — that is untenable. In my view, particular modifications of mind itself are called feeling, perception, and the rest. Just as in your view, mental factors are separately three aggregates. Your statement 'the mode of arising differs' — that too is untenable. If mind and mental factors arise simultaneously, why is it said 'mind arises from two, and mental factors from three'? One who asserts 'only mind exists' — for him, this same reasoning [applies]. Why? For he says: 'First is the moment of consciousness, afterwards [is the moment of] perception and the rest.' Your statement 'association, object, time-period, and cognition are differentiated' — that has already been refuted. Because association does not exist. Your statement 'knowledge as refuge, not

body.text: vijñānapratiśaraṇamiti | cittameva dvidhā vadāmi ekaṃ jñānamaparaṃ vijñānamiti | ato jñānapratiśaraṇaṃ citta[māśrayaṇīyaṃ] na vijñānapratiśaraṇam |
body.translated_text: consciousness as refuge' — I say that mind itself is twofold: one is knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), the other is consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). Therefore [the statement means] knowledge is to be relied upon as a refuge, [not] consciousness.

body.text: yadāha bhavān- bhagavān svayamāha ye cittaniśritāste caitasikā iti | cittotpanno dharmaścaitasika ityucyate | cittaṃ cittādutpannamiti caitasikamityākhyāyate | bhavānāha- bhagavānnāvocanna santi caitasikā iti | kintu vadāmi cittaviśeṣā eva caitasikā iti | yasya yuktirasti [tasya] anuktāpyuktā bhavati | evaṃ [yasya] yuktirnāsti | [tasya] uktāpi anukteva | na tena heturvaktavyaḥ | vakṣyāmaśca cittacaitāsikāḥ saṃjñārthā iti |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'The Blessed One himself said: Those that depend on mind are mental factors' — a <s>dharma</s> arisen from mind is called a mental factor. Mind is designated as a mental factor [because it is] arisen from mind. You have said: 'The Blessed One did not say that mental factors do not exist.' But I say: particular modifications of mind itself are mental factors. For one who has valid reasoning, even what is unstated becomes as if stated. Likewise, for one who lacks valid reasoning, even what is stated becomes as if unstated. Therefore one should not argue merely from that [basis]. And we shall state that mind and mental factors are [merely] designations of concepts (<s>saṃjñārtha</s>).

body.text: sañcinotīti cittam | vedanādayo 'pi sañcayanasabhāgatvāt cittameva | cittañca caitasikaiḥ saha cittādutpadyata iti caitasikamityucyate | caitasikamātramastīti yo vadati sa vadet caitasikadharmā arthākhyā iti | na vaktavyamidaṃ vastutaḥ | ato 'hetuḥ | yaduktaṃ bhavatā kāritrabhedāditi | citte vitarka udabhūditi ca | tadanena pratyuktam | kasmāt | mama cittaviśeṣatvādeva kāritraṃ bhidyate | citta utpannaṃ cittameva citte vitarka udabhūdityucyate | yadavādīḥ saṃkleśo vyavadānañca nirhetukaṃ syāditi | tadapyayuktam | asatyapi caitasike 'sti saṃkleśavyavadānam | ananyalakṣaṇatvācca na santi caitasikāḥ | kasmāt | bhavataścittasamprayuktatvāt caitasikā bhavanti | samprayogaśca nāstīti paścādvakṣyate | ato na santi cittādanye caitasikāḥ |
body.translated_text: 'That which accumulates (<s>sañcinoti</s>) is mind (<s>citta</s>).' Feeling and the rest too, being of a nature similar to accumulation, are mind itself. And mind, together with [what are called] mental factors, is called a mental factor because it arises from mind. One who says 'only mental factors exist' would say that the mental factor <s>dharmas</s> are [merely] conceptual designations (<s>arthākhyā</s>). This should not be said [to have] a real basis. Therefore it is not a [valid] reason. Your statement 'because of the difference of function' and 'in the mind, discursive thought arose' — that is answered by this: Why? In my view, it is precisely because [feeling and the rest] are particular modifications of mind that function is differentiated. [Discursive thought] arisen in mind is itself mind — [so the statement] 'in the mind, discursive thought arose' is said. Your statement 'defilement and purification would be without cause' — that too is untenable. Even without mental factors, there is defilement and purification. And because [mental factors] do not have a separate characteristic, mental factors do not exist. Why? In your view, mental factors exist because they are associated with mind (<s>cittasamprayukta</s>). But association does not exist — this will be stated later. Therefore mental factors separate from mind do not exist.

body.text: na caitasikasattāvargastriṣaṣṭhitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Existence of Mental Factors (<s>na caitasikasattāvarga</s>).

body.text: 64 caitasikanāstitāpradarśanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 64. Chapter on Demonstrating the Non-Existence of Mental Factors (<s>caitasikanāstitāpradarśanavarga</s>)

body.text: yadavocaḥ- lakṣaṇabhedāt santi caitasikā iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | vijñānasya buddhervā [anyeṣāṃ] sarveṣāṃ lakṣaṇādiṣu nāsti viśeṣaḥ | yaccittaṃ rūpaṃ vijānāti saiva buddhirityucyate, saṃjñā ityādyapi | yathā laukikā vadanti yadbhavān vijānātīmaṃ puruṣamiti tat jñānameva vedanā saṃjñā iti jñeyam | yadyeṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ pratiniyataṃ vailakṣaṇyamasti |
body.translated_text: Your statement 'mental factors exist because of the distinction of characteristics' — that is untenable. Why? Among the characteristics and the rest of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) or cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) or [other terms], there is no real distinction. That mind which cognizes form — that itself is called cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>), and so forth. As worldly people say: 'What you cognize about this person' — that knowledge itself should be understood as feeling, perception, and so forth. If these <s>dharmas</s> had a mutually fixed and distinct characteristic

body.text: [tad] abhidhātavyaṃ syāt | vastutastu nabhihitamityato nāsti vailakṣaṇyam | yaduktaṃ prajñā vimucyata iti | tadapyayuktam | hetvabhāvāt | cittavaśāt saṃkleśo 'vidyā cāsti | asmin cittaskandhe saṃkleśo 'vidyā ca sarvathā saṃprayuktā | yaduta avidyāmalinā prajñā saṃkleśamalinaṃ cittamiti | tannirhetukam | evamavidyāvisaṃyogātprajñā vimucyate | saṃkleśavisaṃyogāccittaṃ vimucyate ityapi nirhetukam | api cedaṃ sūtraṃ neyārthakam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- trividhāstravebhyaścittaṃ vimucyata iti | ato jñāyate avidyāto 'pi cittameva vimucyata iti | yaducyate saṃkleśebhyaścittavimuktirvihānam | avidyātaḥ prajñāvimuktiḥ prahāṇamiti | yadi ca saṃkleśebhyaścittaṃ vimucyate avidyātaḥ prajñā vimucyata iti | vyāpādibhyaḥ kiṃ vimucyata iti prativaktavyam | ataścittaṃ vinā na kiñcidvimucyata iti jñātavyam | ataścittamātramasti |
body.translated_text: it should be stated. But in reality it has not been stated — therefore there is no mutual distinction. Your statement 'wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) is liberated' — that too is untenable, because of the absence of a [valid] reason. Through the power of mind, defilement (<s>saṃkleśa</s>) and ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) exist. In this mind-aggregate, defilement and ignorance are associated in every way — namely, 'wisdom stained by ignorance' and 'mind stained by defilement.' That is without [separate] cause. Thus, 'through the disjoining from ignorance, wisdom is liberated' and 'through the disjoining from defilement, mind is liberated' — these too are without [separate] cause. Moreover, this <s>sūtra</s> is of provisional meaning (<s>neyārtha</s>). As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'From the threefold outflows (<s>āsrava</s>), the mind is liberated.' Therefore it is known that it is mind itself that is liberated from ignorance as well. When it is said: 'Liberation of mind from defilements is [mere] suppression (<s>vihāna</s>); liberation of wisdom from ignorance is abandonment (<s>prahāṇa</s>)' — if mind is liberated from defilements and wisdom is liberated from ignorance, then from what is ill-will (<s>vyāpāda</s>) and the rest liberated? This must be answered. Therefore it should be known that apart from mind, nothing is liberated. Therefore only mind exists.

body.text: yadāha bhavān cittasya prādhānyāccittamātramuktamiti | cittasya kaḥ pradhānabhāvo yannāsti prajñādīnām | yaduktaṃ laukikā bhūyasā cittameva vijānanti | ataścittamātramuktamiti | laukikā bhūyasā sukhaṃ duḥkhamapi vijānantīti vedanādayo '[pi] vaktavyāḥ | yadavādīḥ- anyārthavacanaṃ sūtramiti | kasmāccaitasikānanuktvā cittamātraṃ vakti | yadavādīḥ- ekadharmaṃ prajahītha [ityādi] | vacanasyāsya kāraṇamasti | bhagavān sattvānāṃ kleśatāratamyavaśātsadā viṣādākrāntacittaḥ san vadati ayameko dharma iti | asya prahāṇādanye 'pi svayaṃ prahīyante | iti | ato 'hetuḥ | yadavocaḥ- yaduktaṃ nāmalakṣaṇaṃ tadeva caitasikamiti | tat bhavataḥ svasaṃjñānusmaraṇavikalpa[mātram] | nemamarthaṃ sūtraṃ pratipādayati | yadi svasaṃjñānusmaraṇavikalpaṃ karoṣi | kiṃ nāttha nāmalakṣaṇena cittasyālambanamuktamiti | [yasya tu] nyāyaḥ sambhavati | yaduktaṃ sparśo vedanādicaitasikānāṃ hetūkriyata iti | vacanamidaṃ bahudhā duṣṭam | dharmāṇāṃ sasamprayogatve 'pi sparśa eva vedanādīnāṃ hetuḥ na vedanādayaḥ sparśasya | itīdṛśā doṣāḥ santi | ato jñāyate cittamātramasti | na pṛthak caitasikā iti ||
body.translated_text: Your statement 'because mind (<s>citta</s>) is predominant, only mind was mentioned' — what predominance does mind have that wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) and the rest do not? Your statement 'worldly people for the most part know only mind, therefore only mind was mentioned' — worldly people for the most part also know pleasure and pain, therefore feeling (<s>vedanā</s>) and the rest should also be stated. Your statement 'the <s>sūtra</s> speaks with a different intention' — why does it mention only mind without mentioning mental factors? Your citation 'abandon this one <s>dharma</s>' and so forth — there is a reason for this statement. The Blessed One, because of the gradation of defilements in beings, with a mind always afflicted by sorrow, says: 'This is one <s>dharma</s>.' Through the abandonment of this, the others too are abandoned by themselves. Therefore that is not a [valid] reason. Your statement 'what is stated as the name-characteristic (<s>nāmalakṣaṇa</s>) is itself the mental factor' — that is merely your own conceptual elaboration of recollected labels. The <s>sūtra</s> does not teach this meaning. If you make such a conceptual elaboration of recollected labels, why do you not take the name-characteristic as [merely] the object (<s>ālambana</s>) of mind? [Only for the one] whose reasoning is valid [may this be maintained]. Your statement 'contact (<s>sparśa</s>) is made the cause of mental factors such as feeling' — this statement is faulty in many ways. Even if <s>dharmas</s> are associated, contact alone is the cause of feeling and the rest — feeling and the rest are not causes of contact. Such are the faults. Therefore it is known that only mind exists. Mental factors do not exist separately.

body.text: caitasikanāstitāvargaścatuṣṣaṣṭitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Existence of Mental Factors (<s>caitasikanāstitāvarga</s>).

body.text: 65 samprayoganāstitāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 65. Chapter on the Non-Existence of Association (<s>samprayoganāstitāvarga</s>)

body.text: nāsti samprayogaḥ | kasmāt | caitasikadharmāṇāmabhāvāt kena cittaṃ samprayujyate | vedanādilakṣaṇānāṃ naikakālyaṃ śakyate | na ca kāryakāraṇayoryaugapadyamasti | vijñānaṃ saṃjñādīnāṃ hetuḥ | naiṣāṃ dharmāṇāmaikakālyaṃ yaugapadyaṃ vāsti | ato nāsti samprayogaḥ gambhīre pratītyasamutpāda[sūtre]bhagavānāha- asyotpādādidamutpadyata iti | yathā ca bījāṅkurakāṇḍanālapatrapuṣpādīni hetuphalābhyāṃ kramikāni dṛṣṭāni | ato bhavavijñādīnyapi kramikāṇyutpadyeran | yadbhavān manyate kāmādayaḥ kleśā rūpasya saha[bhū]hetavaḥ sahajāḥ syuriti | tadayuktam | na hi rūpaṃ pratyeti | anālambanatvāt | cittacaitasikānāmālambanamasti pratītiścāsti | ataste naikasmin kāle syuḥ sahabhuvaḥ | bahupratītyabhāvāt | ekakāyaścaikasattva ityākhyāyate | ekapratīteḥ | yadyekasmin kṣaṇe bahavaścaitasikāḥ syuḥ | tadā bahvyaḥ pratītayaḥ syuḥ | bahupratītisattvāt bahupuruṣātmakaḥ syāt | sa tu na sambhavati | ato naikasmin kṣaṇe vedanādayo bhavanti |
body.translated_text: Association (<s>samprayoga</s>) does not exist. Why? Because mental factor <s>dharmas</s> (<s>caitasikadharma</s>) do not exist — with what would mind be associated? The characteristics of feeling and the rest cannot be simultaneous. And there is no simultaneity of cause and effect. Consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is the cause of perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>) and the rest. These <s>dharmas</s> do not have simultaneity or co-occurrence. Therefore association does not exist. In the profound <s>sūtra</s> on dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>), the Blessed One said: 'From the arising of this, that arises.' And just as seed, sprout, stalk, stem, leaf, flower, and the rest are seen as successive through cause and effect — so too consciousness and the rest would arise successively. Your view that 'desire (<s>kāma</s>) and other defilements are co-arising causes (<s>sahabhūhetu</s>) of form, being co-arisen' — that is not valid. For form does not [actively] apprehend. Because it has no object (<s>anālambana</s>). Mind and mental factors have objects and [hence] apprehension. Therefore they would not be simultaneous, because of the absence of multiple apprehensions. A single body is called 'a single being' — because of a single apprehension. If at one moment there were many mental factors, then there would be many apprehensions. Because of many apprehensions, there would be a being consisting of many persons. But that is not possible. Therefore, at a single moment, feeling and the rest do not occur.

body.text: kasmātpunaḥ ṣaḍvijñānāni naikakālamutpadyante | (pṛ) vijñānāni kramikamālambanamapekṣya bhavanti | ato naikakālikāni | (u) kasya pratibandhādekaṃ kramikamālambanaṃ na kramaśaḥ ṣaḍvijñānānyutpādayati | jñātavyaṃ pūrvaṃ hetuḥ paścātkāryamiti kramaśa utpādaheturiti | sūtre coktam- cakṣuṣā rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā na nimittagrāhī bhavatīti | yannimittodgrahaṇaṃ tadeva saṃjñākarma | ato bhagavān vijñānakarmānūdya saṃjñākarma pratiṣedhati | ato jñātavyaṃ kasyacidvijñānamasti na saṃjñeti | yo nimittaṃ gṛhṇāti sa dṛṣṭvā gṛhṇāti na darśanakāle | ato jñāyate vijñānādīni kramikānīti | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- cakṣuṣā rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvānuprahṛṣṭacetano bhavati iti | atrāpi pūrvaṃ vijñānakarmoktaṃ paścādvedanādīni | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- dṛṣṭirdarśanamiti | ato jñāyate na sarvaṃ cittaṃ vedanādisamanvitamiti | pañcavijñānānāṃ lakṣaṇena cedaṃ spaṣṭaṃ bhavati | kasmāt | yaścakṣurvijñeye priyāpriyanimittaṃ sāmyanimittañca na gṛhṇāti | tasya
body.translated_text: Why then do the six consciousnesses not arise simultaneously? (Question) Consciousnesses arise depending on successive objects — therefore they are not simultaneous. (Answer) What prevents one successive object from producing the six consciousnesses sequentially? It should be known that the cause comes first and the effect comes afterward — therefore the cause of arising is sequential. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Having seen form with the eye, one should not grasp at signs (<s>nimitta</s>).' The grasping of signs is itself the function of perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>). Therefore the Blessed One, having stated the function of consciousness, prohibits the function of perception. From this it should be known that for some [beings], consciousness exists but not perception. One who grasps signs does so after having seen — not during the time of seeing. Therefore it is known that consciousness and the rest are sequential. Furthermore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Having seen form with the eye, one is delighted in mind.' Here too, the function of consciousness is stated first, then feeling and the rest. Furthermore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Seeing is view.' Therefore it is known that not every mind is accompanied by feeling and the rest. Through the characteristics of the five [sense-]consciousnesses, this becomes clear. Why? One whose eye-consciousness does not grasp the pleasant or unpleasant signs or the sign of indifference in what is to be cognized by the eye —

body.text: nāsti saṃjñā nāpi daurmanasyaṃ vā | vikalpābhāvāt | kecidāhuḥ tasyāpi kāmādayaḥ kleśā na santīti | ato jñāyate nāsti vitarka iti | paryeṣakānantarabhāvī vitarka ityucyate | tacca paścādvakṣyate | ato jñāyate pañcavijñānāmapi vitarko nāstīti | kiñca bhavataḥ pañca vijñānāni na vikalpakāni | tatra kathaṃ vitarkavicārābhyāṃ bhāvyam | cetanāvikalpaḥ pūrvarbhaudārikaḥ san pañcātsūkṣmo bhavatītyato vitarkavicāraustaḥ | yadi pañcavijñāneṣu vitarkavicārau staḥ | tadyathā vadasi mayi tava jñāpanāya prathamata evābhyūhādhīno vitarka utpadyata iti | tadā vitarkakālaḥ | asatyāṃ vijñāpanecchāyāṃ kathamasti vitarkaḥ |
body.translated_text: that one does not have perception, nor does he have dejection (<s>daurmanasya</s>) — because of the absence of conceptual discrimination (<s>vikalpa</s>). Some say that even for him, defilements such as desire do not exist. Therefore it is known that discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>) does not exist [in the five sense-consciousnesses]. <s>Vitarka</s> is defined as 'that which arises immediately following investigation (<s>paryeṣaka</s>).' This will be explained later. From this it is known that even in the five sense-consciousnesses, discursive thought does not exist. Furthermore, according to your [school], the five consciousnesses do not have conceptual discrimination (<s>vikalpa</s>). How then could they be accompanied by discursive thought (<s>vitarka</s>) and investigation (<s>vicāra</s>)? [You may say:] Volition (<s>cetanā</s>), initially gross without discrimination, becomes subtle from the five [sense-consciousnesses] — and therefore discursive thought and investigation exist [in them]. If discursive thought and investigation exist in the five consciousnesses, then as you say: 'For the purpose of informing you, in me, discursive thought first arises depending on deliberation' — that is the time of discursive thought. In the absence of the desire to inform, how could discursive thought exist?

body.text: kecidāhuḥ- pañcavijñāneṣu saṃjñāsti vitarka iti | sa ca vitarkaḥ saṃjñāmupādāyotpadyate | kathañca saṃjñākāle vitarko bhavati | ato 'bhyupeyaṃ pañca vijñānāni asaṃjñāni avitarkāni avicārāṇīti | kasmāt | na hi pañcavijñāneṣu strī puruṣa iti vikalpo 'sti | nāpi vedanādivikalpaḥ | kena tatra vikalpyate | pañcavijñānānāṃ nirvikalpakatvāt tadanantaraṃ manovijñānamutpadyata iti yuṣmābhiruktam | yadi pañcavijñāneṣu
body.translated_text: Some say: 'In the five consciousnesses, perception exists, which is discursive thought.' And that discursive thought arises depending on perception. But how could discursive thought occur at the time of perception? Therefore it must be accepted that the five consciousnesses are without perception, without discursive thought, and without investigation. Why? For in the five consciousnesses, there is no conceptual discrimination of 'woman' or 'man.' Nor is there the discrimination of feeling and the rest. By what then would there be discrimination? Because the five consciousnesses are non-discriminating (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>), you have said that immediately after them, mind-consciousness arises. If in the five consciousnesses

body.text: vikalpo 'sti | kimanantarotpadyamānena manovijñānena | vitarkavicārau ca naikasmin kṣaṇe syātām | audārakasūkṣmayorvirodhāt | ghaṇṭābhighātavat | ādyaśabdo vitarka [kalpaḥ] | antyaśabdo vicāra [kalpaḥ] | sa dārṣṭāntiko 'pyevam | yadi pañcavijñāneṣu vitarkavicārau staḥ | tayoḥ karma vaktavyam | na vaktuṃ vastutaḥ sambhavati | [ato] jñātavyaṃ cittacaitasikāḥ kramikā iti | avidyā prajñā ca viruddhe na yugapatsyātām | kathamekasmin kṣaṇe jñānamajñānañca bhavet | nahyekasmin citte saṃśayasya prasaṅgo 'sti | kasmāt | sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti naikasmin citte samudācarati | cittavyāpārasyedṛśasāmarthyābhāvāt |
body.translated_text: there is conceptual discrimination — what need is there for the mind-consciousness that arises immediately after? And discursive thought and investigation cannot be simultaneous — because of the opposition between the gross and the subtle. It is like the striking of a bell: the initial sound is comparable to discursive thought; the final sound is comparable to investigation. The illustrative example is just so. If discursive thought and investigation exist in the five consciousnesses, their function must be stated. In reality it cannot be stated. Therefore it should be known that mind and mental factors are sequential. Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), being opposed, would not be simultaneous. How could knowledge and ignorance exist at a single moment? For in a single mind, doubt cannot arise. Why? 'Is it a post or a person?' — this does not occur in a single mind, because a single mind does not have the capacity for such dual operation.

body.text: kaścidāha- caitasike smaraṇamatītādhvasañcaraṇam iti | pratyutpannālambanaṃ cittaṃ kathaṃ [tathā] bhaviṣyati | ayaṃ puruṣo mama jñāto māmupakṛtavāniti yat smaraṇam, smṛtvā ca prītijananam tata kathamekasmin citte syāt | icchānicchā ca kathamekasmin citte bhavet | yathoktaṃ sūtre- yo bhikṣava ātmadharmābhirataḥ, tasya dharmo vardhate | yo 'nabhirataḥ tasya dharmo hīyata iti | tat kathamekasmin citte bhaviṣyati | yadyekasmin citte caitasiko 'sti | tadā dharmo vyāmohaḥ syāt | kasmāt | ekasminneva hi citte 'sti jñānamajñānaṃ saṃśayo niścayaḥ śraddhāśraddhā vīryaṃ kausīdyamityevamādyā doṣāḥ | sarve ca caitasikā ekasmina citte pariniṣṭhitāḥ syuḥ | kasya pratibandhāt sukhaṃ dukhaṃ rāgo dveṣa ityādayo na bhavantyekasmin citte | yadyāha bhavān sukhaduḥkhādayo virodhānnaikasmin citte vartanta iti | jñānājñānādayo 'pi mitho virodhānnaikasmin citte varteran | ato nāsti samprayogaḥ |
body.translated_text: Someone says: 'A mental factor is the traversing of the past time-period through recollection.' How could mind, which has a present object, be like that? The recollection 'This person is known to me; he benefited me,' and the generation of delight upon recollecting — how could that be in a single mind? And desire (<s>icchā</s>) and aversion (<s>nicchā</s>) — how could they be in a single mind? As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'O monks, one who delights in self-<s>dharma</s> — for him, <s>dharma</s> increases. One who does not delight — for him, <s>dharma</s> diminishes.' How could that be in a single mind? If mental factors exist in a single mind, then the <s>Dharma</s> would be confused. Why? In a single mind there would be knowledge and ignorance, doubt and certainty, faith and faithlessness, energy and laziness — such faults would arise. All mental factors would be fully established in a single mind. What prevents pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, and the like from occurring in a single mind? If you say: 'Pleasure and pain and the rest do not occur in a single mind because of mutual opposition' — knowledge and ignorance and the rest too, being mutually opposed, would not occur in a single mind. Therefore association does not exist.

body.text: saptasambodhyaṅgasūtre ca bhagavatā caitasikadharmāṇāṃ kramikatvamuktam | "yo bhikṣuścaturṣu smṛtyupasthāneṣu carati ca smṛtisambodhyaṅgaṃ bhāvayati | smṛtau cittaṃ dharmān pravicinoti | dharmāṇāṃ pravicayādviryamārabhate | vīryabalātkuśaladharmān sañcinoti | cittasya vimalā prītirbhavati | prītyā cittaṃ praśrabhyati | praśrabdhyā cittaṃ parigṛhṇāti | cittaparigrahātsamādadhāti | samāhitatvāt rāgadaurmanasyābhyāmupekṣate | upekṣāyāṃ prajānāti" iti caitasikāḥ kramikā bhavanti | aṣṭāṅgikamārgasūtre 'pi krama uktaḥ | yaḥ samyak dṛṣṭiṃ
body.translated_text: In the <s>sūtra</s> on the seven factors of awakening (<s>saptasambodhyaṅga</s>), the Blessed One stated the sequential nature of mental factor <s>dharmas</s>: 'A monk who practices the four foundations of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>) cultivates the mindfulness factor of awakening. When the mind, [established] in mindfulness, investigates <s>dharmas</s> — through the investigation of <s>dharmas</s>, he arouses energy (<s>vīrya</s>). Through the power of energy, he accumulates wholesome <s>dharmas</s>. Stainless joy (<s>prīti</s>) arises in the mind. Through joy, the mind becomes tranquil (<s>praśrabdhi</s>). Through tranquility, the mind becomes collected (<s>parigṛhṇāti</s>). Through the collection of mind, it becomes concentrated (<s>samādhi</s>). Through concentration, one regards with equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>), [free from] passion and dejection. In equanimity, one knows.' Thus mental factors are sequential. In the <s>sūtra</s> on the Noble Eightfold Path too, a sequence is stated: One who obtains right view (<s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s>)

body.text: labhate | sa samyak dṛṣṭyā samyak saṅkalpamutpādayati | yāvatsamyak samādhim | anukramasūtre ca bhagavānāhānandam | śīladharaḥ puruṣo na kaukṛtyabhāvāya cittaṃ praṇidadhāti | śīladharasya puruṣasya cittadharmaḥ kaukṛtyaviratiḥ | kaukṛtyavihīno na tuṣṭilābhāya cittaṃ praṇidadhīta | kaukṛtyavihīnasya cittasya dharmastuṣṭiḥ syāt | tuṣṭasya cittaṃ prīṇāti | prītamanasaḥ kāyaḥ praśrabhyati | kāyapraśrabdhau sukhaṃ vedayate | sukhavedanāyāṃ cittaṃ samādadhāti | cittasamādhāne tattvaṃ prajānāti | tattvavinnirvidyate | nirviṇṇo vimucyate | iti | ato jñāyate caitasikāḥ kramikā iti | aṣṭamahāpuruṣavitarke 'pi krama uktaḥ | yo bhikṣuralpeccho viharati sa santuṣṭo bhavati | santuṣṭaḥ pravivikto bhavati | pravivikto vīryamārabhate | vīryamārabhamāṇaḥ samyaksmṛto bhavati | samyaksmṛtaḥ samāhito bhavati | samāhitaḥ prajñāvān niṣprapañco bhavati | iti | saptaviśuddhāvapi krama uktaḥ | śīlaviśuddhiryāvadeva cittaviśuddhyarthā | cittaviśuddhiryāvadeva dṛṣṭiviśuddhyarthā | dṛṣṭiviśuddhiryāvadeva kāṃkṣāvitaraṇaviśuddhyarthā | kāṃkṣāvitaraṇaviśuddhiryāvadeva mārgāmārgajñānadarśanaviśuddhyarthā | mārgāmārgajñānadarśanaviśuddhiryāvadeva pratipadājñānadarśanaviśuddhayarthā | pratipadājñānadarśanaviśuddhiryāvadeva pratipadāprahāṇajñānadarśanaviśuddhayarthā iti | nidānasūtre 'pi krama uktaḥ | cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpañca mohabhāgīyāvilā smṛtirbhavati | tatra moho 'vidyaiva | mūḍhasya yā prārthanā sā tṛṣṇā | tṛṣṇārtasya yadabhisaṃskaraṇaṃ tatkarma | ityevamādi | mahānidānasūtre 'pi krama ucyate | tṛṣṇāśiraskā nava dharmā [uktāḥ] | tṛṣṇāṃ pratītya paryeṣaṇā | paryeṣaṇāṃ pratītya lābhaḥ | lābhaṃ pratītya viniścayaḥ | viniścayaṃ pratītya chandarāgaḥ | chandarāgaṃ pratītya adhyavasānam | adhyavasānaṃ pratītya parigrahaḥ | parigrahaṃ pratītya mātsaryam | mātsaryaṃ pratītya ārakṣā | ārakṣāṃ pratītya daṇḍādānaśasrādānakalahavigrahavivādāḥ sarve duḥkhopāyāsādayaḥ sambhavanti | iti | srota āpannadharme 'pi krama uktaḥ | satpuruṣaṃ
body.translated_text: generates right intention (<s>samyaksaṅkalpa</s>) through right view, up to right concentration (<s>samyaksamādhi</s>). In the <s>sūtra</s> on sequential [development] too, the Blessed One said to <s>Ānanda</s>: 'A person who maintains moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>) does not apply his mind for the purpose of [generating] remorse (<s>kaukṛtya</s>). For the person who maintains moral conduct, the nature of his mind is freedom from remorse. One freed from remorse does not apply his mind for the purpose of obtaining satisfaction (<s>tuṣṭi</s>). For the mind of one freed from remorse, its nature is satisfaction. When satisfied, the mind becomes joyful (<s>prīṇāti</s>). For one of joyful mind, the body becomes tranquil. In bodily tranquility, one experiences pleasure (<s>sukha</s>). In the experience of pleasant feeling, the mind becomes concentrated. In concentration of mind, one knows reality (<s>tattva</s>). Knowing reality, one becomes disenchanted (<s>nirvidyate</s>). Being disenchanted, one is liberated.' Therefore it is known that mental factors are sequential. In the [sūtra on the] eight reflections of a great person too, a sequence is stated: 'A monk who dwells with few desires is content. Being content, he becomes secluded. Being secluded, he arouses energy. Arousing energy, he becomes rightly mindful. Being rightly mindful, he becomes concentrated. Being concentrated, he becomes wise and free from proliferations (<s>niṣprapañca</s>).' In the seven purifications (<s>saptaviśuddhi</s>) too, a sequence is stated: 'The purification of moral conduct is for the purpose of the purification of mind. The purification of mind is for the purpose of the purification of view. The purification of view is for the purpose of the purification of the overcoming of doubt. The purification of the overcoming of doubt is for the purpose of the purification of the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path. The purification of the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path is for the purpose of the purification of the knowledge and vision of the course of practice. The purification of the knowledge and vision of the course of practice is for the purpose of the purification of the knowledge and vision of the abandonment through the course of practice.' In the <s>Nidānasūtra</s> too, a sequence is stated: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, defiled and turbid mindfulness belonging to the portion of delusion arises. Therein, delusion is ignorance itself. The longing of one who is deluded — that is craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>). The volitional fashioning of one afflicted by craving — that is <s>karma</s>.' And so forth. In the <s>Mahānidānasūtra</s> too, a sequence is stated: 'Nine <s>dharmas</s> headed by craving [are stated]: Dependent on craving, seeking arises. Dependent on seeking, gain arises. Dependent on gain, determination arises. Dependent on determination, desire-and-passion (<s>chandarāga</s>) arises. Dependent on desire-and-passion, resolve arises. Dependent on resolve, appropriation arises. Dependent on appropriation, miserliness arises. Dependent on miserliness, guarding arises. Dependent on guarding, quarrels, disputes, contentions, rod-taking, weapon-taking, and all sufferings and distresses arise.' In the <s>dharma</s> of the stream-enterer (<s>srotāpanna</s>) too, a sequence is stated: 'A good person

body.text: sevamānaḥ saddharmaṃ śṛṇoti | saddharmaṃ śṛṇvan samyaksmṛtimutpādayati | samyaksmṛtipratyayāṃ mārgapratipattimabhyasyati | iti | uktañca sūtre- cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpañca cakṣurvijñānamutpadyate | trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | cittacaittā ekakālikā iti vadatastrayāṇāṃ sannipāto nāsti | ekaikaśa utpadyanta iti vadatastu asti trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ | ityādikāraṇai rnāsti samprayogaḥ |
body.translated_text: — attending upon [a good person], one hears the true <s>Dharma</s>. Hearing the true <s>Dharma</s>, one generates right mindfulness (<s>samyaksmṛti</s>). Conditioned by right mindfulness, one practices the path (<s>mārgapratipatti</s>). And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Dependent on the eye and form, eye-consciousness arises. The conjunction of the three is contact (<s>sparśa</s>).' For those who say that mind and mental factors (<s>cittacaitta</s>) are simultaneous, there is no conjunction of three. But for those who say they arise one by one, there is the conjunction of three. For these and other reasons, there is no association (<s>samprayoga</s>).

body.text: samprayoganāstitāvargaḥ pañcaṣaṣṭitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Existence of Association (<s>samprayoganāstitāvarga</s>).

body.text: 66 samprayogāstitāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 66. Chapter on the Existence of Association (<s>samprayogāstitāvarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) asti samprayogaḥ | kasmāt yaḥ paśyati sa vedayata ayamātmeti | vijñānacittaṃ tamāśrayate | tena samprayuktatvāt | tathā saṃjñāskandhādayo 'pi | yadi nāsti samprayogaḥ kimadhīno 'yaṃ syāt | puruṣasūtra uktam- cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpañca cakṣurvijñānamutpadyate | trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśaḥ | tatsahajā vedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskārādaya iti | asmin mate vividhaṃ nāmāsti yaduta sattvo devo manuṣyaḥ strī puruṣo mahānalpa iti | evamādīni nāmāni sarvāṇi skandhān pratītya bhavanti | yadi cittacaitasikāḥ kramikāḥ tadā skandhadvayaṃ pratītya puruṣo bhavet na skandhapañcakam | kasmāt | nātītānāgataskandhān prati puruṣaḥ sambhavati | bhavānāha- pratyutpanne na santi pañcaskandhāḥ iti | kathamucyeta pañcaskandhān pratītya devamanuṣyādayo bhavantīti | ucyate tu sarvaskandhān pratītya na skandhadvayamātram | ataḥ pañcaskandhān pratītya sattva ityākhyā |
body.translated_text: (Objection) Association exists. Why? Because the one who sees is the same as the one who feels — this is the self. Consciousness-mind relies upon that [self]. Because it is associated with that [self]. Likewise with the perception aggregate (<s>saṃjñāskandha</s>) and the others. If association does not exist, on what would this [consciousness] depend? In the <s>Puruṣa-sūtra</s> it is stated: 'Dependent on the eye and form, eye-consciousness arises. The conjunction of the three is contact. Co-born with that are feeling (<s>vedanā</s>), perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>), formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and the rest.' In this view, there are various names, such as: 'being,' 'god,' 'human,' 'woman,' 'man,' 'great,' 'small,' and so forth. All such names come into being dependent on the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>). If mind and mental factors are sequential, then a 'person' would arise dependent on only two aggregates, not on five. Why? Because a person does not come into being with respect to past and future aggregates. You say: 'In the present, five aggregates do not exist.' Then how could it be said that gods, humans, and the rest come into being dependent on the five aggregates? But it is stated that [they arise] dependent on all the aggregates, not on merely two. Therefore, dependent on the five aggregates, there is the designation 'being.'

body.text: asti ca sūtre samprayogo yadutendriyajñānasamprayuktā śraddhā iti | api coktaṃ sūtre- sparśo vedanāsaṃjñāvitarkaiḥ sahaja iti | api coktaṃ- pañcāṅgikaṃ prathamadhyānamiti | āha ca- vedanādayo vijñānasthitaya iti | yadi vijñānasamprayuktam |
body.translated_text: And in the <s>sūtra</s> there is association, as in: 'Faith associated with the faculties and knowledge.' It is also stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Contact is co-born with feeling, perception, and applied thought (<s>vitarka</s>).' It is also stated: 'The first <s>dhyāna</s> has five factors.' And he said: 'Feeling and the rest are the stations of consciousness (<s>vijñānasthiti</s>).' If [feeling is] associated with consciousness —

body.text: kathaṃ vijñānasthitiṣu vedanādiṣu sthitamidaṃ niśrayate tiṣṭhatīti | kasmāt | nahyucyate vijñānameva vijñānasthitiriti | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- caitasikadharmāścittajāścittaniśritā iti | āha ca- sattvānāṃ cittaṃ dīrgharātraṃ rāgadveṣādisaṃkliṣṭamiti | yadi samprayogo nāsti | kiṃ saṃkleśayati cittam | caitasikāśca prakṛtito dandhā anyonyāśrayamavalambante naḍakalāpavat | api coktaṃ sūtre- yasmin samaye cittamuddhataṃ bhavati | akālastrayāṇāṃ bodhyaṅgānām yaduta dharmapravicayabodhyaṅgasya vīryabodhyaṅgasya prītibodhyaṅgasya | [tatkasya hetoḥ |] uddhataṃ cittaṃ durupaśamaṃ bhavati | [yasmin samaye cittamuddhataṃ bhavati] kālastrayāṇāṃ bodhyaṅgānāṃ bhāvanāyai yaduta praśrabdhisambodhyaṅgasya samādhisambodhyaṅgasya upekṣāsambodhyaṅgasya | [tatkasya hetoḥ uddhataṃ cittamebhirdharmaiḥ] sūpaśamaṃ bhavati | yasmin samaye cittaṃ līnaṃ bhavati | akāla[stasmin samaye] trayāṇāṃ sambodhyaṅgānāṃ yaduta praśrabdhisambodhyaṅgasya samādhisambodhyaṅgasya upekṣāsambodhyaṅgasya | [tatkasya hetoḥ | līnaṃ cittaṃ tadebhirdharmai]rdussamutthāpyaṃ bhavati | [yasmin samaye cittaṃ līnaṃ bhavati |] kāla[stasmin samaye] trayāṇāṃ sambodhyaṅgānāṃ yaduta dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅgasya vīryasaṃmbodhyaṅgasya prītisambodhyaṅgasya | [tatkasya hetoḥ | līnaṃ cittaṃ tadebhirdharmaiḥ] susamuddhāpyaṃ bhavati | iti | ābhidharmikā āhuḥ- ekakālaṃ bhāvanānuyogamanuyuktasya bodhi[pakṣikā] dharmā na viyujyanta iti | ato jñāyate 'sti samprayoga iti ||
body.translated_text: — how is it understood that [consciousness], stationed in the stations of consciousness such as feeling and the rest, abides depending on them? Why? Because it is not said: 'Consciousness itself is the station of consciousness.' Moreover, it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Mental factors (<s>caitasikadharma</s>) are born of mind and depend on mind.' And he said: 'The mind of beings has been defiled by passion (<s>rāga</s>), hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>), and the like for a long time.' If association does not exist, what defiles the mind? Mental factors are by nature sluggish and lean upon each other, like a bundle of reeds. Moreover, it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'At the time when the mind is agitated (<s>uddhata</s>), it is not the right time for the three factors of awakening — namely, the investigation-of-<s>dharmas</s> factor of awakening (<s>dharmapravicayabodhyaṅga</s>), the vigor factor of awakening (<s>vīryabodhyaṅga</s>), and the joy factor of awakening (<s>prītibodhyaṅga</s>). [Why?] Because an agitated mind is difficult to pacify. [At the time when the mind is agitated,] it is the right time for the cultivation of three factors of awakening — namely, the tranquility factor of awakening (<s>praśrabdhisambodhyaṅga</s>), the concentration factor of awakening (<s>samādhisambodhyaṅga</s>), and the equanimity factor of awakening (<s>upekṣāsambodhyaṅga</s>). [Why?] Because an agitated mind is easily pacified by these <s>dharmas</s>. At the time when the mind is sluggish (<s>līna</s>), it is not the right time for the three factors of awakening — namely, the tranquility factor, the concentration factor, and the equanimity factor. [Why?] Because a sluggish mind is difficult to rouse by these <s>dharmas</s>. [At the time when the mind is sluggish,] it is the right time for the three factors of awakening — namely, the investigation-of-<s>dharmas</s> factor, the vigor factor, and the joy factor. [Why?] Because a sluggish mind is easily roused by these <s>dharmas</s>.' The <s>Ābhidhārmikas</s> say: 'For one who is engaged in cultivation at one and the same time, the factors conducive to awakening (<s>bodhipakṣika dharma</s>) are not dissociated.' Therefore it is known that association exists.

body.text: samprayogāstitāvargaḥ ṣaṭṣaṣṭhitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Existence of Association (<s>samprayogāstitāvarga</s>).

body.text: 67 nāstisamprayogavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 67. Chapter on the Non-Existence of Association (<s>nāstisamprayogavarga</s>)

body.text: yaduktaṃ bhavatā- yaḥ paśyati sa vedayate sa ātmeti | tadayuktam | pṛthagjanā mūḍhā mṛṣādṛṣṭimimāmutpādayanti | na vibhajanti vedaneyamidaṃ vijñānaṃ niśrayata iti | yadi te vibhajanti praveśayeyurapi śūnyatām | te cittasantatiṃ dṛṣṭvā avibhajanto vyavahāramātrāsaṅgāttathā
body.translated_text: What you said — 'the one who sees is the same as the one who feels — this is the self' — that is untenable. Deluded ordinary beings (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) generate this false view. They do not discriminate: 'This is feeling, this consciousness depends on it.' If they did discriminate, they would also enter into emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>). They, seeing the continuity of mind, without discriminating, and merely clinging to convention, speak thus —

body.text: vadanti | mūḍhānāṃ vyavahāro na śraddheyaḥ | yadavocaḥ- sarvān skandhān pratītya puruṣo bhavatīti | tatra pañcaskandhānāṃ santatiṃ pratītya puruṣa ityataḥ sarveṣāṃ skandhānāṃ vacanam | yathā loke vadanti- sukhī duḥkhī aduḥkhāsukhīti | naikasmin kāle sambhavanti tisro vedanāḥ | tathā skandhā api | yabdravīṣi- indriyajñānasamprayuktā śraddhā iti | sūtre coktam- anyaiḥ samprayuktamiti | yathocyate- dvau bhikṣāvekatra samprayuktau | iti | āhuśca dveṣasamprayuktaṃ duḥkham | snehaviyuktaṃ duḥkhamiti | bhavatāṃ [mate] rūpaṃ viprayuktamapi saṃvṛttyā samprayuktamityucyate | jñānaśraddhe apyevam | śraddhā yā anityatādi śraddadhate | jñānañca yathāpratīti jñānam | ubhayamekaṃ sādhayatīti samprayuktamityucyate | yadbhavānāha- sparśādvedanādayaḥ sahajā iti | tadayuktam | loke hi kiñcidvastu alpaviruddhamapi sahacaramityucyate | yathā vadanti śiṣyeṇa saha caratīti | yathā ca vadanti rājā mānthātā smṛtimātreṇa svargamāruroheti | tannaiva yujyate | pṛthagjanānāṃ vijñānasyālambanakriyāyāṃ catvāro dharmāḥ kramikā bhavanti- vijñānānantarajā saṃjñā, saṃjñānantarajā vedanā, vedanānantarajā cetanā, cetanā[nantarajāḥ] saumanasyadaurmanasyādayaḥ | tata utpadyante rāgadveṣamohāḥ | ata ucyate sahaivotpadyanta iti |
body.translated_text: — they speak. The convention of the deluded should not be believed. Your statement that 'a person comes into being dependent on all the aggregates' — therein, dependent on the continuity of the five aggregates, [one says] 'person.' Therefore the statement refers to all the aggregates. Just as in the world they say: 'Happy, suffering, or neither-happy-nor-suffering.' The three feelings do not exist at one and the same time. So too with the aggregates. As for your statement: 'Faith associated with faculty-knowledge' — in the <s>sūtra</s> too it is said 'associated with others.' Just as it is said: 'Two monks are associated (<s>samprayukta</s>) at one place.' And they say: 'Suffering is associated with hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>). Suffering is disjoined from affection (<s>sneha</s>).' In your [own] view, even form, though dissociated [from mind], is conventionally called 'associated.' Knowledge and faith are similar — faith is that which has faith in impermanence and so forth. Knowledge is the knowledge of things as they truly are. Because both accomplish one [goal], they are called 'associated.' Your statement that 'feeling and the rest are co-born with contact' — that is untenable. For in the world, even something slightly concordant is called 'accompanying.' Just as they say: 'He walks together with his disciple.' And just as they say: 'King <s>Māndhātā</s> ascended to heaven by mere recollection' — that too does not actually hold. For ordinary beings, in the object-apprehending activity of consciousness, four <s>dharmas</s> arise sequentially: perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>) born immediately after consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), feeling (<s>vedanā</s>) born immediately after perception, volition (<s>cetanā</s>) born immediately after feeling, and then from volition arise pleasurable states (<s>saumanasya</s>), displeasure (<s>daurmanasya</s>), and the like. From those arise passion (<s>rāga</s>), hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>). Therefore it is said that they arise together.

body.text: yaduktaṃ bhavatā- pañcāṅgikaṃ prathamaṃ dhyānamiti | asyāṃ dhyānabhūmau santi tāni pañcāṅgāni | natvaikakālikāni | yathā kāmadhātau tisro vedanāḥ | kasmāt | pūrvokta dharmāṇāmeva paścādbhūmiḥ kathyate | vitarkavicārau ca na saṃprayuktāviti pūrvameva pratyuktam | yadavocaḥ- vijñānasthitaya iti | tatsūtra uktā vijñānasya pratyaya[rūpā] sthitiḥ na niśrayarūpā | kenedaṃ jñāyate | tasminneva hi sūtra uktam- vijñānaṃ rūpaṃ pratītya snehapramodābhyāṃ tiṣṭhati | iti | yadyupyuktaṃ bhavatā- yadi vijñānaṃ vijñānaṃ pratītya tiṣṭhati | tadā pañca vijñānāni sthitayaḥ syuriti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | vijñaptikāle kiñcidvijānāti | vijñātasya citte vedanādaya utpadyante | tatra tṛṣṇodbhavati udbhūtatṛṣṇāpratyayaṃ vijñānaṃ vijñānasthiti rityucyate | ato nocyate vijñānameva vijñānasthitiriti | saptavijñānasthitisūtramidaṃ
body.translated_text: Your statement that 'the first <s>dhyāna</s> has five factors' — in that <s>dhyāna</s> ground, those five factors exist, but they are not simultaneous. Just as the three feelings [exist] in the desire-realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>). Why? Because the ground [of meditation] is stated only for the <s>dharmas</s> previously mentioned. And that applied thought (<s>vitarka</s>) and sustained thought (<s>vicāra</s>) are not associated [with mind simultaneously] has already been answered previously. Your statement about 'the stations of consciousness' — the station spoken of in that <s>sūtra</s> is in the form of a condition for consciousness, not in the form of a support. How is this known? In that very <s>sūtra</s> it is stated: 'Consciousness abides in form by means of attachment (<s>sneha</s>) and delight (<s>pramoda</s>).' If [feeling were] associated with consciousness —

body.text: cintyam | māstu yathārutagrahaṇamiti | śraddhayoghaṃ tarati iti yathā vadanti | tadaparinivaṣṭhitaṃ canam | vastutastu prajñayoghaṃ tarati | idamapi tathā syāt |
body.translated_text: — this should be examined. One should not grasp the literal meaning. Just as they say: 'One crosses [the flood] by the vehicle of faith.' That [statement] is not fully established. But in reality, one crosses by the vehicle of wisdom. This [statement about stations of consciousness] may be similar.

body.text: yaduktaṃ bhavatā- caittāścittāniśritā iti | tadayuktma | pūrvaṃ hi cittaṃ vijānāti | atha saṃjñādayo bhavanti | uktaṃ hi sūtre- vedanādayaścittaniśritā iti | na kuḍyā śritacitravadime caitasikāścittaniśritā ityucyante | yadavocaḥ- caitasikā anyonyaniśritā naḍakalāpavaditi | tadanyasūtraviruddham || yadi samaṃ prayogaḥ, kasmāt caitasikāścittaniśritāḥ | na tu cittaṃ caitasikaniśritam | yadi bravīṣi cittaṃ pūrvamutpadyate tanmahimnā caitasikānāmāśraya iti | tadā sidhyedasmadarthaḥ | nahi citta utpadyamāne caitasikadharmāḥ santi | yadbravīṣi cittaṃ kleśasaṃkliṣṭamityato jñāyate 'smi samprayoga iti | neyaṃ mārganītiḥ | yadi cittaṃ prāk pariśuddhaṃ rāgādibhirāgantukairdūṣitam | tadā sa eva pariśuddhadharmā dūṣyo bhavatīti dharmalakṣaṇaṃ bādhyeta |
body.translated_text: Your statement that 'mental factors are born of mind and depend on mind' — that is untenable. For mind first cognizes. Then perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>) and the rest arise. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Feeling and the rest depend on mind.' The mental factors do not depend on mind like a painting on a wall. Your statement that 'mental factors lean upon each other like a bundle of reeds' — that contradicts other <s>sūtras</s>. If association is equal [between them], why are mental factors said to depend on mind, while mind is not said to depend on mental factors? If you say 'mind arises first, and by its power it is the support for mental factors' — then our meaning is established. For when mind arises, the mental factors do not [yet] exist. Your statement that 'mind is defiled by defilements' — this is not the correct method. If the mind is originally pure (<s>prakṛtipariśuddha</s>) and is corrupted by adventitious defilements (<s>āgantukamala</s>) such as passion and the rest, then that very pure <s>dharma</s> would become corruptible — and the characteristic of <s>Dharma</s> would be violated.

body.text: yathā ca pūrvamuktam- cittaṃ prakṛtipariśuddhamāgantukamalairapakliṣṭamiti | tadidaṃ prativaktavyam | yadi cittaṃ prakṛtipariśuddham | rāgādibhiḥ kiṃ kriyate | yathoktam- citta- saṃkleśāt sattvāḥ sakliśyanti | cittavyavadānātsattvā viśudhyanti iti | tathā ca sattvā api samprayuktāḥ syuḥ | yadi sattvā api samprayuktāḥ syuḥ | yadi sattvā asamprayojyāḥ | rāgādayo 'pi asamprayojyāḥ syuḥ | santatyā dhāvati citte saṃkliṣṭādicittamutpadyate | santānānāṃ dūṣaṇameva saṃkliṣṭacittamityucyate | yaducyate saṃkleśāccittaṃ vimucyata iti | tat cittasantatau yadviśuddhacittamutpadyate | tadvimuktamityucyate | idameva yuktam | yathābhratuṣārādayaścandrasūryābhyāmasamprayuktā api pidhānaṃ kurvantīti [pravādaḥ] | tathā rāgādayo 'pi cittenāsamprayuktā api saṃkleśayantīti [vadanti] | dhūmābhramihikādayaścandrasūryau pidadhatīti pidhānaṃ kathyate | tathā rāgādayo 'pi viśuddhacittamāvṛṇvantīti āvaraṇaṃ bhavati |
body.translated_text: As was said before: 'The mind is pure by nature; it is afflicted by adventitious impurities.' This should be addressed. If the mind is pure by nature, what do passion and the rest do [to it]? As stated: 'Through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled. Through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.' If so, then beings too would be associated [with defilements]. If beings are not subject to association [with defilements], then passion and the rest also should not be subject to association. As the mind runs in continuity, a defiled mind arises [after an undefiled mind]. The corruption of the continuity itself is called 'defiled mind.' When it is said 'the mind is liberated from defilement' — that means that in the continuity of mind, a pure mind arises — that is called 'liberated.' This alone is correct. Just as clouds, frost, and the like, though not associated with the sun and moon, create an obstruction — so too, passion and the rest, though not associated with the mind, [are said to] defile it. Just as smoke, clouds, mist, and the like obstruct the sun and moon — that is called 'obstruction.' Likewise, passion and the rest, obscuring the pure mind, create an obscuration (<s>āvaraṇa</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) abhratuṣārau candrasūryau caikakālikau | saṃkleśacitte tu naivam | ato nāyaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ | (u) āvaraṇasāmyādayaṃ siddha ityato 'navadyam | saṃkleśo 'yaṃ cittasantānaṃ saṃkleśayatīti saṃkleśa ityucyate | caitasikāścittajāścittaniśritā iti yat bhavato vacanaṃ tatpūrvameva pratyuktam | yadavocaḥ- cittacaitasikāḥ prakṛtidandhā iti | tatpratikṣaṇavināśitvāt
body.translated_text: (Objection) Clouds and frost are simultaneous with the sun and moon. But in the case of the defiled mind, it is not so. Therefore this is not a valid analogy. (Reply) Because of the similarity of obstruction, this is established — therefore it is blameless. This defilement defiles the continuity of mind — therefore it is called 'defilement.' Your statement that 'mental factors are born of mind and depend on mind' — that has already been answered previously. Your statement that 'mind and mental factors are sluggish by nature' — because they perish every moment —

body.text: dandha ityucyate | na tu sāhāyyāya mitha ālambane samudācarantīti | ye parasparasahakāriṇaḥ te kañcitkālaṃ tiṣṭheyuḥ | na tu vastuto dṛśyate parasparasahakāritābalam | [ataḥ]kiṃ samprayogeṇa |
body.translated_text: — they are called 'sluggish.' But they do not mutually operate on each other's objects for the purpose of assistance. Those that are mutually cooperative would endure for some time. But in reality, the power of mutual cooperation is not observed. Therefore, what is the use of association?

body.text: bhavato yabdodhyaṅgakālavacanam | tat trīṇi bodhyaṅgāni yathākālaṃ bhāvayedityuktam | natvekasminneva kṣaṇe | yathāha śāriputraḥ saptasambodhyaṅgeṣu ahaṃ svatantravihārī | yasmin cittamuddhataṃ bhavati | tasmin samaye praśrabdhyādīni trīṇi bodhyaṅgāni bhāvayāmīti | bhagavānapi sambodhyaṅgānāmanukramamabocat | yadāha bhavān- aikakālikī sambodhyaṅgānāṃ bhāvaneti | tadayuktam | yadyaikakālikī, saptatriṃśabdodhipakṣikāṇāṃ bhāvanā | tadekakālaṃ bhāvayet dve śraddhe pañcasmṛtyādīn | yanmanyase yathāprāptisthānaṃ [kiñcit] bhāvayatīti | sa evā[nyasya] bhāvanāviyogaḥ | dvayo dhyānādivadanyalabdhavaśāttu aviyoga ucyate | yat saptatriṃśabdodhipakṣikāṇāmekakālaṃ bhāvaneti | na sa mārganayaḥ | kasmāt | nahyekadā bahavo dharmā bhāvayituṃ śakyante |
body.translated_text: Your statement about the timely cultivation of the factors of awakening (<s>bodhyaṅga</s>) — it was said that 'one should cultivate the three factors of awakening at the proper time,' but not in a single moment. As <s>Śāriputra</s> said: 'With regard to the seven factors of perfect awakening, I am an independent dweller. When the mind is agitated, at that time I cultivate the three factors of awakening beginning with tranquility (<s>praśrabdhi</s>).' And the Blessed One too taught the sequential order of the factors of awakening. Your statement 'the cultivation of the factors of awakening is simultaneous' is untenable. If it were simultaneous, the cultivation of the thirty-seven aids to awakening (<s>bodhipakṣika</s>) — one would simultaneously cultivate two kinds of faith and five kinds of mindfulness, and so forth. Your thought that 'one cultivates whatever [factor] one has attained at a given stage' — that itself is the non-separation from the cultivation of another. But it is said to be non-separation because of having obtained the other, just as in the case of two <s>dhyānas</s> and the like. The statement that 'the cultivation of the thirty-seven aids to awakening is simultaneous' — that is not the method of the path. Why? Because one cannot cultivate many <s>dharmas</s> at once.

body.text: nāsti samprayogavargaḥ saptaṣaṣṭitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Existence of Association (<s>nāsti samprayogavarga</s>).

body.text: 68 cittabahutvavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 68. Chapter on the Multiplicity of Consciousness (<s>cittabahutvavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) ājñātaṃ na santi pṛthak caitasikāḥ nāsti ca samprayoga iti | taccittamidānīṃ kimekam uta bahu | kecidvadanti- ekameva cittamutpattivaśādbahu iti | (u) cittaṃ bahu | kasmāt | vijñānameva cittamityucyate | rūpavijñānamanyat gandhādivijñānañcānyat | ato bahūni cittāni | cakṣurvijñānamālokākāśādipratyayānapekṣya anyadevotpadyate | na tathā śrotravijñānam | trayāṇāṃ vijñānaṃ vijñānaviṣayāṇāṃ prāptyotpadyate | manovijñānantu bahupratyayebhya utpadyate | ato jñāyate naikamiti | yadvijñānaṃ nityamityevaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ viṣayaṃ vijānāti | tat kathaṃ viṣayāntaraṃ vijānīyāt | yadi bahūni cittānyutpadyante |
body.translated_text: (Question) It is now understood that there are no separate mental factors (<s>caitasika</s>) and that there is no association. Is that consciousness now one or many? Some say: 'It is one consciousness that becomes many through the force of arising.' (Answer) Consciousness is many. Why? Consciousness itself is called 'mind' (<s>citta</s>). The consciousness of form is one thing and the consciousness of smell and the rest is another. Therefore there are many minds. Eye-consciousness arises differently, depending on conditions such as light, space, and the rest. Ear-consciousness is not like that. The consciousness of three [faculties: nose, tongue, body] arises from the contact of consciousness and its objects. But mind-consciousness arises from many conditions. Therefore it is known that it is not one. If consciousness, being permanent, cognized an object with a single characteristic, how could it cognize a different object? If many minds arise

body.text: tadā jñātuṃ śaknuvanti | yathā jñānaṃ samyak mithyā cānyat | jñānañca niścitaṃ sandigdhaṃ, kuśalamakuśalamavyākṛtaṃ vā sarvamanyadeva | kuśale ca dhyānasamādhivimuktayaḥ catvāryapramāṇāni ṛddhayabhijñādayo 'nye [dharmāḥ] | akuśale ca rāgadveṣamohādayo 'nye | avyākṛte cātītānāgatādayo 'nye | kiñcidvijñānaṃ kāyikavācikakarmasamutthāpakam | kiñcicceryāpathasamutthāpakam | saṃyogato viyogato vā hetusamanantarālambanādhipatīnāṃ pratyekaṃ viśeṣāccittāni bhidyante | viśuddhāviśuddhādivedanānāṃ viśeṣācca cittaṃ bhidyate | kāritraviśeṣācca cittaṃ bhidyate | viśuddhamaviśuddhañca cittaṃ prakṛtitaḥ pratyekaṃ bhidyate | yaccittaṃ prakṛtitaḥ pariśuddhaṃ na tatsaṃkliṣṭam | yathā sūryaraśmiḥ prakṛtito viśuddhā na kadāciddūṣyā bhavati | yat prakṛtito 'viśuddhaṃ na tat viśodhayituṃ śakyate | yathā roma prakṛtitaḥ kṛṣṇaṃ nāvadātaṃ kartumarhati | dānādau vastuto viśuddhaṃ cittamasti | hiṃsādau cāviśuddhaṃ cittam | ato naikaṃ bhavet | sukhaduḥkhādivedanānāṃ vibhāgavaśācca cittamapi naikam | yathocyate bhikṣurvijñānamupabhuṅkte keṣāṃ vijñānaṃ yaduta sukhaduḥkhāduḥkhāsukhānāṃ vijñānam | yadi cittamekam, ekameva vijñānaṃ sarvaviṣayān gṛhṇīyāt | bahucittavādinastu yathendriyaṃ vijñānamutpadyate | ato na sarvaviṣayān gṛhṇīyāt | yadi cittamekam | kasya pratibandhānna sarvaviṣayān gṛhṇāti | ato jñāyate cittaṃ bahu iti |
body.translated_text: then they are able to know. Just as right knowledge and wrong knowledge are different; certain and doubtful knowledge, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [knowledge] — all are different. And within the wholesome, the <s>dhyānas</s>, <s>samādhis</s>, liberations, four immeasurables (<s>apramāṇa</s>), supernatural powers (<s>ṛddhi</s>), higher knowledges (<s>abhijñā</s>), and other <s>dharmas</s> are different. Within the unwholesome, passion (<s>rāga</s>), hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>), delusion (<s>moha</s>), and the rest are different. Within the indeterminate, past, future, and the rest are different. A certain consciousness initiates bodily and vocal <s>karma</s>. Another initiates deportment. Through conjunction and disjunction, and through the individual distinctions of causal, immediately preceding, object, and dominant conditions, minds are differentiated. Through the distinctions of feelings — purified, unpurified, and the rest — mind is differentiated. Through the distinction of function, mind is differentiated. Purified and unpurified mind is differentiated by nature. The mind that is by nature purified is not defiled — just as the rays of the sun are by nature pure and are never corrupted. That which is by nature unpurified cannot be purified — just as hair is by nature dark and cannot be made white. In giving and the rest, there is truly purified mind. In harming and the rest, there is unpurified mind. Therefore [mind] cannot be one. Through the division of feelings such as pleasure, pain, and the rest, mind too is not one. As it is said: 'A monk experiences consciousness — whose consciousness? Namely, the consciousness of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.' If mind were one, a single consciousness would grasp all objects. But for one who holds that there are many minds, consciousness arises according to the sense faculty — therefore it would not grasp all objects. If mind were one, by what obstruction would it not grasp all objects? Therefore it is known that mind is many.

body.text: grāhyabhedādgrāhakamapi bhidyate | yathā kaścitkadācitsvacittaṃ vedayate | kathaṃ svaṃ rūpamātmānaṃ vedayate | yathā cakṣurnātmānaṃ paśyati | asirnātmānaṃ chinatti | aṅgulirnātmānaṃ spṛśati | ataścittaṃ naikam | yathā markaṭopasūtra uktam- yathā markaṭaḥ [araṇya upavane caramāṇaḥ] śākhāṃ gṛhṇāti | tā muktvānyāṃ gṛhṇāti | evameva cittaṃ [rātryā divasasya ca] atyayena anyadevotpadyata anyannirudhyate | iti | yadi cittamekam | ṣaḍvijñānakāyā iti vacanaṃ praṇaṣṭaṃ syāt | sūtre 'pyuktam- kāyaḥ kadāciddaśavarṣāṇyapi tiṣṭhate | yat citta- [mityucyate tat rātryāśca divasasya] atyayena anyadevotpadyate 'nyannirudhyata iti | āha ca- cittamanityasthāyīti bhavitavyam | taccittaṃ santatyā vartate | na pratikṣaṇaṃ chidyate | yathā caikaṃ karma [kṛtaṃ] na punarādeyaṃ bhavati | evaṃ vijñānamapi nālambane
body.translated_text: Because of the differentiation of what is grasped, the grasper too is differentiated. Just as someone sometimes experiences his own mind. How does one's own form experience itself? Just as the eye does not see itself, and a sword does not cut itself, and a finger does not touch itself — therefore mind is not one. As stated in the Monkey <s>Sūtra</s>: 'Just as a monkey, [roaming in a forest or grove,] grasps a branch and, releasing it, grasps another — so too mind, [with the passing of night and day,] arises as one thing and ceases as another.' If mind were one, the statement 'there are six bodies of consciousness (<s>vijñānakāya</s>)' would be destroyed. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The body sometimes lasts even ten years. But what is called mind, [with the passing of night and day,] arises as one thing and ceases as another.' And it is said: 'Mind is impermanent and unstable.' That mind exists as a continuous series (<s>santati</s>) — it is not cut off at every moment. Just as a single <s>karma</s>, once done, cannot be taken up again — so too consciousness does not persist with attachment to an object

body.text: sādaraṃ vartate | tṛṇāgnirnendhane saṅkrāmati | tathā cakṣurvijñānaṃ na śrotraṃ prāpnoti | ato cittaṃ bahu iti ||
body.translated_text: . A grass-fire does not transfer to fuel. Likewise, eye-consciousness does not reach the ear. Therefore mind is many.

body.text: cittabahutvavargaḥ aṣṭaṣaṣṭitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Multiplicity of Consciousness (<s>cittabahutvavarga</s>).

body.text: 69 cittaikatvavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 69. Chapter on the Unity of Consciousness (<s>cittaikatvavarga</s>)

body.text: kaściccodayati- cittamekam | kasmāt | yathoktaṃ sūtre- cittamidaṃ dīrgharātraṃ kāmādibhirupakliṣṭamiti | yadi cittaṃ nānā, na sadopakliṣṭaṃ syāt | ratnahārasūtra uktam- yaścittaṃ sadā śraddhayā śīlena tyāgena śrutena prajñayā ca bhāvayati sa mṛto deveṣūtpadyate iti | dhyānasūtre coktam- prathamadhyānalābhī cittasya paridamanāya prathamadhyānādvitīyadhyānamupasampadya viharati | iti | cittavarge coktam-
body.translated_text: Someone raises [the objection]: Consciousness is one. Why? As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'This mind has been afflicted by desire and the rest for a long time (<s>dīrgharātra</s>).' If mind were manifold, it would not always be afflicted. In the <s>Ratnahārasūtra</s> (Sūtra of the Jewel Necklace) it is said: 'One who constantly cultivates the mind with faith, moral conduct, generosity, learning, and wisdom — upon death, he is reborn among the gods.' And in the <s>Dhyānasūtra</s> (Sūtra on Meditation) it is said: 'One who has attained the first <s>dhyāna</s>, for the taming of the mind, enters into and abides in the second <s>dhyāna</s> from the first <s>dhyāna</s>.' And in the Chapter on the Mind it is said:

body.text:
matsyo yathā sthale kṣipta [okamokata uddhṛtaḥ] |
parispandatīdaṃ cittaṃ māradheyaṃ prahāpayet || iti |
body.translated_text:
Just as a fish, thrown upon dry land, [drawn from its watery home,]
this mind flounders — one should abandon the domain of <s>Māra</s>.

body.text: ato jñāyate cittamekaṃ cañcalamitastato dhāvatīti | saṃyuktapiṭake ca bhikṣurāha-
body.translated_text: From this it is known that mind is one and restless, running here and there. And in the <s>Saṃyuktapiṭaka</s> (Connected Discourses), a monk said:

body.text:
markaṭaḥ pañcadvārāyāṃ kuṭikāyāṃ pasakkiya |
dvāreṇānuparīyāti ghaṭayaṃśca muhurmuhuḥ |
body.translated_text:
Like a monkey entering a hut with five doors,
he goes around door after door, striking again and again.

children.text: tiṣṭha markaṭa mā [dhāvī]rna hi te tat yathā purā |
children.translated_text: Stop, monkey, do not run! It is not for you as it was before.
You are restrained by wisdom; you will not go far.

body.text: ato jñāyate- cittamekaṃ pañcendriyadvāreṣu kāyakuṭikāyāṃ paribhramati | saiva tatprakṛtiḥ | ata āha "mā [dhāvī]rna hi te tat yathāpurā" | iti | āha ca-
body.translated_text: From this it is known that mind is one — it wanders through the five doors of the sense faculties in the hut of the body. Its nature is just that. Therefore he said: 'Do not run! It is not for you as it was before.' And it is said:

body.text:
cittametatsarvakālaṃ yathā dinakaraprabhā |
prajñāvān damayatyeva yathā hastinamaṅkuśam || iti |
body.translated_text:
This mind at all times is like the radiance of the sun.
The wise one tames it, just as [one tames] an elephant with a goad.

body.text: ato jñāyate cittamekamevālambaneṣvaṭatīti | kiñcātmābhāvāccittameva karmakṛtsyāt | ekameva hi cittaṃ karmāṇyabhinirvṛttya punarvipākaṃ vedayate | cittaṃ mriyate cittamutpadyate cittaṃ badhyate cittaṃ mucyate | pūrvānubhūtaṃ cittaṃ smarati | ato jñāyate cittamekamiti | cittamekaṃ sat sañcinoti [vāsanām] | kṣaṇikasya cittasya nāsti sañcayabalam | bhagavataḥ śāsane nāstyātmā | cittamekaṃ sat sattvalakṣaṇaṃ bhavati | yasya cittaṃ bahu | na tasya sattbalakṣaṇaṃ bhavati | dakṣiṇena cakṣuṣā dṛṣṭvā vāmena vijānāti | nahyanyat paśyati anyadvijānāti | ato jñāyate | cittamekamātmanā paśyati ātmanā vijānāti iti |
body.translated_text: From this it is known that a single mind roams among objects. Furthermore, because the self does not exist, mind itself is what performs all <s>karmas</s>. A single mind itself initiates <s>karmas</s> and again experiences their ripening (<s>vipāka</s>). Mind dies, mind is reborn, mind is bound, mind is liberated. Mind remembers what was previously experienced. Therefore it is known that mind is one. Being one, mind accumulates habitual tendencies (<s>vāsanā</s>). A momentary mind does not have the power of accumulation. In the teaching of the Blessed One, there is no self. Mind, being one, has the characteristic of being a sentient being (<s>sattva</s>). For one who holds that mind is many, there would be no characteristic of being a sentient being. Having seen with the right eye, one knows with the left. It is not the case that one sees [with one] and another knows [with the other]. Therefore it is known that mind is one — it sees by itself and knows by itself.

body.text: cittaikatvavarga ekonasaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the sixty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Unity of Consciousness (<s>cittaikatvavarga</s>).

body.text: 70 na cittabahutvavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 70. Chapter on the Non-Multiplicity of Consciousness (<s>na cittabahutvavarga</s>)

body.text: yadyapyuktaṃ bhavatā- rūpādīnāṃ vijñānamanyaditi | na yuktamidam | kasmāt | yadekaṃ cittaṃ tadeva rūpaśabdādigrahaṇarūpāṇi nānākarmāṇi karoti | yathaikaḥ puruṣaḥ pañcachidrake gṛhe sthitaḥ tatra tatra gatān viṣayān gṛhṇāti | tadeva cittaṃ cakṣuṣi lagnamālokadipratyayamapekṣya rūpaṃ paśyati | yathā sa eva puruṣa anyatra sahāyamapekṣya [aparaṃ] kāryaṃ karoti | tasyaiva cittasya vijñeyaṃ vibhaktaṃ bhavati | yathā sa eva pūrvaṃ jñānī san paścādajñānī bhavati | evaṃ mithyājñānaṃ punaḥ samyak jñānaṃ bhavati | yathā sa eva puruṣaḥ pūrvaṃ viśuddhaḥ paścādaviśuddho bhavati | evaṃ yat sandigdhaṃ jñānaṃ tadeva niścitaṃ jñānaṃ bhavati | yathā sa eva puruṣaḥ pūrvaṃ saṃśayitaḥ punarniścito bhavati | yadakuśalaṃ cittaṃ tadeva punaḥ kuśalamavyākṛtañca bhavati | yathā sa eva puruṣaḥ kadācitkuśalaṃ smarati | kadācidakuśalaṃ kadācidavyākṛtañca smarati |
body.translated_text: Although you said 'the consciousness of form and the rest is different' — this is not tenable. Why? One and the same mind performs various functions of grasping form, sound, and the rest. Just as a single person stationed in a house with five openings grasps the objects encountered at each opening. That same mind, attached to the eye and depending on conditions such as light and the rest, sees form. Just as that same person, in another situation, depends on an assistant and performs another task. That same mind's object of cognition is differentiated. Just as that same person, having been knowledgeable before, later becomes ignorant. Likewise, wrong knowledge again becomes right knowledge. Just as that same person, having been purified before, later becomes unpurified. Likewise, doubtful knowledge becomes certain knowledge. Just as that same person, having been uncertain before, later becomes certain. Unwholesome mind becomes wholesome and indeterminate. Just as that same person sometimes remembers what is wholesome, sometimes what is unwholesome, and sometimes what is indeterminate.

body.text: tadeva cittamatītānāgāmīryāpathaprabhedañca karoti | yathā sa eva puruṣo 'tītānāgatādau nāneryāpathān karoti | evaṃ viśuddhaṃ cittamevāviśuddhaṃ bhavati | aviśuddhameva viśuddhaṃ bhavati | yathā sa eva puruṣaḥ pūrvaṃ prasannaḥ paścādaprasanno bhavati | tadeva cittaṃ sukhasamprayuktaṃ paścādduḥkhasamprayuktaṃ bhavati | yathā sa eva puruṣaḥ pūrvamanyaṃ sukhayati paścātpunarduḥkhayati | ata ucyate cittamekaṃ bahukarmaṇe prabhavatīti |
body.translated_text: That same mind also produces the divisions of past, future, and different deportments. Just as that same person performs various deportments with respect to the past, future, and the rest. Likewise, purified mind itself becomes unpurified. And unpurified itself becomes purified. Just as that same person, having been pleased before, later becomes displeased. That same mind, having been associated with pleasure, later becomes associated with pain. Just as that same person, having first delighted another, later causes him pain. Therefore it is said that a single mind is capable of many functions.

body.text: yadavādīḥ- ekameva vijñānaṃ na ṣaḍvivaṣayān gṛhṇātīti | naikaṃ cittamiti | tadayuktam | mama tu indriyapravibhāgādvijñānaṃ pravibhajyate | yat vijñānaṃ cakṣuṣi lagnaṃ tat rūpamātraṃ gṛhṇāti | nānyaviṣayān | anyadapyevam | yadavocaḥ- grāhyabhedādgrāhakabheda iti | tadayuktam | cittadharmatā yadātmānaṃ vijānātīti | yathā pradīpa ātmānaṃ prakāśayati anyānapi prakāśayati | yathā gaṇaka ātmānaṃ gaṇayati anyānapi gaṇayati | evamekameva cittamātmānaṃ vijānāti anyānapi vijānāti | bhavatokto markaṭadṛṣṭānto 'yuktaḥ | yathā markaṭaḥ śākhāṃ gṛhṇāti tāṃ muttkāparāṃ gṛhṇāti | tathā cittamapi ekamālambanaṃ gṛhṇāti | tadutsṛjyāparaṃ gṛhṇāti | ato 'nyaduktameva [yat] svayameva karmābhinirvartayati, svayameva punarvipākaṃ vedayate iti saṃkṣipya pratyavocam | kasmāt | yadi cittamanyat, tadā anyatkaroti, anyadvedayate anyanmṛnmriyate anyajjāyata ityādayo doṣāḥ syuḥ | ato jñāyate cittamekamiti ||
body.translated_text: Your statement 'a single consciousness does not grasp six objects, therefore mind is not one' — that is untenable. In my view, because of the differentiation of sense faculties, consciousness is differentiated. The consciousness attached to the eye grasps form alone — it does not grasp other objects. The others are likewise. Your statement 'because of the differentiation of what is grasped, the grasper too is differentiated' — that is untenable. It is the nature of the mind-<s>dharma</s> that it knows itself. Just as a lamp illuminates itself and also illuminates others. Just as an accountant counts himself and also counts others. Likewise, a single mind knows itself and also knows others. Your monkey analogy is untenable. Just as a monkey grasps a branch and, releasing it, grasps another — so too mind grasps one object and, releasing it, grasps another. As to your other statement that 'it itself initiates <s>karma</s> and itself again experiences the ripening' — I have answered in summary. Why? If mind were different, then one would perform [the action] and another would experience [the result]; one would die and another would be born — and similar faults would arise. Therefore it is known that mind is one.

body.text: na cittabahutvavargaḥ saptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the seventieth chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Multiplicity of Consciousness (<s>na cittabahutvavarga</s>).

body.text: 71 na cittaikatvavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 71. Chapter on the Non-Unity of Consciousness (<s>na cittaikatvavarga</s>)

body.text: atrocyate | yadabravīḥ- cittamekaṃ kāmādinā ciramupakliṣṭam iti | tadayuktam |
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: Your statement 'mind is one and has been afflicted by desire and the rest for a long time' — that is untenable.

body.text: santanyamānacittasyaikaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ dṛśyate | yathā vadanti sandhyāvāt eva prabhātavātaḥ | adyatananadyeva pūrvanadī | [adya] rājasabhāpradīpa eva hyastanapradīpa iti | yathā dantaḥ punarjāta ityucyate | vastutastu pūrvadanto na purnajātaḥ | lakṣaṇasāmyena jātaḥ punarjāta
body.translated_text: The mind that is being continued appears to have a single characteristic. Just as they say: 'The evening breeze is the same as the morning breeze.' 'Today's river is the same as yesterday's river.' 'Today's lamp in the royal assembly hall is yesterday's lamp.' Just as they say: 'The tooth has grown back.' But in reality the former tooth did not grow back. Due to the similarity of characteristics, what has been born is said to have 'grown back.'

body.text: ityucyate | evaṃ cittamanyadapi santatyā cittamekamityucyate | yadavocaḥ- [pūrvānubhūtaṃ cittaṃ] smaratīti | puruṣaḥ kadācidātmanaiva pūrvacittaṃ smarati | yat pūrvacittaṃ tadidānīmāgatamiti kiṃ smṛtena | tenaiva cittena tadeva smaryata iti kathaṃ bhaviṣyati | nahyasti svātmavedakaṃ jñānamekam | ato naikaṃ cittam |
body.translated_text: — it is so called. Thus, though another mind [arises], by continuity it is called 'one mind.' As for what you have said — '[the prior mind] remembers [what was previously experienced]' — a person sometimes remembers his own prior mind. If that prior mind has now come [back], what need is there for memory? That by that very mind, that very [experience] is remembered — how could this be? For there is no single knowledge that is self-aware. Therefore mind is not one.

body.text: yabdravīṣi- [cittaṃ] sañcinotīti | yadi cittaṃ nityamekam | kaḥ sañcayenopakāraḥ | yadi cittaṃ bahu | tadā adharamadhyottamakramasantatyotpadyamānatvādasti sañcayaḥ | bhavatoktaṃ cittaṃ sattvalakṣaṇamiti | yadi cittamekam | tadeva nityaṃ bhavet | yannityam | sa evātmā syāt | kasmāt | idānīṃ kurvan paścātkariṣyan nitya eko 'vikārītyata ātmā bhavati | cittaviśeṣalakṣaṇānabhijñasya cittamekaṃ bhavati | pravāhavaccittaṃ santanyamānamekamiti vadanti | yathā taimirikaḥ keśakalāpamekaṃ paśyati | tadvivecakastu tadbhedaṃ vijānāti | yastu prajñāvān sa cittabhedaṃ vijānāti | kasmāt | brahmādayo vyāmohagatā evaṃ manyante kāyo 'yamanityaḥ cittaṃ vijñānantu nityam iti | yadi brahmādīnāmeva vyāmohaḥ | kaḥ punarvādo 'nyeṣāṃ nityeṣvāsaktānām | ataḥ kuśalacetanāpratyayasāmagrīsamutpanno dharmo nityaḥ syāt | tadviparītastu kṣayī |
body.translated_text: As for what you say — '[mind] accumulates (<s>sañcinoti</s>)' — if mind is permanent and one, what benefit is there in accumulation? If mind is many, then because it arises in a continuity of inferior, middling, and superior stages, there is accumulation. Your statement 'mind has the characteristic of a being (<s>sattva</s>)' — if mind is one, then that very [mind] would be permanent. What is permanent would be the self (<s>ātman</s>). Why? Because acting now and acting later, being permanent, one, and without modification — therefore it would be the self. For one who does not understand the distinctive characteristics of mind, the mind appears to be one. They say that mind, being continuous like a stream, is one. Just as one afflicted with cataracts (<s>taimirika</s>) sees a mass of hairs as one; but one who discriminates knows their distinctions. One who is endowed with wisdom knows the distinctions of mind. Why? <s>Brahmā</s> and others, being in a state of delusion, think: 'This body is impermanent, but mind, consciousness, is permanent.' If even <s>Brahmā</s> and others are deluded, what need to speak of other persons who are attached to permanence? Therefore, a <s>dharma</s> arisen from the assemblage of conditions of wholesome volition (<s>kuśalacetanā</s>) would be permanent. But what is contrary to that would be perishable.

body.text: yaduktaṃ bhavatā- dakṣiṇena dṛṣṭvā vāmena vijānīyāditi | tat jñānabalādanyatpaśyati anyadvijānāti | yathāyaṃ puruṣo granthaṃ racayati | anyaḥ puruṣo vijānāti | anāgatamajātamasadbhūtañcāryajñānabalena vijānāti | atītaṃ vastu asadapi smṛtvā vijānanti anāgatamasadapi [ārya]jñānabalādvijānanti | idaṃ paścāt savistaraṃ vakṣyate ||
body.translated_text: As for what you have said — 'Having seen with the right [eye], one knows with the left' — through the power of knowledge, one sees one thing and knows another. Just as this person composes a text and another person knows it. What is future, unborn, and non-existent is known through the power of noble knowledge (<s>āryajñāna</s>). They know past things, even non-existent, through memory; and they know future things, even non-existent, through the power of noble knowledge. This will be explained later in detail.

body.text: na cittaikatvavarga ekasaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the seventy-first chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Unity of Mind (<s>na cittaikatvavarga</s>).

body.text: 72 cittabahutvapradarśanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 72. Chapter on Demonstrating the Multiplicity of Mind (<s>cittabahutvapradarśanavarga</s>)

body.text: yadavocaḥ- cittamekaṃ bahukarmaṇe prabhavatīti | tadayuktama | kasmāt | samyak pratyāyakātmakaṃ hi cittam, rūpapratyāyanaṃ śabdapratyāyanādanyat | kathaṃ cittamekaṃ bhavati | yathā ghaṭaṃ dhatte hastakarma | na tadeva karmānyadvastu dhatte | tathā yena cittena rūpaṃ gṛhyate |
body.translated_text: As for what you have said — 'Mind, being one, is capable of many actions' — that is untenable. Why? Because mind has the nature of correct cognition (<s>samyak pratyāyaka</s>), and the cognition of form is other than the cognition of sound. How then can mind be one? Just as the action of the hand that holds a pot does not hold another thing with that same action — so too, the mind that grasps form

body.text: na tenaiva śabdaḥ śrūyate | cakṣurvijñānamidañca cakṣurāśrayīkṛtya rūpamālambanīkṛtya bhavati | tadubhayamanityaṃ kṣaṇikam | cakṣurvijñānaṃ kathamakṣaṇikam | yathā vinā vṛkṣaṃ na cchāyānvāste | evaṃ cakṣūrūpayoḥ kṣaṇikatvāt tadāśrityotpannaṃ vijñānamapi kṣaṇikam | kṣaṇikadharmasya nāsti gamanaśaktiḥ | manovarge ca pūrvaṃ bahudhā pratyuktameva | ato na mano gacchatīti |
body.translated_text: does not hear sound with that same [mind]. And this eye-consciousness arises having the eye as its basis and form as its object. Both of these are impermanent and momentary. How then can eye-consciousness be non-momentary? Just as without a tree, a shadow does not persist — so too, because the eye and form are momentary, consciousness arisen depending on them is also momentary. A momentary <s>dharma</s> does not have the power of going. And in the chapter on the mind, this has been refuted in many ways previously. Therefore the mind does not go.

body.text: yadavādiḥ- vijñānaṃ cakṣuṣi lagnaṃ sat ālokamapekṣya paśyati | yathā sa eva puruṣaḥ paśyati śṛṇoti ityādi | tadayuktam | kasmāt | śāstre 'smin dharmaṇāṃ vastutattvamanviṣyate | puruṣaḥ prajñaptisan na dṛṣṭānto bhavitumarhati | puruṣalakṣaṇañcānveṣṭavyam | pañcaskandhāḥ puruṣātmakā iti vadāmaḥ | saṃśayajñānādīni niścayajñānādibhyo 'nyāni na saṃśayajñānādīnyeva niścayajñānādīni ityapi vadāmaḥ | tathā sarvaṃ [vaktavyam] |
body.translated_text: As for what you have said — 'Consciousness, being attached to the eye, sees by depending on light — just as it is the same person who sees, hears, and so forth' — that is untenable. Why? In this treatise, the real nature of <s>dharmas</s> is being investigated. A person, being a mere designation (<s>prajñapti</s>), cannot serve as an illustration. And the characteristic of the person should be investigated. We say that the five aggregates (<s>pañcaskandha</s>) constitute the person. We also say that doubt-knowledge and the rest are different from certainty-knowledge and the rest — doubt-knowledge and the rest are not themselves certainty-knowledge and the rest. Everything should be stated likewise.
