body.text: yadavocaḥ- indriyapravibhāgādvijñānaṃ pravibhajyata iti | tadayuktam | indriyaṃ vijñānajananasya hetupratyayaḥ | yadi vijñānamekam | indriyaṃ kiṃ karoti | [yat] pradīpaṃ dṛṣṭāntatvena kalpayasi | nāyaṃ dṛṣṭānto yuktaḥ | yathā aprakāśitasya prakāśanaṃ karoti pradīpaḥ | na pradīpasvarūpaṃ prakāśayati | ato nātmānaṃ prakāśayati | pradīpenāndhakāre vinaṣṭe [viṣayeṣu] cakṣurvijñānamutpadyate | tadutpannaṃ sat pradīpamapi paśyati | ghaṭādi dravyamapi [paśyati] gaṇakastu ātmarūpamapi jānāti pararūpamapi jānāti | taducyate lakṣaṇajñānam |
body.translated_text: As for what you have said — 'By the division of sense-faculties, consciousness is divided' — that is untenable. The sense-faculty is a causal condition (<s>hetupratyaya</s>) for the production of consciousness. If consciousness is one, what does the sense-faculty do? Your illustration of the lamp is not appropriate. Just as the lamp illuminates what was not illuminated before, it does not illuminate its own form. Therefore it does not illuminate itself. When the lamp destroys darkness, eye-consciousness arises with respect to [visible] objects. That consciousness, having arisen, sees the lamp as well. It sees a pot and other objects as well. But a calculator knows both his own calculations and those of others. That is called characteristic-knowledge (<s>lakṣaṇajñāna</s>).

body.text: yadavocaḥ karmādi | tat karmādidūṣaṇe pratyuktam | ato nāsti sa doṣaḥ | yadi cittamekaṃ nityam | tadāsti karma nāsti vipākaḥ | kasmāt | sākṣāccittaṃ tadāśrita ñca karma bhavati | yadi cittamekam | kaḥ karmavipākaḥ | tathā bandhamokṣādirapi yadavādīḥ- anyat karoti anyadvedayata iti | tadapyayuktam | skandhānāṃ santāno naiko nānyaḥ | antadvayapātāpatteḥ | saṃvṛtisaṃjñayā karmādīnāṃ vacanaṃ na tu paramārthataḥ | ataḥ skandhasantāne so 'yam ityādisaṃjñāvyavahāra ityanavadyam | ato jñāyate cittaṃ bahviti ||
body.translated_text: As for what you have said regarding <s>karma</s> and the rest — that has been answered in the refutation of <s>karma</s> and the rest. Therefore that fault does not apply. If mind is one and permanent, then there would be <s>karma</s> but no ripening (<s>vipāka</s>). Why? Because <s>karma</s> would exist directly in mind and based on that mind. If mind is one, what ripening of <s>karma</s> would there be? Likewise with bondage and liberation and the rest. As for what you have said — 'One agent acts and another experiences' — that too is untenable. The continuity of the aggregates is neither one nor other. Because of the fallacy of falling into both extremes. The statement about <s>karma</s> and the rest is made using conventional designations (<s>saṃvṛtisaṃjñā</s>), not in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārtha</s>). Therefore, in the continuity of the aggregates, the conventional usage 'that is this' and the like is blameless. Therefore it is known that mind is many.

body.text: cittabahutvapradarśanavargo dvisaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the seventy-second chapter, the Chapter on Demonstrating the Multiplicity of Mind (<s>cittabahutvapradarśanavarga</s>).

body.text: 73 kiñcitkālasthāyivijñānavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 73. Chapter on Consciousness that Persists for Some Duration (<s>kiñcitkālasthāyivijñānavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) cittaṃ bahviti nirūpitam | idānīṃ tāni cittāni kiṃ kṣaṇikāni | uta kiñcitkālasthāyīni | kecidāhuḥ- kiñcitkālasthāyīnīti | kasmāt | rūpādīnāṃ pratyāyanāt | yat kṣaṇikaṃ na tat pratyāyayet | ato nāsthāyi bhavati | yadi kṣaṇikaṃ [cittaṃ] tadā rūpādīni na kadāpi pratīyeran | kasmāt | yathā vidyutprabhā kiñcitsthāyinyapi na punaḥ sujñeyā bhavati | kaḥ punarvādaḥ | kṣaṇikaṃ pratyāyayatīti | vastutastu pratyāyayati | ato jñāyate vijñānāni na kṣaṇikānīti | cakṣuḥ pratītya rūpañca cakṣurvijñāna[mutpadyate] ityanayorabhede vijñānamapyabhinnam | cittañca yugapadeva nīlādīni rūpāṇi gṛhṇāti | ato jñāyate 'kṣaṇikamiti |
body.translated_text: (Objection) It has been established that mind is many. Now, are those minds momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), or do they persist for some duration? Some say: 'They persist for some duration.' Why? Because they make objects known (<s>pratyāyana</s>). What is momentary could not make anything known. Therefore [mind] is not non-persisting. If mind were momentary, then forms and the rest would never be cognized. Why? Just as a flash of lightning, even though persisting for a moment, is not well-knowable. What more need be said [about] a momentary [mind] making things known? But in reality it does make things known. Therefore it is known that consciousness is not momentary. 'Depending on the eye and form, eye-consciousness [arises]' — since there is no difference between these two, consciousness too would be undifferentiated. And mind simultaneously grasps blue and other forms. Therefore it is known that it is not momentary.

body.text: yanmanyase- santānato 'dhyavasyatīti | tadapi na yuktam | yadyaikaikaṃ cittaṃ nādhyavasyati | santāno 'pi nādhyavasyet | yathaikasminnandhe rūpamapaśyati bahavo 'pi na paśyeyuḥ | yadi bravīṣi- yathaikastanturna hastinaṃ pratirundhe | bahavastu sañcitāḥ prabhavanti | tathaikaṃ cittaṃ nādhyavasyati | tatsantānastu adhyavasyati | iti | idamapyayuktam | ekaikasmin tantau pratyekamasti kiñcidvalam iti tatsamavāyaḥ prabhavati | cittasyaikasmin kṣaṇe nāsti kiñcitpratyāyakabalam | tasmātsantāno 'pi na pratyāyayet | vastutastu pratyāyayati | ato jñāyate 'kṣaṇikamiti | yadi cittaṃ kṣaṇikamiti | atītānāgatādikarmāṇi niṣprayojanāni syuḥ | kiñcitkālasthāyi tu saprayojanāni karoti | ato jñāyate 'kṣaṇikamiti | anityamapi kiñcitkālamavaśyaṃ tiṣṭhati ||
body.translated_text: If you think — 'Through continuity (<s>santāna</s>), it determines (<s>adhyavasyati</s>)' — that too is not correct. If each individual mind does not determine, a continuity too would not determine. Just as if a single blind person does not see form, many [blind persons] too would not see. If you say — 'Just as a single thread does not restrain an elephant, but many gathered together can; so too a single mind does not determine, but its continuity determines' — this too is untenable. In each individual thread there is some strength — and therefore their combination prevails. But in a single moment of mind there is no power of making things known at all. Therefore a continuity too would not make things known. But in reality it does make things known. Therefore it is known that it is not momentary. If mind were momentary, then past, future, and other actions would be purposeless. But [mind] that persists for some duration performs purposeful actions. Therefore it is known that it is not momentary. Even that which is impermanent necessarily persists for some duration.

body.text: kiñcitkālasthāyivijñānavargastrisaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the seventy-third chapter, the Chapter on Consciousness that Persists for Some Duration (<s>kiñcitkālasthāyivijñānavarga</s>).

body.text: 74 asthāyivijñānavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 74. Chapter on Non-Persisting Consciousness (<s>asthāyivijñānavarga</s>)

body.text: atra pratibrūmaḥ | yaduktaṃ bhavatā- cittaṃ pratyāyakamityato 'kṣaṇikamiti | tadayuktam | cittagatanimittānāṃ balāt [cittaṃ] pratyāyayati | na sthāyibalāt | tathā no cet śabdakarmaṇo na syātpratyāyanam | kasmāt | pratyakṣaṃ paśyāmaḥ khalvidaṃ kṣaṇikamatha ca pratyāyakamiti | ato jñāyate na sthāyitvātpratyāyatīti | samyak pratyayātmakaṃ hi cittam | yannīlaṃ pratyāyayati | na tadeva pītaṃ pratyāyayati | tasmānnīlapratyāyakaṃ kiñcitkālasthāyyapi na pītaṃ pratyāyayati | nīlapratyāyanakālo 'nyaḥ | anīlapratyāyanakālaścānyaḥ | naiko dharmo dvayoḥ kālayoḥ syāt | dharmaḥ kālasamanvitaḥ | kālaśca dharmasamanvitaḥ | graho dvividhaḥ adhyavasāyātmakaḥ anadhyavasāyatmaka iti | yadi vijñānamakṣaṇikam | sarvaṃ grāhyaṃ sākalyenādhyavasyet | mama tu bahuvijñānasantānavaśādutpanno graho 'dhyavasyati | alpasantāne tu nādhyavasyati | vijñānañca viṣayaṃ gṛhṇāti mandaṃ vā kṣipraṃ vā iti cittasya nāsti niyamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Here we reply: As for what you have said — 'Mind is not momentary because it makes things known' — that is untenable. Mind makes things known through the power of marks (<s>nimitta</s>) inherent in the mind, not through the power of persistence. If it were not so, there would be no making-known through the action of sound. Why? We directly perceive that this [sound-action] is momentary and yet it makes things known. Therefore it is known that it is not through persistence that [mind] makes things known. For mind has the nature of correct cognition (<s>samyak pratyaya</s>). That which makes blue known does not make yellow known with that same [mind]. Therefore, even what persists for some duration does not make yellow known while making blue known. The time of making blue known is one; the time of making non-blue known is another. A single <s>dharma</s> cannot be [in] two times. A <s>dharma</s> is conjoined with time, and time is conjoined with <s>dharma</s>. Grasping (<s>graha</s>) is twofold: with determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) and without determination. If consciousness were non-momentary, it would determine all graspable [objects] in their entirety. But for me, the grasping that arises from the force of the continuity of many consciousnesses determines; in a short continuity, it does not determine. And consciousness grasps objects either slowly or quickly — there is no fixed rule for the mind.

body.text: yaduktaṃ bhavatā- āśrayālambanayornāsti bheda iti | kṣaṇikatvāt rūpamāśrayālambanamapi bhinnamevetyarthaḥ sādhitaḥ | yadavādīḥ- yugapad gṛhṇātīti | vijñānaṃ sarvakāyāvayavagrāhakamityato yugapagdraha ityucyate | ato nāstyekaṃ vijñānaṃ sarvagrāhakam | kasmāt | apariniṣpannagrahameva cittamanunirudhyate | [ataḥ] kena labhyate sarvagrāhakaṃ cittamastīti | yadbravīṣi- karmakriyā niṣprayojaneti | tadayuktam | yathā pradīpaḥ kṣaṇiko 'pi prakāśanopayogī | vāyugatakarmāṇi kṣaṇavināśīnyapi padārthān kampayanti | tathā
body.translated_text: As for what you have said — 'There is no difference between the basis and the object' — because of momentariness, form as basis and as object is indeed different — this meaning has been established. As for what you have said — 'It grasps simultaneously' — because consciousness grasps all the parts of the body, it is said to grasp simultaneously. Therefore there is no single consciousness that grasps everything. Why? Consciousness, [with its] grasping still incomplete, ceases. Then how can one say 'there exists a consciousness that grasps everything'? As for what you say — 'The action of <s>karma</s> is purposeless' — that is untenable. Just as a lamp, though momentary, is useful for illumination. Actions in the course of wind, though perishing in a moment, cause objects to shake. Likewise

body.text: vijñānamapi | yathā pradīpādayaḥ kṣaṇikā api [padārtha]grahaṇasamarthā bhavanti | tathā vijñānaṃ kṣaṇikamapi [viṣaya]grahaṇasamarthaṃ bhavati |
body.translated_text: with consciousness too. Just as lamps and the like, though momentary, are capable of grasping objects — so too consciousness, though momentary, is capable of grasping objects.

body.text: atha cittamanovijñānāni kṣaṇikāni | kasmāt | nīlādīrūpasaṅghātaḥ purovartī san vijñānamāśūtpādayati | ato 'sthāyīti jñāyate | puruṣasya kadāciccittaṃ bhavati yadahamekakālaṃ sarvānalambanān gṛhṇāmīti | ato vijñānamasthāyi | yadi vijñānaṃ kiñcitkālaṃ tiṣṭhati | tadā puruṣasya na tadbhānticittamutpadyeta | kasmāt | bījasantānavat kiñcitkālāvasthāyitvāt | na tatra puruṣasya bhrānticittamutpadyate | yadaṅkurakāṇḍādīnyaikālikānīti | ato vijñānaṃ kṣaṇikamiti jñāyate | yo ghaṭaṃ paśyati tasyaiva ghaṭasmṛtirbhavati | darśanānantaraṃ smṛtirbhavatītyataḥ kṣaṇikam | yo vadati vijñānamakṣaṇikamiti | tasyaikameva jñānaṃ samyaṅ mithyā ca sambhavet | ayaṃ puruṣa iti graha eva ayaṃ na puruṣa iti graha iti yathā darśanaṃ bhavati | evaṃ saṃśayagraha eva niścayagrahaḥ syāt | tattu na sambhavati | ato jñāyate kṣaṇikamiti | vikalpādyanekapratyayagrahaṇāt kṣaṇikamiti jñāyate | śabdakarmasantānaśca kṣaṇikaḥ san tatra jñānamutpādayati | ato jñāyate cittaṃ kṣaṇikamiti ||
body.translated_text: Now, mind (<s>citta</s>), thought (<s>manas</s>), and consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) are momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>). Why? Because the aggregate of forms such as blue and the rest, being present before [the perceiver], produces consciousness quickly. Therefore it is known to be non-persisting. A person sometimes has the cognition: 'I grasp all objects at one time.' Therefore consciousness is non-persisting. If consciousness persisted for some duration, then such a mistaken cognition (<s>bhrānti</s>) would not arise in a person. Why? Because, like the continuity of a seed, it persists for some duration — no mistaken cognition arises there that sprout, stalk, and so forth are simultaneous. Therefore it is known that consciousness is momentary. He who sees a pot — in that very person the memory of the pot arises. Because the memory arises immediately after the seeing, [it is known to be] momentary. One who says that consciousness is non-momentary — for him, one and the same knowledge would be both correct and incorrect. Just as the grasping 'this is a person' and the grasping 'this is not a person' occur as if in seeing. Likewise, the grasping of doubt would itself be the grasping of certainty. But that is not possible. Therefore it is known that [consciousness is] momentary. Because of grasping through multiple conditions such as conceptualization (<s>vikalpa</s>) and the rest, it is known to be momentary. And the continuity of sound-action, being momentary, produces knowledge therein. Therefore it is known that mind is momentary.

body.text: asthāyivijñānavargaścatuḥsaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the seventy-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Non-Persisting Consciousness (<s>asthāyivijñānavarga</s>).

body.text: 75 vijñānayaugapadyavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 75. Chapter on the Simultaneity of Consciousnesses (<s>vijñānayaugapadyavarga</s>)

body.text: kaściccodayati | cittaṃ kṣaṇikamiti pratipāditam | idānīṃ vijñānāni kimaikakālikāni | uta kramikāṇi | kecidābhidharmikā vadanti- vijñānānyaikakālikānīti | kasmāt | kaścit sarvān viṣayānekakālaṃ gṛhṇāti | yathaiko ghaṭaṃ paśyan saṅgītadhvanimapi śṛṇoti | ghrāṇena kusumagandhaṃ jighrati | mukhena sagandharasaṃ kavalayati | vyajanavāyuḥ kāyaṃ spṛśati | cetanā ca samīkarotyapaśabdam | ato jñāyate sarvān viṣayānekakālaṃ gṛhṇātīti |
body.translated_text: Someone raises [this question]: It has been established that the mind is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>). Now, do the [types of] consciousness arise simultaneously (<s>aikakālika</s>) or sequentially (<s>kramika</s>)? Certain <s>Ābhidharmikas</s> say: 'The [types of] consciousness arise simultaneously.' Why? Because a certain person grasps all objects at one time. For example, one person, while seeing a pot, also hears the sound of music, smells the fragrance of flowers with the nose, chews food with flavor in the mouth, the fan-wind touches the body, and volition (<s>cetanā</s>) assembles [all these into awareness of] an incorrect utterance. Therefore it is known that one grasps all objects at one time.

body.text: yadyekameva vijñānaṃ kāye sarvasukhaduḥkhe vijānāti | tadā cākṣuṣavijñānenaikena sarvān vṛkṣān gṛhṇīyāt | tattu na sambhavati | katha[mekena] vijñānena mūlaśākhāpatrapuṣpāṇi
body.translated_text: If a single consciousness cognizes all pleasure and pain in the body, then a single visual consciousness would grasp all trees. But that is not possible. How could by a single consciousness the roots, branches, leaves, and flowers

body.text: sarvāṇi jñāyante | ato jñāyate bahūni vijñānāni yugapadekakālamutpannāni sarvān spraṣṭavyān gṛhṇanti iti | nānārūpāṇāṃ jñānamekakālamutpadyate | na tu [yat] nīlajñānam | tadeva pītajñānam | ato jñāyate ekakālaṃ yugapadutpadyante | vahūni vijñānānīti kāyāvayaveṣu ca śīghrataraṃ jñānamutpadyate | ekāvayavagrahaṇakāla eva sarvān gṛhṇāti | bhagavataḥ śāsane ca nāstyavayavī | na hi sambhavatyekameva vijñānaṃ sarvānavayavān gṛhṇātīti | ato ekakālamutpannāni bahūni vijñānāni sarvānavayavān gṛhṇantīti ||
body.translated_text: all be known? Therefore it is known that many consciousnesses, arising simultaneously at one time, grasp all tangibles. Knowledge of various forms arises at one time. But that which is the knowledge of blue is not the same as the knowledge of yellow. Therefore it is known that many consciousnesses arise simultaneously at one time. And in the parts of the body, knowledge arises extremely rapidly. In the very time of grasping one part, it grasps all. And in the teaching of the Blessed One, there is no 'possessor of parts' (<s>avayavin</s>). For it is not possible that a single consciousness grasps all the parts. Therefore many consciousnesses arising at one time grasp all the parts.

body.text: vijñānayaugapadyavargaḥ pañcasaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the seventy-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Simultaneity of Consciousnesses (<s>vijñānayaugapadyavarga</s>).

body.text: 76 vijñānāyaugapadyavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 76. Chapter on the Non-Simultaneity of Consciousnesses (<s>vijñānāyaugapadyavarga</s>)

body.text: atrocyate | yaducyate bhavatā- bahūni vijñānāni yugapadekakālamutpadyanta iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | vijñānaṃ manaskāramapekṣyotpadyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- cakṣuranupahataṃ bhavati | rūpamābhāsagataṃ bhavati | vijñānotpādako manaskāraśca yadi na bhavati | tadā na cakṣurvijñānamutpadyata iti | ato jñāyate vijñānāni manaskāramapekṣya bhavanti naikakālikānīti | sarve cotpattidharmāṇaḥ karmakāraṇādhīnāḥ | cittasyaikaikaśa utpatteḥ | na hi pṛthivīnarakādivipāka ekakālaṃ vedyate | yadi bahūni cittāni yugadutpadyante | tadā yugapadvedanā syāt | na vastutaḥ sambhavati | ato jñāyate vijñānāni naikakālikānīti | vijñānañca śīghrataramālambanaṃ gṛhṇāti | yathālātacakrasya pravṛttiśaighryānnadṛśyate tadvicchedaḥ | tathā vijñānānyapi kālalavasthāyitvānna vibhajyante | yadyaikakālikāni vijñānāni | sarveṣāmutpattidharmāṇāmekakālamekalakṣaṇaṃ yugapadutpattiḥ sambhavet | kaḥ pratibandho 'sti | tathā ca sarvadharmāṇāmutpattaye nāvaśyaṃ yatnaṃ kuryāt | karmākurvannapi
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: Your statement 'many consciousnesses arise simultaneously at one time' is untenable. Why? Consciousness arises in dependence on attention (<s>manaskāra</s>). As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The eye is unimpaired; the form has come into the field of appearance; and if the attention that generates consciousness is not present — then eye-consciousness does not arise.' Therefore it is known that consciousnesses arise in dependence on attention, not simultaneously. And all <s>dharmas</s> that arise are dependent on <s>karma</s> as cause. Because of the arising of mind one at a time — for the ripening of [rebirth in] earth-hells and the like is not experienced simultaneously. If many minds arose simultaneously, then there would be simultaneous feeling. But in reality this is not possible. Therefore it is known that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously. And consciousness grasps its object extremely rapidly. Just as the revolution of a firebrand — because of the speed of its motion, one does not see the break [between positions] — so too the consciousnesses, because of abiding for only a fraction of a moment, are not distinguished [from one another]. If consciousnesses were simultaneous, then for all <s>dharmas</s> that arise, simultaneous arising with a single characteristic would be possible — what obstruction would there be? In that case, for the arising of all <s>dharmas</s>, one would not necessarily need to make effort. Even without performing <s>karma</s>

body.text: mucyeta | na tu tatsambhavati | ato jñāyate vijñānāni naikakālikānīti | kāyaścittānucaraḥ | yadi sarvāṇi cittāni yugapadbhavanti | tadā kāyo vikṣipyeta | atītānāgatādicittānāmekakālamutpatteḥ | vastutastu kāyo na vikṣipyate | ato jñāyate na yugapadbhavanti sarvacittānīti | cakṣuṣā paśyāmaḥ khalu bāhyān bījāṅkurādīn kalamāṃsapeśyādirūpāṇi kaumārayauvanajarākārān kramikān | tathā cittamapi syāt |
body.translated_text: one would be liberated. But that is not possible. Therefore it is known that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously. And the body follows the mind. If all minds arose simultaneously, then the body would be distracted — because of the simultaneous arising of past, future, and other minds. But in reality the body is not distracted. Therefore it is known that all minds do not arise simultaneously. We see with the eye external [things like] seeds, sprouts, and the rest, flesh-masses and other forms, and the aspects of childhood, youth, and old age as sequential. So too should the mind be.

body.text: uktañca sūtre- yadā sukhā vedanā bhavati | tadā [anye] dve vedane niruddhe yaduta duḥkhā vedanā aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā ityādi | yadi vijñānānāṃ yugapadutpādaḥ tadā tisro vedanā ekakālaṃ vedyeran | na tu tadyujyante vastutaḥ | ato jñāyate vijñānāni naikakāla mutpadyanta iti | ekasmin kāya ekacittotpattyā ekaḥ puruṣa ityucyate | vijñānānāṃ yaugapadya ekasmin kāye bahavaḥ puruṣāḥ syuḥ | natvidaṃ yujyate | ata ekasmin kāye vijñānānāṃ yaugapadyaṃ na sambhavati | yaugapadye hi ekakālaṃ sarvān dharmān jānīyuḥ | kasmāt | cakṣuṣi tāvadapramāṇaśatasahasrāṇi vijñānāni bhavanti | evaṃ yāvanmanasyapi | tathā ca [tāni] sarvān dharmān vijānīyuḥ | na tu tadyujyate | ato vijñānāni naikakālikānīti jñāyate |
body.translated_text: And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'When pleasant feeling occurs, at that time the other two feelings have ceased — namely, painful feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,' and so forth. If the arising of consciousnesses were simultaneous, then the three feelings would be experienced at one time. But in reality this is not tenable. Therefore it is known that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously. Through the arising of one mind in one body, it is said 'one person.' If consciousnesses were simultaneous, in one body there would be many persons. But this is not tenable. Therefore the simultaneity of consciousnesses in one body is not possible. If [they were] simultaneous, one would know all <s>dharmas</s> at one time. Why? Because in the eye alone, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of consciousnesses exist. Likewise up to the mind as well. And [in that case, they] would cognize all <s>dharmas</s>. But this is not tenable. Therefore it is known that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.

body.text: (pṛ) kasmādvijñānānyavaśyaṃ kramikāṇi bhavanti | (u) ekaḥ samanantarapratyaya ityato vijñānamekaikamutpadyate | (pṛ) ekaḥ samanantarapratyaya iti kasmāt samyak | īdṛśī dharmatā syāt | tathā bhavatāme kasyātmana ekaṃ manaḥ | tathā mamāpi ekasya manasa ekaḥ samanantarapratyayaḥ | yathā bījasambandhī aṅkurastatsamanantaramutpadyeta | na kāṇḍādyutpādya aṅkuraḥ | evaṃ cittasambandhī dharmaścittakrameṇotpadyeta | nānyadharmotpatti [kramataḥ] | vijñānalakṣaṇaṃ tathā niyataṃ [yat] ekaikodayavyayakramalakṣaṇādhīnam agnilakṣaṇadāhavat | tasmādvijñānānyavaśyaṃ krameṇa bhavanti ||
body.translated_text: (Question) Why do consciousnesses necessarily arise sequentially? (Answer) Because the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>) is one [at a time] — therefore consciousness arises one at a time. (Question) Why is it correct that the immediately preceding condition is one [at a time]? (Answer) Such is the nature of things (<s>dharmatā</s>). Just as in your view, for one self there is one mind — so too for me, for one mind there is one immediately preceding condition. Just as a sprout connected with a seed arises immediately after it — not producing a stalk or the like [before the sprout] — so too, a <s>dharma</s> connected with mind arises in the sequence of mind — not [arising] from the sequence of the arising of another <s>dharma</s>. The characteristic of consciousness is so determined [that it is] governed by the characteristic of arising and ceasing one at a time — just as the burning characteristic of fire. Therefore consciousnesses necessarily arise sequentially.

body.text: vijñānāyaugapadyavargaḥ ṣaṭsaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the seventy-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Non-Simultaneity of Consciousnesses (<s>vijñānāyaugapadyavarga</s>).

body.text: 77 duḥkhasatyaskandhe saṃjñāskandhavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 77. Within the Section on the Truth of Suffering, the Chapter on the Perception Aggregate (<s>saṃjñāskandhavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) ko dharmaḥ saṃjñā | (u) prajñaptisaddharmanimittagrahaṇātmikā saṃjñā | kasmāt | yathoktaṃ sūtre- kecitparīttasaṃjñāḥ kecidbahusaṃjñāḥ kecidapramāṇasaṃjñāḥ kecidakiñcanasaṃjñā iti | vastutastu te bahu kiñcidādidharmā na santi | ato jñāyate saṃjñā prajñaptisaddharmanimittagrahaṇarūpeti | tāḥ saṃjñāḥ bhūyasā viparyāsagatā iṣyante | yathoktam- anitye nityamiti saṃjñāviparyāsaḥ | duḥkhe sukhamiti saṃjñāviparyāsaḥ | anātmani ātmeti saṃjñāviparyāsaḥ | aśubhe śubhamiti saṃjñāviparyāsaḥ | iti | evaṃ śraddhādhimuktivipaśyanā kṛtsnāyataneṣvapi ucyante |
body.translated_text: (Question) What <s>dharma</s> is perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>)? (Answer) Perception has the nature of grasping the mark (<s>nimitta</s>) of a <s>dharma</s> that exists as a designation (<s>prajñaptisaddharma</s>). Why? As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Some have limited perceptions, some have extensive perceptions, some have immeasurable perceptions, some have perceptions of nothingness.' But in reality, those <s>dharmas</s> of 'many,' 'nothing,' and the like do not exist. Therefore it is known that perception has the nature of grasping the mark of a <s>dharma</s> that exists as a designation. Those perceptions are for the most part considered to be perverted (<s>viparyāsagata</s>). As stated: 'Perceiving permanence in what is impermanent — this is the perversion of perception. Perceiving pleasure in what is suffering — this is the perversion of perception. Perceiving self in what is without self — this is the perversion of perception. Perceiving the beautiful in what is impure — this is the perversion of perception.' Likewise, faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), conviction (<s>adhimukti</s>), and insight (<s>vipaśyanā</s>) are also spoken of in the <s>kṛtsnāyatanas</s> (totality-bases).

body.text: saṃjñā tridhā vibhaktā grahālambanā yaduta priyadvepyodāsīnāḥ | tatra tisro vedanāḥ kramaśaḥ samudbhavanti | tā vedanāśca triviṣajananyaḥ | ataḥ saṃjñā duṣṭā | duṣṭatvāt bhagavānāha- saṃjñā prahātavyeti | yathoktam- cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā mā nimittaṃ gṛhvīta iti | ato jñāyate prajñaptisaddharmanimittagrahaṇarūpā saṃjñeti |
body.translated_text: Perception is divided threefold according to the object grasped: the beloved, the hateful, and the indifferent. From these, three feelings arise in order. And those feelings give rise to the three poisons (<s>triviṣa</s>). Therefore perception is defective. Because of its defectiveness, the Blessed One said: 'Perception should be abandoned.' As stated: 'Having seen forms with the eye, do not grasp the mark (<s>nimitta</s>).' Therefore it is known that perception has the nature of grasping the mark of a <s>dharma</s> that exists as a designation.

body.text: (pṛ) prajñaptisaddharmagrahaṇarūpā saṃjñeti nāyamartho yujyate | kasmāt | tathā saṃjñayā hi sarvān kleśān prajahāti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- anityasaṃjñā sādhu bhāvitā sarvaṃ kāmarāgaṃ paryādāpayati | sarvaṃ rūparāgaṃ paryādāpayati | sarvaṃ bhavarāgaṃ paryādāpayati | sarvamauddhatyaṃ paryādāpayati | sarvāmavidyāṃ paryādāpayati | samamasmimānaṃ paryādāpayati | iti | ato jñāyate na prajñaptisaddharmagrahaṇamātrā saṃjñeti | prajñaptidharmagrahaṇarūpā [cet] saṃjñā | tadā na syātkleśānāṃ prahāṇam |
body.translated_text: (Objection) Your view that 'perception has the nature of grasping a <s>dharma</s> that exists as a designation' is not correct. Why? Because through [correct] perception, one abandons all defilements. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The perception of impermanence, when well cultivated, exhausts all desire-and-passion for sensual pleasures, exhausts all desire-and-passion for form, exhausts all desire-and-passion for existence, exhausts all restlessness, exhausts all ignorance, and exhausts the conceit "I am."' Therefore it is known that perception does not merely consist of grasping a <s>dharma</s> that exists as a designation. If perception [were merely] grasping a designative <s>dharma</s>, then there would be no abandonment of defilements.

body.text: ucyate | vastutaḥ prajñeyaṃ saṃjñeti nāmnocyate | yathā vadanti vedakaḥ sarvasmādvimucyate | manasā sarve kleśāḥ prahīyanta iti | yathā ca vadanti akṛṣṇāśuklakarmaṇā sarvāṇi karmāṇi kṣapayatīti | vadanti ca-
body.translated_text: It is replied: In reality, it is wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) that is designated by the name 'perception' (<s>saṃjñā</s>). Just as they say: 'The experiencer is liberated from everything.' And 'by the mind, all defilements are abandoned.' And just as they say: 'By <s>karma</s> that is neither dark nor bright, one exhausts all <s>karmas</s>.' And they say: (

body.text:
śraddhayā vitaratyoghamapramādena cārṇavam |
vīryeṇa duḥkhamatyeti prajñayā pariśudhyati | iti |
body.translated_text:
'By faith one crosses the flood; by diligence, the ocean;
by effort one transcends suffering; by wisdom one is purified' — thus it is said.

body.text: vastutastu prajñayā tarati na tu śraddhādinā | evaṃ prajñaiva saṃjñākhyayocyate | uktañca sūtre- prajñayā balaṃ bhavatīti | yathoktam- āryāstadantevāsino vā prajñābalena sarvān kleśān prajahatīti | ataḥ prajñaiva sarvasaṃyojanasamucchedinī | na tu saṃjñā | saptatriṃśadāryamārgāṅgeṣu noktā saṃjñā | ato na [sā] saṃyojanasamucchedinī | uktañca sūtre- jānan paśyan āsravakṣayaṃ pratilabhate nājānan nāpaśyan iti | triṣvanāsravendriyeṣūktaṃ anājñātamāsyāmindriyamājñendriyamājñātāvīndriyamiti sarvaṃ jñānākhyaṃ bhavati | āha ca bhagavān- prajñāskandho vimuktijñānadarśanaskandho bhavati iti | kiñcāha- dhyānavyatiriktā nāsti sambodhiḥ | sāmyavyatiriktaṃ nāsti dhyānamiti | anukramasūtre coktam- viśuddhaśīladhāriṇo na cittaṃ paritapati yāvadyathābhūtajñānāya cittaṃ samādadhāti iti | dharmajñānādayaḥ sarve prajñākhyāḥ | tisṛṣu ca śikṣāsu adhiprajñāśikṣottamā | āha ca- prajñāsampat vimuktijñānadarśanasampat iti | saptaviśuddhiṣu coktam- pratipadājñāna- darśanavimuktirit | āha ca bhagavān- sarvadharmāṇāṃ yathābhūtajñānamanuttarā prajñā ityucyate | saṃjñā tu naivaṃvidhocyate |
body.translated_text: But in reality, it is by wisdom that one crosses — not by faith and the rest. Thus, wisdom itself is designated by the name 'perception.' And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Through wisdom, there is strength.' As stated: 'The Noble Ones, or their disciples, by the power of wisdom abandon all defilements.' Therefore wisdom alone is the destroyer of all fetters (<s>saṃyojana</s>) — not perception. Among the thirty-seven limbs of the noble path (<s>saptariṃśad āryamārgāṅga</s>), perception is not mentioned. Therefore it is not the destroyer of fetters. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Knowing and seeing, one obtains the destruction of outflows (<s>āsravakṣaya</s>) — not without knowing and seeing.' Among the three undefiled faculties (<s>anāsravendriya</s>), the following are stated: 'the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (<s>anājñātamāsyāmīndriya</s>), the faculty of full knowledge (<s>ājñendriya</s>), and the faculty of one who has fully known (<s>ājñātāvīndriya</s>)' — all are designated by the name 'knowledge.' And the Blessed One said: 'The aggregate of wisdom (<s>prajñāskandha</s>) becomes the aggregate of the knowledge-and-vision of liberation (<s>vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha</s>).' Furthermore he says: 'Apart from <s>dhyāna</s>, there is no awakening (<s>sambodhi</s>); apart from equanimity (<s>sāmya</s>), there is no <s>dhyāna</s>.' And in the <s>Anukramasūtra</s> it is stated: 'For one who maintains purified moral conduct, the mind does not suffer regret, up to [the point where] the mind is concentrated for the knowledge of things as they truly are (<s>yathābhūtajñāna</s>).' The <s>dharmas</s> of <s>dharma</s>-knowledge (<s>dharmajñāna</s>) and the rest are all designated by the name 'wisdom.' And among the three trainings (<s>śikṣā</s>), the training in higher wisdom (<s>adhiprajñāśikṣā</s>) is the highest. And it says: 'The accomplishment of wisdom is the accomplishment of the knowledge-and-vision of liberation.' And among the seven purifications (<s>saptaviśuddhi</s>), it is stated: 'The purification of practice-knowledge-and-vision and liberation.' And the Blessed One said: 'The knowledge of all <s>dharmas</s> as they truly are is called unsurpassed wisdom.' But perception is not spoken of in this manner.

body.text: prajñaiva sarvakleśānāṃ samucchedini na tu saṃjñeti yogo nyānyāḥ | kasmāt | yathāha mahānidānasūtram- yacca sūtre 'vatarati vinaye ca sandṛśyate dharmatāñca na vilomayati tat grāhyam iti | api cāha- samyagarthe sthāpanā yathārtha [grahaṇam] samyak rute sthāpanā yathārūta [grahaṇam] iti | ataḥ sūtre yadyapyuktam anityasaṃjñādayaḥ kleśānāṃ samucchedakā
body.translated_text: That wisdom alone is the destroyer of all defilements, not perception — this accords with reasoning. Why? As the <s>Mahānidānasūtra</s> says: 'What is found in the <s>sūtras</s>, is seen in the <s>Vinaya</s>, and does not contradict the nature of <s>dharma</s> — that is to be accepted.' Furthermore it says: 'Correct establishment in meaning is grasping things as they are; correct establishment in the letter is grasping [the letter] as it is.' Therefore, even though it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s> that 'the perceptions of impermanence and the rest are the destroyers of defilements'

body.text: iti | tathāpi sā prajñaivepi | nyāyato bhavati | āha ca- avidyā sarvakleśānāṃ mūlam | visaṃyogātmajñā vimucyata iti | ato jñāyate prajñayā sarve kleśāḥ prahīyanta iti |
body.translated_text: — even so, that is wisdom itself. This accords with reasoning. And it says: 'Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the root of all defilements. Through disjoining from it, knowledge (<s>ājñā</s>) is liberated.' Therefore it is known that by wisdom all defilements are abandoned.

body.text: (pṛ) bhavatoktaṃ prajñaptisaddharmanimittagrahaṇātmikā saṃjñā iti | kiṃ tannimittam | (u) kecinmanyante- prajñaptidharmo nimittam | prajñaptidharmāḥ pañca atītaḥ anāgataḥ saṅketaḥ saṃyogaḥ pudgala iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | pudgalaḥ pañcaskandhānupādāya siddhaḥ | nimittasyāsiddhyā nāsti prajñaptiḥ | (pṛ) nimittasyārthaḥ kaḥ | (u) yadālambanaṃ tannimittam | kenedaṃ jñāyate | yathoktam- siṃho mṛgarāja iha nadītīre sthitastratra tīre nimittaṃ gṛhītvā oghaṃ tīrtvā niṣkrāmati | tatra yadi nimittaṃ nāsti tadā idaṃ tīraṃ pratinivṛtya [tannimitta]māmaraṇaṃ na muñcati iti | sūtre 'smin vakṣa[mṛgā]dinimittaṃ bhavati | āha ca- bhikṣurnimittaṃ pradarśayatīti | atra cīvarādirnimittam | kiñcāha- bhagavān- īdṛśaṃ nimittaṃ khyāpayatīti | api cāha- [paśu]vadhako rājabhojanāyābhilaṣitaṃ nimittamupādatta iti | āhuśca- prabhātaṃ sūryodayasya nimittamiti | kiñcāha- trīṇi nimittāni yaduta samādhinimittaṃ pragrahanimittamupekṣānimittamiti | tatra samādhyādaya eva nimittāni bhavanti | yaṃ dharmaṃ manasikṛtya cittamālambane badhyate | tat samādhinimittam | cyavanadharmiṇo devaputrasya pañca pūrvanimittāni prādurbhavanti | tatra pañca dharmā eva nimittāni bhavanti | ato jñāyate na prajñaptidharmo nimittamiti | nāpi saṃskāraskandhasaṅgṛhītam | śāriputraḥ pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputrānmukhanimittaṃ gṛhṇāti | uktañca sūtre- cakṣuṣā rūpāṇi
body.translated_text: (Question) You have said: 'Perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>) has the nature of grasping the sign (<s>nimitta</s>) of designated (<s>prajñapti</s>) and real <s>dharmas</s>.' What is that sign? (Answer) Some think: 'The designated <s>dharma</s> is the sign.' The designated <s>dharmas</s> are five: the past, the future, convention (<s>saṅketa</s>), combination (<s>saṃyoga</s>), and the person (<s>pudgala</s>). That is not valid. Why? The person is established depending on the five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>). Because the sign is not established, there is no designation. (Question) What is the meaning of 'sign'? (Answer) Whatever is an object (<s>ālambana</s>) — that is the sign. How is this known? As it is stated: 'A lion, the king of beasts, standing on this bank of a river, having grasped the sign on the far bank, crosses the flood and emerges. If there is no sign on that bank, then he turns back to this bank and does not release that sign until death.' In this <s>sūtra</s>, the sign is of the tree-trunk, wild animals, and the like. And it says: 'A monk displays a sign' — here the sign is the robe and the like. Furthermore it says: 'The Blessed One makes known such a sign.' And it says: 'The animal-slaughterer, for the king's meal, takes up the desired sign.' And they say: 'Dawn is the sign of sunrise.' Furthermore it says: 'There are three signs: the sign of concentration (<s>samādhinimitta</s>), the sign of application (<s>pragrahānimitta</s>), and the sign of equanimity (<s>upekṣānimitta</s>).' Therein, concentration and the rest are themselves the signs. That <s>dharma</s> which, when attended to, binds the mind to its object — that is the sign of concentration. For a divine son (<s>devaputra</s>) subject to passing away, five prior signs (<s>pūrvanimitta</s>) appear. Therein, the five <s>dharmas</s> themselves are the signs. Therefore it is known that the designated <s>dharma</s> is not the sign. Nor is it comprised in the formations aggregate (<s>saṃskāraskandha</s>). <s>Śāriputra</s> grasps the sign of the face from <s>Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra</s>. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Having seen forms with the eye,

body.text: dṛṣṭvā mā nimittaṃ gṛhṇīteti | dharmamudrāyāñcoktam- yo bhikṣuḥ rūpaśabdādinimittaṃ prahīṇaṃ paśyati | nāhaṃ vadāmi sa viśuddhajñānadarśanasya lābhīti | anena jñāyate ālambanameva nimittam | na prajñaptidharma iti |
body.translated_text: one should not grasp the sign.' And in the Seal of <s>Dharma</s> (<s>Dharmamudrā</s>) it is said: 'A monk who sees the sign of form, sound, and the rest as abandoned — I do not say he has obtained purified knowledge and vision.' From this it is known that the object itself is the sign — not the designated <s>dharma</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) nālambanaṃ timittam | kasmāt | animittasamādherapi sālambanatvāt | āha ca rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā mā nimittaṃ gṛhṇīteti | yadyālambanaṃ nimittam | kathaṃ rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā na nimittaṃ gṛhṇāti | (u) nimittaṃ dvividhaṃ duṣṭamaduṣṭamiti | duṣṭanimittaniṣedhārthamāha- rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā na nimittaṃ gṛhṇātīti | animitta[samādhe]rālambanamapi duṣṭamiti paścānnirodhasatya [varge]vakṣyate yat trividha cittanirodhī animittamādāvupasampadya viharatīti | na tu sarvanimittagraho duṣṭaḥ | yaḥ samādhipragrahopekṣānimittādi gṛhṇāti | na tasya doṣo 'sti | nirvāṇañcāsaddharmaḥ | ato na duṣaṇakṛt syāt | yathoktaṃ- dharmanimittasya grāhī na duṣyati iti | prajñaptinimittagrāhiṇastu kleśāḥ samudbhavanti | kasmāt | priyāpriyādivibhaktanimittagrahāt saumanasyadaurmanasyādayaḥ samudbhavanti | tato rāgadveṣādayo doṣā bhavanti | ato jñāyate prajñaptidharmanimittagrahaṇarūpā saṃjñetyucyata iti ||
body.translated_text: (Question) The object is not the sign. Why? Because even the signless <s>samādhi</s> (<s>animittasamādhi</s>) has an object. And it says: 'Having seen forms, one should not grasp the sign.' If the object were the sign, how could one, having seen form, not grasp the sign? (Answer) Signs are of two kinds: defiled (<s>duṣṭa</s>) and undefiled (<s>aduṣṭa</s>). For the purpose of prohibiting the defiled sign, he said: 'Having seen form, one should not grasp the sign.' As for the object of the signless <s>samādhi</s> being defiled — later, in the chapter on the truth of cessation (<s>nirodhasatya</s>), it will be stated that 'one who puts a stop to three kinds of mind enters and abides in the signless [samādhi] at the beginning.' But it is not that all grasping of signs is defiled. One who grasps the signs of concentration, application, and equanimity — there is no fault in that. And <s>Nirvāṇa</s> is a non-existent <s>dharma</s> — therefore it would not be a cause of defilement. As stated: 'One who grasps the sign of <s>Dharma</s> is not defiled.' But for one who grasps the sign of designated [dharmas], defilements arise. Why? From the grasping of signs differentiated as pleasant, unpleasant, and the like, mental pleasure (<s>saumanasya</s>), mental pain (<s>daurmanasya</s>), and the rest arise. From those, faults such as passion (<s>rāga</s>), hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>), and the rest arise. Therefore it is known that perception has the nature of grasping the sign of designated <s>dharmas</s>.

body.text: duḥkhasatyaskandhe saṃjñāskandhavargaḥ saptasaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Within the section on the truth of suffering, this is the seventy-seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Perception Aggregate (<s>saṃjñāskandhavarga</s>).

body.text: 78 duḥkhasatyaskandhe vedanādhikāre vedanālakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 78. Within the section on the truth of suffering, in the topic of feeling: the Chapter on the Characteristics of Feeling (<s>vedanālakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) vedanā katamā | (u) sukhā duḥkhā aduḥkhāsukhā ca | (pṛ) sukhā katamā | duḥkhā katamā | aduḥkhāsukhā ca katamā | (u) kāyacittayorvikāso sukhetyucyate | tayoreva hrāse duḥkhā | ubhayalakṣaṇayo viruddhā aduḥkhāsukhā | (pṛ) imāstisro vedanā aniyatalakṣaṇāḥ | kasmāt | yathā vastvekameva kadācitkāyacitte vikāsayati | kadācit hrāsayati | kadācidubhayavilakṣaṇaṃ bhavati | (u) tadālambanamaniyatam | na tu vedanā | kasmāt | yathaika evāgniḥ kasyāñcidṛtau sukhamutpādayati | kasyāñcidṛtau
body.translated_text: (Question) What is feeling (<s>vedanā</s>)? (Answer) It is pleasant (<s>sukhā</s>), painful (<s>duḥkhā</s>), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant (<s>aduḥkhāsukhā</s>). (Question) What is pleasant? What is painful? What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant? (Answer) The expansion of body and mind is called 'pleasant.' Their contraction is 'painful.' What is opposed to both characteristics is 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant.' (Question) These three feelings have indeterminate characteristics. Why? Because one and the same thing sometimes expands body and mind, sometimes contracts them, and sometimes is different from both. (Answer) It is the object that is indeterminate — not feeling. Why? Just as one and the same fire, in one season, produces pleasure; in another season,

body.text: duḥkham | kasyāñciccāduḥkhāsukham | ālambanajā vedanā tu niyataiva | tadeva vastvekamṛtuvaśāt sukhasya vā heturbhavati | aduḥkhāsukhasya vā heturbhavati |
body.translated_text: pain; and in yet another, neither-pain-nor-pleasure. But feeling born from the object is itself determinate. That same single thing, due to the influence of the season, becomes a cause of pleasure, or a cause of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

body.text: tadālambanaṃ kena kālena sukhaduḥkhādīnāṃ heturbhavati | (u) yatna duḥkhavighātakamasti | tasmin samaye sukhalakṣaṇamutpadyate | yathā kaścit yadā śītārtaḥ tadoṣṇasparśaḥ sukhamutpādayati | (pṛ) nanu sa evoṣṇasparśaḥ utkaṭaḥ san duḥkhakaro bhavati | na tu sukhakaraḥ | ato jñāyate sukhavedanāpi nāstīti | (u) saṃvṛtināmato 'sti sukhavedanā | na tu paramārthataḥ | uṣṇasparśapriyasya kasyacit hitakaro 'pi bhavati | [yasya yadā] pūrvaduḥkhasya pratibandhaḥ | tasmin samaye tasya sukhamutpadyate | yadi pūrvameva duḥkhaviyogaḥ tadoṣṇasparśo na sukhakaraḥ | ato nāsti paramārthataḥ |
body.translated_text: When does that object become a cause of pleasure, pain, and the rest? (Answer) When [the object] is destructive of pain — at that time, the characteristic of pleasure arises. For example, when someone is afflicted by cold, a warm touch produces pleasure. (Question) But is not that very same warm touch, when extreme, a cause of pain, not of pleasure? Therefore it is known that pleasant feeling does not [truly] exist. (Answer) Conventionally (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) and by name, pleasant feeling exists — but not ultimately (<s>paramārthataḥ</s>). A warm touch, for one who loves warmth, can also be beneficial. When there is the obstruction of prior pain — at that time, pleasure arises for that person. If previously there is already separation from pain, then the warm touch does not produce pleasure. Therefore [pleasure] does not exist ultimately.

body.text: (pṛ) yaduktaṃ bhavatā- [saṃvṛti]nāmataḥ sukhamasti iti | tanna yuktam | kasmāt | sūtre bhagavānāha- tisro vedanā iti | yadi nāsti sukhaṃ paramārthataḥ | kathaṃ brūyāt tisro vedanā iti | āha ca- rūpaṃ yadi duḥkhaniyatam | sattvā na tatrāsaṅgamutpādayeyuriti | kiñcāha- rūpasya ka āsvādāḥ ye rūpamupādāya prītisukhajananā iti | kiñcāha- sukhavedanāyā utpadyamānāyāḥ sukhe sthite sukham | niruddhe duḥkham | duḥkhavedanāyā utpadyamānāyā na duḥkhe sthite duḥkham | niruddhe sukham | aduḥkhāsukhavedanāyā na duḥkhaṃ jñāyate na sukhaṃ jñāyate iti | sukhā vedanā puṇyavipākaḥ | duḥkhā vedanā ca pāpavipākaḥ | yadi nāsti paramārthataḥ sukhā vedanā | puṇyapāpayorduḥkhaphalamātraṃ syāt | na tadyuktaṃ vastutaḥ | kāmadhātāvapi sukhā vedanāsti | yadi nāsti paramārthataḥ sā, rūpārūpyadhātū na [sukha]vedanāvantau syātām | na tu yujyate vastutaḥ | kiñcāha- sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ rāgo 'nuśeta iti | yadi nāsti sukhā vedanā, kutra rāgo 'nuśayīta | na vaktavyaṃ duḥkhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ rāgo 'nuśeta iti | ato jñāyate 'sti paramārthataḥ sukhā vedaneti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Your statement 'conventionally, pleasure exists' is not valid. Why? The Blessed One said in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There are three feelings.' If pleasure does not exist ultimately, how could he say 'three feelings'? And he said: 'If form were determined as painful, beings would not generate attachment to it.' Furthermore he said: 'What is the relish (<s>āsvāda</s>) of form? That which, depending on form, generates joy and pleasure.' Furthermore he said: 'When pleasant feeling arises — in pleasure, there is pleasure remaining; when it ceases, there is pain. When painful feeling arises — in pain, there is pain remaining; when it ceases, there is pleasure. When neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling [arises] — neither pain nor pleasure is known.' Pleasant feeling is the ripened result of merit (<s>puṇya</s>). Painful feeling is the ripened result of sin (<s>pāpa</s>). If pleasant feeling does not exist ultimately, then from both merit and demerit there would be only the fruit of suffering — but that is not valid in reality. In the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>) too, pleasant feeling exists. If it does not exist ultimately, then the form and formless realms would not possess [pleasant] feeling — but that is not valid in reality. Furthermore he said: 'In pleasant feeling, passion (<s>rāga</s>) lies latent.' If pleasant feeling does not exist, where would passion lie latent? It cannot be said that 'in painful feeling, passion lies latent.' Therefore it is known that pleasant feeling exists ultimately.

body.text: atrocyate | yadyasti paramārthataḥ sukhā vedanā | kiṃ sukhamiti tasya lakṣaṇaṃ vaktavyam | na tūcyate vastuta | jñātavyaṃ duḥkhaviśeṣasyaiva sukhanimittavyavahāra iti | sarvo lokadhātu ā mahānarakamā ca bhavāgraṃ sarvaṃ duḥkhalakṣaṇam | bahuduḥkhasampīḍitasya mṛduni duḥkhe sukhanimittamutpadyate | yathā kaścit dharmataptaḥ śītasparśaṃ sukhaṃ manyate | tasmāt sūtrāṇi tathāvacanānyaviruddhāni | (pṛ) loke sarvaṃ sukhamiti vaktuṃ sambhavati | mṛduni sukhe duḥkhasaṃjñotpadyate | tathā no cet duḥkhālpatve sukhasaṃjñotpadyata ityapi na vaktuṃ śakyate | (u) duḥkhavedanālakṣaṇasyaudārikatvāt sūkṣmasukhaṃ duḥkhamiti na sambhavati | sukhaṃ sūkṣmamapi nopaghātalakṣaṇaṃ bhavati | kasmāt | na hi paśyāmaḥ kathamapi sūkṣmaṃ sukhamanubhavantaṃ puruṣaṃ bāhumudyamya sudīrghamucchvasantam | sukhā ca vedanā sūkṣmā pravṛttā upaśamalakṣaṇamityucyate | tadyathordhvabhūmau pravṛtta upaśamaḥ | ato yaduktaṃ sūkṣme sukhe duḥkhasaṃjñotpadyata iti tat vacanamātram | bālapṛthagjanānāmalpaduḥkhe sukhasaṃjñā mithyā prādurbhavati iti tu nyāyyam ||
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: If pleasant feeling exists ultimately, then its characteristic 'what is pleasure?' must be stated. But in reality it is not [stated]. It should be known that a particular [lesser] suffering is conventionally called 'pleasure.' The entire world-realm, from the great hells below to the summit of existence (<s>bhavāgra</s>) above — all has the characteristic of suffering. When one who is greatly afflicted by suffering experiences mild suffering, the notion of pleasure arises. Just as someone scorched by heat considers a cold touch to be pleasure. Therefore, the <s>sūtra</s> statements are not contradictory. (Question) It could be said that 'in the world, everything is pleasure' — [that] in mild pleasure, the notion of pain arises. If so, then it cannot be said that 'when suffering is slight, the notion of pleasure arises' either. (Answer) Because the characteristic of painful feeling is gross, it is not possible that subtle pleasure would be called 'pain.' Even subtle pleasure does not have the characteristic of affliction (<s>upaghāta</s>). Why? For we do not see a person experiencing even subtle pleasure raising his arms and sighing deeply. And pleasant feeling, when subtle in its operation, is said to have the characteristic of tranquility (<s>upaśama</s>) — just as [tranquility] operates in the higher realms. Therefore the statement that 'in subtle pleasure, the notion of pain arises' is mere words. It is correct that for foolish ordinary beings (<s>bālapṛthagjana</s>), the false notion of pleasure arises in slight suffering.

body.text: duḥkhasatyaskandhe vedanādhikāre vedanālakṣaṇavargo 'ṣṭasaptatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Within the section on the truth of suffering, in the topic of feeling, this is the seventy-eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of Feeling (<s>vedanālakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 79 saṃskāraduḥkhatāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 79. Chapter on the Suffering of Conditioned Existence (<s>saṃskāraduḥkhatāvarga</s>)

body.text: sarvā vedanā duḥkham | kasmāt | cīvarabhojanādayo hi sarve dūḥkhahetavaḥ na sukhahetavaḥ | kenedaṃ jñāyate | annavastrādiṣūtkaṭeṣu duḥkhamapi vardhata iti pratyakṣaṃ khalu | ato duḥkhahetavaḥ | hastavyathādiduḥkhaṃ lakṣaṇato nidarśayituṃ śakyate | na tathā sukham | annavastrādi vyādhipraśamanam | yathā tarṣitasya pānaṃ na sukhajanakam | kaścidduḥkhapīḍitaḥ duḥkhabhede sukhasaṃjñāṃ janayati | yathā janā maraṇabhītāḥ [anyaṃ] daṇḍaṃ sukhaṃ manyante | daṇḍādānaśastrādānakṣuraśaktayo duḥkhahetutayā niyatāḥ na tathā sukhahetutayā | sarveṣāmavaśyamātyantikaduḥkhatvāt jñātavyaṃ pūrvaṃ [duḥkhaṃ] sadevordhvakālaṃ budhyate pādukākṣayavat | strīrūpādau ca pūrvamutpadyate sukhasaṃjñā | paścādbhavati vidveṣaḥ | ato jñāyate mithyāsaṃjñānusmaraṇena sukhasaṃjñotpadyata iti | mithyasaṃjñānusmaraṇavyāvṛttau tasya doṣaṃ paśyati | strīrūpādīni ucchoṣaṇaśirovyādhyādihetavaḥ | na sukhaṃ bhavati | vairāgye sati tadālambanaṃ tyajyate |
body.translated_text: All feeling is suffering. Why? Robes, food, and the like — all are causes of suffering, not causes of pleasure. How is this known? It is directly perceived that when robes, food, and the like are excessive, suffering increases. Therefore they are causes of suffering. The suffering of hand-pain and the like can be demonstrated by its characteristics — but not so with pleasure. Robes, food, and the like merely alleviate illness. Just as a drink for one who is thirsty does not generate pleasure. When someone afflicted by pain experiences the cessation of pain, he generates the notion of pleasure. Just as people who are afraid of death consider another punishment to be pleasant. Rod-taking, weapon-taking, and blades are determined as causes of suffering — not so as causes of pleasure. Because everything is ultimately painful, it should be known that [suffering] is first [perceived], and then even divine beings in the upper realm come to understand [this], like the wearing out of sandals. And with regard to the form of a woman and such, initially the notion of pleasure arises; afterwards, aversion arises. Therefore it is known that through the recollection of false notions, the notion of pleasure arises. When the recollection of false notions ceases, one sees its faults. The form of a woman and such are causes of emaciation, headache, and the like — not causes of pleasure. When dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) arises, that object is abandoned.

body.text: yadyasti vastutaḥ sukham | kasmāt tyajyate | yasya yatra sukhamabhūt tasya tadeva paścādduḥkhacittajanakamityato jñāyate nāsti sukhamiti |
body.translated_text: If pleasure truly exists in reality, why is it abandoned? That which was once a source of pleasure for someone later becomes the cause of a painful mind — therefore it is known that pleasure does not exist.

body.text: kiñca kāyo duḥkhahetuḥ na sukhahetuḥ | yathāraṇyabhūmau susasyeṣu duṣpraroheṣvapi tṛṇavīraṇāni sūdbhavanti | evaṃ kāyabhūmau duḥkhaskandhāḥ susamudyanti | mṛṣāsukhantu durudbhavaṃ bhavati | kiñca janā duḥkhe sukhaviparyāsamutpādya paścāttatrābhiṣvajante sukhaṃ yadi kiñcidasti | nocyeta viparyāsa iti | yathā nitya ātmā viśuddhaḥ kimapi vastu nāsti | evaṃ sukhamapi | ubhayorviparyastatvāt | janānāṃ kaṭuke duḥkhe sukhacittamutpadyate | yathā bhāravāhī skandhaṃ sukhayati | ato jñāyate nāsti sukhamiti | sūtre ca bhagavatoktam- sukhā bhikṣavo vedanā duḥkhato draṣṭavyā | duḥkhā vedanā śalyato draṣṭavyā | aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā anityato draṣṭavyā | iti | yadyasti niyataṃ sukham | sukhaṃ duḥkhato na draṣṭavyaṃ syāt | jñātavyaṃ pṛthagjanā duḥkhaṃ sukhato gṛhṇantīti | ato bhagavānāha- yatra pṛthagjanānāṃ sukhasaṃjñotpadyate tat duḥkhato draṣṭavyamiti |
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the body is a cause of suffering, not a cause of pleasure. Just as on wild land, even when good crops are difficult to grow, grasses and reeds sprout forth — so too on the ground of the body, aggregates of suffering arise abundantly. But false pleasure is difficult to arise. Furthermore, people generate a perversion of pleasure in suffering and then cling to it. If any pleasure at all existed, it would not be called a perversion. Just as [the notions of] permanence, self, and purity [projected onto things where] no such thing exists — so too with pleasure. Because both are perverted. In people, even in bitter suffering, the notion of pleasure arises — just as a burden-carrier takes comfort in [shifting] his load. Therefore it is known that pleasure does not exist. And the Blessed One said in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'O monks, pleasant feeling should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should be seen as a thorn. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be seen as impermanent.' If pleasure were determined to exist, it should not be seen as suffering. It should be known that ordinary beings grasp suffering as pleasure. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Where ordinary beings generate the notion of pleasure — that should be seen as suffering.'

body.text: imāstisro vedanāśca duḥkhasatyasaṅgṛhītāḥ | yadi vastuto 'sti sukham | kathaṃ duḥkhasatyasaṅgṛhītaṃ syāt | duḥkhameva vastuto 'sti | sukhalakṣaṇantu mṛṣā | kenedaṃ jñāyate | duḥkhacittabhāvanayā hi sarvasaṃyojanāni prajahajāti | natu sukhacittabhāvanayā | ato jñāyate sarvaṃ duḥkhamiti | sarve padārthā duḥkhahetavaḥ | dveṣyavat | dveṣyo dvividhaḥ- ekaḥ duḥkhameva karoti | apara ādau mṛdurapi ante puruṣaṃ hinasti | tadvatpadārthā api kecidādau subhakarā ante tu hiṃsrāḥ | ato jñāyate sarvaṃ duḥkhamiti | sattvānāṃ labdhakāmānāmapi nāsti tṛptiḥ | lavaṇāmbhaḥ pānenātṛptivat ityato duḥkham | kāmaprārthanāvirahaḥ sukhamityucyate | prārthanā tu duḥkham | na paśyāmaḥ kamapi lokamaprārthayamānam | ataḥ sukhavihīnaṃ jānīmaḥ | sarve sattvāḥ kāyikaduḥkhena vā caitasikaduḥkhena vā sadānugamyanta ityataḥ kāyo duḥkhamiti jñāyate |
body.translated_text: These three <s>vedanās</s> (feelings) are included in the <s>duḥkhasatya</s> (truth of suffering). If pleasure truly exists, how could it be included in the truth of suffering? Only suffering truly exists; the characteristic of pleasure is false. How is this known? Through cultivation of the mind on suffering, all <s>saṃyojanas</s> (fetters) are abandoned, but not through cultivation of the mind on pleasure. Therefore it is known that all is suffering. All things are causes of suffering, like an enemy. An enemy is of two kinds: one causes suffering directly; another, though mild at first, harms a person in the end. Likewise, some things are pleasant at first but harmful in the end. Therefore it is known that all is suffering. Even for beings who have obtained their desires, there is no satisfaction — like drinking salt water without being satiated, therefore it is suffering. The absence of longing for desires is called pleasure, but longing itself is suffering. We do not see anyone in the world who is without longing; therefore we know it is devoid of pleasure. All beings are constantly accompanied by either bodily suffering or mental suffering; therefore it is known that the body is suffering.

body.text: kāyaḥ kārāgṛhavatsadā bandhanaḥ | kenedaṃ jñāyate | etatkāyanirodhādvimuktaityucyate | [ato] bandhanaṃ duḥkham | sarve 'pi padārthāḥ kramaśaḥ kutsanīyāḥ | yathā nārakādikāyāḥ grīṣmahemantādyṛtavaḥ bālādīnāmindriyāṇi | śītadharmādi parasparasāpekṣamavasāne
body.translated_text: The body is like a prison, always in bondage. How is this known? Because through the cessation of this body, one is said to be liberated. Therefore bondage is suffering. All things are progressively contemptible — just as the bodies of hell-beings and others, the seasons of summer and winter and so forth, and the sense faculties of children and others. Cold, heat, and other such conditions, being mutually dependent, at the end

body.text: vidvepyaṃ jñāyate | [ataḥ] sarvaṃ duḥkhamiti jñeyam | kāyasya ca bahavaḥ śatravo yadutāśīviṣakāraṇḍaḥ pañcotkṣiptāsikā vadhakāḥ kalyāṇamitravañcanāścorāḥ śūnyagrāme grāmaghātakāścorā mahānadyā avaratīram iti | [imāni]nānāduḥkhāni sadānucaranti [kāyam] | ato jñāyate sarvaṃ duḥkhamiti | kiñca jānīmaḥ sattvānāṃ kāyaḥ sarvaduḥkhairanugamyate yaduta jātiduḥkhaṃ, jarāduḥkhaṃ vyādhiduḥkhaṃ maraṇaduḥkhaṃ vipriyasamāgamaduḥkhaṃ priyaviyogaduḥkhaṃ prārthitādivighātaduḥkham ityādibhiḥ | ato jñāyate kāyo duḥkhakalāpa iti | ātmani sati ātmīyābhiṣvaṅgādyupadravāṇāṃ samudayo 'sti | ato jñāyate kāyo duḥkhanidānamiti |
body.translated_text: are known to be distressing. Therefore all should be known as suffering. The body has many enemies, namely: the basket of venomous snakes, the five executioners with raised swords, the thieves who are treacherous false friends, the village-destroying robbers in an empty village, and the further bank of a great river. These various sufferings constantly attend the body. Therefore it is known that all is suffering. Furthermore, we know that the bodies of beings are accompanied by all sufferings, namely: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of encountering the unpleasant, the suffering of separation from the pleasant, the suffering of frustration of desires, and so forth. Therefore it is known that the body is a mass of suffering. When there is a self, due to attachment to what belongs to the self, there arises an accumulation of calamities. Therefore it is known that the body is the cause of suffering.

body.text: pañca sattvagatayaścatvāra iryāpathāśca sukhavirahitāḥ | kasmāt | yathoktaṃ sūtre- rūpaṃ duḥkhaṃ vedanā saṃjñā saṃskārāṃ vijñānañca duḥkhaṃ iti | rūpa utpadyamāne jarāvyādhimaraṇādayaḥ sarva upadravā utpadyeran | evaṃ vedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskāravijñāneṣvapi | kāyaḥ sadā vyāpriyate kāyavaṅmanobhiḥ kṛtyānyabhisaṃskriyante | kṛtyānāmabhisaṃskaraṇaṃ duḥkhamityucyate | āryāḥ kāyakṣayeṇa hṛṣṭā bhavanti | yadyasti vastutaḥ sukham | kathaṃ sukhādbhraṣṭāḥ pramodyeran | ato jñāyate sarvaṃ duḥkhamiti ||
body.translated_text: The five destinies of beings and the four postures are devoid of pleasure. Why? As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: '<s>Rūpa</s> (form) is suffering, <s>vedanā</s> (feeling), <s>saṃjñā</s> (perception), <s>saṃskārāḥ</s> (formations), and <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) are suffering.' When <s>rūpa</s> (form) arises, aging, illness, death, and all calamities arise. Likewise with <s>vedanā</s>, <s>saṃjñā</s>, <s>saṃskāra</s>, and <s>vijñāna</s>. The body is always active; through body, speech, and mind, actions are constructed. The construction of actions is called suffering. The noble ones are pleased by the destruction of the body. If pleasure truly exists, how would those who have fallen from pleasure rejoice? Therefore it is known that all is suffering.

body.text: saṃskāraduḥkhatāvarga ekonāśītitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Chapter seventy-nine on the suffering of <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned formations).

body.text: 80 duḥkhaprahāṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 80. Chapter on the abandonment of suffering.

body.text: (pṛ) bahubhiḥ kāraṇairbhavatā duḥkhaṃ pratipāditam | athāpi janāḥ sukhaṃ kāmayante | yatra kāmanā tat sukhamiti manyāmahe | (u) pūrvameva pratyuktamidam | pṛthagjanā viparyayāt duḥkhameva sukhato gṛhṇanti | mugdhairuktaṃ kathaṃ śraddheyam | prārthitaṃ labdhvāpi duḥkhato bhāvayet | kasmāt | sarvamanityaṃ vipariṇāme duḥkhajanakam | yathoktaṃ bhagavatā sūtre- rūpārāmā[bhikṣavo] devamanuṣyā rūparatā rūpamuditā rūpavipariṇāmavirāganirodhāt
body.translated_text: (Question) You have demonstrated suffering through many reasons. Yet people still desire pleasure. We think that wherever there is desire, there is pleasure. (Answer) This has already been answered previously. Ordinary persons, due to inversion, grasp suffering as pleasure. How can what is said by the deluded be trusted? Even having obtained what was desired, one should contemplate it as suffering. Why? Because everything is impermanent and produces suffering upon change. As the <s>Bhagavān</s> (the Blessed One) stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'O monks, gods and humans who delight in <s>rūpa</s> (form), who take pleasure in form, who rejoice in form — when form changes, fades, and ceases

body.text: duḥkhaṃ [bhikṣavo] devamanuṣyā viharanti | iti | evaṃ vedanāsaṃskāravijñāneṣvapi | vipariṇāmitvāt jñātavyaṃ duḥkhamiti | janā abhūtasukhamanubhūya tatrāsaṅgamutpādayanti | āsaṅgapratyayā rakṣaṇapālanādayo doṣāḥ samudbhavanti | ataḥ sukhaṃ duḥkhato bhāvayet | sukhañca duḥkhasya dvāram | sukharāgāt tribhyo viṣebhyaḥ sambhavantyakuśalakarmāṇi | [tato]narakādau patito duḥkhopadravānanubhavati | ato jñātavyaṃ sarvaṃ sukhamūlakamiti | sarvaḥ saṃyogo viprayogāntaḥ | viprayoge gāḍhaṃ duḥkhamanubhavati | naitāvatā priyaḥ punarbhavati | ataḥ sukhaṃ duḥkhāntaṃ bhavatīti jñeyam | sukhopakaraṇāmutpādaḥ sattvānāṃ pramoṣaṇāya bhavati | duḥkheṣu ca pātayati | yathā vanyapakṣiṇāmāhāraḥ matsyānāṃ bhakṣaṇapraskandanañca sarvaṃ grahaṇāya bhavati | tathā sukhamapi duḥkhato draṣṭavyam | sukhavedanāyā alpāsvādalabhāyaparimitān doṣān prāpnoti | yathā paśumatsyānāmāsvāditamatyalpam | tadāpadasvatibahulāḥ | ato duḥkhato draṣṭavyam | sukhavedanā ca kleśānāmutpattisthānam | kasmāt | kāyarāgāddhi kāmā apekṣyante | kāmapratyayā vyāpādādayaḥ kleśāḥ krameṇa sambhavanti | sukhavedanā saṃsārasya mūlam | kasmāt | sukhamupādāya hi tṛṣṇā jāyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- tṛṣṇā duḥkhasya mūlam iti | sarveṣāṃ sattvānāmabhisaṃskṛtāni na sukhāya bhavanti | ato duḥkhamūlamityucyate |
body.translated_text: gods and humans, O monks, dwell in suffering.' Likewise with <s>vedanā</s>, <s>saṃskāra</s>, and <s>vijñāna</s>. Because of being subject to change, it should be known as suffering. People, having experienced unreal pleasure, generate attachment to it. From the condition of attachment arise faults such as guarding, maintaining, and so forth. Therefore one should contemplate pleasure as suffering. Pleasure is the gateway to suffering. From attachment to pleasure, unwholesome actions arise from the three poisons. Thereby one falls into hell and other realms and experiences the calamities of suffering. Therefore it should be known that all has pleasure as its root. Every union ends in separation. In separation one experiences intense suffering. Not even by that much does the beloved become one's own again. Therefore it should be known that pleasure ends in suffering. The arising of the means of pleasure serves to delude beings and cast them into suffering — just as food for wild birds, and bait and lures for fish, all serve for capture. Likewise, pleasure should be viewed as suffering. From the slight enjoyment of pleasant <s>vedanā</s> (feeling), one obtains immeasurable faults — just as for livestock and fish, what is savored is very little, yet the calamities thereof are very great. Therefore it should be viewed as suffering. Pleasant <s>vedanā</s> is the birthplace of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). Why? Because from attachment to the body, sensual desires are sought. From the condition of desires, afflictions such as ill-will and others gradually arise. Pleasant <s>vedanā</s> is the root of <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of rebirth). Why? Because based on pleasure, <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) is born. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: '<s>Tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) is the root of suffering.' The conditioned activities of all beings do not lead to pleasure. Therefore it is said that it is the root of suffering.

body.text: sukhavedanā śṛṅkhalāto dustyajatarā | saṃsāre ca sukhakāmanayā badhyate | kasmāt | sukharāgāddhi saṃsāraṃ na muñcati | sukhā vedanā ceyaṃ sadā duḥkhajananī | anveṣaṇakāle kāmanā duḥkham | vighātakāle 'nusmaraṇaṃ duḥkham | lābhakāle na tṛpyati srotaḥ kabalayan sāgara iva | idamapi duḥkham | sukha vedanā atandrīhetuḥ | kasmāt | sattvāḥ sukhasādhanānveṣaṇakāle prapātacaṅkramaṇā[di]doṣamapi sukhato matvā na citte parikhidyante | tasmātprajñāvatā duḥkhamiti bhāvayet | sukhā vedanā karmaṇāṃ pravṛttiheturityucyate | kasmāt | sukharāgāddhi kuśalakarmasu pravartate | sarvamapīdaṃ kāyānubhavasya hetuḥ | kasmāt | sukhamupādāya
body.translated_text: Pleasant <s>vedanā</s> (feeling) is harder to abandon than chains. One is bound in <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of rebirth) by the desire for pleasure. Why? Because due to attachment to pleasure, one does not release <s>saṃsāra</s>. This pleasant <s>vedanā</s> always generates suffering. At the time of seeking, desire is suffering. At the time of frustration, recollection is suffering. At the time of gain, one is not satisfied — like the ocean swallowing a stream. This too is suffering. Pleasant <s>vedanā</s> is the cause of restless striving. Why? Because when beings seek the means to pleasure, even regarding the faults of falling off precipices, walking dangerous paths, and so forth, they think of these as pleasant and do not become weary in mind. Therefore the wise should contemplate it as suffering. Pleasant <s>vedanā</s> is said to be the cause of the arising of actions. Why? Because from attachment to pleasure, one engages in wholesome and unwholesome actions. All of this is the cause of bodily experience. Why? Because based on pleasure

body.text: hi tṛṣṇotpadyate | tṛṣṇāhetunā kāyo 'nubhūyate | sukhavedanā ca nirvāṇasya virodhinī bhavati | kasmāt | sattvāḥ saṃsāre sukhādhyavasānena nirvāṇaṃ nābhilaṣanti | aviraktaḥ sukhavedanāmimāṃ tṛṣyati | tṛṣṇā ca duḥkhasya janakahetuḥ | ataḥ sukhavedanā duḥkhaskandhasya mūlamiti jñāyate | uktañca sūtre- dve ime bhikṣava āśe duṣprajahe | [katame dve] lābhasya jīvitasya ca iti | kāmānāmanucintanī āśā lābhasyāśetyucyate | eṣāṃ kāmānāmupabhogāya yā jīvita pratilābhāyāśā sā jīvitasyāśā | ime dve āśe sukhavedanāmūlike | ataḥ prajñāvatā yathābhūtaṃ sukhavedanālakṣaṇaṃ bhāvayatā duṣprahajā[pi] praheyā |
body.translated_text: <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) arises. Due to the cause of craving, the body is experienced. Pleasant <s>vedanā</s> is an obstacle to <s>nirvāṇa</s>. Why? Because beings, through their conviction that there is pleasure in <s>saṃsāra</s>, do not aspire to <s>nirvāṇa</s>. One who is not dispassionate craves this pleasant <s>vedanā</s>. And <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) is the generative cause of suffering. Therefore it is known that pleasant <s>vedanā</s> is the root of the mass of suffering. It is also stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'O monks, there are two hopes that are difficult to abandon. Which two? The hope for gain and the hope for life.' The hope of anticipating sense pleasures is called the hope for gain. The hope for obtaining life for the enjoyment of these sense pleasures is the hope for life. These two hopes are rooted in pleasant <s>vedanā</s>. Therefore, the wise person, contemplating the true nature of pleasant <s>vedanā</s>, should abandon it even though it is difficult to abandon.

body.text: sukhavedanāsvādo 'pratilabdhavairāgyasya mahāprājñasyāpi cittaṃ kaluṣayati | duṣprajahatvāt sukhavedanātaḥ pragāḍhā bhavati | sukhavedanāsvādaḥ rāgādīnāṃ hetuḥ | sukhavedanāyāmasatyāṃ na kiñcidrajyate | sukhavedanāsvādena tattvajñānaṃ prajahāti | kasmāt | loke hi prājñā avaśyamuttamabhūmyāsvādamupādāyādharāṃ bhūmiṃ tyajanti | ato jñāyate sukhā vedanā duḥkhavedanāmatikrānteti | sattvānāṃ cittamupapattyāyatane 'nubadhyate | yāvadgṛhya janturapi kāye sābhilāṣo bhavati | iti jñātavyaṃ sarvaṃ sukhavedanāsvādāditi | ataḥ sukhāṃ vedanāṃ duḥkhato bhāvayet ||
body.translated_text: The savor of pleasant <s>vedanā</s> (feeling) disturbs the mind even of a greatly wise person who has not yet attained dispassion. Because it is difficult to abandon, pleasant <s>vedanā</s> is deeply entrenched. The savor of pleasant <s>vedanā</s> is the cause of <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and other afflictions. In the absence of pleasant <s>vedanā</s>, nothing whatsoever is desired. Through the savor of pleasant <s>vedanā</s>, one abandons knowledge of reality. Why? Because in the world, even the wise inevitably abandon a lower plane by grasping the savor of a higher plane. Therefore it is known that pleasant <s>vedanā</s> surpasses painful <s>vedanā</s>. The minds of beings become bound to the sphere of rebirth. Even a creature that is to be seized becomes desirous toward the body. Thus it should be known that all this is due to the savor of pleasant <s>vedanā</s>. Therefore one should contemplate pleasant <s>vedanā</s> as suffering.

body.text: duḥkhaprahāṇavargo 'śititamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Chapter eighty on the abandonment of suffering.

body.text: 81 trivedanāvicāravargaḥ
body.translated_text: 81. Chapter on the investigation of the three <s>vedanās</s> (feelings).

body.text: (pṛ) sarvaṃ duḥkhamiti parijñātam | idānīṃ kena vibhaṅgena santi tisro vedanā iti | (u) ekasyā eva duḥkhavedanāyā kālabhedena trayaḥ prakārā bhavanti yat viheṭhakaṃ tat duḥkhamityucyate | viheṭhitaḥ pūrvadūḥkhadhāraṇāya punaduḥkhāntaraṃ paryeṣate | paryeṣitapraṇidhānena mahāduḥkhasya muhūrtamupaśame tasmin (samaye) susukhamityucyate | prītidaurmanasyayoravedane na [kiñcit] praṇidadhāti, na paryeṣate | tasmin samaye aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā ityucyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) It has been fully understood that all is suffering. Now, by what analysis are there three <s>vedanās</s> (feelings)? (Answer) Of the single painful <s>vedanā</s> itself, there are three types due to temporal distinction. That which is tormenting is called suffering. One who is tormented, unable to bear the previous suffering, seeks another suffering as relief. When, through the resolution of what was sought, there is a momentary subsidence of great suffering, at that time it is called pleasure. When one neither resolves nor seeks with regard to feelings of joy and displeasure, at that time it is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant <s>vedanā</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā nāsti | kasmāt sukhaduḥkha eva hyanubhāvye staḥ | aduḥkhāsukhā tu nānubhūyate | (u) puruṣo 'yaṃ tribhiḥ sparśaiḥ spṛṣṭaḥ yaduta duḥkhasparśaḥ sukhasparśa aduḥkhāsukhasparśa iti | hetau sati phalamastīti jñātavyam | yathā kaścit utkaṭatāpalabdhaḥ śītasparśaṃ sukhato 'nubhavati | ūrṣṇasparśaṃ duḥkhataḥ | aśitānuṣṇasparśañca aduḥkhāsukhato 'nubhavati | ato jñāyate astīyamaduḥkhāsukhā vedaneti | yadbhavato matam- aduḥkhāsukhasparśe na vedanotpadyata iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | puruṣa imamaśītānuṣṇasparśanamanubhavati | anubhavajñānālambanaiva vedanā bhavati | kathamāha nāstīti | puruṣaṃ prati ālambanaṃ tridhā vibhaktaṃ priyaṃ dveṣyamudāsīnamiti | priyātsaumanasyaṃ bhavati | dvepyāddaurmanasyam | udāsīnādupekṣā | ato jñāyate saṃjñābhedādimāstisro vedanā bhavanti | ālambanāsvādādimāstisraḥ saṃjñā udyantīti | ālambanaṃ trividham | kiñcidupakārakaṃ kiñcidapakārakam | taccobhayaṃ mitho viruddham | sasukhamasukhaṃ yugapadviruddham | rāgadveṣamohasthānāni [viruddhāni] saprītika maprītikañca viruddham | puṇyāpuṇyāneñjyaphalarūpeṣvālambaneṣu tisro vedanā anupravartante | ato jñāyate astīyamaduḥkhāsukhā vedaneti | yatra cittamanukūlaṃ tatra sukhā vedanā | pratikūlaṃ yatra cittaṃ tatra duḥkhā vedanā | yatra na pratikūlaṃ nānukūlaṃ tatrāduḥkhāsukhā vedanā | lokadharmāścāṣṭau lābho 'lābho nindā praśaṃsā yaśo 'yaśaḥ sukhaṃ duḥkhamiti | pṛthagjanā alābhādiṣu caturdharmeṣu pratikūlacittā bhavanti | lābhādiṣu caturdharmeṣu tu anukūlacittāḥ | vītarāgā āryāstūībhayatrāvaśyamupekṣakā bhaveyuḥ | upekṣaivāsukhāduḥkhā vedanā | ato na sā nāstīti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Neither-painful-nor-pleasant <s>vedanā</s> does not exist. Why? Because only pleasure and pain are experienced. But neither-painful-nor-pleasant is not experienced. (Answer) This person is touched by three types of contact, namely: painful contact, pleasant contact, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact. When the cause exists, the effect should be known to exist. Just as someone afflicted by intense heat experiences cold contact as pleasant, hot contact as painful, and contact that is neither cold nor hot as neither painful nor pleasant. Therefore it is known that this neither-painful-nor-pleasant <s>vedanā</s> exists. Your view that no <s>vedanā</s> arises from neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact is incorrect. Why? Because a person experiences this contact that is neither cold nor hot. <s>Vedanā</s> is precisely the cognition of experience regarding an object. How can you say it does not exist? Objects are divided threefold with respect to a person: agreeable, disagreeable, and neutral. From the agreeable arises <s>saumanasya</s> (mental pleasure). From the disagreeable arises <s>daurmanasya</s> (mental displeasure). From the neutral arises <s>upekṣā</s> (equanimity). Therefore it is known that due to the distinction of perception, these three <s>vedanās</s> arise. From the savoring of objects, these three perceptions arise. Objects are threefold: some are beneficial, some are harmful, and these two are mutually opposed. Pleasure and non-pleasure simultaneously are contradictory. The bases of <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>moha</s> (delusion) are opposed; that which has joy and that which lacks joy are contradictory. In objects that are the results of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable, the three <s>vedanās</s> operate. Therefore it is known that this neither-painful-nor-pleasant <s>vedanā</s> exists. Where the mind is favorable, there is pleasant <s>vedanā</s>. Where the mind is unfavorable, there is painful <s>vedanā</s>. Where it is neither unfavorable nor favorable, there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant <s>vedanā</s>. The eight worldly conditions are: gain and loss, blame and praise, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain. Ordinary persons have unfavorable minds toward the four conditions of loss and so forth; toward the four conditions of gain and so forth, they have favorable minds. But the noble ones who are free from attachment must necessarily be equanimous toward both. Equanimity itself is neither-pleasant-nor-painful <s>vedanā</s>. Therefore it is not the case that it does not exist.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi sparśādipratyayatvāt tisro vedanāḥ santīti | tadā sarve 'pi cittopavicārā vedanāḥ syuḥ | kasmāt | ye cittopavicārāḥ kāyavartinaḥ te sarve 'pi sukhā duḥkhā aduḥkhāsukhā vā bhavanti | (u) [satyaṃ] sarve 'pi cittopavicārā vedanā bhavanti | kasmāt | uktaṃ hi sūtre- aṣṭādaśa manaupavicārāḥ iti tatra kevalamekaṃ manaḥ aṣṭādaśadhāvibhaktaṃ yaduta ṣaṭ saumanasyopavicārāḥ ṣaṭ daurmanasyopavicārāḥ ṣaḍupekṣopavicārā iti | saṃjñāvikalpātkiñcidduḥkhāṅgaṃ kiñcitsukhāṅgaṃ kiñcidupekṣāṅgam | ato jñāyate sarve 'pi cittopavicārā
body.translated_text: (Question) If the three feelings exist because they are conditioned by contact and the rest, then all mental investigations (<s>cittopavicāra</s>) would be feelings. Why? Because all mental investigations that occur in the body are either pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. (Answer) Indeed, all mental investigations are feelings. Why? For it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There are eighteen mental investigations.' Therein, a single mind is divided eighteenfold — namely, six investigations associated with mental pleasure (<s>saumanasyopavicāra</s>), six investigations associated with mental displeasure (<s>daurmanasyopavicāra</s>), and six investigations associated with equanimity (<s>upekṣopavicāra</s>). Through the conceptual distinction of perception, some are constituent parts of suffering, some are constituent parts of pleasure, and some are constituent parts of equanimity. Therefore it is known that all mental investigations

body.text: nāvedanā bhavantīti | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- sarvā vedanā duḥkham iti | ato jñāyate cittopavicāreṣu dehagateṣu sarvaṃ duḥkhamityucyate | āha ca yo rūpasyotpādaḥ sa duḥkhasyotpāda iti | kathaṃ rūpaṃ duḥkhamityucyate | duḥkhahetutvāt | ato jñāyate ālambanamindriyāṇi ca duḥkhajanakānīti | ataḥ sarve 'pi cittopavicārā vedanā ityucyanta iti |
body.translated_text: are not non-feelings. Furthermore, it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'All feelings are suffering.' Therefore it is known that in the mental investigations that occur in the body, everything is called suffering. And it is said: 'The arising of form is the arising of suffering.' How is form said to be suffering? Because it is a cause of suffering. Therefore it is known that objects and sense faculties are generators of suffering. Therefore all mental investigations are called feelings.

body.text: saṃskārāṇāṃ duḥkhatvāt saṃskārān duḥkhato bhāvayet | vipariṇāme duḥkhatvāt sukhāṃ vedanāṃ duḥkhato bhāvayet | duḥkhaduḥkhantu duḥkhameva | itīmāstisro vedanā duḥkhāḥ pratyayasāmagryāṃ samutpannāḥ kṣaṇikāḥ | ata āryā duḥkhataḥ paśyanti | ataḥ sarve 'pi cittasyopavicārā vedanā ityucyante |
body.translated_text: Because formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) are suffering, one should contemplate formations as suffering. Because of the suffering inherent in change (<s>vipariṇāma</s>), one should contemplate pleasant feeling as suffering. As for the suffering of suffering (<s>duḥkhaduḥkha</s>), it is simply suffering. Thus these three feelings are suffering — they arise from the aggregate of conditions and are momentary. Therefore the Noble Ones see them as suffering. Therefore all mental investigations are called feelings.

body.text: (pṛ) kimanāsravā vedanā api duḥkham | (u) duḥkhameva | kasmāt | anāsravā vedanā api āryā anantaraṃ tyajanti | prathamadhyānādārabhya yāvatsarvanirodhasamāpattim | ato duḥkhameva | sāsravadhyānasukhasyānāsravadhyānasukhasya ca ko bhedaḥ | sāsravadhyānānuyāyina ātmahetunā duḥkham | anāsravadhyānāni ca tenaiva duḥkham | ya āryā anāsravacittavihāriṇaḥ te sarvatra paraṃ nirvidyante | ato 'nāsravacitta utpanne paramo nirveda utpadyate | akṣigatarajovat | prākṛtā ajñā duḥkhaṃ sukhato manyante | āryāstu gabhīrajñā bhavāgrānnirviṇṇāḥ kāmadhātunirviṇṇebhyo 'nyebhyo 'pyatimātrāḥ | ato 'nāsravadukhaṃ sāsrava [duḥkhā]datikrāntam | āryā anāsravacittaṃ labdhvā nirvāṇamātronmukhā bhavanti | kasmāt | te tasmin samaye sarve saṃskṛtā duḥkhamiti vyaktaṃ paśyanti | yadyanāsravā vedanā sukhā tadā sukhe prāmodyeran na nirvāṇonmukhacittā bhaveyuḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) Are even undefiled (<s>anāsrava</s>) feelings suffering? (Answer) They are indeed suffering. Why?
