Even undefiled feelings — the Noble Ones immediately abandon them, from the first <s>dhyāna</s> all the way to the cessation attainment (<s>sarvanirodhasamāpatti</s>). Therefore they are indeed suffering. What is the difference between the pleasure of defiled <s>dhyāna</s> and the pleasure of undefiled <s>dhyāna</s>? The defiled <s>dhyāna</s> follower experiences suffering because of the cause of self-attachment. The undefiled <s>dhyānas</s> too are suffering for the same reason. The Noble Ones who abide in the undefiled mind become supremely disenchanted with everything. Therefore, when the undefiled mind arises, supreme disenchantment arises — like dust that has entered the eye. Ordinary beings, lacking knowledge, think suffering is pleasure. But the Noble Ones, with profound knowledge, are disenchanted even with the summit of existence (<s>bhavāgra</s>) — even more intensely than others who are disenchanted with the desire realm. Therefore undefiled suffering surpasses defiled suffering. The Noble Ones, having obtained the undefiled mind, become solely inclined toward <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Why? Because at that time they clearly see that all conditioned things are suffering. If undefiled feeling were pleasant, they would delight in that pleasure and would not become inclined toward <s>Nirvāṇa</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi cittasyopavicārā vedaneti | kathaṃ cittādidharmaḥ pṛthak [na]santi | (u) ekaiva vedanā ālambane nānopavicaratīti vibhaktā bhavati | cittādidharmā api nānālambana upavicaranti | kintu vijñānālambane sati ayaṃ samudācāraścittamityucyate | īdṛśaṃ pūrvavat vaktavyam | imeṣu sarvadharmeṣu kāyagateṣu santi
body.translated_text: (Question) If mental investigations are feelings, how do <s>dharmas</s> beginning with consciousness exist separately [from feeling]? (Answer) A single feeling, moving through various objects, becomes differentiated. <s>Dharmas</s> beginning with consciousness also investigate various objects. But when consciousness is present with its object, this activity is called 'mind.' This should be stated as before. In all these <s>dharmas</s> that occur in the body, there are

body.text: hitādayo viśeṣā ityato vedanetyākhyāyante | bahubhiścittaiḥ kleśā abhinirvartyante | tasmin samaye ca vedanetyucyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ rāgo 'nuśete | duḥkhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ dveṣo 'nuśete | aduḥkhāsukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ moho 'nuśete iti tasmātsaṃjñāvikalpitā ālambane saumanasyādayo dharmā vedanā ityucyante | kasmāt | tasmin samaye hi kleśāḥ samudbhavanti |
body.translated_text: distinctions such as benefit and the rest — therefore they are called 'feelings.' Defilements (<s>kleśa</s>) are produced by many minds. And at that time they are called 'feelings.' As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'In pleasant feeling, passion (<s>rāga</s>) lies latent (<s>anuśete</s>). In painful feeling, hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>) lies latent. In neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, delusion (<s>moha</s>) lies latent.' Therefore, the <s>dharmas</s> of mental pleasure (<s>saumanasya</s>) and the rest, conceptually distinguished by perception with respect to objects, are called 'feelings.' Why? Because at that time, defilements arise.

body.text: (pṛ) ekaikasyāṃ vedanāyāṃ trayaḥ kleśānuśayā bhavanti | kasmānniyamyante sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ rāgo 'nuśeta iti | (u) na duḥkhāyāṃ vedanāṃ rāgo 'nuśayaḥ syāt | mohassarvatrānuśayaḥ | mohabalāddhi duḥkhe sukhasaṃjñotpadyate | vastuno jñānadarśanābhāvāt duḥkhalābhe dveṣa utpadyate | aduḥkhāsukhā vedanāyāssūkṣmatvāt rāgasya dveṣasya vānubhavaḥ | kasmāt | puruṣasya tatra sukhaduḥkhasaṃjñānutpādādvastuno jñānadarśanābhāvācca kevalaṃ mohānuśayaḥ sambhavati | upekṣālambane yadi rāgadveṣau na samudācarataḥ pṛthagjanāstadutkṛṣṭālambanamiti vadanti | ato bhagavānāha- na bhavatāmidamālambanamutkṛṣṭam | ananubhavānna rāgadveṣau samudācārataḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- prākṛtānāṃ yadrupe bhavatyupekṣā sa sarvā rūpaniścitā | yasyedamālambanamutkṛṣṭaṃ tasyāhaṅkāro 'dhiko bhavati | yo nikṛṣṭaṃ karoti tasya punā rāgadveṣau samudbhavata iti | ato jñāyate 'nutkṛṣṭamiti | aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā copaśamalakṣaṇa, ārūpyasamādhivat | upaśāntatvātkleśāḥ sūkṣmaṃ samudācaranti | prākṛtāstatra vimuktisaṃjñāmutpādayanti | ato bhagavānāha- tatrāstyavidyānuśaya iti | ālambanānanubhavātsukhaduḥkhayorapratītiḥ | yo jānāti tadālambanaṃ tasya sukhaduḥkhe spaṣṭaṃ pratīyete | tasmin samaye rāgadveṣau sambhavataḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) In each feeling, three latent defilements (<s>anuśaya</s>) exist. Why is it determined that 'in pleasant feeling, passion lies latent'? (Answer) In painful feeling, passion would not lie latent. Delusion lies latent everywhere. Through the power of delusion, in suffering, the perception of pleasure arises. Due to the absence of knowledge and seeing of things as they truly are, when suffering is obtained, hatred arises. Because of the subtlety of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the experience of passion and hatred [does not arise]. Why? Because in that [state], the person does not generate the perception of pleasure or suffering, and because of the absence of knowledge and seeing of things as they truly are, only the latent tendency of delusion occurs. If in the equanimous object, passion and hatred do not arise, ordinary beings say: 'That object is sublime.' Therefore the Blessed One said: 'This object is not sublime for you. Because you do not experience it, passion and hatred do not arise.' As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'For ordinary beings, whatever equanimity arises regarding form — all of that is determined by form. For one who considers this object sublime, pride (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>) increases. For one who considers it inferior, passion and hatred arise.' From this it is known that it is not sublime. And neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has the characteristic of tranquility, like formless-realm <s>samādhi</s>. Because of its tranquil nature, defilements operate subtly. Ordinary beings generate the perception of liberation therein. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'There, the latent tendency of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) lies latent.' Because of not experiencing the object, there is no awareness of pleasure and suffering. One who knows that object — for him, pleasure and suffering become clear. At that time, passion and hatred occur.

body.text: (pṛ) yastatrālambanaṃ vedayate tasya sukhaduḥkhasaṃjñotpadyeta | ataḥ sukhaduḥkhavedanāmātramasti | (u) puruṣasyāsya tadā tadālambane na sukhacittamutpadyate na ca duḥkhacittam | ato na sukhaduḥkhamātramasti | pūrvoktavat sarvamapi duḥkhaṃ tridhā vibhaktamasti | (pṛ) yadbhavatoktaṃ- tadālambanasyānubhavajñāne punaḥ sukhasaṃjñotpadyata iti | kathaṃ tadanubhavajñānaṃ
body.translated_text: (Question) One who experiences that object would generate the perception of pleasure and suffering. Therefore there is merely pleasant and painful feeling [and nothing else]. (Answer) For this person, at that time, neither a pleasant mind nor a painful mind arises regarding that object. Therefore there is not merely pleasant and painful feeling. As stated before, all suffering too, divided threefold, exists. (Question) As you said: 'When the knowledge of experiencing that object [arises], the perception of pleasure arises again' — how does the knowledge of experiencing

body.text: na sambhavati | avidyayā anubhavajñānam | (u) puruṣasyāsya tasmin ālambane pūrvaṃ nimittagrahāt tatrālambane yadyavidyānuśayo yadi vā rāgadveṣānuśayo 'sti | (pṛ) sukhaduḥkha eva moha utpadyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- sa tāsāṃ vedanānāṃ samudayañcāstagamañcāsvādañcādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ na prajānāti | tasya tāsāṃ vedanānāṃ samudayañcāstagamañcāsvādañcādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtamaprajānato yo 'duḥkhāsukhasyāvedanāyā avidyānuśayaḥ so 'nuśeta iti | ataḥ sukhaduḥkha evāvidyānuśaya udeti | nāduḥkhāsukhāyāṃ [vedanāyām] | (u) sūtramidaṃ svayamāha- vedanānāṃ samudayāstagamādīnavādīn yathābhūtamaprajānato 'duḥkhāsukhāyāmavidyānuśayo 'nuśeta iti | (pṛ) vacanasya sattve 'pi nāyamartho yujyate | kathaṃ sukhaduḥkhayoḥ samudayāstagamādīnavānaprajānato 'duḥkhāsukhāyāṃ vedanāyāmavidyānuśayo 'nuśeta iti | kasmāt anyavastuno 'jñānamanyavastunyanuśayaḥ | ata idaṃ sūtramevaṃ vaktavyam- aduḥkhāsukhāyāḥ samudayādyaprajānato 'duḥkhāsukhāyāṃ vedanāyāmavidyānuśayo 'nuśeta iti | yadi vā tatrāvidyānuśayo nānuśeta iti | (u) tasyāduḥkhāsukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ tridhā cittaṃ bhavati | śāntasaṃjñā aduḥkhāsukhasaṃjñā tajjāduḥkhāsukhabuddhiḥ | mithyājñānena nimittagrāhiṇaḥ sukhabuddhirutpadyate | uttamabhūmisukhāsvādagrāhiṇo duḥkhabuddhirutpadyate | ataḥ sūtre vedanānāmiti bahuvacanamuktam | kasmāt | sarvā vedanā avidyānuśayitāḥ | aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā yathākālaṃ tridhā vibhaktā bhavati | yadā duḥkhāyāḥ samudayādyaprajñānam, tasmin samaye duḥkhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ sukhasaṃjñotpadyate aduḥkhāsukhasaṃjñā cotpadyate | ata ucyate vedanānāṃ samudayādyaprajānato 'vidyānuśayo 'nuśete | aduḥkhāsukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ tu bhūyasāvidyānuśayo 'nuśeta iti ||
body.translated_text: not occur? Through ignorance, there is experiential knowledge. (Answer) For this person, because of previously grasping at signs (<s>nimittāgraha</s>) regarding that object, the latent tendency of ignorance or of passion and hatred exists therein. (Question) Delusion arises only in pleasure and suffering. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'He does not know as it truly is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape of those feelings. For him, regarding those feelings — not knowing as it truly is the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape — the latent tendency of ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling lies latent.' Therefore the latent tendency of ignorance arises only in pleasure and suffering — not in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. (Answer) This <s>sūtra</s> itself says: 'Not knowing as it truly is the arising, passing away, danger, and the rest of feelings — in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent.' (Question) Even though the text says this, this meaning is not tenable. How can it be that from not knowing the arising, passing away, danger, and the rest of pleasure and suffering, the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? Why? Because ignorance regarding one thing serves as the latent tendency in another thing. Therefore this <s>sūtra</s> should be stated thus: 'Not knowing the arising and the rest of neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling], the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.' Or: 'There, the latent tendency of ignorance does not lie latent.' (Answer) For him, in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the mind exists in three ways: the perception of tranquility, the perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and the knowledge of pleasure and suffering born from that [perception]. Through wrong knowledge, grasping at signs, the perception of pleasure arises. For one who grasps the relish of the pleasure of higher states of existence, the perception of suffering arises. Therefore the <s>sūtra</s> uses the plural 'feelings.' Why? Because all feelings are permeated by the latent tendency of ignorance. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, as appropriate, is divided threefold. When there is lack of knowledge regarding the arising and the rest of painful [feeling], at that time the perception of pleasure and the perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arise in painful feeling. Therefore it is said: 'Not knowing the arising and the rest of feelings, the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent.' But in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent for the most part.

body.text: trividhavedanāvicāravarga ekaśītitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the eighty-first chapter, the Chapter on the Investigation of the Threefold Feeling (<s>trividhavedanāvicāravarga</s>).

body.text: 82 vedanāpraśnavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 82. Chapter on Questions about Feeling (<s>vedanāpraśnavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) uktaṃ hi sūtre- tasya cet sukhā vedanotpadyate | sa evaṃ prajānāti- utpannā khalu ma iyaṃ sukhā vedanā iti | ko vedanāṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti | atītānāgatā ca vedanā nopalabhyate | pratyutpannā vedanā tu nātmānaṃ prajānāti | (u) sūtrasyāsya puruṣo
body.translated_text: (Question) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'If a pleasant feeling arises in him, he knows as it truly is: This pleasant feeling has arisen in me.' Who knows feeling as it truly is? Past and future feeling is not apprehended. And present feeling does not know itself. (Answer) This <s>sūtra</s>'s [intention is that] the person

body.text: vedayata ityābhiprāyikaṃ vacanaṃ ityadoṣaḥ | sukhādivedanā kāya āgamya mana ālambate ityato 'pyanavadyam | sukhopakaraṇe sukhamiti vadanti | loke 'pi kāraṇe kāryopacārāt | sa sukhāṃ vedanāmanubhūya nimittaṃ gṛhṇāti | ata ucyate sukhā vedanotpadyate cet sa yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti iti |
body.translated_text: experiences — this is the intended meaning of the statement, and therefore there is no fault. Pleasant and other feelings, having arrived at the body, are apprehended by the mind — and for this reason too it is blameless. Regarding the instrument of pleasure, they say 'pleasure.' In the world too, the effect is figuratively attributed to the cause. Having experienced pleasant feeling, one grasps at signs (<s>nimitta</s>). Therefore it is said: 'If a pleasant feeling arises, he knows as it truly is.'

body.text: (pṛ) yadvedayati sā vedanā | vedyata iti vā vedanā | yadā vedayatīti tadā vedanā sukhādibhinnā | sūtre tūktam- sukhā vedanā duḥkhā vedanā aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā iti | yadi vedyata iti vedanā | kena tadvedyata iti vedayatīti vedanā bhavati | (u) [sukha]kāraṇe sukhamityucyate | yathā tejo duḥkhaṃ tejaḥ sukhamiti | ataḥ kāraṇānubhavajñānaṃ sukhā vedanetyucyate | sattvā imāṃ vedanāṃ vedayanti | ato vedayatīti vedanā bhavati (pṛ) na sattvānāṃ vedanā | uktañca sūtre- vedayatīti vedanā iti | (u) ayaṃ padasyārthaḥ yat sanimittaṃ tat sakāritram | prajñaptau sanimittāmimāṃ sukhāṃ duḥkhāmaduḥkhāsukhāṃ [vedanāṃ] kāyagatāṃ cittamanubhavati | ata ucyate vedayatīti |
body.translated_text: (Question) That which feels (<s>vedayati</s>) — that is feeling. Or: that which is felt (<s>vedyate</s>) — that is feeling. If 'that which feels,' then feeling is different from pleasure and the rest. But the <s>sūtra</s> says: 'Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.' If 'that which is felt,' then by what is it felt? If feeling feels, [there would be circularity]. (Answer) Regarding the cause, [the word] 'pleasure' is used. Just as [one says] 'fire is painful' and 'fire is pleasant.' Therefore the experiential knowledge of the cause is called 'pleasant feeling.' Beings feel this feeling — therefore 'that which feels' is feeling. (Question) Feeling does not belong to beings. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'That which feels — that is feeling.' (Answer) The meaning of the word is that whatever has a sign (<s>nimitta</s>) has a function (<s>kāritra</s>). In designation, the mind experiences this pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling occurring in the body, together with its sign. Therefore it is said: 'It feels.'

body.text: (pṛ) sūtre vedanānāmanubhavadarśanamuktam | yoginastasmin samaye kathamutpadyate sukhaduḥkhāduḥkhāsukhānāṃ nimittam | kiṃ tasya tasmin samaye duḥkhasaṃjñā notpadyate | (u) sarvaṃ duḥkhamityalabdhvā sa tisro vedanā anusmarati | (pṛ) yadi manovijñānavṛttyā catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni bhavanti | kathamucyate kāyikaṃ sukhamiti | (u) sarvāsu vedanāsu evaṃ smṛtyunubandhāt syāt idaṃ kāyikaṃ sukham idaṃ caitasikaṃ sukhamiti | smṛtyupasthānabhāvanākāle kāye sukhasaṃjñotpadyate | tatra smṛtyunubandhāt kāyikaṃ sukhamityucyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) In the <s>sūtra</s>, the experience and seeing of feelings is stated. For the <s>yogin</s> at that time, how does the sign of pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings arise? Does not the perception of suffering arise for him at that time? (Answer) Without having attained [the realization that] everything is suffering, he recollects the three feelings. (Question) If the four foundations of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>) function through the activity of mind-consciousness, how is it said 'bodily pleasure'? (Answer) In all feelings, because of the continuity of mindfulness, it would be: 'This is bodily pleasure, this is mental pleasure.' At the time of cultivating the foundations of mindfulness, the perception of pleasure arises in the body. Because of the continuity of mindfulness there, it is called 'bodily pleasure.'

body.text: (pṛ) yadi sarvā vedanāścaitasikāḥ | kasmāt kāyikī vedanetyucyate | (u) tīrthikānāṃ kṛta ucyate | tīrthikā hi vadanti vedanā ātmaniśritā iti | ato bhagavānāha- vedanāḥ kāyaṃ cittañca niśritā iti | (pṛ) katamā kāyikī vedanā | (u) pañcendriyāṇyupādāyotpadyamānā vedanā kāyikī vedanā | ṣaṣṭhamindriyamupādāyotpadyamānā vedanā caitasikī (pṛ) āsāṃ katamā sāmiṣā katamā nirāmiṣā | (u) kleśā āmiṣāḥ | kleśānuśayitā vedanā sāmiṣā | kleśānanuśayitā vedanā nirāmiṣā |
body.translated_text: (Question) If all feelings are mental factors, why is it said 'bodily feeling'? (Answer) This is said for the sake of the <s>tīrthikas</s>. For the <s>tīrthikas</s> say: 'Feeling depends on the self.' Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Feelings depend on the body and the mind.' (Question) Which is bodily feeling? (Answer) Feeling that arises depending on the five sense-faculties is bodily feeling. Feeling that arises depending on the sixth sense-faculty [mind] is mental feeling. (Question) Among these, which is 'with bait' (<s>sāmiṣā</s>) and which is 'without bait' (<s>nirāmiṣā</s>)? (Answer) Defilements (<s>kleśa</s>) are the 'bait' (<s>āmiṣa</s>). Feeling underlain by defilements is 'with bait.' Feeling not underlain by defilements is 'without bait.'

body.text: (pṛ) katamā duḥkhā vedanā nirāmiṣā | (u) prahīṇāmiṣasya yā duḥkhā vedanā sā nirāmiṣā | āmiṣāṇāṃ viruddhā duḥkhā vedanā itīyaṃ nirāmiṣetyucyate | (pṛ) sāmiṣāṃ nirāmiṣāmuktvā kasmātpunarucyate kāmaniśritā naiṣkramyaniśriteti | kāma eva āmiṣaḥ | naiṣkramyameva nirāmiṣatā | (u) pūrvaṃ sāmānyata uktamāmiṣamiti | idānīṃ punaḥkāma āmiṣaheturiti pravibhajyocyate | yathocyate sūtre- asti sāmiṣā prītiḥ asti nirāmiṣā prītiḥ | asti nirāmiṣato nirāmiṣatarā prītiriti | sāmiṣā prītiriti pañcakāma guṇān pratītyotpadyate prītiḥ | nirāmiṣā prītiriti yaduta prathamadhyāna[jā]prītiḥ | nirāmiṣato nirāmiṣatarāprītiriti yaduta dvitīyadhyānajā prītiḥ | yā vedanā nirvāṇamātrārthā sā naiṣkramyaniścitetyucyate | ataḥ punarucyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) Which painful feeling is 'without bait'? (Answer) The painful feeling of one whose 'bait' has been abandoned is 'without bait.' Painful feeling opposed to the 'bait' — this is called 'without bait.' (Question) Having spoken of 'with bait' and 'without bait,' why is it further said 'dependent on sense-pleasures' (<s>kāmaniśritā</s>) and 'dependent on renunciation' (<s>naiṣkramyaniśritā</s>)? Sense-pleasure itself is the bait. Renunciation itself is the absence of bait. (Answer) Previously, 'bait' was stated generally. Now, it is further analyzed: 'Sense-pleasure is the cause of the bait.' As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There is joy with bait; there is joy without bait; and there is joy more without bait than the baitless.' 'Joy with bait' means the joy that arises depending on the five qualities of sense-pleasure. 'Joy without bait' means the joy born of the first <s>dhyāna</s>. 'Joy more without bait than the baitless' means the joy born of the second <s>dhyāna</s>. Feeling whose sole purpose is <s>Nirvāṇa</s> is called 'determined by renunciation.' Therefore it is stated again.

body.text: (pṛ) pañcasvindriyeṣu kasmādduḥkhā vedanā sukhā vedaneti pratyaṅgaṃ dvidhā vibhaktā | kiṃ nāstyupekṣā vedanā | (u) daurmanasyaṃ saumanasyañcāvaśyaṃ saṃjñāvikalpenotpannam | sukhā duḥkhā tu nāvaśyaṃ saṃjñāvikalpādhīnā | upekṣāvedanāyāṃ saṃjñāvikalpasyātisūkṣmatvānnāsti dvaidham | tṛtīyadhyāne manovijñānaṃ vedyate | kasmātsukhamasti na prītiḥ | (u) susraṃ sarvakāyacittaṃ gahanamāpūrayatīti sukhamucyate | prītistu cittamātramāpūrayati na kāyam | atastṛtīyadhyāne prītiviśeṣaṃ niśrityocyate kāyena sukhaṃ pratisaṃvedayatīti |
body.translated_text: (Question) In the five sense-faculties, why is it divided into two for each — painful feeling and pleasant feeling? Is there no equanimous feeling (<s>upekṣāvedanā</s>)? (Answer) Displeasure (<s>daurmanasya</s>) and elation (<s>saumanasya</s>) necessarily arise through conceptual discrimination (<s>saṃjñāvikalpa</s>). But pleasant and painful [feelings] do not necessarily depend on conceptual discrimination. In equanimous feeling, because conceptual discrimination is extremely subtle, there is no twofold division. In the third <s>dhyāna</s>, mental consciousness is experienced. Why is there happiness (<s>sukha</s>) but not joy (<s>prīti</s>)? (Answer) That which flows well (<s>susra</s>) and fills the entirety of body and mind is called 'happiness.' But joy fills only the mind, not the body. Therefore, in the third <s>dhyāna</s>, depending on the particular [absence of] joy, it is said: 'One experiences happiness with the body.'

body.text: (pṛ) tisṛṣu vedanāsu kā ghaniṣṭhakleśajananī | (u) ābhidharmikāḥ kecidvadanti sukhā vedaneti | kasmāt | pūrvokta [vedanā]pratyayavedanāyā duḥkhataratvāt | [anye] ābhidharmikā vadanti duḥkhā vedaneti | kasmāt | sattvāḥ duḥkhābhihatāḥ sukhārthitvāt ghaniṣṭhaṃ kleśamutpādayanti iti | vividhasukhebhyo 'tyalpaṃ duḥkhamatiricyate | yathā pañcakāmaguṇasampannasya puruṣasya maśakapataṅgadaṃśe yo duḥkhānubhavo bhavati | na tādṛśaṃ rūṣādipañcakāmaguṇānāṃ sukham | yādṛśañca jīvatāṃ putrāṇāṃ śatena sukham, na tadekaputramṛtitulyam | saṃsāre ca duḥkhā vedanā bahulā | na tathā sukhā vedanā | kasmāt | bahavaḥ sattvāḥ
body.translated_text: (Question) Among the three feelings, which is the most intense generator of defilements? (Answer) Certain <s>Ābhidharmikas</s> say: 'Pleasant feeling.' Why? Because the previously stated feeling that conditions [further] feeling is more painful [than itself]. Other <s>Ābhidharmikas</s> say: 'Painful feeling.' Why? Because beings, afflicted by suffering, desiring happiness, generate intense defilements. Even a very small amount of suffering surpasses the various pleasures. For example, for a person endowed with the five qualities of sense-pleasure, the suffering experienced from mosquitoes, moths, and gadflies — [the pleasure] from the five qualities of sense-pleasure such as form and the rest is not equal to that [suffering]. And the happiness from a hundred living sons is not equal to the [suffering of] the death of a single son. And in <s>saṃsāra</s>, painful feeling is predominant, not pleasant feeling. Why? Because many beings

body.text: tisṛṣu durgatiṣūpapannā devamanuṣyebhyo nikṛṣṭāḥ | nāvaśyaṃ svabhāvamadhiṣṭhāya duḥkhasya lābhaḥ | sukhārthitāmadhiṣṭhāya lābho bālābho vāsti | yathā kṣetre tṛṇavīraṇāni svayaṃ prarohanti na sasyāni | duḥkhāṃ vedanāṃ pratītya guruke pāpakarmaṇi pravartate | kasmāt | duḥkhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ pratighānuśayo 'sti | yathoktam- pratigho gurataraṃ pāpam iti |
body.translated_text: are born in the three lower destinies (<s>durgati</s>), inferior to gods and humans. Suffering is not necessarily obtained depending on one's own nature. [Rather] it is obtained depending on the desire for happiness — obtained either by the foolish or not obtained [at all]. Just as in a field, weeds and grass sprout by themselves, not crops. Depending on painful feeling, one engages in heavy evil <s>karma</s>. Why? Because in painful feeling, the latent tendency of aversion (<s>pratighānuśaya</s>) exists. As stated: 'Aversion is a heavier sin.'

body.text: ābhidharmikāḥ kecidāhuḥ- aduḥkhāsukhotpadyate | kasmāt | atrāsti mohānuśayaḥ | sarvakleśānāṃ mūlaṃ mohaḥ | sā ca vedanā sūkṣmā | tatra kleśānāṃ jñānasya duranubhāvatvāt | sā ca vedanā sattvānāṃ prakṛtiḥ | sukhaduḥkhe cāgantuke | sā ca vedanā triṣu dhātuṣu vyāptā | na tathānye dve | vedaneyaṃ cirajīvinī | tadvedanārāgaṃ pratītya jīvati aśīti mahākalpasahasrāṇi duḥkhalakṣaṇān skandhānanubhavati | sā ca nirvāṇavirodhinī | kasmāt | tatra hyutpadyate śāntalakṣaṇaṃ nirvāṇalakṣaṇam | na punaḥ pāramārthikaṃ nirvāṇaṃ labhyate | kiñca sā āryamārgadoṣakaraṇī | yathoktaṃ- visaṃyogasvabhāvaṃ pratītya vimuktirlabhyata iti | sukhā vedanā duḥkhā vedanā tu laukikamārgasyāpi doṣaprāpiṇī | sā ca vedanā āsaṃsāraṃ vyavatiṣṭhate | santānasamucchede samucchidyate | ato ghaniṣṭhakleśajananī ||
body.translated_text: Certain <s>Ābhidharmikas</s> say: 'Neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] [is the most intense generator of defilements].' Why? Because therein exists the latent tendency of delusion (<s>mohānuśaya</s>). Delusion is the root of all defilements. And that feeling is subtle. Therein, because of the difficulty of the influence of knowledge upon defilements [it generates intense defilements]. And that feeling is the natural state (<s>prakṛti</s>) of beings. Pleasant and painful [feelings] are adventitious. And that feeling pervades the three realms (<s>tridhātu</s>); the other two do not [pervade all three] equally. That feeling is long-lasting. Depending on the desire for that feeling, one lives and experiences the aggregates characterized by suffering for eighty thousand great <s>kalpas</s>. And that feeling is opposed to <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Why? Because therein arises the characteristic of peace, the characteristic of <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. But one does not obtain ultimate <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Furthermore, that feeling is detrimental to the noble path. As stated: 'Depending on the nature of disjoining (<s>visaṃyoga</s>), liberation is obtained.' But pleasant feeling and painful feeling are detrimental even to the mundane path. And that feeling persists throughout <s>saṃsāra</s>. It is destroyed [only] upon the destruction of the continuity [of existence]. Therefore it is the most intense generator of defilements.

body.text: vedanāpraśnavargo dvayaśītitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the eighty-second chapter, the Chapter on Questions about Feeling (<s>vedanāpraśnavarga</s>).

body.text: 83 pañcavedanendriyavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 83. Chapter on the Five Feeling-Faculties (<s>pañcavedanendriyavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) sukhendriyaṃ yāvadupekṣendriyaṃ kutra vartate | (u) sukhendriyaṃ duḥkhendriyañca kāyagatam | yathākāyalābhaṃ yāvaccatvāri dhyānāni bhavanti | anyāni trīṇi cittagatāni | yathācittalābhaṃ yāvadbhavāgraṃ bhavati | (pṛ) yathoktaṃ sūtre daurmanasyendriyaṃ prathamadhyāne nirudhyate | saumanasyendriyaṃ tṛtīyadhyāne nirudhyate | sukhendriyaṃ caturthadhyāne nirudhyate upekṣendriyaṃ nirodhasamāpattau nirudhyate | iti | ato bhavaduktamayuktam | (u)
body.translated_text: (Question) Where do the faculty of happiness (<s>sukhendriya</s>) up to the faculty of equanimity (<s>upekṣendriya</s>) operate? (Answer) The faculty of happiness and the faculty of suffering pertain to the body. They exist as far as the [range of] bodily attainment, up to the four <s>dhyānas</s>. The other three pertain to the mind. They exist as far as the [range of] mental attainment, up to the summit of existence (<s>bhavāgra</s>). (Question) As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The faculty of displeasure (<s>daurmanasyendriya</s>) ceases in the first <s>dhyāna</s>. The faculty of elation (<s>saumanasyendriya</s>) ceases in the third <s>dhyāna</s>. The faculty of happiness (<s>sukhendriya</s>) ceases in the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>. The faculty of equanimity (<s>upekṣendriya</s>) ceases in the cessation attainment (<s>nirodhasamāpatti</s>).' Therefore what you have said is untenable. (Answer)

body.text: bhavaduktasūtreṇa duḥkhendriyaṃ prathamadhyāne vartate | bhavatāṃ śāsane tu prathamadhyānaṃ vastuto 'duḥkhendriyam | ato na śraddheyaṃ syādidaṃ sūtram |
body.translated_text: According to the <s>sūtra</s> you have cited, the faculty of suffering (<s>duḥkhendriya</s>) operates in the first <s>dhyāna</s>. But in your teaching, the first <s>dhyāna</s> is in reality without the faculty of suffering. Therefore this <s>sūtra</s> should not be trusted.

body.text: (pṛ) rūpārūpyadhātau kuśaladharmān samyak bhāvayato duḥkhaṃ daurmanasyaṃ nasyāt | (u) traidhātukaṃ sarvaṃ duḥkham | dvayorūrdhvadhātvāraudārike duḥkhe 'satyapi sūkṣmaṃ duḥkhamastyeva | kenedaṃ jñāyate | caturṣu dhyāneṣūcyante catvāri iryāpathāni | yatrāstīryāpatham | tatra sarvaṃ duḥkhaḥ syāt | rūpadhātau ca santi cakṣuḥ śrotrakāyavijñānāni | eṣāṃ vijñānānāṃ yā kācidvedanā sā duḥkhā vā sukhā vā bhavati | ekasmādiryāpathādaparamiryāpathamarthyata ityato jñāyate duḥkhamastīti | sūtre pṛcchati- rūpāṇāṃ ka āsvādaḥ | yaduta rūpaṃ pratītyotpadyate sukhaṃ saumanasyam | kaśca rūpāṇāmādīnavaḥ | yatkiñcanarūpaṃ [sarvaṃ tat] anityaṃ duḥkhaṃ vipariṇāmadharma iti rūpadhātoḥ sarūpatvāt astyāsvādacittaṃ, astyādīnavacittam | ato 'sti sukhaṃ duḥkham | yogī dhyānasamādhiṣu rajyate copekṣate ca | sukhavedanāpratyayatvādavaśyaṃ rajyate | duḥkhavedanāpratyayatvādupekṣate | ato jñāyate 'sti sukhaṃ duḥkhamiti |
body.translated_text: (Question) In the form and formless realms, when one correctly cultivates wholesome <s>dharmas</s>, would not suffering and displeasure arise? (Answer) The entirety of the three realms (<s>traidhātuka</s>) is suffering. Even though gross suffering does not exist in the two upper realms, subtle suffering certainly exists. How is this known? In the four <s>dhyānas</s>, the four postures (<s>iryāpatha</s>) are mentioned. Wherever postures exist, there all suffering would exist. And in the form realm, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and body-consciousness exist. Whatever feeling belongs to these consciousnesses — it is either painful or pleasant. Since from one posture another posture is sought — therefore it is known that suffering exists. The <s>sūtra</s> asks: 'What is the gratification (<s>āsvāda</s>) of forms? The happiness and elation that arise depending on form. And what is the danger (<s>ādīnava</s>) of forms? Whatever form — all of it is impermanent, suffering, and of the nature of change.' Because the form realm is of the same nature as form, there exists a mind of gratification and a mind of [seeing] danger. Therefore there is happiness and suffering. A <s>yogin</s> becomes attached to and becomes equanimous toward the <s>dhyānas</s> and <s>samādhis</s>. He necessarily becomes attached because of pleasant feeling as a condition. He becomes equanimous because of painful feeling as a condition. Therefore it is known that happiness and suffering exist.

body.text: bhagavānāha- vāgādayaḥ prathamadhyānasya śalyam | vitarkacārau dvitīyadhyānasya śalyam | yāvannaivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanasya saṃjñā vedanā ca śalyam iti | śalyamiti duḥkhamityarthaḥ | ato jñāyate duḥkhamiti | sarve 'pi pañcaskandhā duḥkhaṃ vihiṃsanaduḥkham | yathā kāmadhātukavedanā vihiṃsakatvāt duḥkham | ūrdhvadhātukavedanāyā api vihiṃsanamastīti kasmānna duḥkham | yathā kāmadhātau vyādhyādayo 'ṣṭa saṃskārā ucyante | rūpārūpyadhātvorapi tathāṣṭasaṃskārāḥ samānamuktā iti kasmānnāsti duḥkham | rūpadhātāvābhāyā nyūnatā vātiśayo vocyate | ato jñāyate rūpadhātukakarmāpi vibhaktam iti | karmavibhāgādavaśyaṃ duḥkhavipākakarmalābhinā bhavitavyam | āha ca sūtram- atra santīrṣyāmātsaryādayaḥ kleśā
body.translated_text: The Blessed One said: 'Speech and the rest are the thorn of the first <s>dhyāna</s>. Discursive and sustained thought (<s>vitarkacāra</s>) are the thorn of the second <s>dhyāna</s>. Up to: perception and feeling are the thorn of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (<s>naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana</s>).' 'Thorn' means suffering. Therefore it is known that suffering [exists in all realms]. And all five aggregates are suffering — the suffering of being harmed (<s>vihiṃsanaduḥkha</s>). Just as feeling in the desire realm is suffering because of being harmful — the feeling of the upper realms too involves harm — why then is it not suffering? Just as in the desire realm, the eight formations beginning with illness and the like are stated — in the form and formless realms too, eight formations are equally stated — why then is there no suffering? In the form realm, [rebirth may involve] decline, deficiency, or excess. Therefore it is known that <s>karma</s> of the form realm is also differentiated. Because of the differentiation of <s>karma</s>, one necessarily obtains <s>karma</s> whose ripening is suffering. And the <s>sūtra</s> says: 'Herein there exist defilements such as jealousy (<s>īrṣyā</s>), avarice (<s>mātsarya</s>), and the rest

body.text: iti | yathā brahmā brahmāṇamāmantyāha- dhrūvamidaṃ sthānam mā bhavantaḥ śramaṇaṃ gautamamupasaṅkramata iti | āgatyāpi mahābrahmā bhavantamanuyogamāpṛcchati | uktañca sūtre- caturthadhyānamupasampanno 'kuśalān dharmān prajahātīti | api coktaṃ sūtre- tatrāsti mithyādṛṣṭiḥ kleśa iti | īdṛśāḥ kleśā evākuśalā duḥkhavipākaprāpakāḥ syuḥ | kasmānnāsti duḥkham | ābhidharmikā āhuḥ- sarve kleśā akuśalā iti | tatra kathaṃ nāsti duḥkhā vedanā |
body.translated_text: .' Just as <s>Brahmā</s>, summoning another <s>Brahmā</s>, said: 'This abode is permanent — do not, O sirs, approach the renunciant <s>Gautama</s>.' Even the great <s>Brahmā</s>, having come, asks you a question of investigation. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'One who has attained the fourth <s>dhyāna</s> abandons unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>.' Furthermore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Therein there exists wrong view and defilement.' Such defilements, being unwholesome, would produce ripening as suffering. Why then is there no suffering? The <s>Ābhidharmikas</s> say: 'All defilements are unwholesome.' If so, how can painful feeling not exist there?

body.text: uktañca sūtre- rūpārāmā [bhikṣavo] devamanuṣyāḥ rūparatā rūpasamuditāḥ | rūpavipariṇāmavirāganirodhāt duḥkhā [bhikṣavo] devamanuṣyā viharanti | iti | evaṃ yāvadvijñāne 'pi | ato jñāyate sarveṣāmavītarāgāṇāmasti daurmanasyaṃ saumanasyamiti | priya[yoga]pratyayaṃ saumanasyaṃ bhavati | tatpriyaviyogapratyayaṃ daurmanasyaṃ bhavati | prākṛtānāmajñānāṃ kasya śaktibalena priyaprāptipratyayaṃ saumanasyaṃ na bhavati | hānau ca na daurmanasyam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- mārgaṃ pratipannasyaivāyuṣo 'nte rūpe saumanasyaṃ daurmanasya ñca nāsti iti | ato jñāyate sarveṣāṃ prākṛtānāṃ saumanasyaṃ daurmanasyaṃ sadānuvartate iti |
body.translated_text: And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'O monks, gods and humans delight in form, are pleased by form, are gratified by form. Through the change, fading, and cessation of form, gods and humans, O monks, dwell in suffering.' Likewise up to consciousness as well. Therefore it is known that for all who are not free from passion, displeasure and elation exist. Elation arises conditioned by the union with what is beloved. Displeasure arises conditioned by separation from what is beloved. Among ordinary, ignorant people — by whose power of ability does elation conditioned by the attainment of what is beloved not arise? And displeasure not [arise] upon loss? As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'For one who has entered the path, at the end of life, there is neither elation nor displeasure regarding form.' Therefore it is known that for all ordinary beings, elation and displeasure constantly follow.

body.text: bhagavān svayamāha- daurmanasyavigataṃ saumanasyavigatañcaikaṃ cittamupekṣāyāmupavicaratītyayamarhato guṇa iti | ṣaḍupekṣopavicārāścāryacaritānyeva na prākṛtānām | prākṛtāḥ kadācidupekṣāyāmupavicaranti | na tat jñānapratyayatathā | yathoktaṃ sūtre- prākṛtānāṃ yadupekṣācittaṃ sarvaṃ tat rūpaniśritaṃ na rūparāgavimuktam iti | ato jñāyate prākṛtānāṃ nāstyupekṣācittamiti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ rāgānuśayaḥ iti | yadi nāsti tasya sukhā vedanā | kutra rāgo 'nuśayīta |
body.translated_text: The Blessed One himself said: 'A single mind that is free from displeasure and free from elation moves about in equanimity — this is a quality of the <s>Arhat</s>.' And the six equanimous investigations (<s>ṣaḍupekṣopavicāra</s>) are practices of the Noble Ones alone, not of ordinary beings. Ordinary beings sometimes move about in equanimity, but that is not [the equanimity] conditioned by knowledge. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Whatever equanimous mind of ordinary beings — all of that depends on form and is not freed from desire for form.' Therefore it is known that ordinary beings do not have [true] equanimous mind. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'In pleasant feeling, the latent tendency of passion (<s>rāgānuśaya</s>) [is present].' If he does not have pleasant feeling, where would passion become latent?

body.text: yadbhavato mataṃ- kadācidaduḥkhāsukhāyāṃ [vedanāyāṃ] rāgānuśayo 'nuśeta iti | tat sūtre nāsti vacanasthānam | uttamabhūmau ca pravṛtte kāyacitte śāntasukhe na mahadanugṛhīte staḥ | yathoktam- devāḥ kalpasahasramekatra niṣīdanti iti | yadi [te] duḥkhopavicāriṇaḥ
body.translated_text: Your view that 'sometimes in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the latent tendency of passion would become latent' — that has no basis in the <s>sūtra</s>. And in the highest level of existence, when the body and mind are engaged in tranquil happiness, they are not greatly benefited. As stated: 'Gods sit in one place for a thousand <s>kalpas</s>.' If they were those who experience suffering

body.text: na te tadiryāpatheṣu dīrghakālaṃ sthātuṃ śaknuvanti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- saptadināni samāviśya vimuktisukhaṃ vedayata iti | tatra ca praśrabdhisukhaṃ paramam | yathoktaṃ sūtre praśrabdhiriti sukhā vedanā iti | ato jñāyate sarvāsu bhūmiṣu asti sukhā vedaneti | yadbhavato matam- kadācitpraśrabdhisukhaṃ sukhavedanāto bhinnamiti | tadayuktam | yatkiñcidanugrāhakaṃ kāyagataṃ tat sukhamityucyate | ataḥ praśrabdhisukhaṃ na sukhavedanāto bhinnam |
body.translated_text: they would not be able to remain in those postures for a long time. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Having entered [concentration] for seven days, one experiences the bliss of liberation.' And therein, the bliss of tranquility (<s>praśrabdhisukha</s>) is supreme. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Tranquility (<s>praśrabdhi</s>) is pleasant feeling.' Therefore it is known that in all levels of existence, pleasant feeling exists. Your view that 'sometimes the bliss of tranquility is different from pleasant feeling' — that is untenable. Whatever is beneficial and pertains to the body is called 'happiness.' Therefore the bliss of tranquility is not different from pleasant feeling.

body.text: (pṛ) yadyūrdhvadhātukasamādhiṣu sukhaduḥkhasaumanasyadaurmanasyāni santi | kathaṃ dhyānasūtrānuguṇyaṃ bhavet | (u) sūtramidaṃ dharmatālakṣaṇavilomakam | yadyupekṣyate ko doṣaḥ | tatra ca sukhavihāraḥ śānto 'nāsaṅgarūpaḥ | nodbhavati audāriko rāgaḥ pratigho vā | tasmāt ucyate [tatra] nāsti sukhaṃ nāsti duḥkhamiti | tatra ca sukhaduḥkhe sūkṣme na pratīte staḥ | asiśastrādi duḥkhaṃ bandhamaraṇādi daurmanasyañca nāstītyato nāsti duḥkhamiti | yathocyate rūpadhāturanuṣṇāśīta iti | tatrāpi santi catvāri mahābhūtāni | kathaṃ vaktavyam anuṣṇāśīta iti | yaducyate triṣu dhyāneṣu sattvā ekakāyā ekanimittā iti | tatrāpyasti ābhāpravibhāgaḥ | yathā vadanti- yo dhyānavihārī na samyak styānamiddhauddhatyānyapanayati so 'viśuddhābha iti | yathālpajñaḥ puruṣo 'jña ityucyate | yathā ca laukikā vadanti alpalavaṇe bhojane alavaṇamiti | evaṃ tatra saumanalyaṃ daurmanasya ñca na pratītamito nāstītyucyate |

yadbhavadbhirūktaṃ nāsti tatra vitarka iti | uktañca sūtre bhagavatā saṃjñāpratyayo vitarka iti | atra saṃjñāyāṃ satyāṃ kathaṃ nāsti vitarkaḥ | ato jñāyate yāvadbhavāgramasti vitarkadharma iti | [cittasya] audārikatā vitarka iti dhyānadvaye niruddha ityucyate | tasmādūrdhvadhātudvaye 'pi santi sukhaduḥkhādayaḥ ||
iti vedanāskandhaḥ samāptaḥ |

84 duḥkhasatyaskandhe saṃskārādhikāre cetanāvargaḥ
sūtra uktam- ṣaṭ cetanākāyāḥ saṃskāraskandha iti | (pṛ) kā punaścetanā | prārthanā prāṇidhānaṃ cetanā | yathoktaṃ sūtre- avaracetanā avaraprārthanā avarapraṇidhānam | iti |

(pṛ) kasmāt jñāyate prārthanā cetanā iti | (u) uktaṃ sūtre- abhisaṃskurvantīti saṃskārāḥ iti | skandhābhisaṃskāratṛṣṇā prārthanā | yathoktaṃ sūtre abhisaṃskārāḥ tṛṣṇāniśritā iti | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- yathāpi [bhikṣavaḥ] yavakalāpī caturmahāpathe vikṣiptā syāt | [atha] ṣaṭ puruṣā āgaccheyuḥ | [vyābhaṅgihastāste tāṃ yavakalapī ṣaḍibharvyābhāṅgabhi]rhanyuḥ | atha saptamaḥ puruṣa āgacchet | [vyābhaṅgihastaḥ sa yavakalāpīṃ saptamyā vyabhaṅgayā] hanyāt | kiṃ punaridaṃ bhikṣavo bhavatāṃ manasi vipacyate na vā | vipacyate bhagavān | bhagavānāha- evamevāśrutavān pṛthagjano nityaṃ ṣaṭsparśairāhanyate | evaṃ hanyamānaḥ punarāyatibhavāya cetayate | evaṃ hi sa moghapuruṣaḥ suhatataro bhavati | iti | jñātavyaṃ prārthanaiva cetanā iti | kiñcāha- manaḥsañcetanāhāraḥ aṅgārakarṣavat draṣṭavya iti | aṅgāraḥ kasya dṛṣṭāntaḥ | āyatibhavāya cetayata ityasya | āyatibhavaścāṅgārakalpaḥ | sadā duḥkhānāṃ janakatvāt | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- asmīti [bhikṣava] iñjitam | asmīti [bhikṣavaḥ] prapañcitaṃ spanditaṃ

rāgagata iti | yatrāsmīti tatreñjitaṃ manaskṛtaṃ prapañjitaṃ spanditaṃ rāgagatam iti | yo 'bhisaṃskṛto dharmaḥ sa rāgagata ityucyate | [ato] jñātavyaṃ prārthanaiva cetanā iti | kiñcāha- yo bālo janmaprabhṛti maitrīmabhyasyati so 'kuśalaṃ karma karoti cetayate na vā | no bhagavan iti | kāmaprārthanayākuśalaṃ karotīti tadarthaḥ | āha ca cetanā karma cetayitvā ceti | tatra cetanā mānasaṃ karma | cetayitvā karma kāyikaṃ vācikam | cetayitveti prārthayitvā | upālisūtre uktam- nighaṇṭo nāthaputraḥ śītodakapratikṣipta uṣṇodakapratisevī | sa śītodakaṃ prārthayamāno 'labhamānaḥ kālaṃ kuryāt | manassaktadeveṣūpapadyate | ayaṃ śītacetanatvāttatropapadyata iti | ato jñāyate prārthanaiva cetanā iti |

(pṛ) yadbhavanāha- prārthanā cetaneti | sā [prārthanā] tṛṣṇālakṣaṇā na cetanā | kasmāt | sahetusapratyayasūtra uktam- aśrutavataḥ pṛthagjanasya yatprārthitaṃ tṛṣṇaiva sā iti | mahānidānasūtra uktam- tṛṣṇāṃ pratītya paryeṣaṇā ityādi | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- duḥkhī bhūyasā sukhārthī kiṃ na prārthayate iti | āha ca- yadā puruṣaḥ pañcakāmaguṇeṣu rajyate sa rāga eva prārthanā iti | api cāha- tṛṣṇāpratyayamupādānamiti paryeṣaṇaṃ pūrvaṃ bhavati paścādupādānam iti | paryeṣaṇameva tṛṣṇā | tasmāt prārthanā cetanātmiketi bhavatāṃ matamayuktam | yaduktaṃ bhavatā- praṇidhānaṃ cetaneti | tadayuktam | kasmāt upālisūtra uktam- asañcetanikaṃ karma na mahāsāvadyam | asañcetanikamajñānapurassaram | loke 'pi
jñānaṃ cetanaṃ manyate | yathā vadanti ko jñānī idaṃ kuryāt | kaḥ sacetana idaṃ kuryāditi | buddhimānitīmamarthaṃ vyavaharanti | ato jñāyate jñānameva cetaneti |

atra brūmaḥ | praṇidhānaṃ samudaya ityucyate | karmāṅgaṃ praṇidhānaṃ cetanā | yathā kañcitpraṇidadhannāha- ahamanāgate 'dhvani īdṛśaṃ kāyaṃ pratilapsya iti | (pṛ) yadi karmāṅgaṃ praṇidhānaṃ cetaneti | tadā nānāsravā cetanā syāt | cetanā ca tṛṣṇāhetuḥ | yathoktaṃsūtre- manaḥsañcetanāyā [bhikṣavaḥ] āhāre parijñāte tisrastṛṣṇāḥ parijñātā bhavanti | iti | ato jñāyate cetanā tṛṣṇāheturiti | (u) yadbravīṣi nānāsravā cetaneti | tadahamapi na bravīmi astyanāsravā cetaneti | kasmāt | abhisaṃskarotīti saṃskāra iti lakṣaṇāt cetanetyucyate | anāsravadharmasya anabhisaṃskāralakṣaṇatvāt | cetanāhyabhisaṃskāriṇī na nirodhadharmiṇī | yadavocaḥ cetanā tṛṣṇāheturiti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | sā hi tṛṣṇākāryaṃ tṛṣṇāṅgañca | na tṛṣṇāhetuḥ | kāryaprahāṇāddhetuprahāṇamuktaṃ yaduta manaḥsañcetanāhāraprahāṇāt tisṛṇāṃ tṛṣṇānāṃ prahāṇamiti | saṃskārādipratyayāścānena pratyuktāḥ | ato jñāyate tṛṣṇāṅgaṃ cetaneti | tṛṣṇā hi dvividhā hetubhūtā phalabhūtā ceti | hetuḥ tṛṣṇā bhavati phalaṃ prārthanā | prārthanaiva ca cetanā |

codayati | yadi hetvavasthāyāṃ tṛṣṇā phalāvasthāyāṃ cetanā | tadā na cetanā tṛṣṇāṅgaṃ syāt | kasmāt | yo dharmo hetvavasthaḥ so 'nyaḥ phalāvastha ścānyaḥ ityato jñāyate cetanā na tṛṣṇāṅgamiti | yathoktaṃ sahetusapratyaya sūtre mūḍhasya yatprārthitaṃ tṛṣṇaiva sā | tṛṣṇāvato yatkiñcicceṣṭhitaṃ tat karma iti | ataścetanā karmalakṣaṇānugateti tṛṣṇato 'nyā | yasya yasmin vastuni rāgaḥ tasya tasmin vastuni prārthanā | ato rāgāt jāyate prārthanā | prārthanaiva cetanā ato rāgaścetanāhetuḥ |
atrocyate | pūrvamuktaṃ mayā tṛṣṇāṅgaṃ cetaneti | tṛṣṇāyāḥ kevalamādyārambho rāgaḥ | raktasyā[rambhaḥ] prārthanā | yadavocaḥ praṇidhānaṃ [na cetane]ti | na tadyuktam | kasmāt |
praṇidhānaṃ cetanāṅgam | pūrva praṇidhānākhyaṃ karma | paścāt karmaṇi pravṛttiḥ | (pṛ) cetanā manaso 'nyā utānanyā | (u) mana eva cetanā | yathoktaṃ dharmapade-

manasā cet praduṣṭhena bhāṣate vā karoti vā |
tata enaṃ duḥkhamanveti | iti

prasannamanasāpyevam | ato jñāyate mana eva cetaneti | yadi cetanā na manaḥ | kiṃ mānasaṃ karma bhavet | mānasaṃ karma yanmana ālambana upavicarati | ataścetanā mana eva | sāmānyalakṣaṇato manaupavicāraścetanetyuktāpi sā bāhulyena kuśalākaśaladharmagatetyucyate | tasyāścetanāyā bahavaḥ prakārā bhavanti | yadā puruṣaḥ parasattvānāṃ kuśalamakuśalaṃ vā prārthayate | tadā cetanetyākhyāyato | yadālabdhaṃ vastu prārthayate | tadā prārthanā | yadāyatibhavaṃ prārthayate | tadā praṇidhānam | ato jñāyate ekaiva cetanā nānānāmabhirucyata iti |
duḥkhasatye saṃskārādhikāre cetanāvargaścaturaśītitamaḥ |
85 sparśavargaḥ

alambanagataṃ vijñānaṃ sparśa ityucyate | trayāṇāṃ sannipāta itīdaṃ na sparśalakṣaṇam | kasmāt | na hīndriyamālambanaṃ prāpnoti | ata indriyālambanayorna syāt sannipātaḥ | taistribhirālambanaṃ gṛhṇātīti sannipāta ityucyate |

pṛcchati | astyanyaścaitasikadharmaḥ sparśākhyaḥ | kasmāt | dvādaśanidānasūtre hyuktaṃsparśapratyayā vedaneti | āha ca- sparśo vedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskārāṇāṃ heturiti | yadi nāsti sa dharmaḥ | ko hetuḥ syāt | ato jñāyate asti ca caitasika dharmaḥ sparśākhya iti | ṣaṭ ṣaṭkasūtra uktaṃ- ṣaṭa sparśakāyā iti | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre avidyādīnāṃ sparśo [hetu]rdraṣṭavya iti | yadyucyate hetavaḥ prajñaptidharmā iti | na punaḥ pṛthak vaktavyaṃ sa

prajñaptidharma iti | sūtre cāsti dvividhaḥ sparśaḥ eka trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | aparaḥ trayāṇāṃ sannipātāt sparśa iti | ato jñāyate dvividhayoḥ sparśayorekaḥ svarūpasan aparaḥ prajñaptisanniti | yathā dinakaramaṇigomedakānāṃ trayāṇāṃ vibhinnaṃ tejaḥ | candrakāntayoścāpo vibhinnāḥ | pṛthivyādīnāmaṅkurā vibhinnāḥ | evaṃ sparśaścakṣurādīnāṃ vibhinna iti kimastyavadyam | yathā ca bhikṣūṇāṃ samavāyo na bhikṣubhyo 'nyaḥ | skandhānāṃ samavāyo na skandhebhyo 'nyaḥ | na vṛkṣadvayasaṃyogo vṛkṣadvayādbhidyate | na hastadvayasaṃyogo hastadvayādbhidyate | na bahuglānasamavāyo bahuglānebhyo bhidyate | evaṃ sparśo 'pi na cakṣurādibhyo bhidyata iti nāstyavadyam |

atra brūmaḥ | prāguktaṃ mayā [yadā] cittamālambanaṃ gṛhāti tasmin samaye sparśa iti | ataścittaṃ [yasmin] kāle vijñānotpattiheturbhavati | tadanantaraṃ vedanādayo dharmā utpadyante | ṣaṭhṣaṭkasūtre 'pyuktaṃ tasmin samaye sparśaṃ iti | idameva yuktam | na vayaṃ svīkurmaḥ sparśo 'yaṃ dvividha iti | sarvatroktaṃ trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | sparśadvevidhyasūtraṃ sadapi dharmalakṣaṇavirodhādupekṣyam | ata udāhṛtasūtramahetuḥ | yadi sparśo bhidyate jalatejovat | tadā kāritramapi bhidyeta | na tu dṛśyate pratyekaṃ kāritrabhedaḥ | ato jñāyate sa sparśo na tribhyo bhidyata iti |
body.translated_text: Here we reply: As I stated before — when the mind grasps its object, at that time there is contact (<s>sparśa</s>). Therefore, at the time when mind becomes the cause for the arising of consciousness, immediately afterward, <s>dharmas</s> such as feeling and the rest arise. In the <s>Ṣaṭṣaṭkasūtra</s> too it is said: 'At that time, contact [arises].' This alone is valid. We do not accept that 'contact is of two kinds.' Everywhere it is said: 'The conjunction of three is contact.' Even if a <s>sūtra</s> on the twofold nature of contact exists, it should be set aside because it contradicts the marks of <s>Dharma</s>. Therefore the cited <s>sūtra</s> is not a valid reason. If contact were differentiated like water and fire, then its causal efficacy (<s>kāritra</s>) too would be differentiated. But no differentiation of causal efficacy is seen individually. Therefore it is known that contact is not different from the three [factors].

body.text: kiñca yadi sparśaścaitasikadharmaḥ tadā anyebhyaścaitasikebhyo bhidyeta | kasmāt | sparśaścaitasikānāṃ pratyayaḥ | nahi sparśaḥ sparśasya pratyayo bhavati | utpattibhedānna caitasika dharmaḥ | (pṛ) sparśaviśeṣāt sparśapratyayā ścaitasikā iti | na sparśapratyayaḥ sparśaḥ | yathā vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇā na tṛṣṇāpratyayā vedanā | (u) sparśasya kiṃ viśeṣalakṣaṇaṃ yadanyacaitasikānāṃ noktaṃ syāt | na vastuto 'bhidhīyamānamasti | ato 'hetuḥ | vedanādyakālīnā tṛṣṇānantarakālīnā iti vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇā na tu tṛṣṇāpratyayā vedanā | yadi sparśo vyatiriktadharmaḥ | tallakṣaṇaṃ vaktavyam | na tūcyata iti jñātavyaṃ nāsti vibhinnaḥ [sparśa] iti | bhagavān vaidharmye 'pi sparśākhyāmāha | yathāha yo duḥkhopaghātaḥ sa āgatya janakāyaṃ spṛśatīti | āha ca sukhavedanāspṛṣṭena na pramattavyam | na duḥkhavedanāspṛṣṭena vidveṣṭavyam | asyāṃ vedanāyāṃ sparśa iti saṃjñāmāha | bhagavān sūcīlomaṃ yakṣamāha- tava
body.translated_text: Furthermore, if contact were a mental factor (<s>caitasikadharma</s>), then it would differ from the other mental factors. Why? Contact is the condition (<s>pratyaya</s>) of the mental factors. For contact is not the condition of itself. Because of the difference in arising, it is not a mental factor <s>dharma</s>. (Question) Due to a particular kind of contact, mental factors are conditioned by contact — but contact itself is not conditioned by contact. Just as craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) is conditioned by feeling (<s>vedanā</s>), but feeling is not conditioned by craving. (Answer) What distinctive characteristic does contact have that has not been stated for the other mental factors? In reality, nothing can be stated. Therefore that is not a valid reason. Feeling belongs to one time; craving belongs to the immediately subsequent time — therefore craving is conditioned by feeling, but feeling is not conditioned by craving. If contact is a separate <s>dharma</s>, its characteristic must be stated. Since it cannot be stated, it should be known that contact does not exist as a separate [entity]. The Blessed One uses the name 'contact' even for what is dissimilar. As he said: 'That which is a destructive affliction of suffering — that comes and touches (<s>spṛśati</s>) the person's body.' And he said: 'One touched by pleasant feeling should not be heedless. One touched by painful feeling should not be averse.' In this [context of] feeling, he uses the designation 'contact.' The Blessed One said to the <s>yakṣa</s> <s>Sūcīloma</s>: 'Your

body.text: saṃsparśaḥ pāpaka iti kāyamapanayāmi iti | yathā loke vadanti sukha uṣṇasaṃsparśa iti | tathā sparśāhāramapyāhuḥ | pāṇisparśa iti ca vadanti | ataḥ sarvatra kāyavijñānavijñeye vastuni sparśasaṃjñocyate |
body.translated_text: contact is evil — therefore I withdraw my body.' Just as in the world, people say: 'The warm contact is pleasant.' Likewise they speak of 'contact as nutriment' (<s>sparśāhāra</s>). And they say 'the touch of the hand.' Therefore, everywhere, in the object cognizable by body-consciousness, the designation 'contact' is used.

body.text: anyatracoktaṃ- andho na rūpaṃ spṛśati | rūpādyālambaneṣu sparśasaṃjñāñca vakti | iti | tatsparśavyavahārasyāniyatatvānnāsti ca caitasikadharmaḥ pṛthak | yaducyate caitasikaṃ, tatsparśalakṣaṇaviruddham | kasmāt | bhagavānāha- trayāṇāṃ sannipātaḥ sparśa iti | ato jñāyate nāsti pāramārthikaḥ pṛthak caitasikadharma iti | yo dharmaḥ kāyagataḥ sa sparśa ityucyate | yat vedanādīnāṃ caitasikānāṃ hetukriyāṃ prayacchati tasmin samaye sparśa iti nāma pradīyate ||
body.translated_text: It is also said elsewhere: 'A blind man does not touch form.' And in objects such as form and the rest, he uses the designation 'contact.' Because the usage of 'contact' is indeterminate, a separate mental factor <s>dharma</s> does not exist. What is called 'mental factor' contradicts the characteristic of contact. Why? The Blessed One said: 'The conjunction of three is contact.' Therefore it is known that a separate mental factor <s>dharma</s> does not exist ultimately. The <s>dharma</s> that pertains to the body — that is called 'contact.' That which provides the causal function for mental factors such as feeling and the rest — at that time, the name 'contact' is given.

body.text: sparśavargaḥ pañcāśītitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the eighty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Contact (<s>sparśavarga</s>).

body.text: 86 manaskāravargaḥ
body.translated_text: 86. Chapter on Mental Attention (<s>manaskāravarga</s>)

body.text: cittasyābhogo manaskāraḥ | sa manaskāra ābhogalakṣaṇaḥ | ataḥ pratimanaskāraṃ vibhinnaṃ cittamutpadyate | vadanti ca manaskāralakṣaṇaṃ vastavadhāraṇakṛditi | yathoktaṃ sūtreyadi cakṣurādhyātmikamāyatanamanupahataṃ bhavati | rūpaṃ nāhyamāyatanaṃ purovarti bhavati | cittāntarotpādakamanaskāraśca nāsti | tadā na cakṣurvijñānamutpadyata iti |
body.translated_text: The inclination (<s>ābhoga</s>) of mind is mental attention (<s>manaskāra</s>). That mental attention has the characteristic of inclination. Therefore, with each [act of] mental attention, a different mind arises. They also say that the characteristic of mental attention is 'that which causes the determination of an object.' As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'If the internal sense-base of the eye is unimpaired, and if the external sense-base of form is present in front, but there is no mental attention that generates another [mind-moment] — then eye-consciousness does not arise.'

body.text: (pṛ) kiṃ vijñānānāṃ jñānaṃ sarvaṃ manaskārabalenotpadyate kiṃ vā na | (u) na | kasmāt | vijñānānāṃ jñānotpādo naikāntikaḥ | kadācidābhogabalenotpadyate yathā prabalarāgādivarjitānām | kadācidindriyabalādutpadyate yathālokacakṣuṣkaḥ kaṇamṛju parīkṣate | kadācidālambanabalādutpadyate yathā dūrataḥ pradīpaṃ paśyan tasya kampaṃ paśyati | kadācitkuśalamabhyāsādutpadyate yathā śilpakarmādi | kadācitsatyagrahalakṣaṇenotpadyate | yathā rūpādhyavasāyaḥ | kadāciddharmasvarūpata utpadyate yathā kalpāvasāne dhyānam | yadācitkālenotpadyate
body.translated_text: (Question) Does all knowledge of the consciousnesses arise through the power of mental attention, or not? (Answer) No. Why? The arising of knowledge in the consciousnesses is not invariable. Sometimes it arises through the power of inclination — as for those free from intense passion and the rest. Sometimes it arises through the power of the sense-faculty — as when one with worldly eyes examines a sesame seed carefully. Sometimes it arises through the power of the object — as when one seeing a lamp from a distance sees its flickering. Sometimes it arises through habitual cultivation of wholesome [states] — as with craftsmanship and the like. Sometimes it arises through the characteristic of grasping truths — as with the determination of form. Sometimes it arises from the inherent nature of <s>dharmas</s> — as with <s>dhyāna</s> at the end of a cosmic age (<s>kalpa</s>). Sometimes it arises from [the condition of] time

body.text: yathālpāyuṣkānāṃ satvānāmakuśalaṃ cittam | kadācidupapattyāyatanata utpadyate yathā gavājādīnāṃ cittam | kadācitkāyabalāt utpadyate yathā strīpuruṣādīnāṃ cittam | kadācidvayoviśeṣādutpadyate yathā bālādīnāṃ cittam | kadācitklamathatandribhyāmutpadyate | kadācitkarmabalādutpadyate yathā kāmānāṃ vedanā | kadācitsamādhibalādutpadyate yathaikatra pratibaddhacitto vijñāne prakarṣaṃ prajānāti | kadācitsamādhiniyamādutpadyate yathānāvaraṇamārgānantaraṃ vimucyate | kadācicciranirvedādutpadyate yathā kaṭurasanirviṇṇo madhurasamabhilaṣati | kadācidabhirucivaśādutpadyate yathā rūpādīn prati | kadācidrūpadarśanābhilaṣitasya na śabdaśravaṇe tṛptirbhavati | tathā nīlādāvapi | saukumāryādutpadyate yathā lomākṣigataṃ sat cittasya duḥkhajanakaṃ nānyatra gatam | kadācidduḥkhamanādutpadyate yathāpagatākṣirujānnamāsvādyate | kadācidāvaraṇāpagamādutpadyate yathā kāmādyapagame taddoṣān prajānāti | kadācitkramaśa utpadyate | yathā avaraṃ pratītya madhyamamutpadyate | madhyamaṃ pratītyottamam | kadācitsarvata- utpadyate |
body.translated_text: — as with the unwholesome mind of beings of short lifespan. Sometimes it arises from the place of rebirth (<s>upapattyāyatana</s>) — as with the mind of cattle, goats, and the like. Sometimes it arises through the power of the body — as with the mind of women, men, and the like. Sometimes it arises through the specificity of age — as with the mind of children and the like. Sometimes it arises from fatigue and torpor (<s>klamathandri</s>). Sometimes it arises through the power of <s>karma</s> — as with the feeling [experienced] in sensual desires. Sometimes it arises through the power of <s>samādhi</s> — as when one whose mind is fixed on one point knows the excellence of consciousness. Sometimes it arises through the constraint of <s>samādhi</s> — as when one is liberated immediately following the unobstructed path (<s>ānāvaraṇamārga</s>). Sometimes it arises from prolonged disenchantment — as when one disgusted with a bitter taste desires a sweet taste. Sometimes it arises through the power of inclination — as toward form and the like. Sometimes, when one desires to see form, one is not satisfied by hearing sound — likewise with blue and the rest. Sometimes it arises from delicacy (<s>saukumārya</s>) — as when a hair lodged in the eye causes suffering to the mind, but not when lodged elsewhere. Sometimes it arises from the cessation of pain — as when one whose eye-pain has subsided relishes food. Sometimes it arises from the removal of an obstruction — as when, upon the removal of sensual desire and the like, one recognizes those faults. Sometimes it arises gradually — as when, depending on the inferior, the middling arises; depending on the middling, the superior. Sometimes it arises from all [conditions combined].

body.text: (pṛ) yadi sarvavijñānānāṃ jñānaṃ kramalakṣaṇam | kasmāducyate cittāntarajanakamanaskāro nāsti [pṛthaka] iti | (u) tīrthikānāṃ kṛta [ucyate] | tīrthikā hi vadanti ātmamanoyogādvijñānajñānamutpadyata iti | tadvyavahāradūṣaṇāya pradarśayati vijñānajñānāni samanantarapratyayānubandhīnīti | ata evamāha- kasyacit cittāntarajanakamanaskāre 'sati vijñānaṃ notpadyata iti | kasmāt | samanantarapratyayatvāttu vijñānajñānamekaikaṃ pratītyotpadyate | tadyathā vṛkṣaṃ chittvātha pātayati | pūrvamuktaṃ- vijñānāni naikakālikānīti | hetupratyayavaśādvijñānānāṃ jñānamaikaikaṃ krameṇodyate | vijñānadharmāḥ kramikāḥ syuḥ | nātmamanoyogāpekṣiṇaḥ | yathā bāhyavastūni aṅkurakāṇḍanālapatrapuṣpaphalāni kramikāni bhavanti | tathādhyātmikadharmā api | vijñānajñānamaikaikaṃ kramikaṃ bhavati |
body.translated_text: (Question) If the knowledge of all consciousnesses has the characteristic of being sequential, why is it said: 'There is no separate mental attention that generates another [mind-moment]'? (Answer) That was said for the purpose of [refuting] the <s>tīrthikas</s>. For the <s>tīrthikas</s> say: 'Through the conjunction of the self (<s>ātman</s>) and mind, the knowledge of consciousness arises.' To refute that convention, he demonstrates that the knowledge-arisings of consciousness follow the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>). Therefore he said: 'For a certain one, when the mental attention that generates another [mind-moment] does not exist, consciousness does not arise.' Why? Because consciousness-knowledge arises one by one depending on [its] cause as the immediately preceding condition. Just as one first cuts a tree and then fells it. As stated before: 'Consciousnesses are not simultaneous.' Through the power of causes and conditions, the knowledge of consciousnesses rises one by one sequentially. Consciousness-<s>dharmas</s> are sequential — they do not depend on the conjunction of a self and mind. Just as external things — sprouts, stalks, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits — are sequential, so too internal <s>dharmas</s>. Consciousness-knowledge arises one by one sequentially.

body.text: samyak mithyeti manaskāro dvividhaḥ | samyagiti yat yoniśo [manaskāraḥ] | yathā vadanti samyak praśnaḥ samyag dūṣaṇaṃ, dūṣaṇapraśnayoridaṃ sayukti samādhānamiti | dharmāṇāmanityatādi pāramārthikapraśnaḥ samyagityucyate | sādhyasādhanānuvidhānañca samyagityucyate |
body.translated_text: Mental attention is of two kinds: right (<s>samyak</s>) and wrong (<s>mithyā</s>). 'Right' means wise attention (<s>yoniśo manaskāra</s>). As they say: 'A right question, a right refutation — and a reasoned resolution of the question and refutation.' The ultimate investigation of the impermanence and such of <s>dharmas</s> is called 'right.' And the conformity with what is to be proven and the means of proof is called 'right.'

body.text: ato jñāyate yuktayanuyāyimanaskāraḥ tattvamanaskāra ityādayaḥ samyaṅ manaskārāḥ | yathāpudgalaṃ yathākālaṃ manaskāraśca samyaṅ manaskāraḥ | yathā kāmabahulasyāśubhabhāvanā samyaṅmanaskāraḥ | citte 'balīne vyutthānalakṣaṇaṃ smayaṅmanaskāraḥ | etadviparītaṃ mithyāmanaskāraḥ | samyaṅmanaskāraḥ sarvaguṇān sampādayati | mithyāmanaskāraḥ sarvakleśānutthāpayati |
body.translated_text: Therefore it is known that mental attention that follows reasoning, attention to reality, and the like — these are right mental attention. Mental attention that is suited to the person and suited to the time is also right mental attention. For example, the contemplation of the impure (<s>aśubhabhāvanā</s>) for one with much desire is right mental attention. When the mind is weak, the characteristic of arousal is right mental attention. The opposite of this is wrong mental attention. Right mental attention accomplishes all virtues. Wrong mental attention gives rise to all defilements.

body.text: manaskāravargaḥ ṣaḍaśītitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the eighty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on Mental Attention (<s>manaskāravarga</s>).

body.text: 87 chandavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 87. Chapter on Desire (<s>chandavarga</s>)

body.text: sābhilāṣaṃ cittaṃ chandaityucyate | kasmāt | sūtramāha kāmacchanda iti | kāmān chandayatīti kāmacchandaḥ | uktañca sūtre- chando dharmamūlam iti | chanda- prārthanayā sarvadharmānāpnotīti dharmamūlamityucyate | kiñcāha- yadi bhikṣavo mama śāsane tīvracchandā [vartadhve] | tada mama śāsanaṃ suciraṃ tiṣṭhet iti | yaccittaikatānatvenābhilaṣyate | tattīvracchanda ityucyate | ṛddhipāde coktam- chandasamādhiḥ vīryasamādhiḥ cittasamādhirmīmāṃsāsamādhiriti | yaccittenābhilaṣyate sa chandaḥ | ayaṃ vīryasahakāriṇā prajñāsamādhiṃ sañcinotītyebhyaścaturbhyo 'bhilaṣitamṛddhyaṅgamiti nāmabhāg bhavati | āha ca- tvaṃ vihāyasā gamanaṃ chandayasi iti | tenakhalu samayena sa bhikṣuḥ pūrvaṃ svādhyāyabahulo viharati | so 'pareṇa samayenālpotsukastūṣṇīṃbhūtaḥ kaṣāyayati | atha khalu tasminvanaṣaṇḍe adhivasantī devatā tasya bhikṣordharmaśṛṇvantī yena sa bhikṣuḥ tenopasaṅkrāntaḥ | upasaṅkramya taṃ bhikṣuṃ gāthayādhyabhāṣata |
body.translated_text: Mind with aspiration is called 'desire' (<s>chanda</s>). Why? The <s>sūtra</s> says: 'Sensual desire (<s>kāmacchanda</s>)' — one who desires sensual pleasures is [said to have] sensual desire. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Desire is the root of <s>dharmas</s>.' Through the aspiration of desire, one obtains all <s>dharmas</s> — therefore it is called 'the root of <s>dharmas</s>.' Furthermore he said: 'O monks, if you abide with intense desire in my teaching, then my teaching will endure for a long time.' That which is aspired to with one-pointed absorption of mind — that is called 'intense desire.' In the bases of supernatural power (<s>ṛddhipāda</s>) it is said: 'Concentration of desire (<s>chandasamādhi</s>), concentration of energy (<s>vīryasamādhi</s>), concentration of mind (<s>cittasamādhi</s>), concentration of investigation (<s>mīmāṃsāsamādhi</s>).' That which is aspired to by the mind is desire. This, together with energy as its companion, accumulates the concentration of wisdom. From these four, the aspired factor of supernatural power receives its designation. And he said: 'You desire to travel through the sky.' At that time, that monk formerly dwelt devoted to self-study. He, at a later time, with little enthusiasm, remained silent and inactive. Then a deity dwelling in that forest grove, who was listening to that monk's <s>Dharma</s>, approached him and addressed him with a verse:

body.text:
kasmāt dharmapadāni tvaṃ bhikṣurnādhyepi bhikṣubhiḥ sukhaṃ vasan |
śrutvā ca dharmaṃ labhate prasādaṃ dṛṣṭe ca dharme labhate praśaṃsām || iti |
abhūt pūrvaṃ dharmapadeṣu chando yāvadvirāgeṇa samāgato 'smi |
yato virāgeṇa samāgato 'smi yatkiñcidṛṣṭaṃ śrutaṃ vā mataṃ vā |
body.translated_text:
'Why do you, a monk, not study the <s>Dharma</s>-verses? Living happily among monks,
having heard the <s>Dharma</s>, one obtains faith; and in the present life, one obtains praise.'
'There was formerly desire for the <s>Dharma</s>-verses, until I met with dispassion.
Since I met with dispassion, whatever was seen, heard, or thought —'

body.text: ājñāya nikṣepaṇamāhuḥ santa iti | ato jñāyate 'bhilaṣitaṃ chanda iti | abhilaṣitaṃ pratītya kāmeṣuchanda iti kāmacchandaḥ |
body.translated_text: 'The saints say that, having fully understood, one should set it down.' From this it is known that aspiration is desire (<s>chanda</s>). Depending on aspiration toward sensual pleasures, desire for sensual pleasures (<s>kāmacchanda</s>) [arises].

body.text: chandavargaḥ saptāśītitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the eighty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on Desire (<s>chandavarga</s>).

body.text: 88 prītivargaḥ
body.translated_text: 88. Chapter on Joy (<s>prītivarga</s>)

body.text: abhīpsite cittābhiratiḥ prītiḥ | yathoktaṃ- sattvā dhātulakṣaṇenākuśalaprītyā akuśalānuyāyinaḥ | kuśalena kuśalapriyāḥ itīyaṃ prītirityucyate | (pṛ) na dhātuḥ prītirbhavati | kasmāt | bhagavān yat sattvānāṃ nānādhātūn prajānāti tat dhātujñānabalam | yat nānādhimuktīḥ prajānāti tadadhimuktijñānabalam | ato dhātuḥ prītiśca (adhimuktiḥ) vibhinnetiḥ | (u) cirakālābhyāsopacitaṃ cittaṃ dhāturityucyate | yathādhātuca prītirutpadyate | ataścirakālamupacitaṃ cittajñānaṃ dhātujñānabalam | yathādhātusamutpannā prītiriti jñānam adhimuktijñānabalamiti | ata āha- sattvānāṃ yathādhātu santānamanuvartata iti | cirasañcitākuśalacittasyākuśale parā prītirbhavati | cirasañcitakuśalacittasya
body.translated_text: The delight of mind in what is wished for is joy (<s>prīti</s>). As stated: 'Beings, according to their elemental disposition (<s>dhātu</s>), with unwholesome joy, follow the unwholesome. With wholesome [disposition], they love the wholesome' — this is called joy. (Question) The elemental disposition (<s>dhātu</s>) is not joy. Why? When the Blessed One knows the various elemental dispositions of beings, that is the power of knowledge of dispositions (<s>dhātujñānabala</s>). When he knows the various inclinations (<s>adhimukti</s>), that is the power of knowledge of inclinations. Therefore the disposition and joy (and inclination) are distinct. (Answer) The mind accumulated through long habitual practice is called 'disposition' (<s>dhātu</s>). Joy arises in accordance with one's disposition. Therefore, the knowledge of the mind accumulated over a long time is the power of knowledge of dispositions. The knowledge that 'joy arises in accordance with the disposition' is the power of knowledge of inclinations. Therefore he said: 'According to the disposition of beings, the continuum follows along.' For one whose accumulated unwholesome mind is of long duration, there is supreme joy in the unwholesome. For one whose accumulated wholesome mind is of long duration,

body.text: kuśale prītisukham | śītārtasyoṣṇe prītirbhavatīdaṃ dṛṣṭahetukaṃ na dhātujam | ityayaṃ dhātoḥ prīteḥ pravibhāgaḥ ||
body.translated_text: there is joyful pleasure in the wholesome. When someone afflicted by cold finds joy in warmth — that has a visible cause, not born from disposition. This is the distinction between disposition-born and [visibly-caused] joy.

body.text: pritivargo 'ṣṭāśītitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the eighty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on Joy (<s>prītivarga</s>).

body.text: 89 śraddhāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 89. Chapter on Faith (<s>śraddhāvarga</s>)

body.text: cittasya
body.translated_text: The settling of the mind on its object is the characteristic of faith (<s>śraddhā</s>). (Question) Is not this fixed settling a characteristic of wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>)? The fixed settling that belongs to one who has abandoned doubt is the characteristic of wisdom. (Answer) The mental clarity (<s>cetasaḥ prasāda</s>) obtained through the instruction of the Noble Ones, without having seen the <s>dharma</s> oneself — that is called 'faith.' (Question) If so, then one who has seen the <s>dharma</s> oneself would not have faith. (Answer) That is indeed so. An <s>arhat</s> is without faith. As stated in the <s>Dharmapada</s>:

body.text: viṣayasamādhiḥ śraddhālakṣaṇam | (pṛ) nanu niyatasamādhirayaṃ prajñālakṣaṇam | niyatasamādhiḥ prahīṇavicikitsasya bhavatīti prajñālakṣaṇam | (u) dharmaṃ svayamadṛṣṭvā āryopadeśavaśāllabdhaścetasaḥ prasādaḥ śraddhetyucyate | (pṛ) tathā cet svayaṃ dharmadarśinaḥ śraddhā na syāt | (u) satyamevam | arhannaśraddhāvān bhavati | yathoktaṃ dharmapade-

aśraddhaścākṛtajñaśca sandhicchedaśca yo naraḥ |
[hatāvakāśo vāntāśaḥ] sa vai uttamapūruṣaḥ || iti |
body.translated_text:
He who is without faith, ungrateful, and a breaker of bonds,
[who has destroyed occasion and vomited out desires] — he indeed is the supreme person.

body.text: kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- ahaṃ bhagavan asmin vastuni yathā bhagavadvacanaṃ śraddhadha iti | yat svayaṃ dharadarśinaścittaṃ prasīdati | sā[pi] śraddhetyucyate | pūrvaṃ dharmaṃ śrutvā paścātkāyena sākṣātkaroti | tasyeyaṃ cintā bhavati sa dharmaḥ paramārthasatyo na mṛṣeti, cittañca prasīdati | sā śraddhā caturṣu avetyaprasādeṣvantargatā | tadyathā rogī pūrvaṃ bhiṣagvacane śraddadhāna auṣadhamupasevya rogānmuktaḥ paścāttasmin bhiṣaji prasannacitto bhavati | sā śraddhetyucyate |
body.translated_text: Furthermore, it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'I, Blessed One, have faith in this matter just as the Blessed One has spoken.' When the mind of one who has seen the <s>dharma</s> oneself becomes clear, that too is called 'faith.' Having first heard the <s>dharma</s>, one afterwards realizes it directly with the body. For that person, this thought arises: 'That <s>dharma</s> is the ultimate truth — it is not false,' and the mind becomes clear. That faith is included within the four confirmed confidences (<s>avetyaprasāda</s>). Just as a sick person, first having faith in the physician's words, takes medicine and becomes free from disease, afterwards becomes clear-minded toward that physician — that is called 'faith.'

body.text: śraddheyaṃ dvividhā mohajā jñānajeti | mohajā yat kuśalākuśalamacintayataḥ pūraṇādyasadācāryeṣūtpadyamānaścittaprasādaḥ | jñānajā yathā caturṣu [avetya] prasādeṣu buddhādiṣu cittaprasādaḥ | sā tridhā vibhaktā kuśalā akuśalā avyākṛtā ceti | (pṛ) akuśalā śraddhā kleśamahābhūmigataiva āśrāddhya dharmaḥ | neyaṃ śraddhā bhavati | (u) nāyamāśrāddhyadharmaḥ | śraddhā ca prasādalakṣaṇā | akuśalā śraddhāpi prasādalakṣaṇaiva | tathā no cet akuśalā vedanā vedanā na syāt | na ca tadyujyate vastutaḥ | tatastridhaiva vibhaktā | yā śraddhā indriyeṣu gaṇitā vimuktyanugāminī saptatriṃśabdodhipakṣikeṣu gatā sā niyamena kuśalaiva |
body.translated_text: This faith is twofold: born of delusion (<s>mohajā</s>) and born of knowledge (<s>jñānajā</s>). Born of delusion is the mental clarity that arises toward false teachers such as <s>Pūraṇa</s> and others, without considering what is wholesome and unwholesome. Born of knowledge is the mental clarity toward the <s>Buddha</s> and the rest in the four confirmed confidences (<s>avetyaprasāda</s>). That [faith] is divided threefold: wholesome (<s>kuśala</s>), unwholesome (<s>akuśala</s>), and indeterminate (<s>avyākṛta</s>). (Question) Unwholesome faith would simply be the <s>dharma</s> of faithlessness (<s>āśrāddhya</s>) belonging to the great ground of defilements (<s>kleśamahābhūmi</s>). It is not [real] faith. (Answer) It is not the <s>dharma</s> of faithlessness. Faith has the characteristic of mental clarity. Even unwholesome faith has the very characteristic of mental clarity. If that were not so, then unwholesome feeling would not be feeling — but that is not valid in reality. Therefore [faith] is divided precisely into three. That faith which is counted among the faculties (<s>indriya</s>), which leads to liberation (<s>vimuktyanugāminī</s>), and which is included among the thirty-seven limbs of awakening (<s>saptatriṃśad bodhipakṣika</s>) — that is invariably wholesome alone.

body.text: śraddhāvarga ekonanavatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the eighty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Faith (<s>śraddhāvarga</s>).

body.text: 90 vyavasāyavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 90. Chapter on Effort (<s>vyavasāyavarga</s>)

body.text: cetaso 'bhyutsāho vyavasāya ityucyate | sadānyadharmānniśrayate manaskāraṃ vā samādhiṃ vā | tatrāmyutsāhaḥ sadā cittaikāgratāsamudācāraḥ sa vyavasāya ityucyate | trividho vyavasāyaḥ kuśalo 'kuśalo 'vyākṛta iti | yat caturṣu samyakpradhāneṣu antargataḥ sa kuśalaḥ | anyo 'kuśalaḥ | yogī yo 'kuśalānāmādīnave kuśalānāmaniśaṃse ca śraddhadhate | tasya paścādutpadyate vyavasāyo 'kuśalānāṃ prahāṇāya kuśalānāṃ samādānāya | ataḥ śraddhendriyasamanantaraṃ vīryendriyamucyate | kuśadharmagato vyavasāyo vīryamityākhyāyate | sarvahitānāṃ mūlaṃ karoti | tadvyavasāyasahakāratayā manaskārādayo dharmā mahāphalaprāpakā bhavanti | yathā dahanaḥ samīraṇapratilabdhaḥ sarvān dahati ||
body.translated_text: The mental exertion (<s>abhyutsāha</s>) of the mind is called effort (<s>vyavasāya</s>). It always supports other <s>dharmas</s> — attention (<s>manaskāra</s>) or concentration (<s>samādhi</s>). Therein, exertion is the constant arising of one-pointedness of mind — that is called effort. Effort is threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. That which is included in the four right exertions (<s>samyakpradhāna</s>) is wholesome. The other is unwholesome. The <s>yogin</s> who has faith in the danger of unwholesome <s>dharmas</s> and in the benefit of wholesome <s>dharmas</s> — for him, afterwards effort arises for the abandoning of unwholesome [dharmas] and the undertaking of wholesome [dharmas]. Therefore, immediately after the faith faculty (<s>śraddhendriya</s>), the energy faculty (<s>vīryendriya</s>) is stated. Effort directed toward wholesome <s>dharmas</s> is designated as vigor (<s>vīrya</s>). It serves as the root of all beneficial things. Through the cooperation of that effort, <s>dharmas</s> such as attention and the rest become productive of great fruit. Just as fire, augmented by wind, burns everything.

body.text: vyavasāyavargo navatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the ninetieth chapter, the Chapter on Effort (<s>vyavasāyavarga</s>).

body.text: 91 smṛtivargaḥ
body.translated_text: 91. Chapter on Mindfulness (<s>smṛtivarga</s>)

body.text: anubhūtapūrvasya jñānaṃ smṛtiḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- yat ciraviprakṛṣṭānubhūtaṃ smarati na pramuṣati sā smṛtirityucyate |
body.translated_text: Knowledge of what has been previously experienced is mindfulness (<s>smṛti</s>). As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'That which recollects what was experienced long ago and far away, and does not lose it — that is called mindfulness.'

body.text: (pṛ) sā smṛtistrayadhvartinī | kasmāt | uktaṃ hi sūtre smṛtiṃ sarvārthikāṃ [vadāmī]ti | sā smṛtiḥ catuḥsmṛtyupasthānagatā | catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni trayadhvālambanāni ca | kasmātpunaratītamātrālambaneti | (u) tadvacanaṃ sarvakālena bhavati | na tu tryadhvā bhavati | yasmin samaye cittamuddhataṃ bhavati | tadā smṛtirubhayatrānugā | sā sarvatragetyucyate | yaduktaṃ bhavatā catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni tryadhvālambanānīti | tatra pratyutpannā prajñaiva na tu smṛtiḥ | atastathāgato [yadā] pūrvaṃ smṛtināmnā vimuktimuktavān tadā tāmeva prajñetyavocat |
body.translated_text: (Question) That mindfulness extends across the three times. Why? For it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'I declare mindfulness to be all-encompassing.' That mindfulness is included in the four foundations of mindfulness (<s>smṛtyupasthāna</s>). The four foundations of mindfulness have objects belonging to the three times. Why then is it said that [mindfulness] has only past objects? (Answer) That statement applies to all times — but mindfulness does not extend across the three times. At the time when the mind is agitated, mindfulness follows both [past and present]. That is called 'all-encompassing.' As for your statement that the four foundations of mindfulness have objects belonging to the three times — therein, it is wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) regarding the present, not mindfulness. Therefore, when the <s>Tathāgata</s> previously spoke of liberation using the name 'mindfulness,' he [later] called that very thing 'wisdom.'

body.text: (pū) kathaṃ vijñānāntareṇānubhūtaṃ vijñānāntaraṃ smarati | (u) smṛterdharmaṃ evaṃ yat svasantāne yo dharmaḥ [pūrva]mutpannaniruddhaḥ tameva [svasantānikaṃ] viprakṛṣṭaṃ vijñānāntaramālambata iti | jñānānāṃ vijñānadharmaśca tathā yat vijñānāntarānumūtaṃ vijñānāntaraṃ vijānātīti | yathā cakṣurvijñānena vijñātaṃ rūpaṃ manovijñānaṃ vijānāti | anyapudgalenānubhūtamanyaḥ pudgalo vijānāti | yathāryapudgalā yāvatpūrvanivāse dehāntarānubhūtaṃ smṛtibalādvijānānti | (pū) yadi pūrvānubhūtasya jñānaṃ smṛtiriti | ādhunikavijñaptyādidharmāḥ smṛtayaḥ syuḥ | kasmāt | taddharmāṇāmapi pūrvānubhūtopavicārarūpatvāt | (u) vijñaptyādidharmā api smṛtaya ityucyante | yathā bhagavān salyakaṃ nāthaputramavocat pūrvaṃ manasi kṛtvā vyākuruṣva iti | āha ca pūrvānubhuktasukhasmaraṇe kleśa āvirbhavatīti | ato vijñaptyādidharmā api pūrvavastvanusmaraṇarūpā smṛtaya ityucyante | smṛtiriyaṃ gṛhītalakṣaṇājjātā | yasmin dharme gṛhītalakṣaṇamasti | tatra smṛtirbhavati nānyathā | samādhiḥ prajñā ca samādhivarge prajñāvarge ca vakṣyate ||
body.translated_text: (Question) How does one consciousness recollect what was experienced by another consciousness? (Answer) The nature of mindfulness is such: whatever <s>dharma</s> in one's own continuum (<s>svasantāna</s>) has previously arisen and ceased — that very [dharma] belonging to one's own continuum is taken as an object by a different consciousness, even though remote. And the nature of knowledge and consciousness is such that one consciousness knows what was experienced by another consciousness. Just as what is cognized by eye-consciousness regarding form, mind-consciousness also cognizes. And what was experienced by one person (<s>pudgala</s>), another person cognizes. Just as <s>ārya</s> persons, regarding what was experienced in previous abodes in other bodies, cognize it through the power of mindfulness. (Question) If knowledge of what was previously experienced is mindfulness, then contemporary cognitions (<s>vijñapti</s>) and other <s>dharmas</s> would be mindfulness. Why? Because those <s>dharmas</s> too have the nature of investigating what was previously experienced. (Answer) Cognitions and other <s>dharmas</s> are also called mindfulness. Just as the Blessed One said to <s>Salyaka Nāthaputra</s>: 'First bring to mind, then declare.' And it is said: 'When one recollects previously experienced pleasure, defilement manifests.' Therefore cognitions and other <s>dharmas</s>, being of the nature of recollecting previous things, are called mindfulness. This mindfulness arises from a grasped sign. In whichever <s>dharma</s> there is a grasped sign, therein mindfulness occurs — not otherwise. Concentration (<s>samādhi</s>) and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) will be explained in the Chapter on Concentration and the Chapter on Wisdom.

body.text: smṛtivarga ekanavatitamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the ninety-first chapter, the Chapter on Mindfulness (<s>smṛtivarga</s>).

body.text: 92 vitarkavicāravargaḥ
body.translated_text: 92. Chapter on Applied and Sustained Thought (<s>vitarkavicāravarga</s>)
