body.text: prajāpālanāt vadho 'pāpa iti | sa gṛhyadharmasamaḥ | yathā sūnakādīnāṃ lokānāṃ gṛhyadharmāḥ prāṇivadhāḥ sadā kriyamāṇā na pāpavimuktāḥ | tathā kṣatriyasyāpi | sa rājadharmo 'pi hetunā pāpaprāpakaḥ | yadi kṣatriyo rājadharmatvena prāṇān vadhyan apāpo bhavati | tadā sūnakavyādhādayo 'pyapāpāḥ syuḥ | kṣatriyaḥ paraṃ prajāsu karuṇārdracittatayā vairamutsṛjya tadadhīnaṃ puṇyaṃ labhate | yaḥ puruṣajīvitamapaharati | tasya pāpamasti | yathā kaścinmātāpitṛpālanāya paradhanamapaharati | sa puṇyaṃ pāpaṃ vyāmiśraṃ labhate |
body.translated_text: because of protecting the people, killing is not sinful.' That is equivalent to a household custom (<s>gṛhyadharma</s>). Just as for butchers and others in the world, the household customs of constantly performing the killing of living beings are not free from sin — so too for the <s>kṣatriya</s>. That royal duty (<s>rājadharma</s>) also leads to sin through its cause. If a <s>kṣatriya</s>, because it is royal duty, becomes sinless by killing living beings, then butchers, hunters, and the like would also be sinless. A <s>kṣatriya</s>, rather, with a mind moistened by compassion toward his people, abandoning enmity, obtains the merit dependent on that [compassion]. One who takes the life of a person — for him there is sin. Just as someone who steals another's wealth for the sake of supporting his parents — he obtains a mixture of merit and sin.

body.text: (pṛ) mātapitṛpālanāya corayan na pāpaṃ labheta | yathoktaṃ dharmasūtre- yaḥ saptadinānyupavasati | sa caṇḍālādapaharan na pāpamupādatte | yo mumūrṣuḥ sa brāhmaṇādapyupādānaṃ labhate iti | ime duṣkarmaṇā jīvanto 'pi nocyante śīlavyasanina iti | āpannatvāt | yathākāśo na rajasā dūṣyate | tathā te 'pi na pāpena dūṣyante | (u) ukta brāhmaṇa dharma eva- cauryakāle dhanasvāmyāgatya rakṣati | tasmin samaye brāhmaṇena vicārayitavyam | yadi sa dhanasvāmiguṇairasamāno bhavati | tadā taṃ hanyāt | kasmāt | ahamuttamaḥ, nānāprāyaścittaistatpāpaṃ nirharāmi | yadi tena tulyaguṇaḥ | tadā ātmahanane parahanane vā tatpāpamapi tulyam | tasya gurutarapāpasya durharaṇatvāt | yadi dhanasvāmī guṇādhikaḥ | tadā svakāyaṃ tyajet | tatra pāpasyāpanodyatvāt | evaṃ vivekaḥ | corahanane 'pyevaṃ syāt duṣkarmaṇā jīvanta iti yaduktaṃ tatra duṣkarmasattvātkathaṃ puṇyaṃ bhavet |
body.translated_text: (Question) One who steals for the sake of supporting parents would not obtain sin. As stated in the <s>Dharmasūtra</s>: 'One who fasts for seven days — even if he takes from an outcaste (<s>caṇḍāla</s>), he does not incur sin. One who is about to die may take even from a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>.' These people, though living by evil deeds, are not said to have a breach of virtue — because they are in dire straits. Just as space is not defiled by dust, so too they are not defiled by sin. (Answer) It is stated in the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> code itself: 'At the time of theft, the owner of the property comes and protects [it]. At that time, the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should consider: If the property-owner is inferior to himself in qualities, then he should kill him. Why? "I am superior; through various acts of atonement (<s>prāyaścitta</s>), I shall remove that sin." If he is equal in qualities, then the sin of killing oneself and the sin of killing another would also be equal. Because that heavier sin is difficult to remove. If the property-owner is superior in qualities, then one should give up one's own body. Because therein the sin can be expelled.' Such is the discrimination. In the killing of a thief too, it would be the same — [but] as for the statement 'those living by evil deeds,' therein, since evil deeds exist, how could there be merit?

body.text: yadavocaḥ coraṃ purata āgataṃ hanyādeva na vai pāpamahantā tu vindate tat iti | taddūṣitacarameva | kasmāt | yadi purata āgato guṇādhikaḥ | tadā svakāyaṃ tyajet | yadi nāsti pāpamiti | kasmāttathā bhavet | yadabravīḥ veda uktaṃ prāṇivadhaḥ puṇyaprāpaka iti | tatpratyuktameva yaduta badhe nāsti puṇyamiti | yaduktaṃ vastuto martavyasya kasyacidvadhe nāsti pāpamiti | tadā duṣṭacoravadhe 'pi pāpaṃ na syāt | sarve ca sattvāḥ pāpiṣṭhāḥ | skandhakāyānubhavakarmābhisaṃskāritvāt | evañca prāṇivadhena pāpaṃ labheta | tattu na sambhavati |
body.translated_text: As you have said: 'One should indeed kill a thief who comes before one — the killer does not incur sin' — that itself has a flawed conduct. Why? If the one who comes before is superior in qualities, then one should give up one's own body. If there is no sin [in killing], why would that be so? As you have said: 'It is stated in the <s>Veda</s> that killing of living beings produces merit' — that has already been refuted, namely that 'in killing there is no merit.' As for your statement: 'In the killing of one who would really die [anyway], there is no sin' — then in the killing of an evil thief too, there would be no sin. And all beings are sinful — because they are conditioned by the <s>karma</s> of experiencing the aggregate-body (<s>skandhakāya</s>). If so, one would obtain sin through the killing of living beings — but that is not possible.

body.text: (pṛ) ye sattvāḥ pūrvādhvani svayaṃkṛtabadhapratyayāḥ | teṣāmidānīṃ vadhe kasmātpāpaṃ labhyate | cauryādikarmasvapyevaṃ syāt | (u) tathā cet puṇyapāpe na syātām | kasmāt |
body.translated_text: (Question) Those beings who in past lives had the condition of self-caused killing — in their killing now, why is sin obtained? The same would apply to theft and other actions as well. (Answer) If that were so, then merit and sin would not exist. Why?

body.text: ayaṃ puruṣaḥ pūrvādhvakṛtavadhapratyayatvāttadvadho 'pāpaḥ | tatprāṇātipātaviratirapyapuṇyā syāt | evaṃ yaḥ parasmai dadāti tasyāpi na puṇyaṃ syāt | pratigrahītā pūrvādhvani svācaritadānakarmaka idānīṃ tadvipākaṃ labhate | na hi sambhavati nāsti puṇyaṃ pāpamiti | ato jñātavyaṃ sattvānāṃ pūrvādhvakṛtavadhakarmaṇāmapi vadhitā pāpaṃ labhata iti | rāgadveṣamohebhyaḥ samutpannatvāt | ime kleśā mithyāviparyāsāḥ | mithyāviparyastacittotpāda eva pāpaṃ labhate | kaḥ punarvādastaddhetūtthiteṣu kāyavākkarmasu | tena saṃsāro 'navasthaḥ | tathā nocedṛṣayo rāgadveṣādikleśānāmudaye ṛddhe na hīyeran | yadīdaṃ na pāpam | kasya dharmasya viparītaṃ puṇyamityucyeta | jñātavyaṃ pūrvādhvakṛtapratyayānāmapi sattvānāṃ vadhitā pāpavān syāditi | yadyupyuktaṃ tvayā pāpiyān na kiñcitsādhayatīti | tadayuktam | caṇḍālādayo 'pi mantravidhinā puruṣaṃ ghnanti | tathā maharṣayo 'pi akuśalacittena yathābhihitaṃ sādhayanti | te puṇyabalātsādhayantaḥ prāṇātipātātpāpaṃ labhante |
body.translated_text: This person, because of the condition of killing done in past lives, [you say] his killing is sinless. Then the abstention from taking life would also be without merit. Likewise, one who gives to another would also have no merit — [since] the recipient obtains the ripened result of the gift-<s>karma</s> performed in past lives. It is not possible that merit and sin do not exist. Therefore it should be known that even for beings whose killing-<s>karma</s> was done in past lives, the killer obtains sin. Because [killing] arises from passion (<s>rāga</s>), hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>). These defilements are wrong and perverted. A mental arising that is wrongly perverted indeed obtains sin. What need to speak further of bodily and verbal actions arising from those [defilements]? Through that, <s>saṃsāra</s> is without end. If it were not so, then <s>ṛṣis</s>, when defilements of passion, hatred, and the like arise and increase, would not decline [from their attainments]. If this were not sin, in opposition to which <s>dharma</s> would that which is called 'merit' be stated? It should be known that even for beings whose condition was created in past lives, the killer would be sinful. As you have further said: 'A sinful person does not accomplish anything' — that is untenable. Outcastes (<s>caṇḍāla</s>) and others too, through the method of <s>mantras</s>, kill a person. Likewise, great <s>ṛṣis</s> too, with unwholesome minds, accomplish what has been described. They, accomplishing through the power of merit, obtain sin from taking life.

body.text: yadabravīḥ- kaściccittabalena prāṇātipātaṃ kurvan puṇyaṃ prasūte | prāṇadānena pāpamiti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | avaśyaṃ cittabalena puṇyapratyayena puṇyaṃ labhate | na tu cittamātreṇa | yaḥ kuśalacittena gurutalpago brāhmaṇahantā vā bhavati | tena kiṃ puṇyaṃ labhyeta | pārasīkādi paryantabhūmigatānāṃ janānāṃ puṇyabuddhayā mātṛbhaginyādigāmināṃ kiṃ puṇyaṃ bhavet | ato jñāyate puṇyapratyayatvātpuṇyamutpadyate | na tu cittamātreṇa evaṃ steyādāvapi | ato jñāyate vadhādayo 'kuśalā iti | te vadhādayaḥ pareṣāmapakārakatvādakuśalā ityucyante | yadyapi dṛṣṭe kañcitkālaṃ sukhaṃ labhate | paścāttu mahadduḥkhamanubhavati | parāpakāro hyakuśalalakṣaṇam | paśyāmaḥ khalu pratyakṣaṃ bahavaḥ sattvā vadhādīnācaranto bhūyasā tisṛṣu gatiṣu manuṣyagatau ca duḥkhapīḍā anubhavantīti | [ato] jñātavyaṃ duḥkhapīḍā vadhādīnāṃ phalamiti | hetusarūpatvātphalasya | tisṛṣu durgatiṣu pāpāni tīvraduḥkhāni | ato jñāyate vadhādipratyayāttatropapadyanta iti |
body.translated_text: As you have said: 'A certain one, taking life through the power of mind, produces merit; through the gift of life, sin' — that is untenable. Why? Necessarily, through the power of mind with a meritorious condition, one obtains merit — but not through mind alone. One who with a wholesome mind commits grave sexual misconduct (<s>gurutalpaga</s>) or is a slayer of a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> — would he thereby obtain merit? For the people of the borderlands such as <s>Pārasīka</s> and others, who with the notion of merit have sexual relations with mothers, sisters, and the like — would there be merit for them? Therefore it is known that merit arises because of a meritorious condition — not through mind alone. The same applies to theft and the rest as well. Therefore it is known that killing and the rest are unwholesome. Those [acts of] killing and the rest are called unwholesome because they harm others. Even though one may obtain happiness for some time in the present, afterwards one experiences great suffering. Harming others is indeed the characteristic of the unwholesome. We directly perceive that many beings who practice killing and the rest predominantly experience the suffering of affliction in the three [lower] destinies and in the human destiny. Therefore it should be known that the suffering of affliction is the fruit of killing and the rest — because the fruit resembles its cause. In the three lower destinies, sins [ripen as] intense suffering. Therefore it is known that one is reborn there due to the condition of killing and the rest.

body.text: (pṛ) deveṣu maneṣyeṣu caivaṃ syāt | devā api sadā yuddhe 'suraiḥ saha vadhyante |
body.translated_text: (Question) The same would apply among gods and humans as well. Gods too are always killed in battle with the <s>asuras</s>.

body.text: manuṣyeṣu gartagrahaṇayantrajālaviṣaiḥ sattvān ghnanti | (u) devamanuṣyeṣu santi vadhaviratyādayo dharmāḥ | na tu tisṛṣu gatiṣu, iti jñātavyaṃ tatra pāpaṃ tīvraduḥkhamiti | manuṣyā vadhādipratyayena tu prakṣīṇāyurādilābhasukhā bhavanti | [tathā hi] purā manuṣyā apramāṇāyuṣkā abhūvan | candrasūryavatsvakāyaniścaradraśmayaḥ vihāyasā svairacāriṇāḥ | pṛthivī svābhāvikayatheṣṭhadravyāḥ svābhāvikataṇḍulāḥ | sarvamidaṃ vadhādipāpaiḥ praṇaṣṭam | tataḥ punaḥ kṣayo 'bhūt | yāvaddaśavarṣeṣu manuṣyeṣu dhṛtatailasitopalāśālicolayavādayaḥ sarve 'pi tirohitāḥ | ato jñāyate vadhādayo 'kuśalakarmāṇīti | yo vadhahiṃsādibhyo viramati sa punarlābhasukhāyuḥpauṣkalyaṃ labhate | yathāśītivarṣasahasrāyuṣkasya yatheṣṭaṃ kāmā bhavanti | ato jñāyate vadho 'kuśala iti |
body.translated_text: Among humans, with traps, seizures, machines, nets, and poisons, they kill living beings. (Answer) Among gods and humans, there exist <s>dharmas</s> such as abstention from killing. But not in the three [lower] destinies — therefore it should be known that therein sin [produces] intense suffering. But humans, through the condition of killing and the rest, come to have diminished lifespan and diminished happiness of enjoyment. For formerly, humans had immeasurable lifespans. Rays emanated from their own bodies like the sun and moon. They wandered freely through the sky. The earth had naturally desired substances and natural rice-grain. All of this was destroyed by the sins of killing and the rest. Then further decline occurred — until, when humans [lived only] ten years, sesame oil, rock sugar, fine rice, garments, barley, and the rest — all disappeared. Therefore it is known that killing and the rest are unwholesome actions. One who abstains from killing and violence in turn obtains abundance of enjoyment, happiness, and lifespan. Just as for one whose lifespan is eighty thousand years, there are pleasures as desired. Therefore it is known that killing is unwholesome.

body.text: idānīmauttarā vadanti taṇḍulaṃ svābhāvikaṃ vasanaṃ vṛkṣajam | prāṇātipātaviratitvāt | saṃkṣipyedamucyate sattvānāṃ sarvāṇi sukhopakaraṇāni prāṇātipātaviratisamutpannānīti | ato jñāyate prāṇātipātādayo 'kuśalakarmāṇīti | prāṇātipātādidharmāḥ sajjanaiḥ parityājyāḥ | ye buddhā bodhisattvāḥ pratyekabuddhāḥ śrāvakā anye ca bhadantāḥ te sarve tān parityajya viramanti | ato jñāyate 'kuśalā iti |
body.translated_text: Now the northerners say: Rice-grain is natural; garments come from trees — because of abstention from taking life. In brief, this is stated: All the requisites of happiness for beings arise from abstention from taking life. Therefore it is known that taking life and the rest are unwholesome actions. The <s>dharmas</s> of taking life and the rest should be abandoned by the virtuous. All <s>Buddhas</s>, <s>Bodhisattvas</s>, <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s>, <s>Śrāvakas</s>, and other noble ones — they all abandon and abstain from those. Therefore it is known that they are unwholesome.

body.text: (pṛ) prāṇivadhādayaḥ sujanairapyanuśrūyante | yathoktaṃ mede yajñārthaṃ paśuvadho 'nuśrūyata iti | (u) te na sujanāḥ | sujanaḥ sadā parasya hitārthī bhavati | karuṇācittābhyāsī mitrāmitrayoḥ samaḥ | tādṛśaḥ puruṣaḥ kathaṃ prāṇivadhamanuśrāvayet | kāmakrodhakaluṣitacittāḥ santa imaṃ granthaṃ racayāmāsuḥ | [sattvānāṃ] svarge janmābhilāṣī sattvānabhimantrayamānaḥ svapuṇyabalena tatsādhayati | vadhādibhyo vimuktilābhī na tatkaroti | ato jñāyate 'kuśalamiti | (pṛ) vimuktilābhī anyadapi vikālabhojanādi karoti | idamapyakuśalaṃ bhavet | (u) idaṃ pāpaheturiti sujanāḥ pariharantyapi | yo dharmo 'duṣṭaḥ na sa dharmaḥ pariharaṇīyaḥ syāt | vikālabhojanādayo brahmacaryaṃ ghnantītyato 'pi pariharanti | keciddharmāḥ svarūpato 'kuśalā ityataḥ pariharanti yathā madyapānavikālabhojanādayaḥ | ato jñāyate prāṇātipātaḥ svarūpato 'kuśala iti | prāṇātipāto bahujanavidviṣṭaḥ | yathā siṃhavyāghradasyucaṇḍālādayaḥ | yadanena hetunā janavidviṣṭaṃ kathaṃ tadakuśalaṃ na bhavet | yaḥ prāṇātipātavirataḥ sa bahūnāṃ
body.translated_text: (Question) Killing of living beings is also sanctioned by the virtuous. As stated: 'In the <s>Veda</s>, the killing of animals for sacrifice is sanctioned.' (Answer) They are not virtuous. A virtuous person always seeks the welfare of others. One who practices compassionate mind, who is equal toward friend and foe — how would such a person sanction the killing of living beings? Those whose minds were corrupted by desire and anger composed that text. One who desires rebirth in heaven, enticing beings [with promises], accomplishes that through the power of his own merit. One who has obtained liberation does not do that. Therefore it is known that it is unwholesome. (Question) One who has obtained liberation also does other things such as eating at improper times. Would these also be unwholesome? (Answer) The virtuous also avoid this because it is a cause of sin. A <s>dharma</s> that is not harmful — that <s>dharma</s> need not be avoided. Eating at improper times and the like destroy the holy life (<s>brahmacarya</s>) — therefore too they are avoided. Certain <s>dharmas</s> are unwholesome by their own nature — therefore they are avoided, such as drinking intoxicants, eating at improper times, and the like. Therefore it is known that taking life is unwholesome by its own nature. Taking life is detested by the many. Just as lions, tigers, bandits, outcastes, and the like [are detested]. That which, for this reason, is detested by the people — how could it not be unwholesome? One who abstains from taking life is beloved of many

body.text: janānāṃ priyo bhavati | yathā karuṇāvihārī āryāṇāṃ priyaḥ | ato jñāyate vadho 'kuśala iti |
body.translated_text: people. Just as one who abides in compassion is dear to the Noble Ones. Therefore it is known that killing is unwholesome.

body.text: (pṛ) kaścittu prāṇivadhakṛt svavikramavaśājjanānāṃ priyo bhavati | yathā kaścidrājārthaṃ duṣṭacorāṇāṃ hantā rājapriyo bhavati | (u) [pāpa]hetusattvānnātyadhikaṃ priyo bhavati | yathā vadanti yo duṣkarmaṇā rājacittaṃ tarpayati | rājā ca yadi nirviṇṇacitto bhavati | tasya punaḥ sa vimato bhavati | yo durvṛttyā vimato bhavati | sa kathaṃ priyo bhavet | akuśalacārī ātmana evāpriyaḥ | kaḥ punarvādo 'nyeṣām | ato jñāyate prāṇihiṃsākuśaladharma iti | vadhādidharmāḥ tāḍanahiṃsanavandhanādīnāṃ duḥkho padravāṇāṃ hetava ityato jñāyate 'kuśalā iti | (pṛ) ahiṃsādidharmā api duḥkhahetavaḥ | yathā rājā duṣṭacorān vadhitumājñāpāyati | yo na vadhyati taṃ rājā hanti | (u) yo na hanti sa hanyata ityahantāraḥ sarve mariṣyamāṇā bhaveyuḥ | rājaśāsanaviruddhatvādeṣām | yadi rājā jānāti ayamavadhacitta iti tadā avadhitā pratyuta satkriyate | ato jñāyate vadhādayo duḥkhahetavo na tvavadhādayaḥ | yo vadhānācarati | tasya maraṇakāle cittaṃ paritapati | ato jñāyate 'kuśalamiti | vadhādyācaraṇāt na janānāṃ śraddheyaḥ | svayūthyeṣveva na śraddhīyate | kaḥ punarvādaḥ sajjaneṣu | siṃsādyācārī sajātīyairevādhikṣipyate | kaḥ punarvādo 'nyajanaiḥ | hiṃsādyācārī caṇḍālasūnakavyādhādivat sajjanaiḥ dūrataḥ parityajyate | hiṃsādyācaritā na sukhī jana ityucyate | yathā sūnako na kadāpīdṛśakarmaṇā satkāraṃ labhate | sujano guṇāya hiṃsādibhyo viramati | yadi nākuśalam | kasmāt guṇāya viratiṃ sampratyeṣati | dṛṣṭe paśyāmaḥ khalu hiṃsādīnāṃ vipriyaṃ phalaṃ bhavatīti | jñātavyamāgāminyadhvanyapi duḥkhavipākaṃ prāpayatīti | yadi hiṃsādayo nākuśalāḥ | ko dharmaḥ punarakuśalaḥ syāt |
body.translated_text: (Question) But someone who kills living beings becomes dear to people through the power of his own valor. Just as someone who kills wicked thieves for the king's sake becomes dear to the king. (Answer) Because of the [sinful] cause involving [harming] a being, he does not become exceedingly dear. As they say: 'One who satisfies the king's mind through evil deeds — if the king becomes disenchanted in mind, he again becomes disfavored.' One who becomes disfavored through bad conduct — how could he be dear? One who practices the unwholesome is disliked even by himself — what more need be said of others? From this it is known that harming living beings is an unwholesome <s>dharma</s>. <s>Dharmas</s> such as killing and the like are causes of painful consequences such as beating, harming, binding, and the like — from this it is known that they are unwholesome. (Question) <s>Dharmas</s> such as non-harming and the like are also causes of suffering. Just as when the king commands the execution of wicked thieves — one who does not carry out the execution is [himself] punished by the king. (Answer) If one who does not kill is killed, then all non-killers would be about to die — because they oppose the king's command. If the king knows 'this one has a non-killing intention,' then the non-killer is rather honored. From this it is known that killing and the like are causes of suffering, not non-killing and the like. One who practices killing — at the time of death, his mind feels remorse. From this it is known that it is unwholesome. Because of practicing killing and the like, one is not trusted by people. One is not even trusted among one's own companions — what more need be said among virtuous people? One who practices violence and the like is reproached even by his own kind — what more need be said by other people? One who practices violence and the like is abandoned from afar by virtuous people, just like a butcher, hunter, or fowler. One who practices violence and the like is not called a happy person. Just as a butcher never obtains respect through such action. A virtuous person abstains from violence and the like for the sake of merit. If it were not unwholesome, why would one seek abstinence for the sake of merit? In the visible [realm], we indeed see that the fruit of violence and the like is unpleasant. It should be known that in the future course as well, it brings about a painful ripening. If violence and the like are not unwholesome, what <s>dharma</s> then would be unwholesome?

body.text: (pṛ) yadi hiṃsādidharmā akuśalāḥ | tadā dehapoṣaṇaṃ na syāt | kasmāt | na hyasti ahiṃsāsambhavakālaḥ | gatāgate pādotkṣepaṇe pādāvakṣepaṇe vā sadā sūkṣmasattvān vihanti | ātmīyasaṃjñayā paravastūni sadā gṛhṇāti | yathāsvasaṃjñañca mithyā vyavaharati | ato naiva dehapoṣaṇaṃ bhavet | (u) yat hetukṛtaṃ tat pāpam | nāhetukṛtam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- vastusantaḥ sattvāḥ, teṣu sattvasaṃjñāmutpādya jighatsābuddhyā tān hatvā hananapāpaṃ labhanta iti | evaṃ steyādāvapi | (pṛ) yathā viṣaṃ pītavāniti hetāvahetāvubhayathā puruṣaṃ hanti | yathā ca vahniprakramaṇaṃ jñāne 'jñāne ca puruṣaṃ dahati | tathā vedhanādirapi syāt | jñātavyaṃ prāṇihiṃsā hetāvahetau ca pāpaṃ prāpayati | (u) nāyaṃ dṛṣṭānto yuktaḥ | viṣeṇa kāyahiṃsanānmaraṇam |
body.translated_text: (Question) If <s>dharmas</s> such as violence and the like are unwholesome, then the nourishment of the body would not be possible. Why? Because there is no time when non-violence can be accomplished. In going, coming, lifting the foot, and placing the foot down — one always harms subtle beings. With the notion of 'mine,' one always takes the possessions of others. And according to one's own notion, one engages in false conduct. Therefore the nourishment of the body would never be possible. (Answer) What is done intentionally (<s>hetukṛta</s>) is sin — not what is done unintentionally (<s>ahetukṛta</s>). As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There exist beings; generating the notion of a being in them, and killing them with the intention to kill, one obtains the sin of killing.' Likewise with theft and the rest. (Question) Just as one who has drunk poison — whether intentionally or unintentionally, the poison kills the person in both cases. And just as treading on fire — whether knowingly or unknowingly, it burns the person. So too with killing and the like — it should be known that harming living beings produces sin both intentionally and unintentionally. (Answer) This illustration is not valid. Death comes from the body-harming effect of poison.

body.text: puṇyantu cittagatam | kimatra dṛṣṭānto bhavet | vahnivedhanādirapi prabodhe 'sati na duḥkhajanakaḥ | ato na sa dṛṣṭānto yujyate | asati vijñāne na khedaṃ budhyate | sati tu vijñāne budhyate evamasati hetucitte na karma sidhyati | sati tu citte sidhyati | sa dṛṣṭāntastathā syāt | hetau sati pāpam | asati tu nāsti | karmaṇāṃ cittabalātpuṇyapāpavibhāgaḥ | asati hetucitte kathamuccanīcabhāvo bhavet | cikitsāyāmacikitsāyāñcobhayathā puruṣasya duḥkhaṃ jāyate | cittabalātpuṇyapāpavibhāgaḥ | yathā mātustanagrahaṇe bālako na pāpaṃ labhate | anurāgacittābhāvāt | anurāgacittena grahaṇe tu pāpamasti | puṇyaṃ pāpaṃ sarvaṃ cittādhīnaṃ jāyata iti jñātavyam |
body.translated_text: But merit is mental. What illustration could there be for that? Treading on fire and the like too, in the absence of awareness, do not generate suffering. Therefore that illustration is not appropriate. In the absence of consciousness, one does not apprehend pain. But in the presence of consciousness, one does apprehend it — thus, in the absence of an intentional mind, <s>karma</s> is not established; but in the presence of mind, it is established. That illustration should be understood accordingly. When there is intention, there is sin; when there is not, there is none. The classification of merit and demerit of <s>karmas</s> depends on the power of mind. In the absence of an intentional mind, how could there be the distinction of high and low? In both medical treatment and non-treatment, suffering arises for a person. The classification of merit and demerit depends on the power of mind. Just as when a child grasps its mother's breast, it does not obtain sin — because of the absence of a mind of passion. But when grasping with a mind of passion, there is sin. It should be known that merit and demerit all arise depending on mind.

body.text: yadi hetucitte 'satyapi pāpamasti | tadā vimuktilabdho 'pi asati hetau sattvān pīḍayan pāpaṃ labheta | tadā na vimucyeta | pāpiṣṭhānāṃ mokṣābhāvāt | yadi hetovasatyapi puṇyapāpamasti | tadaikameva karma kuśalamakuśalañca syāt | yathā kaścitpuṇyaṃ karma kurvan sattvaṃ hatavānasmīti bhrānto bhavati | tadā tatkarma pāpaṃ puṇyañca syāt | tattu na yujyate | hetāvasati puṇyaṃ pāpaṃ vā nāstīti jñātavyam | yadi vinā cittaṃ karmāsti | tadā kathamidaṃ kuśalaṃ idamakuśalaṃ idamavyākṛtamiti vibhāgaḥ syāt | cittahetunā tvayaṃ vibhāgaḥ | yathā trayaḥ puruṣāḥ sambhūya stūpapradakṣiṇaṃ kurvanti | tatraiko buddhaguṇānusmaraṇāya | dvitīyaḥ steyaharaṇāya | tṛtīyo bhāvaśamanāya | [teṣāṃ] kāyakarmaṇi samāne 'pi kuśalākuśalāvyākṛtavibhāgaścittagata iti jñeyam | kiñcitkarma niyatavipākaṃ, kiñcidaniyatavipākaṃ, kiñciduttamaṃ madhyamamadhamaṃ, dṛṣṭadharmavipākamupapadyavipākaṃ, taduttaravipākamityādi | yadi cittena vinā puṇyapāpaṃ labhyate | kathamayaṃ vibhāgo bhavet | yadi cittavyatiriktaṃ karmāsti asattvasaṃkhyeṣvapi puṇyapāpaṃ syāt | yathā sabhīraṇonmūlitaparvatopadruteṣu sattveṣu samīraṇe pāpaṃ syāt | sugandhikusumasya stūpavihārapatane puṇyaṃ syāt | tattu na sambhavati | ato jñāyate na cittavyatiriktaṃ puṇyapāpamastīti |
body.translated_text: If sin exists even in the absence of an intentional mind, then even one who has obtained liberation, harming beings without intention, would obtain sin. Then he would not be liberated — because there is no liberation for the sinful. If merit and demerit exist even when intention is absent, then one and the same <s>karma</s> would be both wholesome and unwholesome. Just as when someone performing meritorious <s>karma</s> mistakenly thinks 'I have killed a being' — at that time, that <s>karma</s> would be both sinful and meritorious. But that is not valid. It should be known that in the absence of intention, there is neither merit nor demerit. If <s>karma</s> exists apart from mind, then how could there be the classification 'this is wholesome, this is unwholesome, this is indeterminate'? But this classification is [determined] by the mental cause. Just as three persons together perform circumambulation of a <s>stūpa</s>: one for the recollection of the <s>Buddha's</s> virtues, the second for the purpose of stealing, and the third for calming the mind. Although the bodily action is the same, the classification into wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate should be known as mental. Some <s>karma</s> has fixed ripening, some unfixed ripening; some is superior, middling, or inferior; [some is] to be experienced in the present life, in the next birth, or in subsequent [lives], and so forth. If merit and demerit are obtained apart from mind, how could this classification be made? If <s>karma</s> exists apart from mind, then even in non-sentient things there would be merit and demerit. Just as when a wind uproots a mountain and crushes beings, there would be sin in the wind. When a fragrant flower falls on a <s>stūpa</s> or <s>vihāra</s>, there would be merit. But that does not happen. From this it is known that merit and demerit do not exist apart from mind.

body.text: tīrthikā vadanti- upavāsasthaṇḍilaśayanaśalākāvedhādibhirjalapatanadahanapraveśa
body.translated_text: The <s>tīrthikas</s> say: 'Through fasting, sleeping on bare ground, piercing with thorns, and the like — through falling into water, entering fire,

body.text: bhṛgupatanādibhiśca duḥkhapratyayaiḥ puṇyaṃ bhavatīti | tatra prājñā dūṣayanti | tathā cennārakāḥ sattvāḥ sadā dahyante pacyante ca | pretā bubhukṣitāḥ pipāsitāḥ | pataṅgā dahanapraviṣṭāḥ | mīnanakrā jalāvasathāḥ | ajavarāhāśvādayaḥ sadā purīṣakṣetraśāyinaḥ | te 'pi puṇyaṃ labheran | te pratibrūvanti | avaśyaṃ hetucittena tadduḥkhamanubhavatāṃ puṇyaṃ bhavati natvahetucittena | nārakādayo na hetucittena dāhādiduḥkhamanubhavanti | yadi hetucittena vinā puṇyaṃ nāsti | hetucittena vinā pāpamapi nāsti | yadi hetucittena vinā puṇyamasti | nārakādīnāmapi puṇyaṃ syāt | ityevaṃ doṣo 'sti | [iti] | yadi hetucittaṃ vinā puṇyaṃ pāpaṃ vāsti | tadā sujano na syāt | kasmāt | caturṣu iryāpatheṣu sadā sattvān hanti | tattu na sambhavati | hetāvasati nāsti puṇyaṃ pāpamiti jñātavyam | sujanmakṣetrañca na labhet | sadā pāpakattvāt | vastutastu santi brahmakāyikādīnāṃ surucirāḥ kāyā ato jñāyate na hetuṃ vinā puṇyaṃ pāpaṃ vāstīti |
body.translated_text: jumping off cliffs, and other painful practices — merit arises.' The wise refute this: If that were so, then beings in hell are constantly burned and cooked; hungry ghosts (<s>pretas</s>) are hungry and thirsty; moths enter fire; fish and crocodiles dwell in water; donkeys, pigs, horses, and the like always lie in fields of excrement — they too would obtain merit. They reply: 'Necessarily, one who experiences that suffering with an intentional mind obtains merit — but not without an intentional mind. Hell-dwellers and the rest do not experience the suffering of burning and the like with an intentional mind.' If without an intentional mind there is no merit, then without an intentional mind there is no demerit either. If without an intentional mind merit exists, then hell-dwellers and the rest would also have merit — thus the fault exists. If merit and demerit exist without an intentional mind, then there would be no virtuous person. Why? In the four postures (<s>iryāpatha</s>), one always kills beings. But that does not happen. It should be known that in the absence of intention, there is no merit or demerit. And one would not obtain a good birth — because one always commits sin. But in reality, there are radiant bodies of <s>Brahmakāyika</s> deities and the like. From this it is known that without intention, there is no merit or demerit.

body.text: bhāvatāṃ śāsane apariśuddhāhāre pāpaṃ bhavati | yo 'bhipraiti sarvāṇyannapānāni apariśuddhāhārāḥ pāpaprāpakāḥ syuriti | evaṃ surādisparśe so 'brāhmaṇaḥ syāt | pariśuddhena cittena bhojane na punarasti pāpamiti śrutaṃ dṛṣṭavānasi | tadā cittaṃ vinā nāsti puṇyaṃ pāpaṃ vā iti jñātavyam | adhvare ca puṇyacittena paśavo hanyante | tena svarga utpadyeran iti | puṇyacittena hananātpuṇyamasti | tathā no cet sarve prāṇivadhāḥ puṇyaprāpakāḥ pāpaprāpakā vā syuḥ | brāhmaṇamāha- kiñcitsteyamapāpam | yathā saptadinānyanaśanaḥ śūdrādapi pratigṛhṇīyāt | yo mumūrṣuḥ sa brāhmaṇādapi gṛhṇīyāt | putrārthino 'brahmacaryamapāpam iti | hetucitte 'sati na syādīdṛśavibhāgaḥ | ato jñāyate yo hetuṃ vinānyasya viṣaṃ prayacchati | kena sa pāpaṃ labheta | yaḥ sahetu anyasya viṣaṃ prayacchati | viṣaṃ pratyuta vyādhiṃ śamayati | sa puṇyaṃ labheta | kasyacidannaṃ prayacchati | anne cājīrṇe puruṣo mriyate | tata pāpaṃ prāpnuyāt | yadi vinā hetuṃ puṇyapāpe staḥ | tadā dharmo 'yaṃ vyākulaḥ syāt | laukikāḥ sarvavastuṣu cittaṃ śraddadhante | yathā ekameva vacanaṃ prītidveṣajananam | pṛṣṭhatāḍanādirapyevam | ato jñāyate karmāṇi cittādhīnāni iti | [tatra] mānasaṃ karma gariṣṭhamityuttaratna vakṣyate | ato jñāyate karmāṇi cittādhīnānīti | yaḥ
body.translated_text: In your teaching, there is sin in impure food. If one maintains that all food and drink are impure food and bring about sin — then in contact with liquor and the like, one would be a non-<s>brāhmaṇa</s>. 'Have you not heard and seen that when one eats with a purified mind, there is no sin?' Then it should be known that apart from mind, there is no merit or demerit. And in the sacrifice (<s>adhvara</s>), animals are killed with a meritorious mind. Thereby heaven would be produced. Because of killing with a meritorious mind, there is merit. If that is not so, then all killing of living beings would either bring about merit or bring about sin [uniformly]. It is said to the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>: 'Some theft is not sinful. Just as [during] a seven-day fast, one may accept [food] even from a <s>śūdra</s>. One who is about to die may take even from a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>. Sexual misconduct for the sake of a child is not sinful.' If there were no intentional mind, there would not be such a classification. From this it is known: one who, without intention, gives poison to another — by what would he obtain sin? One who, with intention, gives poison to another — if the poison rather cures the disease, he would obtain merit. If someone gives food to another and the person dies from indigestion — from that, one would incur sin. If merit and demerit exist without intention, then this <s>dharma</s> would be confused. Worldly people put their trust in the mind regarding all things. Just as one and the same statement generates either affection or hatred. Striking from behind and the like are also thus. From this it is known that <s>karmas</s> depend on mind. Mental <s>karma</s> is the weightiest — this will be stated later. From this it is known that <s>karmas</s> depend on mind. One who

body.text: prājñaḥ sa pañcakāmaguṇeṣu vasannapi na pāpamāk bhavatīti manaso balam | kasmāt | na hi prājño rūpāṇi dṛṣṭvā mithyāsaṃjñāmutpādayati | ato nāsti rūpāsaṅgadoṣaḥ | tathā śabdādāvapi | yadyanutpannamithyāsaṃjño 'pi pāpavān | tadā sarvāṇi darśanaśravaṇāni pāpāni syuḥ | tathā ca mānasaṃ karma niṣprayojanaṃ syāt | jñānī prajñāśīrṣakaḥ pañcakāmaguṇānanubhavannapi nāsaktimutpādayati | pañcakāmaguṇāḥ santo 'pi cittanirvedānna malinayanti | kimidaṃ na mānasakarmaṇo balam | ato nāsti vinā hetuṃ puṇyapāpapratilābhaḥ |
body.translated_text: is wise, even while dwelling among the five strands of sensual pleasure (<s>pañcakāmaguṇa</s>), does not incur sin — such is the power of mind. Why? For a wise person, having seen forms, does not generate a wrong notion. Therefore there is no fault of attachment to form. Likewise with sound and the rest. If one who has not generated a wrong notion is still sinful, then all seeings and hearings would be sinful. And in that case, mental <s>karma</s> would be purposeless. The wise one, whose head is wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), even while experiencing the five strands of sensual pleasure, does not generate attachment. The five strands of sensual pleasure, though present, do not defile [him] because of the disenchantment of mind. Is this not the power of mental <s>karma</s>? Therefore, without intention, there is no obtaining of merit or demerit.

body.text: codayati | yadbravīṣi parasyānugrahānanugrahau kuśalākuśalalakṣaṇamiti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | yaḥ svakāyaṃ paripālayanpuṇyaṃ karmācarati | tasyātmānaṃ bhojayato 'pi puṇyamasti | caityavihārāvasattvabhūtau | tayoḥ secanaśodhane api puṇyaprāpake | vandanādayastu na parānugrāhakāḥ | kevalaṃ paraguṇavaikalyakarā iti na bhavetpuṇyam | na ca cittamātreṇa puṇyaguṇo bhavati | annavastrābhyāṃ paramupakurvatā tasmin samaye puṇyaṃ labhyate | tathā karuṇā[mātra]cāriṇo na bhavetpuṇyam | yadi caityavihārādayo 'sattvasaṃkhyātāḥ | teṣāṃ yo dhanamapaharati vināśayati vā | na tasya bhavetpāpam | anabhimukhīkṛtya durvacasā paranindane na bhavetpāpam | aśrutatvātkasyāpakarṣaḥ syāt | anyapuruṣe ca duṣṭacittamātramutpādayati na kāyavākkarma karoti | kiṃ punarhīyate | na sa pāpabhāk syāt | kaścidātmānaṃ nindati | kaścidātmānaṃ hanti | kaścitsvayaṃ mithyācarati | kaścicca pāpaṃ labhate | ataḥ kuśalākuśalalakṣaṇaṃ na parānugrahānanugrahamātreṇa bhavati |
body.translated_text: He objects: Your statement that 'benefiting and not-benefiting others is the characteristic of wholesome and unwholesome' is not valid. Why? One who nourishes his own body and practices meritorious <s>karma</s> — for him, even when feeding himself, there is merit. <s>Caityas</s> and <s>vihāras</s> are non-sentient. Watering and cleaning them also brings about merit. But bowing and the like do not benefit others — they merely diminish others' virtues — therefore there would be no merit. And it is not by mind alone that the quality of merit arises. One who benefits another with food and clothing — at that time, merit is obtained. Likewise, one who merely practices compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>) [without action] would not have merit. If <s>caityas</s>, <s>vihāras</s>, and the like are non-sentient, then one who steals or destroys their wealth would have no sin. Criticizing another behind their back would not be sin — because, not having heard, what harm would there be? And when one merely generates a malicious mind toward another person but does not perform bodily or vocal <s>karma</s> — what then is diminished? He would not partake of sin. Someone criticizes himself; someone kills himself; someone himself practices misconduct — and someone [thereby] obtains sin. Therefore, the characteristic of wholesome and unwholesome is not merely benefiting or not-benefiting others.

body.text: atrocyate | yadbravīṣi svadehaṃ pālayataḥ puṇyaguṇo 'stīti | tadayuktam | yadyātmasatkāre puṇyaguṇo 'sti | tadā na kaścitparaṃ satkuryāt | vastutastu puṇyārthī paraṃ satkaroti | yātmārthatā tataḥ puṇyamalpaṃ bhavati | ato jñāyate ātmārthatā na puṇyavatī syāditi | yadāha bhavān ātmapoṣaṇaṃ puṇyakarmācaraṇārthamiti | tat svadehaḥ pareṣāmupakārārtha iti puṣṇāti | tasyāsyāścittabhūmeḥ puṇyaguṇaḥ prasūte | nātmapoṣaṇamātreṇa | yadbravīṣi caityavihārā vasattvabhūtau, tayoḥ secanaśodhane api puṇyaprāpaka iti | tat bhagavadguṇāḥ sattveṣu pūjyā iti smṛtvā janāḥ secante śodhayanti ca | tasya sattvādhīnatvācca puṇyameva labhyate | (pṛ) nirvṛto hi bhagavānasattvabhūtaḥ | uktañca sūtre- na tathāgataḥ san nāsan, nāpi sadasat nāpi ca na san nāsan iti | kathaṃ sattva ityucyeta |
body.translated_text: It is said: Your claim that there is merit in protecting one's own body is not correct. If there were merit in self-care, then no one would honor others. In truth, one who seeks merit honors others; when self-interest is involved, the merit becomes small. Therefore it is known that self-interest does not possess merit. As for your statement that nourishing the self is for the purpose of practicing meritorious <s>karma</s> (action)—one nourishes one's own body for the benefit of others. From that mental disposition, the quality of merit arises—not from mere self-nourishment alone. As for your claim that <s>caityas</s> (shrines) and <s>vihāras</s> (monasteries) are non-sentient, yet watering and cleaning them also yields merit—people water and clean them remembering that the virtues of the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One) are to be honored in sentient beings. Because that depends on sentient beings, merit indeed is obtained. (Objection:) But the <s>Bhagavān</s> has passed into <s>nirvṛti</s> (cessation) and is no longer a sentient being. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The <s>Tathāgata</s> is neither existent nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent.' How then can he be called a sentient being?

body.text: (u) yadi nirvṛto 'sattvabhūtaḥ | tadā anirvṛtakālīnaṃ bhagavantaṃ smṛtvā pūjayantaḥ puṇyaṃ labhante | yathā janāḥ pitarau jananapoṣaṇakālaṃ smṛtvā yajanti | tathā no cet na pitṛpūjā bhavet | tathedamapi | yadbravīṣi vandanādayo na parānugrāhakā iti | tadayuktam | kasmāt | vandanādibhiḥ parasya nānāhitaṃ bhavati | yena paraḥ pūjyānāṃ satkāryo bhavati | ayameva [parā]nugrahaḥ | tenānye 'pi janāḥ satkāraśikṣānanusarantaḥ puṇyaguṇaṃ labhante | parasya vandane svābhimānaṃ bhajyate | akuśāṅgabhaṅgādbahūpakṛtaṃ bhavati | paraguṇāṃśca khyāpayatīti vandanādīnāmīdṛśaṃ hitaṃ bhavati | yadabravīḥ vandanādayaḥ paraguṇavaikalyakarā iti | tadayuktam | vandanaṃ bhakticittena [kriyate] | na tīrthikānāmiva parāpakarṣārthatayā tadācaryate | yathā ca vastradānaṃ yadyapi paraṃ hāpayati | tathāpi paraguṇāpakarṣakameva | tathā ca vastradānenāpi na puṇyaṃ bhavet | ato vandanādīnāṃ gabhīracetanena sabhavyamācaraṇaṃ syāt | yathoktaṃ sūtre- eko bhikṣuḥ snānagṛhe anyasya dehaṃ hastena mārjayati sma | [etacchṛtvā] bhagavān bhikṣūnāmantryāha- ayamupasevako bhikṣurarhan | upasevyamānastu bhinnaśīlaḥ | tathā śikṣayatha yūyam | na siṃhena śvādaya upasevyanta iti |
body.translated_text: (Reply:) If he has attained <s>nirvṛti</s> (cessation) and is no longer a sentient being, then people obtain merit by remembering and worshipping the <s>Bhagavān</s> as he was during his time before <s>nirvṛti</s>—just as people make offerings to their parents remembering the time of their birth and nurturing. If this were not so, there would be no worship of ancestors. The same applies here. Your claim that salutation and other acts do not benefit others is incorrect. Why? Through salutation and such acts, no harm comes to another; rather, it makes the other worthy of honor from those who are venerable. This itself is the benefit to others. Through this, other people too, following the training in respectful conduct, obtain the quality of merit. In bowing to another, one's own pride is broken. Through the breaking of unwholesome components, great benefit is accomplished. And it proclaims the virtues of others—such is the benefit of salutation and similar acts. Your statement that salutation and such acts diminish the virtues of others is incorrect. Salutation is performed with a mind of devotion, not for the purpose of demeaning others as the <s>tīrthikas</s> (non-Buddhist teachers) do. Just as giving cloth, even though it causes another to lose something, is not a diminisher of others' virtues—likewise, if giving cloth also yielded no merit, then salutation and similar acts should be practiced with profound intention. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'A certain <s>bhikṣu</s> (monk) was washing another's body with his hand in the bathing house. Hearing this, the <s>Bhagavān</s> addressed the <s>bhikṣus</s>: This attendant monk is an <s>arhat</s> (worthy one). But the one being attended upon has broken morality. Train yourselves thus—a lion is not served by jackals.'

body.text: yadbhavānāha- na ca cittamātreṇa puṇyaṃ labhata iti | tatra cittaṃ hi sarvaguṇānāṃ mūlam | yat kaścitparasyopakāraṃ cakāra karoti kariṣyati vā sarvaṃ tat kuśalacittamūlakam | yacca parasyāpakāraṃ cakāra karoti kariṣyati vā sarvaṃ tadakuśalacittamūlakam | karuṇācārī ca karuṇācittavipākena sarveṣāmupakaroti yaduta caṇḍavātavṛṣṭyanupatane 'pi sūryācandramasau nakṣatrāṇi ca na bhraśyanti sadā caranti ca | na mahāsamudramudvelayati | na ca mahāgnirdahati | nāpi caṇḍavāta utplāvayati | idaṃ sarvaṃ karuṇāvipākabalam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- yadi sarve lokāḥ karuṇācittamācaranti | tadā kāmāḥ svābhāvikāḥ syuḥ iti | yadbravīṣi caityavihāradhanāpahāre na pāpaṃ syāditi | tat sa puruṣaḥ sattvacittena tadapaharati | yaccaityadhanamapaharati | tatpratyayena apakarṣakaraṇe 'karaṇe vā sarvathā tadādhipatyena pāpaṃ labhate | bhagavati piḍājananānna pāpamastīti bhavato yadi matam | tadā [kaścit] vākpāruṣyādibhirarhantaṃ yojayati | na tadarhato duḥkhaṃ janayati | tasyāpi na pāpaṃ bhavet |
body.translated_text: As for your statement that merit is not obtained by mind alone—the mind is indeed the root of all qualities. Whatever benefit one has done, does, or will do for others, all that has its root in wholesome mind. And whatever harm one has done, does, or will do to others, all that has its root in unwholesome mind. One who practices <s>karuṇā</s> (compassion), through the ripening of a compassionate mind, benefits all beings—namely, even when fierce winds and rains assail, the sun, moon, and stars do not fall but continue their course always; the great ocean does not overflow; the great fire does not burn; nor does the fierce wind blow things away. All this is the power of the ripening of compassion. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'If all worlds practiced the mind of compassion, then desires would become natural.' Your claim that there is no sin in stealing the wealth of <s>caityas</s> (shrines) and <s>vihāras</s> (monasteries)—that person steals with a mind directed toward sentient beings. Whatever shrine wealth he steals, by that condition, whether or not he causes actual deprivation, in every case he obtains sin through that authority. If you think there is no sin in causing harm to the <s>Bhagavān</s>, then someone who subjects an <s>arhat</s> (worthy one) to harsh speech and the like—since that does not produce suffering for the <s>arhat</s>—would also incur no sin.

body.text: yabdravīṣi- anabhimukhanindane na bhavetpāpamiti | tadayuktam | akuśalacittena tatra prayujyate | akuśalacittavattvāt tasmin śṛṇvati aśṛṇvati vāvaśyaṃ duḥkhaṃ janayet | ataḥ pāpaṃ labhate | yaduktaṃ duṣṭacitta[mātra]mutpādya kāyavākkarmākurvato na bhavetpāpamiti |
body.translated_text: Your claim that there is no sin in blaming someone not present is incorrect. An unwholesome mind is applied there. Because of possessing an unwholesome mind, whether that person hears or does not hear, one necessarily generates suffering. Therefore one obtains sin. As for the statement that merely generating a malicious mind, without performing bodily or verbal <s>karma</s> (action), would not constitute sin—

body.text: tadapi na yuktam | parapīḍanāyāviśuddhākuśalacittatvāt [pāpaṃ] janayatyeva | yadi paraprabodhito jānāti tadā tasyāvaśyaṃ duḥkhopāyāso jāyeta eva | yathā cora āgatya paradhanamapaharati | tadā [svāmī] prabudhya yadyapi na jānāti tathāpi tasya [paścāt] pīḍāṃ karotyeva | yadbravīṣī ātmahananamātmanindanañca pāpakaramiti | tadayuktama | yadi svadehaṃ duḥkhayan pāpabhāk bhavati | tadā na ko 'pi sujanmasthānaṃ prāpnuyāt | kasmāt | janā hi caturṣviryāpatheṣu svadehaṃ duḥkhayanti | tathā ca sarve sattvāḥ sadā pāpaṃ labheran yathā parapīḍanā janāḥ | ato na kaścitsusthāne jāyeta | na hyetadyujyate | ato na svadehamātrātpuṇyaṃ pāpaṃ vāstīti jñātavyam | mārgahetutvādvinaye śīlamidaṃ paribaddhaṃ yaḥ kliṣṭacittenātmānaṃ hanti na saṃkleśātpāpaṃ labhata iti |
body.translated_text: that too is incorrect. Because the unwholesome mind is impure, directed toward harming others, it generates sin indeed. If, being alerted by another, one becomes aware, then suffering and distress will necessarily arise for that person. Just as when a thief comes and steals another's wealth—even if the owner, upon waking, does not immediately know, it nevertheless causes him suffering afterward. Your claim that killing oneself and blaming oneself are sinful is incorrect. If one who causes suffering to one's own body incurs sin, then no one would ever attain a good rebirth. Why? Because people cause suffering to their own bodies in the four <s>īryāpathas</s> (postures of daily conduct). Thus all beings would always obtain sin, just as those who harm others do. Therefore no one would be born in a good destination. But this is not reasonable. Therefore it should be understood that there is no merit or sin from one's own body alone. Because it serves as a cause of the path, this precept is established in the <s>Vinaya</s> (monastic discipline): one who kills oneself with an afflicted mind does not obtain sin from the affliction.

body.text: avyākṛtaṃ karmeti | yatkarma na kuśalamakuśalaṃ vā na parasattvānāmupakārakaṃ nāpakārakaṃ tadavyākṛtamityucyate | (pṛ) kasmādavyākṛtamiti nāma | (u) tatkarma nirucyate | yatkarma na kuśalaṃ nākuśalaṃ tadavyākṛtamiti vadanti | kuśalamakuśalañca karma vipākaprāpakam | naitatkarma vipākaprāpakamityavyākṛtam | kasmāt | kuśalamakuśalañca karma prabalam | idantu durbalam | yathā pūtibījaṃ nāṅkuraṃ prarohayati | vipāko dvividhaḥ | kuśalaṃ priyavipākam akuśalamapriyavipākam | avyākṛtantvavipākam | (pṛ) tatra na priya nāpriyopādānaṃ tadavyākṛtavipākamastu | ko doṣaḥ | (u) bhagavānāha- dvidhā vipākaḥ mithyākāyacaryā apriyavipākaprāpiṇī samyakkāyacaryā priyavipākaprāpiṇīti | na tvāha anayorudāsīnamastīti | puṇyaṃ priyalābhamanojñasmṛtivipākam | pāpaṃ tadviparītam | sukhaduḥkhe puṇyapāpayorvipākau | aduḥkhāsukhañca sucaritavipākaḥ | ato jñāyate nāstyavyākṛtavipāka iti |
body.translated_text: Regarding indeterminate <s>karma</s> (action): that <s>karma</s> which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, which neither benefits nor harms other sentient beings, is called <s>avyākṛta</s> (indeterminate). (Objection:) Why is it called <s>avyākṛta</s>? (Reply:) That <s>karma</s> is explained thus: that <s>karma</s> which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome is called <s>avyākṛta</s>. Wholesome and unwholesome <s>karma</s> bring about <s>vipāka</s> (fruition). This <s>karma</s> does not bring about <s>vipāka</s>, hence it is <s>avyākṛta</s>. Why? Because wholesome and unwholesome <s>karma</s> are powerful, while this is weak—just as a rotten seed does not produce a sprout. <s>Vipāka</s> is twofold: wholesome brings pleasant fruition; unwholesome brings unpleasant fruition. But <s>avyākṛta</s> has no fruition. (Objection:) If there is neither pleasant nor unpleasant appropriation, let that be the fruition of indeterminate—what fault is there? (Reply:) The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: '<s>Vipāka</s> is twofold: wrong bodily conduct leads to unpleasant fruition; right bodily conduct leads to pleasant fruition.' He did not say there is a neutral state between these two. Merit has as its fruition pleasant gain and agreeable memory. Sin is the opposite. Pleasure and pain are the fruitions of merit and sin respectively. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant is the fruition of good conduct. Therefore it is known that there is no indeterminate fruition.

body.text: trividhakarmavargaḥ śatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Chapter one hundred on the threefold classification of <s>karma</s> (action).

body.text: 101 duścaritavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 101. Chapter on misconduct (<s>duścarita</s>)

body.text: bhagavānāha- trīṇi duścaritāni kāyaduścaritaṃ vāgduścaritaṃ manoduścaritaṃ iti | kāyābhisaṃskṛtamakuśalaṃ kāyaduścaritam | tat dvividham (1) ekaṃ daśākuśalakarmapathasaṅgṛhītam |
body.translated_text: The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: There are three kinds of misconduct (<s>duścarita</s>): bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Unwholesome action performed through the body is bodily misconduct. It is of two kinds: (1) one that is included in the ten unwholesome <s>karmapatha</s> (action-paths),

body.text: yathā prāṇātipātādattādānakāmamithyācārāḥ | aparaṃ tadasaṅgṛhītam | yathā kaśādaṇḍādhātabandhanasvadāragamanādayaḥ akuśalakarmapathapūrvottaraduṣkarmāṇi ca | (pṛ) prāṇātipātādīni trīṇyakuśalakarmāṇi kiṃ kevalakāyikakarmasvabhāvāni | (u) hananapāpaṃ hananākuśalakarmetyucyate | pāpamidaṃ svakāyenāpi kriyate yatra svakāyena sattvān hanti | vācāpi kriyate yatna sattvān hantuṃ paramājñāpayati | manasāpi kriyate yat kaściccittamutpādayati yena paro mriyate | evamadattādānakāmamithyācārapāpe 'pi | svakṛtantu pūrṇaṃ pāpaṃ labhate | kāyākuśalaṃ karma kāyātmakaṃ vāgātmakaṃ vā | kadāciccittotpāde paro jānāti anena pratyayenāpi pāpakaraṃ prāṇātipātādi kuryāditi | bhūyasā kāyakṛtatvātkāyikaṃ karmetyākhyā | evaṃ vāṅmithyācaritamapi | vācābhisaṃskṛtamakuśalaṃ karma vāṅmithyācaritam | tasyāpi dvaividhyam | yat kenacitpraśne sthāpite taṃ purata eva vañcayati | tadakuśalakarmapathasaṅgṛhītam | anyattadasaṅgṛhītam | abhidhyāvyāpādamithyādṛṣṭyādayo mānasamithyācaritam |
body.translated_text: namely <s>prāṇātipāta</s> (killing), <s>adattādāna</s> (stealing), and <s>kāmamithyācāra</s> (sexual misconduct). The other is not included therein—such as beating with whips, striking with rods, imprisonment, consorting with one's own wife improperly, and the evil deeds preceding and following the unwholesome action-paths. (Objection:) Are the three unwholesome actions beginning with <s>prāṇātipāta</s> exclusively of bodily nature? (Reply:) The sin of killing is called the unwholesome <s>karma</s> of killing. This sin is performed by one's own body when one kills beings with one's own body; it is performed by speech when one commands another to kill beings; it is performed by mind when one generates a mental intention by which another dies. The same applies to the sins of <s>adattādāna</s> (stealing) and <s>kāmamithyācāra</s> (sexual misconduct). But when performed by oneself, one obtains the full sin. Bodily unwholesome <s>karma</s> may be bodily in nature or verbal in nature. Sometimes through a mental arising, another knows and by that condition too, one would commit sinful acts such as <s>prāṇātipāta</s>. Because it is predominantly done through the body, it is called bodily <s>karma</s>. The same applies to verbal misconduct. Unwholesome <s>karma</s> performed through speech is verbal misconduct. It too is of two kinds: when, upon a question being posed, one deceives the questioner to his face—that is included in the unwholesome action-paths. The other is not included therein. <s>Abhidhyā</s> (covetousness), <s>vyāpāda</s> (malice), <s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s> (wrong views), and the like constitute mental misconduct.

body.text: (pṛ) daśākuśalakarmapathānāṃ kasmānmithyādṛṣṭirityākhyā trayāṇāmakuśalamūlānāṃ saṃmoha iti | (u) mithyādṛṣṭiriti saṃmohasya nāmāntaram | saṃmohavivṛddhi sārarūpā mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | na punaḥ saṃmohasya lakṣaṇāntaramasti | abhiṣvaṅgaviparyāsamātraṃ saṃmohaḥ | (pṛ) sūtra uktaṃ- sarvāṇi duścaritāni apriyavipākakarāṇi sucaritāni priyavipākakarāṇīti | priyāpriyalakṣaṇañcāniyatam | yathaikameva rūpaṃ [kasyacit] priyaṃ bhavati [anyasyā] priyaṃ bhavati | atastallakṣaṇaṃ vivecanīyaṃ syāt | (u) sukhameva priyalakṣaṇam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- puṇyavipākaḥ sukhamiti | duḥkhamapriyalakṣaṇam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- pāpātsañjātabhītikā bhavatha | duḥkhahetutvāt iti | (pṛ) sukhameva priyalakṣaṇam | śvavarāhādayo 'nnapurīṣeṇa sukhībhavanti | kimidaṃ puṇyaphalam | (u) idamaviśuddhapuṇyaphalam | yathoktaṃ karmasūtre- yadakāle dadāti aśucirdadāti | laghucittena kaluṣitacittena akṣetre ca dadāti | evamādidānena tadvipākaṃ labhata iti |
body.translated_text: (Objection:) Among the ten unwholesome <s>karmapatha</s> (action-paths), why is the name <s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s> (wrong view) used? <s>Saṃmoha</s> (delusion) is one of the three unwholesome roots. (Reply:) <s>Mithyādṛṣṭi</s> is another name for <s>saṃmoha</s>. <s>Mithyādṛṣṭi</s> is the essential, intensified form of <s>saṃmoha</s>. It does not have a different characteristic from <s>saṃmoha</s>. <s>Saṃmoha</s> is merely attachment and distortion. (Objection:) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'All misconduct produces unpleasant fruition; all good conduct produces pleasant fruition.' But the characteristics of pleasant and unpleasant are indeterminate—just as one and the same form may be pleasant to one person and unpleasant to another. Therefore those characteristics should be carefully distinguished. (Reply:) Pleasure alone is the characteristic of the pleasant. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The fruition of merit is pleasure.' Pain is the characteristic of the unpleasant. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Be fearful of sin, because it is a cause of suffering.' (Objection:) If pleasure alone is the characteristic of the pleasant, then dogs and pigs find pleasure in food and excrement—is this the fruit of merit? (Reply:) This is the fruit of impure merit. As stated in the <s>Karmasūtra</s>: 'When one gives at the wrong time, gives impure things, gives with a frivolous mind, a defiled mind, or gives to an unworthy recipient—through such giving one obtains that corresponding fruition.'

body.text: (pṛ) samyak caritāni priyavipākakarāṇīti sūtra uktvā kasmātpunarucyate sucaritapratyayaṃ svarga utpadyata iti | (u) mithyācāryapi svarga utpadyate | kecidvadanti svarga upapattirduścaritavipāka iti | ataḥ sūtre punarucyate sucaritapratyayaṃ svarga upapadyata iti | duścaritasucarite kuśalākuśalagatikakāyaṃ prāpayataḥ gṛhītakāyastatra sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ vā
body.translated_text: (Objection:) Having stated in the <s>sūtra</s> that good conduct produces pleasant fruition, why is it further stated that heaven arises as a result of good conduct? (Reply:) Even through wrong conduct, heaven may arise. Some say that rebirth in heaven is the fruition of misconduct. Therefore the <s>sūtra</s> further states that heaven arises as a result of good conduct. Misconduct and good conduct cause one to obtain bodies in unwholesome and wholesome destinies respectively; having obtained a body there, one experiences pleasure or suffering

body.text: vedayate | yathā duścaritapratyayaṃ durgatau duḥkhaṃ vedayate | sucaritapratyayaṃ deveṣu manuṣyeṣu vā sukhaṃ vedayate ||
body.translated_text: accordingly. Just as through the condition of misconduct one experiences suffering in lower realms, so through the condition of good conduct one experiences pleasure among <s>devas</s> (gods) or human beings.

body.text: duścaritavarga ekottaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Chapter one hundred and one on misconduct (<s>duścarita</s>).

body.text: 102 sucaritavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 102. Chapter on good conduct (<s>sucarita</s>)

body.text: kāyakṛtaṃ kuśalaṃ kāyasucaritam | tathā vāṅmanasorapi | prāṇātipātādyakuśalakarmatrayaviratiḥ kāyasucaritam | vāgdoṣacatuṣṭayaviratirvāksucaritam | mānasākuśalatrayaviratirmanassucaritam | ivāstisro viratayaḥ saṃvarasaṅgṛhītāḥ yaduta śīladhyānānāsravasaṃvarāḥ | yadvandanavastradānādi kuśalaṃ kāyikaṃ karma tat kāyasucaritam | yat satyabhāṣaṇamṛdubhāṣaṇādi tat vāksucaritam | anabhidhyādi mānasaṃ karma manaḥsucaritam | imāni trīṇi su caritāni |
body.translated_text: Wholesome action performed by the body is bodily good conduct (<s>kāyasucarita</s>). Likewise for speech and mind. Abstention from the three unwholesome bodily actions beginning with <s>prāṇātipāta</s> (killing) is bodily good conduct. Abstention from the four verbal faults is verbal good conduct (<s>vāksucarita</s>). Abstention from the three mental unwholesome actions is mental good conduct (<s>manaḥsucarita</s>). These three abstentions are included in <s>saṃvara</s> (restraint), namely the restraints of <s>śīla</s> (morality), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), and <s>anāsrava</s> (the undefiled). Wholesome bodily <s>karma</s> such as salutation and cloth-giving is bodily good conduct. Truthful speech, gentle speech, and the like constitute verbal good conduct. <s>Anabhidhyā</s> (non-covetousness) and similar mental <s>karma</s> constitute mental good conduct. These are the three kinds of good conduct (<s>sucarita</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) tīrthikā jñaptiṃ vinā prātimokṣaśīlabhājo bhavanti | te śīlasaṃvaraṃ labhante na vā | (u) tīrthikāścittataḥ śīlasaṃvaramutpādayanti | kecit vācāpi gṛhṇanti | anye 'pi śīlasaṃvarasaṅgṛhītaṃ sucaritaṃ labhante yathā daśavarṣāyuṣkasya puruṣasya prāṇātipātaviratisamādānādviṃśativarṣāyuṣkaḥ putra utpadyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) Non-Buddhist teachers (<s>tīrthika</s>) receive the <s>Prātimokṣa</s> moral code without formal announcement (<s>jñapti</s>). Do they obtain the moral restraint of <s>śīla</s> (<s>śīlasaṃvara</s>) or not? (Answer) Non-Buddhist teachers generate the moral restraint of <s>śīla</s> mentally. Some also take it verbally. Others too obtain good conduct included within the moral restraint of <s>śīla</s> — just as when a person with a lifespan of ten years undertakes the abstinence from taking life, a son with a lifespan of twenty years is born.

body.text: (pṛ) sūtra uktaṃ- sucaritaṃ viśuddhacaritaṃ vyupaśamacaritamiti | teṣāṃ ko bhedaḥ | (u) ābhidhārmikā āhuḥ- pṛthagjanānāṃ yat kāyikaṃ vācikaṃ mānasaṃ kuśalaṃ karma tat sucaritamityucyate | śaikṣāṇāṃ saṃyojanaprahāṇāttadeva sucaritaṃ viśuddhacaritamityucyate | aśaikṣāṇāṃ prahīṇasaṃyojanānāṃ visaṃyojanikavyavahāratvāt [tadeva]vyupaśamacaritam | aśaikṣā atyantānutpannākuśalakarmakā ityato vyupaśamacaritā ityucyante | yathoktaṃ- kāyavyupaśamo vāgvyupaśamo manovyupaśama iti | kecidāhuḥ- imāni trīṇi caritāni ekasyaivārthasyavibhinnāni nāmāni | kintu tadbhavyatānurūpatvāt samyagiti śaṃsyate | kleśairviviktatvādviśuddhamiti vadanti | sarvākuśalaviviktatvāt vyupaśama iti | tāni trīṇyapi nārthato bhinnāni |
body.translated_text: (Question) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Good conduct (<s>sucarita</s>), purified conduct (<s>viśuddhacarita</s>), and pacified conduct (<s>vyupaśamacarita</s>).' What is the distinction among them? (Answer) The <s>Ābhidhārmikas</s> say: Whatever wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental <s>karma</s> of ordinary persons (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) — that is called 'good conduct.' For trainees (<s>śaikṣa</s>), because of the abandoning of fetters (<s>saṃyojana</s>), that same good conduct is called 'purified conduct.' For non-trainees (<s>aśaikṣa</s>), who have abandoned fetters and whose activity is the unfettering [of beings], that same [conduct] is 'pacified conduct.' Non-trainees, whose unwholesome <s>karma</s> has absolutely never arisen, are therefore called those of 'pacified conduct.' As stated: 'Pacification of body, pacification of speech, pacification of mind.' Some say: These three conducts are different names for one and the same meaning. But because it accords with its capacity, it is praised as 'right.' Because it is separated from defilements, they call it 'purified.' Because it is separated from all that is unwholesome, it is 'pacified.' These three are not different in meaning.

body.text: (pṛ) ābhidharmikā āhuḥ- cittameva vyupaśamacaritaṃ na cetaneti | kathamayamarthaḥ | (u) trīṇi caritānyapi cittameva | kasmāt | cittavyātiriktā nāsti cetanā | nāsti ca kāyavākkarma | (pṛ) sūtra uktaṃṃ- sucaritadṛṣṭisampanno devadṛśo vā bhavati devasaṃkhyātadṛśo vā bhavati | na sarve sucaritā deveṣūpapadyanta iti | kasmādevaṃ viniścayaḥ | (u) devasaṃkhyāteti vacanādidaṃ jñāpitam | sucarītaśālī yadyapi nāvaśyaṃ deveṣūtpadyate tathāpi ya āryabahumatasthāna utpadyate | sa devasarūpa ityato devasaṃkhyātadṛśa ityucyate | sarve sucaritavanto deveṣūtpadyeran | kecidanyapratyayairviniṣṭā notpadyeran | yat samyaṅmithyāvyāmiśraṃ sucaritaṃ [tatra] mithyācaritasya prābalyānna deveṣūtpadyante | yathoktaṃ sūtre- bhagavānānandamavocat- paśyāmyahaṃ kecana trīṇi suritāni caranto 'pi durgatāvutpadyante | tat teṣāṃ pūrvādhvagataduścaritasya phalavipāka iti | idānīṃ sucaritasyāpi aparipūrṇatvānmaraṇa upasthite mithyādṛṣṭeścittābhimukhyāddargatau patanti | duścaritaśālī susthāna utpadyata itīda mapyevam | ataḥ pṛthagjanatvamaśraddheyam | prabalakarmavaśādupapattivibhedaṃ vedayata iti jñātavyam ||
body.translated_text: (Question) The <s>Ābhidhārmikas</s> say: 'Only the mind is pacified conduct, not volition (<s>cetanā</s>).' How is this meaning [to be understood]? (Answer) All three conducts are indeed the mind. Why? Because there is no volition apart from mind, and there is no bodily and verbal <s>karma</s> [apart from mind]. (Question) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'One endowed with good conduct and right view is reborn with a divine appearance, or is reckoned among the gods.' Not all of good conduct are reborn among the gods. Why is this determination made? (Answer) The statement 'reckoned among the gods' makes known [the following]: Even though one endowed with good conduct does not necessarily take birth among the gods, yet one who is born in a place honored by the Noble Ones is like a god in nature — therefore he is called 'reckoned among the gods.' All those of good conduct would be born among the gods; some, obstructed by other conditions, would not be born [there]. That good conduct which is a mixture of right and wrong — because of the predominance of wrong conduct, they are not born among the gods. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: The Blessed One said to <s>Ānanda</s>: 'I see some who, even while practicing three good conducts, are born in a bad destination. That is the ripened fruit of their misconduct from previous lives.' Now too, because of the incompleteness of good conduct, when death approaches, because the mind turns toward wrong views, they fall into a bad destination. One endowed with misconduct who is born in a good destination — this too is likewise. Therefore the state of being an ordinary person is untrustworthy. One should know that through the force of predominant <s>karma</s>, one experiences the distinction of rebirths.

body.text: sucaritavargo dvayuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and second chapter, the Chapter on Good Conduct (<s>sucaritavarga</s>).

body.text: 103 pratisaṃyuktakarmavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 103. Chapter on <s>Karma</s> Connected to the Realms (<s>pratisaṃyuktakarmavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) sūtra uktaṃ- trividhaṃ karma kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktaṃ karma rūpadhātupratisaṃyuktaṃ karma arūpyadhātupratisaṃyuktaṃ karmeti | kānīmāni | (u) yat karma ānarakādāca paranirmitavaśavartidevādantarāle vipākavedakaṃ tatkāmadhātupratisaṃyuktaṃ karma | ābrahmalokādākaniṣṭhāccāntarāle vipākavedakaṃ karma rūpadhātupratisaṃyuktaṃ karma | ākāśānantyāyatanādānaivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanāccāntarāle vipākavedakaṃ ārūpyadhātupratisaṃyuktaṃ karma | (pṛ) avyākṛtaṃ karma aniyatavipākañca karma kimeteṣu nāntargatam | (u) tatkarmavipākaśca kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktaḥ | kasmāt | tasya dharmasya kāmadhātukavipākatvāt | (pṛ) nanu kāmadhātukadharmāḥ sarve tatkarmavipākāḥ | ato na yujyate | (u) sarve ca kāmadhātukadharmāḥ kāmadhātukakarmavipākā eva | (pṛ) tathā cedidaṃ tīrthikaśāstraṃ yaduta sarvapratisaṃvedyaṃ sukhaṃ duḥkhañca pūrvakarmahetupratyayaṃ bhavatīti | pūrvakarmavipāko yaduta kuśalamakuśalaṃ karma savipākamavipākamiti vyavasāyaguṇasya nāsti yatkiñcanaprayojanam | yadi sarvaṃ karmavipākaḥ | kaḥ punaḥ prayāse guṇaḥ | yasya
body.translated_text: (Question) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There is threefold <s>karma</s>: <s>karma</s> connected to the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>), <s>karma</s> connected to the form realm (<s>rūpadhātu</s>), and <s>karma</s> connected to the formless realm (<s>arūpyadhātu</s>).' What are these? (Answer) Whatever <s>karma</s> produces the experience of ripening in the range from the hells (<s>nāraka</s>) to the <s>Paranirmitavaśavartin</s> gods — that is <s>karma</s> connected to the desire realm. <s>Karma</s> that produces the experience of ripening in the range from the <s>Brahmaloka</s> to the <s>Akaniṣṭha</s> [heaven] — that is <s>karma</s> connected to the form realm. <s>Karma</s> that produces the experience of ripening in the range from the sphere of infinite space (<s>ākāśānantyāyatana</s>) to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (<s>naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana</s>) — that is <s>karma</s> connected to the formless realm. (Question) Is indeterminate (<s>avyākṛta</s>) <s>karma</s> and <s>karma</s> with unfixed ripening not included among these? (Answer) That <s>karma</s> and its ripening are connected to the desire realm. Why? Because the ripening of that <s>dharma</s> belongs to the desire realm. (Question) But all <s>dharmas</s> of the desire realm would be the ripening of that <s>karma</s> — therefore this is not valid. (Answer) Indeed, all <s>dharmas</s> of the desire realm are the ripening of desire-realm <s>karma</s>. (Question) If so, then this is like the non-Buddhist treatise (<s>tīrthikaśāstra</s>) that says: 'All that is experienced — pleasure and suffering — has prior <s>karma</s> as its cause and condition.' [If] the ripening of prior <s>karma</s> — namely wholesome and unwholesome <s>karma</s>, <s>karma</s> with ripening and <s>karma</s> without ripening — [accounts for everything], then there is no purpose whatsoever for the quality of effort. If everything is the ripening of <s>karma</s>, what then is the benefit of exertion? For one whose

body.text: kleśāḥ karmāṇi karmavipākāśca santi tasya vimuktirnāsti | karmavipākasyākṣīṇatvāt | ucyate | yaduktaṃ idaṃ tīrthikaśāstramiti | tadayuktam | tīrthikā hi vadanti sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ paratvamaparatvaṃ pūrvavipākamātramiti | tathā ca na syātpratyutpannapratyayāpekṣā | paśyāmastu vastutaḥ padārthāḥ pratyutpannebhyaḥ pratyayebhyaḥ samutpadyante yathā bījāṅkurādaya iti | ato na vaktavyaṃ sarvaṃ pūrvakarmapratyayādhīnamiti | hetupratyayābhyañca vastūnyutpadyante yathā bījahetukāḥ pṛthivyabākāśakālādipratyayā [aḍkurādayaḥ] | cakṣurvijñānañca karmahetukaṃ cakṣūrūpādipratyayam | ato na tīrthikamithyāśāstrasāmyam | yadbravīṣi pūrvakarmavipāka ityādi | tadayuktam | pratyakṣaṃ khalu phalātphalasantatirutpadyata iti | yathā brīhibhyo brīhayaḥ | evaṃ vipākādvipākotpattau ko doṣaḥ | yathā ajātaputrasya ca caṭakacakravākādīnāñca kāmaḥ, sarpādināṃ kopaḥ, tatsarvaṃ pūrvakarmavipāka iti jñeyam |
body.translated_text: defilements, <s>karmas</s>, and ripened results of <s>karma</s> exist, there is no liberation — because the ripening of <s>karma</s> is inexhaustible. It is replied: Your statement 'this is like the non-Buddhist treatise' is not valid. For non-Buddhists say: 'Pleasure, suffering, superiority, and inferiority are merely the ripening of prior [<s>karma</s>].' If so, there would be no dependence on present conditions. But we see in reality that things arise from present conditions, just as sprouts arise from seeds and the like. Therefore it should not be said that 'everything is dependent on prior <s>karma</s> as its condition.' Things arise from both causes (<s>hetu</s>) and conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>) — just as sprouts and the like arise from the cause of the seed and conditions such as earth, water, space, time, and the rest. And eye-consciousness has <s>karma</s> as its cause but the eye, form, and the rest as its conditions. Therefore there is no similarity with the wrong treatises of non-Buddhists. As for your statement 'it is the ripening of prior <s>karma</s>' and so forth — that is not valid. For it is directly perceived that fruit-continuity arises from fruit. Just as rice arises from rice. In the same way, what fault is there in ripening arising from ripening? Just as the desire of one whose son is unborn, and the desire of sparrows and <s>cakravāka</s> birds, and the anger of serpents and the like — all that should be known as the ripening of prior <s>karma</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi vipākādvipāka utpadyate | tadānavasthā syāt | (u) karmavipākāstrividhāḥ kuśalo 'kuśalo 'vyākṛta iti | kuśalākuśalābhyāṃ vipāka utpadyate nāvyākṛtādityato nānavasthā | yathā brīhibhyo vrīhaya utpadyante | tatra bījādaṅkura utpadyate na tu tuṣādibhyaḥ | evaṃ kuśalākuśalavipākādvipāka utpadyate nāvyākṛtavipākāt | yaduktaṃ bhavatā prayāse na guṇa iti | yadyapi karmaṇo vipāka utpadyate | tathāpi avaśyaṃ yathāśakti paścātsaṃsidhyati | yathā sasyakarmataḥ sasyamutpadyate | tathāpi bījādyapekṣya tat sidhyati | yadāha bhavān- na vimuktirbhavediti | tadapyayuktam | tattvajñānalābhātkarmāṇi kṣīyante | tadyathā dagdhaṃ bījaṃ na punaḥ prarohati | ato nāsti vimukterdoṣaḥ | kiñca ya utpannā dharmāḥ sarve te karmamūlakāḥ | yadi nāsti karmamūlaṃ, kathamutpadyeta | dharmāṇāmutpāde 'sti pratiniyatamaṅgam | yathāyaṃ dharmo niyamena etatpuruṣakāyādutpadyate nānyakāyāt | yadi nāsti karmamūlaṃ, kathamevaṃ pratiniyatavibhāgaḥ syāt |
body.translated_text: (Question) If ripening arises from ripening, then there would be infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>). (Answer) The ripened results of <s>karma</s> are threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Ripening arises from wholesome and unwholesome [karma] — not from indeterminate — therefore there is no infinite regress. Just as rice arises from rice: therein, a sprout arises from the seed, but not from the husk and the like. In the same way, ripening arises from the ripening of wholesome and unwholesome [karma], not from indeterminate ripening. As for your statement 'there is no benefit in effort' — even though ripening arises from <s>karma</s>, still, whatever is possible necessarily comes to fulfillment afterwards according to one's capacity. Just as crops arise from the labor of cultivating crops, yet they come to fulfillment depending on the seed and the rest. As for your statement 'there would be no liberation' — that too is not valid. Through the attainment of the knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>), <s>karmas</s> are exhausted. Just as a burnt seed does not sprout again. Therefore there is no fault regarding liberation. Furthermore, all <s>dharmas</s> that have arisen are rooted in <s>karma</s>. If there is no root of <s>karma</s>, how would they arise? In the arising of <s>dharmas</s>, there is a determinate factor. Just as this <s>dharma</s> necessarily arises from this particular person-body (<s>puruṣakāya</s>), not from another body. If there is no root of <s>karma</s>, how could there be such a determinate distinction?

body.text: (pṛ) dharmā hetumātrajāḥ | yathā māṣānmāṣa utpadyate | [evaṃ sati] ko doṣaḥ | (u) tadapi karmamūlakam | māṣakarmapratyayalābhānmāṣānmāṣa utpadyate | kenedaṃ jñāyate | purā kila janāḥ kuśalamācaritavanta ityataḥ śālitaṇḍulāḥ svata ajāyanta | ato jñāyate karmabhūlakatvāt māṣānmāṣo jāyata iti | (pṛ) nanu sattvasaṃkhyātaṃ vastu khalu pūrvakarmajam | (u) maivam asattvasaṃkhyātaṃ vastvapi karmamūlakam | sarvasattvānāṃ sādhāraṇakarmavipāko yaduta
body.translated_text: (Question) <s>Dharmas</s> are born merely from causes. Just as a bean arises from a bean. If so, what fault is there? (Answer) That too is rooted in <s>karma</s>. Because of obtaining the <s>karma</s>-condition of the bean, a bean arises from a bean. How is this known? It is said that formerly, when people practiced wholesome conduct, rice grains arose spontaneously. From this it is known that, because of being rooted in <s>karma</s>, a bean is born from a bean. (Question) But it is only sentient beings that are born from prior <s>karma</s>. (Answer) Not so — even non-sentient things are rooted in <s>karma</s>. The common ripened result of the <s>karma</s> of all sentient beings — namely

body.text: caṅkramaṇāsthānakarmapratyayalābhāt kṣityādayo bhavanti | prakāśakarmapratyayalābhāccandrasūryādayo bhavanti iti jñātavyaṃ janyaṃ vastu sarvaṃ karmamūlakamiti | (pṛ) yadi janyadharmāḥ karmamūlakāḥ | saṃskṛto 'nāsravaḥ katham | (u) so 'pi karmamūlakaḥ | kasmāt | sarvaṃ pūrvādhvagatadānaśīlādivalādhīnam | ato 'pi karmādisambhūtam | (pṛ) yadyanāsravadharmo 'pi karmasambhūtaḥ | so 'pi pratisaṃyuktadharma ityākhyā syāt | tattu na sambhavati | uktaṃ hi sūtre- asti aprasaṃyuktā vedeneti | (u) anāsravadharmastattvajñānahetukaḥ karmapratyayakaḥ | hetubalamahimnā tu apratisaṃyukta ityucyate |
body.translated_text: because of obtaining the <s>karma</s>-conditions of walking and dwelling, earth and the other [elements] come into being. Because of obtaining the <s>karma</s>-condition of illumination, the moon, sun, and the rest come into being. Thus it should be known that all produced things are rooted in <s>karma</s>. (Question) If produced <s>dharmas</s> are rooted in <s>karma</s>, how can there be conditioned undefiled (<s>anāsrava</s>) [dharmas]? (Answer) Those too are rooted in <s>karma</s>. Why? Because everything depends on the power of giving (<s>dāna</s>), moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), and the like from past lives. Therefore [undefiled dharmas] too arise from <s>karma</s> and the rest. (Question) If even undefiled <s>dharmas</s> arise from <s>karma</s>, they too should be called 'connected <s>dharmas</s>' (<s>pratisaṃyukta</s>) — but that is not possible. For it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There is unconnected feeling.' (Answer) Undefiled <s>dharmas</s> have the knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>) as their cause and <s>karma</s> as their condition. But through the power of the cause, they are called 'unconnected.'

body.text: (pṛ) kiṃ karma kāmadhātuvipākavedakam | kiṃ rūpadhātuvipākavedakam | kimārūpyadhātuvipākavedakam | (u) yaḥ kāmarūpārūpyadhātuṣu daśākuśalakarmāṇi samutpādayati sa kāmadhātau vipākaṃ vedayate | (pṛ) rūpārūpyadhātugato 'pi kimakuśalaṃ karma samutpādayati | (u) tatrāpyakuśalaṃ karma samutpādayati | yathoktaṃ sūtre- tatrāsti mithyādṛṣṭiriti | mithyādṛṣṭiḥ kiṃ nākuśalā | (pṛ) tatra mithyādṛṣṭiravyākṛtā natvakuśalā | (u) nāvyākṛtā | kenaitat jñāyate | uktaṃ hi sūtre bhagavatā- mithyādṛṣṭirduḥkhakleśānāṃ heturiti | mithyādarśinā samutpāditāni kāyavāṅmanaskarmāṇi duḥkhavipākāyabhisaṃskriyante | yathā tiktakāravelle vidyamānāni catvāri mahābhūtāni sarvāṇi tiktarasāni bhavanti | yathā kāmadhātau mithyādṛṣṭirakuśalā | rūpārūpyadhātvorapi tallakṣaṇā akuśalā syāt | lakṣaṇasāmyāt | yathā bako brahmā brahmāṇamāmantrayāha- mopagaccha śramaṇaṃ gautamam | asmāllokāduttārayāma iti | idaṃ manovāgakuśalaṃ rūpadhātau samutpannam | anye 'pi brahma [kāyikā] devāḥ tatra bhavantaṃ tādṛśaṃ puruṣaṃ dūṣayanti | rūpārūpyadhātugatāḥ puruṣā vadanti- idameva nirvāṇamiti | āyuṣo 'nte kāmarūpayorantarābhavameva paśyanti | ito 'nyannirvāṇaṃ nāstīti mithyādṛṣṭirutpanneti anuttamadharmāpavādātkathaṃ nākuśalam | anena jñātavyaṃ tatrāstyakuśalaṃ karmeti | (pṛ) yadi tatrākuśalaṃ karmotpādayanti | tatkarma kiṃsthānapratisaṃyuktam | (u) yadīdamakuśalaṃ karma tadā kāmadhātau vipākaṃ vedayata ityataḥ kāmadhātupratisaṃyuktam |
body.translated_text: (Question) What <s>karma</s> produces ripening to be experienced in the desire realm? What in the form realm? What in the formless realm? (Answer) One who generates the ten unwholesome <s>karmas</s> (<s>daśākuśalakarma</s>) in the desire, form, and formless realms experiences ripening in the desire realm. (Question) Does one who is in the form and formless realms also generate unwholesome <s>karma</s>? (Answer) Even there, unwholesome <s>karma</s> is generated. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There, there is wrong view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>).' Is wrong view not unwholesome? (Question) There, wrong view is indeterminate, not unwholesome. (Answer) It is not indeterminate. How is this known? For it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s> by the Blessed One: 'Wrong view is the cause of painful defilements.' Bodily, verbal, and mental <s>karmas</s> generated by one of wrong views are conditioned for the ripening of suffering. Just as when the four great elements present in bitter gourd are all of bitter taste. Just as wrong view in the desire realm is unwholesome, so too in the form and formless realms it would be unwholesome, having the same characteristic. Just as <s>Baka Brahmā</s> addressed <s>Brahmā</s>: 'Do not approach the ascetic <s>Gautama</s>. We will deliver [you] from this world.' This is unwholesome mental and verbal [action] generated in the form realm. Other <s>Brahmakāyika</s> gods too disparage such a person there. Persons in the form and formless realms say: 'This alone is <s>Nirvāṇa</s>.' At the end of their lifespan, they see only the intermediate existence (<s>antarābhava</s>) between the desire and form [realms]. 'There is no <s>Nirvāṇa</s> other than this' — thus wrong view arises. Because of the denigration of the supreme <s>Dharma</s>, how is it not unwholesome? From this it should be known that even there, unwholesome <s>karma</s> exists. (Question) If they generate unwholesome <s>karma</s> there, to which realm is that <s>karma</s> connected? (Answer) Since this unwholesome <s>karma</s> produces ripening to be experienced in the desire realm, it is connected to the desire realm.

body.text: kuśalaṃ karmāsti uttamaṃ madhyamamadhamamiti | adhamaṃ kāmadhātuvedanīyavipākam | madhyamaṃ rūpadhātuvedanīyavipākam | uttamamārūpyadhātuvedanīyavipākam | kecidāhuḥ-
body.translated_text: Wholesome <s>karma</s> is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. Inferior [karma] has ripening to be experienced in the desire realm. Middling [karma] has ripening to be experienced in the form realm. Superior [karma] has ripening to be experienced in the formless realm. Some say:
