And this passion, following the [course of] time, is: inferior, middling, superior, inferior-inferior, inferior-middling, inferior-superior, middling-inferior, middling-middling, middling-superior, superior-inferior, superior-middling, and superior-superior. And this passion has ten worldly components: namely, having seen a pleasing form, the mind speaks 'this is pleasing.' From that, one generates passion. One makes a resolve. One recollects. One displays [oneself] as one has been trained. One forgets shame and embarrassment (<s>hrī</s> and <s>apatrapa</s>). One always presents oneself. One becomes heedless. One becomes mad. One faints and dies. This is the characteristic of passion.

body.text: rāgalakṣaṇavargo dvāviṃśatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one-hundred-and-twenty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of Passion (<s>rāgalakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 123 kāmahetuvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 123. Chapter on the Causes of Sensual Desire (<s>kāmahetuvarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) kāmo 'yaṃ kathamutpadyate | (u) strīrūpādhyālambane yadi mithyāmanaskāramutpādayati | yadi vā tadrūpe yadi vākāre yadi vā sparśe yadi vā subhāṣite [mithyāmanaskāramutpādayati] | tadā kāmarāga utpadyate | cakṣuḥ śrotrādidvārāsaṃvaraṇe kāmarāga
body.translated_text: (Question) How does this sensual desire (<s>kāma</s>) arise? (Answer) When, in grasping the object of a woman's form, one generates wrong mental attention (<s>mithyāmanaskāra</s>); or in her form, or in her gait, or in her touch, or in her pleasant speech [one generates wrong mental attention] — then desire-passion (<s>kāmarāga</s>) arises. Through non-restraint of the gates of the eye, ear, and other [senses], desire-passion

body.text: utpadyate | bhojane cāmātratājñāne kāmarāga utpadyate | strīrūpasaṃstave kāmarāga utpadyate | sukhāni vedayataḥ kāmarāga utpadyate | mohātkāmarāga utpadyate | aśucisaṃjñājananāt, durvijñānātkāmarāga utpadyate | yathā śuddhaṃ vastra [mapagatakalaṅkaṃ] samyaṅ malena dūṣyate | rāgabahulānāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ saṃvāsena kāmarāga utpadyate | kāyādiṣu cāturbhautikeṣu mithyāmanaskāramutpādayan kāmāhṛto bhavati | apragṛhītavṛttaghaṭavadagrathitakusumavacca | yadi kausīdyānna kuśalaṃ bhāvayati | tadā kāmarāgo 'vakāśaṃ labhate | agamyasthāne gacchan rāgeṇā bhibhūyate | yaduta veśyāṅganāmadyavikrayavadhakakuṭyādayaḥ | tadyathā gṛdhro vā kaṅko vā iti dṛṣṭāntaḥ | aśucyādi vilokya apratihatālambanasya kāmarāgo vegaṃ labhate | sucirādārabhya sadā kāmarāgābhyāsāt rāgānuśayaḥ sidhyati | tadā sūtpādo 'yaṃ bhavati | strīrūpādyalambane prīto nimittaṃ gṛhṇāti paricchedañca gṛhṇāti | nimittagrahaṇaṃ nāma pāṇipādamukhanayanālāpamandahāsakaṭākṣarodananayanabāṣpādinimittānāṃ grahaṇam | paricchedagrahaṇaṃ nāma strī pumāniti saṃsthānaviśeṣavikalpaḥ | evaṃ gṛhītānusmaraṇavikalpasya kāmarāga utpadyate | durbalavicāraṇācitta ālambanamanudhāvati na nigṛhṇāti | tadā kāmarāga utpadyate | yaḥ pravṛttakāmarāgaḥ [tat]kṣāntiṃ vedayan na parityajati | sa kramaśo vardhayati | adhamānmadhyamamutpādayati | madhyamādadhamamutpādayati |
body.translated_text: arises. Through not knowing the proper measure in food, desire-passion arises. Through praise of a woman's form, desire-passion arises. For one who experiences pleasures, desire-passion arises. Through delusion (<s>moha</s>), desire-passion arises. Through generating the perception of the impure (<s>aśuci</s>), because of being difficult to discern, desire-passion arises. Just as a clean garment, free from stain, is properly defiled by dirt. Through association with persons who are abundant in passion, desire-passion arises. Generating wrong mental attention regarding the body and the like, which are composed of the four elements — one becomes captivated by sensual desire. Like a pot whose handle has not been fastened, or like an unstrung garland of flowers. When, through laziness, one does not cultivate the wholesome, then desire-passion finds an opportunity. Going to improper places, one is overpowered by passion — namely, the houses of courtesans, liquor-sellers, slaughterers, and the like. The illustration of the vulture or the heron [applies here]. Having observed the impure and the like, for one whose object is unobstructed, desire-passion gains momentum. Through the habitual practice of desire-passion from a long time past, the latent tendency of passion (<s>rāgānuśaya</s>) is established. Then this [passion] has a subtle arising. Being delighted in the grasping of a woman's form and the like as an object, one grasps the sign (<s>nimitta</s>) and grasps the particularities (<s>pariccheda</s>). 'Grasping the sign' means the grasping of signs such as hands, feet, face, eyes, conversation, gentle laughter, sidelong glances, weeping, tears of the eyes, and the like. 'Grasping the particularities' means the conceptual discrimination of the distinction of shape [as] 'woman' or 'man.' For one who thus recollects and conceptualizes what has been grasped, desire-passion arises. For one whose mind of investigation is weak, [the mind] runs after the object and does not restrain [itself] — then desire-passion arises. One whose desire-passion has set in motion, experiencing patience toward it without abandoning [it] — he gradually increases it. From the inferior, he generates the middling; from the middling, he generates the inferior [again, oscillating].

body.text: kāmarāgasya hitāsvādamātraṃ dṛṣṭvā tadānīnavamajānataḥ kāmarāga utpadyate | ṛtunā ca kāmarāga utpadyate yathā vasantādayaḥ | sthānavaśena ca kāmarāga utpadyate yathā kiñcitsthānaṃ yatra cirādārabhya kāmacāro bahuśo 'bhyastaḥ | dehasyā [vasthā]vaśācca kāmarāgo bhavati | yathā yūno 'rogasya dhanasampannasya | balaśaktyā ca kāmarāgo bhavati | yathā pānauṣadhādiḥ | śubhān manohāriṇaḥ pañcakāmaguṇān yaduta supuṣpitasarārāmaprasannasnigdhavāpīkūpanavameghataṭitsurabhivātavyajanāni labdhavataḥ, pakṣiṇāṃ kalaravaṃ strīṇāṃ sukumārabhūṣaṇarutāni subhāṣitāni vā śṛṇvataḥ kāmarāga utpadyate | karmapratyayena ca kāmarāga utpadyate | yathā viśuddhadātā viśuddhapraṇīteṣu pañcakāmaguṇeṣu saṃpraharṣati | pāpī tu aviśuddheṣu | jātitaśca kāmarāgo
body.translated_text: Seeing only the immediate relish of desire-passion, and not knowing its harmful consequences — desire-passion arises. And desire-passion arises due to the season — such as spring and the rest. And desire-passion arises due to the power of place — such as a certain place where sexual conduct has been frequently practiced over a long time. And desire-passion arises due to the condition of the body — such as for one who is young, healthy, and endowed with wealth. And desire-passion arises due to the force of strength — such as through drinks, medicines, and the like. Having obtained beautiful, captivating five strands of sensual pleasure — namely, a well-flowered pleasure-garden, a clear and pleasant lake or well, new clouds, lightning, a fragrant breeze and fans — hearing the melodious songs of birds, the soft sounds of women's ornaments, or pleasant speech — desire-passion arises. And desire-passion arises due to the condition of <s>karma</s> — just as one who has given in purity rejoices in the five strands of sensual pleasure that are pure and excellent. But a sinner [rejoices] in impure [pleasures]. And desire-passion arises due to birth (<s>jāti</s>)

body.text: bhavati | yathā puruṣaḥ puruṣamicchati | prajñaptāvatyāsaṅge ca kāmarāga utpadyate | [yathā] kaścidantaḥpuṃlakṣaṇo bahistu strīlakṣaṇo vastraveṣavairamaitryādilakṣaṇaśca | alabdhacittasamādhānasya antaḥ sattvaṃ paśyato bahiḥ rūpādi paśyataśca kāmarāgo bhavati | yasya rāgānuśo 'kṣīṇaḥ tṛṣṇāpratyayaśca sammukhī bhavati | tasya mithyāmanaskāra utpadyate | evamādipratyayaiḥ kāmarāgautpadyate ||
body.translated_text: — just as a man desires a man. And desire-passion arises due to attachment to designations (<s>prajñapti</s>) — just as someone who has male characteristics internally but female characteristics externally, and characteristics of clothing, appearance, hostility, friendliness, and the like. For one who has not obtained mental composure (<s>cittasamādhāna</s>), seeing a being internally and seeing form and the like externally — desire-passion arises. For one whose latent tendency of passion (<s>rāgānuśaya</s>) is not exhausted and whose condition of craving (<s>tṛṣṇāpratyaya</s>) is present before [him] — wrong mental attention (<s>mithyāmanaskāra</s>) arises. Through such and similar conditions, desire-passion arises.

body.text: kāmahetuvargastrayoviṃśatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one-hundred-and-twenty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Causes of Sensual Desire (<s>kāmahetuvarga</s>).

body.text: 124 kāmadoṣavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 124. Chapter on the Faults of Sensual Desire (<s>kāmadoṣavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) kāmarāgasya ke doṣāḥ santīti kāmaḥ prahātavyaḥ | (u) kāmarāgo vastuto duḥkham | pṛthagjanā viparyayeṇa mṛṣā [tatra] sukhasaṃjñāmutpādayanti | jñānī tu duḥkhaṃ paśyati | duḥkhaṃ paśyan prajahāti | kāmopādāne nāsti tṛptiḥ | yathā madyapānaṃ tatparitarṣaṇamanuvardhayati | paritarṣaṇavivṛddhyā kaḥ sukhī bhavati | kāmopādānādakuśalāni sahopacīyante | asiśastrādīnāṃ kāmādhīnatvāt | uktañca sūtre- kāmaḥ pāpo laghurdūstyajaḥ | vyāpāda[gato] laghupāpaḥ, vastutaḥ sa [tato 'pi] laghuttaraḥ iti | kāmaḥ punarbhavasya hetuḥ | yathoktaṃ- tṛṣṇāpratyayamupādānaṃ yāvanmahato duḥkhaskandhasya samudaya iti | tṛṣṇāṃ pratītya kāyo bhavati | āha ca duḥkhahetustṛṣṇā bhavatīti | kiñcāha- vidyamānāni duḥkhāni bhikṣavaḥ kasmādbhavantīti manasikṛtvā jānīdhvaṃ [tāni] kāmahetukāni | tṛṣṇāyāśca kāyo heturiti | kiñcāha- kabalīkāre [bhikṣava] āhāre 'sti nandi asti rāgaḥ | ato vijñānaṃ tatra pratiṣṭhitam iti | jñātavyaṃ tṛṣṇā kāyavedanāyāḥ pratyaya iti | ayañca rāgaḥ sadā aśucau samudācarati | yathā stryādiṣu | strīṇāṃ kāyacittamaśuci śakṛnmṛtsu [vidyamāna]vṛścikavat daṣṭvā dūṣayati | sa kāmarāgaḥ sadā mohe samudācarati | yathoktaṃ sūtre- yathā śvā raktaliptamasthikaṅkālaṃ svādayitvā [sva]lālāyogānmanyate yanmadhura[mida]miti | tathā rāgyapi nīrase kāme mithyāviparyāsabalena manyate yadidaṃ rasāsvādamiti |
body.translated_text: (Question) What faults does desire-passion have, that sensual desire should be abandoned? (Answer) Desire-passion is in reality suffering. Ordinary beings, through perversion, falsely generate the perception of pleasure in it. But the wise one sees it as suffering. Seeing it as suffering, he abandons it. In the grasping of sensual desire, there is no satisfaction. Just as the drinking of liquor increases the very thirst for it. Through the increase of thirst, who becomes happy? Through the grasping of sensual desire, unwholesome [states] are accumulated together — because swords, weapons, and the like depend on sensual desire. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Sensual desire is sinful, light [in pleasure], and difficult to abandon. One endowed with malice (<s>vyāpāda</s>) has light sin — in reality, it [i.e., sensual desire] is even lighter [in its pleasure] than that.' Sensual desire is the cause of further rebirth (<s>punarbhava</s>). As stated: 'Clinging (<s>upādāna</s>) conditioned by craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), up to the arising of the great mass of suffering (<s>duḥkhaskandha</s>).' Dependent on craving, the body comes into being. And it says: 'Craving is the cause of suffering.' And further he says: 'Monks, reflect in your minds on why the sufferings that exist arise — [they] are caused by sensual desire.' 'And craving is the cause of the body.' And further he says: 'Monks, in solid food (<s>kabalīkāra āhāra</s>), there is delight (<s>nandī</s>), there is passion (<s>rāga</s>). Therefore consciousness is established therein.' It should be known that craving is the condition of bodily feeling. And this passion always operates in the impure — such as in women and the like. The body and mind of women are impure; like a scorpion dwelling in excrement and mud, it defiles by stinging. This desire-passion always operates in delusion. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Just as a dog, savoring a blood-smeared skeletal bone, because of the mixture with its own saliva, thinks "this is sweet" — so too, the passionate one, in tasteless sensual desire, through the power of wrong perversion, thinks "this is the savoring of flavor."

body.text: yathā māṃsapeśyādayaḥ sasopamā [uktāḥ] | keṣāñcidatīte 'tāgate vā vastuni kāmarāga utpadyate | ato jñāyate mohe sadā samudācaratīti | sattvānāṃ kāmarāgapratyayaṃ sukhamalpaṃ duḥkhaṃ bahu kena kim [syāt] |
body.translated_text: Just as pieces of flesh and the like are described as analogous [to sensual desire]. For some, desire-passion arises with regard to objects in the past or future. From this it is known that [desire-passion] always operates in delusion. The happiness of beings conditioned by desire-passion is small, while the suffering is great — what benefit could there be?

body.text: kāmatṛṣṇāvān sukhahetoḥ sarvaduḥkhānyanubhavati yadutārjanakāle duḥkhaṃ rakṣaṇakāle duḥkhamupabhogakāle 'pi duḥkham | yathā kṛṣivāṇijyasaṃgrāmarājasevāparicaryādīni arjane duḥkhaṃ hānabhītyā rakṣaṇe duḥkhaṃ, pratyutpanne tṛptyabhāvādduḥkham | iṣṭasaṅgame prītiralpā virahe ca duḥkhaṃ bahu | yatho jñāyate kāyo bahudoṣa iti | yathāha bhagavān- kāmatṛṣṇāyāḥ pañcādīnavāḥ- alpāsvādo bahuduḥkhaṃ, saṃyojanādīpanamāmaraṇatṛptirāryavigarhaṇamakuśalaṃ vinā na karaṇam iti | anena kāmarāgeṇa sattvāḥ saṃsārasrotānugāmino nirvāṇāddūrībhavanti | evamādīnyapramāṇānyavadyāni santi | iti jñātavyaṃ kāyo bahudoṣaḥ iti |
body.translated_text: One who has sensual craving (<s>kāmatṛṣṇā</s>) experiences all sufferings for the sake of pleasure — namely, suffering at the time of acquisition, suffering at the time of protection, and suffering at the time of enjoyment. Just as in farming, trade, battle, royal service, attendance, and the like — there is suffering in acquisition; through fear of loss, there is suffering in protection; because of the impossibility of satisfaction in the present, there is suffering. The joy of encountering what is desired is small, and the suffering of separation is great. Therefore it is known that the body is of many faults. As the Blessed One said: 'Sensual craving has five dangers — little enjoyment and much suffering, the kindling of fetters, insatiability until death, the reproach of the Noble Ones, and that it does not cease without the unwholesome.' Through this sensual passion (<s>kāmarāga</s>), beings follow the current of <s>saṃsāra</s> and become far from <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Such and other immeasurable faults exist. Therefore it should be known that the body is of many faults.

body.text: kleśā rāgamupādāya bhavanti yathā kāmarāgāt kleśāḥ sarve samudbhavanti | tṛṣṇānuśaye 'nunmūlite punaḥ punarduḥkhamanubhavati | yathā viṣavṛkṣo 'nucchinnaḥ sadā puruṣaṃ hanti | rāgeṇa sattvā gurvī dhuraṃ vahanti | uktañca sūtre- kāmatṛṣṇā bandhanamityucyate | yathā kṛṣṇaśuklā gauḥ svayamabaddhā rajjunā paramabaddhā | evaṃ cakṣurna rūpabaddhaṃ, rūpañca na cakṣurbaddham, kāmarāgastu tatra baddhaḥ | imaṃ bandhamavalambayato na vimuktirlabhyate | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- pūrvā koṭirna [prajñāyate] avidyānīvaraṇānāṃ sattvānāṃ tṛṣṇāsaṃyojanānāṃ sandhāvatāṃ saṃsaratām iti | api coktaṃ sūtre- rāgaprahāṇādrūpaṃ prahīyate yāvadvijñānaṃ prahīyata iti | rāgo 'yamanityatādibhāvanayā prahīyate | prahīṇe 'smin kāmarāge cittaṃ vimucyate | rūparāgaprahāṇe
body.translated_text: Defilements arise depending on passion (<s>rāga</s>). Just as from sensual passion, all defilements arise. When the latent tendency of craving (<s>tṛṣṇānuśaya</s>) is not uprooted, one experiences suffering again and again. Just as a poison-tree that is not cut down constantly kills a person. Through passion, beings bear a heavy burden. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Sensual craving is called a bond.' Just as a black and white cow — the one is not bound by the rope to the other — so the eye is not bound to form, nor form bound to the eye, but sensual passion is the bond therein. Leaning on this bond, liberation is not obtained. Furthermore, it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The prior limit cannot be discerned — for beings enveloped by the obstruction of ignorance and fettered by the bond of craving, running and wandering [in <s>saṃsāra</s>].' And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Through the abandonment of passion, form is abandoned, up to: consciousness is abandoned.' This passion is abandoned through the cultivation of impermanence and the like. When this sensual passion is abandoned, the mind is liberated. Through the abandonment of passion for form,

body.text: nāsti rūpam | asati rūpe duḥkhaṃ nirudhyate | yāvadvijñāne 'pyevam | jñāyate kāmarāgāḥ sudṛḍhaṃ bandhanamiti |
body.translated_text: there is no form. When there is no form, suffering is brought to cessation. The same applies up to consciousness as well. It is known that sensual passion is an exceedingly firm bond.

body.text: kāmarāgaścoropamaḥ | sattvāstu tadakuśalaṃ na paśyanti | kāmarāgaḥ sadā kusumāramukhataḥ samudācaratītyataḥ paramamakuśalaṃ nāma | kiñca sattvāścittapramodena kāmarāge pravartante yāvanmaśakapipīlikā[daya]ḥ sarve 'pi āhāramaithunayoḥ pravartante | sa kāmarāgo nānākāraṇaiḥ puruṣāṇāṃ cittaṃ badhnāti yaduta mātṛpitṛsvasṛbhaginīpatnīsaṃjñā dhanādayaḥ | satvā āhāramaithunādikāmarāganīvṛtacittāḥ santo janmopādadate | dhyānasamāpattirāga ūrdhvabhūmāvutpadyate | kāmarāgo 'yaṃ saṅgamaṃ karoti | sarveṣāṃ lokānāṃ rucayaḥ pratyekaṃ vibhinnāḥ | rāgātsaṅgacchante | yathā śuṣkāḥ sikatāḥ salilayoge saṃyujyante | saṃsāre kāmatṛṣṇāṃ rasaṃ manyante | yathā rūpāṇāmāsvādādhyavasānamityuktaṃ yaduta rūpaṃ pratītyotpadyate sukhaṃ saumanasyam | asati rāge nāsvādaḥ | āsvāde 'sati saṃsāramāśu prajahāti | sa ca kāmarāgo vimuktiviruddhaḥ | kasmāt | yasmāt sattvāḥ kāmaḥ sukhaṃ dhyānaṃ sukhaṃ samāpattiḥ sukhamiti saṃrajyante | tasmāt vimuktirasukham | [yat] rāgāṅgaprahāṇaṃ tadeva sukhaṃ pariṇamati | yathoktaṃ- yasya vairāgyaṃ sa paramaṃ sukhamanuprāpnoti iti | kiñcāha- yaḥ sarvasukhalābhamicchati tena sarvāṇi kāmasukhāni tyaktavyāni | sarvakāmānāṃ tyāgādātyantikanityasukhaṃ labhata iti | yo mahāsukhaṃ lipsati tenālpasukhamupekṣitavyam | alpasukhopekṣayā apramāṇasukhaṃ pratilabhate |
body.translated_text: Sensual passion is like a thief. But beings do not see its unwholesomeness. Because sensual passion always operates through a pleasant face — therefore it is called 'supremely unwholesome.' Furthermore, beings, through the delight of the mind, engage in sensual passion, even mosquitoes, ants, and the like — all engage in food and sexual intercourse. That sensual passion binds the minds of people through various causes — namely, the notions of mother, father, sister, wife, wealth, and the like. Beings, with minds enveloped by sensual passion for food, sexual intercourse, and the like, take up birth. Passion for <s>dhyāna</s> and attainment produces rebirth in the higher planes. This sensual passion creates association. The tastes of all beings in the world are individually distinct — through passion, they come together. Just as dry sand grains, upon contact with water, become united. In <s>saṃsāra</s>, they consider sensual craving to be a [source of] relish. As it is said: 'The relishing and attachment to form' — namely, depending on form, happiness and elation arise. Without passion, there is no relishing. Without relishing, one quickly abandons <s>saṃsāra</s>. And this sensual passion is opposed to liberation. Why? Because beings become attached [thinking]: 'Sensual pleasure is happiness, <s>dhyāna</s> is happiness, attainment is happiness.' Therefore [they think] liberation is without happiness. But the abandonment of the components of passion — that itself turns into happiness. As stated: 'One who has dispassion attains the supreme happiness.' Furthermore, it is said: 'One who desires the attainment of all happiness must abandon all sensual pleasures. Through the abandonment of all sensual pleasures, one obtains ultimate, permanent happiness.' One who desires great happiness should disregard small happiness. Through the disregard of small happiness, one obtains immeasurable happiness.

body.text: viduṣaśca nāsti pratyekalābha ityuktam | yathā vītarāgatṛṣṇacittasya | yasya cittaṃ rāgatṛṣṇāviviktaṃ tasya sarve duḥkhopāyāsā niruddhāḥ | kāmarāgo 'yaṃ saddharmaṃ vihanti | kasmāt | na hi paramarāgī śīlajātidharmaśāsaneryāpathaśāṃsyapekṣate | nāvavādamādatte | nādīnavaṃ paśyati | nāpi puṇyapāpamālocayati | unmattavat pramattavacca na jānāti kurūpaṃ surūpam | andhavacca na paśyati dhanalābham | yathoktaṃ- kāmarāgo na paśyati hitam | kāmarāgo na vijānāti dharmaṃ andhatamasi ajñānavat | rāgānapagamāt | kiñcoktam-
body.translated_text: And it is said: 'For the wise, there is no individual gain.' Just as for one whose mind is free from passionate craving. For one whose mind is free from passionate craving, all suffering and anguish are brought to cessation. This sensual passion destroys the true <s>Dharma</s>. Why? For one who is supremely passionate does not regard moral conduct, birth, the <s>Dharma</s>-teaching, deportment, or good reputation. He does not accept admonition. He does not see danger. He does not reflect on merit and sin. Like a madman, like a heedless one, he does not know the ugly from the beautiful. Like a blind man, he does not see the gain of wealth. As stated: 'Sensual passion does not see what is beneficial. Sensual passion does not know <s>Dharma</s> — like ignorance in complete darkness.' Because of the non-departure of passion. Furthermore, it is said:

children.translated_text: This sensual passion is an ocean, limitless and fathomless,
with waves and billows, with whirlpools, with sea-monsters, and with <s>rākṣasas</s>.
Thus there are unending perils, uncrossable by human beings.
One who stands on the boat of pure moral conduct, propelled by the wind of right view,

body.text:
nāvikaśca mahān buddhaḥ sanmārgān sampradarśayan |
yathoktabhāvanāyogī so 'yaṃ tarati vai tadā || iti |
body.translated_text:
with the great <s>Buddha</s> as the helmsman, showing the right course —
one who practices meditation as instructed, he indeed crosses over. Thus it is said.

body.text: nāsti kasyacitkleśānāṃ saṃjñāvikalpāsvādo yathā kāmarāgiṇaḥ | sa ca kāmarāgo 'tyantaṃ duṣprajahaḥ | yathoktaṃ- dve ime āśe duṣprajahe | katame dve | lābhāśā jīvitāśā iti |
body.translated_text: No one has such a relish of the conceptual discrimination and delight of defilements as the one who has sensual passion. And this sensual passion is exceedingly difficult to abandon. As stated: 'There are two desires that are difficult to abandon. Which two? The desire for gain and the desire for life.'

body.text: kāmarāgasyedṛśā doṣāḥ santi | kathaṃ jñāyate kāmarāgiṇo lakṣaṇam | (u) kāmarāgabahulaḥ strīrūpakusumagandhamālanṛttavādyagīteṣu pramudito veśyāgṛhapānagoṣṭhīgāmī mahāsamājanāṭakarasikaḥ sānurāgālāpānanditaḥ sadā paritoṣitacittaḥ prasannavadanaḥ sākūtasakākusasmitābhilāṣī durlabhakopaḥ sulabhapramodo bhūyasā dayālucittaḥ punaḥ punarvyādhitacapalagātraḥ svadehādhyāsakta ityevamādi rāgabahulasya lakṣaṇam | lakṣaṇamidaṃ svabhāvabandhenānu gatamityato duṣprajaham | sarve ca kāmarāgā ātyantikaduḥkhāḥ | kasmāt | rāgābhilaṣitasya viprayogo 'vaśyabhāvī | viprayogapratyayaṃ daurmanasyaduḥkhamavaśyabhāvi | yathoktaṃ- rūpasukhino [bhikṣavo] devamanuṣyā rūparāgino rūpamuditā rūpavipariṇāme duḥkhacittā viharanti iti | evaṃ vedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskāravijñāneṣvapi | bhagavān tatra tatra sūtre nānādṛṣṭāntairimaṃ kāmarāgaṃ garhayati yaduta [āśī] viṣopamaḥ, prajñāyuḥkṣayakaratvāt | śalyopamaḥ cittagataduḥkhatvāt | asiśūlopamaḥ kuśalamūlasamucchedakatvāt | agniskandhopamaḥ kāyacittaparidāhatvāt | amitra [bhūtaḥ] duḥkhānāmutpādakatvāt | antaḥsapatnabhūtaḥ manasi
body.translated_text: Such are the faults of sensual passion. How does one know the characteristics of one who has sensual passion? (Answer) One who is predominant in sensual passion delights in the forms of women, flowers, perfumes, garlands, dancing, music, and songs. He frequents the houses of courtesans, drinking halls, and assemblies. He relishes great festivals and theatrical spectacles. He is delighted by amorous conversation. His mind is always gratified. His face is pleasant. He is given to glances with intent, gestures, flashing smiles, and longing. He is difficult to anger and easy to delight. For the most part, he has a compassionate mind. Again and again he has a sickly, restless body. He is attached to his own body — such and the like are the characteristics of one predominant in passion. These characteristics follow through the bond of one's inherent nature — therefore they are difficult to abandon. And all sensual passions are ultimately painful. Why? Separation from what is desired by passion is inevitable. The suffering of displeasure conditioned by separation is inevitable. As stated: 'O monks, gods and humans who delight in form, who are attached to form, who are pleased by form — when form changes, they dwell with a suffering mind.' The same with feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well. The Blessed One, in various <s>sūtras</s>, with various similes, censures this sensual passion — namely, it is like the poison of a serpent, because it destroys wisdom and lifespan; like a thorn, because of the suffering that enters the mind; like a sword-point, because it eradicates wholesome roots; like a mass of fire, because it scorches body and mind; like an enemy, because it produces suffering; like an inner rival, because it is born in the mind;

body.text: jātatvāt | rūḍhamūlopamaḥ durunmūlanatvāt | paṅkabhūtaḥ yaśodūṣakatvāt | vighnabhūtaḥ kuśalamārgāṇāmāvaraṇatvāt | hṛdgataśalyabhūtaḥ antarvyathanāt | akuśalamūlabhūtaḥ sarvākuśalānāmutpādakatvāt | oghabhūtaḥ saṃsārārṇave saṃplābanāt | corabhūtaḥ kuśalasampadapahārāt | evamādyaprahāṇānāmādīnavānāṃ sattvāt kāmarāgaḥ prahātavyaḥ |
body.translated_text: like a deeply-rooted [tree], because it is difficult to uproot; like mire, because it corrupts one's reputation; like an obstruction, because it blocks the wholesome paths; like a thorn lodged in the heart, because of inward torment; like a root of the unwholesome, because it produces all unwholesome [states]; like a flood, because it carries one adrift in the ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s>; like a thief, because it steals the accomplishment of the wholesome. Because such immeasurable dangers, which are not abandoned, exist — sensual passion should be abandoned.

body.text: kāmānāmādinavavargaścatuviṃśatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Dangers of Sensual Pleasures (<s>kāmānāmādīnavavarga</s>).

body.text: 125 rāgaprahāṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 125. Chapter on the Abandonment of Passion (<s>rāgaprahāṇavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) kāmarāgasyedṛśā doṣāḥ santi | kathaṃ prahātavyaḥ | (u) aśuci bhāvanādibhiḥ pratiṣedhayati | anityatādibhāvanādibhiḥ prajahāti | (pṛ) keṣāñcidanityatādibodhanātkāmarāgo vardhate | kathamidam | (u) yaḥ sarvamanityamiti prajānāti na tasya kāmarāgo 'sti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- anityasaṃjñā [bhikṣavaḥ] bhāvitā bahulīkṛtā tadā sarvaḥ kāmarāgaḥ paryādīryate sarvaḥ rūparāgaḥ paryādīryate sarvo bhavarāgaḥ paryādīryate sarvāvidyā paryādīryate sarvo 'smimānaḥ paryādīryate samuddhanyate iti | yaḥ paśyati loko duḥkhaṃ duḥkhahetuḥ rāga iti | tasyāyaṃ rāgaḥ prahīyate | yo nityaṃ smarati mayā jātijarāvyādhimaraṇānyanubhavitavyānīti sa imaṃ rāgaṃ prajahāti | viśuddhasukhe labdhe aviśuddhasukhaṃ tyajati | yathā prathamadhyānalābhe kāmatṛṣṇāṃ tyajati | kāmānāmādīnavānudarśī imāṃ tyajati | ādīnavaśca yathāpūrvamuktaḥ | bahuśrutādiprajñāvivṛdhyā ca kāmarāgaṃ tyajati | jñānasya kleśabhedanasvabhāvatvāt | kuśalapratyayasampannasya kāmarāgaḥ prahīyate yaduta śīlaviśuddhyā dīnyekādaśasamādhyupakaraṇānīti paścānmārgasatye vakṣyate | rūpajñānādīni dharmajñānādīnyupāyāḥ | bhagavān mahābhiṣak | sabrahmacāriṇo 'nucarāḥ | saddharma auṣadham | ātmanā
body.translated_text: (Question) Such are the faults of sensual passion. How is it to be abandoned? (Answer) One counteracts it through the contemplation of the impure (<s>aśubhabhāvanā</s>) and the like. One abandons it through the contemplation of impermanence (<s>anityatā</s>) and the like. (Question) For some, through the awakening to impermanence and the like, sensual passion increases. How is this? (Answer) One who understands that everything is impermanent does not have sensual passion. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'O monks, when the perception of impermanence is cultivated and made abundant, then all sensual passion is exhausted, all passion for form is exhausted, all passion for existence is exhausted, all ignorance is exhausted, all conceit "I am" (<s>asmimāna</s>) is exhausted and eradicated.' One who sees that the world is suffering and that the cause of suffering is passion — for him, this passion is abandoned. One who constantly recollects 'I must experience birth, old age, disease, and death' — he abandons this passion. When pure happiness has been obtained, one abandons impure happiness. Just as upon obtaining the first <s>dhyāna</s>, one abandons sensual craving. One who sees the dangers of sensual pleasures abandons it. And the dangers are as previously stated. Through the increase of wisdom from great learning and the like, one abandons sensual passion. Because it is the inherent nature of knowledge to break through defilements. For one who is furnished with wholesome conditions, sensual passion is abandoned — namely, through the purification of moral conduct, and the eleven instruments of concentration — this will be stated later in the truth of the path (<s>mārgasatya</s>). Knowledges such as knowledge of form and the like, knowledges such as knowledge of <s>dharma</s> and the like — these are the methods. The Blessed One is the great physician. Fellow practitioners of the holy life are the attendants. The true <s>Dharma</s> is the medicine. One's own practice

body.text: yathoktavadācaraṇaṃ virecanam | tadā kāmarāgavyādhiḥ prahīyate | yathā jñāyate rūgṇasya trivastusampannasya tasminneva samaye vyādhiḥ śāmyati iti |
body.translated_text: as instructed is the purging. Then the disease of sensual passion is abandoned. Just as it is known that for a patient furnished with three things, at that very time the disease subsides.

body.text: (pṛ) yathoktaṃ sūtre- aśubha[bhāvanayā] rāgaṃ nirvāpaya iti | kasmāt bhavān bravīti aśubhādi anityatādi ca | (u) sarvāṇi buddhaśāsanāni kleśānāṃ bhedakāni | tathāpi pratyekamasti balaviśeṣaḥ | ādau aśubhayā rāgo vāryate paścādanityatājñānena prahīyate | aśubhayā audariko rāgo 'panīyata itīdaṃ bahūnāṃ jñātameva | rāgānuśayaḥ sūkṣma iti anityatayā prahīyate | kevalamekasmin sūtra īdṛśaṃ vacanamuktam | sarveṣu sūtreṣvanye 'pi prahāṇadharmā uktāḥ | īdṛśapratyaye sati kāmarāgaḥ prahīyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Extinguish passion through the contemplation of the impure (<s>aśubhabhāvanā</s>).' Why do you say 'the impure and the like' and 'impermanence and the like'? (Answer) All the teachings of the <s>Buddha</s> break through defilements. Even so, individually there is a distinction in power. First, through [the contemplation of] the impure, passion is counteracted; afterward, through the knowledge of impermanence, it is abandoned. That through the impure, gross passion is removed — this is known to many. But the latent tendency of passion (<s>rāgānuśaya</s>) is subtle — therefore it is abandoned through impermanence. Only in one <s>sūtra</s> is such a statement made. In all <s>sūtras</s>, other <s>dharmas</s> of abandonment are also stated. When such conditions are present, sensual passion is abandoned.

body.text: rāgaprahāṇavargaḥ pañcaviṃśatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Abandonment of Passion (<s>rāgaprahāṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 126 vyāpādavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 126. Chapter on Ill-Will (<s>vyāpādavarga</s>)

body.text: śāstramāha- vyāpādo dveṣalakṣaṇamiti | yo dviṣyati sa vināśaṃ kartumicchati | parasya tāḍanabandhanamāraṇavihiṃsanāni kartuṃ praṇidadhāti | ekāntato nirākṛtya naiva draṣṭumicchati | ayaṃ dveṣaḥ pratidha ityākhyāyate | gurutaro dveṣa ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī parān nindituṃ daṇḍena tāḍayituñcecchati | [ayaṃ dveṣo] vihiṃsā ityabhidhīyate | madhyamadveṣa ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī [paraṃ] parihartuṃ necchati | kadācit tatputrabhāryādīn vidviṣati | tatrotpadyamāno [dveṣaḥ] krodha ityucyate | adhamadveṣa ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī sadākliṣṭacittaḥ [sa]mrakṣa ityabhidhīyate | avipakvendriya ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī cittagatamakuśalamatyaktvā punarvipākāyecchati | [sa] upanāha ityucyate | vipakvendriya ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī sahasā kiñcit gṛhītvā nānākāraṇai[rna] tyaktumicchati | yathā siṃho nadīṃ vigāhya
body.translated_text: The treatise says: Ill-will (<s>vyāpāda</s>) has the characteristic of hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>). One who hates wishes to destroy. He resolves to beat, imprison, kill, and harm another. He absolutely rejects [the other] and does not even wish to see [him]. This hatred is called <s>pratigha</s> (aversion). The meaning is: the gravest form of hatred. A certain hateful person wishes to censure others and strike them with a rod. This hatred is called <s>vihiṃsā</s> (cruelty). The meaning is: the middling form of hatred. A certain hateful person does not wish to avoid [the other]. Sometimes he hates [the other's] sons, wife, and the like. The hatred that arises therein is called <s>krodha</s> (anger). The meaning is: the inferior form of hatred. A certain hateful person always has an afflicted mind — he is called <s>mrakṣa</s> (hypocrisy). The meaning is: one whose faculties are immature. A certain hateful person, not having abandoned the mental unwholesomeness, desires it again for [future] ripening — he is called <s>upanāha</s> (grudge). The meaning is: one whose faculties have matured. A certain hateful person, having suddenly seized something, does not wish to let go for various reasons. Just as a lion, having plunged into a river,

body.text: tattīranimittaṃ gṛhītvā āmaraṇaṃ na [tato] vinivartate | [sa] pradāśa ityucyate | āgraha ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī hitalābhinaṃ paraṃ dṛṣṭvā citte mātsaryamutpādayati | iyamīrṣyatyucyate | kaścit dveṣī sadā kalahapriyo dhṛṣṭamanovāg bhavati | [ayaṃ] saṃrambha ityucyate | roṣakalaha ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī ciramātsaryeṇa śīlamupadiṣṭo 'pi punaḥ pratilomayati | ayaṃ dveṣa ityākhyāyate | krauryamityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī kiñcidabhīṣṭasya amanaḥprahlādanasya vastuno lābhe kṣubhitacitto bhavati | iyamakṣāntirityucyate | akṣametyarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī asukumāravacanaḥ sadā bhrukuṭilālaso na manaḥ pūrvamālāpaṃ yojayati | iyamapakīrtirityucyate | anāttamanaskatetyarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī sahavāsiṣu sadādhikṣepalolupo bhavati | idamasauratya mityabhidhīyate | adānta ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī kāyavāṅmanobhiḥ satīrthyaṃ saṃspṛṣṭopāyāsaṃ karoti | iayaṃ jigīṣā ityabhidhīyate | upāyāsasparśa ityarthaḥ | kaścit dveṣī sadā garhāprakaṭanaprīto vigītavastupriyaśca bhavati | iyaṃ todanatā ityucyate | upālambha ityarthaḥ |
body.translated_text: having grasped the object of that [hatred], one does not turn away [from it] until death. This is called <s>pradāśa</s> (obstinacy) — meaning 'tenacious grasping.' A certain hateful person, seeing another who has obtained benefit, generates jealousy in the mind. This is called <s>īrṣyā</s> (envy). A certain hateful person, always fond of quarrels, becomes bold in mind and speech. This is called <s>saṃrambha</s> (violent agitation) — meaning 'angry quarreling.' A certain hateful person, though instructed in moral conduct, through long-standing jealousy, again turns against [it]. This is called <s>dveṣa</s> (hatred) — meaning 'cruelty.' A certain hateful person, upon obtaining something undesired and displeasing, becomes agitated in mind. This is called <s>akṣānti</s> (impatience) — meaning 'inability to endure.' A certain hateful person, of ungentle speech, always frowning and idle, does not initiate friendly conversation. This is called <s>apakīrti</s> (ill-repute) — meaning 'displeasure.' A certain hateful person, among those living together, is always eager to disparage. This is called <s>asauratya</s> (disagreeableness) — meaning 'untamed.' A certain hateful person, through body, speech, and mind, causes contact with distress to co-religionists. This is called <s>jigīṣā</s> (desire to conquer) — meaning 'touching with distress.' A certain hateful person, always delighting in publicizing faults and fond of disparaging things, is called <s>todanatā</s> (pricking) — meaning 'reproach.'

body.text: dveṣo 'yaṃ dvividhaḥ- kadācitsattvamupādāya bhavati kadācidasattvamupādāya iti | sattvamupādayotpadyamāno gurutaraḥ pāpaḥ | uttamamadhyamādhamavikalpena navarāśayo bhavanti | navakleśānupādāya navadhā vibhajyate | vinā vastu dveṣapariṇāho daśamo bhavati | idaṃ dveṣalakṣaṇam |
body.translated_text: This hatred is of two kinds: sometimes it arises with reference to a sentient being, sometimes with reference to a non-sentient thing. When arising with reference to a sentient being, the sin is more grave. Through the differentiation of superior, middling, and inferior, there are nine dispositions. Depending on the nine defilements, it is divided ninefold. Without an object, the swelling of hatred becomes the tenth. This is the characteristic of hatred.

body.text: (pṛ) kathaṃ dveṣa utpadyate | (u) amanojñādduḥkhopāyāsādutpadyate | duḥkhavedanāsvabhāvasya asamyak parijñānādvyāpāda utpadyate | garhāvadhataḍanādibhyo vā samutpadyate | durjanasahavṛttyā vā vyāpāda utpadyate yathā saunikavyādhādayaḥ | mandajñānabalādvā dveṣa utpadyate yathā vṛkṣāṇāṃ śākhopaśākhā vāteritā bhavanti | cirasamupacitadveṣānuśayasya āniryātanabhāvaṃ dveṣa utpadyate saunikavyādhasarpāṇāmāgamādvā dveṣa utpadyate | paradoṣānusmṛtipremṇā vā dveṣa utpadyata iti yathā navakleśeṣūktam | kālavaśādvā dveṣa utpadyate yathā daśavayaskādīnām | jātyā vā dveṣa utpadyate yathā sarpādīnām | deśasthānādvā dveṣa utpadyate yathā kānyakubjadeśādau | pūrvamukto rāgajananapratyayaḥ | tadvirodhe dveṣa utpadyate | ātmabuddhimadhyayasya [tatra] mānaparipoṣaṇaṃ padārthādhyavasānañcetyevamādipratyayeṣu satsu dveṣa utpadyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) How does hatred arise? (Answer) It arises from unpleasant [objects] and from the distress of suffering. Through the incorrect comprehension of the inherent nature of painful feeling (<s>duḥkhavedanā</s>), ill-will (<s>vyāpāda</s>) arises. Or it arises from reproach, beatings, striking, and the like. Or ill-will arises from association with wicked persons — just as butchers, hunters, and the like. Or hatred arises through the power of weak knowledge — just as the branches and sub-branches of trees are stirred by wind. For one who has long accumulated the latent tendency of hatred (<s>dveṣānuśaya</s>), hatred arises as a manifestation. Or hatred arises from the approach of butchers, hunters, serpents, and the like. Or hatred arises from the fond recollection of another's faults — as stated regarding the nine defilements. Or hatred arises through the force of time — as in the case of ten-year-olds and the like. Or hatred arises through birth — as in the case of serpents and the like. Or hatred arises from the place — as in the <s>Kānyakubja</s> region and the like. The previously stated conditions that generate passion — when opposed to those, hatred arises. When there is the notion of self, the nourishment of pride, and the determination of objects — when such conditions exist, hatred arises.

body.text: (pṛ) dveṣasya ke doṣāḥ | (u) uktaṃ sūtre- dveṣaḥ kāmarāgād gurutaraṃ pāpam iti | ataḥ suvimokaḥ | vastutastu durvimokaḥ | kintu rāgavanna ciraṃ cittamanuvartate | dveṣo dvidhā santāpakaḥ | ādāvātmānaṃ santāpayati ante paraṃ santāpayati | kiñca dveṣo niyamena narakāya bhavati | dveṣotthakarmaṇāṃ bhūyasā narake pātanāt | dveṣaḥ kuśalapuṇyāni vināśayati yaduta dānaśīlakṣāntayaḥ | imāstrisraḥ karuṇācittajāḥ | dveṣasya karuṇāvirodhitvāt [tāḥ] vināśayati | dveṣajañca karma sarvamante cittaṃ paritāpayati | dveṣendriyavān nirdayatvāt krūracaṇḍāla ityucyate | sattvāḥ sadā duḥkhinaḥ punardveṣeṇa pīḍitāḥ vraṇe prayuktakṣāravat | kiñca sūtre bhagavān svayaṃ dveṣadoṣānāha- dveṣabahulaḥ kutsitaḥ kharvākāro 'praśāntabuddhiśayaḥ sadā bhīrucitto janānāmaśraddheya iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults of hatred? (Answer) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Hatred is a graver sin than sensual passion (<s>kāmarāga</s>).' Therefore it is easily liberated from. But in reality it is difficult to liberate from. However, unlike passion, it does not follow the mind for a long time. Hatred causes burning in two ways: first it burns oneself, and finally it burns others. Moreover, hatred necessarily leads to hell — because <s>karma</s> born of hatred predominantly causes one to fall into hell. Hatred destroys wholesome merits — namely, generosity (<s>dāna</s>), moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), and patience (<s>kṣānti</s>). These three are born of the mind of compassion. Because hatred is opposed to compassion, it destroys them. And <s>karma</s> born of hatred, at the end, torments the mind. One whose faculty of hatred is dominant, because of mercilessness, is called 'a cruel outcaste.' Beings are always suffering — and further oppressed by hatred, like salt applied to a wound. Moreover, in the <s>sūtra</s>, the Blessed One himself declared the faults of hatred: 'One who is abundant in hatred is despicable, of stunted form, of unpeaceful mental disposition, always fearful in mind, and untrustworthy among people.'

body.text: (pṛ) vyāpādabahulasya kāni lakṣaṇāni | (u) dhṛṣṭavāṅmanāḥ sadā anāttamanā bhavati | bhrukuṭikṣepeṇa durabhigamo 'saṃśliṣṭamukhavarṇo durvimokasulabhakopaḥ sadā vyāpādopanāhamudito vigrahabhūṣaṇāyudheṣu prīto durmitrapakṣapātī sajjanavidveṣī, janānāṃ bhīṣaṇāyātathyadhyānacintano 'lpahrayapatrapa ityevamādīni dveṣalakṣaṇāni | imānyanyeṣāṃ vipriyakarāṇi | ataḥ prahātavyāni |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the characteristics of one who is abundant in ill-will (<s>vyāpāda</s>)? (Answer) Bold in speech and mind, he is always displeased. With furrowed brows, he is difficult to approach, of unfriendly facial complexion, difficult to liberate from, quick to anger, always delighting in ill-will and resentment, fond of weapons of conflict and adornment of strife, a partisan of bad friends, hostile toward good people, given to frightening others, engaged in thinking what is untrue, of little shame and moral dread — such and the like are the characteristics of hatred. These cause displeasure in others. Therefore they should be abandoned.

body.text: (pṛ) kathaṃ sa prahātavyo bhaviṣyati | (u) sadā karuṇāmuditāpekṣābhāvanāyāṃ dveṣaḥ prahīyate | dveṣasyādīnavaṃ paśyan dveṣaṃ prajahāti | tattvajñānalābhino dveṣaḥ prahīyate | kṣāntibalācca dveṣaḥ prahīyate | (pṛ) kiṃ nāma kṣāntibalam | (u) yaḥ paragarhādiduḥkhaṃ kṣamate sa kuśaladharmapuṇyaṃ labhate | nākṣāntijamakuśalaṃ labhate | idaṃ kṣāntibalam | kṣāntivihārī śramaṇa ityucyate | kṣāntirhi mārgasyādyaṃ dvāraṃ bhavati | ataḥ śramaṇadharmaṇaḥ kope 'pi na kopavipākaḥ | nindāyāñca na nindāvipākaḥ | tāḍane ca na tāḍanavipākaḥ | yo bhikṣuḥ kṣamāvān sa pravrajyādharmā syāt | vyāpādavato na pravrajitadhardho bhavati | kṣāntiriyaṃ pravrajitadharmaḥ | ya ākāraveṣābhyāṃ bhikṣuḥ bhinnavyavahāro dveṣacittasahagataśca na sa bhavyo bhavati | yastu kṣamāvihārī sa eva karuṇāguṇasavanvitaḥ | kṣamāvihārī svahitaṃ sādhayati | kasmāt | dveṣakārī parān vyābādhituṃ kāmayānaḥ svātmānameva vyābādhate | yāni kāyavāgbhyāṃ paratra pratyuktānyakuśalāni | [teṣā]makuśalānāṃ doṣāḥ śatasahasraguṇamātmanaiva labhyante | ato jñāyate dveṣo mahāntamātmāpakarṣaṃ karoti iti | ataḥ prājñenātmano hitaṃ kartukāmena mahadduḥkhaṃ mahatpāpañcāpākurvatā kṣāntirācaritavyāḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) How shall that [hatred] be abandoned? (Answer) Through the constant cultivation of the contemplation of compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>) and sympathetic joy (<s>muditā</s>), hatred is abandoned. Seeing the danger of hatred, one abandons hatred. For one who has obtained the knowledge of reality, hatred is abandoned. And through the power of patience (<s>kṣānti</s>), hatred is abandoned. (Question) What is the power of patience? (Answer) One who endures the suffering of reproach and the like by others obtains the merit of wholesome <s>dharmas</s>. One does not obtain the unwholesome born of impatience. This is the power of patience. One who abides in patience is called an ascetic (<s>śramaṇa</s>). For patience is the first gate of the path. Therefore, in the <s>dharma</s> of an ascetic, even when there is provocation, there is no ripening of provocation. And when there is blame, there is no ripening of blame. And when there is beating, there is no ripening of beating. A monk who is patient — he would be one whose <s>dharma</s> is that of renunciation. For one abundant in ill-will, there is no <s>dharma</s> of a renunciant. This patience is the <s>dharma</s> of a renunciant. One who, by outward appearance and attire, is a monk but whose conduct is at variance, and who is accompanied by a mind of hatred — he is not capable [of the path]. But one who abides in patience alone is endowed with the virtue of compassion. One who abides in patience accomplishes one's own benefit. Why? One who acts from hatred, desiring to harm others, harms only oneself. Whatever unwholesome [actions] are done in return through body and speech toward others — the faults of those unwholesome [actions] are obtained by oneself a hundred-thousand-fold. Therefore it is known that hatred causes great self-diminishment. Therefore, the wise person, desiring to do what is beneficial for himself, averting great suffering and great sin, should practice patience.

body.text: (pṛ) ko nindādiduḥkhaṃ khamate | (u) yo 'nityatāṃ bhāvayati bahulīkaroti pratibudhyate sarvadharmā kṣaṇikāḥ, nindako vedakaḥ sarvo 'pi kṣaṇika iti | tasya kutra dveṣa utpadyeta | śūnyatācittasya samyak bhāvanayā kṣamamāṇa evaṃ cintayati dharmeṣu vatustaḥ śūnyeṣu ko nindakaḥ ko vā nindāvedaka iti | yadi vastu satyaṃ tadā [ta]dvedanā kṣantavyā | ahaṃ satyato doṣavān iti pūrvapuruṣāḥ satyaṃ vadanti, kasmāt dviṣāmi | yadi vastu satyaṃ | te puruṣāḥ svayameva mṛṣāvādapāpaṃ labheran | kasmādahaṃ dviṣāmīti | aśubhanindāṃ śṛṇvan evaṃ cintayet sarve lokā yathākarma vipākaṃ vedayante | mayā purā idaṃ nindākarma samupacitamāsīt | tadidānīṃ pratyanubhavitavyam | kasmād dviṣyāmīti | yadi cāśubhanindāṃ śṛṇoti taddoṣamātmani bhāvayet | ātmavaśenaiva kāyamanubhavāmi | kāyaśca duḥkhabhājanam | ato nindānubhavitavyeti | kṣāntivihārī evaṃ cintayet padārthāḥ pratītyasamutpannāḥ | idamaśubhaṃ nindākarma śrotravijñānamanovijñānaśabdādisamutpannam | eṣu ahaṃ dvyaṅgasamanvitaḥ | parastu śabdamātrasamanvitaḥ | evañca mamaiva pāpāṅgaṃ bahu | kasmāt dviṣāmi | mayā śabdasyāsya nimittagrahaṇādeva daurmanasyopāyāsāḥ sambhavanti ityahameva duṣṭaḥ | kṣāntimān na parān doṣayati | kasmāt dveṣādīni pāpāni na sattvānāṃ doṣāḥ, sattvā vyādhisamutthāpitacittatvādanīśvarāḥ | yathā bhūtacikitsako bhūtoccāṭanādhyavasito bhūtameva dviṣati na tu rogiṇam | ayaṃ vīryotsukaḥ kuśaladharmāṇāṃ sañcaya ārajyate | ataḥ parapravādān na gaṇayati | buddhānāryasaṅghañca smṛtvā na nindāḥ pramocayati | yathā nindāpaṭavo brāhmaṇādayo buddhaṃ vividhaṃ nindanti | yathā vā śāriputrādiṣu brāhmaṇaiḥ prayujyante 'pavādanindāḥ | kaḥ punarvādo 'smāsu tanupuṇyeṣu |
body.translated_text: (Question) Who endures the suffering of blame and the like? (Answer) One who cultivates and develops impermanence (<s>anityatā</s>) frequently, awakening [to the truth that] all <s>dharmas</s> are momentary — the blamer and the one who experiences [the blame] are all momentary. Where would hatred arise for him? For one who properly cultivates the mind of emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), while enduring, he thinks thus: 'When <s>dharmas</s> are in reality empty, who is the blamer and who is the one who experiences the blame?' If the matter is true, then that experience is to be endured — 'I am in truth faulty' — the ancients speak the truth. Why should I hate? If the matter is not true, then those persons themselves would obtain the sin of false speech. Why should I hate? Hearing unpleasant blame, one should think thus: 'All worldly beings experience ripening according to their <s>karma</s>. I formerly accumulated this <s>karma</s> of blame. Now I must experience its result. Why should I hate?' And if one hears unpleasant blame, one should cultivate [seeing] that fault in oneself: 'By my own doing I experience [this] body. And the body is a vessel of suffering. Therefore blame is to be experienced.' One who abides in patience should think thus: 'Objects arise through dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>). This unpleasant <s>karma</s> of blame arises from ear-consciousness, mind-consciousness, sound, and the like. Among these, I am endowed with two components. But the other person is endowed with sound alone. Thus, my own component of sin is greater. Why should I hate? From my very grasping of the sign of this sound, displeasure and distress arise — therefore I myself am at fault.' One who is patient does not blame others. Why? Because defilements such as hatred and the like are not the faults of beings — beings, having their minds stirred up by disease, are not masters [of themselves]. Just as a spirit-healer, intent on exorcising spirits, hates the spirit itself, not the sick person. This energetic one delights in the accumulation of wholesome <s>dharmas</s>. Therefore he does not regard the words of others. Recollecting the <s>Buddhas</s>, the Noble <s>Saṅgha</s>, and the like, he does not let loose blame. Just as skilled <s>brāhmaṇas</s> and others variously blame the <s>Buddha</s>. Just as <s>brāhmaṇas</s> direct reproach and blame upon <s>Śāriputra</s> and the like. What more need be said of us who are of little merit?

body.text: kiñcedaṃ cintayet lokā akuśabahulā ātmajīvitamahṛtvaiva kaṭukaṃ kurvanti | kiṃ punastāḍananindāmiti | kiñcaivaṃ cintayet- aśubhanindādinā na mama duḥkhamiti vedanā kṣantavyā | yathā bhagavān bhikṣūn śāsti- kāye krakaceṇa vidīrṇe 'pi vedanā kṣantavyā | kā punarnindā iti | idamācaran sadā saṃsārānnirvidyate | nindāyāṃ labdhāyāṃ nirvedaṃ bhūyasā mātrayā suniśritamavagamyākuśalamācarati | sa jānāti ca nindāyā akṣamā ante duḥkhaṃvipākavedanā ityevaṃ cintayan narake mā bhūt pāta iti gurvīmapi nindāṃ vedayate | so 'tīva hryapatrapāsāpekṣaḥ cintayati ahaṃ mahāpuruṣasya bhagavataḥ śrāvako mārgabhāvayitā | [mama]kathamutpādayedakāryaṃ kāyavākkarma iti | kṣānticāribhirbodhisattvaiḥ śakrādibhiśca labhyaṃ kṣāntibalaṃ śrūyate ca | ataḥ kṣāntiḥ kāryā ||
body.translated_text: Moreover, one should think thus: 'Worldly beings, being abundant in the unwholesome, even having their own lives taken away, are made to suffer. How much more so with beatings and blame!' Moreover, one should think thus: 'From unpleasant blame and the like, I do not have suffering' — [thus] the feeling is to be endured. Just as the Blessed One instructed the monks: 'Even when the body is being sawn apart by a saw, the feeling is to be endured. How much more so with blame!' Practicing this, one always develops weariness (<s>nirveda</s>) toward <s>saṃsāra</s>. When blame is received, having firmly understood weariness to a greater measure, one refrains from the unwholesome. And he knows that the result of not enduring blame is painful ripening-feeling — thinking thus, 'Let there be no fall into hell,' he endures even grave blame. He, greatly concerned with shame (<s>hrī</s>) and moral dread (<s>apatrāpā</s>), thinks: 'I am a disciple of the great being, the Blessed One, a cultivator of the path. How could I produce improper bodily and verbal <s>karma</s>?' The power of patience is heard of as obtained by <s>Bodhisattvas</s> who practice patience, by <s>Śakra</s>, and others. Therefore patience should be practiced.

body.text: vyāpādavargaḥ ṣaḍviṃśatyuttaravaśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on Ill-Will (<s>vyāpādavarga</s>).

body.text: 127 avidyāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 127. Chapter on Ignorance (<s>avidyāvarga</s>)

body.text: śāstramāha- prajñaptyanuvartanamavidyā | iti | yathāhuḥ- pṛthagjanā ātmarutamanuvartante | tatra nāsti vastuta ātmā nātmīyam | dharmāṇāṃ samavāyaḥ kevalaṃ prajñaptyā puruṣa ityucyate | pṛthagjanānāmavivekādātmacittaṃ pravartate | ātmacittapravṛttiriyamavidyaiva |
body.translated_text: The treatise says: Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is conformity with conventional designation (<s>prajñaptyanuvartana</s>). As they say: 'Ordinary beings (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) follow the expression "self" (<s>ātma</s>).' Therein, in reality there is no self, nor anything belonging to a self. The conjunction of <s>dharmas</s> is merely designated by convention as a 'person' (<s>puruṣa</s>). For ordinary beings, due to lack of discrimination, the thought of self operates. This operation of the thought of self is itself ignorance.

body.text: (pṛ) bhagavānāha- pūrvāntājñānavidyā iti | kasmāducyate | ātmacittamātramiyamavidyeti | (u) atītādau bahavo bhrāntāḥ | ata āha- tatrājñānamavidyeti | ata āha tasyājñānamavidyeti | sūtre ca vidyāyā artho vivṛtaḥ- yasya kasyacit jñānaṃ vidyeti | keṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ jñānam | rūpamanityamiti yathābhūtajñānam | vedanā saṃjñā saṃskārā vijñānamanityamiti yathābhūtajñānam | vidyāyā viruddhā vidyāvidyā | tathā ca yathābhūtā vidyā avidyaiva |
body.translated_text: (Question) The Blessed One said: 'Ignorance is the non-knowledge of the prior end (<s>pūrvānta</s>).' Why is it said that this ignorance is merely the thought of self? (Answer) Many are deluded regarding the past and the like. Therefore he said: 'The non-knowledge therein is ignorance.' Therefore he said: 'That non-knowledge is ignorance.' And in the <s>sūtra</s>, the meaning of knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) is explained: 'Whatever knowledge anyone has is called knowledge.' Of which <s>dharmas</s> is it knowledge? The knowledge that 'form is impermanent' as it truly is (<s>yathābhūtajñāna</s>). The knowledge that 'feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are impermanent' as it truly is. That which is opposed to knowledge is ignorance. And thus, knowledge as it truly is — [its opposite] is itself ignorance.

body.text: (pṛ) yathābhūtāvidyā yadyavidyā | tarupāṣāṇādidharmā api avidyā syāt | yathābhūtavidyāyā abhāvāt | (u) maivam | tarupāṣāṇāni cācittakāni na pūrvāntādi vikalpayanti | avidyā tu vikalpinīti na tarupāṣāṇayoḥ samānā | (pṛ) avidyā nāma dharmābhāvaḥ | yathā puruṣasya cakṣuṣā rūpādarśanaṃ nādarśanadharmo bhavati | ato vidyāyā abhāvamātramavidyā | na dharmāntaram | (u) maivam | yadyabhāvo 'vidyā | pañcaskandheṣu asti pudgala iti mithyākalpanā ghaṭaśakale ca suvarṇasaṃjñotpadyata iti kasmādbhavati | ato jñāyate mithyāvikalpasvabhāvāvidyā | na tu vidyāyā abhāvo 'vidyeti | avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārādayaḥ santatyā pravartante | yadyabhāvaḥ kathamutpādayet | (pṛ) na vidyā avidyā iti cet idānīṃ vidyāṃ vihāya sarve dharmā abhāvāḥ syuḥ | ato naiko dharmo 'vidyā bhavati | (u) avidyeyaṃ svalakṣaṇata ucyate nānyadharmataḥ | yathocyate akuśalamevākuśalasvarūpaṃ nāvyākṛtam |
body.translated_text: (Question) If the non-knowledge of things as they truly are is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), then even <s>dharmas</s> such as trees, stones, and the like would be ignorance — because of the absence of knowledge of things as they truly are. (Answer) Not so. Trees and stones are without mind; they do not conceptually discriminate about prior [and future] existences and the like. But ignorance has conceptual discrimination — therefore it is not the same as trees and stones. (Question) Ignorance is the absence of a <s>dharma</s>. Just as a person's not-seeing of form with the eye is not a <s>dharma</s> of non-seeing. Therefore ignorance is merely the absence of knowledge — not a separate <s>dharma</s>. (Answer) Not so. If ignorance were mere absence, then why does the false conceptualization arise — namely, 'there is a person (<s>pudgala</s>) in the five aggregates,' and 'in a potsherd, the perception of gold arises'? From this it is known that ignorance has the nature of false conceptualization — not that the absence of knowledge is ignorance. Formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) and the rest, conditioned by ignorance, operate in continuity. If [ignorance] were mere absence, how could it produce [anything]? (Question) If [you say] that what is not knowledge is not ignorance, then, leaving aside knowledge, all <s>dharmas</s> would be absences. Therefore no single <s>dharma</s> would be ignorance. (Answer) This ignorance is called [so] from its own characteristic, not from [the characteristic of] another <s>dharma</s>. Just as it is said: 'The unwholesome is of the nature of unwholesomeness itself, not indeterminate.'

body.text: tathāvidyāpi | kusūlaṃ puruṣākāramapi puruṣagatyabhāvāt apuruṣa ityucyate | evamiyaṃ vidyā savikalpāpi yathābhūtaṃ na prajānātītyavidyetyucyate | na tarupāṣāṇayorapi tathā |
body.translated_text: So too with ignorance. Even a granary in the shape of a person is called 'non-person' because of the absence of the movement of a person. In the same way, this [kind of knowledge], even though having conceptual discrimination, is called 'ignorance' because it does not know things as they truly are. It is not the same as trees and stones.

body.text: (pṛ) yānyuktāni arūpamapratighamanāsravamasaṃskṛtamiti tāni sarvāṇi tadanyābhidhāyakāni | kasmādavidyāpi naivam | (u) asti kadācidayaṃ nyāyaḥ | akuśalādiṣu tu naivaṃ bhavati | (pṛ) kecidāhuḥ- vidyāyā abhāvamātramavidyeti | yathā prakāśābhāve tama iti | (u) loke dvidhā vadanti- vidyāyā abhāvo 'vidyeti | kadācidviparītā vidyā avidyeti | vidyāyā abhāvo 'vidyeti yathā vadanti loke- adho 'rūpadarśī, badhiro 'śabdaśroteti | viparītā vidyā avidyeti- yathā rātrau sthāṇuṃ dṛṣṭvā puruṣa iti buddhirbhavati | puruṣaṃ vā dṛṣṭvā sthāṇubuddhiḥ | yadi kaścididamiti yathābhūtaṃ na prajānāti | tadajñānam | mithyācittaṃ kleśaḥ | ayaṃ saṃskārāṇāṃ pratyayaḥ | arhataḥ samucchedānna santi avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ | yadi na vidyā avidyeti | arhato buddhadharmeṣu vidyā nāstīti vidyāvidyā syāt | yo 'vidyāvān na so 'rhan | [ato] jñātavyaṃ pṛthagasti avidyāsvarūpam | idaṃ mithyācittamiti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Those [terms] that have been stated — 'formless' (<s>arūpa</s>), 'without resistance' (<s>apratigha</s>), 'without outflows' (<s>anāsrava</s>), 'unconditioned' (<s>asaṃskṛta</s>) — all of those designate what is other [than themselves]. Why is ignorance not likewise? (Answer) Sometimes this principle [of defining by negation] applies. But with the unwholesome and the like, it is not so. (Question) Some say: 'Ignorance is merely the absence of knowledge. Just as in the absence of light, there is darkness.' (Answer) In the world, they speak in two ways: 'The absence of knowledge is ignorance,' and sometimes 'perverted knowledge is ignorance.' 'The absence of knowledge is ignorance' — just as in the world they say: 'A blind person is a non-seer of form; a deaf person is a non-hearer of sound.' 'Perverted knowledge is ignorance' — just as at night, having seen a post, the cognition arises: 'It is a person.' Or having seen a person, the cognition of a post [arises]. When someone does not know this [thing] as it truly is, that is non-knowledge. The wrong mind is a defilement. This is the condition of formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>). For <s>Arhats</s>, through complete eradication, there are no formations conditioned by ignorance. If [you say] that what is not knowledge is ignorance, then for an <s>Arhat</s>, because there is no knowledge of <s>Buddha</s>-<s>dharmas</s>, there would be the ignorance of [not knowing] knowledge. One who has ignorance is not an <s>Arhat</s>. Therefore it should be known that ignorance has a separate essential nature — namely, this wrong mind.

body.text: sarve kleśā asyā avidyāyā aṅgāni | kasmāt | sarveṣāṃ kleśānāṃ mithyācāra [rūpa]tvāt | te puruṣāṇāṃ cittāvaraṇā andhatamorūpāḥ | yathāha- kāmarāgī na dharmaṃ paśyati, kāmarāgī na puṇyaṃ paśyati iti | tatkāmopādātā andhatamobhūmaḥ | evaṃ krodhamohāvapi | sarve kleśāḥ saṃskārāṇāmutpādakāḥ | uktantu sūtre- avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārā iti | ato jñāyate sarve kleśā avidyā iti | aśūnyatādarśino nityamastyavidyā | kliṣṭāvidyāmātraṃ sarvasaṃskārāṇāṃ pratyayaḥ | viparītā vidyā avidyetyucyate | adṛṣṭaśūnyabhāvasya nityamastīyamavidyā | ato jñāyate avidyāṅgāni sarve kleśā iti |
body.translated_text: All defilements are limbs of this ignorance. Why? Because all defilements have the nature of wrong conduct. They are obstructers of beings' minds, of the nature of blind darkness. As it says: 'One with passion for sensual pleasures does not see the <s>dharma</s>; one with passion for sensual pleasures does not see merit.' Thus the appropriation of sensual desires is the ground of blind darkness. So too with anger and delusion. All defilements produce formations. But it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Formations are conditioned by ignorance.' From this it is known that all defilements are ignorance. For one who does not see emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), there is always ignorance. The mere defiled ignorance (<s>kliṣṭāvidyā</s>) is the condition of all formations. Perverted knowledge is called ignorance. For one who has not seen the state of emptiness, this ignorance always exists. From this it is known that all defilements are limbs of ignorance.

body.text: (pṛ) avidyā kathamutpadyate | (u) asaddhetuṃ śrutvā cintayato 'vidyotpadyate | yathā asti dravyamastyavayavī asti cit, sarve dharmā akṣaṇikāḥ, nāsti punarbhavaḥ | śabda ātmā, sa ca nityaḥ, tṛṇavṛkṣādayaḥ sacetanā ityevamādimithyāgrahe sati avidyotpadyate | asatkāraṇairvāvidyotpadyate | yaduta durmitrasaṃstavo 'saddharmaśravaṇaṃ mithyāmanaskāro mithyāsamudācāra
body.translated_text: (Question) How does ignorance arise? (Answer) Ignorance arises when one hears and contemplates a wrong cause. Such as: 'There exists a substance (<s>dravya</s>), there exists a possessor of parts (<s>avayavin</s>), there exists consciousness (<s>cit</s>); all <s>dharmas</s> are non-momentary; there is no rebirth; sound is the self (<s>ātman</s>), and it is permanent; grasses, trees, and the like are sentient' — when such wrong grasping exists, ignorance arises. Or ignorance arises from wrong causes (<s>asatkāraṇa</s>) — namely, association with bad friends (<s>durmitra</s>), hearing the wrong <s>dharma</s> (<s>asaddharmaśravaṇa</s>), wrong attention (<s>mithyāmanaskāra</s>), wrong conduct (<s>mithyāsamudācāra</s>)

body.text: ityebhiścaturbhiḥ kāraṇairavidyotpadyate | anyakleśajananapratyayāḥ sarve 'vidyājananahetavaḥ | avidyāhetubhyaścāvidyotpadyate | yathā yavebhyo yavāḥ śālibhyaḥ śālayaḥ | evaṃ yatrāsti sattvakalpanā, tatrāvidyotpadyate | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- mithyāmanaskārapratyaye 'vidyotpadyata iti | mithyāmanaskāraścāvidyāyā nāmāntarameva | puruṣaṃ dṛṣṭvā astīti buddheḥ pūrvameva puruṣamanaskāra utpadyate paścānniścaya ityato 'vidyetyucyate | idamubhayaṃ pūrvāparalakṣaṇamanyonyasahāyamutpadyate | yathā vṛkṣātphalaṃ bhavati phalādvṛkṣaḥ |
body.translated_text: — from these four causes, ignorance arises. All conditions that generate other defilements are also causes that generate ignorance. And ignorance arises from the causes of ignorance [itself]. Just as barley arises from barley, and rice from rice. In the same way, wherever there is the conceptualization of a being (<s>sattvakalpanā</s>), there ignorance arises. Furthermore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Conditioned by wrong attention (<s>mithyāmanaskāra</s>), ignorance arises.' And wrong attention is just another name for ignorance. Having seen a person, before the cognition 'exists' [arises], the attention directed toward the person arises first, and afterwards the determination [follows] — therefore it is called 'ignorance.' These two — [wrong attention and ignorance] — having prior and posterior characteristics, arise as mutual supports. Just as from a tree fruit arises, and from a fruit a tree.

body.text: avidyāyāḥ ke doṣāḥ | (u) sarve vipattyupāyāsā avidyādhīnāḥ | kasmāt | [yasmāt] avidyātaḥ samutpadyante rāgādayaḥ kleśāḥ | tebhyo 'kuśalaṃ karma | tataḥ kāyānubhavaḥ | tatpratyayo vividhavipatyupāyāsānāṃ pratilābhaḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- avidyānivṛtasya [bhikṣavo vālasya] tṛṣṇāsamprayuktasyaivamayaṃ kāyaḥ samudāgata iti | siṃha nādasūtre coktam- upādānāni tṛṣṇānidānānīti | gāthā cāha-
body.translated_text: What are the faults of ignorance? (Answer) All misfortunes and distresses are dependent on ignorance. Why? Because from ignorance arise defilements such as passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the rest. From those, unwholesome <s>karma</s>. From that, the experience of the body. From that condition, the obtaining of manifold misfortunes and distresses. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'For the foolish monk obstructed by ignorance, conjoined with craving — thus this body has come to be.' And it is stated in the <s>Siṃhanāda Sūtra</s>: 'Appropriations (<s>upādāna</s>) have craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) as their origin.' And the verse says:

body.text:
yāḥ kāścidimā durgatayo 'smiṃlloke paratra ca |
avidyāmūlakāḥ sarvā icchālobhasamucchrayāḥ || iti |
body.translated_text:
Whatever bad destinies exist in this world and the next —
all are rooted in ignorance, arising from desire and greed.

body.text: avidyāsamutpannatvātsarvakleśānām | pṛthagjanā vedayante [sukhata] imān skandhān pañca [ye] 'śucayo 'nityā duḥkhāḥ śunyā anātmakāḥ | ya āryāḥ te tān duḥkhān vedayante | samyaṅmanaskārātpañca skandhān prajahāti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- ātmasaṃjñā mithyāviparyāsa iti prajānato na punarutpadyata iti | ato 'vidyāpratyayo bandho vidyāpratyayo mokṣa iti | loke sattvā avidyābalādalpādabhiniveśādbahūnādīnavān na paśyanti | yathā śalabhā agnau patanti | yathā vā matsyā aṅkuśaṃ gilanti | tathā sattvā api dṛṣṭe 'lpāsvādagṛddhā bahūnādīnavān na pratīkṣante | tīrthikagranthairutpannamithyādṛṣṭikā vadanti na santi puṇyādīni iti | sarvamiyamavidyā | asatāṃ mārgo 'kuśalahetuḥ | akuśalahetuḥ sarvo 'vidyā |
body.translated_text: Because all defilements are produced by ignorance, ordinary beings experience these five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) [as] pleasant — those that are impure, impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self. But the Noble Ones experience them as suffering. Through right attention (<s>samyaṅmanaskāra</s>), one abandons the five aggregates. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Knowing that the perception of self (<s>ātmasaṃjñā</s>) is a wrong perversion, it does not arise again.' Therefore, bondage is conditioned by ignorance; liberation is conditioned by knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>). In the world, beings, through the power of ignorance, cling to small things and do not see the many dangers. Just as moths fall into fire. Or just as fish swallow the hook. So too, beings, greedy for small pleasures in what is visible, do not anticipate the many dangers. Those whose wrong views have arisen through the treatises of non-Buddhists (<s>tīrthika</s>) say: 'Merit and the like do not exist.' All of this is ignorance. The path of the wicked is the cause of the unwholesome. Every cause of the unwholesome is ignorance.

body.text: mithyādṛṣṭyā kṛtakarmaṇā bhūyasā narake patanti | mithyādṛṣṭayaḥ sarvā avidyayotpadyante | buddho bhagavān sarvajñaḥ śāstā trayāṇāṃ dhātūnāṃ samyak caryāviśuddha āryavinīta ityādi tīrthikā na vivicya prajānanti | yathā sadratnamandhā nirākurvanti | ime 'vidyāyā doṣāḥ |
body.translated_text: Through <s>karma</s> done with wrong view, one for the most part falls into hell. All wrong views arise from ignorance. That the <s>Buddha</s>, the Blessed One, the Omniscient One, the Teacher, who has purified the right practice of the three realms, who has disciplined the Noble Ones — and the rest — non-Buddhists do not discriminately understand. Just as the blind reject a precious jewel. These are the faults of ignorance.

body.text: kiñca sarvasattvānāṃ vipattyupāyasavipralopādayaḥ sarve 'vidyādhīnāḥ | sarve ca lābhasaṃsiddhiprakarṣā vidyādhīnāḥ | yo vardhitāvidyaḥ sa ekāntato 'vīcinarake patati | yathā kalpādau janā āsvādastuccha ityanabhijñāya [tatra] rāgādhyavasāyamutpādayāmāsuḥ | ato rūpabalāyurādayo vinaṣṭāḥ | ato jñātavyamavidyayā sarve lābhāḥ pramuṣitā iti | iyamavidyā ca tatprajñānamātreṇa prahīyate | rāgādibhistu na tathā | rāgacitte nāsti krodhaḥ | krodhacitte nāsti rāgaḥ | avidyā tu sarvacitteṣu vartate | abhāvitaprajñasya cāvidyā sadā citte vartate | sarvakleśeṣu avidyā prabalā | yathoktaṃ sūtre- avidyā pāpīyasī gurvī durvimokā ca iti | avidyā ca dvādaśanidānānāṃ mūlam | asatyāmavidyāyāṃ karmāṇi nopacīyante na saṃsidhyanti | kasmāt | nahyasti arhatāṃ sattva[saṃjñā]lakṣaṇam | avidyāvirahānna karmāṇyu pacīyante | karmaṇāmanupacayādvijñānādīnyaṅgāni na punaḥ prādurbhavanti ato jñāyate avidyā sarvaduḥkhānāṃ mūlamiti |
body.translated_text: Furthermore, all misfortunes, distresses, deceptions, and the like of all beings are dependent on ignorance. And all gains, accomplishments, and excellences are dependent on knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>). One whose ignorance has increased falls without exception into the <s>Avīci</s> hell. Just as at the beginning of the <s>kalpa</s>, beings, not understanding that the taste [of food] was trivial, generated the determination of attachment toward it. Therefore form, strength, lifespan, and the rest were destroyed. From this it should be known that through ignorance all gains are lost. This ignorance is abandoned merely through that wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>). But with passion and the rest, it is not so. In a mind of passion, there is no anger. In a mind of anger, there is no passion. But ignorance operates in all minds. For one whose wisdom is uncultivated, ignorance always operates in the mind. Among all defilements, ignorance is the most powerful. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Ignorance is the worst, the heaviest, and the most difficult to liberate from.' Ignorance is the root of the twelve links of dependent origination (<s>dvādaśanidāna</s>). In the absence of ignorance, <s>karmas</s> are not accumulated and do not come to fruition. Why? For <s>Arhats</s> do not have the characteristic of the perception of a being (<s>sattvasaṃjñā</s>). Because of being free from ignorance, <s>karmas</s> are not accumulated. Because of the non-accumulation of <s>karma</s>, the limbs such as consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) and the rest do not appear again. From this it is known that ignorance is the root of all suffering.

body.text: pratyakṣaṃ dṛśyate khalu asminnaśucikāya āsaṅgaḥ, anitye nityasaṃjñā ca | yathā riktamuṣṭirbālānāmullāpanāya | yathā ca māyā mūḍhānāṃ puraḥ pradarśayati mṛdaṃ suvarṇamiti | prākṛtā mūḍhā dṛṣṭe pāpādhiṣṭhitā abhidhānenollapanīyā bhavanti | tathā lokā api cakṣuṣā aśuci dṛṣṭvā tadvañcitā bhavanti | caittā dharmā kṣaṇikāḥ, nimittagrahaṇādutpadyante | kṣaṇike rūpe mohānnimittaṃ gṛhṇanti | tathā śabdādāvapi | tasmāddurvimokā | ime 'vidyāyā doṣāḥ |
body.translated_text: It is directly perceived that there is attachment to this impure body, and the perception of permanence in what is impermanent. Just as an empty fist [is shown] to beguile children. And just as a magician displays before the deluded [the illusion that] earth is gold. Common, deluded beings, established in sin regarding what is visible, are to be beguiled by words. So too, beings in the world, having seen the impure with the eye, are deceived by it. Mental <s>dharmas</s> are momentary; they arise from the grasping of signs (<s>nimittagrahaṇa</s>). Through delusion, they grasp signs in momentary form. Likewise also with sound and the rest. Therefore [ignorance] is the most difficult to liberate from. These are the faults of ignorance.

body.text: (pṛ) avidyābahulasya puṃsaḥ kāni lakṣaṇāni | (u) ayaṃ bhayasthāne nirbhayo bhavati | susthāne prītivigataḥ sajjanadveṣī durjanasnidgho 'bhiprāyasya viparyayagrāhī priyamitre sadā pratikūlaḥ tucchavastuṣu sāragrāhī alpahrayapatrapo na vicikitsāpratīkṣī, na pareṣāṃ tarpaṇa ātmanāpi durniṣevaṇo mūḍho 'vijñātā sujīrṇamalinavastro bhramati | ramyapradeśādaśucipradeśamandhakāre prayāti | ātmanaivātmānaṃ mahāniti ślāghamānaḥ parasya laghūkaraṇe tṛpyati | apathenātmaguṇān prakaṭayati | doṣaṃ doṣa iti na vijānāti | hitaṃ hitamiti na vijānāti | apariśuddho 'nairyāṇiko bhāṣaṇe 'paṭuḥ sadā krodhopanāhamuditaḥ paropadeśaṃ viparyayato gṛhītvā [tatra] paramādhyāvasito durlabhamabhyasya suvinaśvaraṃ labhate | labdhasyāpi
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the characteristics of a person dominated by ignorance? (Answer) Such a person is fearless in a place of danger, devoid of joy in a good place, hating good people, affectionate toward bad people, grasping the opposite of what is intended, always hostile to dear friends, grasping substance in trivial things, having little shame and moral dread, not anticipating consequences, not satisfying others, himself practicing what is harmful, wandering about deluded, unknowing, wearing old and soiled clothes. He goes from a pleasant place to an impure place, into darkness. He praises himself, [thinking] 'I am great,' and finds satisfaction in belittling others. He displays his own qualities by a wrong path. He does not know a fault as a fault. He does not know what is beneficial as beneficial. Impure, not inclined toward liberation, unskilled in speech, always excited by anger and resentment, he grasps the instruction of others in a perverted way and is supremely fixated on that. Having practiced what is rare, he obtains what is easily perishable. Even of what he has obtained

body.text: nārtha vetti | viditamapi mithyā viparyayati | evamādilakṣaṇāni sarvāṇyavidyādhīnāni | ato jñāyate 'vidyāpramāṇaduṣṭā ataḥ prahātavyeti |
body.translated_text: he does not understand the purpose. And even what he understands, he wrongly perverts. Such and other characteristics are all dependent on ignorance. From this it is known that ignorance is immeasurably corrupt — therefore it should be abandoned.

body.text: (pṛ) kathaṃ prahātavyā | (u) tattvajñānaṃ bhāvayato 'vidyā prahīyate | (pṛ) skandhadhātvāyatanānāṃ jñānamapi tattvajñānam | kasmātsūtra uktam- avidyāyā bhaiṣajyaṃ pratītyasamutpādaḥ pratītyasamutpādabhāvanā vā iti | (u) tīrthikā bahavo bhrāntāḥ | hetau bhrāntā vadanti- īśvarā dayo lokakāraṇamiti | vastutastu bhrāntā vadanti- asti dravyamastyavayavītyādi | pratītyasamutpādā[di]dvayaṃ bhāvayato ['vidyā] prahī yate | (pṛ) pratītyasamutpādo 'vidyāyā bhaiṣajyam | kasmāducyate dvayamiti | (u) anyajñānasaṃjihīrṣayā | skandhadhātvāyatanādi bhāvayannapi avidyāṃ bhinatti | mithyādṛṣṭimātraṃ gurutarāvidyā | mithyādṛṣṭiśca pratītyasamutpādapraheyā | ato dvayamityucyate | evaṃ rāgadveṣāvapi | laukikā bhūyasā ghaṭādipade bhrāntāḥ | yathā ghaṭapadaṃ śṛṇvato manasi saṃśaya udeti kiṃ rūpādiḥ ghaṭaḥ kiṃvā rūpādivyatirikto 'nyo 'sti ghaṭa iti | evaṃ pañcaskandhātmakaḥ puruṣaḥ kiṃ vā tadvyatirikto 'nyo 'sti puruṣa iti | samāhitacittaḥ kāya evātmā kāyādanya ātmā iti śāśvatocchadākhye 'ntadvaye na patati | yaḥ prajānāti ghaṭaḥ pratītyasamutpanno rūparasagandhasparśamaya iti | evaṃ rūpādayaḥ skandhaḥ puruṣa iti | [sa] evaṃ prajānan nāmajaṃ saṃśayaṃ prajahāti | idaṃ nāma dharmāṇāṃ paramārthaṃ sañchādayati | yathāha devatāparipṛcchāsūtram-
body.translated_text: (Question) How is [ignorance] to be abandoned? (Answer) Through cultivating the knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>), ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is abandoned. (Question) The knowledge of the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>), elements (<s>dhātu</s>), and sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>) is also knowledge of reality. Why then is it stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The medicine for ignorance is dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>), or the cultivation of dependent origination'? (Answer) Many <s>tīrthikas</s> are confused. Confused regarding the cause, they say: '<s>Īśvara</s> and the like are the cause of the world.' Confused regarding reality, they say: 'There exists substance (<s>dravya</s>), there exists a possessor of parts (<s>avayavin</s>),' and the like. Through cultivating the twofold [analysis beginning with] dependent origination, ignorance is abandoned. (Question) Dependent origination is the medicine for ignorance. Why is it said 'twofold'? (Answer) With the desire to include other knowledge [as well]. Even cultivating the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, one destroys ignorance. Wrong view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>) alone is the more serious form of ignorance. And wrong view is to be abandoned through dependent origination. Therefore it is called 'twofold.' The same applies to passion (<s>rāga</s>) and hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>) as well. Worldly people are for the most part confused regarding terms such as 'pot' and the like. Just as when one hears the word 'pot,' doubt arises in the mind: 'Is the pot [nothing but] form and the like, or is there something other than form and the like that is the pot?' In the same way: 'Is the person constituted of the five aggregates, or is there something other than them that is the person?' One whose mind is concentrated does not fall into the two extremes called 'eternalism' (<s>śāśvata</s>) and 'annihilationism' (<s>uccheda</s>), [namely the views that] 'the self is identical with the body' and 'the self is other than the body.' One who understands that 'the pot is dependently originated, made of form, taste, smell, and touch' — likewise [understands that] 'the aggregates such as form and the rest are the person.' Understanding thus, he abandons the doubt born of names. This name conceals the ultimate reality (<s>paramārtha</s>) of <s>dharmas</s>. As the <s>Devatāparipṛcchā Sūtra</s> says:

body.text:
nāma sarvamadhvabhāvi nāma bhūyo na vidyate |
ekadharmasya nāmno 'sya sarve dharmā vaśānugāḥ || iti |
body.translated_text:
'Name pervades all time-periods; beyond name, nothing more exists.
To this single [thing called] name of a <s>dharma</s>, all <s>dharmas</s> are subservient.' Thus it is said.

body.text: kiñcāha- lokasya samudayaṃ paśyato 'bhāvadṛṣṭirnirudhyate | lokasya nirodhaṃ paśyato bhāvadṛṣṭirnirudhyate | iti | api coktam- saṃskārāṇāṃ santatiṃ pañcaskandhānāṃ saṃsaraṇaṃ vadanti | ime 'vidyādīnavāḥ pratītyasamutpādaṃ bhāvayato nirudhyanta iti | ukta ñca sūtre- yaḥ pratītyasabhutpādaṃ paśyati sa dharmaṃ paśyati | yo dharmaṃ paśyati sa buddhaṃ
body.translated_text: Furthermore it says: 'For one who sees the origination of the world, the view of non-existence (<s>abhāvadṛṣṭi</s>) ceases. For one who sees the cessation of the world, the view of existence (<s>bhāvadṛṣṭi</s>) ceases.' And it is also said: 'They speak of the continuity of formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>), the transmigration of the five aggregates. These faults beginning with ignorance cease for one who cultivates dependent origination.' And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'One who sees dependent origination sees the <s>Dharma</s>. One who sees the <s>Dharma</s> sees the <s>Buddha</s>

body.text: paśyatīti | evaṃ yo nāmajaṃ saṃśayaṃ prajahāti so 'parapratyayaḥ paramārthato buddhaṃ paśyati | atastattvajñānādavidyā kṣīyate | pratītyasamutpādaṃ samyak prajānan tattvajñānaṃ pratilabhate | saṃkṣepata uktaṃ caturaśītidharmaskandhe- yā kācana prajñā sarvā sāvidyāvyāvartinīti | avidyā ca sarvakleśānāṃ mūlaṃ sarvakleśānāṃ sahakāriṇī cetyevaṃ pratītyasamutpāda [jñāne] avidyā prahīyate ||
body.translated_text: .' Thus, one who abandons the doubt born of names, being independent of others, sees the <s>Buddha</s> in the ultimate sense. Therefore, through the knowledge of reality, ignorance is exhausted. One who correctly understands dependent origination obtains the knowledge of reality. In brief, it is stated in the Eighty-four <s>Dharmaskandhas</s>: 'Whatever wisdom there is — all of that averts ignorance.' And ignorance is the root of all defilements and the companion of all defilements — thus, through [the knowledge of] dependent origination, ignorance is abandoned.
