body.text: avidyāvargaḥ saptaviṃśatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one-hundred-and-twenty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on Ignorance (<s>avidyāvarga</s>).

body.text: 128 mānavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 128. Chapter on Conceit (<s>mānavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) trayaḥ kleśāḥ saṃsārasya mūlamityuktam | ato 'nyaḥ punarasti na vā | (u) asti mānākhyaḥ | (pṛ) katamo mānaḥ | (u) mithyācittenātmana unnatirmāna ityucyate | māno 'yaṃbahuvidhaḥ | avara ātmani unnatirmānaḥ | sameṣu samatāmanyatāpi māna ityucyate | tatrātmabuddhinimittagrahadoṣasattvāt | sameṣu ātmana unnatirmahāmānaḥ | viśiṣṭeṣu ātmana unnatirabhimānaḥ | pañcasu skandheṣu ātmanimittagraho 'smimānaḥ | asmimāno dvividho nimittapradarśano 'nimittapradarśana iti | nimittapradarśanaḥ pṛthagjanānāmātmamāno yaduta rūpamātmā, rūpavānātmā, ātmani rūpaṃ, rūpa ātmā iti darśanam, evaṃ yāvadvijñānamapi | iti viṃśatidhā pradarśanāt nimittapradarśanaḥ | animittapradarśanaḥ śaikṣajanānāmasmimānaḥ | yathā sthaviraḥ kṣemaka āha- na khalvāyuṣman rūpamasmīti vadāmi, na vedanā, na saṃjñā, na saṃskārā, na vijñānam, [nāpyanyatra vijñānādasmīti vadāmi] | api ca ma āyuṣman pañcasūpādānaskandheṣu anusahagato 'smīti mānaḥ asmīticchandaḥ asmītyanuśayo 'samuddhataḥ | [ityādi] | ayamasmimāna ityucyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) It has been stated that the three defilements (<s>kleśa</s>) are the root of <s>saṃsāra</s>. Is there yet another [defilement] or not? (Answer) There is — it is called conceit (<s>māna</s>). (Question) What is conceit? (Answer) The elevation of oneself through a wrong-minded (<s>mithyācitta</s>) [attitude] is called conceit. This conceit is of many kinds. The elevation of oneself [when one is] inferior is [ordinary] conceit (<s>māna</s>). Regarding oneself as equal to equals is also called conceit — because therein there is the fault of grasping the mark (<s>nimittagraha</s>) of self-notion. The elevation of oneself regarding equals is great conceit (<s>mahāmāna</s>). The elevation of oneself regarding superiors is overestimation (<s>abhimāna</s>). The grasping of the mark of a self in the five aggregates is the conceit 'I am' (<s>asmimāna</s>). The conceit 'I am' is of two kinds: that which manifests a mark (<s>nimittapradarśana</s>) and that which does not manifest a mark (<s>animittapradarśana</s>). 'That which manifests a mark' is the self-conceit of ordinary beings (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) — namely, the view that 'form is the self, the self possesses form, form is in the self, the self is in form,' and likewise up to consciousness as well. Thus, through twenty modes of manifestation, it is 'that which manifests a mark.' 'That which does not manifest a mark' is the conceit 'I am' of learners (<s>śaikṣa</s>). Just as the Elder <s>Kṣemaka</s> said: 'Indeed, Venerable One, I do not say "I am form," nor "I am feeling," nor "I am perception," nor "I am formations," nor "I am consciousness" — [nor do I say "I am something other than consciousness"].  But, Venerable One, in the five aggregates of clinging, the conceit "I am" accompanies me, the desire "I am" [accompanies me], and the latent tendency "I am" has not been uprooted,' and so forth. This is called the conceit 'I am.'

body.text: yaḥ srotaāpattyādiphalaviśeṣānapratilabhya pratilabdhavāniti vadati so 'dhimānaḥ | (pṛ) alābhe kasmādbhavati lābhabuddhiḥ | (u) dhyānābhyāse 'lpāsvādalābhāt saṃyojanā nuśayaṃ vyāvartayati na punaścitte samudācarati | ato 'yaṃ māno bhavati | śrutacintāmayaprajñābalena ca sadā kalyāṇamitramupasadya [ta]tsamudācāravivekamabhirocayati | pañcaskandhānāṃ lakṣaṇamalpaṃ jñātvā srotaāpattyādiphalasaṃjñāmutpādayati | [aya]madhimānaḥ |
body.translated_text: One who, without having obtained the distinction of the fruits of stream-entry and the rest, says 'I have obtained them' — that is over-estimation (<s>adhimāna</s>). (Question) In the absence of attainment, why does the notion of attainment arise? (Answer) Through the practice of <s>dhyāna</s>, having obtained a small taste [of concentration], one turns away the fetters and latent tendencies (<s>saṃyojanānuśaya</s>) — they no longer arise in the mind. Therefore this conceit arises. And through the power of wisdom born of learning and reflection (<s>śrutacintāmayaprajñā</s>), always approaching good spiritual friends (<s>kalyāṇamitra</s>), one delights in their discriminating detachment. Having known a little of the characteristics of the five aggregates, one generates the perception of having attained the fruits of stream-entry and the rest. This is over-estimation (<s>adhimāna</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) adhimānasya ke doṣāḥ | (u) ante daurmanasyopāyāsairbhavitavyam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- yo bhikṣuḥ kathayati ahaṃ samuddhatavicikitsaḥ pratilabdhamārga iti | [tasya] purata evaṃ kathayet- atigabhīraḥ pratītyasamutpādo lokottaradharma iti | yadyayaṃ bhikṣurvastuto 'pratilabdhamārgaḥ | [tadāsya] imaṃ dharmaṃ śṛṇvataḥ kaukṛtyopāyāso bhavati | ato yatnenādhimānamimaṃ samucchindyāt | adhimānini buddhā bhagavanto mahākāruṇikā api [taṃ] dūrīkṛtya na dharmāvavādaṃ kurvanti | ataḥ samucchindyāt | kiñcādhimānī dharmasya mithyādarśane viharati | ato nāsti tāttviko guṇaḥ | tadyathā vaṇik gabhīramahāsamudragato ratnābhāseṣvāsakto bhavati | tathāyamapi buddhaśāsanārṇavagataḥ alpaṃ dhyānasukhaṃ pratilabhya pāramārthikamārga iti tatrāsaṅgaṃ janayati | adhimānī ante maraṇakāle na mārgaṃ vedayate | ato yatnena pāramārthikatattvajñānamanviṣyāt | adhimānī svārthaṃ vināśayati sammohañca bardhayati | alabdhe labdhasaṃjñāvatvāt | ato nātmānamātmanaiva vañcayet | iti kṣipraṃ visṛjet |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults of over-estimation? (Answer) At the end, there must be displeasure and distress. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'A monk who says "I have uprooted doubt, I have obtained the path" — one should speak to him in this manner: "Extremely profound is dependent origination, a supramundane <s>dharma</s>." If that monk has in reality not obtained the path, then upon hearing this <s>dharma</s>, remorse and distress arise in him.' Therefore one should strive to eradicate this over-estimation. The <s>Buddhas</s>, the Blessed Ones, the greatly compassionate, even toward one who has over-estimation, keep him at a distance and do not give him instruction in the <s>Dharma</s>. Therefore one should eradicate it. Furthermore, one who has over-estimation dwells in a wrong vision of the <s>Dharma</s>. Therefore there is no genuine virtue. Just as a merchant who has entered the depths of the great ocean becomes attached to false gems. So too, this [person], having entered the ocean of the <s>Buddha's</s> teaching, having obtained a small happiness of <s>dhyāna</s>, generates attachment [thinking] 'this is the ultimate path.' One who has over-estimation, at the end, at the time of death, does not experience the path. Therefore one should strive diligently to seek the ultimate knowledge of reality (<s>pāramārthikatattvajñāna</s>). One who has over-estimation destroys his own welfare and increases delusion — because of having the perception of having attained what has not been attained. Therefore one should not deceive oneself by oneself. Hence one should quickly abandon it.

body.text: yaduttamaṃ puruṣamavaraṃ vadanti | tadayathā bhavatīti ayathāmāna ityucyate | ayaṃ svayamucco 'pi svātmabhāvamavanamayati | yadaguṇāḥ santa ātmānamunnamayanti | tanmithyāmāna ityucyate | akuśaladharmairātmana uccakaraṇamapi mithyāmānaḥ | yat sujane pūjye pṛṣṭhato 'satkāra uddhatamānaḥ saḥ | ityādi mānalakṣaṇam |
body.translated_text: When one calls a superior person 'inferior' — that, being untrue, is called 'wrong conceit' (<s>ayathāmāna</s>). This person, even though himself elevated, brings down his own self-respect. When those without virtues elevate themselves — that is called 'false conceit' (<s>mithyāmāna</s>). Self-elevation through unwholesome <s>dharmas</s> is also false conceit. Disrespecting a virtuous, venerable person behind their back is arrogant conceit (<s>uddhatamāna</s>). Such and the like is the characteristic of conceit.

body.text: (pṛ) kathaṃ māna utpadyate | (u) skandhānāṃ paramārthalakṣaṇamajānānāṃ māna
body.translated_text: (Question) How does conceit arise? (Answer) For those who do not know the ultimate characteristic of the aggregates, conceit

body.text: utpadyate | yathoktaṃsūtre- ye kecit [śramaṇā brāhmaṇā vā] anityena rūpeṇa [duḥkhena vipariṇāmadharmeṇa] śreṣṭho 'hamasmīti samanupaśyanti | sadṛśo ['hamasmāti samanupaśyanti] hīno ['hamasbhīti samanupaśyanti] kimanyatra yathābhūtasyādarśanāt | evaṃ yāvadvijñānamiti | skandhānāṃ paramārthalakṣaṇaṃ jānatāṃ nāsti mānaḥ | kāyānusmṛtiṃ bhāvayato nāsti mānaḥ | yathā gauḥ śṛṅgamapekṣya tīkṣṇo bhavati | tacchṛṅge gate na bhavati | kāyo 'śuciḥ navadvāreṣu malaprasrāvī | kaḥ prājña imamapekṣya ucco 'smīti [manyeta] evamādikāyānusmṛtipratyaye tu nāsti mānaḥ | prājño jānāti sarve sattvā yadi vā daridrī yadi vā dhanī yadi vā pūjyo yadi vā jadhanyaḥ sarve 'pi asthimāṃsasnāyusirāpañcasandhipeśīkalalasamavāyamayakāyāḥ, jātijarāvyādhimaraṇadaurmanasyaparidevaduḥkhopāyāsasamanvitā rāgakrodhādipuṇyapāpakarmayuktā narakādidurgatibhāginaśceti | kathamutpādayenmānam | ābhyantaraṃ bāhyaṃ cittaṃ pratītyasamutpannaṃ sarvaṃ kṣaṇikamiti paśyato na bhavati mānaḥ | cittasamādhiñca samyak bhāvayato na bhavati mānaḥ | kasmāt | nimitte 'nugate hi māna utpadyate | asati nimitte kutra mānamutpādayet | kiñca prājñasya śīlādiṣu satsu na bhavati mānaḥ | kasmāt | śīlādayo hi sarve eṣāṃ kleśānāṃ kṣayakarāḥ | asatsu guṇeṣu kaḥ prājño 'sadvastuni mānamutpādayet | anityatādilakṣaṇaṃ bhāvayato māno nirudhyate | kaḥ prājño 'nityena duḥkhena aśucinā padārthena mānaṃ kuryāt |
body.translated_text: arises. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Whatever ascetics or <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, [regarding] impermanent form [that is suffering and of the nature of change], contemplate "I am superior" — or contemplate ["I am equal"] — or contemplate "I am inferior" — what is this but not seeing as it truly is?' Likewise up to consciousness. For those who know the ultimate characteristic of the aggregates, there is no conceit. For one who cultivates the mindful contemplation of the body (<s>kāyānusmṛti</s>), there is no conceit. Just as a bull, depending on its horns, becomes fierce. When those horns are gone, it is not [fierce]. The body is impure, exuding filth from the nine openings. What wise person, depending on this, would think 'I am superior'? Through such contemplation of the body and the like as a condition, there is no conceit. The wise person knows that all beings — whether poor or wealthy, whether venerable or lowly — all possess bodies that are an assemblage of bones, flesh, sinews, veins, the five joints, and membranous tissue; [all are] endowed with birth, old age, disease, death, displeasure, lamentation, suffering, and distress; [all are] connected with <s>karmas</s> of merit and sin born of passion, anger, and the like; [all are] partakers of the lower destinies such as hell and the rest. How could one generate conceit? For one who sees that the internal [mind], the external [world], and the mind are all dependently originated and momentary — there is no conceit. And for one who correctly cultivates the concentration of mind (<s>cittasamādhi</s>), there is no conceit. Why? Because conceit arises when a mark (<s>nimitta</s>) is followed. When there is no mark, where would one generate conceit? Furthermore, for the wise person who possesses moral conduct and the like, there is no conceit. Why? Because moral conduct and the like are all destroyers of these defilements. When virtues are absent, what wise person would generate conceit regarding an unreal object? For one who cultivates the characteristics of impermanence and the like, conceit ceases. What wise person would generate conceit regarding an impermanent, suffering, and impure object?

body.text: (pṛ) mānasya ke doṣāḥ | (u) mānātkāyo bhavati | kāyātsarvaṃ duḥkhaṃ pravartate | yathāha bhagavān sūtre- yadāhaṃ māṇavako 'bhūvam, na tadā mānalakṣaṇamājñāsiṣam ahamiti vedanāvyākaraṇaṃ kutracidutpatsyata iti | anyamānānāmaprahīṇatvāt | sarve kleśā nimittagrahānuvartinaḥ | ahamiti nimitteṣu mahat | ato jñāyate mānātkāyo bhavatīti | māno 'yaṃ mohabhāgīyaḥ | kasmāt | cakṣuṣā rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā ahaṃ paśyāmītyāha | māno 'yamanītyā ca pravartate | kasmāt | sarve lokā anityā duḥkhā anātmakāḥ | kathamanena māno bhavati | ato rāgadveṣamohāḥ paramānītayaḥ | manoddhitaṃ karma tīkṣṇaṃ gurukañca |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults of conceit? (Answer) Through conceit, the body comes into being. Through the body, all suffering proceeds. As the Blessed One said in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'When I was a young student (<s>māṇavaka</s>), I did not at that time know the characteristic of conceit — namely, "I" — that feeling-declaration [of selfhood] that was to arise somewhere.' Because of the non-abandonment of other forms of conceit. All defilements follow the grasping of marks. In marks, the mark 'I' is the greatest. Therefore it is known that through conceit the body comes into being. This conceit belongs to the class of delusion (<s>moha</s>). Why? Having seen form with the eye, one says 'I see.' And this conceit proceeds based on what is unreal (<s>anītya</s>). Why? All worlds are impermanent, suffering, and without self. How can there be conceit regarding this? Therefore passion, hatred, and delusion are supremely unreal. Mental <s>karma</s> is sharp and grave.

body.text: gabhīrāsaktatvāt | rāgoddhitantu nedṛśaṃ bhavati | mānabalādrāgādayo vardhante | anena rāgeṇa labdho gotrādimānastu vipulaṃ vardhate | asmimānapratyayaṃ pravartate nīcakulam | siṃhavyāghra vṛkeṣvapi bhavati | asmātpratyayānnarake patati | mānasya santyevamādīnyapramāṇānyavadyāni |
body.translated_text: Because of deep attachment. But [<s>karma</s>] produced by passion is not like that. Through the power of conceit, passion and the like increase. Through this passion [strengthened by] the conceit of lineage and the like, [they] grow extensively. Dependent on the conceit 'I am' as its condition, one revolves in low births. It exists even among lions, tigers, and wolves. Through this condition, one falls into hell. The faults of conceit are thus immeasurable.

body.text: (pṛ) kiṃ mānabahulasya lakṣaṇam | (u) ayaṃ samupāttadhārṣṭyo duḥsahabhāṣaṇo 'satkāracitto 'lpabhayaḥ svairācāramuditaḥ svayañca mahāduḥśāsano yatkiñcijjadhanya[mapi]svayaṃ bahumānī, parakutsanapriyāluritīme doṣā durapaneyāḥ | ato jñāninā nācaritavyāḥ | māno 'yaṃ sarvaguṇānāṃ vighaṭakatayā pravartate ||
body.translated_text: (Question) What is the characteristic of one who is full of conceit? (Answer) This [person] is bold and presumptuous, difficult to converse with, disrespectful in mind, little afraid, delighted in willful conduct, himself extremely difficult to discipline, and regarding even the most inferior thing as highly esteemed by himself, and delights in disparaging others — these faults are difficult to remove. Therefore the wise person should not practice them. This conceit operates as the destroyer of all virtues.

body.text: mānavargo 'ṣṭhāviṃśatyuttaraśatattamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one-hundred-and-twenty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on Conceit (<s>mānavarga</s>).

body.text: 129 vicikitsāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 129. Chapter on Doubt (<s>vicikitsāvarga</s>)

body.text: śāstramāha- vicikitsā nāma tattvārthe buddhyaviniścaḥ kimasti vimuktiḥ kiṃ vā nāsti | kimasti kuśalamakuśalam | uta na | kimasti ratnatrayam | uta na iti |
body.translated_text: The treatise says: Doubt (<s>vicikitsā</s>) is the non-determination of the intellect regarding the meaning of reality — namely: 'Does liberation exist or not? Do wholesome and unwholesome exist or not? Do the Three Jewels (<s>ratnatraya</s>) exist or not?'

body.text: (pṛ) vṛkṣe saṃśayo bhavati kiṃ sthāṇuḥ kiṃ vā puruṣa iti | mṛtpiṇḍe saṃśayo bhavati kiṃ mṛtpiṇḍaḥ uta kokila iti | madhukare saṃśayo bhavati kiṃ madhukaraḥ kiṃ vā jambūphalamiti | sarpe saṃśayo bhavati kiṃ sarpaḥ kiṃ vā rajjuriti | ghoṭakamṛge saṃśayo bhavati kiṃ prabhā kiṃ vā salilaṃ iti | evamādayaḥ saṃśayahetavaścākṣuṣavijñānajanakāḥ | dhvanau saṃśayo bhavati kiṃ mayūrakṛta uta manuṣyakṛta iti | gandhe saṃśayo bhavati kimutpalagandhaḥ uta saṃparkagandha iti | rase saṃśayo bhavati kiṃ māṃsarasa uta māṃsābhāsarasa iti | sparśe saṃśayo bhavati kimautpattikatantava uta paripakvatantava iti | mānasavijñānantu nānāvidhasaṃśayajanakam | yathā kimayaṃ dharmo dravyavān uta guṇamātram | vimastyātmā uta na ityevamādayaḥ kiṃ saṃśayā na santi |
body.translated_text: (Question) Regarding a tree, doubt arises: 'Is it a stump or a person?' Regarding a lump of clay, doubt arises: 'Is it a lump of clay or a cuckoo?' Regarding a bee, doubt arises: 'Is it a bee or a <s>jambū</s> fruit?' Regarding a snake, doubt arises: 'Is it a snake or a rope?' Regarding a mirage-deer, doubt arises: 'Is it a gleam or water?' Such and similar causes of doubt are generators of visual consciousness. In sound, doubt arises: 'Was it made by a peacock or by a person?' In smell, doubt arises: 'Is it the scent of a lotus or a composite scent?' In taste, doubt arises: 'Is it the flavor of meat or a semblance of meat-flavor?' In touch, doubt arises: 'Is it a naturally-produced thread or a ripened thread?' But mind-consciousness generates various kinds of doubt. Such as: 'Does this <s>dharma</s> possess substance or is it merely a quality? Does the self exist or not?' — and the like. How could such doubts not exist?

body.text: atra brūmaḥ | sthāṇurvā puruṣo va ityevamādibhistu na kleśā bhavanti | na ca te punarbhavasya pratyayā bhavanti | kṣīṇāsravāṇāmapyetatsambhavāt |
body.translated_text: Here we reply: From 'Is it a stump or a person?' and the like, defilements do not arise. And they are not conditions for further rebirth. Because they occur even for those whose outflows are exhausted (<s>kṣīṇāsrava</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) vicikitseyaṃ kathamutpadyate | (u) dvividhadharmadarśanaśravaṇajñānairvicikitsā bhavati | kasmāt | pūrvaṃ dvidhāvasthitaṃ padārthaṃ sthāṇuṃ puruṣañca dṛṣṭvā paścāddūrataḥ paśyati
body.translated_text: (Question) How does this doubt (<s>vicikitsā</s>) arise? (Answer) Through seeing, hearing, and knowing <s>dharmas</s> of two kinds, doubt arises. Why? Having previously seen two things in different positions — a stump and a person — and afterward seeing from a distance

body.text: puruṣādi vastu tadā saṃśeta sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti | tadā mṛdādāvapi | dvidhāśravaṇam- yadi kaścicchṛṇoti asti puṇyaṃ pāpamiti | paścācchṛṇoti loke nāstīti | ataḥ saṃśayo bhavati | dvidhājñānam- yadā deve varṣati nadī samṛddhā bhavati | jalasetubhede 'pi nadī samṛddhā | yathā deve vivṛkṣati pipīlikāpotānyaṇḍavāhīni | kasmiṃścit [kutracit] khanatyapi aṇḍasaṃkrānto gacchati | mayūrakūjanaṃ puruṣo 'pi kartuṃ śaknoti | kiñcidvastu dṛśyaṃ yathā ghaṭaḥ | kiñcidadṛśyaṃ yathālātacakram | adṛśyaṃ vastu yathā vṛkṣamūlaṃ pṛthivyāmadhastāt jala[sthaṃ]vā | kiñcidavastu adṛśyañca yathā dvitīyaṃ śiraḥ tṛtīyo bāhuḥ | evamādibhirdvidhādharmadarśanaśravaṇajñānaiḥ saṃśayo bhavati |
body.translated_text: an object such as a person, one then doubts: 'Is it a stump or a person?' Likewise with clay and the rest. 'Hearing of two kinds' — if someone hears 'Merit and demerit exist' and afterward hears 'In the world, they do not exist' — from that, doubt arises. 'Knowledge of two kinds' — when the god rains, the river swells; when a water-dam breaks too, the river swells. Just as when the god is about to rain, ants carry their egg-bundles; [but] even when someone digs in a certain place, [ants] move carrying their eggs. A peacock's cry can be made by a person too. Some objects are visible — such as a pot. Some are invisible — such as the circle of a firebrand. An invisible object — such as the root of a tree, underground or in water. Something that is both non-existent and invisible — such as a second head or a third arm. Through such seeing, hearing, and knowing <s>dharmas</s> of two kinds, doubt arises.

body.text: aparīkṣya darśanācca saṃśayo bhavati | yathātidūrādibhiraṣṭapratyayaiḥ | dvidhāśraddhāvattvena ca saṃśayo bhavati | yathā kaścidvadati- asti paraloka iti | [anyaḥ] kaścidvadati nāstīti | ubhayorapi puruṣayoḥ śraddhāvataḥ saṃśayo bhavati | vimate vastuni yāvadviśiṣṭalakṣaṇaṃ na paśyati tāvatsaṃśayo bhavati | viśiṣṭalakṣaṇaṃ paśyatastu saṃśayo na bhavati | (pṛ) kathaṃ viśiṣṭhalakṣaṇaṃ paśyati | (u) darśanaśravaṇajñānānāṃ viniścayādvigatasaṃśayo bhavati | bhagavacchāsane yaḥ kāyena dharmatālakṣaṇaṃ sākṣātkaroti | so 'tyantavigatasaṃśayo bhavati | yathā bodhisattvo bodhimaṇḍe niṣaṇṇo 'vadat vyavasāyena brāhmaṇalabdhaṃ gamīraṃ dharmamabhisametya pratyayān jānan paśyaṃśca prakṣīṇasaṃśayajālo bhaveyamiti | sadyuktiprajñālābhinaśca saṃśayaḥ prahīyate | yathā jñānī saṃskārāṇāṃ pratītyasamutpādaṃ śrutvā vijñāya ca nirdhāsyati saṃsāro 'nādirityevamādi |
body.translated_text: Doubt also arises from seeing without examination — such as through the eight conditions of being too far away and the like. And doubt arises through trusting two [authorities] — just as someone says 'The next world exists' and someone else says 'It does not exist.' When one trusts both persons, doubt arises. Regarding an object about which there is uncertainty, as long as one does not see a distinguishing mark, doubt exists. But for one who sees the distinguishing mark, doubt does not exist. (Question) How does one see the distinguishing mark? (Answer) Through the determination of seeing, hearing, and knowledge, one becomes free from doubt. In the teaching of the Blessed One, one who directly realizes the characteristic of the nature of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>dharmatālakṣaṇa</s>) with the body — he becomes completely free from doubt. Just as the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, seated at the seat of awakening (<s>bodhimaṇḍa</s>), said: 'Through determination, having comprehended the profound <s>Dharma</s> obtained by <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, knowing and seeing the conditions — I would become one whose net of doubt is destroyed.' And for one who obtains wisdom conjoined with correct reasoning, doubt is abandoned. Just as the wise one, having heard and understood the dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>) of conditioned things, will ascertain 'Saṃsāra is beginningless' and so forth.

body.text: (pṛ) vicikitsāyāḥ ke doṣāḥ | (u) vicikitsābahulasya laukikaṃ lokottaraṃ sarvaṃ na sidhyati | kasmāt | sandidghaḥ pumān na kāryaṃ karma karoti | yat karoti tat jaghanyaṃ bhavati | sādhayitumakṣamatvāt | uktañca sūtre- vicikitsā cittasyānuprarohaḥ | tadyathā satṛṇakṣetre 'nuprarohabahulatvādanyatṛṇānyeva na prarohanti | kiḥ punaḥ śālisasyādīni |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults of doubt? (Answer) For one who is full of doubt, nothing is accomplished — neither worldly nor supramundane. Why? A person who is in doubt does not perform the <s>karma</s> that should be done. What he does becomes inferior — because of being unable to accomplish [it]. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Doubt is the non-growth of the mind. Just as in a field overgrown with weeds, because of the abundance of non-growth, other grasses alone grow — what more need be said of rice and other crops?

body.text: evaṃ cittaṃ vicikitsāprasṛṣṭamasadvastunyeva samādadhāti | kiṃ punaḥ samyak samādhau iti | kiñcāha bhagavān- vicikitsā nāma tamaso rāśiriti | sa tamaso rāśistrividhaḥ atīto 'nāgataḥ pratyutpanna iti | sa tamaso rāśirātmadṛṣṭīnāmuttisthānam | puruṣo 'yaṃ cittaṃ samādadhāno 'pi mithyā samādadhāti | vinā bhagavacchāsanaṃ na samyaksamādhimān iti vaktuṃ śakyate | bahavaḥ sattvā āmaraṇaṃ vicikitsāvinaṣṭāḥ | tadyathāha- aṣṭakādayaḥ pañcābhijñā maharṣayaḥ saṃśayālīḍhā vipannā iti | saṃśayānasya dānādi kurvataḥ puṇyamavipākaṃ vā syādalpavipākaṃ vā | kasmāt | imāni puṇyakarmāṇi cittodgatāni | tasya puruṣasya cittaṃ sadā vicikitsākaluṣitamityato nāsti kuśalam | uktañca sūtre- vicikitsitacitto dānaṃ datvā pratyantabhūmau vipākaṃ vedayata iti | kasmāt | vicikitsābahulo naikāgracitto yathākālaṃ pāṇibhyāṃ prayacchati | nāpi vividhaṃ satkāracittamutpādayati | ataḥ pratyantabhūmau kṣudraṃ vipākaṃ vedayate | tadyathā pāyāsyādayaḥ kṣudrarājāḥ |
body.translated_text: Likewise, a mind pervaded by doubt settles only on unreal objects — what more need be said of correct <s>samādhi</s>?' And further the Blessed One said: 'Doubt is a mass of darkness.' That mass of darkness is threefold: past, future, and present. That mass of darkness is the basis for views of self (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>). This person, even while composing his mind in <s>samādhi</s>, composes it wrongly. Without the teaching of the Blessed One, it cannot be said that he has right <s>samādhi</s>. Many beings are destroyed by doubt until death. As it says: '<s>Aṣṭaka</s> and the others, the great seers endowed with the five superknowledges (<s>pañcābhijñā</s>), were consumed by doubt and perished.' For one who, while doubting, performs giving and the like — the merit would either be without ripening or of small ripening. Why? These meritorious <s>karmas</s> arise from the mind. That person's mind is always defiled by doubt — therefore there is no wholesomeness. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'One who, with a doubting mind, gives a gift, experiences ripening in a border-region.' Why? Because one who is full of doubt, lacking one-pointed mind, gives with his hands at the appropriate time but does not generate a diversified mind of honor. Therefore he experiences a paltry ripening in a border-region. Just as <s>Pāyasī</s> and the like — petty kings.

body.text: (pṛ) nāstīyaṃ vicikitsā | kasmāt | vicikikitsā nāma caitasikadharmaḥ | caitasikāśca kṣaṇikāḥ | san na vicikitsā | asan api na vicikitsā | naikaṃ cittaṃ sat asaditi bhavati | ato nāstīti jñāyate | (u) nāhaṃ vadāmi kṣaṇikeṣvasti vicikitseti | anirdhāritacittasantāno vicikitsetyākhyāyate | na tasmin samaye cittaṃ nirdhārayati ayaṃ sthāṇurayaṃ puruṣa iti | satanyamānamidaṃ cittamaśraddadhānatvādāvilam | mithyādarśanādasti vā nāsti veti vicikitsanna śraddadhate |
body.translated_text: (Question) This doubt does not exist. Why? Doubt is a mental factor (<s>caitasikadharma</s>). And mental factors are momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>). Being [existent], it is not doubt. Being non-[existent], it too is not doubt. A single mind cannot be both existent and non-existent. Therefore it is known that [doubt] does not exist. (Answer) I do not say that doubt exists in momentary [states]. A continuity of undetermined mind is designated as 'doubt.' At that time, the mind does not determine: 'This is a stump; this is a person.' This extending mind, because of non-trusting, is turbid. Through wrong seeing, [one wonders] 'does it exist or not' — doubting, one does not trust.

body.text: aśraddheyaṃ dvividhā vicikitsāsambhavā mithyādarśanasambhavā iti | vicikitsāsambhavā laghutarā | mithyādarśanasambhavā tu gurutarā | śraddhā ca dvividhā samyadgarśanasambhavā śravaṇasambhaveti | samyadgarśanasambhavā śraddhā dṛḍhā bhavati śravaṇasambhavā tu naivaṃ bhavati ||
body.translated_text: Non-trusting (<s>aśraddhā</s>) is twofold: born from doubt and born from wrong view (<s>mithyādarśana</s>). Non-trusting born from doubt is lighter. Non-trusting born from wrong view is heavier. And faith (<s>śraddhā</s>) is twofold: born from right seeing (<s>samyagdarśana</s>) and born from hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>). Faith born from right seeing is firm. But faith born from hearing is not so.

body.text: vicikitsāvarga ekonatriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one-hundred-and-twenty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Doubt (<s>vicikitsāvarga</s>).

body.text: 130 satkāyadṛṣṭivargaḥ
body.translated_text: 130. Chapter on the View of the Personal Self (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭivarga</s>)

body.text: pañcasu skandheṣu ātmabuddhiḥ satkāyadṛṣṭiḥ | vastuta ātmano 'bhāvātpañcaskandhālambinītyucyate | kāyaḥ pañcaskandhātmakaḥ | tatrotpannā [ātma]dṛṣṭiḥ satkāyadṛṣṭirityucyate | nirātmaka ātmanimittagrahaṇāt dṛṣṭirityākhyāyate |
body.translated_text: The notion of self (<s>ātmabuddhi</s>) in the five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) is the view of the personal self (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>). Because the self does not exist in reality, it is said to take the five aggregates as its object. The body (<s>kāya</s>) consists of the five aggregates. The view of self (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>) that arises therein is called <s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>. Because of grasping the sign of a self in what is selfless, it is designated as 'view' (<s>dṛṣṭi</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) pañcasu skandheṣu ātmeti nāmakaraṇe ko doṣaḥ | yathā ghaṭādayaḥ padārthāḥ pratyekaṃ svalakṣaṇāḥ | na tatrāsti doṣaḥ | tathātmāpi | skandhavyatirikta ātmāstīti brūvatastu doṣaḥ syāt | (u) yadyapi na skandhavyatirikta ātmetyucyate | tathāpīdaṃ duṣṭam | kasmāt | tīrthikā hi vadanti- ātmā nityaḥ | asminnadhvani kṛtakarmaṇāmante vipākavedanāt iti | evaṃ bruvataḥ pañcaskandhā eva nityāḥ syuḥ | ātmavādī manyate ātmā eka iti | tathā sati pañcaskandhā eka eva syuḥ | ityayaṃ doṣaḥ | ātmagrahaśca duṣṭaḥ | kasmāt | ātmabuddhau hi ātmīya [buddhi]rasti | ātmīye sati rāgadveṣādayaḥ sarve kleśāḥ samudbhavanti | ato jñāyata ātmabuddhiḥ kleśānāmutpattisthānamiti | yadyapīme na vadanti skandhavyatirikta ātmeti | [tathāpi] skandheṣu nimittagrahānna [teṣāṃ] śūnyatāyāmavacaranti | śūnya[tā]yāmanavacaraṇātkleśāḥ sambhavanti | kleśebhyaḥ karma sambhavati | karmato duḥkham | evaṃ jananamaraṇasantāno 'vicchinno bhavati | ima ātmakalpanayā kāyaśiraścakṣurhastapādasyaudārikaṃ vivekameva na labhante | kiṃ punaḥ skandhānāṃ vivekam | eka ātmā nitya ātmeti samādānāt | yo na vivecayati | ko 'vakrāmati śūnya[tāyā]m | ātmadarśīnirvāṇabhīta ātmā na bhaviṣyatīti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- pṛthagjanāḥ śūnyānātmatāṃ śrutvā mahābhītimutpādayanti ātmā na bhaviṣyati | ato nāsti kiñcidupalabhyamiti | evaṃ pṛthagjanā yāvatpāmopahataṃ kāyaṃ prārthayamānā na nirvāṇāya prayante | yaḥ śūnyatājñānapratilābhī sa punarnirbhīto bhavati | yathohopasenasūtram-
body.translated_text: (Question) What fault is there in designating the self in the five aggregates? Just as objects such as pots and the like, each having their own characteristics — there is no fault therein. Likewise with the self. If one were to say that the self exists apart from the aggregates — that would be a fault. (Answer) Even though one does not say the self exists apart from the aggregates, this is still defective. Why? The <s>tīrthikas</s> say: 'The self is permanent. In this course, at the end of <s>karmas</s> performed, there is the experience of ripening.' For one who speaks thus, the five aggregates themselves would be permanent. The proponent of self believes 'the self is one.' If so, the five aggregates would be one only. Thus there is this fault. And the grasping of self is defective. Why? In the notion of self (<s>ātmabuddhi</s>), there is the notion of 'mine' (<s>ātmīya</s>). When 'mine' exists, all defilements such as passion, hatred, and the rest arise. From this it is known that the notion of self is the basis for the arising of defilements. Even though they do not say 'the self exists apart from the aggregates,' because of grasping the sign in the aggregates, they do not practice emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>). Because of not practicing emptiness, defilements arise. From defilements, <s>karma</s> arises. From <s>karma</s>, suffering. Thus the continuity of birth and death becomes unbroken. Through this imagining of self, they do not even obtain the gross discrimination of body, head, eyes, hands, and feet — what more need be said of the discrimination of the aggregates! Because of accepting 'the self is one, the self is permanent.' One who does not discriminate — who would enter into emptiness? The seer of self, fearing <s>Nirvāṇa</s> [because] 'the self will not exist' — as stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Ordinary beings, hearing of emptiness and selflessness, generate great fear — [thinking] "The self will not exist! Therefore nothing is to be obtained."' Thus, ordinary beings, as far as desiring even this body afflicted by disease, do not strive for <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. One who has obtained the knowledge of emptiness becomes fearless. As in the <s>Upasena Sūtra</s>:

body.text:
brahmacaryaṃ sucaritaṃ mārgaścāpi subhāvitaḥ |
tuṣṭa āyuḥkṣaye bhoti rogasyāpagame yathā || iti |
body.translated_text:
The holy life has been well practiced, and the path has been well cultivated;
one is content at the exhaustion of life, just as at the departure of a disease.

body.text: ātmāstīti yo vadati sa mithyādṛṣṭau patati | yadyātmā nityaḥ tadā sukhaduḥkhayorvikāro na syāt | asati vikāre nāsti puṇyaṃ pāpaṃ vā | yadyanitya ātmā | tadā nāsti paralokaḥ | svabhāvato vimuktasyāpi nāsti puṇyaṃ pāpaṃ vā | ato jñāyate satkāyadṛṣṭirgurutaraṃ pāpamiti | kiñca satkāyadṛṣṭiko 'tyantamūḍhaḥ | pṛthagjanāḥ sarve satkāyadṛṣṭyā vikṣiptacittā bhavanti | atyāsaṅgāt saṃsāre yātāyātā bhavanti | yo nairātmyaṃ paśyati tasya yātāyātaṃ samucchidyate |
body.translated_text: One who says 'the self exists' falls into wrong view. If the self is permanent, then there would be no modification of pleasure and suffering. In the absence of modification, there is no merit or demerit. If the self is impermanent, then there is no next world. For one who is liberated by his own nature too, there is no merit or demerit. From this it is known that the view of the personal self (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>) is an extremely grave sin. Furthermore, the holder of <s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s> is utterly deluded. All ordinary beings have their minds scattered by <s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>. Because of excessive attachment, they become wanderers going to and fro in <s>saṃsāra</s>. One who sees selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>) — for him, the going to and fro is cut off.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi pañcaskandhā anātmakāḥ | kasmāt satvānāṃ tatrātmabuddhirbhavati | (u) martyo devaḥ pumān strī iti nāmanimittaṃ śṛṇvataḥ saṃjñāvikalpādātmabuddhirutpadyate | na tu hetunā | hetvabhāvenātmabuddhirutpadyate yaduta yadyātmā nāsti kaḥ sukhaṃ sukhaṃ vedayet, iryāpathavyavahāroddhitapuṇyapāpakarmaṇā vipākaṃ [ko] vedayeteti | anādau saṃsāre ca cirasañcitamātmanimittantu tadanuśayasādhanam | yathā ghaṭādinimittam | ata ātmabuddhirutpadyate | sarvavedanāskandheṣu ātmabuddhirutpadyate na tu vedanāyām | ata ucyata ātmamatiryatrotpadyate tatrātmāstīti | kasmāt | na hi sarvatrātmamatirbhavati | vyāmohādātmamatirutpadyate | tadyathā andha[kalpa]sya śakalādi labdhvā suvarṇamaṇisaṃjñā bhavati | kiñcāyaṃ śūnyatāvivekajñānālābhī mohātpaśyatyātmānam | tadyathā māyā[marīcī]gandharvanagarālātacakrādiṣu astīti matirbhavati |
body.translated_text: (Question) If the five aggregates are without self, why do beings have the notion of self therein? (Answer) Through hearing designative signs such as 'mortal,' 'god,' 'man,' 'woman' — from the conceptual discrimination of perception, the notion of self arises. But not through a [valid] reason. In the absence of a reason, the notion of self arises — namely: 'If the self does not exist, who would experience pleasure? Who would experience the ripening of <s>karma</s> from deportment, conduct, upholding, and merit and demerit?' And in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, the sign of self long accumulated — that is the establishment of its latent tendency. Just as the sign of a pot and the like. Therefore the notion of self arises. The notion of self arises in all the feeling-aggregates — not in feeling [alone]. Therefore it is said that the notion of self exists wherever it arises. Why? Because the notion of self does not exist everywhere. Through delusion, the notion of self arises. Just as a blind person, having obtained a piece of broken pottery and the like, generates the perception of gold and jewels. And further, this one who has not obtained the knowledge of the discrimination of emptiness, through delusion sees a self. Just as in illusions, mirages, <s>Gandharva</s>-cities, circles of firebrands, and the like — the notion 'this exists' arises.

body.text: (pṛ) paśyāmaḥ khalu pratyakṣaṃ rūpakāye keśanakharomādyavayavān pratyekaṃ vibhinnān | kaḥ sacetanastānātmānaṃ manyeta | (u) kecitpaśyanti ātmānaṃ yavasadṛśaṃ sarṣapādisamānaṃ hṛdayāntarvartinañca | brāhmaṇānāmātmā śuklaḥ | kṣatriyāṇāmātmā pītaḥ | vaiśyānāmātmā raktaḥ | śūdrāṇāmātmā kṛṣṇa iti | uktañca vede-
body.translated_text: (Question) We directly perceive that in the material body there are individual parts — hair, nails, body-hair, and the like — each distinct. What sentient being would consider them to be the self? (Answer) Some see the self as resembling a barley grain, equal to a mustard seed in size, dwelling within the heart. The self of <s>brāhmaṇas</s> is white; the self of <s>kṣatriyas</s> is yellow; the self of <s>vaiśyas</s> is red; the self of <s>śūdras</s> is black. And it is stated in the <s>Veda</s>:

body.text: purāsīnmahān puruṣa ādityavarṇaḥ tamasaḥ parastāt | tamevaṃ vidvānamṛta iha bhavati | nānyaḥ panthā vidyate ['yanāya] | aṇoraṇiyān mahato mahīyān ātmā guhāyāṃ nihito 'sya jantoḥ | tamakratuḥ paśyati [vītaśokaḥ] sūtraṃ maṇigaṇeṣviva |
body.translated_text: 'In the beginning there was a great <s>Puruṣa</s>, of the color of the sun, beyond darkness. Knowing him thus, one becomes immortal here — there is no other path to go.' 'Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the self (<s>ātman</s>) is hidden in the cave of this creature. One who is free from desire sees [him], the serene one, free from sorrow — like a thread among rows of jewels.'

body.text: evaṃ kecinmanyante rūpamātmeti | sthūlacetanā āhuḥ vedanātmeti | vṛkṣaśilādau vedanāyā abhāvāt jñeyaṃ vedanaivātmeti | madhyamacetanā āhuḥ saṃjñā ātmā, sukhaduḥkhayoratītayorapi [tat] saṃjñāvadātmeti buddhi[sattvā]t | sūkṣmacetanā āhuḥ saṃskāra ātmeti | ghaṭādāvatīte 'pi [tat] cetanāvānātmeti buddheḥ | paramasūkṣmacetanā āhu- vijñānamātmeti | cetanāpi audārikī | cetanāyāmasyāmatītāyāmapi [tat] vijñānavānātmeti buddheriti jānanti | [yasya] pañcasu skandheṣu ātmabuddhirbhavati | na sa vivecayati vedanādīn skandhān | rūpaṃ cittañca sammiśrya ātmasaṃjñā samutpadyate | yathā rūpādicaturdharmasāmānye ghaṭasaṃjñotpadyate | rūpādivibhāgena viṃśatibhāgaiḥ paśyati rūpamātmeti | kasmāt | rūpavānayamātmeti pratīto dharmo vedanādīnāmāśrayaḥ | vedanādaya ime rūpe pratibaddhā ityata ucyate rūpa[vān] ātmeti | kecidvedanādigataṃ rūpaṃ paśyanti | vedanādaya ime 'nupalabhyamānadharmā ityato rūpamāśrayante | yathā ākāśo 'nupalabhya ityataḥ pṛthivyādaya āśrīyante | eva [mātmadṛṣṭe] viṃśatibhāgā mohādbhavanti |
body.translated_text: Thus some think: 'Form is the self.' Those of gross understanding say: 'Feeling is the self.' Because there is no feeling in trees, stones, and the like — therefore it should be known that feeling alone is the self. Those of middling understanding say: 'Perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>) is the self' — because even when pleasure and suffering are past, there is still that perception-possessing self, from the existence of consciousness. Those of subtle understanding say: 'Formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) are the self' — because even when pots and the like are past, there is still that volition-possessing self, from the existence of consciousness. Those of supremely subtle understanding say: 'Consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is the self' — [because] even volition is gross; even when this volition has passed, there is still that consciousness-possessing self, from the existence of consciousness — so they understand. For one who has the conception of self with respect to the five aggregates, he does not discriminate the aggregates of feeling and the like. Mixing form and mind, the perception of self arises — just as from the general nature of the four <s>dharmas</s> beginning with form, the perception of a 'pot' arises. By dividing into form and the rest, one sees twenty aspects [of the self-view]: 'Form is the self.' Why? Because this self is one that has form — it is an established <s>dharma</s>, the substrate of feeling and the rest. These — feeling and the rest — are bound in form. Therefore it is said: 'The self has form.' Some see form as included in feeling and the like. These — feeling and the like — are imperceptible <s>dharmas</s>; therefore they take refuge in form. Just as space is imperceptible, and therefore earth and the other [elements] take refuge [in it]. Thus, from delusion, twenty aspects of the view of self arise.

body.text: (pṛ) cakṣurādiṣu kasmānnocyata ātmeti bhāgaḥ | (u) asti ca | yathoktaṃ sūtre- yadyāha kaścit yaccakṣurayamātmeti | tanna yujyate | kasmāt | cakṣurutpannavināśi | yadi cakṣurayamātmā | tadā ātmā utpannavināśī syāt | cakṣurādīni pṛthak pṛthagviśiṣṭalakṣaṇāni | yadyucyate cakṣurātmeti | śrotrādayo nātmā syuḥ | tattu na
body.translated_text: (Question) Why is it not said that the eye and the like [sense-bases] are also aspects [of the self-view]? (Answer) There are [such aspects]. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'If someone says "the eye is this self" — that is not valid. Why? The eye is subject to arising and perishing. If the eye were the self, then the self would be subject to arising and perishing.' The eyes and the like have individually distinct characteristics. If one says 'the eye is the self,' then hearing and the rest would not be the self. But that is not

body.text: yujyate | yadi śrotrādayaḥ punarā[tmā] | tadā eka eva pumān bahvātmā syāt | rūpādīnāṃ saviśeṣatvāt vaktuṃ śakyaṃ rūpamevā na vedanādaya iti |
body.translated_text: valid. If hearing and the rest were again the self, then a single person would have many selves. Because form and the rest have distinctive [characteristics], it is possible to say 'form alone [is the self], not feeling and the rest.'

body.text: (pṛ) nāstyātmeti yadvacanam | sāpi mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | kathamidam | (u) asti satyadvayam | paramārthato 'styātmeti yadvacanaṃ sā satkāyadṛṣṭiḥ | saṃvṛtito nāsti ātmeti vacanaṃ mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | lokasatyato 'styātmā paramārthato nāstyātmeti vacanaṃ samyak dṛṣṭiḥ | paramārthato nāsti saṃvṛtito 'stīti vadan na dṛṣṭau patati | evamasti nāstīti vacanaṃ jñeyam | yathā vyāghrī svapotaṃ mukhenāpaharati atiniṣṭhuragrahaṇe kṣataṃ [bhavediti] atiśithilagrahaṇe bhraṃśo [bhavediti] | evamāstitvaṃ pratipannaścetsatkāyadṛṣṭau patati | ātmanāstitvaṃ pratipannaścenmithyādṛṣṭau patati | kṛtahānamakṛtābhyāgama ubhayaṃ duṣṭam | nāstīti pratipannasya [kṛta]hānam | ātmāstīti pratipannasyā [kṛtā]bhyāgamaḥ | ataḥ sūtra uktaṃ- dvāvantau parihāryāviti | paramārthato nāstīti vadan saṃvṛtito 'stīti ca vadan antadvayaṃ parityajya madhyamāyāṃ pratipadi caratītyākhyāyate | buddhaśāsanamavivādamanutkarṣaṇam | paramārthato nāstītyuktau paṇḍito notkarṣati | saṃvṛtito 'stītyuktau pāmaro na vivadate | tathāgataśāsane 'śāśvatānucchedā pariśuddhā madhyamā pratipat | paramārthato nāstitayā na śāśvataḥ | saṃvṛtitostitayā nocchedaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) The statement 'There is no self' — that too is wrong view. How is this? (Answer) There are two truths. The statement 'the self exists ultimately (<s>paramārthataḥ</s>)' — that is the view of the personal aggregate (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>). The statement 'there is no self conventionally (<s>saṃvṛtitaḥ</s>)' is wrong view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>). The statement 'the self exists according to worldly truth (<s>lokasatya</s>) but does not exist ultimately (<s>paramārthataḥ</s>)' is right view (<s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s>). One who speaks saying 'it does not exist ultimately but exists conventionally' does not fall into [wrong] view. Thus the statements 'it exists' and 'it does not exist' should be understood. Just as a tigress carries her cub in her mouth — if the grip is too firm, it would be injured; if too loose, it would fall. So too, if one adopts 'it exists,' one falls into the view of the personal aggregate (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>). If one adopts 'the self does not exist,' one falls into wrong view. 'What has been done is lost, and what has not been done does not arrive' — both are faulty. For one who adopts 'it does not exist,' what has been done is lost. For one who adopts 'the self exists,' what has not been done arrives. Therefore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Both of these extremes are to be avoided.' Speaking 'it does not exist ultimately' and 'it exists conventionally,' one abandons both extremes and is said to walk in the middle path. The teaching of the <s>Buddha</s> is non-contentious and non-disparaging. When one says 'it does not exist ultimately,' the wise person does not disparage. When one says 'it exists conventionally,' the ignorant person does not contend. In the teaching of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the purified middle path is neither eternalist nor annihilationist. Through not existing ultimately, it is not eternalist. Through existing conventionally, it is not annihilationist.

body.text: (pṛ) yo dharmaḥ paramārthato nāsti sa sutarāṃ nāstīti syāt | kena punarucyate saṃvṛtito 'stīti | (u) sarvairlaukikairvyavahriyate astīti yaduta karma karmavipāko yadi vā bandho yadi vā mokṣa iti | ime sarve mohajāḥ | kasmāt | ime pañcaskandhāḥ śūnyā māyopamāḥ jvālāvacca santānenotpannatvāt | pṛthagjanānāṃ titīrṣayā astītivacanamanuvartate | yadi nāstīti vadet | tadā pṛthagjanā vyāmuhya yadi vā ucchedavāde pateyuḥ yadi vā skandhānāṃ nāstītākathane avineyāḥ syuḥ | puṇyapāpādikarmabhirbandho vā mokṣo vā na sidhyet | yastaṃ mohavādaṃ vināśayati | saḥ svayameva śūnyatāyāmavatarati | tadāsya sarvā mithyādṛṣṭayo na bhavanti | ataḥ paramārthasatyaṃ paścāducyate | yathā strīpuṃnimittavyāvṛttaye kāyapratyavekṣaṇamādāvupadiśyate | atha keśaromanakhādibhiḥ kāyavikalpalakṣaṇa[mupadiśyate] pañcaskandhamātramastīti | atha śūnyatālakṣaṇena pañcaskandhanirodhalakṣaṇa[mupadiśyate] | pañcaskandhanirodhalakṣaṇaṃ paramārthasatyamityucyate | saṃvṛtyāstīti kathane na tadā punaḥ paramārthato
body.translated_text: (Question) A <s>dharma</s> that does not exist ultimately would all the more not exist — why then is it said 'it exists conventionally'? (Answer) All worldly people engage in the convention 'it exists' — namely <s>karma</s>, the ripening of <s>karma</s>, bondage, or liberation. All of these arise from delusion. Why? These five aggregates are empty, illusion-like, and arise in continuity like a flame. For ordinary beings, following their desire [to cross over], the statement 'it exists' is maintained. If one were to say 'it does not exist,' then ordinary beings, being confused, would either fall into the annihilationist view, or through the declaration that the aggregates do not exist, they would become unteachable. Through <s>karmas</s> of merit, sin, and the like, neither bondage nor liberation would be established. One who destroys that deluded view — he himself enters into emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>). At that time, all his wrong views do not exist. Therefore, the ultimate truth (<s>paramārthasatya</s>) is stated afterward. Just as, to avert the signs of female and male, the contemplation of the body (<s>kāyapratyavekṣaṇa</s>) is first taught. Then, through hair, body-hair, nails, and the like, the analytical characteristic of the body is taught — 'there are merely the five aggregates.' Then, through the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of the cessation of the five aggregates is taught. The characteristic of the cessation of the five aggregates is called 'the ultimate truth.' In the conventional statement 'it exists,' at that time one does not yet require the statement 'it does not exist ultimately.'

body.text: nāstīti vacanamapekṣyate | uktañca sūtre- yaḥ sarvadharmān niḥsvabhāvān prajānāti sa śūnyatāyāmavatarati | iti | ato jñāyate pañca skandhā api na santīti | uktañca paramārthaśūnyatāsūtre- cakṣurādi paramārthato nasti | asti tu saṃvṛtita iti | mahāśūnyatāsūtra uktam- yadidaṃ jarāmaraṇamiti vacanaṃ yadi vāyaṃ puruṣo jarāmaraṇa[-lakṣaṇa] iti vacanaṃ | yadi vā tīrthikānāṃ vacanaṃ kāya eva jīvaḥ, yadivānyaḥ kāyo 'nyo jīva itīdamekārthakaṃ, vyañjanameva nānā | kāya eva jīvaḥ anyaḥ kāyo 'nyo jīva itīdaṃ vacane na brahmacaryaṃ bhavati | yaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ ayaṃ puruṣo jarāmaraṇa[lakṣaṇa] iti nairātmyasyābhidhānam | yaḥ pratiṣedha idaṃ jarāmaraṇamiti tat jarāmaraṇasya vyāvartanam | yāvadavidyāyāḥ iti | ato jñāyate paramārthato na jarāmaraṇādi | saṃvṛtyā tūcyate jātipratyayaṃ jarāmaraṇam | iyamucyate madhyamā pratipat | kiñcoktaṃ rādhasūtre- rūpaṃ rādha yūyaṃ vikirata vidhamata vidhvaṃsata vikrīḍanakaṃ kuruta [tṛṣṇā]kṣayāya [pratipadyata] tadyathā pāṃsvāgārikāḥ | avastutvāt kṣayāya bhāvyā iti | skandhā api kṣayāya [bhāvyāḥ] | paramārthato 'bhāvāt skandhavṛttilakṣaṇavṛttimanusarato nātmamatiratyantaṃ prahīyate | hetupratyayānāmanirodhāt | yathā vṛkṣaḥ paraśunā chinno bhasmasātkṛtaḥ | tathāpi [tatra] vṛkṣasaṃjñāmanuvartate | yadā tu mahāvāte opūyate jalena vā pravāhitaḥ tadā vṛkṣasaṃjñā nirudhyate | evaṃ yadā vidhvaṃsitāni vikrīḍanakaṃ kṛtāni vikīrṇāni vidhmātāni niruddhāni pañcaskandhalakṣaṇāni, tasmin samaye śūnyatālakṣaṇaṃ sampannaṃ bhavati | yathāha sūtram- rādha yūyaṃ [rūpaṃ] vidhvaṃsata vikrīḍanakaṃ kuruta vikirata vidhamata bhāgaśo vidalayata sattvakṣayāya iti | asmin sūtra uktam- pañcaskandhā anityāḥ sattvaśūnyāḥ na santīti | pūrvasmin sūtra uktam- pañcaskandhā vikīrṇā niruddhāḥ te dharmaśūnyā bhavanti iti ||
body.translated_text: And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'One who understands all <s>dharmas</s> as without own-nature (<s>niḥsvabhāva</s>) enters into emptiness.' Therefore it is known that even the five aggregates do not exist. And it is stated in the <s>Paramārthaśūnyatā Sūtra</s>: 'The eye and the rest do not exist ultimately; but they exist conventionally.' The <s>Mahāśūnyatā Sūtra</s> states: 'The statement "this is old age and death" and the statement "this person has the characteristic of old age and death" — or the statement of the non-Buddhists (<s>tīrthika</s>) "the body is identical with the life-force (<s>jīva</s>)" or "the body is different from the life-force" — these have one and the same meaning, only the words are different. [Whether] "the body is identical with the life-force" [or] "the body is different from the life-force" — in [either of] these statements, the holy life does not exist. The negation "this person has the characteristic of old age and death" is the designation of non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>). The negation "this is old age and death" is the removal of old age and death [as ultimately real]. Up to: the same with ignorance.' Therefore it is known that old age, death, and the rest do not exist ultimately. But conventionally it is said: 'Old age and death are conditioned by birth.' This is called the middle path. Furthermore, it is stated in the <s>Rādha Sūtra</s>: '<s>Rādha</s>, you — scatter form, destroy it, demolish it, make it a plaything, practice for the exhaustion of craving — just as children [play] with sand houses.' Because it has no substance, it is to be contemplated for the purpose of exhaustion. The aggregates too are to be contemplated for the purpose of exhaustion. Because they do not exist ultimately, one who follows the characteristic of the continuity of the aggregates — his conception of self is not completely abandoned. Because causes and conditions have not ceased. Just as a tree, though cut by an axe and reduced to ashes — even so, the perception of 'tree' continues. But when it is blown away by a great wind, or washed away by water — at that time the perception of 'tree' ceases. In the same way, when the characteristics of the five aggregates have been demolished, made into a plaything, scattered, blown away, destroyed, and brought to cessation — at that time the characteristic of emptiness is accomplished. As the <s>sūtra</s> says: '<s>Rādha</s>, you — demolish [form], make it a plaything, scatter it, blow it away, break it apart piece by piece for the exhaustion of beings.' In this <s>sūtra</s> it is stated: 'The five aggregates are impermanent, empty of beings, and do not exist.' In the previous <s>sūtra</s> it is stated: 'The five aggregates, having been scattered and brought to cessation, are empty of <s>dharmas</s>.'

body.text: satkāyadṛṣṭivargastrīṃśatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, the Chapter on the View of the Personal Aggregate (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭivarga</s>).

body.text: 131 anta[graha]dṛṣṭivargaḥ
body.translated_text: 131. Chapter on the View of Grasping at Extremes (<s>antagrāhadṛṣṭivarga</s>)

body.text: dharmāḥ samucchidyante vā śāśvatā vā iti yadidaṃ vacanaṃ tadanta[graha]dṛṣṭirityucyate | kecidābhidharmikā āhuḥ- yadā kaścidāha ātmā śāśvato vā aśāśvato veti iyamevāntagrahadṛṣṭiḥ na sarve dharmāḥ[śāśvatā vā aśāśvatā vā] iti | kasmāt | dṛṣṭaṃ khalu pratyakṣaṃ [yat] bāhyaṃ vastu samucchidyata iti | uktañca sūtre- astīti darśanaṃ śāśvatagrahaḥ | nāstīti darśanamucchedagraha iti | kāya eva jīva ityucchedadṛṣṭiḥ | anyaḥ kāyo 'nyo jīva iti śāśvatadṛṣṭiḥ | nāsti karma paraṃ maraṇāditi ucchedadṛṣṭiḥ | asti karma paraṃ maraṇāditi śāśvatadṛṣṭiḥ | asti ca nāsti ca karma paraṃ maraṇādityatra yadastīti sa śāśvata[vādaḥ] yannāstīti sa ucchedavādaḥ | naivāsti na ca nāstītyapyevam |
body.translated_text: The statement that '<s>dharmas</s> are annihilated' or 'they are eternal' — this is called the view of grasping at extremes (<s>antagrāhadṛṣṭi</s>). Certain <s>Ābhidharmikas</s> say: 'When someone says "the self is eternal" or "the self is non-eternal" — this alone is the view of grasping at extremes, not [the view that] all <s>dharmas</s> are eternal or non-eternal.' Why? Because we directly see that external things are annihilated. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The view "it exists" is the grasping of eternalism. The view "it does not exist" is the grasping of annihilationism.' 'The body is identical with the life-force' is the annihilationist view. 'The body is different from the life-force' is the eternalist view. 'There is no <s>karma</s> beyond death' is the annihilationist view. 'There is <s>karma</s> beyond death' is the eternalist view. 'There is and there is not <s>karma</s> beyond death' — therein, what says 'there is' is eternalism; what says 'there is not' is annihilationism. 'Neither is there nor is there not' — this too is the same.

body.text: (pṛ) ayaṃ caturtho graho na dṛṣṭiḥ syāt | (u) lokasatyato 'pi pudgalarahitatvāddharmāṇāṃ dṛṣṭirityucyate | śāśvato 'śāśvataḥ antavānanantavānityādi catuṣkoṭikamapyevam | uktañca sūtre- ṣaṭ sparśāyatanāni nirudhyante santyanyānīti śāśvatavādaḥ | na santyanyānīti uccheda[vāda] iti | ātmā pūrvamakarot paścātkariṣyatīti yaddarśanaṃ sā śāśvatadṛṣṭiḥ ātmā pūrvaṃ nākarot paścānna kariṣyatītīyamucchedadṛṣṭiḥ | api cāha mithyādṛṣṭisūtram- puruṣasya saptakāyāḥ pṛthivyaptejovāyavaḥ sukhaṃduḥkhaṃ jīvitamiti | mriyamāṇasya catvāri mahābhūtāni tammūlapratiśaraṇānīndriyāṇyākāśapratiśaraṇāni iti | kiñcāha- kṣureṇa ca krakacena prāṇino hatvā [eka]māṃsapuṃñca kuryāt nāsti [tato nidānaṃ]pāpaṃ [nāsti pāpasyāgama] iti | iyamucchedadṛṣṭiḥ | brahmajālasūtra ucchedadṛṣṭilakṣaṇamuktam | asti paralokaḥ yaḥ kārakaḥ sa eva vedaka iti yadvacanam | iyaṃ śāśvatadṛṣṭirityucyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) This fourth grasping would not be a view. (Answer) Because <s>dharmas</s> are devoid of a person even according to worldly truth, it is called 'a view.' 'Eternal, non-eternal; finite, infinite' and the like — the fourfold proposition (<s>catuṣkoṭika</s>) too is the same. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: '"The six sense-bases of contact (<s>sparśāyatana</s>) cease — are there others [beyond]?" is eternalism. "There are no others" is annihilationism.' 'The self previously acted and will act in the future' — that view is the eternalist view. 'The self did not previously act and will not act in the future' — this is the annihilationist view. Furthermore, the <s>Mithyādṛṣṭi Sūtra</s> says: 'A person has seven bodies: earth, water, fire, wind, pleasure, suffering, and life-force.' 'When one who is dying — the four great elements return to their fundamental resting-places, and the sense-faculties return to space as their resting-place.' Furthermore it says: 'With a razor and a saw, having killed living beings, one should make a single heap of flesh — there is no sin from that cause, and no arrival of sin.' This is the annihilationist view. In the <s>Brahmajāla Sūtra</s>, the characteristic of the annihilationist view is stated. 'There is another world; the doer is the experiencer' — this statement is called the eternalist view.

body.text: (pṛ) śāśvatocchedadṛṣṭiḥ kathamutpadyate | (u) yena hetunā bhavati tathāgataḥ paraṃ maraṇāditi vadanti tato nidānaṃ śāśvatadṛṣṭirbhavati | yena hetunā na bhavati tathāgataḥ paraṃ maraṇāditi vadanti tato nidānamucchedadṛṣṭirbhavati | (pṛ) kathamiyaṃ dṛṣṭiḥ prahīyate | (u) śūnyatāṃ samyagbhāvayato nāstyātmadṛṣṭiḥ | asatyāmātmadṛṣṭau nāstyantadvayam | yathoktaṃ yamakasūtre- nāstyaikakasmin skandhe tathāgataḥ | nāsti samudite skandhe tathāgataḥ | nāsti cānyatra skandhāttathāgataḥ | evaṃ dṛṣṭa eva dharme [tathāgato] 'nupalabhyamānaḥ | kathaṃ vaktavyaṃ [yathā] kṣīṇāsravo 'rhan kāyasya bhedā [ducchetsyati vinaṃkṣyati] na bhavati paraṃ maraṇāditi | ato jñāyate nopalabhyate pudgala iti | pudgalasyānupalambhādātmadṛṣṭiḥ śāśvatocchedadṛṣṭiśca nāsti | dharmāḥ pratityasamutpannā iti paśyato nāstyantadvayam | yathā punaruktam- lokasamudayaṃ paśyato 'bhāvadṛṣṭirnirudhyate | lokanirodhaṃ paśyato bhāvadṛṣṭirnirudhyata iti | madhyamāyāṃ pratipadi viharataścāntadvayaṃ nirudhyate | kasmāt | dharmāṇāṃ santatyotpādaṃ paśyata ucchedadṛṣṭi rnirudhyate | [teṣāṃ] kṣaṇikatāṃ paśyataḥ śāśvatadṛṣṭirnirudhyate | kiñcoktam- na pañcaskandhāstathāgataḥ | na cāsti anyatra skandhāttathāgata iti | ato jñāyate nocchedo na śāśvata iti | kāyādanya upalabhyata ityato naikaḥ kāyena bhavati | sahāyaṃ sattva ityato nānyo bhavati | pañcaskandhāḥ punaḥ santanyanta ityataḥ sattvo jāyate mriyata iti vaktameva na prabhavati | santānena pravṛttatvādanya iti na vaktuṃ śakyate | santānasyaikatvenābhidhānāt |
body.translated_text: (Question) How do the views of eternalism and annihilationism (<s>śāśvatocchedadṛṣṭi</s>) arise? (Answer) Through whatever reason they say 'The <s>Tathāgata</s> exists after death' — from that arises the eternalist view (<s>śāśvatadṛṣṭi</s>). Through whatever reason they say 'The <s>Tathāgata</s> does not exist after death' — from that arises the annihilationist view (<s>ucchedadṛṣṭi</s>). (Question) How is this view abandoned? (Answer) For one who correctly cultivates emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), there is no view of self (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>). In the absence of the view of self, there are not the two extremes (<s>antadvaya</s>). As stated in the <s>Yamaka Sūtra</s>: 'The <s>Tathāgata</s> is not in any single aggregate. The <s>Tathāgata</s> is not in the combination of aggregates. Nor is the <s>Tathāgata</s> other than the aggregates. Thus, the <s>Tathāgata</s> is unobtainable even in the present <s>dharma</s>. How then can it be said that the <s>Arhat</s> whose outflows are exhausted, at the breaking up of the body, will be annihilated, will perish, and will not exist after death?' From this it is known that the person (<s>pudgala</s>) is unobtainable. Because the person is unobtainable, neither the view of self nor the views of eternalism and annihilationism exist. For one who sees that <s>dharmas</s> are dependently arisen (<s>pratītyasamutpanna</s>), there are not the two extremes. As it has been further stated: 'For one who sees the origination of the world, the view of non-existence (<s>abhāvadṛṣṭi</s>) ceases. For one who sees the cessation of the world, the view of existence (<s>bhāvadṛṣṭi</s>) ceases.' And for one who abides in the middle path (<s>madhyamā pratipad</s>), the two extremes cease. Why? For one who sees the arising in continuity (<s>santatyutpāda</s>) of <s>dharmas</s>, the annihilationist view ceases. For one who sees their momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatā</s>), the eternalist view ceases. Furthermore it is stated: 'The five aggregates are not the <s>Tathāgata</s>. Nor is the <s>Tathāgata</s> other than the aggregates.' From this it is known: neither annihilation nor eternality. Because something other than the body is perceived, it is not one with the body. Because the being exists together [with it], it is not other. Because the five aggregates continue in continuity — therefore it is not possible to say 'the being is born and dies.' Because it operates through continuity, it cannot be said to be 'other.' Because [successive] continuities are designated as one.

body.text: ime skandhāste skandhāścānya ityabhidhānāt śāśvatavādo na bhavati | svasantānapratyayabalena pravartata ityata ucchedavādo na bhavati |
body.translated_text: Because it is said that 'these aggregates are different from those aggregates,' the eternalist doctrine does not hold. Because [the continuum] operates through the power of the conditions of one's own continuum (<s>svasantāna</s>), the annihilationist doctrine does not hold.

body.text: antagrahadṛṣṭivarga ekatriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, the Chapter on the View of Grasping Extremes (<s>antagrahadṛṣṭivarga</s>).

body.text: 132 mithyādṛṣṭivargaḥ
body.translated_text: 132. Chapter on Wrong View (<s>mithyādṛṣṭivarga</s>)

body.text: vastutaḥ satsu dharmeṣu nāstīti cittotpādanaṃ mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | yathā vadanti na santi catussatyāni trīṇi ratnānītyādi | ūktañcasūtre- katamā bhikṣavo mithyādṛṣṭiḥ, nāsti dattaṃ nāstīṣṭaṃ, nāsti hutaṃ, nāstisukṛtaduṣkṛtānāṃ phalaṃ vipākaḥ | nāstyayaṃ lokaḥ nāsti paro lokaḥ, nāsti mātā nāsti pitā, na santi sattvā aupapātikāḥ, na santi śramaṇabrāhmaṇāḥ samyaggatāḥ samyak pratipannā ya imaṃ lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ svayamabhijñāya sākṣātkṛtya pravedayanti- kṣīṇā me jātiruṣitaṃ brahmacaryaṃ kṛtaṃ karaṇīyaṃ nāparamitthatvāya iti | dattaṃ [yat] parahitāya prayacchati | iṣṭhaṃ iti vedokto devānāṃ kṛte yāgaḥ | hutamiti devebhyo ghṛtādidravyahomaḥ | sukṛtamiti trayāṇāṃ sukṛtakarmaṇāmiṣṭaphalapratilābhaḥ | duṣkṛtamiti trayāṇāṃ duṣkṛtakarmaṇāmaniṣṭaphalapratilābhaḥ | sukṛtaduṣkṛtakarmaṇāṃ [phalaṃ] vipākaḥ ihalokaśubhāśubhakīrtyādiḥ devakāyādayaḥ pāralauke vipākaśca | ayaṃ loka iti vartamānaḥ | paraloka iti anāgataḥ | mātā pitā janakau | sattva aupapātika iti asmāllokātparalokagantā | arhanniti kṣīṇāsravaḥ | yadidaṃ sarvaṃ nāstīti sā mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | sattvānāṃ saṃkleśo vyavadānaṃ jñānadarśanamajñānadarśanam- idaṃ sarvamahetukam | nāsti balaṃ nāsti vīryam | nāsti ca teṣāṃ phalamityādi mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | saṃkṣipyedaṃ brūmaḥ- yadviparyayacittaṃ sarvaṃ tanmithyādṛṣṭiḥ iti | tadyathā anitye nityasaṃjñā, duḥkhe sukhasaṃjñā, aśucau śucisaṃjñā, anātmani
body.translated_text: The generation of the thought 'it does not exist' regarding <s>dharmas</s> that exist in reality is wrong view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>). Such as saying: 'The four noble truths do not exist, the Three Jewels do not exist,' and so forth. And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'What, monks, is wrong view? [Thinking:] "There is no gift given, no offering, no sacrifice, no fruit or ripening of well-done or ill-done actions, no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously born beings, no ascetics or <s>brāhmaṇas</s> who, having rightly gone, rightly practiced, realize this world and the other world through their own superknowledge, and declare: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'"' 'Gift' (<s>datta</s>) is what one gives for the benefit of others. 'Offering' (<s>iṣṭa</s>) is the Vedic sacrifice performed for the sake of the gods. 'Sacrifice' (<s>huta</s>) is the offering of ghee and other substances into fire for the gods. 'Well-done' (<s>sukṛta</s>) is the obtaining of desired fruit through the three kinds of well-done <s>karma</s>. 'Ill-done' (<s>duṣkṛta</s>) is the obtaining of undesired fruit through the three kinds of ill-done <s>karma</s>. 'Fruit and ripening of well-done and ill-done actions' is [results such as] good and bad reputation and the like in this world, and rebirth in divine bodies and the like in the next world. 'This world' is the present. 'The other world' is the future. 'Mother and father' are the parents. 'Spontaneously born beings' (<s>aupapātika</s>) are those who go from this world to the other world. '<s>Arhat</s>' is one whose outflows are exhausted. That all of this 'does not exist' — that is wrong view. 'The defilement and purification of beings, knowledge and vision and non-knowledge and non-vision — all of this is without cause. There is no power, there is no effort, and there is no fruit of those' — and so forth is wrong view. In brief we say: Whatever perverted mind — all of that is wrong view. Such as the perception of permanence in the impermanent, the perception of pleasure in suffering, the perception of purity in the impure,

body.text: ātmasaṃjñā anutkṛṣṭa utkṛṣṭasaṃjñā, utkṛṣṭe cānutkṛṣṭasaṃjñā, vyavadānamārge avyavadānamārgasaṃjñā, avyavadānamārge ca vyavadānamārgasaṃjñā, abhāve bhāvasaṃjñā, bhāve cābhāvasaṃjñā ityevamādīni viparyayacittāni | abhidharme yāḥ pañcadṛṣṭayaḥ brahmajālasūtre ca dvāṣaṣṭidṛṣṭayaḥ sarvā[stā] mithyādṛṣṭayo bhavati |
body.translated_text: the perception of self in what is without self, the perception of superiority in what is not superior, the perception of non-superiority in what is superior, the perception of a path of purification in what is not a path of purification, the perception of a non-purifying path in what is a path of purification, the perception of existence in non-existence, the perception of non-existence in existence — such perverted minds. In the <s>Abhidharma</s>, the five [wrong] views, and in the <s>Brahmajāla Sūtra</s> the sixty-two views — all of those are wrong views.

body.text: mithyādṛṣṭiḥ kathamamutpadyate | (u) mohādutpadyate | ahetau hetvābhāse cāsaṃkliṣṭāsaktatvādbhavati | sukhahetāvāsaṅgādvadati nāsti duḥkhamiti | bhraṣṭaśūnyatāmārgatvādvadanti nāsti duḥkhamiti | na hi duḥkhavedako 'stīti | laukikāḥ padārthā ahetukā apratyayā iti yadvadanti | yadi vā vadanti īśvarādihetukā na tṛṣṇāhetukā iti | idaṃ nāsti samudaya iti | yena hetunā vadanti nāsti nirvāṇamiti | anyathā vā vadanti nirvāṇam | idaṃ nāsti nirvāṇamiti | asati nirvāṇamārge kena prāpyeta | atha vā vadanti asti vimuktermārgāntaramupavāsādiriti | idaṃ nāsti mārga iti | nāsti buddha iti | te vadanti dharmā apramāṇāḥ | kathamekaḥ puruṣaḥ sarvān jānīyāt iti | atha vā manyante buddhaḥ puruṣāṇāṃ pūjyo nāsti puruṣa ityato nāsti [sa] buddha iti draṣṭavyam | kleśānāṃ kṣayābhāvānnāsti dharmaḥ | samyakcaryayā taddharmapratilābhino na santītyato nāsti saṅghaḥ | dattasya dṛṣṭaphalānupalambhādvadanti nāsti dattamiti | uktañca sūtre- nāsti dattam | tadanumānamapyanaikāntikam | loke kaściddānābhirato daridro bhavati | kṛpaṇastu dhanika ityādibhiḥ nāsti kāraṇairvadanti dattamiti | nāstīṣṭaṃ nāsti hutamityapyevam | yadyagnau prakṣiptaṃ dravyaṃ bhasmasādbhavati | tasya kiṃ phalamasti | nāsti sukṛtaṃ duṣkṛtaṃ, nāsti ca sukṛtaduṣkṛtānāṃ [phalaṃ] vipākaḥ | yadi jīvo nityaḥ tadā nāsti sukṛtaṃ duṣkṛtam | yadi jīvo 'nityaḥ tadā nāsti paralokaḥ | nāsti paro loka ityato nāsti sukṛtaṃ duṣkṛtaṃ, nāsti sukṛtaduṣkṛtānāṃ vipākaḥ, nāstyayaṃ loka iti | avayavaśaḥ pravibhajyamānā dharmā atyantābhāvatāṃ pratigacchanti | nāsti paro loka iti | maraṇātparaṃ na bhavati pratītyasamutpāda ityato vadanti nāsti paro loka iti | nāsti mātā pitā | te 'pyavayavaśaḥ pravibhajyamānāḥ prakṣīyante | vadanti ca gomayamupādāya krimayo bhavanti | na hi gomayaṃ krimīṇāṃ pitarau | ye mastakādayaḥ śarīrāvayavāḥ, na ta eva matāpitroḥ śarīrāvayavāḥ | dharmāṇāṃ kṣaṇikatvāt mātā pitā ca kiṃ karoti | na sattvā aupapātikā iti | sattvadharmābhāvādayaṃ loka eva nāsti | kiṃ puna[stadūrdhva]kāyaṃ vedayata iti |
body.translated_text: How does wrong view arise? (Answer) It arises from delusion (<s>moha</s>). And it arises because of non-attachment to and non-defilement by what is not a cause but has the appearance of a cause (<s>ahetau hetvābhāsa</s>). Through attachment to the cause of pleasure, one says 'suffering does not exist.' Having fallen from the path of emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), they say 'suffering does not exist' — for 'there is no one who experiences suffering.' Worldly people say that things are 'without cause and without condition.' Or else they say 'they have <s>Īśvara</s> and the like as their cause, not craving as their cause.' This is [the denial that] 'origination does not exist.' Through whatever reason they say '<s>Nirvāṇa</s> does not exist,' or state <s>Nirvāṇa</s> differently — this is [the denial that] '<s>Nirvāṇa</s> does not exist.' When <s>Nirvāṇa</s> does not exist, by what path would it be attained? Or they say 'there exists another path to liberation, such as fasting and the like' — this is [the denial that] 'the path does not exist.' 'The <s>Buddha</s> does not exist' — they say: '<s>Dharmas</s> are immeasurable. How could a single person know all of them?' Or they think: 'The <s>Buddha</s> is honored among persons. There is no person — therefore there is no <s>Buddha</s>.' Because of the non-exhaustion of defilements, 'the <s>Dharma</s> does not exist.' Because those who through right practice obtain that <s>dharma</s> do not exist, 'the <s>Saṅgha</s> does not exist.' Because no visible fruit of giving is perceived, they say: 'Gift-giving does not exist.' And it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Gift-giving does not exist.' And even the inference thereof is inconclusive. In the world, someone devoted to giving becomes poor, while a miser becomes wealthy — through such reasons they say 'gift-giving does not exist.' 'Offering does not exist, sacrifice does not exist' — this is likewise. If the substance cast into fire becomes ash, what fruit could it have? 'Well-done and ill-done do not exist, and there is no fruit or ripening of well-done and ill-done actions.' If the self (<s>jīva</s>) is permanent, then there is no well-done and ill-done. If the self is impermanent, then there is no other world. Because there is no other world, there is no well-done and ill-done, no fruit or ripening of well-done and ill-done actions, and no this world. When things are analyzed part by part, they reach utter non-existence. 'The other world does not exist' — after death, dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>) does not occur — therefore they say 'the other world does not exist.' 'Mother and father do not exist' — they too, when analyzed part by part, are exhausted. And they say: 'From cow dung, worms come into being. Surely cow dung is not the parents of worms. The parts of the head and the rest of the body are not the very same parts of the body of the mother and father. Because <s>dharmas</s> are momentary, what do mother and father do?' 'Spontaneously born beings do not exist' — because of the non-existence of a being-<s>dharma</s>, this very world does not exist. How much more would one experience something beyond the body?

body.text: cetanākhyaḥ sattvo 'yaṃ kiṃ kāyātmakaḥ kimakāyātmakaḥ | yadi kāyātmakaḥ | tadā cakṣuṣā paridṛśyamāno 'yaṃ kāyaḥ khanyamāno mṛdbhavati | hūyamāno bhasma bhavati | krimibhuktaḥ purīṣaṃ bhavati | ato nāstyaupapātikaḥ | akāyātmaka ityayaṃ dvividho yadi cittātmako yadi vā cittavyatirikta iti | yadi cittātmakaḥ, tadā caittadharmaḥ | caittadharmaśca pratikṣaṇamutpattivināśī, na sthāyī | kimuta paradehaṃ prāpnuyāt | yadi cittavyatiriktaḥ tadā nātmamatiḥ | parasya citta eva nātmamatiḥ, kimutācittasthāne | ato nāstyaupapātikaḥ |
body.translated_text: This being, called 'consciousness' (<s>cetanā</s>) — is it corporeal (<s>kāyātmaka</s>) or incorporeal (<s>akāyātmaka</s>)? If corporeal, then this body, seen with the eye, when dug up becomes earth, when burned becomes ash, and when eaten by worms becomes excrement. Therefore there is no spontaneously born being. If incorporeal, this is twofold: either of the nature of mind (<s>cittātmaka</s>) or distinct from mind (<s>cittavyatirikta</s>). If of the nature of mind, then it is a mental <s>dharma</s>. And a mental <s>dharma</s> arises and perishes every moment — it does not endure. How could it reach another body? If distinct from mind, then there is no notion of self. Even in another's mind there is no notion of self — how much more so in a mindless state? Therefore there is no spontaneously born being.

body.text: nāstyarhanniti | sa kṣudhitaḥ sarvān dṛṣṭvā annaṃ prārthayate | śīte satyauṣṇyaṃ prārthayate | tāpe śītaṃ prārthayate | ninditaḥ kupyati | satkṛtastṛpyati | ato nāsti kṣīṇāsravaḥ | sūtre kecidvadanti- nāstyarhanniti | idaṃ sūtramanusṛtya sā mithyādṛṣṭirbhavati | saṃkleśa iti | kāya eva saṃkleśaḥ | ato vadantyakāraṇamiti | jñānadarśanamajñānadarśanamapyevam | nāsti balaṃ nāsti vīryamiti | paśyāmaḥ khalu sarve sattvāḥ prajñaptikāraṇakā iti | kecidvadanti īśvaraḥ [svātantryeṇa] karaṇīyaṃ karotīti | paśyāmaśca sarvān sattvān karmakāraṇatantrān na svatantrān | ato vadanti nāsti balaṃ nāsti vīryaṃ [nāsti] ca tatphalamiti |
body.translated_text: 'The <s>Arhat</s> does not exist' — he, when hungry, sees all [food] and begs for food. When it is cold, he seeks warmth. In heat, he seeks coolness. When blamed, he becomes angry. When honored, he is satisfied. Therefore, there is no one whose outflows are exhausted. Some say in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The <s>Arhat</s> does not exist.' Following this <s>sūtra</s>, that wrong view arises. 'Defilement' — the body itself is defilement. Therefore they say 'it is without cause.' Knowledge and vision, and non-knowledge and non-vision — this is likewise. 'There is no power, there is no effort' — we see indeed that all beings have designation as their cause. Some say: '<s>Īśvara</s>, through his own sovereignty, does what is to be done.' And we see that all beings are governed by the chain of <s>karma</s>, not self-governed. Therefore they say: 'There is no power, there is no effort, and there is no fruit of those.'

body.text: anitye nityasaṃjñeti | yena kāraṇena kṣaṇika[vādaḥ] khaṇḍyate | tena kāraṇena śāśvatadṛṣṭirutpadyate | vadanti ca dharmā nirudhyamānāḥ punaḥ paramāṇavo bhavantīti | [anye] kecidvadanti mūlaprakṛtau pratiyantīti | dharmāṇāṃ vināśe 'pi saṃjñānusmaraṇāt sukhaduḥkhe vedayate | tasya śāśvatadṛṣṭirutpadyate | āhuśca jīvo nityaḥ | śabdo 'pi nitya iti | ebhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ śāśvatadṛṣṭirbhavati |
body.translated_text: 'The perception of permanence in the impermanent' — by whatever reason the doctrine of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikavāda</s>) is refuted, by that reason the eternalist view arises. And they say: '<s>Dharmas</s>, upon ceasing, again become atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>).' Others say: 'They return to the primordial nature (<s>mūlaprakṛti</s>).' Even in the destruction of <s>dharmas</s>, through the recollection of designations, one experiences pleasure and suffering. For that person, the eternalist view arises. And they say: 'The self (<s>jīva</s>) is permanent. Even sound is permanent.' Through such reasons, the eternalist view arises.

body.text: duḥkhe sukha[saṃjñe]ti | yena kāraṇena vadanti asti sukhamiti | yathā pūrvamuktaṃ trivedanāvarge | anena kāraṇenotpadyate sukhasaṃjñā | aśucau śucisaṃjñeti | kāye 'bhyāsaṅgāt cakṣuṣā aśuci dṛṣṭvā śucisaṃjñāmutpādayanti | keciccintayanti- ātmā puruṣalakṣaṇalabdhaḥ | asya puruṣasya kāyamaśuciṃ paśyāmaḥ | asti punaḥ sattvo yena śucīkriyata iti | ebhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ śucisaṃjñotpadyate |
body.translated_text: 'The perception of pleasure in suffering' — by whatever reason they say 'pleasure exists' — as was previously stated in the Chapter on the Three Feelings. Through that reason, the perception of pleasure arises. 'The perception of purity in the impure' — because of attachment to the body, having seen the impure with the eye, they generate the perception of purity. Some think: 'The self (<s>ātman</s>) has the characteristic of a person. We see that this person's body is impure. But there is a being by which it is made pure.' Through such reasons, the perception of purity arises.

body.text: anātmani ātmasaṃjñeti | skandhānāṃ santānena pravṛttiṃ dṛṣṭvā ekalakṣaṇaṃ gṛhṇāti |
body.translated_text: 'The perception of self in what is without self' — having seen the operation of the aggregates in continuity, one grasps a unitary characteristic.

body.text: tadā ātmeti manyante | yathā ca pūrvamutpannaṃ satkāyadṛṣṭeḥ kāraṇam | anenaiva kāraṇenātmasaṃjñā sambhavati | anutkṛṣṭa utkṛṣṭasaṃjñeti | pūraṇādiṣu tīrthikācāryeṣu utkṛṣṭasaṃjñāmutpādayanti | brahmā svayamāha- ahamasmi mahābrahmā prabhurdevānāṃ kartā jagata ityevamādi | kecidāhuḥ- yadi kaścitpañcakāmānāṃ sukhavedanāsampannaḥ ayamutkṛṣṭa dharma iti | kecitpunarāhuḥ - yadi kaścidviraktaḥ prathamadhyāna[mārabhya]yāvaccaturthadhyānamupasampadya viharati ayamutkṛṣṭa dharma iti | kecidāhuḥ- loke pratyakṣadṛṣṭeṣu brāhmaṇāḥ pūjyāḥ | parekṣeṣu sattveṣu devāḥ pūjyā iti | iyamanutkṛṣṭa utkṛṣṭasaṃjñeti | utkṛṣṭe cānutkṛṣṭasaṃjñeti | sarveṣu sattveṣu buddhaḥ paramapūjyaḥ | kecittasmin anutkṛṣṭasaṃjñāmutpādya vadanti- ayaṃ kṣatriyaḥ alpakālikaśikṣāmārgaḥ | buddhavacanañca na cāṭukāvya[vat] kleśagurukaṃ na vedasadṛśam | tadutkṛṣṭamiti na vadanti | santi saṅghe catuṣkoṭikāḥ pudgalā ityato 'nutkṛṣṭaḥ | evamutkṛṣṭe 'nutkṛṣṭasaṃjñāmutpādayanti |
body.translated_text: then they think 'this is the self.' And the previously arisen cause of the view of the perishable collection (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>) — by this very cause, the perception of self arises. [The next perversion is] the perception of the superior in what is not superior (<s>anutkṛṣṭa utkṛṣṭasaṃjñā</s>). They generate the perception of superiority in non-Buddhist teachers such as <s>Pūraṇa</s> and the like. <s>Brahmā</s> himself said: 'I am the Great <s>Brahmā</s>, lord of the gods, creator of the world' — and so forth. Some say: 'If someone is endowed with the pleasant feeling of the five sensual pleasures — this is the superior <s>dharma</s>.' Others say: 'If someone, being dispassionate, enters and abides in the first <s>dhyāna</s> up to the fourth <s>dhyāna</s> — this is the superior <s>dharma</s>.' Some say: 'In the world, among those who are directly seen, <s>brāhmaṇas</s> are to be revered. Among unseen beings, the gods are to be revered.' This is the perception of the superior in what is not superior. And the perception of the not-superior in what is superior: Among all beings, the <s>Buddha</s> is supremely to be revered. But some, generating the perception of non-superiority in him, say: 'He is a <s>kṣatriya</s>, [following] a path of training for a short time. And the word of the <s>Buddha</s> is not like flattering poetry, not heavy with defilements, not like the <s>Vedas</s>.' They do not say it is superior. 'There are persons of four categories in the <s>Saṅgha</s>' — therefore it is not-superior. Thus they generate the perception of non-superiority in what is superior.

body.text: avyadānamārge vyavadānamārgasaṃjñeti | yatkecidāhuḥ- bhasmatīrthādisnānaiḥ puruṣaḥ śudhyatīti | kecidāhuḥ- jananamaraṇayoḥ kṣayo 'vasānaṃ vyavadānamārga iti | śīladhāraṇa brahmacaryamātra āsajya devapūjādayaśca [vyavadānamārga ākhyāyeta] īśvara [prasādena] ca viśuddhiṃ labhata iti ca vadanti | kecidāhuḥ- tapaścaryayā pūrvatanīnakarmakṣayo vyavadānamārga iti | [kecidāhuḥ]- laśunaṃ tyaktvā dadhinavanītādinā viśuddhiṃ labhate | punaḥ prayataḥ snātvā brahmayajñapaṭhanatadūrdhvabhojanaṃ viśuddhimārga iti | ebhirnānāvidhairasanmārgairvimukti rlabhyate natvaṣṭhāṅgikaviśuddhimārgeṇeti |
body.translated_text: [The next perversion is] the perception of the path of purification in what is not the path of purification (<s>avyavadānamārge vyavadānamārgasaṃjñā</s>). Some say: 'A person is purified through bathing in ashes, holy fords, and the like.' Some say: 'The cessation and end of birth and death is the path of purification.' Some say, clinging merely to the upholding of moral conduct and the practice of the holy life: 'Worship of gods and the like [is the path of purification],' and 'Through the grace of <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), one obtains purification.' Some say: 'Through the practice of austerities (<s>tapaścaryā</s>), the exhaustion of prior <s>karma</s> is the path of purification.'
