[Some say]: 'Having abandoned garlic, one obtains purification through curds, fresh butter, and the like. Again, having purified [oneself] and bathed, the recitation of the <s>Brahmā</s>-sacrifice (<s>brahmayajña</s>) and eating after that is the path of purification.' Through these various wrong paths, liberation is [said to be] obtained — but not through the eightfold path of purification.

body.text: bhāve 'bhāvasaṃjñeti | yat dharmā lokasatyataḥ santo 'pi abhāva ityucyante | abhāve bhāvasaṃjñeti yaducyate santi dravyāṇi astyavayavīti | santi saṃkhyāparimāṇādayo guṇā ityapi vadanti | sāmānyalakṣaṇaṃ pṛthaktvalakṣaṇaṃ samavāyañca vadanti | prakṛtikālādayo 'satpadārthāḥ santīti ca vadanti | ebhiḥ kāraṇairutpannāni viparyayacittāni mithyādṛṣṭayo bhavanti | āsu mithyādṛṣṭiṣu viśiṣya catasro dṛṣṭayaḥ | anyā ya ugrakleśā sā mithyādṛṣṭiḥ |
body.translated_text: [The next perversion is] the perception of non-existence in what exists (<s>bhāve abhāvasaṃjñā</s>): <s>dharmas</s> that exist according to worldly truth are said to be 'non-existent.' [And] the perception of existence in what is non-existent (<s>abhāve bhāvasaṃjñā</s>): as when it is said 'There exist substances (<s>dravya</s>),' 'There exists a possessor of parts (<s>avayavin</s>).' And they also say: 'There exist qualities (<s>guṇa</s>) such as number, measure, and the like.' And they assert a universal characteristic (<s>sāmānya</s>), a particular characteristic (<s>pṛthaktva</s>), and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). And they say: 'Non-existent entities such as <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), <s>Kāla</s> (time), and the like exist.' From these causes arise perverted minds, which are wrong views (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>). Among these wrong views, four views are distinguished. Any other that is an intense defilement — that is [also] wrong view.

body.text: (pṛ) iyaṃ mithyādṛṣṭiḥ kathaṃ prahīyate | (u) sūtre bhagavatā proktasamyakdṛṣṭyā prajahāti | (pṛ) samyagdṛṣṭiḥ kathamutpadyate | (u) yo darśanaśravaṇānvayajñānaiḥ samyagviniścinoti | tasya samyagdṛṣṭirbhavati | samyaksamādhiṃ bhāvayataḥ samyagdṛṣṭirutpadyate | yathāha sūtram- samāhito yathābhūtaṃ prajānātīti | na vikṣiptacitta [ityarthaḥ] |
body.translated_text: (Question) How is this wrong view abandoned? (Answer) As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>, one abandons it through right view (<s>samyakdṛṣṭi</s>) proclaimed by the Blessed One. (Question) How does right view arise? (Answer) One who correctly determines [things] through the knowledges of direct seeing, hearing, and inference — for him, right view exists. For one who cultivates right concentration (<s>samyaksamādhi</s>), right view arises. As the <s>sūtra</s> says: 'One who is concentrated knows things as they truly are' — meaning: one whose mind is not distracted.

body.text: (pṛ) asyā mithyādṛṣṭeḥ ke doṣāḥ | (u) sarve doṣā vipattivyasanāni ca mithyādṛṣṭyā bhavanti | sa āha- nāsti pāpaṃ nāsti puṇyaṃ sukṛtaduṣkṛtānāṃ phalaṃ vipāka iti | ato dṛṣṭadharma eva na santi suvṛttāni | kiṃ punaranāgatāni | evaṃ dūṣitasukṛtaduṣkṛtaḥ pumān samucchinnakuśalamūla ityucyate | sa niyatamavīcau patiṣyati | yathoktaṃ ṣaṭpādābhidharme- krimipipīlikāhananaṃ puruṣahananād gurutaram iti | sa mithyādṛṣṭikaḥ puruṣaḥ lokadūṣakaḥ satvānāṃ bhūyasāpakārāya pravartate | yathā viṣavṛkṣo hiṃsāyai prarohati | tena kṛtaṃ kāyikaṃ vācikaṃ mānasaṃ karma sarvamaśubhavipākāya bhavati | yathoktaṃ sūtre- mithyādṛṣṭikasya [bhikṣavaḥ] puruṣapudgalasya yatkāyakarma yathādṛṣṭisamāttaṃ samādattaṃ yacca vākkarma........yacca manaḥkarma yā cetanā yā prārthanā yaḥ praṇidhiḥ ye ca saṃskārāḥ sarve te 'niṣṭāya akāntāya amanāpāya ahitāya duḥkhāya saṃvartate | tadyathā tiktakālābubījaṃ koṣātakībījaṃ picumandabījamādrāyāṃ pṛthivyāṃ nikṣiptaṃ yaccaiva pṛthivīrasamupādīyate yaccāporasaṃ tejorasaṃ vāyurasamupādīyate sarvaṃ tat tiktakatvāya kaṭukatvāya asātatvāya saṃvartate | [tatkasya hetoḥ] bījaṃ hi bhikṣavaḥ pāpakam | evameva mithyādṛṣṭikasya puruṣapudgalasya cittacaitasikā dharmā aniṣṭāya [akāntāya
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults of this wrong view? (Answer) All faults, misfortunes, and calamities come about through wrong view. He says: 'There is no sin, there is no merit, there is no fruit or ripening of good deeds or bad deeds.' Therefore, in this very present life, there are no good conducts. How much less in future lives! A person whose [understanding of] good deeds and bad deeds is thus corrupted is said to be 'one whose wholesome roots are completely cut off.' He will certainly fall into the <s>Avīci</s> hell. As stated in the <s>Ṣaṭpādābhidharma</s>: 'The killing of worms and ants is more grave than the killing of a person.' Such a person of wrong view, a corrupter of the world, operates predominantly for the harm of beings — just as a poison tree grows for the purpose of injury. Whatever bodily, verbal, or mental <s>karma</s> is done by him — all leads to unwholesome ripening. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'O monks, for a person of wrong view, whatever bodily <s>karma</s> is undertaken and carried out in accordance with that view, whatever verbal <s>karma</s>... whatever mental <s>karma</s>, whatever volition, whatever aspiration, whatever resolution, and whatever formations — all of these conduce to what is undesired, unwanted, unpleasant, unhelpful, and to suffering. Just as a bitter gourd seed, a ridged-gourd seed, or a <s>picumanda</s> (neem) seed, planted in moist earth, whatever earth-essence it absorbs, whatever water-essence, fire-essence, or wind-essence it absorbs — all of that conduces to bitterness, pungency, and unpleasantness. Why is that? Because the seed, O monks, is bad. In the same way, for a person of wrong view, the mental and mental-factor <s>dharmas</s> conduce to what is undesired, [unwanted

body.text: amanāpāya ahitāya duḥkhāya] saṃvartate | [tatkasya hetoḥ] dṛṣṭirhi bhikṣavaḥ pāpikā iti | atastasya puruṣapudgalasya kṛtamapi dānādi neṣṭaphalaṃ bhavati | pūrvakṛtamithyādṛṣṭicittena vinaṣṭatvāt | tatkṛtasyāśubhamevādhimātraṃ bhavati | pāpakacittasya cirasañcitatvāt |
body.translated_text: unpleasant, unhelpful, and to suffering]. Why is that? Because the view, O monks, is bad.' Therefore, for that person, even acts of giving and the like that have been done do not bear desirable fruit — because they are destroyed by the prior mind of wrong view. What is done by him is overwhelmingly unwholesome — because of the long accumulation of the sinful mind.

body.text: saṃvareṇa ca kaścidasaddharmaṃ pratiroddhuṃ śaknoti | asya puruṣapudgalasya nāsti sukṛtaṃ duṣkṛtamityato na yataḥ kutaścitprativiratiḥ | atyantapramatto 'saddharma carati | hryapatrapākhyadvividhaśukladharmasabhinnaḥ paśusamo bhavati | yaśca vadati nāsti sukṛtaṃ duṣkṛtaṃ veti sa sadā citte 'kuśalameva kāṅkṣate | tasya saddharmasamādāpanakāraṇameva nāsti | kasmāt na hi sa sajjanamupagacchati | nā[pi] saddharmaṃ śṛṇoti | tasya duṣkṛtacittaṃ sūtthānaṃ bhavati | sukṛtacittaṃ durutpādam | duṣkṛtasya sūtthānatvātsukṛtasya kāraṇameva nāsti | evaṃ krameṇa duṣkṛtopacaye samucchinnakuśalamūlo bhavati |
body.translated_text: And through restraint, someone is able to resist the wrong <s>dharma</s>. But for this person, because he holds that 'there is no good deed or bad deed,' there is no abstention from anything whatsoever. Being extremely heedless (<s>pramatta</s>), he practices the wrong <s>dharma</s>. Having broken the two white <s>dharmas</s> called shame (<s>hrī</s>) and moral dread (<s>apatrāpā</s>), he becomes like an animal. And one who says 'there is no good deed or bad deed' always craves only the unwholesome in the mind. For him, there is simply no cause for undertaking the true <s>Dharma</s>. Why? Because he does not approach good people. Nor does he hear the true <s>Dharma</s>. His mind of bad deeds arises easily. The mind of good deeds arises with difficulty. Because the mind of bad deeds arises easily, there is simply no cause for good deeds. Thus, through the gradual accumulation of bad deeds, his wholesome roots become completely cut off.

body.text: mithyādṛṣṭikasya puruṣapudgalasya dusthānagata ityākhyā | yathā nārakāḥ sattvā na mārgapratilābhapravaṇāḥ | tathā ca pudgalo madhyamadeśa utpanna iṣṭāniṣṭavivekāya ṣaḍindriyasampanno 'pi na mārgapratilābhapravaṇo bhavati | mithyādṛṣṭikasya nāsti [yatkiñcit] duṣkṛtamakuṭam | nāsti viratirlaghoralpādvā [duṣkṛtāt] | alpamapyakuśalaṃ kurvan narake patati | karmaṇo 'sya gurupāpakacittena samutpannatvāt | yathā karmavarge narakavimocakaṃ karma ityanena kāraṇena tatpuruṣakṛtaṃ sarvaṃ narakāya saṃvartate | na ca sa pāpakamakuśalaṃ karma kṣapayati | akuśaladharmasya sadā cittagatatvāt | durlabhā ca tasyottarottarānnarakādvimuktiḥ | kasmāt | samucchinnakuśalamūlasya hi yadā kuśalaṃ na pravartate tadanantaraṃ narakānnaiva vimuktiḥ | citte mithyādṛṣṭikatvāt tasya kuśalamūlaṃ kathaṃ pravarteta | mithyādṛṣṭikaḥ pudgalo 'cikitsyaḥ tadyathā samupasthitamaraṇanimitto rogī | cikitsakaḥ sannapi na cikitsituṃ śaknoti | evamayamapi | anyakuśalarahitatvādyāvad buddhā api na cikitsante | ato 'vaśyamavīcyāṃ patati ||
body.translated_text: Such a person of wrong view is called 'one who has gone to a bad place.' Just as beings in hell are not inclined toward obtaining the path, so too this person — even though born in the central region, endowed with the six faculties for discriminating the desirable from the undesirable — is not inclined toward obtaining the path. For a person of wrong view, there is no bad deed that is not committed. There is no abstention from even a slight or minor bad deed. Even doing a small amount of unwholesome [karma], he falls into hell — because his <s>karma</s> arises from a mind of grave sinfulness. As stated in the Chapter on <s>Karma</s>: 'The <s>karma</s> that liberates from hell' — for this reason, everything done by that person conduces to hell. And he does not exhaust sinful, unwholesome <s>karma</s> — because the unwholesome <s>dharma</s> is always present in his mind. His liberation from hell is extremely difficult to obtain. Why? For one whose wholesome roots are completely cut off, when the wholesome does not operate, at that time there is no liberation from hell. Because his mind is of wrong view, how would his wholesome root operate? A person of wrong view is incurable — just as a sick person upon whom the sign of death has appeared — even though a physician is present, he cannot be treated. So too with this one. Because of being devoid of all other wholesomeness, even the <s>Buddhas</s> cannot treat him. Therefore he necessarily falls into the <s>Avīci</s> hell.

body.text: mithyādṛṣṭivargo dvātriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, the Chapter on Wrong View (<s>mithyādṛṣṭivarga</s>).

body.text: 133 parāmarśadvayavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 133. Chapter on the Two Kinds of Clinging (<s>parāmarśadvayavarga</s>)

body.text: abhūtavastuni idameva satyamanyanmithyeti vacanaṃ dṛṣṭiparāmarśa ityucyate | pūrvokte 'nutkṛṣṭadharma utkṛṣṭasaṃjñāviniścayo 'pi dṛṣṭiparāmarśaḥ |
body.translated_text: Regarding a non-existent object, the statement 'This alone is true, the other is false' is called view-clinging (<s>dṛṣṭiparāmarśa</s>). The previously stated determination that generates the perception of the superior in what is not a superior <s>dharma</s> — that too is view-clinging.

body.text: (pṛ) dṛṣṭiparāmarśasya ke doṣāḥ | (u) sa puruṣo nyūnaguṇaṃ labdhvā ātmānaṃ pūrṇaṃ manyate | tasya guṇañcātivakti | kasmāt | akuśale vastuni atyantakuśalasaṃjñāmutpādya vīryamārabhate | tena hetunā ca paścātparitapati | viduṣāṃ parihāsyaśca bhavati | anutkṛṣṭe utkṛṣṭasaṃjñāyāḥ kṛtatvāt | yo 'nutkṛṣṭamutkṛṣṭaṃ vadati sa bālo mūḍhasaṃjñaḥ | yathāndho ghaṭaśakale suvarṇasaṃjñāmutpādya cakṣuṣmatāṃ laghu hāsyo bhavati | dṛṣṭiparāmarśasyedṛśā doṣāḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults of view-clinging? (Answer) That person, having obtained an inferior quality, considers himself complete. And he exaggerates his own virtue. Why? Having generated the perception of extreme wholesomeness in an unwholesome object, he exerts effort. Through that cause, he later suffers remorse. And he becomes an object of ridicule among the wise — because of having generated the perception of the superior in what is not superior. One who calls what is not superior 'superior' is a fool with a deluded mind — just as a blind person, having generated the perception of gold in a potsherd, becomes an easy object of ridicule among those who have eyes. Such are the faults of view-clinging.

body.text: yat kaścit bodhimupekṣamāṇaḥ snānādiśīlena viśuddhiprāptiṃ kāṅkṣate tat śīlavrataparāmarśa ityucyate | (pṛ) nanu śīlena na viśuddhilābhaḥ | (u) prajñayaiva viśuddhilābhaḥ | śīlantu prajñendriyasya mūlam | (pṛ) ke doṣāḥ śīlavrataparāmarśasya | (u) ye doṣā uktā dṛṣṭiparāmarśasya "nyūnaṃ vastu [labdhvā] sampūrṇaṃ manyate ityādinā ta eva doṣāḥ | śīlavrataparāmarśapratyayamatyadhikaṃ duḥkhānyanubhavati | yaduta śītoṣṇavedanā, bhasmabhūmitarukaṇṭakādiṣu śayanaṃ jalahradāgnipraveśo bhṛgupatanamityādi | paraloke 'pi atimātraduḥkhavipākaḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- govratikaḥ saṃsiddha[vrata]ḥ [kāyasya bhedātparaṃ maraṇāt] gavāṃ sahavyatāmupapadyate | asaṃsiddho narake patati iti | sa tamasaḥ tamaḥ praviśati | yatastaṃ dharmaṃ samādadāno dṛṣṭadharme duḥkhamanubhavati | ūrdhvamapi duḥkham | sa gurutaraṃ pāpañca vindate | kasmāt | adharmaṃ dharmaṃ matvā saddharmaṃ vināśayati | saddharmacaryāpabādakaśca bahūn sattvān narake pātayati | suviśuddhadharmasya pṛṣṭhīkṛtatvāt | sañcitamahāpāpo 'vaśyamavīcinarake vipākamanubhavati |
body.translated_text: When someone, disregarding awakening (<s>bodhi</s>), desires the attainment of purification through mere observance of bathing and the like — that is called precept-and-vow-clinging (<s>śīlavrataparāmarśa</s>). (Question) Is it not through moral conduct that one obtains purification? (Answer) One obtains purification through wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) alone. But moral conduct is the root of the faculty of wisdom. (Question) What are the faults of precept-and-vow-clinging? (Answer) The same faults stated for view-clinging — namely, 'having obtained an inferior thing, one considers it complete' and so forth — those very faults [apply here]. Through the condition of precept-and-vow-clinging, one experiences exceedingly great sufferings — namely, the feelings of cold and heat, lying on ashes, ground, trees, and thorns, entering water, ponds, and fire, falling from cliffs, and so forth. In the next life too, there is excessively great ripening of suffering. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'One who practices the ox-vow (<s>govratika</s>), having perfected [that] vow, [upon the dissolution of the body after death] is reborn in the company of cattle. If [the vow is] imperfected, he falls into hell.' He enters from darkness into darkness. Because, in undertaking that <s>dharma</s>, he experiences suffering in this very present life. And hereafter too there is suffering. And he incurs graver sin. Why? Mistaking what is not <s>Dharma</s> for <s>Dharma</s>, he destroys the true <s>Dharma</s>. And being one who obstructs the practice of the true <s>Dharma</s>, he causes many beings to fall into hell — because of having turned his back on the supremely pure <s>Dharma</s>. Having accumulated great sin, he necessarily experiences the ripening in the <s>Avīci</s> hell.

body.text: ato
body.translated_text: Therefore

body.text: anācārādvirama | mā cara mithyāmārgam | kasmāt ya ādito nācarati tasya mārgacaraṇaṃ sukaram | mithyācāraparāhatacittasya tu duṣkaro mārgapraveśaḥ | śatrurapi
body.translated_text: desist from misconduct. Do not practice the wrong path. Why? For one who does not practice [the wrong path] from the beginning, the walking of the [true] path is easy. But for one whose mind is struck by wrong practice, entry upon the path is difficult. Even an enemy

body.text: na tathā pudgalaṃ glapayati yathā mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | kasmāt | na hi śatrustathā pudgalaṃ paribhāvayati yathā mithyādṛṣṭayanugāmināṃ tīrthikācaritānāṃ nānāduḥśīlānāṃ nagnatānirlajjatābhasmarajaḥkāyatākeśolluñcchanādīnāṃ samādānam | mithyādṛṣṭikaḥ sarvasmāllaukikahitakāmāt bhraśyati | dṛṣṭadharme pañcakāmaguṇebhyo bhraśyati | tadūrdhvaṃ sugatisukhānnirvāṇācca bhraśyati | sukhaṃ prārthayitvā duḥkhaṃ labhamāno vimuktiṃ prārthayitvā bandhaṃ labhamānaḥ puruṣaḥ kiṃ na mattaḥ | tat kasmāt | [ya] ekenānnadānapratyayena svarge janmalābhārho bhavati | tasya puruṣasya mithyācāracāritvāt dānāya kāyajīvite satyapi na kiñcana hitaṃ bhavati ||
body.translated_text: does not debilitate a person as much as wrong view does. Why? Because an enemy does not humiliate a person as much as [does] the undertaking of the various immoral practices of non-Buddhist teachings that follow upon wrong view — such as nakedness, shamelessness, covering the body with ashes and dust, tearing out the hair, and the like. A person of wrong view falls away from all worldly beneficial desires. In this very present life, he falls away from the five strands of sensual pleasure (<s>pañcakāmaguṇa</s>). Hereafter, he falls away from the happiness of a good destination and from <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. A person who, having desired happiness, obtains suffering, and having desired liberation, obtains bondage — is he not deluded? And why is that? One who, through the mere condition of a single gift of food, would be worthy of obtaining birth in heaven — because of that person's practice of wrong conduct, even though his body and life exist for the purpose of giving, nothing beneficial comes of it.

body.text: parāmarśadvayavargastrayastiṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Two Kinds of Clinging (<s>parāmarśadvayavarga</s>).

body.text: 134 upakleśavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 134. Chapter on the Secondary Defilements (<s>upakleśavarga</s>)

body.text: gurucittasya svāpakāmatā middham | cittasamādhānāya prabodhaviratiḥ svāpaḥ | viṣayeṣu vikṣiptacittatā auddhatyam | cittākāṃkṣite daurmanasyabandhaḥ kaukṛtyam | tadyathā kṛtamakartavyamakṛtañca kartavyamiti | kuśalakuhanakuṭilacittaṃ māyā | māyācittavṛttinirvartanaṃ śāṭhyam | svakṛtākuśalasyāhrepaṇamāhrīkyam | saṅghe kṛtākuśalasyāhrepaṇamanapatrāpyam | akuśalānugaṃ cittaṃ pramādaḥ | yadasantaṃ guṇaṃ khyāpayati tena janā vadanti astīti | [sā] kuhanā | lābhasatkārāyādbhutaṃ prakhyāpya pareṣāṃ manaḥprahlādinī vāk lapanā | paradravyalipsayā tallipsāmupagūhya vadati idaṃ vastu sundaramityādi | tannaimittikatā | yadetatpuruṣanindāyai anyaṃ stauti- tava pitā vyavasāyī tvantu neti | [tat] niṣpeṣikatā | yat dānena dānaṃ prārthayamāno vadati- idaṃ dānavastu amukātpatyantāllabdhamityādi |
body.translated_text: The desire for sleep when the mind is heavy is drowsiness (<s>middha</s>). The desisting from wakefulness for the sake of mental composure is sleep (<s>svāpa</s>). The scattering of the mind toward objects is restlessness (<s>auddhatya</s>). The bondage of displeasure regarding what is desired by the mind is remorse (<s>kaukṛtya</s>) — namely, 'I did what should not have been done, and I did not do what should have been done.' A mind that is deceitfully and crookedly wholesome is deceit (<s>māyā</s>). The enactment of a conduct born of a deceitful mind is dissimulation (<s>śāṭhya</s>). Shamelessness regarding one's own unwholesome deeds is lack of shame (<s>āhrīkya</s>). Shamelessness regarding unwholesome deeds committed in the <s>Saṅgha</s> is lack of moral dread (<s>anapatrāpya</s>). A mind that follows the unwholesome is heedlessness (<s>pramāda</s>). That which proclaims a non-existent virtue, whereby people say 'it exists' — that is hypocrisy (<s>kuhanā</s>). Speech that pleases the minds of others by proclaiming something marvelous for the sake of gain and honor is flattery (<s>lapanā</s>). Concealing one's desire for another's property, one says 'This thing is beautiful' and the like — that is hinting (<s>naimittikatā</s>). That which praises another in order to reproach a person — 'Your father was industrious, but you are not' — that is belittling (<s>niṣpeṣikatā</s>). That which, desiring to obtain a gift through [giving a] gift, says 'This gift-material was obtained from such-and-such a great person' and the like —

body.text: tat lābhena lābhajigṛkṣā | yat puruṣasya nidrāvyādhau niratiḥ sā tandrītyucyate | yā mārgacaryākāraṇasudeśasaṃpattāvapi sadotkaṇṭhitatā [sā] aratirityucyate | yat puruṣasya kāyasya jṛmbhaṇā adamanaṃ styānamiddhasya pratyayaḥ sā vijṛmbhikā | ya āhāre bahvalpatādamanānabhijñaḥ | [sa] ādito 'dama ityucyate | yo nātimātravyavasāyī bhavati | [sa] vivartyacitta ityucyate | yo mahāmātrāṇāṃ vacanaṃ na satkaroti na bibheti | so 'bahumānītyucyate | akuśalarucikaḥ puruṣaḥ pāpamitra ityucyate | ityādaya upakleśāḥ | kleśebhya utpannatvāt ||
body.translated_text: that is seeking gain through gain (<s>lābhena lābhajigṛkṣā</s>). A person's fondness for the illness of sleep is called indolence (<s>tandrī</s>). That which is constant discontent even when there is the attainment of a good place fit for practicing the path — that is called aversion (<s>arati</s>). A person's yawning of the body and non-restraint, which is the condition of torpor and drowsiness — that is called yawning (<s>vijṛmbhikā</s>). One who is ignorant of the restraint of eating much or little in food — he is called 'unrestrained' (<s>adama</s>) from the outset. One who does not make effort excessively — he is called 'of distracted mind' (<s>vivartyacitta</s>). One who does not honor the words of elders and does not fear them — he is called 'disrespectful' (<s>abahumānī</s>). A person who delights in the unwholesome is called a 'bad friend' (<s>pāpamitra</s>). These and the like are the secondary defilements (<s>upakleśa</s>). Because they are produced from the defilements.

body.text: upakleśavargaścatustriṃduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one-hundred-and-thirty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Secondary Defilements (<s>upakleśavarga</s>).

body.text: 135 akuśalamūlavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 135. Chapter on the Unwholesome Roots (<s>akuśalamūlavarga</s>)

body.text: trīṇyakuśalamūlāni yaduta lobhadveṣamohāḥ | (pṛ) madamānādyapi akuśalamūlaṃ syāt | kasmāttīṇyevoktāni | (u) sarve 'pi kleśā strayāṇāṃ kleśānāmaṅgānyeva | mānādikaṃ mohāṅgam | ato na pṛthagucyate | trayaḥ kleśā sāvānāṃ cetasi bhūyasā vartante | na mānādi | sarveṣāmavītarāgāṇāṃ maśakapipīlikāparyantānāmime trayaḥ kleśā eva cittavartinaḥ | naivaṃ madamānādiḥ | rāge sati dveṣo 'kuśalamūlaṃ bhavati | anuraktasya virodhe dveṣo 'nupravartate | mohastu dvayormūlam | kasmāt | yasya nāsti mohaḥ na tasya rāgadveṣau | yathoktaṃ sūtre- daśākuśalakarmāṇi trividhāni lobhadveṣamohajānīti | na tūktaṃ mānādijānīti | santi ca tisra eva vedanā na punarasti caturthī | āsu tisṛṣu vedanāsu trayaḥ kleśā anuśayā bhavanti | yadyasti pṛthaṅ mānādiḥ | kasyāṃ vedanāyāmanuśayaḥ syāt | tadvastuto nābhidhātuṃ śakyate | [iti] jñātavyaṃ tāni trīṇyeva kleśamūlānīti |
body.translated_text: The three unwholesome roots (<s>akuśalamūla</s>) are greed (<s>lobha</s>), hatred (<s>dveṣa</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>). (Question) Intoxication (<s>mada</s>), conceit (<s>māna</s>), and the like could also be unwholesome roots. Why are only three stated? (Answer) All other defilements are merely limbs of these three defilements. Conceit and the like are limbs of delusion. Therefore they are not stated separately. The three defilements for the most part operate in the minds of those with outflows (<s>sāsrava</s>), not conceit and the like. For all those not free from passion — down to mosquitoes and ants — these three defilements alone operate in the mind, not intoxication, conceit, and the like. When there is passion, hatred becomes an unwholesome root — because when there is attachment, hatred arises in opposition [to what threatens the attachment]. But delusion is the root of both [passion and hatred]. Why? One who does not have delusion does not have passion or hatred. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The ten unwholesome <s>karmas</s> are of three kinds — born of greed, hatred, and delusion.' But it is not stated 'born of conceit and the like.' And there are exactly three feelings, no fourth. In these three feelings, the three defilements are latent tendencies (<s>anuśaya</s>). If conceit and the like were separate [roots], in which feeling would their latent tendency exist? That cannot in reality be stated. Therefore it should be known that those three alone are the roots of defilements.

body.text: (pṛ) kasmātsukhavedanāyāṃ rāgo 'nuśayaḥ | (u) pratyakṣaṃ hi tatra tasyotpattiḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- sukhavedanīyasparśaṃ labhamānasya bhavati prītiḥ | duḥkhavedanīyasparśaṃ labhamānasya bhavati aprītiḥ | tasya vedanānāmudayavyayāsvādādīnavanissaraṇānāṃ yathābhūtāprajñānāt | iti | aduḥkhāsukhavedanāyāmavidyānuśayaḥ | kasmāt | nahyayamārūpyadhātvāptānāṃ skandhānāṃ santānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti | tadā [khalvasya] tatra bhavati nirvāṇasaṃjñā vā vimuktisaṃjñā vā aduḥkhāsukhasaṃjñā vā ātmasaṃjñā vā | ata uktaṃ- aduḥkhāsukhavedanāyāṃ moho 'nuśayo bhavatīti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Why is passion the latent tendency in pleasant feeling? (Answer) Because its arising therein is directly perceived. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'For one who obtains a contact to be experienced as pleasant, there arises delight. For one who obtains a contact to be experienced as painful, there arises displeasure. For him, there is no knowledge as it truly is of the origination and passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape of these feelings.' In neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the latent tendency of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) becomes latent. Why? Because he does not understand as it truly is the continuity of the aggregates attained in the formless realm. At that time, there arises for him the perception of <s>Nirvāṇa</s>, or the perception of liberation, or the perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, or the perception of self. Therefore it is said: 'In the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, delusion is the latent tendency.'

body.text: (pṛ) anuśayāḥ kiṃ dharme 'nuśerate ki vā sattve 'nuśerate | (u) dharmānupādāya sattvabuddhirbhavati | sattvabuddhimanusṛtya vedanā vedyante | vedanā anusṛtya lobhādayaḥ kleśānuśayāḥ | ato jñāyate dharmānupādāyotpanno 'nuśayaḥ sattve 'nuśeta iti | kasmāt tat jñāyate | yasya sattvasyāprahīṇaḥ so 'nuśayaḥ tasya so 'nuśayo 'nuśete | yasya tu prahīṇaḥ na tasyānuśete 'nuśayaḥ | yadi dharme 'nuśayo 'sti | dharmāṇāṃ nityasattvādanuśayā nityānuśayāḥ syuḥ | nityasyāprahātavyatvāt | asattvasaṃkhyāto 'pi sānuśayaḥ syāt | tathā cet puruṣasyānuśayo 'stīti bhittyādiranuśayavān syāt | puruṣasya vijñānamastīti bhittyādirapi vijñānavān syāt | nedaṃ vastuto 'sti | tathārhanna syāt | anyeṣāṃ puruṣapudgalānāmanuśayo 'stīti [so] 'nuśayavān[syāt] |
body.translated_text: (Question) Do the latent tendencies (<s>anuśaya</s>) become latent in <s>dharmas</s> or in sentient beings? (Answer) Depending on <s>dharmas</s>, the notion of a being arises. Following the notion of a being, feelings are experienced. Following feelings, the latent tendencies of defilements such as greed and the like [become latent]. Therefore it is known that the latent tendency, having arisen depending on <s>dharmas</s>, becomes latent in the sentient being. How is this known? The latent tendency that has not been abandoned by a being — that latent tendency becomes latent in that being. But the one that has been abandoned does not become latent in that [being]. If the latent tendency were in <s>dharmas</s> — since <s>dharmas</s> always exist — the latent tendencies would always be latent. Because what is permanent cannot be abandoned. Even one who is not counted as a sentient being would have latent tendencies. If that were so, since a person has latent tendencies, a wall and the like too would have latent tendencies. Since a person has consciousness, a wall and the like too would have consciousness. But this is not so in reality. Then an <s>Arhat</s> too would not be [free]. Since other persons and beings have latent tendencies, he [too] would have latent tendencies.

body.text: (pṛ) ayamanuśayaḥ aprahīṇaḥ san anuśete | prahīṇassannānuśete | (u) dvidhānuśayo 'nuśete | (1) ālambanatonuśayanam (2) samprayogato 'nuśayanamiti | ayamanuśayo yadi prahīṇo yadi vāprahīṇaḥ sa ālambanataḥ saṃprayogataśca | kasmāducyate prahīṇaḥ san nānuśeta iti | tathā cet tṛtīyānuśayanalakṣaṇaṃ vaktavyam | anabhidhānāt jñātavyaṃ nāstīti | anuśayo bhūmyantarālambano nānuśete | ato jñāyate sattvamātre 'nuśayo na dharma iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) This latent tendency, when not abandoned, becomes latent; when abandoned, it does not become latent. (Answer) In two ways does a latent tendency become latent: (1) through its object (<s>ālambana</s>), and (2) through its association (<s>samprayoga</s>). This latent tendency, whether abandoned or not abandoned, [is related to something] through object and through association. Why then is it said 'when abandoned, it does not become latent'? If that were so, a third mode of latent tendency would have to be stated. Because it is not stated, it should be known that it does not exist. A latent tendency whose object is in another plane (<s>bhūmi</s>) does not become latent [in that plane]. Therefore it is known that the latent tendency is in the sentient being alone, not in <s>dharma</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) dvidhānuśayo 'nuśeta (1) ālambanato 'nuśayaḥ (2) samprayogato 'nuśaya iti | eṣāṃ sattvānāmanuśayā nālambanato na samprayogataḥ | kathaṃ bhaviṣyatyanuśayaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) The latent tendency becomes latent in two ways: (1) through the object, and (2) through association. For these beings, the latent tendencies are neither through the object nor through association. How would they be latent tendencies?

body.text: (u) pratyuktapūrvamidam- anuśayā dharmamupādāyotpannāḥ sattve 'nuśerata iti | yathoktamabhidharmakāye- kāmadhātukasattvānāṃ katyanuśayā ityādi | yadi sattveṣu nānuśayīran | kathametādṛśaḥ praśnaḥ syāt |
body.translated_text: (Answer) This has already been replied to: The latent tendencies, having arisen depending on <s>dharmas</s>, become latent in sentient beings. As stated in the <s>Abhidharmakāya</s>: 'For beings of the desire realm, how many latent tendencies [exist]?' and so forth. If they were not latent in sentient beings, how could such a question exist?

body.text: (pṛ) yadyanuśayaḥ sattve 'nuśete | sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ rāgo 'nuśaya iti sūtroktaṃ virudhyeta | (u) nedaṃ pāryantikaṃ vacanam | vaktavyaṃ khalu sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ samutpanno rāgaḥ sattve 'nuśeta iti | (pṛ) sa rāgo rūpādīnupādāyāpi bhavati | kuto 'trocyate kevalaṃ sukhavedanāmupādāya bhavatīti | (u) saṃjñānusmaraṇavikalpaprītyādinā rāga utpadyate na tu rūpādimātrāt | (pṛ) duḥkhavedanāmupādāyāpi rāgo bhavati | yathā vadanti- sukhī na prārthayate duḥkhī tu bahu prārthayate | kasmātkevalamuktaṃ sukhavedanāto bhavatīti | (u) na duḥkhavedanayā rāga utpadyate | duḥkhasya pīḍanātmakatvāt puruṣasya sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāmeva rāga utpadyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) If the latent tendency becomes latent in sentient beings, the statement in the <s>sūtra</s> that 'passion is latent in pleasant feeling' would be contradicted. (Answer) This is not the final [meaning of the] statement. What should be said is that passion, having arisen in pleasant feeling, becomes latent in the sentient being. (Question) That passion also arises depending on form and the like. Why is it said here that it arises depending solely on pleasant feeling? (Answer) Passion arises through perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>), recollection (<s>anusmaraṇa</s>), conceptual discrimination (<s>vikalpa</s>), joy (<s>prīti</s>), and the like — but not from form and the like merely. (Question) Passion also arises depending on painful feeling. As they say: 'One who is happy does not desire; but one who is suffering desires much.' Why is it stated that it arises solely from pleasant feeling? (Answer) Passion does not arise from painful feeling. Because suffering has the nature of affliction, passion arises in the person only in pleasant feeling.

body.text: (pṛ) aduḥkhāsukhāyāṃ vedanāyāmapi rāgānuśayo 'nuśete | kasmāduktaṃ kevalaṃ sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāmiti | (u) aduḥkhāsukhavedanāḥ sukha[rūpa]tvāt [tatra] puruṣasya rāga utpadyate | ata ucyate sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ rāgānuśaya iti | tāsu triṣu vedanāsu trayaḥ kleśā anuśayā ityatastraya evocyante ||
body.translated_text: (Question) In neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling too, the latent tendency of passion becomes latent. Why is it stated solely 'in pleasant feeling'? (Answer) Because the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has the nature of pleasure, passion arises in the person therein. Therefore it is said: 'In pleasant feeling, the latent tendency of passion.' In these three feelings, the three defilements as latent tendencies — therefore only three are stated.

body.text: akuśalamūlavargaḥ pañcatriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one-hundred-and-thirty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Unwholesome Roots (<s>akuśalamūlavarga</s>).

body.text: 136 saṅkīrṇakleśavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 136. Chapter on Miscellaneous Defilements (<s>saṅkīrṇakleśavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) sūtra uktam- traya āsravāḥ- kāmāsravo bhavāsravo 'vidyāsrava iti | katame ime | (u) kāmadhātāvavidyāṃ varjayitvā anye sarve kleśāḥ kāmāsravā ityucyante | evaṃ rupārūpyadhātvorbhavāsravaḥ | traidhātukī cāvidyā avidyāsravaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There are three outflows (<s>āsrava</s>): the outflow of sensual pleasures (<s>kāmāsrava</s>), the outflow of existence (<s>bhavāsrava</s>), and the outflow of ignorance (<s>avidyāsrava</s>).' What are these? (Answer) In the desire realm, excluding ignorance, all other defilements are called the outflow of sensual pleasures. Likewise in the form and formless realms, [they constitute] the outflow of existence. Ignorance pertaining to the three realms is the outflow of ignorance.

body.text: (pṛ) āsravāḥ kathaṃ vardhante | (u) uttamādhamadhyamadharmaiḥ kramaśo vardhante | rūpādiviśiṣṭālambanalābhācca vardhante | (pṛ) ime traya āsravāḥ; kathaṃ vadanti saptāsravā iti | (u) vastuta āsravā dvividhāḥ satyadarśanaheyā [ye] āsravāṇāṃ mūlabhūtāḥ | bhāvanāheyā [ye] āsravāṇāṃ phalabhūtāḥ | pañcabhirārāsravasahakāribhiḥ pratyayai militvā sapta bhavanti | te kleśā eva | bhagavānarthata āha- traya āsravāḥ, catvāra oghāḥ, catvāro bandhāḥ, catvāryupādānāni, catvāro granthā ityādi |
body.translated_text: (Question) How do the outflows increase? (Answer) They increase progressively through superior, middling, and inferior <s>dharmas</s>. And they increase through obtaining a distinguished object such as form and the like. (Question) There are these three outflows — how is it said that there are seven outflows? (Answer) In reality, the outflows are of two kinds: those to be abandoned by the seeing of the truth (<s>satyadarśanapraheya</s>), which are the root of the outflows; and those to be abandoned by cultivation (<s>bhāvanāpraheya</s>), which are the fruit of the outflows. Combined with the five companion conditions that aid the outflows, they become seven. They are just the defilements. The Blessed One, according to the meaning, said: 'There are three outflows, four floods (<s>ogha</s>), four bonds (<s>bandha</s>), four clingings (<s>upādāna</s>), four fetters (<s>grantha</s>),' and the like.

body.text: (pṛ) catvāra oghāḥ kāmaugho bhavaugho dṛṣṭyodho 'vidyaugha iti | katama ime | (u) dṛṣṭimavidyāñca varjayitvā tadanye kāmadhātukakleśāḥ sarve kāmaugha ityucyate | rūpārūpyadhātukabhabaugho 'pyevam | sarvā dṛṣṭayo dṛṣṭayaughaḥ | avidyā avidyaughaḥ | (pṛ) ogheṣu kasmāt dṛṣṭyaughaḥ pṛthagucyate | nāsraveṣu | (u) tīrthikā bahavo dṛṣṭivāhitāḥ | ata ogheṣu pṛthagucyate | cyutiṃ bahatīti oghaḥ | trīn bhavān badhnātīti bandhaḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) The four floods are: the flood of sensual desire (<s>kāmaugha</s>), the flood of existence (<s>bhavaugha</s>), the flood of views (<s>dṛṣṭyaugha</s>), and the flood of ignorance (<s>avidyaugha</s>). What are these? (Answer) Excluding views and ignorance, all other defilements of the desire realm are called the flood of sensual desire. The flood of existence pertaining to the form and formless realms is likewise. All views constitute the flood of views. Ignorance constitutes the flood of ignorance. (Question) Among the floods, why is the flood of views stated separately, but not among the outflows? (Answer) Many <s>tīrthikas</s> are carried away by views. Therefore among the floods it is stated separately. 'Flood' (<s>ogha</s>) means that which carries one away from the [good] destiny. 'Bond' (<s>bandha</s>) means that which binds one to the three existences.

body.text: (pṛ) catvāryupādānāni- kāmopādānaṃ dṛṣṭyupādānaṃ śīlavratopādānamātmavādopādānamiti | katamānīmāni | (u) ātmano 'bhāvāt tadvādopādānamātmavādopādānam | astyātmeti paśyato 'ntadvayaṃ bhavati- ayamātmā nityo 'nityoveti | anitya ityavadhārayan pañcakāmaguṇānupādatte | nāsti paraloka iti dṛṣṭasukha āsajyate | nitya ityavadhārayan mandendriyaḥ pāralaukikasukhamākāṃkṣamāṇaḥ śīlavratamupādatte | kiñcittīkṣṇendriya evaṃ cintayati- yadi jīvo nityaḥ tadā aduḥkhasukhavikāraḥ, tadā puṇyapāpābhāvāditi mithyādṛṣṭimutpādayati | evamātmavādamupādāyaiva catvāryupādānāni bhavanti |
body.translated_text: (Question) The four clingings (<s>upādāna</s>) are: clinging to sensual pleasures (<s>kāmopādāna</s>), clinging to views (<s>dṛṣṭyupādāna</s>), clinging to rules and observances (<s>śīlavratopādāna</s>), and clinging to the doctrine of self (<s>ātmavādopādāna</s>). What are these? (Answer) Because the self does not exist, the clinging to the doctrine of self is the assertion [of its existence]. For one who sees 'the self exists,' there arise two extremes: 'Is this self permanent or impermanent?' One who determines 'It is impermanent' clings to the five strands of sensual pleasure. [Thinking] 'There is no other world,' he becomes attached to the happiness of what is directly visible. One who determines 'It is permanent,' being of dull faculties, desiring happiness in the other world, clings to rules and observances. But one of sharp faculties thinks thus: 'If the living being (<s>jīva</s>) is permanent, then it is without the transformation of suffering and happiness; then, because of the non-existence of merit and sin,' he generates wrong view. Thus, depending on the doctrine of self itself, the four clingings arise.

body.text: (pṛ) catvāro granthāḥ abhidhyākāyagrantho vyāpādaḥ kāyagranthaḥ śīlavrataparāmarśaḥ kāyagranthaḥ idaṃ satyābhiniveśaḥ kāyagrantha iti | katama ime | (u) paradravyābhidhyayā anyasminnadadati dveṣabuddhimutpādayati, kaśāśastrādinā [gṛhṇāti] | gṛhasthānāmidaṃ vigrahamūlam, sukhāntanuvartanamityucyate | yaḥ śīlavrataparāmarśakaḥ kāmayate anena śīlavratena viśuddhiṃ labheya iti | tasyedameva tathyamanyanmithyeti dṛṣṭirbhavati | idaṃ pravrajitānāṃ vivādamūlaṃ, duḥkhāntānuvartanamityucyate | pañca skandhāḥ kāya ityucyante | catvāra ime granthā avaśyaṃ kāyavāṅmayā iti kāyagrantha ityucyante | kecidāhuḥ- catvāra ime dharmā jananamaraṇe saṅgra 'thnantīti granthāḥ |
body.translated_text: (Question) The four fetters (<s>grantha</s>) are: the fetter of the body of covetousness (<s>abhidhyākāyagrantha</s>), the fetter of the body of ill-will (<s>vyāpādakāyagrantha</s>), the fetter of the body of grasping at rules and observances (<s>śīlavrataparāmarśakāyagrantha</s>), and the fetter of the body of dogmatic clinging to [the view] 'this alone is truth' (<s>idaṃsatyābhiniveśakāyagrantha</s>). What are these? (Answer) Through covetousness for another's property, one who does not give to another generates a mind of hatred and seizes [the property] with whips, weapons, and the like. This is the root of conflict for householders and is called 'following the pursuit of pleasure.' One who grasps at rules and observances desires: 'Through these rules and observances, may I obtain purification.' For him, there arises the view: 'This alone is true; the other is false.' This is the root of conflict for renunciants and is called 'following the pursuit of suffering.' The five aggregates are called 'body' (<s>kāya</s>). These four fetters necessarily involve body and speech — therefore they are called 'fetters of the body.' Some say: 'These four <s>dharmas</s> tie [beings] in the knot of birth and death — therefore they are called fetters (<s>grantha</s>).'

body.text: (pṛ) pañca nīvaraṇāni- kāmacchando vyāpādaḥ styānamiddhaṃ auddhatyakukṛtyaṃ vicikitsā ceti | katamānīmāni | (u) puruṣasya kāmeṣu abhiniveśādvyāpādo 'nuvartate | yathoktaṃ sūtre- tṛṣṇāta utpadyate vyāpādaḥ | īrṣyādayaḥ kleśāḥ kaśāśastrādiduścaritāni ca kāmacchandādutpadyante iti | puruṣo 'yaṃ kāyacittayo rāgadveṣaparikṣipyamāṇayorbahuvyāpāraiḥ
body.translated_text: (Question) The five hindrances (<s>nīvaraṇa</s>) are: sensual desire (<s>kāmacchanda</s>), ill-will (<s>vyāpāda</s>), sloth-and-torpor (<s>styānamiddha</s>), restlessness-and-remorse (<s>auddhatyakukṛtya</s>), and doubt (<s>vicikitsā</s>). What are these? (Answer) From a person's fixation on sensual pleasures, ill-will follows. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'From craving, ill-will arises.' Defilements such as jealousy (<s>īrṣyā</s>) and the rest, and misconduct such as [employing] whips, weapons, and the like arise from sensual desire. This person, when body and mind are agitated by passion and hatred, with many activities

body.text: paricchinnayośca styānamiddhamicchati | styānamiddhena kiñcidviśramya punā rāgadveṣavikṣiptacitto na dhyānasamādhiṃ labhate | cittasya bāhyālambanānuvartanādauddhatyaṃ bhavati | aśuddhakarmakasya puruṣasya citte sadā daurmanasyakaukṛtyaṃ bhavati | vikṣiptacittatvātkaukṛtyacittatvācca sadā vicikitsate- vimuktirasti naveti | yathā rājakumāro 'ciravataṃ śramaṇoddeśamavocat |
body.translated_text: and when exhausted, desires sloth-and-torpor. Having rested a little through sloth-and-torpor, with a mind again distracted by passion and hatred, he does not obtain <s>dhyāna</s> and <s>samādhi</s>. From the mind following external objects, restlessness (<s>auddhatya</s>) arises. For a person of impure conduct, in the mind there is always displeasure-and-remorse (<s>daurmanasyakaukṛtya</s>). Because of having a distracted mind and a remorseful mind, one constantly doubts: 'Does liberation exist or not?' Just as the royal prince <s>Aciravata</s> said to the novice monk (<s>śramaṇoddeśa</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) kasmānnīvaraṇamityākhyā | (u) kāmacchando vyāpādaśca śīlaskandhaṃ nivṛṇutaḥ | auddhatyakukṛtyaṃ samādhiskandhaṃ nivṛṇoti | sthānamitthaṃ prajñāskandham | kecit teṣāṃ nīvaraṇānāṃ varjanāya vadanti- idaṃ kuśalamidamakuśalamiti | sa tatra vicikitsate kimasti kiṃ vā nāstīti | sā vicikitsā siddhā skandhatrayaṃ nivṛṇoti | eṣu pañcasu nīvaraṇeṣu trīṇi dṛḍhabalānīti kevalaṃ nīvaraṇamityucyante | anye dve nīvaraṇe tanubale iti dvau dharmau sāṃsargikau | ime dve nīvaraṇe jananakāraṇasahite ityataḥ sāṃsargike ityucyeta | styānamiddhasya pañcadharmāḥ pratyayā yaduta cāñcalyamaratirvijṛmbhikā, āhāre 'mātratā cetaso 'valīnatā iti | auddhatyakaukṛtyasya catvāro dharmāḥ pratyayāḥ- jñātivitarko janapadaḥvitarko 'maraṇavitarkaḥ, pūrvatanīnakrīḍitasukhitālāpitahasitānusmaraṇamiti | imāni jananakāraṇāni | pratipakṣo 'pi samānaḥ | styānamiddhasya prajñā pratipakṣaḥ | auddhatyakukṛtyasya samādhiḥ pratipakṣaḥ | nivāraṇamapi samānam | ime dve sāṃsargike nīvaraṇe | ime pañcadharmā nīvaraṇāni vā bhavanti | anīvaraṇāni vā bhavanti | kāmadhātvāptā akuśalā nīvaraṇāni | anyātrānīvaraṇāni |
body.translated_text: (Question) Why are they designated 'hindrances' (<s>nīvaraṇa</s>)? (Answer) Sensual desire and ill-will obstruct the aggregate of moral conduct (<s>śīlaskandha</s>). Restlessness-and-remorse obstruct the aggregate of concentration (<s>samādhiskandha</s>). Sloth-and-torpor [obstruct] the aggregate of wisdom (<s>prajñāskandha</s>). Some, for the purpose of averting those hindrances, say: 'This is wholesome, this is unwholesome.' He doubts therein: 'Does it exist or does it not exist?' That doubt, once established, obstructs all three aggregates. Among these five hindrances, three have strong power — therefore they alone are called 'hindrances.' The other two hindrances have weak power — therefore those two <s>dharmas</s> are composite (<s>sāṃsargika</s>). These two hindrances are said to be composite because they include their generative causes. The five conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>) of sloth-and-torpor are: restlessness (<s>cāñcalya</s>), discontent (<s>arati</s>), yawning (<s>vijṛmbhikā</s>), improper measure in food (<s>āhāre amātratā</s>), and depression of mind (<s>cetaso avalīnatā</s>). The four conditions of restlessness-and-remorse are: thought of relatives (<s>jñātivitarka</s>), thought of one's country (<s>janapadavitarka</s>), thought of immortality (<s>amaraṇavitarka</s>), and the recollection of former play, happiness, conversation, and laughter (<s>pūrvatanīnakrīḍitasukhitālāpitahasitānusmaraṇa</s>). These are the generative causes. The antidote (<s>pratipakṣa</s>) is also the same [i.e., composite]. The antidote of sloth-and-torpor is wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>). The antidote of restlessness-and-remorse is concentration (<s>samādhi</s>). The obstruction is also the same. These two are composite hindrances. These five <s>dharmas</s> are hindrances or they are not hindrances. Those belonging to the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>) that are unwholesome are hindrances. Those belonging elsewhere are not hindrances.

body.text: pañcāvarabhāgīyeṣu saṃyojaneṣu kāmacchando vyāpādaḥ śīlabrataparāmarśaḥ avaragamanārthatvādavarabhāgīyāni | tadyathā govratikaḥ saṃsiddhaḥ kāyasya bhedātparaṃ maraṇāt
body.translated_text: Among the five lower fetters (<s>pañcāvarabhāgīyasaṃyojana</s>), sensual desire (<s>kāmacchanda</s>), ill-will (<s>vyāpāda</s>), and clinging to rules and rituals (<s>śīlavrataparāmarśa</s>) are called 'lower' because they have the purpose of going to the lower [destinies]. Just as one who observes the ox-vow (<s>govratika</s>), having accomplished [the vow], after the breaking up of the body, after death

body.text: gavāṃ sahavyatāmupapadyate | asaṃsiddho narake patati | vicikitsā vairāgyasya vighnabhūtā | satkāyadṛṣṭiścaturṇāṃ mūlam | itīmāni pañca | kāmacchandavyāpādau kāmadhātornātivartete | satkāyadṛṣṭirātmabuddhernātivartate | śīlavrataparāmarśo 'varadharmānnātivartate | vicikitsā pṛthagjanatvānnātivartate | kāmacchandavyāpādau kāmadhātuṃ nātikrāmataḥ | atikrame punarākṣipyate | anyāni trīṇi pṛthagjanatvaṃ nātikrāmanti | ata ucyante 'varabhāgīyānīti |
body.translated_text: is reborn in the company of cattle. If not accomplished, one falls into hell. Doubt (<s>vicikitsā</s>) obstructs dispassion. The view of the personal self (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>) is the root of the [other] four. These are the five. Sensual desire and ill-will do not go beyond the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>). The view of the personal self does not go beyond the notion of self (<s>ātmabuddhi</s>). Clinging to rules and rituals does not go beyond the lower <s>dharmas</s>. Doubt does not go beyond the state of an ordinary being (<s>pṛthagjanatva</s>). Sensual desire and ill-will do not transcend the desire realm. Upon transcending it, one is drawn back again. The other three do not transcend the state of an ordinary being. Therefore they are called 'lower' (<s>avarabhāgīya</s>).

body.text: pañcordhvabhāgīyāni [auddhatyaṃ māno 'vidyā rūparāgaḥ arūparāgaḥ |] auddhatyasya dhyānasamādhividhātitvānna cittamupaśāmyati | idamauddhatyasya nimittagrahānuvartanānmānaḥ pravartate | nimittagrāhi cittamidamavidyāsambhūtamityato rūparāgo 'rūparāgaśca staḥ | tāni pañca saṃyojanāni śaikṣajanānāmūrdhvasamudācaraṇārthatvādūrdhvabhāgīyānītyucyante | tāni śaikṣajanānāṃ citta ucyante na pṛthagjanānām | (pṛ) auddhatyaṃ kasmāt rūpārūpyadhātukaṃ saṃyojanaṃ na kāmadhātukam | (u) tatra sthūlakleśābhāvādauddhatyaṃ vyaktaṃ bhavati | tadauddhatyaṃ samādhibhaṅge balavadityataḥ saṃyojanamityucyate | tadūrdhvabhāgīyaṃ samucchedayato vimuktirlabhyate | keṣāñcit rūpe ārūpye ca vimuktisaṃjñā bhavati | tatpratiṣedhāyocyate santyūrdhvabhāgīyāni saṃyojanānīti |
body.translated_text: The five upper fetters (<s>pañcordhvabhāgīya</s>) [are: restlessness (<s>auddhatya</s>), conceit (<s>māna</s>), ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), passion for the form realm (<s>rūparāga</s>), and passion for the formless realm (<s>arūparāga</s>).] Because of restlessness's disruption of <s>dhyāna</s> and <s>samādhi</s>, the mind does not become tranquil. Conceit operates through following this grasping of the sign [of restlessness]. Ignorance is born from this mind that grasps signs — therefore passion for the form realm and passion for the formless realm exist. These five fetters are called 'upper' (<s>ūrdhvabhāgīya</s>) because they pertain to the higher operation of those in training (<s>śaikṣa</s>). They are called [fetters] of those in training — not of ordinary beings. (Question) Why is restlessness a fetter of the form and formless realms and not of the desire realm? (Answer) Because in those [higher realms], gross defilements are absent, restlessness becomes clearly manifest. That restlessness, being powerful in the disruption of <s>samādhi</s>, is therefore called a 'fetter.' By completely cutting off those upper fetters, liberation is obtained. For some, the perception of liberation arises in the form realm and the formless realm. To refute that, it is said: 'There are upper fetters.'

body.text: pañca mātsaryāṇi- āvāsamātsaryaṃ, kulamātsaryaṃ, lābhamātsaryaṃ, varṇamātsaryaṃ dharmamātsaryamiti | [tatra] āvāsamātsaryam- ahameva atra vasāmīti nānyān prayojayati | kulamātsaryam- kulamidamahameva praviśāmīti nānyān prayojayati | satsvapyanyeṣu ahamevotkṛṣṭa iti | lābhamātsaryamiti- ahamevātra dānaṃ lapsya mānyebhyaḥ prayacchatu iti | anye santyo 'pi mā māmatikrāmantu | varṇamātsaryam- māmeva varṇaya, mānyān | anyān varṇayannapi mā māmatiricyatu iti | dharmamātsaryam- ahameva dvādaśāṅgapravacanārthaṃ jānāmi | gabhīramartharahasyaṃ jānannapi na pravadāmīti |
body.translated_text: The five kinds of avarice (<s>mātsarya</s>) are: avarice regarding dwelling-place (<s>āvāsamātsarya</s>), avarice regarding families (<s>kulamātsarya</s>), avarice regarding gains (<s>lābhamātsarya</s>), avarice regarding praise (<s>varṇamātsarya</s>), and avarice regarding the <s>Dharma</s> (<s>dharmamātsarya</s>). 'Avarice regarding dwelling-place' — 'I alone shall dwell here' and one does not encourage others [to stay]. 'Avarice regarding families' — 'I alone shall enter this family' and one does not encourage others. Even though others exist [who could visit], [one thinks:] 'I alone am superior.' 'Avarice regarding gains' — 'I alone shall receive the gift here; let others give elsewhere.' Even though others are present, 'May they not surpass me!' 'Avarice regarding praise' — 'Praise me alone, not others.' Even when praising others, 'May he not surpass me!' 'Avarice regarding the <s>Dharma</s>' — 'I alone know the meaning of the twelve-fold teaching (<s>dvādaśāṅgapravacana</s>).' Even knowing profound and secret meanings, 'I will not expound them.'

body.text: (pṛ) pañca mātsaryāṇāṃ ke doṣāḥ | (u) ima āvāsādayo bahūnāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ sādhāraṇāḥ | ayantu svakulaṃ tyaktvā sādhāraṇabhūteṣu mātsaryamutpādayati | ityayaṃ doṣakleśaḥ | sa vimukternaiva bhāgī bhavati | kasmāt | sa sādhāraṇabhūtān dharmāneva na tyajati | kaḥ punarvādaḥ
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults of the five kinds of avarice? (Answer) These dwelling-places and the rest are common to many persons. But this person, having abandoned his own family, generates avarice toward things that are common. This is the fault of this defilement. He is never a partaker of liberation. Why? He does not relinquish even <s>dharmas</s> that are common — what more need be said

body.text: svīyān pañca skandhān tyajatīti | sa ca pretādīnāṃ durupapattyāyataneṣu patati | lābhanivṛttacittasya māna utpadyate | sajjanānanyān laghūkṛtya narake patati | anyebhyo dānabhaṅgānmanuṣyadehaṃ lābhamāno daridro bhavati | mātsaryacittena dātarguṇaṃ pratigrahīturdeyañca samucchedayatītyato gurutaraṃ pāpaṃ labhate | dharmamatsaro 'ndhādipāpabhāgbhavati | tadyathā jātyandhasya sapatnabahulānāñca janma na svātantrayaprāpakam | āryagarbhācca parihīyate | triṣu adhvasu daśasu dikṣu [gatānāṃ] buddhānāṃ śatruḥ san saṃsāre saṃsaran sadā mūḍho bhavati | sajjanān dūrīkaroti | sajjanadūrīkaraṇādakuśalaṃ vinā na vartate | akuśalaṃ trividham- akuśalākuśalaṃ mahākuśalaṃ akuśalamadhyākuśalamiti | akuśalaṃ prāṇātipātādattādānādi | mahākuśalaṃ yadātmahananaṃ, parastyātmahananasamādāpanaṃ, svayaṃ mātsarya[karaṇaṃ] parasya mātsaryasamādāpanam | sa dharmamātsaryeṇa bahūn puruṣānukuśale pātayati | buddhadharmamārgañca kṣapayati | yathoktaṃ sūtre- santyāvāsamātsaryasya pañca doṣāḥ- anāgatasya subhikṣorāgamanāya necchati | āgataṃ punastarjayanna tṛpyati | gamanāyānucintayati | saṅghadeyaṃ gopayati | saṅghadeyeṣu ātmīyabuddhiṃ karoti | kulamātsaryasya pañca doṣāḥ- kulābhiniveśādavadātavasanaistulyasukhaduḥkho bhavati | dhanāyāvadātavasanaṃ prajahāti | pratigrahīturdānaṃ labhate | tadubhayaprahāṇāttasmin kule varcaḥ kuṭyāṃ bhūtatvāyotpadyate | lābhamātsaryasya pañca doṣāḥ- sadā sambhārasambhavāya klamati | dvayorbhedena lābhī bhavati | sajjanān nindati sadā daurmanasyacittaḥ | varṇamātsaryasya pañca doṣāḥ- anyeṣāṃ varṇaṃ śrutvā vyākulakaṣāyacitto bhavati | śatasahasreṣu lokeṣu aśuddhacittaḥ sajjanānadhikṣipati | ātmonnatyā parānavanamati | duryaśo 'ntardhāpayati iti | sarveṣāṃ mātsaryāṇāṃ sāmānyata ime doṣāḥ santi- prabhūtadhanasañcayaḥ | pariṣadbhīrutā, bahujanavidveṣitā, sadā vyākulacittatā, ātmanaḥ sadaikākitā, avarakule janma ityevamādayo 'pramāṇāḥ pañcamātsaryāṇāṃ doṣāḥ |
body.translated_text: of relinquishing one's own five aggregates! And he falls into the difficult-to-arise destinations of hungry ghosts (<s>preta</s>) and the like. One whose mind is turned away from gains generates conceit. Disparaging virtuous persons, he falls into hell. Through obstructing others' gifts, when obtaining a human body, he becomes destitute. With an avaricious mind, by destroying the virtues of the giver and the gift and the recipient — from that, one obtains extremely grave sin. One avaricious regarding the <s>Dharma</s> becomes a partaker of sins such as congenital blindness and the like. Just as the birth of the congenitally blind, and those with many enemies — birth that does not bring independence. And one falls away from the embryo of nobility (<s>āryagarbha</s>). Being an enemy of the <s>Buddhas</s> of the three time-periods and the ten directions, wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>, one is always deluded. One distances oneself from virtuous persons. Because of distancing from virtuous persons, one does not proceed without the unwholesome. The unwholesome is threefold: unwholesome-unwholesome, great-unwholesome, and middling-unwholesome. 'Unwholesome' is taking life, taking what is not given, and the like. 'Great unwholesome' is self-killing, inducing another to kill himself, oneself practicing avarice, and inducing another to practice avarice. Through <s>Dharma</s>-avarice, one causes many persons to fall into the unwholesome. And one destroys the path of the <s>Buddha-Dharma</s>. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There are five faults of avarice regarding dwelling-place: one does not wish a prosperous newcomer to come. One is not satisfied with threatening those who have arrived. One plans for their departure. One hides what belongs to the <s>Saṅgha</s>. And regarding what belongs to the <s>Saṅgha</s>, one generates the notion of ownership.' The five faults of avarice regarding families: through attachment to families, one becomes equal in pleasure and suffering with the white-robed [householders]. For the sake of wealth, one abandons the white-robed [identity]. The recipient obtains a gift. Through the destruction of both [family and renunciant roles], in that family, one is reborn as an insect in a house due to [the force of] that existence. The five faults of avarice regarding gains: one always toils for the arising of provisions. Through the division of the two [parties], one becomes a gainer. One always disparages virtuous persons with a mind of displeasure. The five faults of avarice regarding praise: hearing the praise of others, one becomes agitated and disturbed in mind. In hundreds of thousands of worlds, with an impure mind, one disparages virtuous persons. Through self-elevation, one looks down on others. One conceals ill repute. The general faults of all forms of avarice are: the accumulation of abundant wealth, fear of assemblies, being hated by many people, always having a disturbed mind, always being alone, birth in an inferior family — such and similar immeasurable faults belong to the five kinds of avarice.

body.text: pañca cetaḥ khilāḥ- [ihāyuṣmanto bhikṣuḥ] śāstari vicikitsate, dharme vicikitsate, śīle vicikitsate, śikṣāyāṃ vicikitsate | yo bhikṣuḥ śāsturmahāpuruṣāṇāñca
body.translated_text: The five mental barrennesses (<s>cetaḥkhila</s>) are: [Here, friends, a monk] doubts the Teacher; doubts the <s>Dharma</s>; doubts moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>); doubts the training (<s>śikṣā</s>). And the monk who, when someone praises the Teacher and great persons

body.text: varṇavādī, tasmin jane anāttamanā āhatacitto bhavati | ayaṃ pañcamaḥ | śāstari vicikitsaka evaṃ cintayati- kiṃ śāstā mahān, kiṃ vā pūraṇādayaḥ iti | dharme vicikitsaka [evaṃ cintayati] kiṃ śāstuḥ pravacanamutkṛṣṭamuta vedasyeti | śīle vicikitsate kiṃ śāstṛproktaṃ pravacanamutkṛṣṭaṃ, kiṃ vā kukkaṭaśvādivratamiti | śikṣāyāṃ vicikitsate kiṃ mānapānādi dharmo nirvāṇaṃ gamayati uta neti | anāttamanā āhata [citto] vyāpādabuddhyā bhayagauravacittaṃ vinā sajjanān garhayati | ebhiḥ pañcabhiḥ dharmairvipraluptacitto, na nānākuśalendriyāṇyavaṣṭambhayati | ataścetaḥ khila ityucyate |
body.translated_text: — toward that person, one becomes displeased and hostile in mind. This is the fifth. One who doubts the Teacher thinks thus: 'Is the Teacher great, or are <s>Pūraṇa</s> and the others [great]?' One who doubts the <s>Dharma</s> [thinks]: 'Is the Teacher's doctrine superior, or is the <s>Veda</s>'s?' One who doubts moral conduct [thinks]: 'Is the conduct taught by the Teacher superior, or are the vows of the cock, dog, and the like?' One who doubts the training [thinks]: 'Do the <s>dharmas</s> of mindfulness such as mindfulness of breathing and the like lead to <s>Nirvāṇa</s>, or not?' One who is displeased and hostile in mind — through a mind of malice, without the mind of fear and reverence, one censures virtuous persons. Through these five <s>dharmas</s>, one's mind is despoiled, and one does not steady the various wholesome faculties. Therefore it is called 'mental barrenness' (<s>cetaḥkhila</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) kasmācchāstrādau vicikitsate | (u) so 'bahuśratatvādvicikitsate | bahuśrutasya tu vicikitsā ālpīyasī bhavati | sa ca bālo mūḍho 'jño na tathāgatadharmānyadharmayorvivekaṃ prajānāti | ato vicikitsate | dharme ca nāsvādaṃ labhate | ataśca | vicikitsate | na ca vedadīn granthān śṛṇoti adhyeti vā | janairvarṇitaṃ śrutvā utkṛṣṭacittamutpādayati | adhvanyadhvani bahulamithyāvicikitsaḥ sadā kaluṣitacittatayā śāstrādau vicikitsate | yathā śāsturupasthāyakaḥ sunakṣatraḥ | sa ca mithyādṛṣṭibahulaiḥ puruṣaiḥ samānakṛtyatayā vicikitsate | kiñca vedavyākaraṇādīni mithyādṛṣṭisūtrāṇyadhīyānaḥ paribhinnasamyakprajño bhavati ityato vicikitsate | dharmāṇāṃ [yathāśrute] 'rthe prītaḥ kusmṛtiṃ janayan na sūtrakṛdāśayaṃ labdhuṃ śaknoti | ato vicikitsate sarvadā svahitālābhapratyayataḥ śāstrādiṣu vicikitsate |
body.translated_text: (Question) Why does one doubt the Teacher and the rest? (Answer) He doubts because of being unlearned. For one of great learning, doubt is slight. And this foolish, deluded, ignorant person does not know the distinction between the <s>dharmas</s> of the <s>Tathāgata</s> and other <s>dharmas</s>. Therefore he doubts. And he does not obtain the relish of the <s>Dharma</s>. Therefore too he doubts. And he does not hear or study texts such as the <s>Vedas</s> and the like. Having heard the praise by others, he generates a mind of elevation. In journey after journey, with abundant wrong doubts, always with a defiled mind, he doubts the Teacher and the rest. Just as <s>Sunakṣatra</s>, the attendant of the Teacher. And through association with persons abundant in wrong views, he doubts. Moreover, studying <s>Vedas</s>, grammars, and the like — <s>sūtras</s> of wrong views — he has his right wisdom destroyed, and therefore he doubts. Being pleased with the literal meaning of <s>dharmas</s> as heard, generating wrong recollection, he is unable to obtain the intention of the <s>sūtra</s>-composer. Therefore he doubts. Always, from the condition of not obtaining one's own welfare, he doubts the Teacher and the rest.

body.text: pañca cetaso vinibandhāḥ- yaḥ kāyo 'vigatarāgo sa kāya āsajyate | kāmeṣvavītarāgaḥ kāmeṣvāsajyate | gṛhasthena prabrajitasya samāgamaḥ | āryavacane ceto na prahṛṣyati | alpahitavastunātmānaṃ pūrṇaṃ manyate | tatra catvāro vinibandhāḥ kāmarāgamupādāyodbhavanti | ya ādhyātmikātmabhāve 'vigatarāgaḥ sa bāhyarūpādikāmeṣvāsajyate | ata ubhayoḥ samāgamamabhilaṣati | abhilāṣāvyākulatayā āryavacane upaśamapradarśane dharme na prahṛṣyati | ataḥ śīlabāhuśrutyadhyānasamādhyādiṣvalpaṃ hitaṃ vastu labdhvā tenātmānaṃ pūrṇaṃ manyate | tadalpahitavastvabhiniveśānmahāhitaṃ vismarati | prājñastu nālpahitābhiniviṣṭo mahāhitaṃ vighnayet |
body.translated_text: The five mental fetters (<s>cetaso vinibandha</s>) are: One who has not abandoned passion for the body is attached to the body. One who has not abandoned passion for sensual pleasures is attached to sensual pleasures. Association of a householder with a renunciant. The mind does not delight in the words of the Noble Ones. One considers oneself fulfilled with a small beneficial thing. Therein, four fetters arise depending on sensual passion (<s>kāmarāga</s>). One who has not abandoned passion for the inner self-existence is attached to external sensual pleasures of form and the like. Therefore one desires the association of both. Because of the agitation of desire, one does not delight in the <s>Dharma</s> that demonstrates tranquility through the words of the Noble Ones. Therefore, having obtained only a small beneficial thing in moral conduct, learning, <s>dhyāna</s>, concentration, and the like, one considers oneself fulfilled. Because of clinging to that small beneficial thing, one forgets what is greatly beneficial. But the wise one, not clinging to what is of small benefit, would not obstruct what is of great benefit.

body.text: ayaṃ yadyaṣṭākṣaṇavihīnaḥ [saḥ] puruṣakāyaṃ duṣkaraṃ labdhvavānityataścittaikāgryeṇa vīryamārabheta | pṛthagjanatā cāśraddheyā | asya samagrasya pratyayasya vigame 'nye pratyayā bhavanti | [iti] naivāryamārge 'vatarati [pṛthagjanaḥ] | alpahitamakāmayamānaḥ pravrajyāphalavipākaṃ labhate | mriyamāṇaśca na vipratisarati | svaparahitañca karoti | saguṇeṣveva nābhiniviśate | kaḥ punarvādo 'kuśale dharme | ataḥ [sa] samyagācāra ityucyate | pṛthagjanādīnavā na kimapi saṃkleśayanti |
body.translated_text: If this [person] is free from the eight unfavorable conditions (<s>aṣṭākṣaṇa</s>), having obtained the difficult-to-obtain human body, he should then undertake effort with one-pointed mind. And the state of being an ordinary person (<s>pṛthagjana</s>) is not to be trusted. When the totality of his conditions disappears, other conditions arise — thus the ordinary person does not enter the noble path. One who does not desire small benefit obtains the ripened fruit of going forth (<s>pravrajyā</s>). And at the time of dying, he does not have remorse. He accomplishes what is beneficial for both himself and others. He does not cling even to virtuous qualities — what need to speak of unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>? Therefore he is said to be of right conduct. The dangers of being an ordinary person do not trouble him in any way.

body.text: (pṛ) ke pṛthagjanānāmādīnavāḥ | (u) sūtra uktaṃ- pṛthagjano viṃśatidhā svacittaṃ nigṛhyaivaṃ cintayet- mama vibhinnākāraveṣamātrasya vṛthā, na kiñcillabhyam, aśubhena [pathā] mariṣyāmi, mahābhayārṇave patiṣyāmi, tadbhayasthāne na jñāsyāmyabhayasthānaṃ, nāpi jñāsyāmi mārgaṃ, na dhyānasamādhīn lapsye, asakṛtkāyaduḥkhamanubhaviṣyāmi, duṣparihārā bhaviṣyantyaṣṭāvakṣaṇāḥ, śatruḥ sadānusariṣyati, sarve mārgā vivṛtāḥ, durgateravimokṣaḥ, apramāṇadṛṣṭibhiḥ sadā vinibandhaḥ, pañcasvānantaryeṣu apratibandhaḥ, anādiḥ saṃsāro nāntavān, akurvato na puṇyapāpapratilābhaḥ | kuśalākuśalayorna pratinidhilābhaḥ | na saddharma karomi, naivāsti sukhalayaḥ kṛtayoḥ kuśalākuśalayornaiva vismṛtirvināśo vā āmaraṇaṃ na dānto bhaviṣyāmi iti | ete viṃśatidharmāḥ kaṃ na dūṣayanti | kartavyamayaṃ kṛtavānityataścittaṃ na vipratisarati | [kāmā]bhiniviṣṭhasya gārhasthyadharmaḥ pravrajyādharmaścana sidhyataḥ | ato nālpahite 'bhiniveśet |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the dangers of being an ordinary person? (Answer) It is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'An ordinary person should discipline his own mind in twenty ways and reflect thus: "For me, of diverse appearance, garb, and measure, [all is] in vain; nothing is obtained. I shall die by an unwholesome path and fall into the great ocean of fear. In that place of fear, I shall not know the place of safety; nor shall I know the path; nor shall I obtain <s>dhyāna</s> and concentration. Repeatedly I shall experience bodily suffering. The eight unfavorable conditions will be difficult to avoid. The enemy will always pursue me. All paths are exposed. There is no liberation from a bad destiny. There is always bondage through immeasurable views. There is no protection against the five heinous crimes (<s>ānantarya</s>). <s>Saṃsāra</s> is beginningless and without end. Without acting, there is no obtaining of merit or sin. Of the wholesome and the unwholesome, there is no obtaining in exchange. I do not practice the true <s>Dharma</s>. There is no shelter of happiness. Of the wholesome and unwholesome that have been done, there is neither forgetfulness nor destruction. Until death, I shall not be tamed."' These twenty <s>dharmas</s> — whom do they not corrupt? [But one who reflects:] 'I have done what was to be done' — his mind does not have remorse. For one who is attached to sensual pleasures, neither the household <s>dharma</s> nor the <s>dharma</s> of going forth succeeds. Therefore one should not cling to what is of small benefit.

body.text: saptānuśayāḥ | (pṛ) kleśāḥ kasmādanuśaya ityucyante | (u) jananamaraṇasantāne sadā sattvamanurvartata ityanuśayaḥ | tadyathā dhātrī sadā bālamanuvartate | yathā vāvimukto vātajvaraḥ | yathā vā ṛṇī anudinamucchavasati | yathā vā anapagatamākhuviṣam | taptāyasaḥ kṛṣṇalakṣaṇam | yathā vā yavasyāḍkuraḥ | svayaṃdattadāsapatratvam | yathā vā praṇaṣṭasya vastunaḥ sākṣijanaḥ | yathā prajñā kramaśaḥ samupacīyamānā[sti] | yathā karma sadopacīyāmānam | yathā jvālā santanyate | evaṃ krameṇa santatyā vardhata ityanuśaya ityucyate |
body.translated_text: The seven latent tendencies (<s>anuśaya</s>). (Question) Why are defilements called 'latent tendencies'? (Answer) Because they constantly follow the being throughout the continuity of birth and death — [therefore they are called] latent tendencies. Just as a nurse constantly follows a child. Or just as an unreleased wind-fever. Or just as a debtor sighs day after day. Or just as unremoved rat-poison. Like the black mark on heated iron. Or just as the sprout of barley. Like the document of one who has given himself as a slave. Or just as the witnesses of a lost property. Just as wisdom gradually accumulated exists. Just as <s>karma</s> constantly accumulated. Just as a flame continues in succession. Thus, growing gradually in continuity — that is called 'latent tendency.'

body.text: (pṛ) ayamanuśayaḥ kiṃ cittasamprayuktaḥ kiṃ vā cittaviprayuktaḥ | (u) cittasamprayuktaḥ | kasmāt | rāgādayo 'nuśayalakṣaṇāḥ | ime 'nuśayalakṣaṇāḥ saumanasyasamprayuktāḥ | yadidaṃ saumanasyaṃ cittaviprayuktamitīdaṃ na yujyate | saumanasyamidaṃ yadi sukhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ vartate [tadā] rāgānuśaya ityucyate | rāgo nāmāsaṅgaḥ | cittaviprayukte nāsaṅgabhāvo 'sti | ato jñāyate 'nuśayāścittasamprayuktā iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) Is this latent tendency associated with mind (<s>cittasamprayukta</s>) or dissociated from mind (<s>cittaviprayukta</s>)? (Answer) It is associated with mind. Why? Passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the rest have the characteristic of latent tendency. These, having the characteristic of latent tendency, are associated with mental happiness (<s>saumanasya</s>). Now, the statement that this mental happiness is dissociated from mind — that is not valid. If this mental happiness operates in pleasant feeling, then it is called 'the latent tendency of passion' (<s>rāgānuśaya</s>). Passion means attachment (<s>āsaṅga</s>). In what is dissociated from mind, there is no state of attachment. Therefore it is known that the latent tendencies are associated with mind.

body.text: (pṛ) na yukta[mida]m | anuśayā na cittasamprayuktāḥ | kasmāt | uktaṃ hi sūtre- bālānāṃ maithunacittameva nāsti | kaḥ punarvādo maithunarāgasāmarthyam | rāgānuśayānuśayitāśca bhavanti iti | kiñcāha- nāsti cetanā nāsti vikalpaḥ | vijñāpratiṣṭhitamālambanañcāsti iti | kiñcoktaṃ sūtre- satkāyadṛṣṭisamucchede 'nuśayāḥ sahaiva samucchidyante iti | āryamārgaśca na kleśānāṃ yaugapadyaṃ labhate | ata āryamārgasamutpādaścittaviprayuktānuśayasamucchedakaḥ | tathā nocet āryamārgeṇa kasya samucchedaḥ syāt | yadi nāsti cittaviprayukto 'nuśayaḥ | pṛthagjanāḥ śaikṣajanāśca yadā kuśalacitte 'vyākṛtacitte ca vartante | tadā arhantaḥ syuḥ | anuśayaśca paryavasthānahetuḥ | anuśayātparyavasthānamutpadyate | paryavasthānalabdho 'nuśayo vardhate | ato jñāyate 'nuśayāścittaviprayuktā iti | yadi kaścitkuśalāvyākṛtacitto 'pi sānuśaya ityucyate | yasya nāsti cittaviprayukto 'nuśayaḥ | kuto 'nuśayavān bhavati | ato jāyate 'nuśayaścittaviprayukta iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) That is not valid. The latent tendencies are not associated with mind. Why? For it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Infants do not even have the thought of sexual intercourse — what need to speak of the capacity for sexual passion? Yet they are underlain by the latent tendency of passion.' Furthermore, it says: 'There is no volition, there is no conceptual discrimination, yet there is an object in which consciousness is established.' Furthermore, it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'When the view of the personal aggregate (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>) is eradicated, the latent tendencies are eradicated together with it.' And the noble path does not occur simultaneously with defilements. Therefore, the arising of the noble path eradicates the latent tendencies that are dissociated from mind. If it were not so, what would the noble path eradicate? If there is no latent tendency dissociated from mind, then ordinary persons and learners (<s>śaikṣa</s>), when they are in a wholesome or indeterminate mind, would be <s>Arhats</s>. And the latent tendency is the cause of [active] envelopment (<s>paryavasthāna</s>). From the latent tendency, envelopment arises. The latent tendency obtained through envelopment grows. Therefore it is known that the latent tendencies are dissociated from mind. If someone, even while having wholesome or indeterminate mind, is said to have latent tendencies — [then] for one who has no latent tendency dissociated from mind, how could he be one who has latent tendencies? Therefore it is known that the latent tendency is dissociated from mind.

body.text: atrocyate | na yuktamidam | yaduktaṃ bālānāmasati rāge rāgānuśayo 'stīti | tadayuktam | bālānāṃ rāgāpanayanauṣadhālābhādaprahīṇakāmarāgā ityato rāgānuśayo 'nuśete | yathā bhūtasamāviṣṭo 'nudbhavakāle 'pi bhūtasamāviṣṭa ityucyate | kasmāt | tadvyādhipraśamanamantroṣadhānāmalābhāt | yathā ca caturdinajvarārto dinadvaye [jvarā]nudbhave 'pi jvarārta ityucyate | yathā vā ākhuviṣamanapanītavyādhitvāddhanagarjane prādurbhavati | evaṃ yasmin citte 'nuśayāpanayanamoṣadhamapratilabdham | [tat] aprahīṇā[nuśaya]mityucyate | anye 'pi praśnāḥ sāmānyataḥ pratyuktā eva | yaducyate bhavatā nāsti cetanā nāsti vikalpaḥ vijñānasyamālambanamasti iti | tadapi aprahīṇānuśayatvāt | yadāha bhavān- satkāyadṛṣṭiranuśayena saha samucchidyata iti | bhavataḥ paryavasthānaṃ cittasamprayuktam | anutpattikāle |
body.translated_text: Here it is replied: That is not valid. Your statement that 'for infants, even without passion, the latent tendency of passion exists' — that is not valid. For infants, because of not obtaining the medicine for removing passion, their sensual passion is unabandoned — therefore the latent tendency of passion lies latent. Just as one possessed by a spirit, even at the time when [the spirit] has not manifested, is called 'spirit-possessed.' Why? Because of not obtaining the mantra-medicine for pacifying that disease. And just as one afflicted by a four-day fever, even on the two days when the fever has not manifested, is called 'afflicted by fever.' Or just as rat-poison, because the disease has not been removed, manifests at the roar of thunder. In the same way, a mind in which the medicine for removing latent tendencies has not been obtained — that is called 'one whose latent tendencies are unabandoned.' The other questions too have been answered in general terms. Your statement that 'there is no volition, there is no conceptual discrimination, yet there is an object of consciousness' — that too is because of the unabandoned state of latent tendencies. Your statement that 'the view of the personal aggregate is eradicated together with the latent tendencies' — according to your [view], envelopment (<s>paryavasthāna</s>) is associated with mind. At the time of non-arising,

body.text: prahīṇameva | evamanuśayo 'pi | āryamārgakāle 'vidyamānamapi prahīṇamityucyate | virodhidharmapratilambhāt | yadbravīṣi- mārgaḥ kleśaiḥ saha naikakāliko 'stīti | [tat]aprahīṇatvādastītyucyate | yadavocaḥ pṛthagjanāḥ śaikṣajanāśca yadi kuśalāvyākṛtacittagatāḥ, tadā arhantaḥ syuriti | prahīṇa[kleśo] 'rhan | teṣāntvaprahīṇa[kleśa]tvāt | yathā kaścinmāsavarjanadharmamasamādāno māṃsamabhuñjannapi na varjitamāṃsa ityucyate | avidyāmithyāsmṛtimithyāsaṅkalpādayaḥ santītyato 'prahīṇāḥ kleśāstadā samutpadyante | arhatastu nāsti saheturiti nānyaiḥ sāmyam | yaduktaṃ tvayā paryavasthānalabdho 'nuśayastu vardhata iti | tadayuktam | sarve kleśā uttamamadhyamāvaradharmairvardhante, na paryavasthānalābhāt | yadbraṣīṣi kuśalāvyākṛtacittagato 'nuśayavān syāditi | tadapi aprahīṇatvādanuśayavānityucyate | ebhiḥ kāraṇairjñāyate 'nuśayā na [citta]viprayuktā iti |
body.translated_text: it is already abandoned. The same with the latent tendency too. At the time of the noble path, even though it does not exist [manifestly], it is said to be 'abandoned' — because of the obtaining of the opposing <s>dharma</s>. Your statement that 'the path does not occur simultaneously with defilements' — [the latent tendency] is said to exist because of being unabandoned. Your statement that 'if ordinary persons and learners, when in wholesome or indeterminate mind, would be <s>Arhats</s>' — an <s>Arhat</s> is one whose defilements are abandoned. But for them, because their defilements are unabandoned, [they are not Arhats]. Just as someone who has not undertaken the vow of abstaining for one month, even though he is not eating meat, is not called 'one who has abandoned meat.' Because ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), wrong mindfulness (<s>mithyāsmṛti</s>), wrong intention (<s>mithyāsaṅkalpa</s>), and the like exist — therefore the defilements are unabandoned. They arise at that time. But for an <s>Arhat</s>, because there is no cause — therefore he is not the same as others. Your statement that 'the latent tendency obtained through envelopment grows' — that is not valid. All defilements grow through <s>dharmas</s> of superior, middling, and inferior [quality] — not through the obtaining of envelopment. Your statement that 'one in wholesome or indeterminate mind would have latent tendencies' — that too is said to have latent tendencies because of the unabandoned state. Through these reasons, it is known that the latent tendencies are not dissociated from mind.

body.text: aṣṭa mithyāmārgāḥ- mithyādṛṣṭiryāvanmithyāsamādhiriti | ayathābhūtaviparyaya jñānadarśanānmithyādṛṣṭiḥ yāvanmithyāsamādhiḥ | (pṛ) samyagājīvo mithyājīvaśca na kāyavākkarmavyatiriktau | kasmātpṛthagucyate | (u) mithyājīvaḥ pravrajitānāṃ dussamucchedatvāt pṛthagucyate | mithyājīvo [yena] māyāśāṭhyādayaḥ pañcadharmāḥ puṣṭiṃ labhante sa mithyājīvaḥ | saṃkṣipyedamucyate- pravrajitānāmakāryaṃ dhanārjanakarma yaduta rājasevāvāṇijyarogacikitsādikarma | anādeyañca prāṇidhadhanadhānyādi | ādāne mithyājīvaḥ | vinaye yatpratiṣiddhaṃ tena ca svātmajīvanaṃ mithyājīvaḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- pañca vāṇijyānyupāsakenākaraṇīyānīti | (pṛ) kena kuryājjīvitam | yathādharmabhikṣayā jīvet | na mithyājīvaṃ jīvet | kasmāt | aviśuddhacetasā saddharmaṃ praṇāśayati | mārgayogānavaṣṭambhāt | mārgāvacara evaṃ cintayet- bhagavataḥ śāsane 'vatāro mārgācaraṇārthaḥ na
body.translated_text: The eight wrong paths (<s>mithyāmārga</s>) are: wrong view (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>) up to wrong concentration (<s>mithyāsamādhi</s>). Through knowledge and vision that are perverted and not in accordance with reality — [there is] wrong view up to wrong concentration. (Question) Right livelihood (<s>samyagājīva</s>) and wrong livelihood (<s>mithyājīva</s>) are not distinct from bodily and verbal <s>karma</s>. Why are they stated separately? (Answer) Wrong livelihood is stated separately because it is difficult for renunciants to eradicate. Wrong livelihood is that through which the five <s>dharmas</s> of deception (<s>māyā</s>), flattery (<s>śāṭhya</s>), and the like flourish. In brief, this is stated: For renunciants, the improper activity of earning wealth — such as royal service, trade, medical treatment, and the like — is not to be done. And what is not to be accepted — such as the wealth, grain, and the like of living beings. To accept [such things] is wrong livelihood. Whatever is prohibited in the <s>Vinaya</s> — to live by that is wrong livelihood. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There are five trades that a lay follower (<s>upāsaka</s>) should not engage in.' (Question) By what means should one live? One should live by lawful begging (<s>dharmabhikṣā</s>). One should not live by wrong livelihood. Why? Because with an impure mind, one destroys the true <s>Dharma</s>. Because there is no firm support in the practice of the path. One who is a practitioner of the path should reflect thus: 'My entry into the teaching of the Blessed One is for the purpose of practicing the path, not

body.text: jīvanārtha iti | ataḥ saddharmābhirataḥ pariśuddhajīvanamācaret | bhikṣurbhikṣadharme suniṣṇātaḥ syāt | yo mithyājīvanamācarati, na [sa] bhikṣudharmā bhavati ||
body.translated_text: for the purpose of [mere] living.' Therefore, one who delights in the true <s>Dharma</s> should lead a purified life. A monk (<s>bhikṣu</s>) should be well-versed in the <s>dharma</s> of begging. One who practices wrong livelihood does not possess the <s>dharma</s> of a monk.

body.text: saṅkīrṇakleśavargaḥ ṣaṭtriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on Miscellaneous Defilements (<s>saṅkīrṇakleśavarga</s>).

body.text: 137 navasaṃyojanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 137. Chapter on the Nine Fetters (<s>navasaṃyojanavarga</s>)
