body.text: kiñca vimuktyarthī śīlasamādhiprajñā vimuktijñānadarśanaskandhānutpādayati | eṣāṃ ka upayogaḥ | [te] sarve kleśānāṃ nirodhāya bhavanti jñānī taddhitaṃ dṛṣṭvā tān skandhānupāśrayate | ato jñāyate kleśapratyayaḥ kāya iti | kleśāśca krameṇa nirudhyante | prahīṇatrividhasaṃyojanaḥ srotaāpattiphalabhāg bhavati | tanukāmacchandādikaḥ sakṛdāgāmiphalabhāk | prakṣīṇakāmadhātusaṃyojano 'nāgāmiphalabhāk | dhyānasamādhiṣvapi ayaṃ kramaḥ | atyantakṣīṇasarva[saṃyojanaḥ] arhatphalabhāg bhavati | evaṃ kleśānāṃ kramaśo nirodhātkāyo 'pi kramaśo nirudhyate | īśvarādikāraṇatve na syātkramanirodhaḥ | ato jñāyate kleśapratyayaḥ kāya iti | sujanā rāgādīnāṃ kleśānāṃ prahāṇaṃ prārthayante | draṣṭavyamavaśyaṃ rāgādipratyayamidānīmāyatyāñca glānyupāyāsān labhanta ityato 'vaśyaṃ [teṣāṃ] prahāṇaṃ prārthayante | tathā no cenna prahāṇaprārthanā syāt | ye vadanti īśvarādayaḥ kāyasya heturiti | te 'pi prārthayante kāmacchandādīnāṃ prahāṇam | ato jñāyate kāmacchandādipratyayaḥ kāya iti | vidvān prajñayā vimuktiṃ labhante | [ato] ajñānādvadhyata iti jñeyaṃ bhavati | tasmāt jñāyate kleśapratyayaḥ kāyo bhavatīti |
body.translated_text: Furthermore, one who desires liberation cultivates the aggregates of moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), concentration (<s>samādhi</s>), wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), liberation (<s>vimukti</s>), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (<s>vimuktijñānadarśana</s>). What is their purpose? They all exist for the cessation of defilements. The wise one, having seen the benefit thereof, relies on those aggregates. From this it is known that the body arises through the condition of defilements. And the defilements are gradually ceased. One who has abandoned the three fetters (<s>saṃyojana</s>) becomes a partaker of the fruit of stream-entry (<s>srotaāpattiphala</s>). One whose sensual desire and the like are attenuated becomes a partaker of the fruit of once-returning (<s>sakṛdāgāmiphala</s>). One whose fetters of the desire realm are exhausted becomes a partaker of the fruit of non-returning (<s>anāgāmiphala</s>). This same gradation [applies] in <s>dhyāna</s> and concentrations as well. One whose all fetters are completely exhausted becomes a partaker of the fruit of <s>Arhatship</s> (<s>arhatphala</s>). Thus, through the gradual cessation of defilements, the body too is gradually ceased. If God and the like were the cause, there would be no gradual cessation. From this it is known that the body arises through the condition of defilements. Good persons desire the abandonment of passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the other defilements. It should be understood that they inevitably receive, now and in the future, the sickness and distress conditioned by passion and the rest — therefore they necessarily desire their abandonment. If it were not so, there would be no desire for abandonment. Those who say God and the like are the cause of the body — they too desire the abandonment of sensual desire and the rest. From this it is known that the body arises through the condition of sensual desire and the rest. The wise obtain liberation through wisdom. Therefore it should be known that one is destroyed by ignorance. From this it is known that the body arises through the condition of defilements.

body.text: bhagavānāha- tatra tatra sūtre nandirāgakṣayātsamyagvimuktiṃ labhata iti | kasmāt | cakṣūrūpādayo hi na bandhā ityucyante | nandirāgādayastu bandhāḥ | nandirāgabhaṅgāt cittaṃ samyagvimucyate | samyagvimuktaṃ cittaṃ nirvāṇe 'vatarati | ato jñāyate kleśapratyayaḥ kāyo bhavatīti | animittānākāraśūnyatayā hi vimuktiṃ pratilabhate | ato jñāyate kleśapratyayaḥ kāya iti | kasmāt | dharmāṇāṃ śūnyatādarśanamevānimittapratilābhaḥ | nimittanirodhānna punarbhavaṃ praṇidadhāti | ataḥ śūnyatā vimokṣamukhamityucyate | tadviparyaye bandhaḥ | ityādinā kleśādhīnaḥ kāyo bhavatīti pradarśitam ||
body.translated_text: The Blessed One said in various <s>sūtras</s>: 'Through the destruction of delight and passion (<s>nandirāga</s>), one obtains right liberation.' Why? Because the eye, form, and the like are not called 'bonds' — but delight, passion, and the like are bonds. Through the destruction of delight and passion, the mind is rightly liberated. A mind that is rightly liberated enters <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. From this it is known that the body arises through the condition of defilements. Through signlessness (<s>animitta</s>), absence of activity (<s>anākāra</s>), and emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), one obtains liberation. From this it is known that the body arises through the condition of defilements. Why? The seeing of the emptiness of <s>dharmas</s> is itself the attainment of signlessness. Through the cessation of signs, one does not resolve upon renewed existence. Therefore emptiness is called a 'door of liberation' (<s>vimokṣamukha</s>). In the opposite case, there is bondage. Through such [reasoning] and the like, it has been demonstrated that the body arises dependent on defilements.

body.text: vidyāhetuvargaścatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and fortieth chapter, the Chapter on the Cause of Ignorance (<s>vidyāhetuvarga</s>).

body.text: iti
body.translated_text: Thus the aggregate of the truth of origination (<s>samudayasatyaskandha</s>) is completed.

body.text: samudayasatyaskandhaḥ samāptaḥ |
atha nirodhasatyaskandhaḥ
body.translated_text: Now, the aggregate of the truth of cessation (<s>nirodhasatyaskandha</s>).

body.text: 141 nirodhasatyaskandhe ādyaḥ prajñaptisthāpanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 141. The first chapter in the aggregate of the truth of cessation: Chapter on the Establishment of Conventional Designation (<s>prajñaptisthāpanavarga</s>).

body.text: śāstramāha- trividhacittānāṃ nirodho nirodhasatyaṃ yaduta prajñapticittaṃ dharmacittaṃ śūnyatācittam | (pṛ) kathameṣāṃ trayāṇāṃ cittānāṃ nirodhaḥ | (u) prajñapticittaṃ bahuśrutapratyayajñānena vā nirudhyate | cintanāpratyayajñānena vā nirudhyate | dharmacittamūṣmagatādidharmeṣu śūnyatābuddhayā nirudhyate | śūnyatācittaṃ nirodhasamāpattyavataraṇena nirudhyate | yadi vānupadhiśeṣanirvāṇe 'vatarataḥ santānasamucchede nirudhyate |
body.translated_text: The treatise says: The cessation of the three kinds of mind is the truth of cessation (<s>nirodhasatya</s>) — namely, the mind of conventional designation (<s>prajñapticitta</s>), the mind of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>dharmacitta</s>), and the mind of emptiness (<s>śūnyatācitta</s>). (Question) How is the cessation of these three kinds of mind [achieved]? (Answer) The mind of conventional designation is ceased either through knowledge born of learning (<s>bahuśrutapratyayajñāna</s>), or through knowledge born of reflection (<s>cintanāpratyayajñāna</s>). The mind of <s>dharmas</s> is ceased through the realization of emptiness in the <s>dharmas</s> of the heat stage (<s>ūṣmagata</s>) and the like. The mind of emptiness is ceased through entry into the attainment of cessation (<s>nirodhasamāpatti</s>). Or, for one who enters <s>Nirvāṇa</s> without remainder (<s>anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa</s>), it is ceased through the cutting off of the continuity.

body.text: (pṛ) katamā prajñaptiḥ | (u) skandhānupādāya ye vikalpā tadyathā pañcaskandhānupādāya puruṣa ityucyate | rūparasagandhasparśānupādāya ghaṭa ityucyate ityādi | (pṛ) kasmādiyaṃ prajñaptiḥ | (u) sūtre bhagavānāha-
body.translated_text: (Question) What is conventional designation (<s>prajñapti</s>)? (Answer) Depending on the aggregates, whatever conceptual constructions [arise] — for example, depending on the five aggregates, it is said 'a person.' Depending on form, taste, smell, and touch, it is said 'a pot,' and so forth. (Question) Why is this a conventional designation? (Answer) In the <s>sūtra</s>, the Blessed One said:

body.text:
yathāhyaṅgasambhārādbhavati śabdo ratheti ca |
evaṃ skandheṣu satsveva bhavati sattveti saṃvṛtiḥ || iti |
body.translated_text: 'Just as from the assemblage of parts arises the word "chariot," so too, when the aggregates exist, there is the convention "being."'

body.text: yathā ca bhagavān bhikṣūnavocat- dharmā anityā duḥkhāḥ śūnyā anātmānaḥ pratītyasamutpannā aniyatasvabhāvā nāmamātramanusmaraṇamātraṃ bhogamātram | imāneva pañcaskandhānupādāya nānā nāma pravartate sattvo manuṣyo deva ityādi iti | sūtre 'smin vastusato dharmasya pratiṣedhāducyate nāmamātramiti |
body.translated_text: And the Blessed One said to the monks: '<s>Dharmas</s> are impermanent, suffering, empty, without self, dependently originated, of no fixed own-nature — mere names, mere recollections, mere enjoyments. Depending on these very five aggregates, various names proceed — being, human, god, and so forth.' In this <s>sūtra</s>, because the really existent <s>dharma</s> is negated, it is said 'mere name.'

body.text: kiñcāha bhagavān- dve satye paramārthasatyaṃ saṃvṛtisatyamiti | paramārthasatyaṃ yaduta
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the Blessed One said: 'There are two truths: ultimate truth (<s>paramārthasatya</s>) and conventional truth (<s>saṃvṛtisatya</s>).' Ultimate truth is

body.text: rūpādayo dharmā nirvāṇañca | saṃvṛtisatyaṃ yat prajñaptimātraṃ niḥsvabhāvam | yathā rūpādipratyayo ghaṭaḥ sidhyati | tathā pañcaskandhapratyayaḥ puruṣaḥ sidhyati | (pṛ) yadi paramārthato nāstīdam | lokasatyasya ka upayogaḥ | (u) laukikāḥ sattvā lokasatyamupādāyopayojayanti | kenedaṃ jñāyate | yathā citrito 'gnirityuktau janāḥ śraddadhante | buddhā bhagavanto laukikānāṃ prajñaptito viyojanāya lokasatyena vyavaharanti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- nāhaṃ [bhikṣavo] lokena vivadāmi | lokaśca mayā vivadati | na [bhikṣavaḥ] dharmavādī [kenacilloke] vivadati | iti |
body.translated_text: <s>dharmas</s> such as form and the rest, and <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Conventional truth is what is mere designation, without own-nature (<s>niḥsvabhāva</s>). Just as a pot is established through the conditions of form and the like, so a person is established through the conditions of the five aggregates. (Question) If this does not exist ultimately, what is the use of worldly truth? (Answer) Worldly beings employ it through the convention 'it exists' — namely, <s>karma</s>, the ripening of <s>karma</s>, bondage, or liberation. All of these arise from delusion. How is this known? Just as when one says 'painted fire,' people believe [it is real]. The <s>Buddhas</s>, the Blessed Ones, employ worldly truth in order to lead worldly beings away from conventional designation. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'I, monks, do not dispute with the world. It is the world that disputes with me. One who speaks <s>Dharma</s> does not dispute with anyone in the world.'

body.text: purā kila janā vastūpabhogakāmanayā vahuvastunāmutpattikāle ghaṭa ityādi nāma sthāpayāñcakruḥ | saddharme sati nopayogo labhyeta | ato lokasatyamityucyate | satyadvaya ukte bhagavataḥ śāsanaṃ suviśuddham | paramārthatastu vidvān na viśiṣyate | lokasatyato bālairna vivadante | satyadvayaṃ vadan na śāśvatoccheda [dṛṣṭau] patati | na patati mithyādṛṣṭau sukhānte duḥkhānte ca | karmavipākādi sarvaṃ sidhyet | lokasatyaṃ buddhānāṃ śāsanavinayamūlam | yaduta dānaśīlayorvipākaḥ susthāna upapattiḥ | anena dharmeṇa taccittaṃ damayitvā mārgaśāsanaṃ grāhayitvā paścātparamārthasatyamupadiśati | evaṃ jinaśāanamādāvagādhagabhīram- tadyathā mahāsamudraḥ kramaśo gabhīraḥ | ato lokasatyaṃ vadanti | yo mārgasya lābhajñānaṃ sādhayati [sa] paramārthadharmopadeśārho bhavati | yathā bhagavata evaṃ cetaḥ parivitarka udabhut- paripavkāḥ khalu rāhulasya [bhikṣoḥ] vimuktiparipacanīyā dharmāḥ yannūnamahaṃ rāhulaṃ uttara āsravānāṃ kṣaye vinayeyamiti | tadyathā ghrāṇapākaḥ tadvināśe sukhaṃ janane durbhedanam | evaṃ lokasatyena cittaṃ damayitvātha paramārthajñānena vināśayati | uktañca sūtre- dharmāṇāṃ pravicayapūrvakaṃ nirvāṇaṃ parijñātavyamiti | yogī pūrvaṃ dharmāḥ [kiṃ] prajñaptisantaḥ [kiṃ vā] paramārthasanta iti jñātvā paścānnirodhasatyaṃ sākṣātkaroti | kleśāḥ sthūlasūkṣmakrameṇa nirudhyante | yathā keśaromādinimittena strīpuruṣādinimittaṃ nirudhyate | rūpādininimittena keśaromādinimittaṃ nirudhyate |
body.translated_text: Formerly, it is said, people desiring the enjoyment of things established names such as '<s>ghaṭa</s>' (pot) and so forth at the time of the origination of many things. Without the true <s>Dharma</s>, no practical benefit could be obtained. Therefore it is called <s>lokasatya</s> (conventional truth). When the two truths are taught, the teaching of the <s>Bhagavat</s> is thoroughly purified. From the standpoint of <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate truth), however, the wise person is not distinguished. From the standpoint of <s>lokasatya</s>, the ignorant do not dispute. One who speaks of the two truths does not fall into the views of eternalism or annihilationism. One does not fall into wrong views, whether regarding the end of pleasure or the end of suffering. All matters such as <s>karmavipāka</s> (the ripening of action) and so forth would be established. <s>Lokasatya</s> is the root of the teaching and discipline of the <s>Buddhas</s>; namely, the ripening of <s>dāna</s> (generosity) and <s>śīla</s> (morality) is rebirth in a good destination. Having tamed the mind with this <s>dharma</s> and having caused it to accept the teaching of the path, afterward one teaches <s>paramārthasatya</s> (ultimate truth). Thus the teaching of the <s>Jina</s> (Victor) is at first gradually deep — just as the great ocean is progressively deep. Therefore they teach <s>lokasatya</s>. One who accomplishes the knowledge of attaining the path becomes worthy of instruction in <s>paramārthadharma</s> (ultimate truth). Just as the <s>Bhagavat</s> had this thought arise in his mind: 'Surely the <s>dharmas</s> that ripen liberation are mature in the <s>bhikṣu</s> <s>Rāhula</s>; let me now train <s>Rāhula</s> further in the destruction of the <s>āśravas</s> (defilements).' Just as the ripening of a boil brings pleasure upon its bursting yet is difficult to break open, so having tamed the mind with <s>lokasatya</s>, one then destroys it with <s>paramārthajñāna</s> (ultimate knowledge). And it is said in the <s>sūtra</s>: '<s>Nirvāṇa</s> is to be fully known through the prior investigation of <s>dharmas</s>.' The <s>yogī</s> first knows whether <s>dharmas</s> exist as <s>prajñapti</s> (designation) or as <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate reality), and afterward directly realizes <s>nirodhasatya</s> (the truth of cessation). The <s>kleśas</s> (defilements) are destroyed in the order of coarse to subtle. Just as by means of the sign of hair and body-hair, the sign of woman and man and so forth is destroyed; by means of the sign of <s>rūpa</s> (form) and so forth, the sign of hair and body-hair is destroyed;

body.text: atha śūnyatādinimittena rūpādinimittaṃ nirudhyate | yathā kīlena kilo 'panīyate | ato lokasatyamucyate |
body.translated_text: Then by means of the sign of <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness) and so forth, the sign of <s>rūpa</s> (form) and so forth is destroyed. Just as a peg is removed by means of another peg. Therefore it is called <s>lokasatya</s> (conventional truth).

body.text: lokasatyena madhyamā pratipatsādhyate | kasmāt | pañcaskandhāḥ santānena pravartanta iti nocchedaḥ | kṣaṇikā iti na śāśvataḥ | śāśvatocchedavinirmukta iti madhyamā pratipat | yathoktaṃ sūtre- lokasamudayaṃ paśyataḥ nāstīti dṛṣṭirna bhavati | lokanirodhaṃ paśyataḥ astīti dṛṣṭirna bhavati iti | ata ucyate lokasatyam | lokasatyato bhagavataḥ śāsanaṃ sarvaṃ satyameva yaduta astyātmā nāstyātmā ityādi paryāyāḥ | lokasatyato 'styātmeti vadato nāstyavadyam | paramārthato nāstyātmeti vadataśca satyam |
body.translated_text: Through <s>lokasatya</s> (conventional truth), the middle way (<s>madhyamā pratipat</s>) is established. Why? Because the five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) proceed in a continuum (<s>santāna</s>), therefore it is not annihilationism. Because they are momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), therefore it is not eternalism. Being free from both eternalism and annihilationism is the middle way. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'For one who sees the arising of the world, the view "it does not exist" does not arise. For one who sees the cessation of the world, the view "it exists" does not arise.' Therefore it is called <s>lokasatya</s>. From the standpoint of <s>lokasatya</s>, all the teaching of the <s>Bhagavat</s> is true indeed — namely, such statements as 'there is a self' or 'there is no self' and so forth. From the standpoint of <s>lokasatya</s>, there is no fault in saying 'there is a self.' And from the standpoint of <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate truth), saying 'there is no self' is true.

body.text: lokasatyena pratidūṣaṇaṃ sthāpyate | paramārthatastu prativacanam | asti vastutaḥ sattva iti yā dṛṣṭiḥ ayaṃ mahāmohaḥ | nāstīti yadvacanaṃ tadapi mohatamasi pātayasi | kasmāt | iyaṃ bhāvābhāvadṛṣṭiḥ śāśvatocchedātmikā | yena yogino bhāvāntānnirgamya abhāvānte patanti | lokasatye 'sati kena nirgamaṃ labheran | yadapratilabdhaśūnyatāprajño vadati nāsti sattva iti | iyaṃ mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | jananamaraṇavedakaḥ sattvo nāstīti vacanaṃ hi mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | yadi śūnyatābuddhipratilābhī vadati nāsti sattva iti | na tadā doṣaḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- arhantī bhikṣuṇī pāpīyāṃsaṃ māramavocat-
body.translated_text: Through <s>lokasatya</s> (conventional truth), a refutation is established. But from the standpoint of <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate truth), there is a reply. The view that there truly exists a being (<s>sattva</s>) — this is great delusion (<s>mahāmoha</s>). The statement that it does not exist also causes one to fall into the darkness of delusion. Why? Because this view of existence and non-existence partakes of eternalism and annihilationism, by which <s>yogins</s>, having emerged from the extreme of existence, fall into the extreme of non-existence. Without <s>lokasatya</s>, how could they obtain an exit? When one who has not attained the wisdom of <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness) says 'there is no being,' this is <s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s> (wrong view). The statement that the being who experiences birth and death does not exist is indeed wrong view. But if one who has attained the understanding of <s>śūnyatā</s> says 'there is no being,' then there is no fault. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>, the <s>arhatī bhikṣuṇī</s> (nun who is an arhat) said to the evil <s>Māra</s>:

body.text:
kiṃ nu sattva iti pratyeṣi māradṛṣṭigataṃ nu te |
śuddhasaṃskārapuñjo 'yaṃ neha sattva upalabhyate || iti |
body.translated_text:
'Why do you presume a being (<s>sattva</s>), O <s>Māra</s>? Is this your view?
This is merely a heap of pure <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations); no being is found herein.'

body.text: kiñcāha-
body.translated_text: And furthermore she said:

children.translated_text: This body is a continuum of <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), empty and devoid of anything;
Like an illusion, like a magical creation, it deceives the eyes of ordinary people.
Like a thorn, like an abscess, it is an enemy, a robber-foe;
It is suffering, empty, without self, subject to birth, decay, and destruction.

body.text: iti |
body.translated_text: Thus.

body.text: (pṛ) sarvasyāpi nāsti yatkiñcana cittam | kasmāt keṣāñcinmithyādṛṣṭirityucyate keṣāñcitparamārthadṛṣṭiriti | (u) yasya puruṣasya śūnyatātattvajñānaṃ notpannaṃ tasyāstyātmeti matirbhavati | ato nāstyātmeti śrutvaiva santrāsamutpādayati | yathāha bhagavān- ye bālāḥ pṛthagjanāḥ śūnyo nāstyātmā, na punaḥ karoti iti śrutavantaḥ te mahābhītā bhavanti | iti | ato jñāyate apratilabdhaśūnyatājñānaḥ astyātmeti matyā nirvāṇādbibheti | tadā mithyādṛṣṭirbhavati | pratilabdhaśunyatājñānastu nāsti mūlata āgatiriti prajānāti | tadā nāsti kiñcana bhayamiti | apratilabdhaśūnyatātattvo nāsti kiñcanetidṛ ṣṭyā durgatau patati yadutocchedadṛṣṭi[rūpa]mithyādṛṣṭiḥ | yo 'yaṃ lokasatyato 'styātmeti prajñāya asti karmaphalamiti śraddadhānaḥ paścāt saṃskārā anityā utpattinirodhalakṣaṇā iti bhāvayitvā nirodhaṃ sākṣātkaroti | [tasya] ātmabuddhyabhāve kāmacittaṃ nirudhyate | sa yadi nāsti kiñcaneti vacanaṃ śṛṇoti | tadā nāsti kaścana doṣaḥ | ata ucyate lokasatyam |
body.translated_text: (Question) Since for all there is nothing whatsoever that is mind, why is it said that for some it is <s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s> (wrong view) and for others it is <s>paramārthadṛṣṭi</s> (ultimate view)? (Answer) For a person in whom the true knowledge of <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness) has not arisen, there arises the notion 'there is a self.' Therefore, merely upon hearing 'there is no self,' he generates fear. As the <s>Bhagavat</s> said: 'Those foolish ordinary persons (<s>pṛthagjanāḥ</s>) who have heard that [all is] empty, that there is no self, and that there is no further agent — they become greatly frightened.' Therefore it is known that one who has not attained the knowledge of <s>śūnyatā</s>, through the notion 'there is a self,' fears <s>nirvāṇa</s>. Then it becomes <s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s> (wrong view). But one who has attained the knowledge of <s>śūnyatā</s> understands that fundamentally there is no coming. Then there is no fear whatsoever. One who has not attained the truth of <s>śūnyatā</s>, through the view 'there is nothing whatsoever,' falls into a bad destination — this being the wrong view in the form of annihilationism (<s>ucchedadṛṣṭi</s>). One who, from the standpoint of <s>lokasatya</s>, understands 'there is a self' and has faith that there is the fruit of <s>karma</s>, afterward, having contemplated that <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations) are impermanent and characterized by arising and cessation, directly realizes cessation (<s>nirodha</s>). In the absence of the notion of self, the mind of desire is destroyed. If such a one hears the statement 'there is nothing whatsoever,' then there is no fault. Therefore it is called <s>lokasatya</s> (conventional truth).

body.text: kecittīrthikā apavadanti śramaṇo gautamaḥ paramārthata ātmānaṃ dūṣayatīti | ato bhagavānāha- lokasatyato vadāmi asti sattva iti | samyagdṛṣṭiṃ prakāśayan vadāmi santi sattvāḥ sandhāvantaḥ saṃsaranta iti | iyaṃ samyagdṛṣṭiriti vadāmi | pṛthagjana mithyāmanaskārānniḥsattve vastusaditi vacanaṃ, tanmithyāmanaskārasya dūṣaṇam | na sattvasya dūṣaṇam | yathā ghaṭādayaḥ prajñaptyocyante | tatra na rūpādayo ghaṭāḥ | na rūpādivyatirikto ghaṭaḥ | evaṃ na rūpādayaḥ skandhāḥ sattvaḥ | nāpi rūpādivyatiriktaḥ sattvaḥ | yathā rūpādīnupādāya prajñaptimatikrāmati | evaṃ nirodhalakṣaṇena rūpādīnatikrāmati | dṛṣṭāntenārthaḥ suvibhajyate | yathā citritaḥ pradīpaḥ pradīpa ityukto 'pi na pradipavṛttiko bhavati | evaṃ ghaṭo 'stīti kathito 'pi na vastusan bhavati | santi pañcaskandhā ityuktā api na paramārthāḥ ||
body.translated_text: Certain <s>tīrthikas</s> (non-Buddhist teachers) criticize, saying 'the ascetic <s>Gautama</s> refutes the self from the ultimate standpoint.' Therefore the <s>Bhagavat</s> said: 'From the standpoint of <s>lokasatya</s> I say there is a being (<s>sattva</s>). Illuminating right view (<s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s>), I say beings exist, running and transmigrating. This I call right view.' The statement of an ordinary person (<s>pṛthagjana</s>), due to wrong mental attention (<s>mithyāmanaskāra</s>), that a thing truly exists where there is no being — that is the refutation of wrong mental attention, not the refutation of the being. Just as pots and so forth are spoken of as <s>prajñapti</s> (designation): therein, <s>rūpa</s> (form) and so forth are not the pot, nor is the pot something apart from <s>rūpa</s> and so forth. Likewise, <s>rūpa</s> and the other <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) are not the being, nor is the being something apart from <s>rūpa</s> and so forth. Just as one transcends <s>rūpa</s> and so forth by means of <s>prajñapti</s> (designation), so one transcends <s>rūpa</s> and so forth by means of the characteristic of cessation (<s>nirodhalakṣaṇa</s>). The meaning is well distinguished by an analogy: just as a painted lamp, though called a 'lamp,' does not function as a lamp, so a pot, though spoken of as existing, does not exist as a real thing. Even though the five <s>skandhas</s> are said to exist, they are not ultimate realities.

body.text: prajñaptisthāpanavarga ekacatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: Chapter on the Establishment of Designation (<s>Prajñaptisthāpanavarga</s>), the one hundred and forty-first.

body.text: 142 prajñaptilakṣaṇavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 142. Chapter on the Characteristics of Designation (<s>Prajñaptilakṣaṇavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) kathaṃ ghaṭādayaḥ prajñaptitaḥ santi na vastutaḥ | (u) (1) prajñaptau nimittapradarśanamasti na paramārthe | yathā vadanti idaṃ rūpaṃ idaṃ ghaṭarūpamiti | na vaktuṃ śakyata [idaṃ] rūparūpamiti | nāpi vaktuṃ śakyata idaṃ vedanādirūpamiti | (2) pradīpo rūpasahagamāt prajvalatīti [vadanti] sparśasahagamātpradahatīti | paramārthadharmastu naivaṃ dṛśyate | kasmāt | vijñānaṃ nānyasahagamādvijānātīti | vedanāpi nānyasahagamādvedayata iti | ato jñāyate sahabhāvaḥ prajñaptisanniti | (3) anyadharmamupādāya prajñaptisan sidhyati | yathā rūpādīnupādāya ghaṭaḥ | paramārthadharmastu nānyadharmamupādāya sidhyati | kasmāt | yathā vedanā nānyadharmamupādāya sidhyati | (4) prajñaptiśca nānādharmavatī | yathā pradīpaḥ prakāśate pradahati ca | naivaṃ dṛśyate paramārthadharmaḥ | kasmāt | yathā vedanā na vedayate vijānāti ca | (5) rathaśabdo rathāṅgādiṣu bhavati | rūpādiśabdastu na padārthe vartata | ityevaṃ vibhāgaḥ | rathāṅgādayo rathasādhanāḥ pratyayāḥ | na tatrāsti rathaśabdaḥ | tathā ca rathakāraṇe nāsti rathadharmaḥ | tadupādāya tu rathaḥ sidhyati | ato jñāyate rathaḥ prajñaptiriti | (6) rūpādiśabdenoktā rūpādayo labhyante | ghaṭādiśabdenoktā ghaṭādayastu na labhyante | ato jñāyate ghaṭādayaḥ prajñaptaya iti | (7) prajñaptau cittaṃ vikṣipati, na samādadhāti | yathā kaścidaśvaṃ dṛṣṭvā vadati- aśvaṃ paśyāmīti | kaścidaśvakāyaṃ paśyāmīti | kaściccarma paśyāmīti | kaścidromāṇi vā paśyāmīti | kaścidvadati vīṇāśabdaṃ śṛṇomīti | kaścit tantrīnādaṃ śṛṇomīti | kaścidvadati kusumaṃ jighrāmīti | kaścitkusumagandhaṃ jighrāmīti | kaścidvadati surāṃ pibāmīti | kaścitsurārasaṃ pibāmīti | kaścidvadati puruṣaṃ spṛśāmīti, kaścit puruṣakāyaṃ spṛśāmīti, kaścit puruṣabhujaṃ spṛśāmiti, kaścit puruṣahastaṃ spṛśāmīti, kaścit puruṣasyāṅguliṃ spṛśāmīti, kaścit puruṣasyāṅguliparva spṛśāmiti | manovijñānamapi sattvādau vikṣipati yaduta kāyaḥ sattvaḥ cittaṃ sattva iti | evaṃ rūpādaya eva ghaṭa athavā rūpādivyatirikto ghaṭa ityādi | paramārthavacane tu cittaṃ samādadhāti na vikṣipati | rūpaṃ paśyāmīti [vat] śabdamapi paśyāmīti na vaktuṃ śakyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) How do pots and so forth exist as <s>prajñapti</s> (designation) but not as real things? (Answer) (1) In <s>prajñapti</s> there is a display of characteristics, but not in <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate reality). As they say: 'this is form (<s>rūpa</s>),' 'this is the form of a pot' — but one cannot say 'this is the form of form.' Nor can one say 'this is the form of <s>vedanā</s> (feeling) and so forth.' (2) A lamp, because it accompanies <s>rūpa</s> (form), is said to 'blaze'; because it accompanies <s>sparśa</s> (contact), it is said to 'burn.' But <s>paramārthadharma</s> (ultimate reality) is not seen in this way. Why? Because <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) does not cognize by accompanying something else. <s>Vedanā</s> (feeling) also does not feel by accompanying something else. Therefore it is known that co-existence (<s>sahabhāva</s>) is of the nature of <s>prajñapti</s>. (3) A thing existing as <s>prajñapti</s> is established by depending on another <s>dharma</s>. Just as a pot depends on <s>rūpa</s> and so forth. But <s>paramārthadharma</s> is not established by depending on another <s>dharma</s>. Why? Just as <s>vedanā</s> is not established by depending on another <s>dharma</s>. (4) <s>Prajñapti</s> possesses multiple properties. Just as a lamp both illuminates and burns. <s>Paramārthadharma</s> is not seen in this way. Why? Because <s>vedanā</s> does not both feel and cognize. (5) The word 'chariot' (<s>ratha</s>) applies to the wheels and other parts. But the word '<s>rūpa</s>' and so forth does not apply in this way to the object. Thus is the distinction. The wheels and other parts are the conditions that produce the chariot. The word 'chariot' does not exist therein. Likewise in the cause of the chariot there is no chariot-property. But the chariot is established in dependence upon them. Therefore it is known that the chariot is a <s>prajñapti</s> (designation). (6) When spoken of with the word '<s>rūpa</s>' and so forth, <s>rūpa</s> and so forth are apprehended. But when spoken of with the word 'pot' and so forth, pots and so forth are not apprehended. Therefore it is known that pots and so forth are <s>prajñaptis</s> (designations). (7) In <s>prajñapti</s>, the mind is distracted and does not concentrate. For example, someone seeing a horse says 'I see a horse'; another says 'I see the body of a horse'; another says 'I see the hide'; another says 'I see the hairs.' Someone says 'I hear the sound of a <s>vīṇā</s>'; another says 'I hear the sound of the strings.' Someone says 'I smell a flower'; another says 'I smell the fragrance of the flower.' Someone says 'I drink liquor'; another says 'I drink the taste of the liquor.' Someone says 'I touch a person'; another says 'I touch the person's body'; another says 'I touch the person's arm'; another says 'I touch the person's hand'; another says 'I touch the person's finger'; another says 'I touch the person's finger-joint.' The mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) is also distracted regarding beings and so forth — namely, 'the body is the being,' 'the mind is the being,' and so forth. Likewise, '<s>rūpa</s> and so forth are the pot' or 'the pot is something apart from <s>rūpa</s> and so forth,' and so on. But when speaking of <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate reality), the mind concentrates and is not distracted. One cannot say 'I see <s>rūpa</s>' and also 'I see sound.'

body.text: (8) jñeyādau [sarva]mavyapadeśyamapi astītyucyate | [yat vyapadiśyate] iyaṃ prajñaptiḥ yathā ghaṭādayaḥ | ato jñāyate ghaṭādayaḥ prajñaptisanta iti | kasmāt | rūpādayo dharmā jñeyādāvanabhidheyā iti na vyapadiśyante | yathā rūpādayaḥ svalakṣaṇena vyavadeśyāḥ | na ghaṭādayaḥ svalakṣaṇena vyapadiśyante | ata ime prajñaptisanta iti jñāyate | (9) kecit astīti prajñaptilakṣaṇaṃ vadanti | idaṃ lakṣaṇamanyatra vartate na prajñaptau | yathoktaṃ sūtre- karma viduṣo 'viduṣaśca lakṣaṇamiti | yaḥ kāyavāṅmanobhiḥ kuśalaṃ karoti sa vidvān | yaḥ kāyavāṅmanobhirakuśalaṃ karma karoti so 'vidvān | kāyavākkarma catvāri mahābhūtānyupādāya tiṣṭhati | mānasaṃ karma cittamāśrayate | imāni trīṇi kathaṃ viduṣo 'viduṣaśca lakṣaṇam | ato jñāyate nāsti prajñapteḥ svalakṣaṇam | (10) prajñaptilakṣaṇamanyatra vartamānamapi na punarekam | yathoktam- śalyaviddha iva rūpyate iti | rūpyata iti rūpalakṣaṇam | vedayata iti vedanālakṣaṇe puruṣa ucyate | yathāha bhagavān- vidvān mūḍhaśca sarvaḥ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ vedayate | vidvān sukhe duḥkhe na kāmamutpādayati | bahvādinimittodgrahaṇaṃ saṃjñālakṣaṇamityapi puruṣa evocyate | yathāha- prabhāmahaṃ paśyāmi rūpamahaṃ paśyāmīti | [saṃskṛta]mabhisaṃskarotīti saṃskāralakṣaṇe 'pi puruṣa evocyate | yathāha- ayaṃ puruṣapudgalaḥ puṇyopagaṃ saṃskāramabhisaṃskaroti | apuṇyopagaṃ saṃskāramabhisaṃskaroti | āneñjyopagaṃ saṃskāramabhisaṃskarotīti | vijānātīti vijñānalakṣaṇe 'pi puruṣa evocyate | yathāha- [kṣipraṃ] dharmaṃ vijānāti vijño jihvā sūparasaṃ yathā | iti | ato yadanyatragatamuktamapi bahulakṣaṇamucyate | idaṃ prajñaptilakṣaṇam | rūpādi[sva]lakṣaṇaṃ nānyatragataṃ nāpi bahulakṣaṇam |
body.translated_text: (8) Among knowable objects and the like, even what cannot be designated by all is said to 'exist.' [That which is designated] — this is conventional designation (<s>prajñapti</s>), such as pots and the like. From this it is known that pots and the like are conventionally existent (<s>prajñaptisat</s>). Why? <s>Dharmas</s> such as form and the like, being inexpressible among knowable objects and the like, are not designated [as such]. Just as form and the like are to be designated by their own characteristics (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), pots and the like are not designated by their own characteristics. From this it is known that they are conventionally existent. (9) Some say that 'existence' is the characteristic of conventional designation. This characteristic occurs elsewhere, not in conventional designation. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: '<s>Karma</s> is the characteristic of the wise and the unwise.' One who does what is wholesome through body, speech, and mind — he is wise. One who does unwholesome <s>karma</s> through body, speech, and mind — he is unwise. Bodily and verbal <s>karma</s> subsists dependent on the four great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>). Mental <s>karma</s> depends on mind (<s>citta</s>). How are these three the characteristic of the wise and the unwise? From this it is known that conventional designation has no own-characteristic. (10) Even though the characteristic of conventional designation occurs elsewhere, it is not singular. As stated: 'One is affected as if struck by a thorn' — 'is affected' is the characteristic of form. 'Experiences' is the characteristic of feeling (<s>vedanā</s>), but a person is spoken of. As the Blessed One said: 'Both the wise and the deluded experience pleasure and suffering. The wise one, regarding pleasure and suffering, does not generate craving.' The grasping of signs (<s>nimitta</s>) such as multiplicity and the like is the characteristic of perception (<s>saṃjñā</s>), yet a person is spoken of. As stated: 'I see radiance, I see form.' '[That which is] conditioned (<s>saṃskṛta</s>) — one conditions' is the characteristic of formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>), yet a person is spoken of. As stated: 'This person-individual (<s>puruṣapudgala</s>) conditions meritorious formations. He conditions demeritorious formations. He conditions imperturbable formations.' 'Cognizes' is the characteristic of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), yet a person is spoken of. As stated: 'The discerning one quickly comprehends the <s>Dharma</s>, just as the tongue [comprehends] a fine flavor.' Therefore, what is stated elsewhere and spoken of with multiple characteristics — this is the characteristic of conventional designation. The own-characteristic of form and the like does not occur elsewhere, nor does it have multiple characteristics.

body.text:
(11) yo dharmaḥ sarveṣāmanuśayakaraḥ sa prajñaptisan | paramārthadharmastu nānuśayakaraḥ | anuśayā hi puruṣaṃ kurvanti | (12) prajñaptau ca na jñānotpādo bhavati | purovartirūpādiṣu jñānotpādo bhavati | taduttaraṃ manovijñānena vikalpayati ghaṭamahaṃ paśyāmītyādi | ghaṭasya jñānamavaśyaṃ rūpādyapekṣam | kasmāt | rūparasagandhasparśānupādāya hi ayaṃ ghaṭa iti vyavahāraḥ | paramārthajñānantu na yatkiñcidapekṣya bhavati |
(13) prajñaptau ca bhavati saṃśayaḥ yathā sthāṇurvā puruṣo vā iti | rūpādiṣu tu na saṃśayo bhavati rūpaṃ vā kiṃ vā śabda iti | (pṛ) rūpādāvapi saṃśayo bhavati kimasti rūpaṃ kiṃ vā nāsti rūpamiti | (u) nedaṃ yuktam | rūpaṃ paśyan naiva saṃśete ayaṃ śabda iti | anyasmāt kāraṇāt saṃśayo bhavati kimasti rūpaṃ kiṃ vā nāsti rūpamiti | yathā rūpaṃ śūnyamiti śrutvā punā rūpaṃ paśyan saṃśete kimasti kiṃ vā nāstīti | nirodhasatyaṃ paśyato 'yaṃ saṃśayaḥ prahīyate | (pṛ) nirodhasatye 'pi saṃśayo bhavati kimasti nirodhaḥ kiṃ vā nāsti nirodha iti | (u) abhiniviṣṭeṣu saṃśayo bhavati na tu nirodhasatye | asti nirodha iti mataṃ nāsti nirodha iti matañca yaḥ śṛṇoti tasya bhavati saṃśayaḥ kimasti kiṃ vā nāstīti | sa tadā na nirodhasatyaṃ paśyati | kasmāt | nirodhasatyaṃ paśyato na punaḥ saṃśayo bhavati | ato jñāyate saṃśayotpādasthale prajñaptirasti |
body.translated_text:
(11) Whatever <s>dharma</s> produces latent tendencies (<s>anuśaya</s>) in all [beings] — that is conventionally existent. But an ultimate <s>dharma</s> does not produce latent tendencies. For latent tendencies operate upon a person (<s>puruṣa</s>). (12) And in conventional designation, there is no arising of knowledge. Knowledge arises regarding form and the like that are present before [the perceiver]. Subsequently, through mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>), one conceptualizes: 'I see a pot,' and so forth. Knowledge of the pot necessarily depends on form and the like. Why? For the convention 'this is a pot' operates dependent on form, taste, smell, and touch. But ultimate knowledge (<s>paramārthajñāna</s>) does not arise dependent on anything whatsoever.
(13) And in conventional designation, doubt arises — such as 'Is it a post or a person?' But in form and the like, doubt does not arise — such as 'Is it form or sound?' (Question) Even in form and the like, doubt arises: 'Does form exist or does form not exist?' (Answer) This is not valid. One who sees form does not at all doubt 'this is sound.' Doubt arises from other causes: 'Does form exist or does it not exist?' — just as, having heard 'form is empty,' upon again seeing form, one doubts 'does it exist or does it not exist?' This doubt is abandoned when seeing the truth of cessation (<s>nirodhasatya</s>). (Question) Even regarding the truth of cessation, doubt arises: 'Does cessation exist or does it not exist?' (Answer) Doubt arises regarding those who are attached, but not regarding the truth of cessation. One who hears the opinion 'cessation exists' and the opinion 'cessation does not exist' — for that person, doubt arises: 'Does it exist or does it not exist?' At that time, he does not see the truth of cessation. Why? For one who sees the truth of cessation, doubt does not arise again. From this it is known that conventional designation exists in the domain where doubt arises.

body.text: (14) ekasmin vastuni bahuvijñaptyutpattilābhe prajñaptirasti | yathā ghaṭādau | paramārthadharme tu na tathā | kasmāt | rūpādau na bhavanti śrotrādivijñaptayaḥ | (15) bahvāyatanasaṅgṛhītaṃ prajñaptisat | yathā ghaṭādayaḥ | ataḥ kecidvadanti prajñaptisat caturmahābhūtasaṅgṛhītam | paramārthadharmastu na bahvāyatanasaṅgrahaṃ labhate | (16) yat niḥsvabhāvaṃ sat kriyāsamarthaṃ bhavati | idaṃ prajñaptisat | yathā puruṣaḥ karotīti | puruṣasvabhāvaḥ karmasvabhāvaśca na paramārtha upalabhyate | snehadveṣādivikalpo yaḥ kaścana sa sarvaḥ prajñaptisan | na paramārthasan | kasmāt | rūpādidharmāṇāṃ sākṣāddarśane na snehadveṣādisaṃjñotpadyate | (17) gamyate āgamyata ityādi, ucchidyate vinaśyati ityādi, dāhyate
body.translated_text: (14) When multiple cognitions arise regarding a single object, conventional designation exists — such as with pots and the like. But regarding an ultimate <s>dharma</s>, it is not so. Why? Regarding form and the like, cognitions of the ear-faculty and the like do not arise. (15) What is included in many sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>) is conventionally existent — such as pots and the like. Therefore some say that the conventionally existent is included in the four great elements. But an ultimate <s>dharma</s> is not included in many sense-bases. (16) That which, being without own-nature (<s>niḥsvabhāva</s>), is an existent capable of functioning — this is conventionally existent. Such as 'a person acts.' The own-nature of a person and the own-nature of action are not obtained ultimately. Whatever conceptual discrimination (<s>vikalpa</s>) of attachment, aversion, and the like — all of that is conventionally existent, not ultimately existent. Why? In the direct perception of <s>dharmas</s> such as form and the like, conceptions such as attachment and aversion do not arise. (17) Going, coming, and the like; being cut off, being destroyed, and the like; being burned

body.text: pradāhyate ityādi yā kācana kriyā sarvā sā prajñaptisatī | na paramārthasatī | kasmāt | paramārthadharmāsyādāhyatvāt | avināśyatvāt | puṇyapāpādikarma sarvaṃ prajñaptisat | kasmāt | prāṇātipātādi pāpaṃ prāṇātipātaviratyādi puṇyaṃ sarvaṃ na paramārthasat | (18) prajñaptisadāpekṣikam- yathā idaṃ, tat, guru laghu, dīrghaṃ hrasvaṃ, mahadalpaṃ, ācāryaḥ antevāsī, pitā putraḥ ārya anārya ityādi | paramārthastu nāpekṣikaḥ | kasmāt | rūpaṃ nānyapadārthamapekṣya śabdādīn sādhayatīti | na śūnyatayā prajñaptikhaṇḍanaṃ prajñaptisat | yathā vṛkṣān niśritya vanaṃ khaṇḍyate | mūlakāṇḍaṃ niśritya vṛkṣaḥ khaṇḍayate | rūpādi niśritya mūlakāṇḍaṃ khaṇḍyate | tathā śūnyatayā yat khaṇḍanaṃ tattu paramārthasat | yathā rūpādi śūnyatayā khaṇḍyate |
body.translated_text: being scorched, and the like — whatever activity there may be, all of that is conventionally existent, not ultimately existent. Why? Because an ultimate <s>dharma</s> is not burnable, not destructible. All meritorious and sinful <s>karma</s> is conventionally existent. Why? Taking life (<s>prāṇātipāta</s>) and the like is sinful; abstaining from taking life and the like is meritorious — all of this is not ultimately existent. (18) The conventionally existent is relational (<s>āpekṣika</s>) — such as 'this,' 'that,' 'heavy,' 'light,' 'long,' 'short,' 'great,' 'small,' 'teacher,' 'student,' 'father,' 'son,' 'noble,' 'ignoble,' and the like. But ultimate [reality] is not relational. Why? Form does not establish sound and the like by depending on another category of object. It is not through emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>) that conventional designation is refuted as conventionally existent. Just as a forest is refuted by relying on trees, a tree is refuted by relying on root and trunk, root and trunk are refuted by relying on form and the like — so too, the refutation through emptiness is ultimately existent. Just as form and the like are refuted through emptiness.

body.text: (19) śūnyatācāryāyatanānuvartanaṃ prajñaptisat | nairātmyacaryāyatanānuvartanantu paramārthasat | (20) santi catvāro vādāḥ- ekatvaṃ, nānātvaṃ, anirvacanīyatvaṃ, abhāva iti | ete catvāro vādāḥ sāvadyāḥ | ato jñāyate ghaṭādayaḥ prajñaptisanta iti |
body.translated_text: (19) Following the domain of the teacher of emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>) is conventionally existent. But following the domain of the practice of non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>) is ultimately existent. (20) There are four doctrines: unity (<s>ekatva</s>), plurality (<s>nānātva</s>), inexpressibility (<s>anirvacanīyatva</s>), and non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>). These four doctrines are faulty. From this it is known that pots and the like are conventionally existent.

body.text: ekatvam- rūparasagandhasparśā eva ghaṭa iti | nānātvam rūpādīn vihāyānyo 'sti ghaṭa iti | anirvacanīyatvam- rūpādaya eva vā ghaṭaḥ kiṃ vā tadvayatirikto ghaṭa iti na nirvaktuṃ śakyate | abhāvaḥ- nāstyayaṃ ghaṭa iti | ime catvāro vādā ayuktāḥ | ato jñāyate ghaṭaḥ prajñaptiriti |
body.translated_text: Unity [means]: 'Form, taste, smell, and touch are themselves the pot.' Plurality [means]: 'Apart from form and the like, there is another pot.' Inexpressibility [means]: 'Whether the pot is just form and the like, or whether the pot is other than them — this cannot be expressed.' Non-existence [means]: 'This pot does not exist.' These four doctrines are untenable. From this it is known that the pot is a conventional designation.

body.text: prajñaptilakṣaṇavargo dvicatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and forty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Characteristics of Conventional Designation (<s>prajñaptilakṣaṇavarga</s>).

body.text: 143 ekatvakhaṇḍanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 143. Chapter on the Refutation of Unity (<s>ekatvakhaṇḍanavarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) eṣāmekatvādīnāṃ caturṇāṃ vādānāṃ ke doṣāḥ | (u) ekatvavāde doṣo yaduta rūpādīnāṃ dharmāṇāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ pratyekaṃ vibhaktam | yadi ghaṭa ekaḥ, tadā na sambhavati | rūpādīni naikaikaṃ pṛthivīdhāturityucyante | tatsamavāyaḥ kathaṃ pṛthivī bhavet | kasmāt | yadyekaiko 'śvo na gaurbhavati | tatsamavāyaḥ kathaṃ gaurbhavet | (pṛ) yathā ekaikaṃ tilaṃ na kalāpaṃ sādhayati | tatsamavāyastu sādhayati | evaṃ rūpādīnyekaikaṃ na pṛthivīṃ sādhayanti | tatsamavāyastu sādhayati | (u) na yujyate | kasmāt | tilakalāpaḥ prajñaptisan | ekatvādi tu paramārthadharme vicāryate | iti kathaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ syāt |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults of these four doctrines of unity and the rest? (Answer) The fault in the doctrine of unity is that the characteristics of <s>dharmas</s> such as form and the like are individually distinct. If the pot were one [with them], that would be impossible. Form and the like individually are not each called 'earth element' (<s>pṛthivīdhātu</s>). How then could their combination be earth? Why? If each individual horse is not a cow, how could their combination be a cow? (Question) Just as each individual sesame seed does not constitute a heap, but their combination does — so too, form and the like individually do not constitute earth, but their combination does. (Answer) This is not valid. Why? A heap of sesame seeds is conventionally existent. But here [we are] examining unity and the like regarding an ultimate <s>dharma</s>. Therefore how could this serve as an example?

body.text: rūparasagandhasparśāścatvāro dharmāḥ | pṛthivī tu ekadharmaḥ | na catvāra ekaḥ syāt | yadi catvāra ekaḥ | eko 'pi catvāraḥ syāt | tattu na sambhavati | ato jñāyate rūpādaya eva na pṛthivīti | laukikā vadanti- pṛthivīrūpaṃ pṛthivīgandhaḥ pṛthivīrasaḥ pṛthivīsparśaṃ iti | na paśyāmo rūparūpamiti vadantaṃ yaṃ kañcana | anyadharmalakṣaṇenāvaśyaṃ pradarśyate- yathā amukasya puruṣasya kuṭīti | (pṛ) idaṃ nānyadharmalakṣaṇena pradarśanaṃ, svadharmeṇaiva svātmapradarśanam | yathā śilāpuruṣasya hastapādamiti | kasmāt | na hi hastapādavyatiriktaḥ śilāpuruṣo 'sti | evaṃ rūpādivyatiriktā pṛthivī yadyapi nāsti | tathāpi svātmarūpeṇaiva svātmapradarśanaṃ [iti vadataḥ] ko doṣaḥ | (u) yadyucyate pṛthivī rūpādinā svātmānameva pradarśayatīti nāyaṃ nyāyo bhavati | śīlāpuruṣadṛṣṭānto yadyapi bhavatoktaḥ | sa dṛṣṭāntastu na yuktaḥ | kasmāt | śilāpuruṣasya hasta iti pradarśane tadanyaḥ kāyaḥ śilāpuruṣa iti syāt | śūnyatāyāmapi ca astītyabhidhīyate | yathā vadanti śilāpuruṣasya kāya iti | tasmin samaye śilāpuruṣa eva na punastadanyo 'stītyucyate | yathā bhagavānāha- santyasmin kāye keśā romāṇi raktaṃ māṃsaṃ ityādi | tāni keśādīni vihāya nāstyanyaḥ kāyaḥ | keśādīnāṃ niśrayasthānamidaṃ pṛthagasadapi [astīti] abhidhīyate | ato jñāyate śilāpuruṣa iti vacanamapi mṛṣāvacanam, iti | yadi śilāpuruṣadṛṣṭāntena pṛthivīṃ sādhayasi | tathāpi nāsti pṛthivī | bhavatāṃ sūtre uktaṃ- rūparasagandhasparśavatī pṛthivīti | iyaṃ pṛthivyeva nāsti kāyavat | ato jñāyate rūparasagandhasparśā eva, naivāstīyaṃ pṛthivīti |
body.translated_text: Form, taste, smell, and touch are four <s>dharmas</s>. But earth is one <s>dharma</s>. Four cannot be one. If four were one, then one would also be four. But that is impossible. From this it is known that form and the like alone [exist], not earth. Worldly people say: 'the form of earth,' 'the smell of earth,' 'the taste of earth,' 'the touch of earth.' But we do not see anyone saying 'the form of form.' [Earth] is necessarily indicated by the characteristic of another <s>dharma</s> — just as 'the hut of such-and-such a person.' (Question) This is not indication by the characteristic of another <s>dharma</s>, but the indication of one's own self by one's own <s>dharma</s>. Just as 'the hands and feet of the stone person (<s>śilāpuruṣa</s>).' Why? For there is no stone person apart from hands and feet. Thus, even though earth apart from form and the like does not exist, what fault is there in saying [it is] the indication of one's own self by one's own form? (Answer) If you say that earth indicates its own self by form and the like, this principle does not hold. Although you have cited the example of the stone person, that example is not valid. Why? In the indication 'the hand of the stone person,' the body other than [the hand] would be the stone person. But even in emptiness, it is said to 'exist' — just as they say 'the body of the stone person.' At that time, 'stone person' is just the same [stone] — it is not said that something other than it exists. Just as the Blessed One said: 'In this body there are hairs, body-hairs, blood, flesh,' and so forth. Apart from those hairs and the like, there is no other body. This body is declared as the locus of dependence for hairs and the like — though individually non-existent, [it] is said to 'exist.' From this it is known that the statement 'stone person' is also a false statement. If you establish earth by the example of the stone person, then earth too does not exist. In your <s>sūtra</s> it is stated: 'Earth possesses form, taste, smell, and touch.' This earth itself does not exist, like the body. From this it is known that form, taste, smell, and touch alone [exist] — this earth does not exist.

body.text: guṇānāñca na lakṣaṇaṃ pradarśayituṃ śakyate | rūpaṃ gandhavaditi na vaktuṃ śakyate | rūparasagandhasparśavatī pṛthivī iti tu vaktuṃ śakyate | ato naikatvamiti | rūpādibuddhiḥ pṛthivībuddhiśca pṛthak | ato jñāyate rūpādīni na pṛthivīti | anyadrūpādīnāṃ nāma anyat pṛthivyā nāma | (pṛ) buddhibhedo nāmabhedaśca sarvaḥ saṃyoge bhedavān | (u) yadi buddhirnāmasaṃyogamātreṇāsti | [tadā] saṃyogo nāmamātraṃ bhavet | tathā ca pṛthivī nāmamātramasti | iti nāstyekatvavādaḥ |
body.translated_text: And the characteristics of qualities cannot be demonstrated. It is not possible to say 'form possesses smell.' But it is possible to say 'earth possesses form, taste, smell, and touch.' From this it is known that form and the like are not earth. The cognition of form and the like and the cognition of earth are separate. From this it is known that form and the like are not earth. The name of form and the like is different; the name of earth is different. (Question) The differentiation of cognition and the differentiation of name all exist in combination. (Answer) If cognition and name exist merely through combination, then combination would be merely nominal. And likewise, earth would be merely nominal. Therefore the doctrine of unity does not stand.

body.text: pṛthivī sa sarvendriyajñeyā bhavati | kenedaṃ jñāyate | puruṣa evaṃ cintayati- pṛthivīṃ paśyāmi, pṛthivīṃ rasayāmi, pṛthivīṃ spṛśāmi iti | yadi rūparasagandhasparśāḥ pṛthivī | na
body.translated_text: Earth is knowable by all sense-faculties. By what is this known? A person thinks thus: 'I see earth, I taste earth, I touch earth.' If form, taste, smell, and touch are earth, then not

body.text: syāt rūpamātre pṛthivīṃ paśyāmīti pṛthivīsaṃjñā | gandhādāvapyevam | vastutastu na rūpamātre pṛthivī jñāyate | ato jñāyate na rūpādīnyeva pṛthivīti | prajñaptisaṃjñākāraṇe ekasminnavayave ca prajñaptisaṃjñābhidhīyate | yathā kaścid vṛkṣaśākhāṃ chindan vadati- vṛkṣaṃ chindāmi, vanaṃ chindāmīti ca | guṇānāṃ sīmāni dravyāṇi anyāni | tatra yadyasti kāraṇam | nānena sidhyati ekatvavādaḥ |
body.translated_text: it might be that, perceiving earth in mere form, one applies the designation 'earth.' The same applies to smell and so forth. But in reality, earth is not cognized in mere form alone. Therefore it is known that form and the rest are not identical with earth. In the case of conventional designation, the designation is applied even to a single part. Just as someone cutting a branch of a tree says 'I am cutting the tree' or 'I am cutting the forest.' Substances are the boundaries of qualities, and they are different. If there is a reason for that, the doctrine of unity (<s>ekatvavāda</s>) is not established by this.

body.text: sāṃkhyāḥ punarāhuḥ- pañca guṇāḥ pṛthivīti | tadapyayuktam | kasmāt | yathā pūrvamuktaṃ- śabdo rūpādivyatiriktaḥ kṣaṇikaḥ santānapravṛttaḥ | na caturmahābhūtasādhanaheturiti | ato jñāyate na sarvāṇi bhautikāni śabdavantīti ||
body.translated_text: The <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> further say that the five qualities constitute earth. That too is untenable. Why? As stated before — sound is distinct from form and the rest, is momentary, and proceeds in a continuum. It is not caused by the four <s>mahābhūtas</s> (great elements). Therefore it is known that not all material things possess sound.

body.text: ekatvakhaṇḍanavargastricatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: The chapter on the Refutation of Unity is the one hundred and forty-third.

body.text: 144 nānātvakhaṇḍanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 144. Chapter on the Refutation of Plurality

body.text: (pṛ) nānātvavāde ke doṣāḥ | (u) rūpādīn vihāya nāsti pṛthivī | kasmāt | kena tat jñāyate | na hi rūparasagandhasparśān vihāya pṛthivībuddhirutpadyate | rūpādidharmeṣvevotpadyate | kasmāt | yathā anyat rūpaṃ anye śabdādayaḥ | na ca śabdādīnapekṣya rūpabuddhirutpadyate | yadi rūpādivyatiriktā pṛthivī | rūpādīnyanapekṣyāpi pṛthivībuddhiḥ syāt | na vastutastānyanapekṣya bhavati | ato nāsti pṛthivī pṛthak | (pṛ) nānyadharmamanapekṣya bhavati | avaśyaṃ rūpalakṣaṇamapekṣya rūpabuddhirbhavati | (u) sāmānyalakṣaṇakhaṇḍanavarge vakṣyate | na rūpavyatiriktaṃ rūpalakṣaṇaṃ pṛthagastīti | ato na yujyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults in the doctrine of plurality? (Answer) Apart from form and the rest, there is no earth. Why? How is that known? Indeed, the cognition of earth does not arise apart from form, taste, smell, and touch. It arises only with respect to the properties of form and so forth. Why? Just as form is one thing and sound and the rest are different — the cognition of form does not arise dependent on sound and the rest. If earth were distinct from form and the rest, the cognition of earth should arise even without depending on form and the rest. But in reality it does not arise without depending on them. Therefore earth does not exist separately. (Question) [Cognition] does not arise without depending on the property of another. The cognition of form necessarily arises depending on the defining characteristic of form. (Answer) It will be stated in the chapter on Refutation of Universal Characteristics that the defining characteristic of form does not exist separately from form. Therefore this is not tenable.

body.text: pṛthivyādipṛthagdharmasya nendriyaṃ jñāpakam | ato jñāyate na pṛthak santi pṛthivyādayo dharmā iti | (pṛ) pṛthivyādayo dvīndriyagrāhyā yaduta kāyendriyagrāhyāścakṣurindriyagrāhyāḥ | kena tat jñāyate | cakṣuṣā dṛṣṭvā jānīmo 'yaṃ ghaṭa iti | kāyendriyeṇa spṛṣṭvāpi jānīmaḥ ayaṃ ghaṭa iti | ato nendriyagrāhyā iti bhavato vacanamayuktam | (u) tathā cet ghaṭo 'yamindriyacatuṣṭayagrāhyaḥ syāt | ghrāṇenāpi mṛta jighryate | rasanayāpi mṛt rasyate | (pṛ) ghrāṇarasanābhyāṃ na gṛhṇāti ghaṭam | kasmāt | na hyandhakāre vivecayati ghaṭo vā jighrayate kapālaṃ vā | ghaṭo vā rasyate kapālaṃ vā iti | (u) yadyapi na vivecayati kiṃ ghaṭa uta kapālamiti | tathāpi mṛdi jñānaṃ bhavati mṛdaṃ
body.translated_text: There is no sense faculty that makes known a property of earth and the rest as separate. Therefore it is known that the properties of earth and the rest do not exist separately. (Question) Earth and the rest are grasped by two sense faculties — namely the body-sense and the eye-sense. How is that known? Having seen with the eye, we know 'this is a pot.' Having touched with the body-sense too, we know 'this is a pot.' Therefore your statement that they are not grasped by the senses is untenable. (Answer) If so, the pot should be grasped by four sense faculties. For by the nose too, clay is smelled. By the tongue too, clay is tasted. (Question) One does not grasp a pot by the nose and tongue. Why? For in darkness one cannot discriminate whether it is a pot that is being smelled or a potsherd, whether it is a pot being tasted or a potsherd. (Answer) Even though one cannot discriminate whether it is a pot or a potsherd, still the cognition arises regarding clay: 'I smell clay,' 'I taste clay'

body.text: jighrāmi, mṛdaṃ rasayāmīti | yadi ghaṭa udgatamukhaṃ khanyate | tadā dṛṣṭvā spṛṣṭvā vā na nirdhārayati kimayaṃ ghaṭa śarāvaḥ kiṃ vā ghataśakalamiti | ato jñāyate cakṣurindriyaṃ kāyendriyañca na ghaṭaṃ gṛhṇīyāt iti | andhakāre ghaṭabuddhirutpannāpi na vivecayati suvarṇaghaṭo rajataghaṭo vā iti | ato jñāyate cakṣurindriyaṃ kāyendriyamapi na ghaṭaṃ gṛhṇīyāt | ghrāṇendriyaṃ jihvendriyaṃ puṣpaphalakṣīrasurādīn dharmān gṛhṇāti | cakṣurindriyaṃ kāyendriyantu na gṛhṇāti | yathā [cakṣuḥ] puṣpādi paśyati na vivicya jānāti gandhaḥ surabhirasurabhirvā raso madhuro 'madhuro vā ityādi | ato yadi mataṃ cakṣuḥkāyendriyābhyāṃ jānīmo dravyaṃ na ghrāṇajihvābhyāmiti | nedaṃ sambhavati | yathā ghrāṇajihve dravyaṃ pṛthakkṛtya na vikalpayataḥ | tathā cakṣuḥkāyendriye api dravyamapṛthagbhūtamapi na vikalpayataḥ |
body.translated_text: . If a pot is dug up with its mouth protruding, then even having seen or touched it, one cannot determine whether this is a pot, a saucer, or a pot-fragment. Therefore it is known that the eye-sense and the body-sense do not grasp the pot. Even when the cognition of a pot arises in darkness, one cannot discriminate whether it is a golden pot or a silver pot. Therefore it is known that the eye-sense and the body-sense also do not grasp the pot. The nose-sense and the tongue-sense grasp properties such as those of flowers, fruits, milk, liquor, and so forth. But the eye-sense and the body-sense do not grasp these. Just as [the eye] sees flowers and the like but does not discriminately know whether the smell is fragrant or unfragrant, whether the taste is sweet or not sweet, and so forth. Therefore, if you hold that by the eye-sense and body-sense we know substance but not by the nose and tongue — this is not possible. Just as the nose and tongue do not separate substance and discriminate it, so too the eye-sense and body-sense also do not discriminate substance even though it is not separate.

body.text: pañcendriyeṣu prajñaptigrāhakaṃ jñānaṃ nāsti | ato jñāyate prajñaptirna cakṣuḥkāyaghrāṇajihvendriyairlabhyate | ṣaṣṭhasya tvasti prajñaptijñāpakaṃ jñānam | kasmāt | manovijñānasya sarvadharmālambanatvāt | cakṣuryadi rūpaṃ paśyati arupañca paśyati | tadā śabdādīnamapi paśyet | tathā cet śrotrādīnīndriyāṇi nāvaśyakāni syuḥ | na tu sambhavati | ataścakṣuḥkāyendriyābhyāṃ na dravyaṃ gṛhyate | (pṛ) rūpeṇa dravyopalabdhau cakṣuḥ paśyati | na tu sarvo rūpātpṛthagbhūto dharmo dṛśyaḥ | (u) rūpeṇa ghaṭopalabdhiritīdaṃ na yujyate | kasmāt | kaḥ karoti ghaṭarūpam | saṃyogamātramidam | ato na rūpeṇa ghaṭopalabdhiḥ | yadi ca dṛśyadharmeṇa tadanyadharma upalabhya dṛśyo bhavati | ghaṭādinādṛśyadharmeṇa rupolabdhiriti rūpamapi adṛśyaṃ syāt | ghaṭo 'pi dvividhaḥ syāt dṛśyo 'dṛśya iti | dṛśyadharmasyādṛśyopalabdhyarthatvāt | yadyavaśyaṃ rūpādidharmasyopalabdhatvāt cakṣurādīndrayagrāhyamiti | [tadā] rūpalakṣaṇaṃ cakṣurindriyagrāhyamiti na syāt | kasmāt | bhavatāṃ sūtre rūpamupādāya (=rūpahetukaṃ) indriyeṇa rūpaṃ dṛśyamitīdaṃ rūpalakṣaṇaṃ punaralakṣaṇaṃ bhavati | tathā tu rūpalakṣaṇamadṛśyamiti syāt | ato na yujyate |
body.translated_text: Among the five sense faculties, there is no cognition that grasps conventional designation. Therefore it is known that conventional designation is not obtained through the eye, body, nose, or tongue senses. But the sixth [sense, i.e., mind] does have cognition that makes known conventional designation. Why? Because <s>manovijñāna</s> (mental consciousness) has all <s>dharmas</s> as its objects. If the eye sees form and also sees non-form, then it should also see sound and the rest. In that case, the ear and other sense faculties would not be necessary. But that is not possible. Therefore, substance is not grasped by the eye-sense and body-sense. (Question) When substance is apprehended through form, the eye sees it. But not every property separate from form is visible. (Answer) The apprehension of a pot through form is not tenable. Why? Who makes 'pot-form'? This is merely a conjunction. Therefore there is no apprehension of a pot through form. Moreover, if through a visible property another property of it is apprehended and becomes visible, then since a pot and the like [have] an invisible property, the apprehension of form [through that invisible property] would mean form too should be invisible. And a pot would be of two kinds — visible and invisible — because a visible property serves for the apprehension of the invisible. If you insist that because the property of form and the rest is apprehended, it is grasped by the eye and other senses — then the defining characteristic of form should not be grasped by the eye-sense. Why? In your <s>sūtra</s> it says: 'Depending on form (i.e., caused by form), form is seen by the sense faculty' — this defining characteristic of form becomes again a non-characteristic. Thus the defining characteristic of form would be invisible. Therefore this is not tenable.

body.text: yadi rūpopalabdhyā dṛśyamiti | [tarhi] sarvāṇīndriyāṇi dravyaṃ jānīyuḥ | śrotrendriyamapi ākāśaṃ jānīyāt śabdopalambhāt | kāyendriyeṇa vāyuṃ jānīyāt sparśopalambhāt |
body.translated_text: If [you say] something is visible because of the apprehension of form, then all sense faculties should know substance. The ear-sense too should know <s>ākāśa</s> (space) because of the apprehension of sound. The body-sense should know <s>vāyu</s> (wind) because of the apprehension of touch.

body.text: bhavatāṃ mate tu na yujyate | ato nedaṃ dharmamupalambhayati | (pṛ) anye dharmā nopalabdhikarāḥ | rūpamātramupalabdhikaram | (u) maivam | na tatrāsti vinigamanā rūpamātramupalabdhikaraṃ nānye dharmā iti | yathā bhavānāha mahatyanekadravyavattvāt rūpāccopalabdhiriti | evaṃ rūpahetukaṃ rūpamupalabhyate | rūpalakṣaṇopalambhena rūpaṃ taduttaramupalabhyam | na rūpamātramupalabdhikaramiti | evamukte ['pi] na pūrvoktadoṣaparihāraḥ |
body.translated_text: But according to your view, this is not tenable. Therefore this [argument] does not make the property apprehensible. (Question) Other properties are not the cause of apprehension. Only form alone is the cause of apprehension. (Answer) Do not say so. There is no decisive determination there that form alone is the cause of apprehension and not other properties. Just as you say that apprehension is from form because a large [object] possesses many substances — so too, form is apprehended as caused by form. Through the apprehension of the defining characteristic of form, form is subsequently apprehended. It is not that form alone is the cause of apprehension. Even when stated thus, the previously stated fault is not avoided.

body.text: anyakālaṃ rūpabuddhirutpadyate anyakālañca ghaṭabuddhiḥ | ato rūpāt ghaṭopalambhe ka upakāraḥ | yathā andho 'bhyastaghaṭaparimāṇo vinaṣṭacakṣuṣko 'pi spṛṣṭvā ghaṭaṃ jānāti | ato na rūpamātraṃ darśanasya kāraṇam | andhaḥ kāyendriyeṇa ca vāyuṃ jānāti | ato na rūpamātropalambhāt jñānamutpadyate | bhavatāṃ sūtre 'pyuktam- kāyāgataspṛṣṭaḥ sparśo na pṛthivyaptejasāṃmiti jñātavyam- adṛṣṭaliṅgo vāyuriti | tadapyayuktam | kasmāt | andha imaṃ vāyuṃ jānannapi na jānāti vāyurayaṃ kiṃ dṛśyaḥ kiṃvā adṛśya iti | puruṣaścakṣuṣā saṃkhyāparimāṇādīn dharmān paśyati | na tatrāsti rūpopalabdhiḥ | gandhamāghrāyāpi agandhadharme jñānaṃ labhate | rasaṃ rasayitvāpi arasadharme jñānaṃ labhate | ato 'vaśyaṃ rūpolambhena dravyaṃ tadūrdhva jñeyamitīdamayuktam |
body.translated_text: The cognition of form arises at one time, and the cognition of a pot arises at another time. Therefore, what benefit does form provide for the apprehension of a pot? Just as a blind person who has previously experienced the dimensions of a pot, even with destroyed eyesight, knows a pot by touching it. Therefore, form alone is not the cause of seeing. A blind person also knows wind by the body-sense. Therefore, cognition does not arise merely from the apprehension of form. In your <s>sūtra</s> too it is said: 'Touch that comes to the body is not [the touch] of earth, water, or fire' — one should know that wind has invisible characteristics. That too is untenable. Why? A blind person who knows this wind still does not know whether this wind is visible or invisible. Moreover, a person sees with the eye such properties as number, dimension, and so forth. There is no apprehension of form there. By smelling a fragrance too, one obtains cognition of a property that is not smell. By tasting a flavor too, one obtains cognition of a property that is not flavor. Therefore, the claim that substance must necessarily be known subsequently through the apprehension of form is untenable.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi rūpopalambho darśanasya na kāraṇam | ye saṃkhyāparimāṇādayo dharmāḥ [te] adṛśyadravyagatāḥ, vāyuśca dṛśyaḥ syāt | (u) asmanmate rūpaṃ vihāya nāstyanyo dharmo dṛśyaḥ | ato jñāyate mate ['smin] yatra rūpamutpannamasti tatra cakṣuḥ paśyati | cakṣuṣā dṛṣṭarūpasyaiva ghaṭasaṃjñā bhavati | yasmin dharme nāstyutpannaṃ rūpam, tatra sacakṣuṣkasyāpi notpadyate 'nyaghaṭasaṃjñā | ato rūpadi vihāya pṛthagasti ghaṭa itīdaṃ na nyāyyam ||
body.translated_text: (Question) If the apprehension of form is not the cause of seeing, then properties such as number, dimension, and so forth should belong to invisible substances, and wind should be visible. (Answer) In our view, apart from form, there is no other property that is visible. Therefore it is known that in this view, wherever form has arisen, there the eye sees. The designation 'pot' belongs only to the form seen by the eye. In a property where form has not arisen, even for one who has eyesight, the cognition 'this is some other pot' does not arise. Therefore, that a pot exists separately from form and the rest — this is not logically valid.

body.text: nānātvakhaṇḍanavargaścatuścatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: The chapter on the Refutation of Plurality is the one hundred and forty-fourth.

body.text: 145 anirvacanīyatvakhaṇḍanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 145. Chapter on the Refutation of Inexpressibility

body.text: (pṛ) anirvacanīyatve ke doṣāḥ | paramārthadharmo naikatvanānātvābhyāmanirvacanīyaḥ | kasmāt | na hetudṛṣṭāntau staḥ idamanirvacanīyamiti jñāpayitum | rūpādayo dharmāḥ paramārthasantaḥ | ato nānirvacanīyāḥ | dharmāḥ pratyekaṃ sasvalakṣaṇāḥ | yathā rūpaṇalakṣaṇaṃ rūpam | na nānātvalakṣaṇam | kathamucyate 'nirvacanīyamiti | vijñānaviśeṣāddharmaviśeṣaḥ | yathā cakṣurvijñānena rūpaṃ jñāyate, na śabdādi | ato 'sya nānirvacanīyatā | rūpaṃ rūpāyatanasaṅgṛhītaṃ na śabdādisaṅgṛhītam | yadyanirvacanīyatvamicchasi | idaṃ rūpamidaṃ rūpamiti nirvacanīyamasti | rūpamidamarūpamidamiti anirvacanīyam | evaṃ śabdādayo 'pi | dharmāṇāṃ kramaḥ saṃkhyā cāsti | yadyanirvācyāḥ | tadā dharmā asaṃkhyāḥ syuḥ | kasmāt | prathamaṃ dvitīyamiti lakṣaṇabhedasyābhāvāt | ato jñāyate paramārthato nānirvācyāḥ dharmāḥ prajñaptāveva ekatvanānātvasatvāducyate 'nirvācya iti ||
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults in inexpressibility? <s>Dharmas</s> in the ultimate sense are inexpressible as either unity or plurality. Why? There are no reasons or examples to make known that something is inexpressible. <s>Dharmas</s> such as form and the rest exist in the ultimate sense. Therefore they are not inexpressible. Each <s>dharma</s> has its own characteristic. For example, the characteristic of form is form. It is not the characteristic of plurality. How can it be called 'inexpressible'? From the distinctness of cognition, there is distinctness of <s>dharmas</s>. Just as form is known through visual consciousness, not sound and the rest. Therefore it has no inexpressibility. Form is included in the <s>rūpāyatana</s> (form-base), not in sound and the rest. If you wish for inexpressibility — 'this is form, this is form' is expressible; 'this is form, this is non-form' is inexpressible. So too for sound and the rest. <s>Dharmas</s> have sequence and number. If they were inexpressible, then <s>dharmas</s> would be uncountable. Why? Because there would be no distinction of characteristics such as 'first' and 'second.' Therefore it is known that in the ultimate sense, <s>dharmas</s> are not inexpressible. Only in conventional designation, because of unity, plurality, and existence, they are called 'inexpressible.'

body.text: anirvacanīyatvakhaṇḍanavargaḥ pañcacatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: The chapter on the Refutation of Inexpressibility is the one hundred and forty-fifth.

body.text: 146 abhāvakhaṇḍanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 146. Chapter on the Refutation of Non-existence

body.text: (pṛ) abhāvavāde ke doṣāḥ | (u) abhāvatve na puṇyapāpādīnāṃ vipāko vimuktyādayaḥ sarve dharmāḥ | vidyamānaṃ nāstīti grahe sa graho 'pi abhāvaḥ syāt | vaktuḥ śrotuścābhāvāt | asti nāstīti vādāḥ śraddhayoktāḥ pratyakṣajñānaśraddhayā vā bhavanti anumitijñānaśraddhayā vā bhavanti | sūtramranthānusāreṇa vā bhavanti | yatkiñcana nāstīti yat vacanaṃ tadeṣu triṣu na bhavati | sūtraṃ vānusarāma iti bhavatāmāśayo [yaḥ] nāyaṃ yujyate | sūtrāśayo 'pi duḥsaṃvādaḥ | kadācidastītyāha kadācinnāstītyāha | kathaṃ śraddhāṃ gṛhṇīmaḥ | yadyanumānajñānaṃ śraddadhyāt | avaśyaṃ pratyakṣapūrvakamanumitijñānaṃ bhavet | ghaṭādayo dharmā idānīṃ pratyakṣadṛṣṭāḥ santi | jñānajanakatvāt | yo jñānajanakaḥ dharmo 'sti nābhāva[rūpaḥ] |
body.translated_text: (Question) What are the faults in the doctrine of non-existence? (Answer) If [all were] non-existent, there would be no fruition of merit, demerit, and the rest, nor liberation, nor any <s>dharmas</s> whatsoever. If what exists is grasped as non-existent, that very grasping too would be non-existent — because the speaker and listener would also be non-existent. Statements of 'it exists' or 'it does not exist' are spoken either through faith in direct perception or through faith in inferential knowledge, or in accordance with <s>sūtras</s> and treatises. The statement 'nothing whatsoever exists' does not fall under any of these three. Or if your intention is 'we follow the <s>sūtra</s>' — this is not tenable either. The purport of the <s>sūtras</s> is also contradictory — sometimes it says 'it exists,' sometimes it says 'it does not exist.' How can we place faith [in one alone]? If one has faith in inferential knowledge, then inferential knowledge must necessarily be preceded by direct perception. <s>Dharmas</s> such as pots and the rest are now directly perceived to exist, because they generate cognition. A <s>dharma</s> that generates cognition exists and is not of the nature of non-existence.

body.text: idānīṃ ghaṭaśarāvādayaḥ saviśeṣā dṛśyante | yadi sarve 'bhāvāḥ | kaḥ saviśeṣaḥ syāt | mithyāsaṃjñayā saviśeṣā iti bhavatāṃ matam | kasmāt ākāśe ghaṭādīn na vikalpayati | mohātpadārthabuddhirutpadyata iti bhavatāṃ matam | sarveṣāmabhāvatve moho 'pyabhāvaḥ syāditi kena pravarteta | sarve dharmā abhāvā iti bhavata āśaye jñānamidaṃ kiṃ pratītya bhavati | na hi jñānānyabhāvapratyayenotpadyante | padārthān jānātīti jñānam | nedaṃ jñānamabhāva iti vācyam | yadyatyantābhāvā iti | tadā sarve janā yathābhipretaṃ yatkiñcana kuryuḥ | kintvāryā dānaśīlakṣāntyādikuśalakarmābhiratā akuśaladharmaviviktāśca bhavanti | ato jñāyate nābhāvā iti | ghaṭādayo dharmāḥ pratyakṣajñeyāḥ | bhavāṃstvāha- pratyakṣaṃ sarvamabhāvarūpamiti | abhāvadharmakatvācca na sūtre śraddadhīta | tathā ca kena kāraṇenāha- sarvamabhāva iti | ataḥ sarvamabhāva itīdaṃ [na] spaṣṭaṃ bhavet | yadi kāraṇena na prakāśayati [tadā] paragṛhītaṃ prakṛtitaḥ sidhyet | paravādasya siddhatvāt bhavatāṃ dharmo vinaśyet | yo bhāvaḥ kāraṇena sādhyaḥ na so 'bhāva ityucyate ||
body.translated_text: Now, pots, potsherds, and so forth are seen as having distinctions. If all are non-existent, what distinction could there be? Your view is that they have distinctions through false designation. Then why does one not imagine pots and such in empty space? Your view is that cognition of real objects arises from delusion. But if all are non-existent, delusion too would be non-existent — so by what would it be set in motion? In your view that 'all <s>dharmas</s> are non-existent,' on what basis does this knowledge arise? For cognitions do not arise from a condition of non-existence. Knowledge means knowing objects — this knowledge cannot be called non-existent. If [you say] they are absolutely non-existent, then all people would do whatever they pleased. But the noble ones (<s>ārya</s>) delight in wholesome actions such as generosity (<s>dāna</s>), morality (<s>śīla</s>), patience (<s>kṣānti</s>), and so on, and they are free from unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>. Therefore it is known that [all things] are not non-existent. <s>Dharmas</s> such as pots are knowable by direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). But you say that all direct perception is of the nature of non-existence. And since it has the character of non-existence, one should not have faith in the <s>sūtra</s>. Moreover, by what reason do you say 'all is non-existent'? Therefore 'all is non-existent' would [not] be clearly established. If you do not demonstrate it with a reason, then the opponent's position would be established by default. Since the opponent's thesis is established, your doctrine would perish. That which is a real entity established by a reason — that is not called non-existent.

body.text: abhāvakhaṇḍanavargaḥ ṣaṭcatvāriṃśaduttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: The chapter on the refutation of non-existence (<s>abhāvakhaṇḍanavarga</s>), the one hundred and forty-sixth.

body.text: 147 abhāvasthāpanavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 147. The chapter on the establishment of non-existence (<s>abhāvasthāpanavarga</s>).

body.text: abhāvavādyāha- yadyapi vacasā śūnyatāṃ khaṇḍayasi | tathāpi dharmāṃḥ paramārthato 'bhāvāḥ | indriyairviṣayāṇāmanupalambhāt | kasmāt | na hyasti dharmāṇāmavayavī grāhyaḥ | ataḥ sarve dharmā agrāhyāḥ | agrāhyādabhāvā[tmakāḥ] | avayavinyagrāhye 'pi avayavā grāhyā iti bhavato yanmatam | tanna yuktam | nāvayaveṣu buddhirbhavati | kasmāt | sthūlaghaṭādīnāṃ padārthānāmeva grāhyatvāt | na cāvayavā avayavinaṃ kurvanti | kasmāt | avayavinamupādāya hi avayavā ucyante | avayavino 'bhāvādavayavā api na santi | dravyeṣu guṇeṣu asatsu nāvayavāḥ santi | ato na santyavayavāḥ | sūkṣmāvayavān paśyato 'vayavabuddhiḥ sadā bhavati na ghaṭabuddhiḥ | kasmāt | avayavān nityaṃ smarato ghaṭabuddhirnaiva bhavet | yadyavayavasmaraṇapūrvakaṃ ghaṭabuddhirbhavati | tadā ghaṭabuddhirvilambya bhavet | na vastuto vilambya
body.translated_text: The proponent of non-existence (<s>abhāvavādin</s>) says: Even though you refute emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>) with words, still, <s>dharmas</s> are ultimately non-existent, because the sense faculties (<s>indriya</s>) do not apprehend their objects. Why? Because there is no composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) of <s>dharmas</s> that can be grasped. Therefore all <s>dharmas</s> are ungraspable. Being ungraspable, they are of the nature of non-existence. Your view that even when the composite whole is ungraspable, the parts (<s>avayava</s>) can be grasped — that is not correct. There is no cognition of the parts. Why? Because only gross objects like pots are graspable. Moreover, parts do not constitute the composite whole. Why? Because parts are so called only in dependence on a composite whole. In the absence of the composite whole, parts too do not exist. When substances (<s>dravya</s>) and qualities (<s>guṇa</s>) do not exist, parts do not exist. Therefore parts do not exist. For one who sees subtle parts, there is always cognition of parts but never cognition of the pot. Why? One who constantly remembers the parts would never have cognition of the pot. If cognition of the pot arises preceded by recollection of parts, then the cognition of the pot would arise with a delay. In reality, it does not arise with a delay

body.text: bhavati | ato nāvayavāḥ smaryante | ghaṭaṃ dṛṣṭvā yannāvayavavikalpabuddhirbhavati saiva ghaṭabuddhiḥ |
body.translated_text: . Therefore the parts are not remembered. Upon seeing a pot, the very cognition that does not involve differentiation of parts — that itself is the cognition of the pot.

body.text: sarve cāvayavā abhāvā[tmakāḥ]ḥ | kasmāt | sarvehyavayavā avayavaśo bhidyamānā aṇutāṃ yānti | aṇuśo bhidyamānā atyantābhāvatāṃ pratiyanti | sarveṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ niṣṭhā śūnyatābuddhijananamavaśyam | ato 'vayavāḥ paramārthato 'bhāvatmakāḥ | avayavavādinaḥ satyadvayabhaṅgaḥ syāt | kasmāt | yo vadati nāstyavayavī kevalamavayavāḥ santīti | tasyātītāgāmidarśanaprahāṇādīni karmāṇi na syuḥ | evañca lokasatyaṃ nāsti | bhavān paramārthaṃ śūnyatāṃ manyate | paramārthe cābhāvātmakā avayavāḥ | ato jñāyate avayavamātravacanaṃ na satyadvaye 'vatārayati | satyadvaye 'navatārādabhāvaḥ |
body.translated_text: Moreover, all parts are of the nature of non-existence. Why? Because all parts, when broken down part by part, reach atoms (<s>aṇu</s>). When atoms are broken down, they reach absolute non-existence. The generation of the cognition of emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>) regarding all <s>dharmas</s> is inevitable. Therefore parts are ultimately of the nature of non-existence. For the proponent of parts, the doctrine of the two truths (<s>satyadvaya</s>) would be violated. Why? One who says 'there is no composite whole, only parts exist' — for such a person, actions such as seeing past and future and abandoning [defilements] would not be possible. Thus the conventional truth (<s>lokasatya</s>) does not exist. You consider the ultimate truth to be emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>). And in the ultimate, parts are of the nature of non-existence. Therefore it is known that the assertion of mere parts does not lead to the two truths. From not leading to the two truths, [the result is] non-existence.

body.text: yo dharmo 'paneyaḥ so 'bhābātmakaḥ | yathā avayavānupādāya avayavī nirākriyate | avayavāntarāṇyupādāya pūrvāvayavā nirākriyante | ato 'yamavayavavādo 'bhāvātmakaḥ | rūpādīnyapi abhāvātmakāni | kasmāt | na hi cakṣuḥ sūkṣmaṃ rūpaṃ paśyati | na ca mano gṛhṇāti pratyutpannaṃ rūpam | ato rūpamagrāhyam | cakṣurvijñānaṃ na vikalpayati idaṃ rūpamiti | manovijñānantu atīte anāgate vartate na rūpe vartate | ato nāsti kiñcidrūpavikalpakam vikalpakābhāvādrūpamagrāhyaṃ bhavati | nādyavijñānaṃ rūpaṃ vikalpayati | tathā dvitīyādivijñānānyapi | ato nāsti kiñcidrūpavikalpakam |
body.translated_text: Whatever <s>dharma</s> can be removed is of the nature of non-existence. Just as the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is negated by taking away its parts (<s>avayava</s>), and the prior parts are negated by taking away the intermediate parts — therefore this doctrine of parts is of the nature of non-existence. Form (<s>rūpa</s>) and the rest too are of the nature of non-existence. Why? Because the eye does not see subtle form. Nor does the mind (<s>manas</s>) grasp present form. Therefore form is ungraspable. Visual consciousness (<s>cakṣurvijñāna</s>) does not conceptualize 'this is form.' Mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>), however, operates regarding the past and future, not regarding form. Therefore there is nothing that conceptualizes form. Due to the absence of a conceptualizer, form becomes ungraspable. The first consciousness does not conceptualize form. Likewise the second and subsequent consciousnesses. Therefore there is nothing that conceptualizes form.

body.text: (pṛ) cakṣurvijñānena rūpe gṛhīte tato manovijñānamanusmarati | ato na nāsti vikalpakamiti | (u) cakṣurvijñānaṃ rūpaṃ dṛṣṭvā niruddhameva | tata ūrdhvaṃ manovijñānamutpadyate | manovijñānamidaṃ na rūpaṃ paśyati | adṛṣṭvā kathamanusmaret | yadyadṛṣṭvānusmaret | andho 'pi rūpamanusmaret | na vastuto 'nusmarati | ato manovijñānaṃ nānusmarati | (pṛ) cakṣurvijñānānmanovijñānamutpadyate | ato 'nusmarati | (u) maivam | kasmāt | sarvāṇi caramacittāni cakṣurvijñānamupādāya samutpannāni anusmareyuḥ | naiva vismareyuḥ | tasmādutpannatvāt |
body.translated_text: (Objection:) When form has been grasped by visual consciousness (<s>cakṣurvijñāna</s>), then mental consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>) recollects it. Therefore it is not the case that there is no conceptualizer. (Reply:) Visual consciousness, having seen form, ceases. After that, mental consciousness arises. This mental consciousness does not see form. Without seeing, how could it recollect? If it could recollect without seeing, then even a blind person would recollect form. In reality, one does not recollect [in that way]. Therefore mental consciousness does not recollect. (Objection:) Mental consciousness arises from visual consciousness. Therefore it recollects.
