The maximum lifespan of <s>pretas</s> (hungry ghosts) is seven thousand years. The lifespan of those in <s>Pūrvavideha</s> is two hundred and fifty years. The lifespan of those in <s>Avaragodānīya</s> is five thousand years. The lifespan of those in <s>Uttarakuru</s> is a fixed one thousand years. The lifespan of those in <s>Jambudvīpa</s> is either an immeasurable <s>kalpa</s> or ten years. The lifespan of the <s>devas</s> of the <s>Cāturmahārājika</s> heaven is five thousand years. Up to the <s>Bhavāgra</s> (summit of existence), the lifespan is eighty thousand years. Therefore it is known that everything in the three realms is impermanent.

body.text: tribhiḥ śraddhābhiśca śraddhīyate 'nityamiti | dṛṣṭe nāsti kaściddharmo nityaḥ | āptavacane 'pi na kaściddharmo nityaḥ | anumitijñāne 'pi nāsti kaścinnityaḥ | dṛṣṭapūrvakatvādanumānasya | yadyasti kiñcinnityaṃ sthānam | ko vidvān sarvadharmanirodha[pūrvaṃ] vimuktimabhilaṣet | ko
body.translated_text: Impermanence is established through three kinds of faith. By direct perception, no <s>dharma</s> is permanent. By the words of authoritative persons, no <s>dharma</s> is permanent. By inferential knowledge also, nothing is permanent, since inference is based on what has been directly perceived. If there were some permanent state, what wise person would desire liberation preceded by the cessation of all <s>dharmas</s>? Who

body.text: vā neṣyāt | sukhavedināṃ sadā saṃvāsaṃ priyaṃ vā vastutastu vidvān sarvathā vimuktimeva prārthayate | ato jñāyate samudayadharma na nityaṃ bhavatīti | atha punarvaktavyaṃ samudayadharma sarvaṃ kṣaṇikaṃ muhūrtamapi na tiṣṭhati | kaḥ punarvādo nityaṃ bhavatīti |
body.translated_text: would not desire the constant companionship of pleasant feelings and beloved things? But in truth, the wise person seeks only liberation in every way. Therefore it is known that what has the nature of arising is not permanent. Furthermore, it should be stated that everything having the nature of arising is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>) and does not endure even for an instant. What need then to speak of it being permanent?

body.text: (pṛ) anityasaṃjñāśraddhā kiṃ karoti | (u) kleśān vināśayati | yathoktaṃ sūtre- anityasaṃjñā bhāvitā [bahulīkṛtā] sarvaṃ kāmarāgaṃ paryādāti | sarvaṃ rūparāgaṃ [paryādāti | sarvaṃ] bhavarāgaṃ [paryādāti] | sarvamasmimānaṃ [paryādāti sarvā]mavidyāṃ paryādāti iti | (pṛ)
body.translated_text: (Question) What does faith in the perception of impermanence accomplish? (Answer) It destroys the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'The perception of impermanence, when cultivated and made abundant, completely exhausts all desire-attachment (<s>kāmarāga</s>), completely exhausts all form-attachment (<s>rūparāga</s>), completely exhausts all existence-attachment (<s>bhavarāga</s>), completely exhausts all the conceit "I am" (<s>asmimāna</s>), and completely exhausts all ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>).'

body.text: (pṛ) maivam | anityasaṃjñeyaṃ kāmarāgamapi vardhayati | yathā kaścit subhikṣakālo na dīrgha iti budhyan maithunarāga āsajyate | kusumaṃ nāticiraṃ navaṃ bhavatīti jānan sukhāyāśu tadupabhuṅkte | parasya [dayitājanasya] surūpaṃ na nityaṃ bhavatīti jānan maithunarāgaṃ drutataraṃ vardhayati | evamanityajñānavaśātkāmarāga utpadyate | ato nānityasaṃjñā kāmarāgaṃ vināśayati | kecidanityamiti jānanto vadhādikamapi kurvanti | yāvattiryañcaḥ anityamiti jānanto 'pi na kleśān bhindanti | ato 'nityasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayato na kaścidupakāro bhavati | (u) anityatvādviyogaduḥkhamutprekṣamāṇaḥ subhikṣakālasukhajīvitadhanamānāni tyajanti | viduṣo nānena prīticittamutpadyate | prīticittābhāve na kāmacittamutpadyate | vedanāṃ pratītya hi tṛṣṇā bhavati | vedanānirodhe tṛṣṇā nirudhyate | ato jñāyate anityasaṃjñā kāmarāgaṃ samucchedayatyeva | yaśca dharmo 'nityaḥ, so 'nātmā ityanityamanātma ca bhāvayato yogino nātmabuddhirbhavati | ātmabuddhyabhāve ātmīyabuddhirna bhavati | ātmīyabuddhyabhāvāt kutra kāmarāgaḥ syāt | anityasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayan svaparakāyaṃ kṣaṇikaṃ maraṇa[dharma] ca paśyati | kathaṃ rāgamutpādayet | yogī prārthitaṃ sarvamanityaṃ vipralopanamiti anuyāti | tadā tucchaṃ bhavati | tucchatvāt na kāmarāgamutpādayati | yathā kaścidvālakaḥ śūnye hastaḥ tuccha iti jñātvaiva na [tatra]saṅgaṃ janayati | kiñca sattvā nādhruvavastuṣu prīyante | yathā kaścit bhaṅguratvāt bhājane na pramudyate | yathāpi ca kācinnārī amukasya puruṣasyāyurna saptadinānyeṣyatīti śrutvā [vadati] satsvapi subhikṣakālārjavabahumānadhanaprabhāvabaleṣu ko vā prīyeta iti | jano 'yaṃ samyaganityasaṃjñā- [bhāvana]yā na kāmarāgamutpādayati | vidvān hi punarāvṛttipatanādiduḥkhamanusmaran yāvaddivyakāmeṣvapi nāsajyate | kevalamuktimeva prārthayate | anityasaṃjñā kāmarāgaṃ vardhayatīti yadbhavānavocat tadayuktam |
body.translated_text: (Question) This is not so. This perception of impermanence also increases desire-attachment. Just as someone, knowing that a time of abundance will not last long, becomes attached to sexual desire; knowing that a flower will not remain fresh for long, one quickly enjoys it for pleasure; knowing that the beauty of another's beloved will not last forever, one increases sexual desire more rapidly. Thus, due to the knowledge of impermanence, desire-attachment arises. Therefore the perception of impermanence does not destroy desire-attachment. Some, knowing things to be impermanent, even commit murder and such acts. Even animals, though knowing impermanence, do not destroy their <s>kleśas</s>. Therefore cultivating the perception of impermanence brings no benefit. (Answer) Contemplating the suffering of separation due to impermanence, people abandon the pleasures of times of abundance, livelihood, wealth, and honor. For the wise person, delight of mind does not arise from this. In the absence of delight, desire-mind does not arise. For <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) arises dependent on <s>vedanā</s> (feeling). With the cessation of <s>vedanā</s>, <s>tṛṣṇā</s> ceases. Therefore it is known that the perception of impermanence completely uproots desire-attachment. And whatever <s>dharma</s> is impermanent, that is non-self — thus, for the practitioner who contemplates impermanence and non-self, the notion of self does not arise. In the absence of self-notion, the notion of 'mine' does not arise. In the absence of the notion of 'mine,' where would desire-attachment exist? One who cultivates the perception of impermanence sees one's own and others' bodies as momentary and subject to death. How could one generate attachment? The practitioner pursues the understanding that all that is desired is impermanent and subject to dissolution. Then it becomes empty. Due to its emptiness, one does not generate desire-attachment. Just as a child, knowing an empty hand to be empty, does not generate attachment to it. Moreover, beings do not delight in unstable things. Just as someone does not rejoice in a vessel because of its fragility. And just as a woman, hearing that a certain man's life will not last seven days, says: 'Even though there are times of abundance, honesty, honor, wealth, power, and strength, who would delight in them?' This person, through the correct cultivation of the perception of impermanence, does not generate desire-attachment. The wise person, remembering the suffering of return, falling, and such, does not become attached even to divine pleasures, but seeks only liberation. What you said — that the perception of impermanence increases desire-attachment — is incorrect.

body.text: yadi kaścidaprahīṇāsmimāno bhavati | tadā sa bāhyaṃ vastvanityaṃ paśyan śocyate | priyabaloviparihāṇyā ca kāmaprārthatāṃ karoti | pṛthagjano 'yaṃ prahīṇakāmasukho ['pi] na viyogaduḥkhaṃ prajānāti | tadyathā kaścidbālako mātrā tāḍitaḥ punarmātaramevāyāti | vidvāṃstu duḥkhahetau sthita eva na duḥkhaṃ nirodhyamiti jñātvā tyajati duḥkhahetuṃ yaduta pañcaskandhān | ayaṃ yogī ābhyantaraskandhān paribhettuṃ anātmasaṃjñāṃ pratilabhate | bāhyavastuvināśe 'pi na śokena pīḍyate | anātmapratilābhī kiṃ punaḥ prārthayīta anityasajñyapi na kiñcitprārthayate |
body.translated_text: If someone has not abandoned the conceit 'I am' (<s>asmimāna</s>), then seeing external things as impermanent, one grieves. Due to the loss of beloved strength, one desires sense pleasures. This ordinary person, though having abandoned the pleasure of desire, does not realize the suffering of separation. Just as a child, struck by his mother, comes back to his mother again. But the wise person, knowing that suffering is not ceased while remaining in the cause of suffering, abandons the cause of suffering, namely the five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates). This practitioner, in order to discern the internal <s>skandhas</s>, attains the perception of non-self (<s>anātmasaṃjñā</s>). Even when external things are destroyed, one is not afflicted by grief. One who has attained the perception of non-self — what more would one desire? Even the perception of impermanence does not cause one to desire anything.

body.text: anityasaṃjñā ceyaṃ yadi duḥkhe 'nātmasaṃjñāṃ notpādayati | tadā sā kleśavināśanasampannā na bhavati | ata uktaṃ sūtre- ekāgreṇa cittena pañcaskandhānanityān bhāvayet | ya ādhyātmikān skandhān aparibhidya bahirdhā vastu anityaṃ paśyati | tasya sātmasaṃjñatvāt śoka utpadyate | tadeyamasamyagbhāvanā bhavati | iti | anityamiti paśyatāmapi na nirvedavirāga utpadyate | yathā aurabhrikavyādhādīnām | eṣāṃ satyapi anityajñāne na sādhubhāvanā bhavati | kaścitsamyagbhāvayannapi nānavarataṃ bhāvanāṃ vyavasyati | tasya kāmacittamante viparyasyati | ata ucyate- ekagracitteteti | kiñca kaścit anitya[saṃjñā]malpakālaṃ bhāvayati | kleśāstu bahavaḥ | na [tān] paribhettumalaṃ bhavati | yathā alpamauṣadhaṃ bahvī rvyādhīrna vināśayati | tathedamapi | ata ucyate- ekāgracittena anityamiti samyambhāvanā kleśān vināśayati | iti |
body.translated_text: And if this perception of impermanence (<s>anityasaṃjñā</s>) does not give rise to the perception of non-self (<s>anātmasaṃjñā</s>) with respect to suffering, then it is not endowed with the capacity to destroy the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>). Therefore it is stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'With a one-pointed mind, one should contemplate the five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>) as impermanent. One who, without analyzing the internal aggregates, sees external objects as impermanent — for such a person, because of the perception of self, grief arises. This is incorrect contemplation.' Even among those who see things as impermanent, disenchantment and dispassion (<s>nirvedavirāga</s>) do not arise, just as in the case of butchers, hunters, and the like. Even though they possess knowledge of impermanence, proper contemplation does not occur for them. Someone, even while contemplating correctly, does not persist in contemplation without interruption. For such a person, the mind of desire overturns at the end. Therefore it is said: 'with a one-pointed mind.' Furthermore, someone contemplates the perception of impermanence for only a short time. But the afflictions are many. It is not sufficient to overcome them, just as a small amount of medicine does not destroy many diseases. So too is this case. Therefore it is said: 'With a one-pointed mind, correct contemplation of impermanence destroys the afflictions.'

body.text: dharmā anityā iti jñānameva tattvajñānam | sati tattvajñāne na bhavanti kāmādayaḥ kleśāḥ | kasmāt | avidyāpratyayatvāt kāmādīnām | iti anitya[saṃjñā] na kāmarāgasaṃvardhanīti veditavyam | kiñcānityasaṃjñā sarvān kleśānupaśamayati | yogī yadi prajānāti vastvidamanityamiti | na tadā [tatra]sakāmo bhavati | puruṣo 'yamavaśyaṃ mariṣyatīti prajānan kasmai dviṣyāt | kaḥ sacetano mriyamāṇaṃ dviṣyāt | yadi dharmā anityāḥ, kathaṃ tata uddhatasaṃjñāmutpādayet | dharmā anityā iti jñānānna moha utyadyate | mohānudayānnavicikitsādayo bhavanti | ato jñāyate anitya[saṃjñā] kleśānāṃ virodhinīti ||
body.translated_text: The knowledge that <s>dharmas</s> are impermanent is itself the knowledge of reality (<s>tattvajñāna</s>). When there is knowledge of reality, afflictions such as desire (<s>kāma</s>) do not arise. Why? Because desire and the rest are conditioned by ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). Thus it should be understood that the perception of impermanence does not promote desire and attachment (<s>kāmarāga</s>). Moreover, the perception of impermanence (<s>anityasaṃjñā</s>) pacifies all afflictions. If the <s>yogī</s> understands that this thing is impermanent, then he does not have desire for it. A person who knows 'this one will certainly die' — toward whom would he bear hatred? What sentient being would hate one who is dying? If <s>dharmas</s> are impermanent, how could one give rise to the perception of arrogance regarding them? From the knowledge that <s>dharmas</s> are impermanent, delusion does not arise. From the non-arising of delusion, doubt (<s>vicikitsā</s>) and the rest do not occur. Therefore it is known that the perception of impermanence is opposed to the afflictions.

body.text: anityasaṃjñāvargastrisaptattyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, the Chapter on the Perception of Impermanence (<s>anityasaṃjñāvarga</s>).

body.text: 174 duḥkhasaṃjñāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 174. Chapter on the Perception of Suffering (<s>duḥkhasaṃjñāvarga</s>)

body.text: yo dharmo bādhātmakaḥ tad duḥkhamityucyate | tatrividham- duḥkhaduḥkhaṃ vipariṇāmaduḥkhaṃ saṃskāraduḥkhamiti | pratyutpanne vastuto duḥkhaṃ yadasiśastrādi tad duḥkhaduḥkham | priyāṇāṃ punarbhāryādīnāṃ viyogakāle yadbhavati duḥkham, idaṃ vipariṇāmaduḥkham | śūnyānātmajñānalābhino yaccittaṃ bhavati saṃskṛtadharmāḥ sarve viheṭhanā iti | tatsaṃskāraduḥkham | tadduḥkhānuyāyi cittaṃ duḥkhasaṃjñā |
body.translated_text: That <s>dharma</s> which is of the nature of affliction — that is called suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>). It is of three kinds: the suffering of suffering (<s>duḥkhaduḥkha</s>), the suffering of change (<s>vipariṇāmaduḥkha</s>), and the suffering of conditioned formations (<s>saṃskāraduḥkha</s>). The suffering that is actually present, such as from swords and weapons — that is the suffering of suffering. The suffering that arises at the time of separation from beloved ones such as wives — this is the suffering of change. For one who has attained the knowledge of emptiness and non-self, the mental state that 'all conditioned <s>dharmas</s> are vexation' — that is the suffering of conditioned formations. The mind that follows upon such suffering is the perception of suffering (<s>duḥkhasaṃjñā</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) duḥkhasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayatā kiṃ hitaṃ labhyate | (u) duḥkhasaṃjñāyāṃ phalānnirvedo bhavati | kasmāt | na hi duḥkhasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayitā kāmaprītiṃ sevate | tatprītyabhāvānna tṛṣṇā bhavati | yogī yadi dharmā duḥkhamiti prajānāti | tadā na saṃskārānanubhavati | dharmā anityā anātmakā api na duḥkhajanakāḥ tadā naiva tyājyāḥ | duḥkhatvāttu tyājyāḥ | duḥkhatyāgādvimucyate | sarve sattvā atitarāṃ bhītā bhavanti yadidaṃ duḥkhamiti | yadi taruṇo vṛddho vā pāmaraḥ paṇḍito vā āḍhyo daridro vā jānāti idaṃ duḥkhalakṣaṇamiti | [tadā] sarve te nirviṇṇā bhavanti | sarve yogacāriṇaḥ puruṣā nirvāṇe śāntopaśamasaṃjñotpādakā bhavanti | sarveṣāṃ saṃsāre duḥkhasaṃjñotpādanāt | kenedaṃ jñāyate | ye sattvāḥ kāmadhātvāptaduḥkhopadrutā bhavanti | te prathamadhyāne śāntasaṃjñāmutpādayanti | evaṃ bhavāgraduḥkhopadrutā nirvāṇe śāntasaṃjñāmutpādayanti |
body.translated_text: (Question) What benefit is obtained by one who cultivates the perception of suffering (<s>duḥkhasaṃjñā</s>)? (Answer) From the fruit of the perception of suffering, disenchantment (<s>nirveda</s>) arises. Why? Because one who cultivates the perception of suffering does not indulge in the pleasure of desires. From the absence of that pleasure, craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) does not arise. If the <s>yogī</s> understands that <s>dharmas</s> are suffering, then he does not experience conditioned formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>). <s>Dharmas</s> that are impermanent and without self, if they do not produce suffering, need not be abandoned. But because they are suffering, they should be abandoned. Through the abandonment of suffering, one is liberated. All beings are extremely frightened, thinking 'this is suffering.' Whether young or old, whether foolish or wise, whether wealthy or poor — if one knows 'this has the characteristic of suffering,' then all of them become disenchanted. All practitioners (<s>yogacārin</s>) give rise to the perception of peace and tranquility in <s>nirvāṇa</s>, because the perception of suffering in <s>saṃsāra</s> is produced in all. How is this known? Those beings who are afflicted by the suffering attained in the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>) give rise to the perception of peace in the first <s>dhyāna</s>. Likewise, those afflicted by the suffering at the peak of existence give rise to the perception of peace in <s>nirvāṇa</s>.

body.text: saṃsāre 'styavadyaṃ yaduta duḥkham | yathoktaṃ sūtre- yat rūpaṇamanityaṃ duḥkhaṃ vipariṇāmadharma, ayaṃ rūpasyādīnava iti | avidyayābhiniviṣṭamidaṃ duḥkham | kenedaṃ jñāyate | sattvānāṃ paramārthato duḥkhe sukhasaṃjñotpādāt | paramaduḥkhasaṃjñotpādanāttu nirvidyante | ato bhagavānāha- ye duḥkhaṃ budhyanti teṣāmahaṃ duḥkhamāryasatyaṃ vyākaromi iti | tatra bhagavān lokasatyamupādāya imamarthaṃ prakāśayati | sarvadevamanuṣyāṇāṃ yatra sukhasaṃjñā bhavati | tatra mama śrāvakā duḥkhasaṃjñāmutpādayanti | utpannaduḥkhasaṃjñā nirvidyanta iti | paramamohapadaṃ
body.translated_text: In <s>saṃsāra</s> there is that which is blameworthy, namely suffering. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'That form which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change — this is the danger of form.' This suffering is clung to through ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). How is this known? Because beings, in ultimate reality, give rise to the perception of pleasure regarding suffering. But through giving rise to the perception of supreme suffering, they become disenchanted. Therefore the <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'Those who understand suffering — for them I declare suffering as a Noble Truth (<s>āryasatya</s>).' Therein the <s>Bhagavān</s>, relying on conventional truth, illuminates this meaning: 'Where all gods and humans have the perception of pleasure, there my disciples (<s>śrāvaka</s>) give rise to the perception of suffering. Having given rise to the perception of suffering, they become disenchanted.' The supreme ground of delusion is

body.text: yad duḥkhe sukhasaṃjñotpādanam | anayā saṃjñayā ca sarvasattvānāṃ saṃsāre yātāyātānāṃ mānasaṃ kliśyati | duḥkhasaṃjñāpratilābhinastu mucyante |
body.translated_text: the giving rise to the perception of pleasure regarding suffering. Through this perception, the minds of all beings who come and go in <s>saṃsāra</s> are afflicted. But those who attain the perception of suffering are liberated.

body.text: caturbhirāhāraiścordhvadehaṃ samāpadyate | tatra duḥkhasaṃjñayā āhārān prajahāti | yathā putramāṃsakhādanam, yathā vā niścarmagobhakṣaṇam, yathā aṅgārakarṣubhakṣaṇam | yathā śaktiśatadhārāvalepanam | tathābhūte 'ṣvāhāreṣu sarvaṃ duḥkhārthakam | tathā duḥkhasaṃjñayā āhārān prajahāti | duḥkhasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayato mano na catasṛṣu vijñānasthitiṣu sukhaṃ viharati sarvatra duḥkhadarśitvāt | yathā mugdhāḥ śalabhāḥ sukhasaṃjñayā pradīpe patanti | vidvān agnirdahatīti jñātvā [taṃ] parīharati | prākṛtā api tathā avidyāmohādūrdhvadehāgnau patanti | vidvāṃstu duḥkhasaṃjñayā vimucyate | sarvañca traidhātukaṃ duḥkhaṃ duḥkhasamudayaḥ | duḥkhā vedanā duḥkham | duḥkhajanakaṃ duḥkhasamudayaḥ | [idānī]maduḥkhamapi avaśyaṃ cirādduḥkhaṃ janayati | ato loke sarvaṃ duḥkhamiti bhāvayet | nirviṇṇacittā dharmān vedayanto vimucyante ||
body.translated_text: Through the four kinds of nutriment (<s>āhāra</s>), one attains a higher body. Through the perception of suffering, one abandons nutriments. Just as the eating of one's own child's flesh, or just as the eating by a skinless cow, or just as the eating from a pit of burning coals, or just as the anointing with a hundred-bladed spear — in such nutriments, everything is for the sake of suffering. Thus, through the perception of suffering, one abandons nutriments. For one cultivating the perception of suffering, the mind does not dwell in pleasure in the four stations of consciousness (<s>vijñānasthiti</s>), because it sees suffering everywhere. Just as deluded moths, with the perception of pleasure, fall into a lamp, but a wise person, knowing that fire burns, avoids it — so too, ordinary people, through the delusion of ignorance, fall into the fire of higher existence. But the wise one, through the perception of suffering, is liberated. All of the three realms (<s>traidhātuka</s>) is suffering and the origin of suffering. Painful feeling is suffering. That which produces suffering is the origin of suffering. Even what is presently not suffering will inevitably produce suffering in the long run. Therefore one should contemplate: 'Everything in the world is suffering.' Those with disenchanted minds, experiencing <s>dharmas</s>, are liberated.

body.text: duḥkhasaṃjñāvargaścatussaptatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Perception of Suffering (<s>duḥkhasaṃjñāvarga</s>).

body.text: 175 anātmasaṃjñāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 175. Chapter on the Perception of Non-Self (<s>anātmasaṃjñāvarga</s>)

body.text: yogī sarve dharma bhaṅgavipariṇāmalakṣaṇā iti paśyati | yasmin rūpe āttmatayābhiniviśate idaṃ rūpaṃ vipariṇāmadharma | tadvipariṇāmadharmajñānādātmacittaṃ pariharati | tathā vedanādīnapi | yathā kaścit girinirjharānuvāhito yatkiñcidavalambya tadvihāya mucyate | tathā yogyampi tadātmatayā kalpayati | tadvipariṇāmadharma dṛṣṭvā anātmakaṃ prajānāti | ato 'nātmake 'nātmasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayati |
body.translated_text: The <s>yogī</s> sees that all <s>dharmas</s> are characterized by breaking apart and change. Regarding the form to which one clings as self — this form is subject to change. Through the knowledge that it is subject to change, one abandons the notion of self. Likewise with feeling (<s>vedanā</s>) and the rest. Just as someone carried along by a mountain torrent, grasping whatever is available, lets go and is freed — so too, the practitioner designates that as self. Seeing that it is subject to change, he understands it as non-self. Therefore, regarding what is non-self, he cultivates the perception of non-self (<s>anātmasaṃjñā</s>).

body.text: (pṛ) anātmasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayan kiṃ hitaṃ labhate | (u) anātmasaṃjñābhāvayitā duḥkhasaṃjñāṃ paripūrayati | pṛthagjanā ātmasaṃjñayā paramārthato duḥkhe na duḥkhaṃ paśyanti | anātmasaṃjñayā tu atyalpe 'pi duḥkhe tadupaghātaṃ budhyate | anātmasaṃjñayā copekṣācittaṃ samudācarati | kasmāt | ātmasaṃjñayā hi ātmā naśyediti bibhyanti | yadi paramārthaṃ
body.translated_text: (Question) What benefit does one cultivating the perception of non-self (<s>anātmasaṃjñā</s>) obtain? (Answer) One who cultivates the perception of non-self fulfills the perception of suffering (<s>duḥkhasaṃjñā</s>). Ordinary people (<s>pṛthagjana</s>), due to the perception of self, do not see suffering in what is ultimately suffering. But through the perception of non-self, even in the slightest suffering, one recognizes its harm. Through the perception of non-self, the mind of equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>) arises. Why? Because through the perception of self, they fear that the self might perish. If the ultimate reality

body.text: jānāti tadā hāyapati duḥkhamanātmakaṃ vināśyamiti | tadā samudācaratyupekṣā | anātmasaṃjñayā ca nityasukhaṃ bhavati | kasmāt | sarvamanityam | tatra yadi ātmātmīyacittamutpādayati | tadā ātmā na bhavet, ātmīyamapi na bhavet, sadā duḥkhamevāsti iti vadet | nāstyātmātmīyamiti cintayato dharmeṣu vinaṣṭheṣu na duḥkhamutpadyate |
body.translated_text: is known, then one understands that suffering is non-self and subject to destruction. Then equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>) arises. Through the perception of non-self, there is also perpetual happiness. Why? Because everything is impermanent. If regarding that, one gives rise to the thought of self and what belongs to self — then if the self does not exist and what belongs to self also does not exist, one would say 'there is always only suffering.' For one who contemplates 'there is no self nor what belongs to self,' when <s>dharmas</s> are destroyed, suffering does not arise.

body.text: anātmasaṃjñayā ca yoginaścittaṃ viśudhyati | kasmāt | sarve hi kleśā ātmadṛṣṭisambhūtāḥ | idaṃ vastu ātmano hitamityataḥ kāmarāga utpadyate | idaṃ vastu ātmano 'hitamityato dveṣapratitha utpadyate | anenātmaivābhimānajanakaḥ | ahamāyuṣo 'nte kariṣyāmi na kariṣyāmiti dṛṣṭivicikitsā bhavati | evamātmanaiva sarve kleśāḥ samudbhavanti | anātmasaṃjñayā tu sarve kleśāḥ samucchidyante | kleśānāṃ samucchedāt cittaṃ viśudhyati | cittaviśuddhyā ca kāñcanaṃ loṣṭaṃ candanamasidhārāṃ praśaṃsāṃ nindāñca samaṃ manyate | priyavipriyairviviktaṃ cittaṃ sunivṛttaṃ śāntaṃ bhavati | ato jñāyate 'nātmasaṃjñakasya cittaṃ viśudhyatīti | anātmasaṃjñāṃ vihāya nāstyanyo mārgo vimuktiprāpakaḥ | kasmāt | yadyātmavādī prajānāti nāstyātmā nāstātmīyamiti | evaṃ vyavasitaṃ cittamutpādayanneva vimucyate |
body.translated_text: Through the perception of non-self, the mind of the <s>yogī</s> is also purified. Why? Because all afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) arise from the view of self (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>). 'This thing is beneficial to the self' — from this, desire and attachment (<s>kāmarāga</s>) arise. 'This thing is harmful to the self' — from this, hatred and aversion (<s>dveṣapratigha</s>) arise. Thus the self itself is the generator of pride (<s>abhimāna</s>). 'At the end of my life, will I do this or will I not?' — thus arise wrong views and doubt (<s>dṛṣṭivicikitsā</s>). In this way, all afflictions arise from the self alone. But through the perception of non-self, all afflictions are completely cut off. Through the complete cutting off of afflictions, the mind is purified. Through the purification of the mind, one regards gold and a clod of earth, sandalwood and a stream of ink, praise and blame as equal. The mind, free from the pleasant and unpleasant, well-restrained, becomes peaceful. Therefore it is known that the mind of one with the perception of non-self is purified. Apart from the perception of non-self, there is no other path that leads to liberation. Why? If one who holds the doctrine of self understands 'there is no self, there is nothing belonging to self,' then by giving rise to such a determined mind, one is liberated.

body.text: (pṛ) maivam | kadācidanātsaṃjñayā punaḥkāmacittamutpadyate | yathā strīrūpe rāgaḥ | tatsarvamanātmasnehāt | nairātmyamanusaranneva puṇyapāpaṃ sañcinoti | kasmāt | svakāyasyopakāre 'pakāre vā na puṇyapāpam | (u) sātmakacittaḥ kāmarāgamutpādayati | svakāye puruṣasaṃjñāṃ parakāye ca strīsaṃjñāmutpādya [tatra] abhiniviśate | tadabhiniveśotpādaśca prajñaptyā bhavati | tallakṣaṇaiva prajñaptiḥ | ato na nairātmyaṃ kāmacittajanakam | anātmacittaśca na karmāṇi sañcinoti | yathā arhato 'nātmasaṃjñayā na karmāṇi sañcīyante | anātmasaṃjñeyaṃ sarveṣāṃ kleśānāṃ karmaṇāñca samucchedinī | ata[stāṃ] bhāvayet ||
body.translated_text: (Question) This should not be so. Sometimes through the perception of non-self, the mind of desire arises again, such as attachment to a woman's form. All of that comes from attachment to what is non-self. Even while following non-self, one accumulates merit and demerit. Why? Because there is no merit or demerit in benefiting or harming one's own body? (Answer) One with the notion of self gives rise to desire and attachment (<s>kāmarāga</s>). By giving rise to the perception of 'man' regarding one's own body and the perception of 'woman' regarding another's body, one clings to that. The arising of that clinging occurs through conventional designation (<s>prajñapti</s>). That designation is only a characterization. Therefore non-self is not the producer of the mind of desire. And the mind of non-self does not accumulate <s>karma</s>. Just as for an <s>Arhat</s>, through the perception of non-self, <s>karmas</s> are not accumulated. This perception of non-self is the complete destroyer of all afflictions and <s>karmas</s>. Therefore one should cultivate it.

body.text: anātmasaṃjñāvargaḥ pañcasaptatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Perception of Non-Self (<s>anātmasaṃjñāvarga</s>).

body.text: 176 āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 176. Chapter on the Perception of Repulsiveness Regarding Nutriment (<s>āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñāvarga</s>)

body.text: sarvaṃ duḥkhajananamāhārakāmādbhavati | āhārācca maithunarāgaḥ sahotpadyate | kāmadhātau yāni santi duḥkhāni sarvāṇi tāni annapāna maithunarāgaṃ pratītya bhavanti | āhārakāmasamucchedāya pratikūlasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayet |
body.translated_text: All production of suffering arises from the desire for nutriment (<s>āhāra</s>). From nutriment, sexual desire (<s>maithunarāga</s>) also co-arises. Whatever sufferings exist in the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>), all of them arise dependent on food, drink, and sexual desire. For the complete cutting off of the desire for nutriment, one should cultivate the perception of repulsiveness (<s>pratikūlasaṃjñā</s>).

body.text: yathā kalpādau sattvāḥ svargādāgatya loke 'smin upapādukā abhūvan | [te] prabhāsvarakāyāḥ khecarāḥ svatantrā bhūtvā pṛthivīrasamādāvaśnuvan | tadaśanabahulāḥ praṇaṣṭapramātiśayā abhūvan | evaṃ krameṇa jarāvyādhimaraṇaśālinaḥ yāvadvatsaraśataṃ bhūyasā duḥkhaiḥ pīḍitāḥ | āhārābhiniveśavaśāt sarve te tādṛśemyaḥ phalemyaḥ praṇaṣṭāḥ | ata āhāraṃ yoniśo bhāvayet | annapānābhiniveśānmaithunarāga utpadyate | tato 'nye kleśā bhavanti | tebhyo 'kuśalaṃ karma kurvanti akuśalakarmataḥ trīn doṣān vardhayitvā devamanuṣyāṇāmapakurvanti | tasmāt sarvāḥ kleśavipattaya āhārakāmāt bhavanti jarāvyādhimaraṇalakṣaṇāni annapānādhīnāni |
body.translated_text: Just as at the beginning of the cosmic age (<s>kalpa</s>), beings, having come from heaven to this world, were spontaneously born (<s>upapāduka</s>). They had luminous bodies, traveled through the sky, and were independent. Then they consumed the essence of the earth and other things. Having consumed much food, their extraordinary powers were destroyed. Thus gradually, they came to possess aging, disease, and death, and were afflicted by suffering for as much as a hundred years. Due to their attachment to nutriment, all of them were destroyed by those consequences. Therefore one should wisely contemplate nutriment. From attachment to food and drink, sexual desire (<s>maithunarāga</s>) arises. From that, other afflictions arise. Due to those, they perform unwholesome <s>karma</s>. Through unwholesome <s>karma</s>, increasing the three faults, they harm gods and humans. Therefore all calamities of affliction arise from the desire for nutriment. The characteristics of aging, disease, and death are dependent on food and drink.

body.text: āhāro 'yaṃ sthāne paramamabhiniveśayati | kāmarāgo gururapi na puruṣaṃ kleśayati | yathā āhārakartā | yadi vā bālo vṛddho gṛhasthaḥ pravrajito vā anāhārapīḍito bhavati | āhāramimaṃ bhuṅktvā anāsaktamanā bhavet | avirāgī atitarāṃ khidyate | yathā asidhārāvalepanī, yathā vā viṣa[siktau]ṣadhasevakaḥ | yathā vā viṣasarpapoṣakaḥ | ato bhagavānāha- bhāvitacitta idamāhārayet | nāhārakāmāya tadduḥkhapīḍitaḥ syāt iti | kecittīrthikā [api] niraśanavratamācaranti | ato bhagavānāha- nāsyāhārasyopacchedāt vimucyate | kintu yoniśo manasi kṛtvā āhārayediti | ye samucchinnāhārāḥ teṣāṃ kleśā na kṣīyante | ahitaṃ tīvramaraṇameva bhavati | ato bhagavānāha- āhāre 'smin pratikūlasaṃjñāṃ janayet, nāsti tato 'vadyamiti |
body.translated_text: This food firmly establishes attachment to a place. Even heavy sensual passion (<s>kāmarāga</s>) does not afflict a person as much as food does. Whether a child, an elder, a householder, or a renunciant — when afflicted by lack of food, having eaten this food, one should be of unattached mind. One who is not dispassionate (<s>avirāgī</s>) is exceedingly distressed — just as one who licks a sword's edge, or one who uses medicine mixed with poison, or one who nourishes a poisonous snake. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'One whose mind is cultivated should eat this food. One should not be afflicted by the suffering of craving for food.' Certain non-Buddhist ascetics (<s>tīrthika</s>) also practice the vow of fasting. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'One is not liberated through the cutting off of this food. Rather, having wisely reflected (<s>yoniśo manasi kṛtvā</s>), one should eat.' For those who have completely cut off food, their defilements are not destroyed — only harmful, severe death results. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'One should generate the perception of repulsiveness regarding this food — there is no fault in that.'

body.text: (pṛ) kathamāhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā kuryāt | (u) ayaṃ kāyasvabhāvo 'kuśalaḥ | atyuttaramasamāhāraphalaṃ sarvamaśuci | atastato nirvindyāt | surabhigandhamadhurapānabhojanāni śucikāla eva kāyasya hitakarāṇi | dantena carvitaṃ lālayā siktaṃ liṅgaṃ vāntavadāmāśayapatitaṃ kāyasya hitakaram | ato jñāyate 'śucīti | idamannapānamajñānātsukham | yadi kaścinmadhuramāhāraṃ labhamāno 'pi punarvāntaṃ na bhunakti | iti jñātavyamajñānabalāttanmadhuraṃ manyata iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) How should one generate the perception of repulsiveness regarding food? (Answer) The nature of this body is unwholesome. The exceedingly superior fruit of undigested food is entirely impure. Therefore one should become disenchanted with it. Fragrant, sweet drinks and foods are beneficial to the body only during the time of purity. Chewed by the teeth, moistened with saliva, [the food's] appearance, having fallen into the stomach like vomit, is beneficial to the body. Therefore it is known to be impure. This food and drink are [considered] pleasant only through ignorance. Even someone who obtains sweet food does not eat it again once vomited. Therefore it should be known that through the power of ignorance, one considers it sweet.

body.text: āhārapratyayaṃ kṛṣikarma sevārjanaṃ saṃrakṣaṇamityevañjātīyaduḥkhānyanubhavati | tatpratyayamapramāṇāni pāpāni kurvanti | yadaśuci sarvaṃ tadāhārādhīnam | asatyāhāre kena
body.translated_text: On account of food, one experiences sufferings of this kind — farming, service, earning, and guarding. On account of that, one commits immeasurable sins. Whatever is impure — all of that depends on food. When food does not exist, by what

body.text: bhavanti tvagasthiraktamāṃsoccārādīnyaśucīni vastūni | yā durgatayorvarcaḥkuṭīkrimyādayaḥ te sarve gandharasābhiniveśādatrotpadyante | yathoktaṃ karmavarge- yastarṣito mriyate sa jalakrimibhāvenotpadyate | nibiḍasthāne mṛtaḥ pakṣiṣūtpadyate | maithunarāgeṇa mṛto yonāvutpadyate | ityevamādi | ya etadāhāravivikta sa mahāsukhaṃ pratilabhate | yathā rūpadhātau nirvāṇe cotpadyate | āhārānuvartanataḥ kṛṣṇādiduḥkhaṃ bhavati | evamāhāro 'śucirduḥkha iti dṛṣṭvā pratikūlasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayet ||
body.translated_text: do the impure substances such as skin, bones, blood, flesh, excrement, and the like come into being? Those in the bad destinies — worms in latrines and the like — all of them are born there through attachment to smell and taste. As stated in the Chapter on <s>Karma</s>: 'One who dies parched with thirst is born as a water-worm. One who dies in a confined place is born among birds. One who dies with passion for sexual intercourse is born in the womb.' And so forth. One who is free from this food obtains great happiness — just as in the form realm (<s>rūpadhātu</s>) and in <s>Nirvāṇa</s>, [such happiness] arises. Through following food, suffering such as toil and the like arises. Thus, seeing that food is impure and suffering, one should cultivate the perception of repulsiveness.

body.text: āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñāvargaḥ ṣaṭsaptatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Perception of Repulsiveness Regarding Food (<s>āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñāvarga</s>).

body.text: 177 sarvaloke 'nabhiratisaṃjñāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 177. Chapter on the Perception of Non-Delight in All the World (<s>sarvaloke'nabhiratisaṃjñāvarga</s>)

body.text: yogī paśyati lokeṣu sarvaṃ duḥkham, citte ca nāsti kiñcitsukhamiti | ayañca yogī bhāvayati prītiviviktaṃ samādhiṃ tadyathā anātmasaṃjñāṃ duḥkhasaṃjñāmāhāre pratikūlasaṃjñāṃ maraṇasaṃjñām | ityādi | tadā tasya cittaṃ na sarvaloke 'bhiramate | api cāyaṃ paśyati- yatpriyaṃ tatkāmarāgavardhanam, yadvipriyaṃ tat dveṣapratighavardhanamiti | ata ubhayatra nābhiramate | dhanikasya pālanādiduḥkhamastīti dṛśyate | daridrasyākiñcanyaduḥkhaṃ dṛśyate | susthāniko duḥsthāne patiṣyamāṇo dṛśyate | duḥsthāniko dṛṣṭe duḥkhānyanubhavan dṛśyate | pratyutpanno dhaniko 'vaśyaṃ patiṣyāmi, idañca kāmādīnāṃ vihṛtisthānamiti prajānāno dṛśyate | pratyutpanno daridro na pratyayopalabhyanirgama iti prajānānaḥ | ato na savaloke 'bhiramate | alpatarāśca sattvāḥ susthāna utpannāḥ, bahutarā durgatau patanti | yathoktaṃ sūtre- alpatarāḥ susthāna utpadyante bahutarā dusthāna utpadyante | tadādīnavaṃ dṛṣṭvā nirvāṇameva prārthayante | iti | puruṣo 'yaṃ paśyati kāmādayo doṣāḥ kleśāssadā santānamanuvartanta iti | yathā krodhāsevī puruṣo 'vakāśe labdhe punarbadhyate | asmin vadhake kathamabhirameta | kleśādutpannamakuśalaṃ karma sadānuvartamānaṃ dṛśyate | naivākuśalakarmaphalānmucyate | yathoktaṃ sūtre-
body.translated_text: The <s>yogin</s> sees that in the worlds everything is suffering, and that in the mind there is not the slightest happiness. And this <s>yogin</s> cultivates a <s>samādhi</s> free from joy (<s>prīti</s>) — such as the perception of non-self (<s>anātmasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of suffering (<s>duḥkhasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of repulsiveness regarding food, and the perception of death (<s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s>). And so forth. Then his mind does not delight in all the world. Moreover, this [yogin] sees: 'What is pleasant increases sensual passion (<s>kāmarāga</s>); what is unpleasant increases aversion and ill-will (<s>dveṣapratigha</s>).' Therefore he does not delight in either. The wealthy are seen to have suffering of guarding and the like. The poor are seen to have the suffering of destitution. One in a good place is seen as about to fall into a bad place. One in a bad place is seen experiencing sufferings directly. The presently wealthy person, knowing 'I will certainly fall, and this is the pleasure-ground of sensual desires and the like,' is seen [to suffer]. The presently poor person, knowing 'I cannot find a way out through conditions' [suffers likewise]. Therefore he does not delight in all the world. Fewer beings are born in good places; more fall into bad destinies. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Fewer are born in good places; more are born in bad places.' Having seen that danger, they aspire only to <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. This person sees that the faults of sensual desires and the like — the defilements — always follow the mental continuum. Just as a person given to anger, having found an opportunity, is bound again — how would one delight in such a murderer? Unwholesome <s>karma</s> born from defilements is seen always following [one]. One is never freed from the fruit of unwholesome <s>karma</s>. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>:

body.text:
sa cettu pāpakaṃ karma kariṣyati karoṣi vā |
na te duḥkhātpramoko 'sti, utpātyāpi palāyataḥ || iti |
body.translated_text:
If you will commit sinful <s>karma</s>, or are committing it now,
there is no escape from suffering for you, even if you fly up and flee.

body.text: ato nābhiramate | jātyādīnyaṣṭa duḥkhāni sadā sukṛtinamanuvartante | kiṃ punaḥ pāpinam | evaṃ kathaṃ loke abhirameta | tadyathā āśīviṣakaraṇḍaḥ pañcokṣiptāsikā vadhakāḥ śūnye grāme coraḥ | tādṛśānyavaratīrāṇi duḥkhāni sadā sattvānanuvartante | kathaṃ tatrābhirameta | tadyathā lavaṇatiktatṛṣṇānadīvāhitaḥ pañcakāmaguṇaviṣaśalya [viddhaḥ] avidyāndhakārāṅgārakarṣau [patitastādṛśāni] duḥkhāni sattvānanuvartante | kathaṃ [tatra] abhirameta | yogī upaśamasukhamalpaṃ vipattikleśaduḥkhāni bahūnīti prajānāti | kasmāt, [yasmāt] pratidīnaṃ lokaistūyamānā vanaṣaṇḍaprasūtasphītaphalasamṛddhiśālino ['pi] bhūpā na dīrghakālasukhalābhino dṛśyante | sukhasampraharṣiṇo 'lpāḥ | duḥkhavedinastu bahavaḥ | ato na sarvaloke 'bhiramate |
body.translated_text: Therefore one does not delight. The eight sufferings such as birth and the like always follow even the meritorious — how much more the sinful! Thus, how would one delight in the world? Just as a basket of poisonous snakes, five sword-bearing executioners, a thief in an empty village — such unabating sufferings always follow beings. How would one delight therein? Just as one carried by a river of salty, bitter thirst, pierced by the poisonous arrow of the five strands of sensual pleasure (<s>pañcakāmaguṇa</s>), fallen into the burning coals of the darkness of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) — such sufferings follow beings. How would one delight therein? The <s>yogin</s> knows that the happiness of peace (<s>upaśama</s>) is little and the sufferings of calamity and defilement are many. Why? Because even kings who are daily praised, who dwell in forest groves bearing abundant fruit and thriving prosperity, are not seen to obtain happiness for a long time. Those rejoicing in happiness are few; those experiencing suffering are many. Therefore one does not delight in all the world.

body.text: (pṛ) saṃjñāmimāṃ bhāvayan kāni hitāni vindate | (u) nānāvidhalokalakṣaṇeṣu na cittamabhiniviśate | tāṃ saṃjñāṃ bhāvayatā kṣipraṃ mokṣo labhyate | saṃsāre ca dīrghakālaṃ [na]tiṣṭhati | ayaṃ yogī hitaṃ jñānaṃ vindate | sadā sarvatrādīnavabhāvitvāt | asya ca citte na kleśā udbhavanti |
body.translated_text: (Question) What benefits does one obtain by cultivating this perception? (Answer) In the various characteristics of the world, the mind does not become attached. By cultivating that perception, one quickly obtains liberation. And one does not remain in <s>saṃsāra</s> for a long time. This <s>yogin</s> obtains beneficial knowledge — because of always seeing danger everywhere. And in his mind, defilements do not arise.

body.text: udbhave vāśu nirudhyante | yathā taptāyaḥkapāle patitaṃ jalabindu | yogī loke nābhiramata ityataḥ paramopaśame 'bhiramate | yo lokānnirviṇṇaḥ sa upaśame parame 'bhiramate | tasmāt sarvaloke 'nabhiratisaṃjñāṃ bhāvayet ||
body.translated_text: Even if they arise, they quickly cease — just as a drop of water that falls on a heated iron plate. The <s>yogin</s> does not delight in the world — therefore he delights in supreme peace (<s>paramopaśama</s>). One who is disenchanted with the world delights in supreme peace. Therefore one should cultivate the perception of non-delight in all the world.

body.text: sarvaloke 'nabhiratisaṃjñāvargaḥ saptasaptatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: This is the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Perception of Non-Delight in All the World (<s>sarvaloke'nabhiratisaṃjñāvarga</s>).

body.text: 178 aśubhasaṃjñāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 178. Chapter on the Perception of Impurity (<s>aśubhasaṃjñāvarga</s>)

body.text: (pṛ) aśubhasaṃjñāṃ kathaṃ bhāvayet | (u) yogī paśyati kāyasya bījamaśubhaṃ yaduta mātāpitoraśucimārgajaśukraśoṇitasaṅghātaḥ | kāyo 'yamaśucibhiḥ saṃsiddho yaduta jīrṇāhāraprasvedaprasnigdhaḥ | upapattisthānañcāśuci yaduta mātuḥ kukṣau paripūrṇamaśuci bhavati |
body.translated_text: (Question) How should one cultivate the perception of impurity (<s>aśubha</s>)? (Answer) The <s>yogin</s> sees that the seed of the body is impure — namely, a combination of semen and blood born from the impure passage of the mother and father. This body is constituted by impurities — namely, it is smeared with old food and sweat. The place of birth is also impure — namely, in the mother's womb, the impurity is complete.

body.text: viṇmūtrādyaśucipadārthāḥ sambhūya kāyaṃ kurvanti | navasu dvāreṣu sadāśucīni sravanti | kāyo 'yaṃ yatra nikṣipyate tadeva sthānamamaṅgalamaśuci | annaṃ pānaṃ vastraṃ puruṣakāyagataṃ parīhitaṃ sarvaṃmaśuci bhavati | pareṣāṃ dūṣaṇañca bhavati | kāyasyāsya padārthaḥ sarvo 'śuciḥ | yathā snānajalaṃ yadi vā snānapātrādi | kāyotthaṃ keśanakhaśiṅkhāṇaśleṣmādi sarvamaśuci | dṛśyate ca mṛtakāyo 'śucitaḥ | kāyo 'yaṃ mriyamāṇaḥ kimanyo bhavati | ādita ārabhyāyamaśuciriti veditavyam | jāyamānastu ātmabuddhiviparyayāt śucirityucyate | mṛtaspṛṣṭī aśucirbhavati | keśanakhādi sadā mṛtavastu | apramāṇā mṛtakrimayaśca sadā kāyaṃ spṛśanti | ato jñātavyaṃ kāyo 'yamādita ārabhyāśuciriti | aśucilūkṣāmakṣikāmaśakādayaḥ sarvā aśucikrimayaḥ sarvadāgatya kāyaṃ spṛśantītyaścāśuciḥ | kāyo 'yaṃ varcaḥkuṭīvat sadāśucipūrṇaḥ | tatpratītya varcaḥkuṭyāṃ sahasradhā krimayo bhavanti | tathāyaṃ kāyo 'pi |
body.translated_text: Impure substances such as excrement, urine, and the like come together to constitute the body. Impurities constantly flow from the nine openings. This body — wherever it is placed, that very place becomes inauspicious and impure. Food, drink, and clothing that come in contact with a person's body — all become impure. And they defile others. The substance of this body is entirely impure — just as bathing water, or bathing vessels, and the like. Everything arising from the body — hair, nails, phlegm, mucus, and the like — all is impure. And a dead body is seen to be impure. Is this body, when dying, something different? From the very beginning, it should be understood that it is impure. But when born, through the perversion of the notion of self, it is called 'pure.' One who touches a dead person becomes impure. Hair, nails, and the like are always dead matter. Immeasurable dead parasites always touch the body. Therefore it should be known that this body is impure from the very beginning. Impure lice, flies, mosquitoes, and the like — all impure parasites — always come and touch the body, and thus it is impure. This body, like a latrine, is always full of impurities. Just as a thousand worms are born in a latrine dependent on it, so too is this body.

body.text: kāyo 'yaṃ śmaśānasamaḥ | kasmāt | mṛtakāyasya hi sthānaṃ śmaśānamityucyate | ayaṃ kāyo 'pi bahvayo mṛtakrimayo 'tra tiṣṭhanti | ayaṃ kāyo 'śuciṃ karoti | yāni śucisthānāni surabhikusumavastramālādīni [tāni] sarvāṇyetatkāyavaśādaśucīni bhavanti | brāhmaṇā mṛtagṛhe prasūtikāgṛhe ca nāhāramupabhuñjanti | aśucitvāt | asmin kāye tu śatasahasradhā krimayaḥ sadā jāyante mriyante ca | tadā nopabhojyānnapāno bhavet | ato jñāyate 'śuciriti | loke ca narakamaśuci | kāyo 'yaṃ krimiśatasahasrāṇāṃ narakam | ato 'śuciḥ | kāyo 'yaṃ sadā snānamapekṣate | yadi śuciḥ | kimarthaṃ snānamapekṣate | surabhikusumagandhamālālaṅkṛto 'yaṃ kāyaḥ iti veditavyaṃ kāyo 'yaṃ svabhāvato 'śuciriti | prajñaptyā śucibhiḥ bāhyairalaṅkriyate | ayaṃ manuṣyakāyaḥ paramamaśuciḥ | yathānyeṣāṃ sattvānāṃ carmaromanakhadantamajjāsthimāṃsāni kadācidupayujyante | manuṣyakāye tu naikamasti grāhyam | paramāśucitvāt | yathotpalapadbhapuṇḍarīkapuṣpādīni aśucisabhūtatvādaśucīni bhavanti | na tathā kāyo 'yamanyapadārthairaśucīkriyate | prakṛtita evāśuciḥ | kāyo 'yaṃ yadi śuciḥ | tadā na vastreṇācchādayet | yathā puruṣo vastrācchāditamalarāśiḥ parān vañcayati | tathā strī ācchādanābharaṇācchāditakāyā puruṣaṃ mohayati | tathā puruṣo 'pi | [ato] jñātavyamaśuciriti | samantato 'yaṃ kāyaḥ sadā aśuci nissārayati yaduta navarandhrāṇi aśucidvārāṇi romakūpeṣu ca naikamasti śuci |
body.translated_text: This body is like a charnel ground. Why? Because the place where a dead body lies is called a charnel ground. In this body too, many dead parasites reside. This body creates impurity. Whatever places are pure — fragrant flowers, garments, garlands, and the like — all of them become impure on account of this body. <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> do not eat food in a house of death or in a house of childbirth — because of impurity. Yet in this body, parasites in hundreds of thousands are constantly being born and dying. Therefore food and drink should not be consumed [in its presence]. From this it is known to be impure. And in the world, hell is [considered] impure. This body is a hell for hundreds of thousands of parasites. Therefore it is impure. This body always requires bathing. If it were pure, why would it require bathing? This body is adorned with fragrant flower-garlands and ornaments — from this it should be understood that this body is impure by nature. Through designation, it is adorned with external pure [things]. This human body is supremely impure. Just as the skin, hair, nails, teeth, marrow, bones, and flesh of other beings are sometimes utilized — but in the human body, not a single thing is to be taken, because of its supreme impurity. Just as lotuses, water-lilies, and <s>puṇḍarīka</s> flowers, being of impure origin, become impure — this body is not made impure by other substances; it is impure by its very nature. If this body were pure, one would not cover it with clothing. Just as a person, covering a heap of filth with cloth, deceives others — so a woman, with her body covered by garments and ornaments, deludes a man. So too does a man [delude others]. Therefore it should be known to be impure. On all sides, this body is constantly discharging impurity — namely, the nine openings are gates of impurity, and in the pores of the hair too, not a single thing is pure.

body.text: (pṛ) aśubhasaṃjñābhāvanā kasya hitasya lābhāya bhavati | (u) strīpuruṣayoḥ śubhasaṃjñayā kāmarāga utpadyate | tasmātkāmarāgātpāpakānāṃ dvāramaprāvriyate | aśubhasaṃjñābhāvanāyāntu kāmarāgāṇāṃ nigraho bhavati | kasmāt | ayaṃ hi kāyo durgandhamalairaśuciścarmāvṛtatvātparaṃ na jñāyate | vasanācchāditāśucirāśyābhāsavat śucipriyavastu parivarjayet | yogī cāyaṃ vinīlakalohitakādisaṃjñayā sarvakāyaṃ paryādāti | kāyaparyādānāt na kāmarāgo bhavati | pratyakṣaṃ dṛśyate ca vinīlakalohitakādirūpam | (pṛ) yadvastuto 'vinīlakam, tat kasmādvinīlakaṃ paśyati | (u) adhimuktivalādyogī tat vinīlakaṃ gṛhṇāti | sarvāṇi rūpāṇi ca vinīlakalohitakāni paśyati |
body.translated_text: (Question) For the attainment of what benefit is the cultivation of the perception of impurity (<s>aśubhasaṃjñā</s>)? (Answer) Through the perception of beauty (<s>śubhasaṃjñā</s>) regarding women and men, sensual passion (<s>kāmarāga</s>) arises. From that sensual passion, the door to sins is opened. But through the cultivation of the perception of impurity, there is the restraint of sensual passions. Why? This body, being impure with foul-smelling filth, is not known [as impure] because it is covered by skin. One should avoid what appears pure and pleasant, like a heap of impurity covered by garments. And this <s>yogin</s>, through the perception of the livid (<s>vinīlaka</s>), the blood-smeared (<s>lohitaka</s>), and the like, pervades the entire body. Through the pervading of the body [with this perception], sensual passion does not arise. And the livid, blood-smeared, and other forms are directly perceived. (Question) What is in reality not livid — why does he see it as livid? (Answer) Through the power of determination (<s>adhimukti</s>), the <s>yogin</s> grasps it as livid. And he sees all forms as livid, blood-smeared, and the like.

body.text: (pṛ) bhāvaneyaṃ kasmānna viparyastā bhavati | (u) kāyo 'yaṃ vinīlakalohitabhāgīyaḥ | yathoktaṃ sūtre- asti vṛkṣe viśuddhatā iti | vinīlakalohitakalakṣaṇaṃ sadā bhāvayan anyāni rūpāṇyabhibhavati | yathā [indra]nīlamaṇiprabhā sphaṭikarūpaṃ tiraskaroti | evaṃ vinīlakalohitakādilakṣaṇaṃ dīrghakālaṃ bhāvayato 'śubha[saṃjñā] sampūrṇā bhavati | aśubhasaṃjñāyāṃ na maithu rāga utpadyate | anutpanne maithunarāge sāṃvṛtasarvāpattivimukho nirvāṇameyānuyāti | aśubhasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayata idṛśaṃ hitaṃ labhyate |
body.translated_text: (Question) Why is this meditation not erroneous? (Answer) This body belongs to the category of the blue-black and red. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There is purity in the tree.' By constantly meditating on the characteristic of the blue-black and red, one overcomes other forms. Just as the radiance of a sapphire (<s>indranīlamaṇi</s>) eclipses the form of crystal, so by meditating for a long time on the characteristic of the blue-black and red and so forth, the <s>aśubhasaṃjñā</s> (perception of the impure) becomes complete. When the <s>aśubhasaṃjñā</s> (perception of the impure) is present, sexual desire does not arise. When sexual desire has not arisen, one is freed from all calamities that are concealed and proceeds toward <s>Nirvāṇa</s>. Such benefit is obtained by one who cultivates the <s>aśubhasaṃjñā</s> (perception of the impure).

body.text: aśubhabhāvanāvargo 'ṣṭasaptatyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: The chapter on the meditation on the impure (<s>aśubhabhāvanā</s>) is the one hundred and seventy-eighth.

body.text: 179 maraṇasaṃjñāvargaḥ
body.translated_text: 179. Chapter on the perception of death (<s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s>).

body.text: yogīmaraṇasaṃjñayā jīvite 'dhruvacitto bhavati | ityataḥ [tāṃ] bhāvayet | ayaṃ sadā kuśaladharmeṣu paramamabhirato 'kuśaladharmān prajahāti | kasmāt | sattvā bhūyasā maraṇavismaraṇādakuśalaṃ karma kurvanti | yadā tu maraṇamanusmaranti tadā prajahati | satatamaraṇānusmaraṇācca mātāpitṛbhrātṛsvasṛjñātisālohitaparijanādiṣu rāgatṛṣṇālpīyasī bhavati | maraṇasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayataḥ svasya hitaṃ bhavati yaduta cittaikāgryeṇa kuśaladharmāṇāmupacayaḥ |
body.translated_text: Through the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death), the <s>yogī</s> becomes one whose mind recognizes the impermanence of life. Therefore, one should cultivate it. Such a person, being supremely delighted in <s>kuśaladharmas</s> (wholesome qualities), abandons <s>akuśaladharmas</s> (unwholesome qualities). Why? Because beings for the most part perform <s>akuśala karma</s> (unwholesome actions) due to forgetting death. But when they recollect death, they abandon them. Through constant recollection of death, attachment and craving toward mother, father, brothers, sisters, relatives, kinsmen, and attendants becomes diminished. For one who cultivates the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death), there is personal benefit, namely the accumulation of <s>kuśaladharmas</s> (wholesome qualities) through one-pointedness of mind.

body.text: laukikāḥ sattvā bhūyasā parihitābhiratā svahitaṃ tyajantyeva | kiñcāyaṃ kṣiprameva mucyate | kasmāt | ājavañjavamanughāvatāṃ hi lokānāṃ sadā maraṇaṃ bhavati | ayantu maraṇanirvedā dvimuktimeva prārthayate |
body.translated_text: Worldly beings, for the most part delighting in the welfare of others, simply abandon their own welfare. Moreover, this one is quickly liberated. Why? For beings who rush about heedlessly, death is always present. But this one, through disenchantment with death, seeks only the two kinds of liberation.

body.text: (pṛ) kathaṃ maraṇasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayet | (u) sarvamanityamiti pūrvaṃ sāmānyata uktam | idānīntu kāyo 'nitya iti mātraṃ bhāvayet | skandhānāṃ santānasamucchedo maraṇa saṃjñetyucyate | kāyo 'yaṃ bāhyavastvapekṣayāpyanityataraḥ | tadyathā mṛṇmaye ghaṭe 'dhruvalakṣaṇam | tadapyatikrānto 'yaṃ kāya iti yogī bhāvayati | kasmāt | mṛṇmayo 'yaṃ ghaṭo yadi [samyak] prayogapālitaḥ kadācit ciraṃ tiṣṭhet | ayaṃ kāyastu ciratamaṃ tiṣṭhamāno na vatsaraśatamatikrāmati | adhruvatvānmaraṇasaṃjñāmanusmaret | kiñcāyaṃ kāyaḥ paripanthidharmaiḥ sambahulaḥ yadutāśiśastragadāvadhakacoraprapātapānabhojanāparipācanātiśītātigharmavātavyādhayaḥ | saṃkṣepataḥ sarve sattvā asattvāśca kāyasya paripanthino dharmā draṣṭavyāḥ | ato bhāvayenmaraṇasaṃjñām |
body.translated_text: (Question) How should one cultivate the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death)? (Answer) Previously it was stated in general that everything is impermanent. But now one should meditate specifically that the body is impermanent. The cessation of the continuity of the <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) is called the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death). This body is even more impermanent than external objects. For example, there is the characteristic of impermanence in an earthen pot. The <s>yogī</s> meditates that this body exceeds even that. Why? This earthen pot, if properly maintained, might sometimes last a long time. But this body, even at its longest duration, does not exceed a hundred years. Due to its impermanence, one should recollect the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death). Moreover, this body is beset by many hostile conditions, namely: killing by cold, weapons, clubs, murderers, thieves, falling from heights, improper drink and food, excessive cold, excessive heat, wind, and disease. In brief, all beings and non-beings should be regarded as hostile conditions for the body. Therefore, one should cultivate the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death).

body.text: kiñca yogī paśyati kāyaḥ kṣaṇikanityo vipariṇāmalakṣaṇo naikaṃ kṣaṇamapyārakṣya iti | ato maraṇasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayati | yogī dṛṣṭadharme ca paśyati bālyayauvanavārdhakyāni savyādhīni nirvyādhīni vā na maraṇaparihārīṇīti | evaṃ kāyenāpi bhavitavyamityanusmṛtya maraṇasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayati | kiñca yogī paśyati aniyatavipākaṃ karma | na sarvakarmāṇi kṣīyante āyurvarṣaśatairapi | karmaṇo 'niyatatvānmaraṇamapyaniyataṃ iti | ato maraṇasaṃjñāmanusmaret | anādau ca saṃsāre 'sti karmāpramāṇama | asti kiñcitkarma anyakarmaṇo varaṇakam | mamāpi bhavedakālikamaraṇakarma | iti kathamasminnāyuṣi[yogī] śraddadhīta | kiñca yogī paśyati maraṇamatiprabhaviṣṇu, na sāntvavacanenollāpanīyaṃ dhanenānuneyaṃ vigraheṇa vā mocanīyam | yathā mahati śaile caturbhyo digbhya āgate nāsti palāyanasthānam |
body.translated_text: Furthermore, the <s>yogī</s> sees that the body is momentarily impermanent, characterized by transformation, and cannot be preserved even for a single moment. Therefore, one cultivates the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death). The <s>yogī</s> also sees in the present life that childhood, youth, and old age — whether with illness or without illness — do not escape death. Recollecting that the same must happen to this body, one cultivates the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death). Furthermore, the <s>yogī</s> sees that the ripening of <s>karma</s> is indefinite. Not all <s>karmas</s> are exhausted even in a hundred years of life. Because <s>karma</s> is indefinite, death too is indefinite. Therefore, one should recollect the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death). In beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>, there is immeasurable <s>karma</s>. Some <s>karma</s> obstructs other <s>karma</s>. I too might have <s>karma</s> that causes untimely death — how then could the <s>yogī</s> trust in this lifespan? Furthermore, the <s>yogī</s> sees that death is supremely powerful; it cannot be appeased by gentle words, placated by wealth, or released by force. Just as when a great mountain approaches from the four directions, there is no place to flee.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi kaścidyamaṃ santaparyati | tadā maraṇānmucyate | (u) ayaṃ bālo mūḍha[evaṃ] vadati | yamaḥ prāṇināmutpādane vadhe cāsvatantrabalaḥ | kevalaṃ parāmṛśati kiṃ kuśalacārī kiṃ vākuśalacārīti | vipākavedanāyāṃ kṣīyamāṇāyāṃ hiṃsrakakāyapratyayaṃ mriyate | ato yogī kāyo 'niśrayo 'śaraṇo maraṇavartmagata iti paśyan maraṇasaṃjñāmanusmarati | kiñca yogī sadā paśyati kāyo 'yaṃ jarāvyādhiparipīḍito 'dhruvasvabhāvaḥ pratikṣaṇamutpannavināśī
body.translated_text: (Question) If someone propitiates <s>Yama</s>, then is one freed from death? (Answer) This is what a fool, a deluded person, says. <s>Yama</s> does not possess independent power over the birth and killing of living beings. He merely examines whether one has practiced virtue or non-virtue. When the <s>vedanā</s> (feeling) of karmic ripening is being exhausted, one dies due to conditions involving a destructive body. Therefore, the <s>yogī</s>, seeing that the body is without refuge, without shelter, and has entered the path of death, recollects the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death). Furthermore, the <s>yogī</s> constantly sees that this body is afflicted by old age and disease, has an impermanent nature, and arises and perishes at every moment.

body.text: vijñānasantānavinaṣṭa ityato maraṇasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayati | kiñcāyaṃ yogī paśyati maraṇaṃ niyataṃ jīvitamaniyatam | aniyatānniyataṃ viśiṣyata ityato maraṇasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayati |
body.translated_text: The continuum of <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) is destroyed — therefore one cultivates the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death). Moreover, this <s>yogī</s> sees that death is certain while life is uncertain. Since what is certain surpasses what is uncertain, therefore one cultivates the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death).

body.text: (pṛ) kasmāt jarāvyādhyādisaṃjñā anuktvā maraṇasaṃjñāmātramucyate | (u) jarāvyādhyabhibhūtaḥ puruṣo na parikṣīyate | vyādhirbalaṃ harati jarā yauvanaṃ harati | jñātisālohito dhanamanyacca[harati] | kāyastu tathāpi tiṣṭhati | maraṇaṃ punaḥ sarvamapaharati | jarāvyādhyādi ca maraṇasya pratyayaḥ | ato na pṛthagucyate | uktañca sūtre- maraṇaṃ nāma mahātāmastram araśmikamarakṣaṇam asahāyakamanupasthāpakaṃ paramabhayasthānaṃ iti | ato maraṇasaṃjñāmanusmaret | kiñca sattvā maraṇapratyayaṃ paralokādvibhyati | traidhātuke sarvasyāsti maraṇaṃ na tathā jarā vyādhiśca |
body.translated_text: (Question) Why is only the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death) taught without mentioning the perception of old age, disease, and so forth? (Answer) A person overcome by old age and disease does not completely perish. Disease takes away strength; old age takes away youth; relatives and kinsmen take away wealth and other things. But the body still remains even so. Death, however, takes away everything. Moreover, old age, disease, and so forth are conditions for death. Therefore, they are not stated separately. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Death is a great darkness, without light, without protection, without companions, without support, and is the place of supreme fear.' Therefore, one should recollect the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death). Furthermore, beings fear the next world due to death being its condition. In the <s>traidhātuka</s> (three realms), all have death, but not all have old age and disease.

body.text: (pṛ) yadi sattvān vihāya nāsti maraṇasaṃjñā | sattvā eva prajñaptisantaḥ | yogī kasmādimāṃ saṃjñāṃ bhāvayati | (u) vinaśvarasattvalakṣaṇa[jñāna]vihīno maraṇādvibheti | yo maraṇasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayati | na sa bibheti | ato bhāvayet | anityasaṃjñādayo mārgasya pratyāsannāḥ | aśubhāhāre pratikūlamaraṇasaṃjñādayo mārgaviprakṛṣṭāḥ | mārgapratilābhī īdṛśasaṃjñayā cittaṃ pragṛhṇāti |
body.translated_text: (Question) If apart from beings there is no <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death), and beings are merely designations, why does the <s>yogī</s> cultivate this perception? (Answer) One who lacks knowledge of the characteristic of perishable beings fears death. One who cultivates the <s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of death) does not fear. Therefore, one should cultivate it. The <s>anityasaṃjñā</s> (perception of impermanence) and others are proximate to the path. The perceptions of the impure, repulsiveness of food, and death are distant from the path. One who has attained the path restrains the mind through such perceptions.

body.text: maraṇasaṃjñāvarga ekonāśīttyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: The chapter on the perception of death (<s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s>) is the one hundred and seventy-ninth.

body.text: 180 antimasaṃjñātritayavargaḥ
body.translated_text: 180. Chapter on the final triad of perceptions (<s>antimasaṃjñātritaya</s>).

body.text: prahāṇasaṃjñeti | yathā caturṣu samyakpradhāneṣūktam- utpannānāṃ pāpakānāmakuśalānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ prahāṇāya [chandaṃ janayati vyāyamati]vīryamārabhate | [cittaṃ pragṛhṇāti pradadhāti] iti | ime ca pāpakā akuśalā dharmā narakādiduḥkhakleśānāṃ pratyayāḥ | pāpakīrtiśabdānāṃ cittaparitāpādiduḥkhānāñca mūlam | tasmātprajahyāt |
body.translated_text: The <s>prahāṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of abandonment) — as stated in the four <s>samyakpradhānas</s> (right efforts): 'For the abandonment of arisen evil, unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>, one generates desire, strives, arouses effort, applies and exerts the mind.' These evil, unwholesome <s>dharmas</s> are the conditions for the suffering and <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) of the hells and so forth. They are the root of ill repute and of sufferings such as mental torment. Therefore, one should abandon them.

body.text: (pṛ) kathaṃ prajahāti | (u) dharmāṇāmakaraṇaṃ pratibdhastasmin samaye prajahāti | ayoniśo manaskāraḥ kāmarāgādīnāṃ kleśānāṃ pratyayaḥ | tanmanaskāraprahāṇāt te dharmāḥ prahīyante | (pṛ) imāṃ prahāṇasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayan kiṃ hitaṃ vidante | (u) tāṃ saṃjñāṃ bhāvayan sadā na pāpakān dharmānanuvartate | kartavya[meva] karoti | aṣṭāvakṣaṇāṃśca varjayati | puruṣasyātmahitaṃ yadutakleśānāṃ prahāṇam | kleśaprahāṇābhirati dharmacī varasaṃvṛtaliṅgasya pravrajitasya hitam tayā nocet svakāyameva manyeta | yadi yogī prahāṇasaṃjñābhāvanāyāmabhirataḥ, tadā buddhe dharmapūjāṃ karoti |
body.translated_text: (Question) How does one abandon them? (Answer) By non-performance of <s>dharmas</s>; when obstructed, at that time one abandons them. <s>Ayoniśo manaskāra</s> (improper mental attention) is the condition for <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) such as <s>kāmarāga</s> (sensual desire) and so forth. Through the abandonment of that mental attention, those <s>dharmas</s> are abandoned. (Question) What benefit does one who cultivates this <s>prahāṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of abandonment) obtain? (Answer) One who cultivates that perception never follows evil <s>dharmas</s>; one does only what should be done and avoids the eight unfavorable conditions. A person's own welfare is the abandonment of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). Delight in the abandonment of <s>kleśas</s> is the welfare of the renunciant whose outward mark is the best <s>dharma</s>-conduct. Without it, one would care only for one's own body. If the <s>yogī</s> delights in the cultivation of the <s>prahāṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of abandonment), then one performs the worship of the <s>Dharma</s> toward the <s>Buddha</s>.

body.text: virāgasaṃjñā nirodhasaṃjñā iti | rāge cātyantānutpanne virāgo bhavati | tadvirāgānusmaraṇameva virāgasaṃjñā | (pṛ) prahāṇasaṃjñaiva virāgasaṃjñeti matam | kasmātpunarucyate | (u) prahāṇāllabhyate virāgam | prahāṇaṃ nāma kāmarāgasyāpanayanam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- kāmarāgasya prahāṇāt pañcaskandhāḥ prahīyante iti | prahāṇasaṃjñā ca virāgasaṃjñā | kasmāt | tasmin samaye nāsti kāmaḥ, tasya dharmasya prahāṇaṃ bhavati | ato virāgasaṃjñālābhino duḥkhakleśāḥ nirudhyante | yathoktaṃ sūtre- vītarāgo vimucyate iti | vimuktilābha eva prahāṇam | anupadhiśeṣa[nirvāṇaṃ] praviṣṭhasya nirodho bhavati | uktañca sūtre- trayaḥ svabhāvāḥ prahāṇasvabhāvo virāgasvabhāvo nirodhasvabhāva iti | yaducyate prahāṇasvabhāvo virāgasvabhāva iti tadarhata eva bhavati | sa hi prahīṇasarvakleśastraidhātukaviraktaḥ soṣadhiśeṣanirvāṇe tiṣṭhati | yaducyate nirodhasvabhāva iti tadāyuṣo 'nte jīvitavyapagame prahīṇasantānasya | nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇaṃ samāpannasyaiva bhavati |
body.translated_text: The <s>virāgasaṃjñā</s> (perception of dispassion) and the <s>nirodhasaṃjñā</s> (perception of cessation) are as follows: When desire has utterly ceased to arise, there is <s>virāga</s> (dispassion). The recollection of that <s>virāga</s> itself is the <s>virāgasaṃjñā</s> (perception of dispassion). (Question) It is held that the <s>prahāṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of abandonment) is itself the <s>virāgasaṃjñā</s> (perception of dispassion). Why then is it stated again? (Answer) Through abandonment, <s>virāga</s> (dispassion) is obtained. Abandonment means the removal of <s>kāmarāga</s> (sensual desire). As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Through the abandonment of <s>kāmarāga</s> (sensual desire), the five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) are abandoned.' The <s>prahāṇasaṃjñā</s> is also the <s>virāgasaṃjñā</s>. Why? Because at that time there is no desire, and the abandonment of that <s>dharma</s> occurs. Therefore, for one who has attained the <s>virāgasaṃjñā</s>, the suffering and <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) cease. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'One who is free from desire is liberated.' The attainment of liberation itself is abandonment. For one who has entered <s>anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa</s> (nirvāṇa without remainder), there is cessation. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'There are three natures: the nature of abandonment, the nature of dispassion, and the nature of cessation.' What is called the nature of abandonment and the nature of dispassion pertains only to the <s>Arhat</s>. For the <s>Arhat</s> has abandoned all <s>kleśas</s>, is dispassionate toward the <s>traidhātuka</s> (three realms), and abides in <s>sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa</s> (nirvāṇa with remainder). What is called the nature of cessation pertains to one whose continuum has been severed at the end of the lifespan, at the departure of the vital force, and who has attained <s>nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa</s> (nirvāṇa without remainder).

body.text: asti ca dvidhā vimuktiḥ prajñāvimuktiścetovimuktiriti | yadabhihitaṃ prahāṇamiti tat avidyāṃ prajahātīti prajñā vimucyate | yadvirāga iti tat tṛṣṇāṃ vivarjayatīti ceto vimucyate | dvayorvimuktayoḥ phalaṃ nirodho bhavati | yatprahāṇasaṃjñetyabhidhānaṃ tadevāvidyāsravaprahāṇasyābhidhānaṃ yannirodhasaṃjñeti tadanayordvayoḥ phalam | yathoktaṃ sūtre- sarvasaṃskārāṇāṃ prahāṇāt prahāṇam | sarvasaṃskāreṣu virāgādvirāgaḥ | sarvasaṃskārāṇāṃ nirodhāt nirodha iti | tathā ceme traya ekasyaiva nāmāntaram | yo 'nityasaṃjñāṃ
body.translated_text: Moreover, there are two kinds of <s>vimukti</s> (liberation): <s>prajñāvimukti</s> (liberation through wisdom) and <s>cetovimukti</s> (liberation of mind). What is called abandonment refers to 'one abandons <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)' — thus one is liberated through <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom). What is called dispassion refers to 'one renounces <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving)' — thus the mind is liberated. The fruit of both liberations is cessation. What is designated as the <s>prahāṇasaṃjñā</s> (perception of abandonment) is itself the designation for the abandonment of the <s>āsrava</s> (defilement) of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). What is called the <s>nirodhasaṃjñā</s> (perception of cessation) is the fruit of both of these. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: 'From the abandonment of all <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned formations), there is abandonment. From dispassion toward all <s>saṃskāras</s>, there is dispassion. From the cessation of all <s>saṃskāras</s>, there is cessation.' Thus these three are merely different names for the same thing. One who cultivates the <s>anityasaṃjñā</s> (perception of impermanence)

body.text: yāvannirodhasaṃjñāṃ bhāvayati sa kṛtasarvakṛtyo niruddhasarvakleśaḥ prahīṇaskandhasaṃyojanasantatirnirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇaṃ samāpadyate |
body.translated_text: up to the <s>nirodhasaṃjñā</s> (perception of cessation) — such a one, having accomplished all tasks, with all <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) ceased, the continuum of the <s>skandha</s> (aggregate) fetters severed, attains <s>nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa</s> (nirvāṇa without remainder).

body.text: antimasaṃjñātritayavargo 'śītyuttaraśatatamaḥ |
body.translated_text: The chapter on the final triad of perceptions (<s>antimasaṃjñātritaya</s>) is the one hundred and eightieth.

body.text: 181 samādhipariṣkāreṣu ādyapañcasamādhipariṣkāravargaḥ
body.translated_text: 181. Chapter on the first five accessories of <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), among the accessories of <s>samādhi</s>.

body.text: (pṛ) pūrvamuktaṃ bhavatā- mārgasatyaṃ [dvividhaṃ] yat samādhiḥ tatpariṣkāraśceti | tatra samādhiruktaḥ | samādhipariṣkāra idānīṃ vaktavyaḥ | yasmāt sati samādhipariṣkāre samādhiḥ sidhyati na tvasati | (u) samādhipariṣkārā ya ekādaśadharmāḥ- (1) pariśuddhaśīlatā, (2) abhisambodhipratilābhaḥ, (3) indriye guptadvāratā, (4) bhojane mātrajñatā, (5) rātryā ādyāntimabhāge jāgaraṇatā, (6) kuśalavitarkasampannatā, (7) kalyāṇādhimuktisampannatā, (8) pradhānīyāṅgasampannatā, (9) vimuktyāyatanasampannatā, (10) anāvaraṇatā, (11) anāsaṅgitā iti |
body.translated_text: (Question) You previously stated that the <s>mārgasatya</s> (truth of the path) is twofold, namely <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) and its accessories. There, <s>samādhi</s> has been discussed. Now the accessories of <s>samādhi</s> should be explained, for <s>samādhi</s> is accomplished when the accessories of <s>samādhi</s> are present, but not when they are absent. (Answer) The accessories of <s>samādhi</s> are the following eleven <s>dharmas</s>: (1) purity of <s>śīla</s> (moral conduct), (2) attainment of <s>abhisambodhi</s> (perfect awakening), (3) guarding the doors of the sense faculties (<s>indriya</s>), (4) moderation in food, (5) wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night, (6) endowment with wholesome thought (<s>kuśalavitarka</s>), (7) endowment with virtuous resolve (<s>kalyāṇādhimukti</s>), (8) endowment with the factors of exertion (<s>pradhānīyāṅga</s>), (9) endowment with the bases of liberation (<s>vimuktyāyatana</s>), (10) freedom from obstruction (<s>anāvaraṇatā</s>), and (11) freedom from attachment (<s>anāsaṅgitā</s>).

body.text: pariśuddhaśīlateti | akuśalakarmaṇo viratiḥ śīlam | akuśalakarmāṇi yāni prāṇātipātādattādānakāmamithyācārāṇi trīṇi kāyikakarmāṇi | mṛṣāvāda piśunavācā paruṣavācā sampralāpa itīme catvāri vācikakarmāṇi | ebhyaḥ pāpakebhyo viratiḥ śīlam | vandanapratyudgamanānuvrajanapūjādisaddharmācaraṇamapi śīlamityucyate | śīlaṃ samādhihetuṃ karotīti samādīyate | tathā hi tadyathā suvarṇakāraḥ pūrvaṃ sthūlamalamapanayati | evaṃ prathamataḥ śīlasamādānena sthūlān śīladoṣānapanayati | paścātsamādhyādinā anyān sūkṣmadoṣānapanayati | yasmādasati śīlasamādāne dhyānasamādhirna bhavati | śīlasamādāna pratyayāttu dhyānasamādhiḥ sulabho bhavati | yathoktaṃ sūtre- śīle mārgasya mūlaṃ
body.translated_text: Regarding 'one whose <s>śīla</s> (moral conduct) is purified': abstention from unwholesome action is <s>śīla</s>. The unwholesome actions are: killing (<s>prāṇātipāta</s>), stealing (<s>adattādāna</s>), and sexual misconduct (<s>kāmamithyācāra</s>) — these are the three bodily actions. False speech (<s>mṛṣāvāda</s>), divisive speech (<s>piśunavācā</s>), harsh speech (<s>paruṣavācā</s>), and idle chatter (<s>sampralāpa</s>) — these are the four verbal actions. Abstention from these evil deeds is <s>śīla</s>. The practice of wholesome conduct (<s>saddharmācaraṇa</s>) such as salutation, rising to greet, accompanying, worship, and so forth is also called <s>śīla</s>. <s>Śīla</s> is undertaken because it creates the cause for <s>samādhi</s> (concentration). For just as a goldsmith first removes the coarse impurities, so too, first through the undertaking of <s>śīla</s>, one removes the coarse moral faults, and afterward through <s>samādhi</s> and so forth one removes the other subtle faults. Because without the undertaking of <s>śīla</s>, <s>dhyāna-samādhi</s> (meditative concentration) does not arise. But through the condition of undertaking <s>śīla</s>, <s>dhyāna-samādhi</s> is easily attained. As stated in the <s>sūtra</s>: '<s>Śīla</s> is the root of the path,

body.text: sopānañceti | kiñcāha- śīla prathamaratha[vinīta]m iti | prathamaṃ ratha[vinīta]manabhiruhya dvitīyaṃ ratha[vinītaṃ]kathamabhirohati | api cāha- śīlaṃ samā bhūmiḥ | imāṃ samāṃ bhūmiṃ vyavasthāpya catvāri satyāni paśyati iti | āha ca- dve bale | [katame dve |] pratisaṃkhyābalaṃ bhāvanābalañceti | pratisaṃkhyābalaṃ śīlasamādānameva | bhāvanābalaṃ mārgaḥ | pūrva śīlabhedāpattiṃ śīlasamādānahitañca pratisaṃkhyayā vicārya śīlaṃ samādatte | paścāt pratilabdhamārgaḥ pāpakātprakṛtyā viramati | kiñcāha- śīlaṃ bodhivṛkṣasya mūlamiti | asati mūle nāsti vṛkṣaḥ | ataḥ pariśuddhaśīlāvaśyakī |
body.translated_text: and its staircase.' Furthermore it says: '<s>Śīla</s> is the first relay chariot.' Without mounting the first relay chariot, how can one mount the second relay chariot? Moreover it says: '<s>Śīla</s> is level ground.' Having established this level ground, one sees the four truths. And it says: 'There are two powers. What are the two? The power of analytical reflection (<s>pratisaṃkhyābala</s>) and the power of cultivation (<s>bhāvanābala</s>).' The power of analytical reflection is precisely the undertaking of <s>śīla</s>. The power of cultivation is the path. First, by analytically reflecting upon the danger of breaking <s>śīla</s> and the benefit of undertaking <s>śīla</s>, one undertakes <s>śīla</s>. Afterward, having attained the path, one naturally abstains from evil. Furthermore it says: '<s>Śīla</s> is the root of the tree of <s>bodhi</s> (awakening).' Without a root there is no tree. Therefore the purity of <s>śīla</s> is indispensable.

body.text: dharma[tā] ca tathaiva syāt | asati śīlasamādāne na bhavati dhyānasamādhiḥ | tadyathā vyādhicikitsāyā auṣadhamapekṣyate | tathā kleśavyādhicikitsāyā asati śīle na sampadyata auṣadham | āha ca- pariśuddhaśīlasya cittaṃ nānutapyati | yāvadviraktacitto vimucyata iti | ime sarve guṇāḥ śīlasamādānādhīnāḥ | ataḥ samādhipariṣkāra ityucyate |
body.translated_text: The nature of <s>dharma</s> is likewise. Without the undertaking of <s>śīla</s>, <s>dhyāna-samādhi</s> (meditative concentration) does not arise. Just as medicine is required for the treatment of disease, so too for the treatment of the disease of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), without <s>śīla</s> the medicine is not accomplished. And it says: 'For one whose <s>śīla</s> is purified, the mind does not burn with remorse; and so the mind, becoming dispassionate, is liberated.' All these virtues depend on the undertaking of <s>śīla</s>. Therefore it is called a requisite of <s>samādhi</s> (<s>samādhipariṣkāra</s>).

body.text: asti ca karmāvaraṇaṃ, kleśāvaraṇaṃ, anayordvayoḥ phalaṃ vipākāvaraṇam | pariśuddhaśīlasyemāni trīṇyāvaraṇāni na bhavanti | anāvṛtacittasya samādhiḥ sidhyati | pariśuddhaśīlo na vikṣipatītyato niyamena nirvāṇamadhigacchati gaṅgāsrotasi dāruskandhavat | pariśuddhaśīlasamādānāt vyavasthāṃ karoti | śīlasamādānaṃ kāyikaṃ vācikamakuśalaṃ karma pratiṣedhayati | dhyānasamāpattirmānasamakuśalaṃ karma pratiṣedhayati | evaṃ kleśānāṃ pratiṣedhe pratilabdhatattvajñānasyātyantikaprahāṇaṃ bhavati |
body.translated_text: There is the obstruction of <s>karma</s> (<s>karmāvaraṇa</s>), the obstruction of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) (<s>kleśāvaraṇa</s>), and the result of both — the obstruction of ripening (<s>vipākāvaraṇa</s>). For one whose <s>śīla</s> is purified, these three obstructions do not arise. For one whose mind is unobstructed, <s>samādhi</s> is accomplished. One whose <s>śīla</s> is purified is not distracted, and therefore necessarily attains <s>nirvāṇa</s>, like a log in the current of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> river. Through the undertaking of purified <s>śīla</s>, one establishes stability. The undertaking of <s>śīla</s> prevents unwholesome bodily and verbal action. The attainment of <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) prevents unwholesome mental action. Thus, when the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) are prevented, for one who has attained the knowledge of reality, there is final and complete abandonment.

body.text: mārgavarge 'sakṛddarśitaṃ śīlaṃ stambhabhūtamiti | dhyānasamādhicittanagarasya śīlaṃ parighā bhavati | saṃsāraughataraṇasya śīlaṃ setuḥ | sajjanapariṣadi praveśasya śīlaṃ mudrā | aṣṭāṅgikāryakṣetrasya śīlaṃ pārabhūtam | yathā pārarahite kṣetre jalaṃ na tiṣṭhati | evaṃ pariśuddhaśīle 'sati samādhijalaṃ na tiṣṭhati | (pṛ) kaḥ pariśuddhaśīlaḥ | (u) yo gogī pāpakriyānabhiratādhyāśayaḥ paralokaparivādādibhyo bibhyati | [sa] pariśuddhaśīla ityucyate | kiñca yogī cittaviśuddhaye pariśuddhaśīlo bhavati | yathoktaṃ saptamaithunarāgasūtre- kāye 'nāpattike 'pi cittamapariśuddhamityataḥ śīlamapyapariśuddhamiti | śīlabhedapratyayāḥ
